Specifically, Article 2 grants British subjects the right to reside in, trade freely within, and buy and sell without monopolies in the Dominican Republic under most-favored-nation privileges, with corresponding rights granted to Dominican citizens in British dominions. Additionally, Article 3 stipulates that tonnage, import, and export duties levied on vessels and goods from either nation shall not exceed those levied on national vessels and goods.

records.headline: The Dominican Republic. TREATY OF PEACE, AMITY, COMMERCE AND NAVIGATION, BETWEEN HER BRITANNIC MAJESTY AND THE DOMINICAN REPUBLIC.
records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* reported that the Dominican Republic declared the slave trade to be an act of piracy punishable by death. To help prevent this trade, the republic agreed to permit British warships—acting under specific treaty instructions—to visit vessels sailing under the Dominican flag that are reasonably suspected of slave trading within twenty leagues of the Dominican coast. If suspicions are confirmed, the detained vessel is to be sent to Santo Domingo and delivered to local authorities for prosecution under Dominican law.
records.summary_es: El *New York Herald* informó que la República Dominicana declaró la trata de esclavos crimen de piratería conminado con pena capital. A fin de coadyuvar a su erradicación, la república consintió en facultar a los cruceros de guerra británicos —conforme a instrucciones capitulares precisas— para inspeccionar embarcaciones que arbolasen insignia dominicana bajo fundada sospecha de tráfico de esclavos en un radio de veinte leguas de las costas dominicanas. De comprobarse el delito, la presa sería remitida a Santo Domingo y consignada a los tribunales de la República para su procesamiento conforme al derecho patrio.

records.full_text:
IN THE NAME OF THE MOST HOLY TRINITY.
Her Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, and the President of the Dominican Republic, being desirous to consecrate the formal recognition of the independence of the same, and to conclude a treaty of peace and friendship, and to regulate thereby the commercial intercourse between the dominions and subjects of her Majesty, and the territories and citizens of the Republic, they have for this purpose named as their respective Plenipotentiaries, that is to say:—
Her Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, Sir Robert Hermann Schomburgk, Doctor of Philosophy, Knight of the Royal Prussian Order of the Red Eagle, of the Royal Saxon Order of Merit; of the Legion of Honor of the French Republic; Her Consul to the Dominican Republic;
And the President of the Dominican republic, Senor Jose Maria Medrano, Minister Secretary of State for the departments of police and the interior, and charged with those of Justice, Public Instruction, and Foreign Affairs;
Who, after having communicated to each other their respective full powers, found in good and due form, have agreed upon and concluded the following articles:—
Art. 1. There shall be perpetual peace and friendship between her Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, her heirs and successors, and the Dominican republic, and between their respective subjects and citizens.
Art. 2. There shall be reciprocal freedom of commerce between the British dominions and the Dominican republic. The subjects of her Britannic Majesty may reside in and trade to any part of the territories of the republic, to which any other foreigners are or shall be admitted. They shall enjoy full protection for their persons and properties. They shall be allowed to buy from and sell to whom they like without being restrained or affected by any monopoly, contract, or exclusive privilege of sale or purchase whatever; and they shall moreover enjoy all other rights and privileges which are or may be granted to any other foreigners, subjects or citizens of the most favored nation.
The citizens of the Dominican republic shall, in return, enjoy similar protection and privileges in the dominions of Her Britannic Majesty.
Art. 3. No tonnage, import or other duties or charges shall be levied in the Dominican republic on British vessels, or on goods imported or exported in British vessels, than are or may be provided to be levied on national vessels, or on the like goods imported or exported in national vessels; and in the same manner, no tonnage, import, or other duties or charges shall be levied in the British dominions on vessels of the republic, or on goods imported or exported in those vessels, beyond what are or may be levied on national vessels, or on the like goods imported or exported in national vessels; or from the ports upon the commerce, without prejudice whatever to the provisions of the fourth article, exclusively reserved to national vessels of each of the the two countries respectively.
Art. 4. Merchandise or goods coming from the British dominions in any vessels, or coming from British vessels from any country, shall not be prohibited in the Dominican republic, nor be subjected to higher duties than are levied on the same kinds of merchandise or goods, coming from any other foreign country, or imported in any other vessels.
All articles, the produce of the republic, may be exported therefrom by British subjects and British vessels, on as favorable terms as by the subjects and citizens and vessels of any other foreign country.
Art. 5. The protection of the government of the republic shall be afforded to all British vessels, their crews and goods. If any British vessel should be wrecked on the coast of the republic, the local authorities shall afford them aid, and secure them from plunder, and shall cause all articles saved from the wreck to be restored to their lawful owners. The amount of salvage dues in such cases shall be settled, in case of dispute, by arbitrators chosen by both parties.
Art. 6. It being the intention of the two contracting parties to bind themselves by the present treaty, to treat each other on the footing of the most favored nation, it is hereby agreed between them, that any favor, privilege, or immunity whatever in matters of commerce and navigation, which either contracting party has actually granted, or may hereafter grant, to the subjects or citizens of any other State, shall be extended to the subjects or citizens of the other contracting party, gratuitously, if the concession in favor of that other State shall have been gratuitous, or in return for a compensation as nearly as possible of proportionate value and effect, to be adjusted by mutual agreement if the concession shall have been conditional.
Art. 7. Each contracting party may appoint Consuls for the protection of its trade, in the dominions or territories of the other; but no such Consul shall enter upon the exercise of his functions until he shall have been admitted and approved, in the usual form, by the government of the country to which he is sent.
The respective agents and Consuls of each of the two contracting parties residing within the dominions or territories of the other, shall enjoy the same rights, immunities, privileges and exemptions which are or may be granted to the diplomatic agents or Consuls of equal rank, of the most favored nation.
Art. 8. The subjects of her Britannic Majesty residing in the Dominican republic shall not be disturbed, persecuted, or annoyed on account of their religion, but they shall have perfect liberty of conscience therein, and exercise their creed either within their own private houses, or in the said or particular chapels. Liberty shall also be granted to them to bury in the Dominican republic, in the manner, they may freely establish and maintain, their subjects who may die in the territories of the said republic. In like manner, the citizens of the Dominican republic shall enjoy, within all the dominions of Her Britannic Majesty, a perfect and entire liberty of conscience, and shall be allowed to exercise their religion publicly or privately, within their own dwelling houses, or in the chapels and places of worship appointed for that purpose.
Art. 9. Slavery being perpetually abolished in the Dominican republic, and having been already declared by her an act of piracy punishable with the pain of death, the Dominican republic engages to permit any British vessel of war, which may be furnished with special instructions under the treaties between Great Britain and foreign powers, and with the formalities as are provided for in such cases by the said treaties relative to the prevention of the infamous slave trade, to visit any vessels sailing under the Dominican flag, which may, upon reasonable grounds, be suspected of being engaged in this vile trade in slaves; it being understood that the distances and places between which the right of visit shall be exercised as restricted as they are in the treaties with other powers, for Cuba and Porto Rico, shall likewise refer to the same distance of twenty leagues from the coasts of the Dominican republic; and if, by the result of the visit, it shall appear to the officer in command of such British vessel of war that the suspicions of the commander are well grounded, the vessel shall be sent, without delay, to the port of Santo Domingo, in the Dominican republic, and shall be delivered up to the local authorities, to be proceeded against according to the laws of the republic.
It is understood that the present article shall not be extended to other cases, which might occasion a vexatious and unnecessary visit to the Dominican vessels in their voyages and commercial enterprises; but that, with the aid of the Dominican authorities, authorized to expect protection and assistance; and, if the case should arise, which, however, is not to be supposed, that the Dominican republic should receive a conviction of having suffered a vexatious molestation, it rests with her to withdraw it, after having given a year's previous notice thereof.
Art. 10. In order that the two contracting parties may have the opportunity of hereafter treating and agreeing upon such other arrangements as may tend still further to the improvement of their mutual interests, and to the promotion of the commerce of their respective subjects and citizens, it is agreed that the present treaty shall remain in force for the term of ten years from the date of the exchange of the ratifications, and either of the contracting parties shall have the right of giving to the other party notice of its intention to terminate at the expiration of the said ten years the stipulations of the present treaty; and the present treaty shall cease to be binding after ten years, and all notice that might be given and amity shall remain obligatory to both nations.
Art. 11. The present treaty shall be ratified, and the ratifications shall be exchanged at Santo Domingo, within the space of eight months, or sooner, if possible, counted from the date of this treaty, or sooner, if shall be possible.
In witness whereof, the respective plenipotentiaries have signed the same, and affixed thereto the seals of their arms.
Done at Santo Domingo, the sixth day of March, in the year of our Lord eighteen hundred and fifty.
(L. S.) ROBERT H. SCHOMBURGK.
(L. S.) JOSE MARIA MEDRANO.

ADDITIONAL ARTICLES.
As the circumstances of the Dominican with the Haytien nation might oblige the Dominican republic to modify the third article, it is hereby especially understood and agreed between the two contracting parties, that the Dominican republic shall have perfect liberty of making during the space of ten years such changes as she may think fit in her duties, notwithstanding the stipulation of article 3 aforesaid; but the subjects of her Britannic Majesty shall not be restrained or affected by any monopoly, contract or exclusive privilege of purchase or sale; and as her disposition is constant to afford and protect commerce, it should enter in her views to adopt any measures of limited or except in the case that the existing laws should continue.
The present additional article shall have the same force and validity as if it were inserted, word for word, in the treaty signed this day. It shall be ratified at the same time. And in consequence of the exception in article 3, it is to be understood that the sanction or disapprobation of the treaty is naturally reserved to Her Britannic Majesty.
In testimony whereof the undersigned have, in virtue of their full powers, signed and sealed the present article.
Done at Santo Domingo, the sixth day of March, in the year of our Lord eighteen hundred and fifty.
(L. S.) ROBERT H. SCHOMBURGK.
(L. S.) JOSE MARIA MEDRANO.
Ratified in the city of St. Domingo, September 27, 1850. BUENAVENTURA BAEZ.
DR. JOSE MARIA CAMINERO.

records.headline: News from Haiti to October 15 states that hostilities have actually commenced between the Haitians and Dominicans
records.summary_en: News from Haiti to October 15 states that hostilities have actually commenced between the Haitians and Dominicans, with about 500 Dominican troops driving back Soulouque's vanguard at the Pass of Bonica, and a Haitian brig of war with 200 men captured off Scott's Bay by two Dominican schooners and carried into Macao Roadstead. It adds that the Emperor marched on the 11th from Petit Goave, at the head of his staff and 400 guards, to take the field in person, and that the hostilities had disastrously affected the island's trade, with no coffee to be had and cutting of logwood and mahogany restricted.
records.summary_es: Noticias de Haití hasta el 15 de octubre afirman que las hostilidades han comenzado realmente entre haitianos y dominicanos, con unos 500 soldados dominicanos rechazando la vanguardia de Soulouque en el Paso de Bonica y un bergantín de guerra haitiano con 200 hombres capturado frente a Scott's Bay por dos goletas dominicanas y llevado a la rada de Macao. Añade que el emperador marchó el día 11 desde Petit-Goâve, al frente de su estado mayor y 400 guardias, para tomar el campo en persona, y que las hostilidades habían afectado desastrosamente el comercio de la isla, sin café disponible y con el corte de palo de tinte y caoba restringido.

records.headline: The New-York Daily Tribune reports, reprinting a Boston Traveller item of the 26th
records.summary_en: The New-York Daily Tribune reports, reprinting a Boston Traveller item of the 26th, that the people of the Dominican Republic were expecting a United States expedition to attack the Haitians, in which event a strong Dominican force would march to assist the enterprise. Under the heading 'From Hayti,' letters from Cape Haytien to the 2d instant state that all the laborers from that part of the country had joined the army against St. Domingo. The letters add that the Haitians were in high spirits because United States claims of about £300,000, which United States Agent Mr. Green had warned would be enforced by a naval fleet within six weeks, had not been backed by the appearance of any fleet, leading them to declare that the United States dared not send one and to denounce the affair as a humbug.
records.summary_es: Reproduciendo una nota del Boston Traveller del día 26, el New-York Daily Tribune informa que el pueblo de la República Dominicana esperaba una expedición de los Estados Unidos para atacar a los haitianos, en cuyo caso una fuerte tropa de dominicanos marcharía para apoyar la empresa. Bajo el encabezado 'From Hayti', cartas de Cabo Haitiano hasta el día 2 del corriente indican que todos los jornaleros de esa parte del país se habían unido al ejército contra Santo Domingo. Las cartas añaden que los haitianos estaban muy regocijados porque las reclamaciones por unas £300,000 a favor de ciudadanos estadounidenses, que el agente de los Estados Unidos, el Sr. Green, había advertido serían exigidas por una flota en seis semanas, no habían sido respaldadas por la aparición de ninguna escuadra, lo que los llevó a afirmar que los Estados Unidos no se atrevían a enviarla y a denunciar todo el asunto como una farsa.

records.headline: Late from St. Domingo—Peace Declared Between the Haytiens and Dominicans.
records.summary_en: According to an account from St. Domingo City received via the brig *George Otis* and reported from Boston on November 30, 1850, a treaty of peace between the Haytiens and Dominicans had been concluded through the intervention of the English and Americans, following some brief fighting that caused no serious loss. An English man-of-war was in port at the time of the treaty. The newspaper also reported on a separate railway collision near Batavia involving an emigrant train and an express train, which resulted in fatalities and injuries.

Un navío de guerra británico se encontraba fondeado en la rada al ajustarse el convenio. La gaceta daba cuenta por separado de un siniestro ferroviario cerca de Batavia entre un tren de emigrantes y un convoy expreso, saldado con víctimas mortales y heridos.

records.full_text: Accounts from St. Domingo City, to the 2d instant, received by the brig George Otis, represent that, through the intervention of the English and American agents, a treaty of peace between the Dominicans and Haytiens had been concluded. Previous to this there had been some brisk fighting between the contending parties, but no serious loss had been sustained by either party. There was, at the time of the treaty, an English man-of-war in port.

records.headline: Under the headline 'From St. Domingo,' the Daily National Intelligencer reports
records.summary_en: Under the headline 'From St. Domingo,' the Daily National Intelligencer reports that accounts from the city of San Domingo up to November 6 state that intelligence had arrived there that Emperor Souloque of Haiti was about to make a descent upon the Dominican Republic. In response, the Dominican Government was making extensive defensive preparations. The paper adds that rumors—which it characterizes as unfounded—had reached St. Domingo that the United States was fitting out an expedition against Haiti, in which case the Dominican Government intended to march a strong force into Souloque's territory to cooperate with the United States.
records.summary_es: Bajo el titular 'From St. Domingo', el Daily National Intelligencer informa que las noticias de la ciudad de Santo Domingo hasta el 6 de noviembre indican que se había recibido información allí de que el emperador Souloque de Haití estaba a punto de lanzarse sobre la República Dominicana. En respuesta, el Gobierno dominicano realizaba extensos preparativos de defensa. El periódico añade que habían llegado a Santo Domingo rumores —que califica de infundados— de que los Estados Unidos estaban preparando una expedición contra Haití, en cuyo caso el Gobierno dominicano tenía la intención de hacer marchar una fuerte tropa hacia los dominios de Souloque para cooperar con los Estados Unidos.

records.summary_en: The *Polynesian* reported that the Dominican Republic was preparing to repel an expected invasion by Hayti under Faustin, with Santa Ana placed in chief command of the army. Additionally, a treaty with England acknowledging Dominican independence was celebrated at a public dinner attended by the British Consul—who stated England would not interfere in the contest—while no American consul or shipmasters were present. Under this new treaty, British vessels are allowed to enter Dominican ports at a fifty percent lower tonnage duty than American vessels.
records.summary_es: El *Polynesian* reseñó que la República Dominicana se aprestaba a rechazar la temida invasión acaudillada por Faustino, habiéndosele encomendado a Santana la comandancia suprema de las tropas. Celebróse asimismo con un banquete de Estado la ratificación del tratado con Inglaterra que sancionaba la soberanía dominicana, al que asistió el cónsul británico —quien manifestó que su gobierno se abstendría de intervenir en la refriega—, registrándose la ausencia del cónsul o patrones de barcos norteamericanos. Conforme a las cláusulas estipuladas, las naves británicas gozaban de una franquicia del cincuenta por ciento en el canon de tonelaje en fondeaderos dominicanos frente a los cargueros de Estados Unidos.

records.full_text:
The Commissioners on Mexican Claims have this morning completed their awards. They amount to forty thousand dollars less than the sum appropriated to meet them, of one million and a quarter of dollars.

Major Donelson publishes a letter in the Union this morning, three columns and a half long, to the editor of the Union, upon assuming the editorial control of that journal. The Major endeavors to make the compromise a tower of patriotism above the ordinary spirit of party; but says that 'if the ultra Democratic party of this nation can be brought together in no other way than by an abandonment of the Union, or a compromise with the enemies of the compromise, we can never consent to buy peace on such terms.' He thinks the Democratic party, nevertheless, will unite on a constitutional basis, and elect the next President.

The intelligence brought by the last arrival from England, relative to the movement of British naval force, is considered to have a direct bearing upon the movements of Southern adventurers. It is supposed that the British vessels which have been dispatched may first meet the West India fleet somewhere near the shores of St. Domingo, for the purpose of obtaining redress, instant and immediate, from the Emperor of the black republic; while the adventurers from the Southern States may effect a landing on Dominica, and unite with those forces to assault the black republic in the flank. It is very true that our government at Washington can't declare war, or commence hostilities, without an act of Congress, but it can connive at the movement of a body of armed men, who may choose to emigrate to Dominica.

The intelligence brought by a letter from Mr. Riddle, United States Commissioner to the World's Fair, relative to the space allotted to the United States, is believed to be very onerous and expensive. The custom house commission on each package amounted to nearly $2, besides which, all the duties, tares, draperies, &c., for the display of goods, have to be provided by each nation, and those of other countries are very brilliant. He has had to employ a number of clerks to make out a descriptive catalog. Among these, he says, he is behind hand, owing to the late hour at which goods arrived.

The charge against Collector Lewis, of Philadelphia, after a full investigation by the President and Secretary of the Treasury, has been dismissed.

The Hon. John M. Clayton arrived here yesterday.

records.summary_en: The *Wilmington Journal* reported on April 25, 1851, that because St. Domingo (the Dominican Republic) was unrecognized by the United States, it was regarded as a piratical government rather than a nation requiring an act of Congress for military action. The newspaper suggested that U.S. vessels fitted out at Norfolk and New York could join other American ships to demand redress from the "emperor" of Hayti or demolish his regime. Additionally, it noted rumors that expeditions from the Southern States purportedly bound for Cuba were likely intended to land on the Dominican part of the island to assist the Dominicans and revolutionize the social and political condition of the blacks.
records.summary_es: El *Wilmington Journal* comunicó el 25 de abril de 1851 que, por carecer de reconocimiento oficial por parte de Estados Unidos, Santo Domingo (la República Dominicana) era conceptuado más bien como un gobierno pirático que como una nación formal que demandase una ley del Congreso para emprender acciones militares. La hoja apuntaba que buques de guerra estadounidenses alistados en Norfolk y Nueva York podrían concurrir con otras unidades navales para exigir satisfacciones al «emperador» de Haití o derribar su régimen. Recogía además comentarios de que expediciones armadas procedentes de los estados del Sur, supuestamente destinadas a Cuba, tendrían por objeto desembarcar en la parte dominicana para auxiliar a los naturales y trastocar el ordenamiento político y social de las poblaciones negras.

records.summary_en: Captain Hollins of the schooner Mary Chilton, from Port-au-Prince, reports that the Chamber of Deputies had been in session to consider the American government's proposition relative to acknowledging the independence of the Dominicans. It was generally believed the day the Chilton sailed that the Chamber had rejected the proposition and had also rejected a claim for the detention of the American brig Leander and the imprisonment of her captain, that the Haitians were daily expecting the American squadron, and that five conspirators against the Empire had been shot.

records.full_text:
ONE DAY LATER FROM HAYTI.—A letter from Porte-au-Prince, dated April 10, published in the New York Journal of Commerce, says that the Haytien Congress have not yet made a decision on the offer of mediation between the Haytiens and Dominicans, by the three commercial powers. This is one day later than the report that the offered mediation had been rejected. A Boston dispatch of the 1st inst. has the following:
The schooner October, from Porte-au-Prince, with advices to April 13, arrived here to-day. It is currently reported at St. Domingo that the Chambers had refused to comply with the demands of the American Commissioner, or to make peace. Emperor Soulouque was preparing to march on St. Domingo with all his forces. He had dismissed his Cabinet, and replaced them with men who were in favor of war.
The steamboat General Taylor arrived at Port-au-Prince on the 10th April, and was offered for sale.

records.headline: A correspondent signing 'AB.' writes to the New-York Daily Tribune
records.summary_en: A correspondent signing 'AB.' writes to the New-York Daily Tribune that Mr. Walsh is dissatisfied with the Haitian government's answer and is about to depart immediately on the French steamer Crocodile for the City of St. Domingo. The writer sees no reason to suppose that peace or a truce will be agreed to with the eastern part of the island on any basis other than incorporating both under one government, comparing foreign intervention there to British or French intervention if South Carolina were to secede from the United States. Nevertheless, the correspondent reports being informed that Soulouque, despite having made sufficient preparations for his planned expedition against 'Dominica' (the Dominican Republic), will delay it out of deference to the three powers engaged in the proposed mediation.

El autor no ve motivos para suponer que se acuerde la paz o una tregua con la parte oriental de la isla sobre otra base que no sea la incorporación de ambas bajo un solo gobierno, comparando la intervención extranjera allí con una intervención inglesa o francesa si Carolina del Sur se separara de los Estados Unidos. records.headline: Summarizing an account from the Revue, the New-York Daily Tribune details
records.summary_en: Summarizing an account from the Revue, the New-York Daily Tribune details a proposed American colonization scheme in 'Dominica' (the Dominican Republic) under which settlers would import goods from the United States duty-free, own all mines on their grants exempt from taxation, and enjoy both Dominican citizenship rights and United States immunities. The colonists would form a special military corps under the Republic's authority with officers named by themselves or the Company, while the Republic would advance 30-year bonds at 10 percent interest to purchase two sea steamers to carry mails and emigrants between Santo Domingo and New York. Emigrants would receive free passage and freight, with the government paying the Company in 10 percent bonds £20 for each emigrant over 12 years old and $10 for each under, and retaining the right to take the steamers for war purposes upon repaying the Company's payments toward the original advance. The Tribune remarks that the Revue writer's aim is to excite France to annex the Dominican state.
records.summary_es: Resumiendo un relato de la Revue, el New-York Daily Tribune detalla un proyecto de colonización estadounidense en 'Dominica' (la República Dominicana) según el cual los colonos importarían mercancías de los Estados Unidos libres de derechos, serían propietarios de todas las minas en sus concesiones exentas de impuestos y gozarían tanto de los derechos de los ciudadanos dominicanos como de las inmunidades de los Estados Unidos. Los colonos formarían un cuerpo militar especial bajo la autoridad de la República con oficiales nombrados por ellos mismos o por la Compañía, mientras que la República adelantaría bonos a 30 años con un interés del 10 por ciento para comprar dos vapores marítimos destinados al transporte de correspondencia y emigrantes entre Santo Domingo y Nueva York. El Tribune observa que el propósito del autor de la Revue es incitar a Francia a anexarse el Estado dominicano.

records.full_text:
THE INTERNATIONAL MAGAZINE FOR JUNE. Price 25 cents.
This number is one of the best and most attractive yet issued. It contains a great variety of interesting and valuable matter, among which we notice a very interesting and well-written account of the mission of Mr. Robert M. Walsh to Hayti, as Special Agent of the United States. Mr. Walsh's instructions were to act in concert with the agents of France and Great Britain in an endeavor to induce the Emperor Soulouque to recognize the independence of the Dominican Republic. The writer gives a very graphic description of the character and court of the sable monarch, and of the progress and results of the mission. He represents Mr. Walsh as having acted with great energy and decision, and at various places in Hayti, as threatening to blockade and bombard Port-au-Prince in case Soulouque should still refuse to recognize the eastern part of the island as separate and independent. Armed coercion was apparently as familiar to him as his own title of "Special Agent," and his dreams by night and his talk by day seem to have been mainly of seventy-fours, frigates, paixhans, bomb-shells, rockets and thirty-two pounders. An inexorable and most unmitigated "interventionist" was Mr. Walsh, and if his advice had been followed, the "Napoleon of the West" would have been taught a lesson which he would not soon have forgotten. The Magazine contains also a great variety of other interesting matter, including several original stories and poems, and a large number of well-executed wood-cuts.

records.headline: An envoy's failure to bring the Emperor at Port-au-Prince to reason
records.summary_en: An envoy's failure to bring the Emperor at Port-au-Prince to reason is reported by The National Era. The envoy returned home, and the scheme was pursued with the Dominican Government through written proposals signed by Duff Green and B. B. Green at Washington on August 20, 1850. The proposals called for introducing a large body of American colonists into St. Domingo, granting 50 acres of land to each person and an additional square mile to each family of five. Settlers in 'Dominica' (the Dominican Republic) were to enjoy full Dominican civil rights as well as United States immunities, duty-free importation of goods from the United States, and tax-exempt ownership of all mines found on their grants. They were also to form a special military corps under the Republic's authority with officers named by themselves or the company, while the Republic would advance 30-year bonds bearing 10 percent interest to purchase two sea steamers for transporting mails and emigrants from Santo Domingo.

The correspondent stated that their political objective in communicating the proposals was solely to help protect the Dominicans from attacks by their black neighbors, the Haytiens. Additionally, the excerpt referenced efforts by English, French, and American consuls to dissuade the black Emperor (Soulouque) from invading Dominican territory in order to restore peace to the island.

records.headline: In a historical sketch using the paper's period language, the writer traces Santo Domingo from Spanish rule to independence
records.summary_en: In a historical sketch using the paper's period language, the writer traces Santo Domingo from Spanish rule to independence moves, saying Boyer entered and occupied Dominica, which his successors kept until 1843, when Santana led a revolt, drove out the Haitians and established a free government. For this site's framing, Boyer's entry is reported as the paper presented it; historically the period was an invasion and occupation of the Dominican Republic, not a merger of the two countries.
records.summary_es: En un bosquejo histórico que usa el lenguaje de época del periódico, el autor traza Santo Domingo desde el dominio español hasta los movimientos de independencia, diciendo que Boyer entró y ocupó Dominica, que sus sucesores mantuvieron hasta 1843, cuando Santana lideró una revuelta, expulsó a los haitianos y estableció un gobierno libre. Para el marco de este sitio, la entrada de Boyer se reporta como la presentó el periódico; históricamente el período fue una invasión y ocupación de la República Dominicana, no una fusión de los dos países.

records.headline: The Vermont Watchman and State Journal reports that Sir Robert discovered
records.summary_en: The Vermont Watchman and State Journal reports that Sir Robert discovered aboriginal remains consisting of a circle containing a granite idol nearly six feet in length. According to the paper, he never encountered such a monument during all his travels in Guiana, and it indicates a much greater advancement than that possessed by the races currently inhabiting that territory or those who inhabited the island of St. Domingo when Columbus landed. Sir Robert made the discovery during one of the journeys undertaken under the command of the British government to acquaint himself with the capabilities and population of the Dominican Republic, and he is now preparing to travel to the province of Cabao, where Columbus landed.

records.headline: Citing the New York Sun and the June 15 issue of the Gaceta of St. Domingo
records.summary_en: Citing the New York Sun and the June 15 issue of the Gaceta of St. Domingo, The Daily Crescent reports on several official documents addressed to the Dominican people and army by President Buenaventura Baez. The documents concern an incursion by a column of Haitian infantry into the territory of St. Domingo on May 29, in violation of the existing truce between the Haitians and the Dominicans. According to the Gaceta, the Haitians were repulsed and tranquility has been restored to the frontier, while President Baez's spirited address to the army strongly denounces the conduct of the Haitian Government and the aims of Emperor Soulouque.
records.summary_es: Citando al New York Sun y la edición del 15 de junio de la Gaceta de Santo Domingo, The Daily Crescent informa sobre varios documentos oficiales dirigidos al pueblo y al ejército dominicanos por el presidente Buenaventura Báez. Los documentos se refieren a la incursión de una columna de infantería haitiana en el territorio de Santo Domingo el 29 de mayo, en violación de la tregua existente entre haitianos y dominicanos. Según la Gaceta, los haitianos fueron rechazados y la tranquilidad ha sido restablecida en la frontera, mientras que la enérgica alocución del presidente Báez al ejército denuncia duramente la conducta del Gobierno haitiano y las pretensiones del emperador Soulouque.

records.summary_en: According to the newspaper report dated July 19, 1851, dates from St. Domingo up to the 30th indicate that markets were glutted with American provisions, coffee was depressed, and an excessive issue of government paper money negatively impacted business while political affairs remained tranquil. The report also notes that the emperor's address had a grand effect, and his coronation would soon be solemnized with a general amnesty and the return of exiles.
records.summary_es: Con arreglo a la relación de prensa del 19 de julio de 1851, partes recibidos de Santo Domingo hasta el día 30 denotaban saturación de provisiones estadounidenses en plaza, cotizaciones deprimidas para el café y quebranto mercantil causado por emisiones desmedidas de papel moneda fiscal, en tanto la situación política discurría pacífica. La nota añade que el mensaje del emperador produjo viva impresión y que su unción imperial se solemnizaría en breve con indulto general y repatriación de desterrados.

records.summary_en: An account attributed to the New York Express says Soulouque in good faith sent 2,000 men to the Dominican frontier to notify the people there of the truce agreed with the commissioners of France, England and the United States, but the commanding general, without authority, seized the undefended frontier town of Galeta and pronounced it conquered. It says the Dominicans, enraged, mustered in force and beat off the Haitians with some killed and wounded on the Haitian side, and that the commissioners would renew their efforts for a permanent peace in the autumn.

Dice que los dominicanos, enfurecidos, se reunieron en fuerza y rechazaron a los haitianos con algunos muertos y heridos del lado haitiano, y que los comisionados renovarían sus esfuerzos por una paz permanente en el otoño.

records.headline: Reprinting an item from the London News, The Granite Farmer describes
records.summary_en: Reprinting an item from the London News, The Granite Farmer describes a granite monument nearly six feet in length discovered by Sir Robert during one of the journeys he undertook under the command of the British government to study the capabilities and population of the Dominican Republic. The paper notes that the monument indicates a much greater advancement than that possessed by the races currently inhabiting that territory or those who lived on the island of St. Domingo when Columbus landed. It adds that Sir Robert is preparing to travel to the provinces of Cibao, described as the most interesting district of the republic and the classical ground where Columbus landed.
records.summary_es: Reproduciendo una nota del London News, The Granite Farmer describe un monumento de granito de casi seis pies de largo descubierto por Sir Robert durante uno de los viajes que emprendió bajo las órdenes del Gobierno británico para conocer las capacidades y la población de la República Dominicana. El periódico señala que el monumento demuestra un adelanto mucho mayor que el que poseen las razas que habitan actualmente ese vasto territorio o las que habitaban la isla de Santo Domingo cuando desembarcó Colón. Añade que Sir Robert se prepara para realizar un viaje a las provincias del Cibao, descritas como el distrito más interesante de la república y el suelo clásico donde desembarcó Colón.

records.headline: The idea and the wish to dissolve the com pulsory union
records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that after the expulsion of Boyer in 1843 and the accession of Gen. Riviere, the Dominicans seized an opportunity while the garrison was reduced to capture the remaining troops, proclaim a provisional independent government in early January 1844, and issue a revolutionary manifesto on January 16, 1844. It described the Dominican population as consisting of pure whites—who were the intellectually predominant and ruling class—and mixed races of various colors, all of whom were constitutionally declared equal citizens before the law. Additionally, the excerpt noted that Santana, the Dominican liberator and first President, resigned in 1848 and was succeeded by Jimenez, who was described as a traitor.
records.summary_es: El periódico relató que tras el derrocamiento de Boyer en 1843 y la exaltación del general Rivière, los dominicanos aprovecharon la mengua de la guarnición para reducir a las tropas restantes, proclamar un gobierno provisional independiente a principios de enero de 1844 y promulgar una manifestación revolucionaria el 16 de enero de 1844. Describía a la población dominicana integrada por blancos puros —que constituían la clase intelectualmente rectora y gobernante— y razas mixtas de diversos matices, proclamados todos constitucionalmente ciudadanos iguales ante la ley. Añadía el extracto que Santana, libertador dominicano y primer presidente, renunció en 1848 y fue sucedido por Jimenes, a quien se tildaba de traidor.

records.summary_en: The paper recounts that Soulouque never recognized the Dominican Republic, kept up a state of war and constantly threatened new expeditions, until the representatives of France, England and the United States intervened. It says he refused to make peace or agree to a ten-year truce but promised to suspend the war virtually and proclaimed that Dominicans could come in and trade with assurance of kind treatment, though a Haitian officer who crossed the frontier under a flag of truce to carry the proclamation was driven back with a few killed and wounded.
records.summary_es: El periódico relata que Soulouque nunca reconoció la República Dominicana, mantuvo un estado de guerra y amenazó constantemente con nuevas expediciones, hasta que intervinieron los representantes de Francia, Inglaterra y los Estados Unidos. Dice que se negó a hacer la paz o a aceptar una tregua de diez años, pero prometió suspender la guerra en la práctica y proclamó que los dominicanos podían venir a comerciar con garantía de buen trato, aunque un oficial haitiano que cruzó la frontera con bandera de tregua para llevar la proclamación fue rechazado con algunos muertos y heridos.

records.headline: The Turks Island Gazette reports that President Baez, after some months in retirement with his family at Azua
records.summary_en: The Turks Island Gazette reports that President Baez, after some months in retirement with his family at Azua, returned to Santo Domingo on Saturday the 6th and entered the city under a salute of guns, escorted by his life guards and four hundred dragoons to the National Palace. The same report describes General Santana, old and in poor health, making his slow way to Santiago, where the military guard turned out to salute him, on his way to assume command of the Dominican army assembled on the frontier, as Soulouque had joined his army at Port au Prince with the avowed purpose of invading Dominican territory.
records.summary_es: La Turks Island Gazette informa que el presidente Báez, después de algunos meses de retiro con su familia en Azua, regresó a Santo Domingo el sábado 6 y entró en la ciudad bajo una salva de cañonazos, escoltado por su guardia personal y cuatrocientos dragones hasta el Palacio Nacional. El mismo informe describe al general Santana, viejo y de salud quebrada, haciendo su lento camino hacia Santiago, donde la guardia militar salió a saludarlo, en ruta a asumir el mando del ejército dominicano reunido en la frontera, pues Soulouque se había unido a su ejército en Puerto Príncipe con el propósito declarado de invadir el territorio dominicano.
records.passage: President Baez, after spending some months in retirement with his family at Azua, returned to St. Domingo, on Saturday, the 6th inst. and entered the city under a salute of [illegible] guns. The elite of the Dominican army, newly accoutred and uniformed, received His Excellency, who was escorted by his life guards and four hundred dragoons from Azua, Bani, and San Cristobal; the body guard were in full dress, and wore their splendid new brass helmets, ornamented with horse tails; the cavalcade rode to the National Palace, through streets ornamented with flags, and followed by the troops. The triumphal entry into Rome of Scipio Africanus was less ostentatious than President Baez's appearance in the city of St. Domingo, on the morning of the 6th inst. and we may be allowed to remind our readers that Scipio subsequently lost his popularity with the Roman people when he claimed for himself and the Senators a station at public festivals which the laws of the republic did [illegible] either. La nota observaba asimismo que las informaciones recibidas eran enteramente parciales.

records.headline: How They Do It.
records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that after being left to themselves by Colombia and Spain, the Dominicans were invaded and subjugated by Haytian President Boyer under the pretext of aid. Under Haytian rule, local institutions and the University of Santo Tomas de Aquinas were destroyed, public edifices were dismantled, and property was confiscated due to constitutional laws forbidding white property ownership. Consequently, many Dominicans fled the country while the rest remained stripped of their means to leave.
records.summary_es: El diario relató que, tras quedar desamparados por Colombia y España, los dominicanos fueron invadidos y sojuzgados por el mandatario haitiano Boyer so pretexto de auxilio. Bajo la dominación haitiana, las instituciones vernáculas y la Universidad de Santo Tomás de Aquino fueron desmanteladas, los edificios públicos arruinados y los bienes confiscados en virtud de preceptos constitucionales que vedaban a los blancos el derecho de propiedad. En consecuencia, numerosos dominicanos huyeron de la patria, en tanto los restantes quedaron desprovistos de recursos para emigrar.

records.full_text: HOW THEY DO IT.—Some time in 1849, Mr. King, of Georgia, then a member of the House of Representatives, made a speech on the subject of the recognition of the independence of Hayti, in which he gave a brief history of the manner in which the Dominicans were brought under the yoke of the Haytians. In 1821, the Spanish part of the island of St. Domingo declared its independence of Spain, and sent commissioners to ask admission as one of the States of that republic. The Colombians were then too much engaged with their own affairs to undertake the defence of the Dominicans. Spain, engaged in the vain effort of reclaiming her other more populous and valuable colonies, left the Dominicans to themselves. Boyer, then president of Hayti, called out his whole military force, and passing the frontier, under pretence of aiding the Dominicans, took possession of the country, and annexed it to Hayti.

records.headline: The paper argues that unless a new system replaces the present mode of dealing with such questions, Soulouque will succeed
records.summary_en: The paper argues that unless a new system replaces the present mode of dealing with such questions, Soulouque will succeed in his project of subduing the Dominicans, a project it says is in reality warmly sustained by England. It argues that under Mr. Fillmore the United States lost what Mr. Calhoun's system had gained — holding Soulouque in check and upholding the Dominicans without direct intervention or protectorate — and has been trapped into a coalition with France and England in which it will exercise but nominal influence in Haitian affairs.
records.summary_es: El periódico argumenta que, a menos que un nuevo sistema reemplace el modo actual de tratar estas cuestiones, Soulouque tendrá éxito en su proyecto de subyugar a los dominicanos, un proyecto que, dice, en realidad es apoyado calurosamente por Inglaterra. Argumenta que bajo el Sr. Fillmore los Estados Unidos perdieron lo que el sistema del Sr. Calhoun había ganado —mantener a Soulouque a raya y apoyar a los dominicanos sin intervención directa ni protectorado— y han quedado atrapados en una coalición con Francia e Inglaterra en la que ejercerán solo una influencia nominal en los asuntos haitianos.

records.headline: The New York Herald reports that a colonel serving as a representative in the Congress of the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: The New York Herald reports that a colonel serving as a representative in the Congress of the Dominican Republic has sailed for the United States on an important political mission to Washington. Explaining that 'Dominica' (the Dominican Republic) is a former Spanish colony and now a republic occupying the eastern and larger section of the island, the paper contrasts it with the western Empire of Haiti, whose recently crowned emperor is ambitious to control the entire island and whose designs—along with the policies of England and France—remain suspected. The Herald presumes the envoy's mission concerns these relations between the Haitian empire and the Dominican republic, and asks whether the Dominicans, whom it deems entitled to United States protection, will receive it from Mr. Webster.
records.summary_es: The New York Herald informa que un coronel que se desempeña como representante en el Congreso de la República Dominicana ha zarpado hacia los Estados Unidos en una importante misión política con destino a Washington. Explicando que 'Dominica' (la República Dominicana) fue originalmente una colonia española y es ahora una república que ocupa la sección oriental y más extensa de la isla, el periódico la contrasta con el Imperio de Haití en el extremo occidental, cuyo emperador recientemente coronado ambiciona toda la isla y cuyos designios —junto con la política de Inglaterra y Francia— siguen despertando sospechas. El Herald presume que la misión del enviado se refiere a estas relaciones entre el imperio haitiano y la república dominicana, y se pregunta si los dominicanos, a quienes considera con derecho a la protección estadounidense, la recibirán del Sr. Webster.

records.summary_en: Under the headline 'Important from St. Domingo,' the Alexandria Gazette reprints a New York Herald item reporting a private letter from St. Domingo dated April 21. According to the letter, Col. T. S. Heniker, a representative in the Congress of the Dominican Republic, sailed on a brig that recently arrived at Boston, bound for Washington on an important political mission. The article notes that 'Dominica' (the Dominican Republic), originally a Spanish colony and now a republic, forms the eastern and larger section of the island, whereas the western end, nearly the size of New Jersey, constitutes the Empire of Haiti under the recently crowned Emperor Soulouque.

records.headline: The New-York Daily Tribune reports that the Haitian ruler has refused
records.summary_en: The New-York Daily Tribune reports that the Haitian ruler has refused to acknowledge the independence of the Dominican Republic and warned that unless the Haitian flag is hoisted there, he will march against the Dominicans in October. In response, the Dominicans are preparing to meet him on the frontier with a force of six thousand men and are busily repairing their frontier fortifications. Meanwhile, the Dominican Government guarantees land grants with indisputable title to all settlers, with five hundred Germans expected to settle at Cape Isabella, and is encouraging the cultivation of tobacco as the new crop comes in rapidly. A market report notes that American produce was in demand and lists St. Domingo coffee at $12 per hundredweight.
records.summary_es: El New-York Daily Tribune informa que el gobernante haitiano se ha negado a reconocer la independencia de la República Dominicana y ha advertido que, a menos que se ice allí la bandera haitiana, marchará contra los dominicanos el próximo mes de octubre. En respuesta, los dominicanos hacen preparativos para enfrentarlo en la frontera con una fuerza de seis mil hombres y reparan activamente sus fortificaciones fronterizas. Entretanto, el Gobierno republicano garantiza concesiones de tierras con título indisputable a todos los colonos, esperándose el asentamiento de quinientos alemanes en Cabo Isabela, y fomenta el cultivo de tabaco mientras la nueva cosecha entra con rapidez. Un informe de mercado señala que los productos estadounidenses tenían demanda y cotiza el café de Santo Domingo a $12 por quintal.

records.full_text: The latest news from Hayti is to the 20th ultimo. The Emperor Soulouque still refused to acknowledge the independence of the Dominican republic, and would not agree to an exchange of prisoners. He had threatened the messengers who went to Port-au-Prince to effect the exchange that unless the Haytien flag was hoisted he would march against them in October next. Arrangements were making to meet him on the frontier, under General Santana, with a force of 6,000 men. The Dominicans are also busily employed repairing their fortifications.

records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* reported that the Dominican Republic comprises about two-thirds of the island of Hayti and occupies a position of significant commercial importance, though its ability to meet the annual interest on a £760,000 loan was doubted. The article noted that the Dominican population is estimated at 200,000 of Spanish origin (including whites, blacks, and a mixed race), contrasting it with Hayti proper, which was under the despotic rule of Emperor Soulouque, possessed a population of 700,000 all-black citizens, and barred white persons from holding property. Furthermore, the excerpt stated that the entire island had been united under the Haytien government from 1821 until 1844, when Dominica separated due to Haytien violations of annexation terms and a refusal to permit white immigration.

El escrito consignaba que la población dominicana se estimaba en 200.000 almas de origen español (comprendiendo blancos, negros y razas mixtas), contrastándola con Haití propiamente dicho, sometido al mando tiránico del emperador Soulouque, con un censo de 700.000 habitantes exclusivamente de raza negra y con leyes que prohibían a los blancos poseer bienes raíces. records.full_text: The fact is believed to be simply that the President was authorised in 1851 to negotiate for a loan, but that such a loan would require the sanction of the Legislature, and that it is doubtful if this could be obtained for anything like the amount named. At the same time, it is impossible to comprehend the purpose for which it can be required. The depreciated paper circulation might be bought up for £30,000, and the idea of a State with only 200,000 inhabitants, and scarcely yet sure of its independence, or secure from the domestic intrigues peculiar to all races of Spanish origin, taking upon itself a debt of £760,000 simply to promote enterprise and immigration, is preposterous. The interest and sinking fund upon this would be nearly £60,000 per annum, and the entire revenue of the republic is supposed not to exceed £60,000. If the country, after a war with Haiti, and experiencing financial difficulties, should be in a condition to need an advance, it is not such an exaggeration as is likely to take place at present; and, as far as regards the promoters of enterprise, it will be enough if the English public deal with any specific project that may be brought forward, after a due examination of their merits. Raybaud as the French Consul General at Hayti, while the French war steamer *L'Ardent* departed St. Domingo on July 14 for Puerto-Plata carrying the resident French Consul. records.headline: The paper says the Republic of San Domingo, in the eastern portion of the island, has long excited the jealousy of Soulouque
records.summary_en: The paper says the Republic of San Domingo, in the eastern portion of the island, has long excited the jealousy of Soulouque and his predecessors, and that frequent wars between the two powers have impoverished the whole island. It says that in the last twelve months exhausted resources on both sides produced a tacit cessation of hostilities that either side could resume, while Soulouque was crowned, recruited and re-equipped his army, and distributed honors and titles.
records.summary_es: El periódico dice que la República de Santo Domingo, en la parte oriental de la isla, ha despertado desde hace tiempo los celos de Soulouque y de sus predecesores, y que las frecuentes guerras entre las dos potencias han empobrecido toda la isla. Dice que en los últimos doce meses el agotamiento de recursos de ambas partes produjo un cese tácito de hostilidades que cualquiera de las partes podría reanudar, mientras Soulouque era coronado, reclutaba y reequipaba su ejército y distribuía honores y títulos.

records.summary_en: Under the headline 'Important Movement Concerning Hayti,' the Staunton Spectator reports that two American gentlemen serving as officers in the army of the Dominican Republic have arranged with parties in the United States to purchase a steamer to transport a large number of emigrants to 'Dominica' (the Dominican Republic). records.headline: Under the headline 'Important Movement Concerning Hayti,' The National Era reports
records.summary_en: Under the headline 'Important Movement Concerning Hayti,' The National Era reports that two American officers of the army of the Dominican Republic have arranged with parties in the United States to buy a steamer to carry a large number of emigrants to 'Dominica' (the Dominican Republic), where eight hundred men have reportedly enlisted for colonization on advantageous terms. In editorial commentary, the paper notes the constant hostility between the Government of Haiti and the eastern part of the island styled the Dominican Republic, asks whether this hostility is fomented by white Americans who have gained a foothold there, and remarks that this so-called Republic is about as much a reality as the Mosquito King.
records.summary_es: Bajo el titular 'Important Movement Concerning Hayti', The National Era informa que dos oficiales estadounidenses del ejército de la República Dominicana han hecho arreglos con ciertas partes en los Estados Unidos para comprar un vapor con el fin de llevar un gran número de emigrantes a 'Dominica' (la República Dominicana), donde se dice que ochocientos hombres ya se han alistado para la colonización en condiciones ventajosas. En un comentario editorial, el periódico señala la constante hostilidad entre el Gobierno de Haití y la parte oriental de la isla denominada República Dominicana, se pregunta si dicha hostilidad no es fomentada por los estadounidenses blancos que han logrado establecerse allí, y afirma que esa llamada República tiene tanta realidad como el Rey de los Mosquitos.

records.headline: The Portsmouth Inquirer reports that two American officers in the army of the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: The Portsmouth Inquirer reports that two American officers in the army of the Dominican Republic have arranged with parties in the United States to purchase a steamer to transport a large number of emigrants to 'Dominica' (the Dominican Republic), and that eight hundred men have already enlisted for colonization on advantageous terms. Commenting on the movement, the paper predicts that eight hundred Americans in the 'Republic of Dominica' will soon make its exports an important item in the West India trade. From a political standpoint, it adds that eight hundred enterprising Americans will not only suffice to protect the Dominicans against the Haitian Emperor, but will also be likely to carry the war into his territory with an eye to extending the area of freedom.

Comentando sobre el movimiento, el periódico predice que ochocientos estadounidenses en la 'República de Dominica' pronto harán de sus exportaciones un rubro importante del comercio de las Indias Occidentales. Desde un punto de vista político, añade que ochocientos estadounidenses emprendedores no solo bastarán para proteger a los dominicanos contra el emperador haitiano, sino que muy probablemente llevarán la guerra a su territorio con miras a extender el área de la libertad.

records.headline: The Richmond Enquirer reports that after a change in the State Department defeated
records.summary_en: The Richmond Enquirer reports that after a change in the State Department defeated an earlier movement, Mr. Green called the President's attention to papers on file alleging that Mr. Webster had been induced to oppose recognizing the independence of the Dominican Republic by representations from New York and Boston merchants holding large contracts with Solouque for ships, arms, and military supplies. According to Green, the papers proved that persons in the United States were cooperating with the British and French governments in expectation that England and France would aid in conquering the Dominicans and ultimately annexing Cuba and the other West Indian islands. After Green protested against sacrificing the Dominicans by withholding recognition, the President promised to inquire into the facts and professed willingness to recognize both governments, while propositions for a colonization contract sent to confidential persons in St. Domingo were intercepted by French agents and published in Paris and the United States.
records.summary_es: El Richmond Enquirer informa que, después de que un cambio en el Departamento de Estado frustrara un movimiento anterior, el Sr. Green llamó la atención del Presidente sobre documentos archivados según los cuales el Sr. Webster había sido inducido a oponerse al reconocimiento de la independencia de la República Dominicana por gestiones de comerciantes de Nueva York y Boston que tenían grandes contratos con Solouque para el suministro de buques, armas y pertrechos militares. Según Green, los documentos probaban que ciertas personas en los Estados Unidos cooperaban con los gobiernos británico y francés con la expectativa de que Inglaterra y Francia ayudarían a conquistar a los dominicanos y finalmente anexar Cuba y las demás islas de las Indias Occidentales. Tras la protesta de Green contra sacrificar a los dominicanos al negarles el reconocimiento, el Presidente prometió investigar los hechos y manifestó su disposición a reconocer a ambos gobiernos, mientras que las propuestas para un contrato de colonización enviadas a personas de confianza en Santo Domingo fueron interceptadas por agentes franceses y publicadas en París y en los Estados Unidos.

records.summary_en: The Southern Sentinel reports that two American officers of the army of the Dominican Republic have made arrangements with parties in the United States to purchase a steamer to transport a large number of emigrants to 'Dominica' (the Dominican Republic). According to the paper, eight hundred men have already enlisted for colonization among the Dominicans under terms described as highly advantageous to men of enterprise and intelligence. The Sentinel adds that the New York Herald, which it remarks always pretends to know more than its neighbors, claims to have secret intelligence that the enterprise is a filibuster movement intended for the conquest of the island of Haiti.

Según el periódico, ochocientos hombres ya se han alistado para la colonización entre los dominicanos bajo condiciones descritas como muy ventajosas para hombres de empresa e inteligencia. El Sentinel añade que el New York Herald, del cual comenta que siempre pretende saber más que sus vecinos, afirma poseer inteligencia secreta de que se trata de un movimiento filibustero destinado a la conquista de la isla de Haití.

records.headline: The Morning Star reports Mr. Green's statements concerning Boston merchants
records.summary_en: The Morning Star reports Mr. Green's statements concerning Boston merchants who held large contracts with Soulouque for ships, arms, and military supplies, and papers allegedly proving that persons in the United States were cooperating with the British and French governments in expectation that England and France would aid Soulouque to conquer the Dominicans and ultimately annex Cuba and the other West Indian islands. According to the account, Green protested against allowing Mr. Webster to sacrifice the Dominicans by withholding recognition of their independence; the President promised to inquire into the facts, professed his willingness to recognize both governments, and stated he could not legally prevent Green from obtaining a colonization contract from the Dominican government. After propositions sent to confidential persons in St. Domingo were intercepted by French agents and published in Paris and the United States, Green investigated conditions in St. Domingo and concluded that unless the United States counteracts British and French policy, the white population on the eastern part of the island will be compelled to acknowledge the dominion of Soulouque's government.
records.summary_es: El Morning Star informa sobre las declaraciones del Sr. Green acerca de comerciantes de Boston que tenían grandes contratos con Soulouque para el suministro de buques, armas y pertrechos militares, así como de documentos que, según afirma, probaban que ciertas personas en los Estados Unidos cooperaban con los gobiernos británico y francés con la expectativa de que Inglaterra y Francia ayudarían a Soulouque a conquistar a los dominicanos y finalmente anexar Cuba y las demás islas de las Indias Occidentales. Según el relato, Green protestó contra permitir que el Sr. Webster sacrificara a los dominicanos al negarles el reconocimiento de su independencia; el Presidente prometió investigar los hechos, manifestó su disposición a reconocer a ambos gobiernos y declaró que no podía impedir legalmente que Green obtuviera un contrato de colonización del Gobierno dominicano. Después de que las propuestas enviadas a personas de confianza en Santo Domingo fueran interceptadas por agentes franceses y publicadas en París y en los Estados Unidos, Green indagó la situación real en Santo Domingo y concluyó que, a menos que los Estados Unidos contrarresten la política británica y francesa, los blancos de la parte oriental de la isla se verán obligados a reconocer el dominio del gobierno de Soulouque.

records.headline: The Rhode-Island Weekly Post reports that advices from St. Domingo
records.summary_en: The Rhode-Island Weekly Post reports that advices from St. Domingo to October 3 state that vague rumors of an expedition from the United States to St. Domingo caused considerable excitement in the republic for a time, though all had become quiet by the latest accounts. According to the report, the public believed that these unfounded rumors were circulated by persons seeking to foment internal trouble and aid schemes to overthrow the government. In response, Dominican President Baez issued a manifesto prohibiting foreigners from disembarking at any ports in the republic other than St. Domingo, Azua, and one other designated port except in cases such as shipwreck, closing La Romana and Samana for six months, and banning the importation of firearms and ammunition.
records.summary_es: El Rhode-Island Weekly Post informa que las noticias de Santo Domingo hasta el 3 de octubre indican que vagos rumores sobre una expedición procedente de los Estados Unidos hacia Santo Domingo causaron considerable agitación en la república por un tiempo, aunque según los últimos informes todo había vuelto a la calma. De acuerdo con la nota, el pueblo creía que esos rumores infundados eran difundidos por personas interesadas en fomentar disturbios internos y apoyar planes para destruir al gobierno. En respuesta, el presidente dominicano Báez emitió un manifiesto que prohíbe a los extranjeros desembarcar en cualquier puerto de la república salvo Santo Domingo, Azua y otro puerto habilitado, excepto en casos como naufragio, cierra La Romana y Samaná por seis meses y prohíbe la importación de armas de fuego y municiones.

records.headline: The New York Herald reports that several French warships have taken
records.summary_en: The New York Herald reports that several French warships have taken possession of a Dominican peninsula (printed 'Sa mata' and 'Samsna') with designs to hold it as a naval station. Recalling an article it published the previous April, the paper states that an intrigue had been going on for years between Dominican President Buenaventura Baez and Major Reybaud, the French Consul to Haiti, aimed at allowing France to obtain a foothold in 'Dominica' (the Dominican Republic), conquer the western part of the island, extinguish Soulouque and his empire, and restore the entire island to French dominion. According to the Herald, the scheme had the cooperation of President Baez and a clique of French residents, whereas the mass of the citizens, being Spaniards, were hostile to any measure subjecting them to France. The paper adds that some two years earlier President Baez wrote to the French Consul General in Port-au-Prince offering to place the country under French protection at whatever sacrifice—which the April article hinted was the peninsula now seized—and more recently made an even stronger appeal to France.
records.summary_es: The New York Herald informa que varios buques de guerra franceses han tomado posesión de una península dominicana (impresa como 'Sa mata' y 'Samsna') con el propósito de mantenerla como estación naval. records.full_text:
THE FRENCH MOVEMENT IN ST. DOMINGO.

American, French, and Spanish Views of the Question.

THE NEW CASUS BELLI.

[From the New York Herald of April 21, 1852.]
OUR PORT-AU-PLAT CORRESPONDENCE.
PORT-AU-PLAT, Dominican Republic, February, 1852.
I have on former occasions addressed a word to you, to draw the attention of the public of the republic, respecting what it pleases our present administration to throw dust into the eyes of the United States citizens. I mean the false information which the President officially stated in his message, that the differences between the Dominican republic and the Haytian empire were arranged, while such a desirable event is as far off as ever—thanks to the intrigue of public agents.

I may as well advise; for if you will refer to the Revue des Deux Mondes, for May, 1851, its pages corporate more than a sentiment, since Mr. M. Barrot, a member of the Assembly, contains an article on the empire of Hayti and the Dominican republic, which, it is confidently reported, has the French Consul in Port au Prince for author. Now, for its author, and is so filled up with misstatements that it is impossible that the reviewer in Paris could assemble a print contained therein to insert similar stuff it is clumsily attempted, in these pages, to make it appear that the Dominican republic desires a French protectorate over St. Domingo, is the most ardent desire of the Dominican population, who would see with pleasure their President, Senor Baez, (who, to his shame be it said is more Frenchman than Dominican,) and a small clique of French partisans, surrender the republic, although the inhabitants utterly despise Johnny Crapaud with as deep a hatred as ever did their Haytian neighbors.

I am now resident here for some years, during which time I have studied the character of the Haytians, and remarkably; and I must confess that the steady exercise of French diplomatic agents in Hayti, for some years past, inspires me with a suspicion that those agents have only had one aim—namely, to get hold under some plausible appearance of the Dominican republic and to conquer afterwards the western part, under the black ribbon, with comparative facility, thereby restoring the 'Queen of the Antilles' to the dominion of France; or, if you will, since the Dictator has restored 'the eagles' of Napoleon to the French army, to the claws of the rapacious bird, which, although it may resemble ours in form, has no relationship with it in character.

The supposition of an intended protectorate in St. Domingo is further strengthened by the arrival of the Prince de Joinville and the Duke d'Aumale in Hayti, during the presidency of General Guerrier. The children of Louis Philippe, the late King of the French, came to Hayti under the pretext of paying the Montalais their legacy, which was left by the late King of Hayti to the widow of Prince de Joinville's brother, the late Prince of Joinville, and to her sister-in-law, the Duchess of Orleans; but the real object of their visit was to prepare the way for the French fleet to come and occupy Cuba and Porto Rico to her sister, bidding the young princes a very cool adieu, and telling them they had better turn back, as they would find nothing there to do, and to render it in time the stronghold of these seas, and to conquer the rest of Hayti.

The Emperor's downfall and the revolution interrupted the intrigue, but scarcely had Louis Napoleon reached the presidency than the old schemes of Louis Philippe's agent were recommendations, and found a warm supporter in a French agent, named Mr. Raybaud, who was sent to the Dominican republic, clever, educated and French in heart, although a Dominican citizen.

The Revue des Deux Mondes tells us that this patriotic citizen had proposed to Mr. M. Barrot, the French Consul in Port au Prince—'You have only to give us your support, or a company of 2,000 men, to convince France of our sincere desire to place ourselves under her protectorate.' But Mr. Raybaud, although a Dominican citizen, was so far from having the modesty to refuse the proposal, that he had even the face to ask for more—namely, that 5,000 French troops should be sent to occupy the republic of Dominica.

So far from having the modesty, or to make statements from the executive of the Dominican republic, will be still more surprised if they continue to deny them for a short distance. They will find that Mr. Senor Baez, the President of Dominica, actually sent Mr. Raybaud to induce the acceptance of the young republic, foot and arm, of the French flag, and to place it under the protectorate of France; and that, at this moment, Mr. Raybaud (Mr. Green)—sent to St. Domingo with full powers from President Baez, to treat on this subject; so that, as long as there is a spark of hope that France will accept my proposals, I will wait with resignation.'

The author of these precious state papers from St. Domingo sent to Paris, where he went to further the object of his mission to produce the annexation of St. Domingo to the French empire, was Mr. Raybaud, although it is well known that another agent, whose name was kept secret, while the English cabinet employed only intrigue, which altogether failed.

The objects of Mr. Green's mission are well-known to the public of Dominica, although it was stated by the president's partisans that he was merely sent to Paris to purchase arms, &c. But Mr. Raybaud (Green), whose real name was known, selected young Green, who by the situation he had formerly held in Mexico, seemed to be a proper person for the mission to Paris; and his brother, who is now in his cabinet, although he never affirmed his connection with it.

I need not tell you how Mr. Green succeeded in his cabinet at Aranjuez. I never heard of any; but I can tell you what he did in Paris, and also what Mr. Baez's Carminero, then Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Dominican republic, did in London. Mr. Carminero was offered him the protectorate, promising that the British flag should be hoisted in St. Domingo; but Mr. Carminero refused it in the name of his government, and that the same Mr. Carminero, as soon as he found that Mr. Green was sent to London, sent the British Cabinet a diplomatic note, in which he declined to accept any such proposals.

The intention of Mr. Raybaud was not to produce an aggrandizement, but desired merely the prosperity of Dominica, and to avoid the trouble of getting a new prince to govern the republic. He added however, should France reject the offer, that if the Dominican republic can flag, it would be the sign to him to strike the British flag. Now, is it not surprising that after such facts, the city of a person who fabricates falsehoods in his message to Congress, in the manner of Mr. Fillmore, could assert such fables?

To show how far he abuses the Ministers of France and England, he says, 'We have offered to the United States to place ourselves under her protection, but no answer was given.' Now, no such proposal was ever made by Mr. Baez to the United States. He also says, 'We have offered to the Dominican flag to be hoisted in St. Domingo.' Now, this is another falsehood of Mr. Fillmore. Mr. Fillmore says, 'We have offered the Dominican flag to be hoisted in St. Domingo.' He says, 'We are forced by the French to consent.' This is another falsehood of Mr. Fillmore. Now, this is another falsehood of Mr. Fillmore, who says, 'We are forced by the French to consent.' Our lethargy, he says, 'has prevented us from accepting the offer, or the financial obstacles that might be given as an excuse to us for not having accepted it.' Now, no such excuse can be made, for no offer was ever made to us. We have not even the trouble to carry it there—it is all a invention of Mr. Fillmore; and we are sure that, if such a proposal had been made to the Dominican republic, the New World the future entrepot of the two hemispheres would not have been rejected. But Mr. Fillmore, it is openly, may be objected to us: 'Good God! because it is a secret.' If it is a secret, how does Mr. Fillmore and his friends know of it? because it such a legitimate and honorable mission that it must be kept secret. Yes, because others already dispute themselves publicly for the Dominican republic; and Mr. Fillmore, who has done so far for the eight years has answered to the gut vice of the cabinet of Paris.

Answer to Mr. Green: But if Mr. Green might succeed under such circumstances, the diplomatic tendency of the British cabinet, although it may seem so, is entirely different; how different with the Dictator, Louis Napoleon at the head of the French army, and the article of the Revue des Deux Mondes, written by Mr. Raybaud, is still more surprising. If we look at the article in the Revue des Deux Mondes, written by Mr. Raybaud, we find that the writer, after describing the state of Hayti, says that the French flag, hoisted in Dominica, would be a strong inducement for France to accept the proposal; and he adds that the French government ought to accept it, because it would give France the key of the Gulf of Mexico, and enable her to conquer Hayti, and to regain the control of the Queen of the Antilles. records.headline: An editorial in the Tribune addresses rumors that France has taken
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Tribune addresses rumors that France has taken possession of the peninsula of Samaná, criticizing rival newspapers for sensational bluster. The paper argues that the Dominican Republic is an independent government, virtually though not officially recognized by the United States, that has sought French protection or annexation of its own free will. The editorial maintains that the Monroe declaration contains no principle justifying American interference with the Dominican Republic's decisions, distinguishing its sovereign status from that of Cuba, which remains a Spanish dependency.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en el Tribune aborda los rumores de que Francia ha tomado posesión de la península de Samaná, criticando a los periódicos rivales por sus aspavientos sensacionalistas. El periódico sostiene que la República Dominicana es un gobierno independiente, virtual aunque no oficialmente reconocido por los Estados Unidos, que ha buscado la protección francesa o la anexión por su propia voluntad. El editorial afirma que la declaración de Monroe no contiene ningún principio que justifique la interferencia estadounidense en las decisiones de la República Dominicana, distinguiendo su condición soberana de la de Cuba, que sigue siendo una dependencia española.
