records.headline: The Dispatch reports rumors that French warships have occupied
records.summary_en: The Dispatch reports rumors that French warships have occupied Samaná to establish a naval station. The paper recalls its earlier reporting on an intrigue between Dominican President Buenaventura Báez and the French consul to Haiti to secure France a foothold in "Dominica," from which French forces might conquer Haiti and restore the entire island to French rule. According to the article, while Báez and local French residents supported placing the country under French protection and offering Samaná, the Dominican population remained firmly hostile to French dominion.

Según el artículo, aunque Báez y los residentes franceses locales apoyaban poner el país bajo la protección francesa y ofrecer Samaná, la población dominicana se mantuvo firmemente hostil a la dominación francesa.

records.headline: An editorial in the Daily Union discusses the reported surrender
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Daily Union discusses the reported surrender, by the Dominican president, of his country's independence to French domination under the pretext of protection against Haitian Emperor Faustin Soulouque. The paper contends that ceding Samaná and establishing a French naval depot would give France supreme control over the Dominican Republic. While expressing skepticism that France intends to conquer Haiti or the whole island, the editorial warns that Samaná possesses one of the world's finest natural harbors. Stationed there, the paper asserts, a French fleet would command the Mona Passage, threatening American trade routes and coasts.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en el Daily Union analiza los informes que indican que el presidente dominicano ha entregado la independencia de su país a la dominación francesa bajo el pretexto de protección frente al emperador haitiano Faustin Soulouque. El diario sostiene que la cesión de Samaná y el establecimiento de un depósito naval francés otorgarían a Francia un control supremo sobre la República Dominicana. Aunque expresa escepticismo de que Francia pretenda conquistar Haití o la isla entera, el editorial advierte que Samaná posee uno de los mejores puertos naturales del mundo. Estacionada allí, afirma el periódico, una flota francesa dominaría el paso de la Mona, amenazando las rutas comerciales y las costas estadounidenses.

It says Great Britain and France instructed their agents to menace Soulouque with hostility if he refused, but he persisted in his designs against Dominica and would in no manner acknowledge its independence, so the utmost the mediating powers could effect was the prolongation of an existing truce, and it praises Mr. Walsh's mission.

records.headline: The paper reports late news from Haiti: Soulouque has recruited and re-equipped his army and placed it on as effective a footing
records.summary_en: The paper reports late news from Haiti: Soulouque has recruited and re-equipped his army and placed it on as effective a footing as the empire's resources would permit, distributing eagles, crosses of the Legion of Honor, ranks and titles to ensure or reward the fidelity of his army. It summarizes the Emperor's address from the throne to the Senate as analyzing the condition of the empire — public works, the budget, internal and external trade, custom houses, the crops, the army and navy, foreign relations and public instruction — and as stating that the army and navy are on a respectable footing.
records.summary_es: El periódico informa noticias recientes de Haití: Soulouque ha reclutado y reequipado su ejército y lo ha puesto en un pie tan eficaz como lo permitían los recursos del imperio, distribuyendo águilas, cruces de la Legión de Honor, rangos y títulos para asegurar o recompensar la fidelidad de su ejército. Resume el discurso del emperador desde el trono ante el Senado como un análisis de la condición del imperio —obras públicas, presupuesto, comercio interno y externo, aduanas, cosechas, ejército y marina, relaciones exteriores e instrucción pública— y como una afirmación de que el ejército y la marina están en un pie respetable.

“By some means, publicity has been given to the correspondence between the State Department and Mr. Robert M. Walsh, its agent in the negotiation for the pacification of Hayti. In the various papers which constitute this correspondence, the motives and purposes of the Administration in proffering its good offices in behalf of the Dominican republic are frankly and clearly set forth.

“In 1821 the Spanish portion of the Island of St. Domingo voluntarily subjected itself to the government of Hayti, then presided over by Boyer. On the expulsion of Boyer, and on account of the wrongs and grievances which they had endured, with a repetition of which they were menaced, the Dominicans threw off the subjection of negro government and established an independent republic. To this step the Spanish inhabitants of St. Domingo were driven by the necessity of self-preservation. Not only were their political rights and their liberty invaded and trampled upon by the black barbarians of Hayti, but the doom of indiscriminate slaughter and extermination was incessantly held before them in the threats of the Macaya and Dessalines.

“By the most imperious necessity, then, were the Dominicans impelled to set up an independent government. Nevertheless, their act of separation was regarded as a revolt by the negroes of Hayti, who prepared to reduce the rebel whites to subjection by the strong arm of force. All the efforts of the Haytien government were unequal, how ever, to the reconquest of Dominico. The Spaniards defended themselves with valor and energy, and, despite the disparity of numbers, successfully repelled the invasions of their foes. They achieved and established their independence. France formally recognised the republic of Dominica. England and the United States recognised it by their acts. Still Soulouque refused to acknowledge the independence of the Dominicans, and persisted in his efforts to reduce them to subjection. In this juncture, under the apprehension of a very formidable attack by Soulouque, the Dominican government solicited the mediation of the United States,

records.full_text:
HAYTI AND ST. DOMINGO.

The official paper of France (the Moniteur) lately contained an article from which we translate the following paragraphs:

“The Emperor Faustin I, immediately upon his accession to power, manifested his hostile views against the people of the eastern part of the island of Hayti, who, after the fall of the President Boyer, in 1844, had proclaimed their independence and established the Dominican Republic.

“The first essay of the Haitien Emperor, however, was not fortunate; defeated at the battle of the Ocoa, in 1849, his armies were entirely broken up, and he was obliged to retire, followed by the Dominicans, who would have carried their successes much further had it not been for the friendly mediation of the Powers which intervened in the conflict.

“On this occasion France was naturally called upon to act the first part. In 1843, in fact, before the division of the island had taken place, and when the eastern part was yet under the Haytien yoke, the inhabitants of the province of St. Domingo had, of their own accord, invoked the protection of the King of the French, and offered, on this condition, to deliver up to him the peninsula and bay of Samana.

“This treaty, accepted by M. Ferdinand Barrot, was ratified at Paris early in 1844. Soon after France fulfilled the first engagement it had assumed, by causing the Dominican movement to be supported by Vice Admiral de Moges, commander of the West India squadron. Strong in this support, the Dominicans were enabled to maintain their separation, and on the 27th February, 1844, hoisted the national flag.

“When, however, the French Government came to be called upon to carry out the conditions of the treaty of 1843, the Chamber of Deputies was not favorably inclined to it; they found that it would be dangerous to accept a military post in the proximity of a colony which had so cruelly escaped from us, and in the possession of which an attempt might be made to establish ourselves; moreover, and above all, the Chamber did not like to take up a position which seemed to engage us to assume in future the permanent protectorate of the Dominican Republic.

“These considerations prevailed: the treaty of 1843 was abandoned; the peninsula of Samana was not occupied; but France, nevertheless, remained the declared protectress of the new State, and it was in this capacity that she afterwards offered her mediation to put an end to the contest between the Haitiens and the Dominicans.”

The readers of the Intelligencer will not have forgotten that this was the project which was defeated by the unremitted vigilance and resolute conduct of the lamented Commodore Knox. The scheme is far from being abandoned, as the public may soon have occasion to perceive. England has already secured an island (the island of Alta Vela) in the same quarter, but having an eye to an establishment on that very point of Samana.

records.headline: The West-Jersey Pioneer describes defensive regulations issued
records.summary_en: The West-Jersey Pioneer describes defensive regulations issued by the Dominican government restricting passenger landings at Azua and Puerto Plata, requiring special permits at Santo Domingo, and barring the importation of arms and ammunition. The paper views these measures as an absurd overreaction to unfounded rumors of an impending filibustering expedition from the United States, which harms Dominican commerce. The editorial insists that no responsible American group has organized an invasion of the island, asserting that the United States government would promptly declare any such filibuster illegal and surrender the invaders to justice.
records.summary_es: El West-Jersey Pioneer describe las regulaciones defensivas emitidas por el gobierno dominicano que restringen el desembarco de pasajeros en Azua y Puerto Plata, exigen permisos especiales en Santo Domingo y prohíben la importación de armas y municiones. El periódico considera estas medidas como una reacción absurda y desmedida ante rumores infundados de una inminente expedición filibustera desde los Estados Unidos, lo que perjudica el comercio dominicano. El editorial insiste en que ningún grupo estadounidense respetable ha organizado una invasión de la isla, afirmando que el gobierno de los Estados Unidos declararía de inmediato ilegal cualquier intento filibustero y entregaría a los invasores a la justicia.

records.headline: Our National Reputation.
records.summary_en: The *West-Jersey pioneer* reported on December 18, 1852, that recurring American expeditions against Cuba and the Rio Grande caused neighboring regions—including St. Domingo, which barred its doors against foreigners—to view American commercial enterprises with extreme suspicion as disguised filibuster incursions. The newspaper lamented that these actions damaged the reputation of the United States, causing foreign nations to regard the American government as a piratical force rather than an honorable republic.

El periódico deploraba que tales desafueros menoscabaran el crédito de Estados Unidos, incitando a las potencias extranjeras a considerar al gobierno estadounidense como una potencia corsaria antes que como una república honorable.

records.full_text: From the Saturday Gazette. OUR NATIONAL REPUTATION. The United States is rapidly becoming the terror of the world. We are a nation of filibusters and colonizers of weaker nations, whose territories lie within range of our commerce or speculation. New Grenada is alarmed at the infusion of our population into her territories, and last, of all, the little republic of St. Domingo has been in a panic about a report, received by way of Turks Island, to the effect that an American steamer had put into Puerto Plata, but had fled on sight of an English steamer, and that this solitary steamer was bound to land a force that would take possession of the Dominican Republic and straightway annex it to the dominions of Uncle Sam. However absurd such a report might be made, it is wild to suppose that the government of the United States would sanction it, or shoulder the responsibility of it. It would rather have declared the whole affair illegal and outrageous, and done every thing to give up the lawless invaders to the justice of the injured government. That such would have been the result, we have an assurance in the policy laid down by our government, in various administrations, when similar troubles have been menacing us with Canada, Cuba and Mexico. But neither the declared policy nor the actual practice of a government can give confidence to foreign powers, so long as the shameless spirit of encroachment, annexation and revolution exists as it does among so large a portion of the American people. The lawlessness of a class inspires more faith than the promises of a President, and the reputation of the nation suffers for the shamelessness of a faction. Thus it is that every commercial enterprise that is set on foot in an American port is at once looked upon as a Fillibuster expedition in disguise. Cuba shakes in her shores at the sight of an American steamer; St. Domingo bars her doors on all foreigners, lest a stray American invader may come in and upset her government, and we shall next hear that Soulouque, the supreme, the Emperor of Hayti, drawing a cordon across his land frontier and fortifying his ports, to prevent his Imperial domains from being carried off bodily to be annexed to the great American Republic. While we can laugh at the folly of these foreign fears, we cannot help lamenting that the name of the United States should have fallen into such an odium as to justify, in the slightest degree, such absurd alarms. But, thanks to the oft-repeated and shameless enterprises upon cuba and the Rio Grande, the government of the republic fought for by the fathers, and identified in all honor by Washington and those around him, has now come to be looked on as a species of piratical craft cruising in all seas, and ready to plunder and capture all foreign property. It is beginning to be a sort of national Rob Roy, whose policy is '—the simple plan, That they shall take who have the power, And they shall keep who can.' Right-minded citizens, who respect national honesty and deem acts of national wrong as shameful as pocket-picking, should set their faces against all movements that may tend to strengthen the opprobrium into which we have fallen among foreign governments. The mere fact of our being a nation of unexampled prosperity, and rapidly growing in wealth and power, should not satisfy us, so long as we are looked upon abroad as a lawless people, with a government incapable of checking the growing popular frenzy for annexation. There is something more than mere power and wealth to be attained by a nation—and that is the reputation as well as the fact of national integrity.

records.headline: The editorial calls it preposterous for The Union to talk of the United States assuming a protectorate over the Dominican
records.summary_en: The editorial calls it preposterous for The Union to talk of the United States assuming a protectorate over the Dominican Republic, or over any of the republics south of the United States, and says the true American policy is to keep clear of all protectorates. It argues that the Dominicans themselves would refuse and repudiate such protection, having instead solicited France for eight years, so that an American protectorate would have to be enforced at the cannon's mouth while France's would be welcomed.
records.summary_es: El editorial califica de absurdo que The Union hable de que los Estados Unidos asuman un protectorado sobre la República Dominicana, o sobre cualquiera de las repúblicas al sur de los Estados Unidos, y sostiene que la verdadera política estadounidense es mantenerse alejada de todo protectorado. Argumenta que los propios dominicanos rechazarían y repudiarían tal protección, pues en cambio la han solicitado a Francia durante ocho años, de modo que un protectorado estadounidense tendría que imponerse a cañonazos, mientras que el de Francia sería bien recibido.

records.headline: The Intelligencer reprints remarks from the New York Tribune
records.summary_en: The Intelligencer reprints remarks from the New York Tribune. They concern rumors that France had taken possession of the peninsula of Samaná. According to the quoted extract, American diplomacy faced three choices: returning the Dominicans to Haitian rule, maintaining their independence only to see them annexed to France, or annexing them directly to the United States. The Tribune observed that the Dominican people rejected the third option attempted by the Greenes and preferred French annexation under Napoleon III. The Intelligencer comments that domestic slavery severely weakens American external influence, making appeals to the Monroe doctrine in Santo Domingo pointless.
records.summary_es: El Intelligencer reproduce comentarios del New York Tribune acerca de los rumores de que Francia había tomado posesión de la península de Samaná. De acuerdo con el extracto citado, la diplomacia estadounidense enfrentaba tres opciones: devolver a los dominicanos al dominio haitiano, mantener su independencia solo para verlos anexionados a Francia, o anexionarlos directamente a los Estados Unidos. El Tribune observó que el pueblo dominicano rechazó la tercera opción intentada por los Greene y prefirió la anexión francesa bajo Napoleón III. El Intelligencer comenta que la esclavitud interna debilita gravemente la influencia exterior estadounidense, haciendo inútiles las apelaciones a la doctrina Monroe en Santo Domingo.

records.summary_en: The *Daily National Intelligencer* reported that a mission by the Creole Minister of Foreign Affairs failed to persuade the Haitian Emperor Soulouque to sign a peace treaty or a ten-year truce with St. Domingo. Soulouque argued that the island was naturally one and indivisible, viewing the Dominicans as rebels who had no right to secede, and therefore peremptorily declined the propositions through his Senate. However, the Emperor's Minister of Foreign Affairs subsequently volunteered a positive assurance that hostilities against the Dominicans would not be renewed.
records.summary_es: El *Daily National Intelligencer* refirió que la legación encabezada por el canciller de origen criollo no logró inducir al emperador haitiano Soulouque a pactar un tratado de paz ni una tregua decenal con Santo Domingo. Soulouque adujo que la isla era indivisible por naturaleza, conceptuando a los dominicanos como facciosos sin potestad para segregarse, por cuya causa desestimó rotundamente las proposiciones ante su Senado. Con todo, el ministro de Negocios Extranjeros imperial brindó ulteriormente seguridades formales de que no se reanudarían las hostilidades contra los dominicanos.

The December number, for January, 1853, will be the first of the forty-first volume of the Knickerbocker Magazine.
Since the price of subscription has been reduced from five to three dollars a year, the circulation of the Knickerbocker has been increased nearly four to one. In many places ten are sold where there was but one before, and through the year it has been steadily increasing. It is now offered as cheap as any of the Magazines, all things considered. Instead of making new and prodigious promises, we submit a few extracts from notices of late numbers, which we might extend to a number of pages.
Those familiar with the Editor's monthly "gossip" with his readers have, doubtless, with ourselves, admired the taste and judgment displayed in the selection of articles that adorn its pages. It is a sufficient guarantee that no contribution is admitted to its pages that is not in every way worthy of his perusal. When storms and wild tempests are abroad, and the "stormy spirit of the storm" is out, and all is drear and desolate without, ask for no more agreeable companion than the KNICKERBOCKER. Its contents impart valuable information, its sallies of genuine wit are a sovereign specific for all the "ills that flesh is heir to," and it never fails to drive away the "blue devils" of the horrors, and time passes merrily on.—[Courier, Burlington, Vermont.]
[National Intelligencer, Washington.]
'The December number of the Knickerbocker is a capital one. It contains a very interesting article on "The Creole Minister of Foreign Affairs," which gives a graphic account of the mission of the late Mr. Walsh to the Court of the Emperor of Hayti. Mr. Walsh was sent by the United States Government to negotiate a treaty of peace between the Emperor and the Government of St. Domingo. He had several interviews with the Creole Minister of Foreign Affairs, but failed to accomplish the object of the mission. Neither persuasion nor argument could induce the Emperor to make a definite treaty of peace, or a truce of ten years, with the Government of St. Domingo, which he regarded as a rebel whose subjection was necessary to the maintenance of his own authority. He argued that nature had designed the whole island to be under one Government, that the constitution of Hayti so declared it, and that he was bound to maintain the integrity of his empire. The article is well written, and contains much interesting information.'
'The Knickerbocker has been and will be a fact of its own: it is a sort of "institution." We never yet took up a new number of its pages, filled with articles not printed from English authors, but we felt a sort of "home-feeling" in its company and welcome.'—New York Christian Inquirer.

records.headline: The National Era publishes diplomatic instructions for an American commissioner
records.summary_en: The National Era publishes diplomatic instructions for an American commissioner to act impartially in mediating the conflict between Haiti and the Dominican Republic. The envoy is instructed not to deny justice to Haitian Emperor Faustin Soulouque because of his African race and monarchical system, nor to favor the Dominican government solely for its Castilian lineage and republican form. The dispatch explains that the commercial interests of France, Great Britain, and the United States require regional peace, enabling Haiti to repay French debts and opening expanded markets for all three powers.
records.summary_es: The National Era publica instrucciones diplomáticas que ordenan a un comisionado estadounidense actuar con imparcialidad al mediar en el conflicto entre Haití y la República Dominicana. Se instruye al enviado a no denegar justicia al emperador haitiano Faustin Soulouque debido a su raza africana y sistema monárquico, ni a favorecer al gobierno dominicano únicamente por su linaje castellano y forma republicana. El despacho explica que los intereses comerciales de Francia, Gran Bretaña y los Estados Unidos requieren la paz regional, lo que permitiría a Haití pagar sus deudas francesas y abriría mercados más amplios para las tres potencias.

records.summary_en: The newspaper criticizes United States policy toward Hayti, attributing it to slavery-dominated diplomacy and the failure to recognize Hayti's independence. It reports that, following domestic interference and joint bullying with foreign governments, the French have taken possession of Samana as a naval station under the pretext of intervening for Dominica. The publication warns that this acquisition will allow France to monitor American commerce and facilitate hostile actions against the United States in the event of war.

La publicación previene que dicho enclave consentirá a Francia vigilar las rutas mercantiles norteamericanas y propiciar acometidas bélicas contra Estados Unidos en coyunturas de guerra.

But we have not yet reached the final result of our indefensible conduct towards Hayti. As we have already said, had we recognised her independence, and exchanged with her the usual international courtesies, we should have enjoyed the largest portion of her valuable trade, and obtained an influence over her, beneficial to her internal interests, and protective against foreign aggression. In obedience to a blind and bigoted sectional Interest, we have pursued an opposite policy, and now retribution is about to overtake us. We have interfered impertinently in her domestic affairs, we have united with foreign Governments in bullying her—and now, one of these Governments, if the latest intelligence be correct, has taken possession of a most important station on the island, on pretence of making its intervention for Dominica more effective, but in reality with a view to secure a most important naval station, close upon our shores. Samana has been taken possession of by the French, by whom, it is stated, it is to be held as a naval station. And its positien is such, that it will enable France to keep an eye upon our commerce, and, in the event of war, facilitate hostile movements against our shores. And this is the result of negro-phobia—of Slavery domination—of pro-slavery diplomacy—of the base policy which we have pursued towards that important island.

records.summary_en: The *Wilmington Journal* reported on December 24, 1852, that the Dominican Republic had long sought French protection and offered annexation, a step the current French Emperor was taking to secure a strategic point for monitoring American movements regarding Cuba under existing treaties. The newspaper contrasted the history of the former Spanish portion—which achieved independence without a servile insurrection and retained a white and mixed population superior in society and education—with the former French portion (Hayti), where a violent slave uprising had occurred.
records.summary_es: El *Wilmington Journal* comunicó el 24 de diciembre de 1852 que la República Dominicana procuró largamente el patronato de Francia y propuso su anexión, resolución que el actual soberano galo aprovechaba para guarecer un apostadero estratégico desde el cual observar las maniobras norteamericanas respecto a Cuba al amparo de las convenciones vigentes. El diario contrastaba los antecedentes de la antigua sección española —que conquistó su autonomía sin insurrecciones de esclavos y preservó un vecindario blanco y mestizo más encumbrado en cultura y letras— con la antigua colonia francesa (Haití), teatro de un sangriento levantamiento servil.

records.headline: The paper defends the Fillmore administration's mediation, arguing that the Monroe declaration was aimed at European colonization
records.summary_en: The paper defends the Fillmore administration's mediation, arguing that the Monroe declaration was aimed at European colonization and aggressive intervention, not at France and Great Britain cooperating with the United States to pacify Haiti. It says the Dominicans besought the mediating powers to protect them, and that the powers interfered only to shield a feeble community from destruction.

Dice que los dominicanos suplicaron a las potencias mediadoras que los protegieran, y que las potencias intervinieron solo para escudar a una comunidad débil de la destrucción.

records.headline: The Daily Union prints an item from the New Orleans Picayune
records.summary_en: The Daily Union prints an item from the New Orleans Picayune. It summarizes news from the Santiago newspaper Correo del Cibao. The Dominican journal denounces the licensing of cockpits in central Santiago as a remnant of barbarism and features theological debates between Catholic clergy and Protestant missionaries. A correspondent in the Dominican paper also complains of irregular postal deliveries and a serious lack of physicians in many towns. In addition, the Portuguese schooner Ceres was detained at Puerto Plata for alleged involvement in the slave trade and sent to Santo Domingo for judicial proceedings.
records.summary_es: The Daily Union publica una nota del New Orleans Picayune que resume noticias del periódico santiagués Correo del Cibao. El periódico dominicano denuncia la autorización de galleras en el centro de Santiago como un vestigio de barbarie y presenta debates teológicos entre el clero católico y misioneros protestantes. Un corresponsal en el diario dominicano también se queja de las entregas postales irregulares y de una grave falta de médicos en muchas localidades. Además, la goleta portuguesa Ceres fue detenida en Puerto Plata por presunta participación en la trata de esclavos y enviada a Santo Domingo para procedimientos judiciales.

records.headline: The National Intelligencer reprints a New York Commercial Advertiser report
records.summary_en: The National Intelligencer reprints a New York Commercial Advertiser report based on the arrival of the schooner Sarah Maria from Port-au-Prince. The dispatch notes that the vessel brings no intelligence regarding the election of the President of the Dominican Republic, whose Electoral College was appointed to convene on the first Monday in December. Furthermore, neither the vessel nor dispatches to the 30th ultimo from Santo Domingo by way of New Orleans mention any French seizure of the peninsula of Samaná.
records.summary_es: El National Intelligencer reproduce un informe del New York Commercial Advertiser basado en la llegada de la goleta Sarah Maria desde Puerto Príncipe. El despacho señala que la nave no trae noticias sobre la elección del presidente de la República Dominicana, cuyo Colegio Electoral debía reunirse el primer lunes de diciembre. Además, ni la embarcación ni los despachos del 30 del mes anterior desde Santo Domingo por la vía de Nueva Orleans mencionan toma francesa alguna de la península de Samaná.

records.headline: The Dominican Republic appears to have come under the protection of France
records.summary_en: The Dominican Republic appears to have come under the protection of France against Emperor Faustin Soulouque of Haiti, an article in the Eastern Times observes. The paper notes that a French naval depot has been established at the Dominican port of Samaná, affording an advantageous position to observe Cuban developments. The editorial expresses surprise that France, having recently replaced its own republic with an imperial regime, would protect a West Indian republic whose inhabitants have previously demonstrated their ability to defend themselves.
records.summary_es: Un artículo en el Eastern Times observa que Francia parece haber asumido la protección de la República Dominicana frente al emperador Faustin Soulouque de Haití. El periódico señala que se ha establecido un depósito naval francés en el puerto dominicano de Samaná, lo que brinda una posición ventajosa para observar los acontecimientos en Cuba. El editorial expresa sorpresa de que Francia, habiendo sustituido recientemente su propia república por un régimen imperial, proteja a una república antillana cuyos habitantes han demostrado anteriormente su capacidad para defenderse por sí mismos.

records.headline: The Liberator denounces an unnamed New York filibustering newspaper
records.summary_en: The Liberator denounces an unnamed New York filibustering newspaper for endorsing Duff Green's project of colonizing the "Republic of Dominica" with armed emigrants under the guise of protection. Quoting the rival editor, William Lloyd Garrison's paper highlights the argument that because Washington never recognized Haiti, its citizens are outlaws whom armed American companies may rightfully dispossess by seizing the empire portion of the island. The editorial condemns the writer as an unmasked villain and scoundrel while warning against such predatory schemes of national robbery.
records.summary_es: The Liberator denuncia a un periódico filibustero no identificado de Nueva York por respaldar el proyecto de Duff Green de colonizar la «República de Dominica» con emigrantes armados bajo el pretexto de protección. Al citar al editor rival, el periódico de William Lloyd Garrison destaca el argumento de que, como Washington nunca reconoció a Haití, sus ciudadanos son forajidos a quienes las compañías armadas estadounidenses pueden legítimamente despojar apoderándose de la porción imperial de la isla. El editorial condena al autor como un villano y canalla confeso, al tiempo que advierte contra tales planes predatorios de despojo nacional.

The ongoing truce was attributed in part to the depletion of the Haitian treasury following Soulouque’s lavish coronation ceremonies. Un observador, el comisionado Walsh, dedujo que la independencia dominicana sólo podría asegurarse a la postre por la vía de las armas contra Haití.

records.headline: Past diplomatic negotiations between France and the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: Past diplomatic negotiations between France and the Dominican Republic are recounted in a French newspaper report translated by The Texas Republican. According to the article, protracted negotiations resulted in a treaty drafted in December 1843 to establish French protection over the emerging state. The reported terms bound France to support Dominican independence, required the Dominican Republic to cede the peninsula of Samaná for a permanent French establishment, and made the French governor of Samaná the representative of the protectorate. The paper adds that the agreement was accepted by Ferdinand Barrot and supported by the French naval squadron.
records.summary_es: The Texas Republican traduce un informe de un periódico francés que relata negociaciones diplomáticas pasadas entre Francia y la República Dominicana. Según el artículo, prolongadas negociaciones dieron como resultado un tratado redactado en diciembre de 1843 para establecer la protección francesa sobre el naciente Estado. Los términos consignados obligaban a Francia a respaldar la independencia dominicana, requerían que la República Dominicana cediera la península de Samaná para un establecimiento francés permanente y convertían al gobernador francés de Samaná en el representante del protectorado. El periódico añade que el acuerdo fue aceptado por Ferdinand Barrot y respaldado por la escuadra naval francesa.

records.headline: Under the heading "France and St. Domingo," the Tribune translates
records.summary_en: Under the heading "France and St. Domingo," the Tribune translates an article from the Courrier du Havre responding to American and British complaints over rumored French designs on Samaná. The French paper questions Anglo-American objections to foreign acquisitions and provides historical context regarding Dominican independence. The account states that during the 1844 independence movement against Haitian rule, Dominican leader Pedro Santana sought a foreign protector and turned to France, initiating long and difficult negotiations with a hesitant French cabinet.
records.summary_es: Bajo el encabezado «Francia y Santo Domingo», el Tribune traduce un artículo del Courrier du Havre que responde a las quejas estadounidenses y británicas sobre supuestos planes franceses en Samaná. El diario francés cuestiona las objeciones angloamericanas a las adquisiciones extranjeras y aporta contexto histórico sobre la independencia dominicana. El relato afirma que durante el movimiento de independencia de 1844 contra el dominio haitiano, el líder dominicano Pedro Santana buscó un protector extranjero y recurrió a Francia, iniciando negociaciones largas y difíciles con un indeciso gabinete francés.

records.summary_en: On January 19, 1853, *The Republic* reported that Mr. Soulé submitted a resolution requesting the President to provide the Senate with State Department information concerning American citizens' claims against Hayti and correspondence from the 1849 special agent who reported on the condition of the Island of St. Domingo. The newspaper also noted that Mr. Brooke withdrew a resolution regarding the suspension of official relations with Nicaragua's minister for later introduction in Executive session. Additionally, the Senate considered Mr. Cass's joint resolutions reaffirming the Monroe Doctrine and applying it to Cuba.

La gaceta registró asimismo que el Sr. Brooke retiró una moción tendiente a interrumpir los lazos diplomáticos con el ministro de Nicaragua a fin de someterla en sesión secreta. El Senado atendió además las resoluciones conjuntas del senador Cass que revalidaban la Doctrina Monroe aplicándola a Cuba.

The article compared this French action to supporting South Carolina in seceding from the Federal Union and suggested that the Emperor of Hayti would be justified in considering the French debt cancelled if France does not disclaim the acts. records.summary_en: Letters from France dated in late November make no mention of a pretended occupation of Saint Domingo, noting instead that French vessels were stationed at Port-au-Prince to watch Soulouque's movements. The report also states that no peace treaty has been signed between the Dominican Republic and the Haytian Empire, raising expectations that hostilities would resume following the expiration of the armistice. Additionally, M. Max. Raybaud's May mission as French Plenipotentiary was to sign a Treaty of Commerce and Navigation with the Dominican Republic, which has now been ratified.

Por lo demás, la misión de mayo de M. Max Raybaud como plenipotenciario consistió en suscribir un Tratado de Comercio y Navegación con la República Dominicana, el cual quedó ratificado.

records.summary_en: Based on the provided excerpt, *The Nevada journal* reported that while diplomatic relations might not be established with Hayti, a serious question would arise for the United States if France should reclaim possession of the island of St. Domingo. Additionally, the *Charleston Mercury* and other Southern papers opposed the acquisition of Cuba, arguing it would ultimately reduce Cuba to the social and industrial condition of St. Domingo.

records.headline: From Our Paris Correspondent.
records.summary_en: The *Daily National Intelligencer* reported on foreign newspaper discussions regarding rumored French acquisitions, specifically the alleged occupation of the Samana peninsula by French forces and a possible French protectorate over the Dominican Republic. French sources, such as *La Patrie* and the *Journal des Débats*, dismissed reports of a territorial seizure, attributing the presence of the French frigate *la Sibylle* to a routine cruise following an epidemic in Martinique. Additionally, the *Journal des Débats* recalled that a decade prior, the Dominican Republic had offered a protectorate to Louis Philippe to protect against western neighbors, which was interrupted by the 1848 revolution.
records.summary_es: El *Daily National Intelligencer* resumió el debate en diarios del exterior respecto a supuestas anexiones francesas, singularmente la alegada ocupación de la península de Samaná por destacamentos galos y un previsible protectorado sobre la República Dominicana. Fuentes de prensa francesas como *La Patrie* y el *Journal des Débats* descartaron una usurpación de tierras, explicando que la navegación de la fragata gala *la Sibylle* obedecía a un crucero ordinario tras una epidemia sufrida en Martinica. El *Journal des Débats* rememoró además que diez años atrás la República Dominicana brindó el protectorado a Luis Felipe para guarecerse de sus convecinos occidentales, proyecto truncado por la revolución de 1848.

This curious note was elicited by the evident sensation produced in the political circles (if there can be said to be political circles now in France) by the appearance of a pamphlet entitled Limites de la France, the object of which was to indicate the tendency of the new Government to total conquest, or at least the absorption of all nations and fractions of nations west of the Alps and the Rhine. Sensation becoming so deep, the pamphlet in question was really intended to indicate the line of policy intended to sound public opinion upon the subject. The Government, soliciting this impression, and innocent of preparing, seeing that its silence was being interpreted in a manner dangerous, deemed it best—as Government is bound to do under such circumstances—instantly did, what it had formerly done in relation to the pamphlet which preceded the Empire, and which was used under its cover for the preparation of the empire; and what it did, not with regard to a compromising document upon Swiss affairs, published by a member of the Government, came out and repudiated all connection with the document, in the Moniteur of yesterday, the 5th of January, in the French, following and satisfactory terms:
"There have appeared recently several works, one among others under a title which seems calculated to excite—they seem to be intended to flatter tendencies which are supposed to exist in the French nation. The Moniteur repels all connection with the authors of these works, of which the spirit is as far removed from the intentions of the Emperor as from his loudly-declared policy."
After this, it is to be hoped that the most suspicious and incredulous as to the origin and intent of Limites de la France will submit his error, and abandon his apprehensions. To be sure, the Empire has come, as predicted by the pamphleteers of two and three years ago, and the said pamphleteers are now high in imperial favor. But that I don't pretend to be any thing more than a remarkable coincidence, which if I were a French writer it would be very indiscreet to remark upon. To be sure, the document on Swiss affairs, of which the existence was so positively denied, was afterwards published, in totidem verbis. That was certainly unlucky; but it does not authorize the suspicion, and still less the plain charge, that the disclaimer above quoted from the Moniteur is not irreproachably sincere and correct.
Extraordinary movement in the high functionary world has taken place in France upon the occasion of the new year. A decree of the 31st December nominated thirty-three new Senators. This body may now consist of 150 members, besides the ex-officio members, i. e. the French princes, the cardinals, marshals, and admirals of France. Six seats, original creation, by the decree of 1852, still remain, therefore, yet unfilled, in order to complete the Senate, forty-four nominations to make. These will doubtlessly be held back, only to be used to reward possible future exigencies. I must mention some of the names of the new Senators. The MARQUIS DE DAMPIN, the MARQUIS DE LAROCHEJAQUELIN, and the DUKE DE MOUCHY. These are three Legitimists, who have rallied to the Empire. In the Senate, M. DUPIN (ainé) has been replaced by Henry V. upon whom they wished to impose their own peculiar views as to the political course he should pursue. Legitimism has lost almost from history one of its most illustrious names, which he inherited, coming with all the luster that approved devotion to a principle, loyal fidelity to the King, and chivalric heroism could cast upon it, of which he never had any thing to bestow upon a cause, but which he has to-day honored by the connection with it in his person of the Senatorial dignity under an imperial Bonaparte. We have also M. DE HEECKEREN, late Baron DE ANTHES. This is the person who went to England to arrange Sir HUDSON LOWE after the death of Napoleon I, and who went to Russia, who was so grossly and publicly insulted the keeper of the Emperor. Beside these three, we have in the Senate three names of note: then M. FIALIN DE PERSIGNY, the devoted Minister of Louis Napoleon on 2d December, 1851; CLARY; SANTOUR DE LA TRESSONIER; MARSHAL VAILLANT; LUGUI; LUCIEN BONAPARTE, cousin of the Emperor Napoleon III, and son of Lucien Bonaparte; the DUKE DE BASSANO, and TASSCHER DE LA PAGERIE, cousin of the Empress.
The military enterprise of Count G. DE RAOUSSET-BOULBON in Northern Mexico, has, as might be expected, excite here a marked interest. The Paris papers give a large share in their columns to the latest news from the scene of operations. The Assemblée Nationale publishes the following letter from the French adventurer, written, it would seem, when just upon the eve of starting upon his expedition. If it has not yet appeared in print in the United States, it will be read with interest:
"I have for a year devoted my whole life, all my resources, all my exertions to the realization of a colossal enterprise, one of the boldest which has been witnessed for a long time. I have fully succeeded in my combinations, and I am now about to put my projects into execution. I start with two hundred men, adventurous, resolute, and full of faith. I shall find reinforcements in the country. I have foot soldiers, horsemen, and cannon, and I am about to put my project into execution..."
The Moniteur, among its foreign items, has merely stated the fact of the conquest of Count RAOUSSET-BOULBON—but the semi-official comments, in a tone, however, which would indicate a thorough consciousness of the danger of the ground they were treading on, and of the immenseness of collision with the United States, if this Government should give the slightest intimation of an intention to profit by the victory of the French band of adventurers in Northern Mexico, for the establishment of "a nascent colony" or by asserting the protectorate of an independent State upon the North American continent or on the borders of the United States. But I apprehend no such result. Whatever may be his personal instincts, by those of a victorious, NAPOLEON III. will seek other vent for his lust of enlarged dominion. He meditates other conquests; for the success of which he desires, IF NOT WINS THE AID, AT LEAST THE NEUTRALITY OF THE UNITED STATES. He is conscious, moreover, of many reasons not to provoke us by assuming a sovereignty or a protectorate in defiance with the policy loudly proclaimed by the United States for the last thirty years, and which no European State has dared to contest for the space of even one year. The Count, would-be imitator of Cortez, must therefore, in spite of himself, remain a buccaneer with the products of his enterprise, unless the Mexicans should succeed in repelling him, or unless we should nip his "nascent" glories in the bud by purchase from Santa Anna, and Santa Anna should not succeed to become a citizen of our Republic, or seek his ancient leader, Santa Anna, to the conquest of yet another province from Mexico. The Constitutionnel, I say, in putting allusions to the same subject, before summing up her article, as follows: "This column, which left California to seek its fortune in Mexico, is acting, be it well understood, on its own account, on its own risk and responsibility. It is a romantic episode, but one of an exclusively private character, to which, as between State and State, no importance attaches except as a matter of curiosity. It is strictly for the satisfaction of that word which we borrow from the Courrier des Etats Unis all the new details with which here column is filled..."
This Journal, I remember, has found phrases much less academic than "romantic episode," "column of adventurous spirit," "enterprising spirit," when it attempted to stigmatize the very similar, and certainly equally excuseable, invasions of American citizens into neighboring countries by citizens of our own "enterprising" population. Far be it from me to justify or even to palliate those invasions; but I dislike to see France engaging in these culpable adventures. The French journals have found no terms too severe by which to stigmatize them. I only insist that equal justice be rendered to all, and that an act be not qualified as enterprising, admirable, romantic, chivalrous, or heroic, when it happens to be French or American origin.
The occupation of Samana, in the Dominican Republic, by a portion of the French fleet in the West Indies, has been matter of lively interest here during the last week. What appeared in the official Journal, but—we well understand—La Patrie, a more or less semi-official sheet, thus explains the fact, which it seems has been sadly exaggerated and misinterpreted in the United States. It would certainly add something to the value of this explanation if it had appeared in the official journal; but we well understand how the official would seem not too anxious to show that this Government has avoided interference with the well-known American policy touching European acquisitions of territory or influence on our side of the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. La Patrie would have hardly ventured the following explanation of the Samana affairs if it were not true:
"English and American papers speak of an occupation by the French forces of the peninsula Samana. This news is like all those of the same sort (a very profound invention of the same sort), destitute of all foundation. A mark that the French semi-official) which many foreign sheets, and among them those of the United States, have given to the corvette La Silphide, which had remained in the West Indies, had no other purpose than a change of air. It proceeded upon a cruise in the seas of the Dominican Republic to give a passage to the French Consul, who had previously requested to report upon the news given to him in that country."
The Journal des Débats, alluding to the same report, had previously rated as quite unworthy of credit the supposition that the French Government had seized upon, with intention to appropriate, the eastern portion of the Island or St. Domingo; but regarded as at any rate less improbable than the news that Louis III. had accepted the protectorate of the Dominican Republic. And it calls to mind, in this connection, the fact that ten years ago the Republic offered the protectorate to Louis Philippe, in order to secure it from hostile invasion by its neighbors of the West end. Before Louis Philippe had positively accepted or refused the protectorate, a revolution broke out in Paris and led to negotiations. They were afterwards renewed, and the proposition was finally rejected by France under the Republic. It was apprehended that NAPOLEON III, so solicitous to increase the influence, and especially the maritime force of France in the West Indies, had reviewed and reversed the decision of the statesmen of the Republic. But I feel sure that NAPOLEON III. will commit no such folly; that he has too lively a sense of the "reproach of humiliation and effacement," which he says rests upon France, to seek glory for her at St. Domingo, when opportunities near home, of more facile execution, of better promise; opportunities in which he would be better supported by the strong national instincts, by the fierce, inextinguishable antipathies of his subjects, than he would be were he to throw down his glove to the young giant of America. Selfish, doubtless, and unjust those instincts and evoke those antipathies, and it will require the supreme efforts of all Europe to stay the deluge which may be made to pour upon it from France. A war with the United States would not stir up in France and array for action those terrible elements which would constitute the force of NAPOLEON III, and make him almost invincible if he sagaciously chooses the moment and the occasion for foreign war. records.headline: The Weekly National Intelligencer cites French press accounts
records.summary_en: The Weekly National Intelligencer cites French press accounts explaining naval movements that sparked American rumors regarding the occupation of Samaná. According to the semi-official paper La Patrie, the frigate La Sibylle left Martinique after an epidemic merely to cruise the Antilles for crew health, and its appearance in Dominican waters generated false reports of military occupation. Meanwhile, the Journal des Débats dismissed reports that France seized the eastern part of the island, though it deemed a French protectorate over the Dominican Republic plausible. The Débats recalled that the republic previously offered Louis Philippe the protectorate before the 1848 revolution intervened.
records.summary_es: El Weekly National Intelligencer cita reseñas de la prensa francesa que explican movimientos navales que suscitaron rumores en los Estados Unidos sobre la ocupación de Samaná. Según el diario semioficial La Patrie, la fragata La Sibylle abandonó Martinica tras una epidemia simplemente para realizar un crucero por las Antillas por la salud de su tripulación, y su presencia en aguas dominicanas generó falsos reportes de ocupación militar. En tanto, el Journal des Débats desestimó que Francia se hubiera apoderado de la parte oriental de la isla, si bien consideró verosímil un protectorado francés sobre la República Dominicana. El Débats recordó que la república había ofrecido anteriormente el protectorado a Luis Felipe antes de que sobreviniera la revolución de 1848.

records.headline: The Daily Union comments that Dominican offers of a protectorate
records.summary_en: The Daily Union comments that Dominican offers of a protectorate, previously rejected by King Louis Philippe and the Second Republic, have been renewed to Emperor Napoleon III with greater prospects of acceptance. The paper reprints an extract from the Congressional Globe copying a Kingston letter to the Courrier des États-Unis that welcomes French protection over the Dominican Republic. The correspondent argues that French control would safeguard Cuba from American filibusters and shield the fertile eastern part of the island against aggressive Haitian incursions, urging the French Empire to accept what earlier governments declined.
records.summary_es: The Daily Union comenta que los ofrecimientos dominicanos de un protectorado, previamente rechazados por el rey Luis Felipe y la Segunda República, han sido renovados ante el emperador Napoleón III con mayores probabilidades de aceptación. El diario reproduce un extracto del Congressional Globe que copia una carta de Kingston dirigida al Courrier des États-Unis que celebra la protección francesa sobre la República Dominicana. El corresponsal sostiene que el control francés resguardaría a Cuba de los filibusteros estadounidenses y protegería la fértil parte oriental de la isla frente a agresivas incursiones haitianas, instando al Imperio francés a aceptar lo que gobiernos anteriores declinaron.

records.headline: A Paris correspondent examines a French press article arguing that France had missed chances to extend its influence
records.summary_en: A Paris correspondent examines a French press article arguing that France had missed chances to extend its influence in America. The article says the peninsula of Samana and the whole Dominican Republic were offered to the French government in exchange for its flag and protection, and the correspondent suspects Napoleon III is now seriously considering a larger French role in America.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal en París examina un artículo de la prensa francesa que sostiene que Francia había perdido oportunidades de extender su influencia en América. El artículo dice que la península de Samaná y toda la República Dominicana fueron ofrecidas al gobierno francés a cambio de su bandera y su protección, y el corresponsal sospecha que Napoleón III está considerando ahora seriamente un papel francés mayor en América.

records.headline: The National Intelligencer publishes a translation of a French essay
records.summary_en: The National Intelligencer publishes a translation of a French essay discussing the expansion of French influence in the Americas. The writer recalls that the peninsula of Samaná and the entire Dominican Republic were previously offered to the French government in exchange for its flag and naval protection. The author explains that this proposal was rejected not because of Spanish or British opposition, but because of parliamentary timidity and opposition within the French Chambers under earlier regimes. Under the Empire, the essay concludes, the French government is finally liberated from legislative indecision.
records.summary_es: El National Intelligencer publica la traducción de un ensayo francés que examina la expansión de la influencia francesa en las Américas. El autor recuerda que la península de Samaná y toda la República Dominicana fueron ofrecidas anteriormente al gobierno francés a cambio de su bandera y protección naval. El texto explica que esta propuesta fue rechazada no por oposición española o británica, sino por la timidez parlamentaria y la resistencia de las Cámaras francesas bajo regímenes anteriores. Bajo el Imperio, concluye el ensayo, el gobierno francés se encuentra finalmente liberado de la indecisión legislativa.

records.headline: An editorial in the National Era censures American diplomacy
records.summary_en: An editorial in the National Era censures American diplomacy for interfering as a partisan in Hispaniola to resist Haitian supremacy while disregarding the Monroe Doctrine. The paper argues that Washington's policy achieved nothing—gaining neither a foothold in "Dominica," nor the favor of the Dominican government, nor colonial opportunities in that white republic, while opening the door to French influence at Samaná. The editorial then quotes a paragraph from the National Intelligencer reporting the arrival of the Spanish steamer Isabel II at Havana from Santo Domingo, where the vessel was warmly received, confirming that rumors of Samaná's cession to France were unfounded.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en el National Era censura a la diplomacia estadounidense por intervenir como partidaria en La Española para oponerse a la supremacía haitiana, ignorando la doctrina Monroe. El periódico sostiene que la política de Washington no logró nada: no obtuvo ni un punto de apoyo en «Dominica», ni el favor del gobierno dominicano, ni oportunidades colonizadoras en esa república blanca, al tiempo que abrió la puerta a la influencia francesa en Samaná. Luego, el editorial cita un párrafo del National Intelligencer que reporta la llegada a La Habana del vapor español Isabel II procedente de Santo Domingo, donde fue recibido con entusiasmo, confirmando que los rumores de la cesión de Samaná a Francia carecían de fundamento.

records.summary_en: A vessel claimed as a prize by the Dominican government was declared piracy under republic laws, resulting in prison sentences of two years for the captain, mate, and pilot, and one year for the rest of the crew. Court proceedings revealed a questionable letter involving Senor Jose Maria Pando, the Spanish commercial agent at Curacao, regarding instructions and financial advances for the ship via a merchant in Porto Plata. Additionally, the Dominican Republic celebrated the February 15 inauguration of General Santana as president.
records.summary_es: Una embarcación apresada como presa de guerra por el gobierno dominicano fue condenada por piratería bajo el ordenamiento legal patrio, dictándose penas de dos años de prisión para el capitán, contramaestre y práctico, y un año para los restantes tripulantes. Las audiencias sacaron a luz una sospechosa misiva que comprometía a don José María Pando, agente comercial español en Curazao, tocante a instrucciones y adelantos de caudales girados al navío a través de un comerciante de Puerto Plata. Por su parte, la República Dominicana conmemoró con regocijo la asunción de mando del general Santana como mandatario el 15 de febrero.

records.headline: The Republic reports that the Archbishop of Santo Domingo was summoned
records.summary_en: The Republic reports that the Archbishop of Santo Domingo was summoned before the Dominican National Congress for refusing to take the required constitutional oath of fidelity. When the archbishop declared he preferred banishment over sanctioning a heretical constitution, President Pedro Santana furnished him with passports, placed a national ship at his disposal, and granted him four thousand dollars for travel expenses. Touched by this unexpected generosity, the prelate withdrew his refusal and agreed to swear allegiance. The president ordered the oath ceremony conducted with full religious pomp in the Cathedral, followed by a Te Deum across all churches.
records.summary_es: The Republic informa que el arzobispo de Santo Domingo fue citado ante el Congreso Nacional dominicano por negarse a prestar el juramento constitucional de fidelidad requerido. Cuando el arzobispo declaró que prefería el destierro antes que sancionar una constitución herética, el presidente Pedro Santana le entregó sus pasaportes, puso un buque nacional a su disposición y le otorgó cuatro mil dólares para gastos de viaje. Conmovido por esta inesperada generosidad, el prelado retiró su negativa y aceptó jurar lealtad. El presidente ordenó que la ceremonia de juramento se celebrara con toda la pompa religiosa en la Catedral, seguida de un Te Deum en todas las iglesias.

records.headline: The Watchman and Observer reports that Dominican President Pedro Santana summoned
records.summary_en: The Watchman and Observer reports that Dominican President Pedro Santana summoned Archbishop Don Tomás de Portes before the National Congress for ecclesiastical interference in civil functions. When called upon to swear allegiance, the prelate refused to take the oath to what he termed an accursed and heretical constitution, stating he would choose exile instead. President Santana promptly provided him with a passport, a national vessel, and $4,000 for his journey, though the archbishop subsequently reconsidered, took the constitutional oath, and was restored to his ecclesiastical duties.
records.summary_es: El Watchman and Observer informa que el presidente dominicano Pedro Santana citó al arzobispo don Tomás de Portes ante el Congreso Nacional por la intromisión eclesiástica en funciones civiles. Al ser llamado a jurar lealtad, el prelado se negó a prestar juramento a lo que denominó una constitución maldita y herética, afirmando que prefería el exilio. records.summary_en: The Hannibal Journal reports on a conflict in the Dominican Republic between President Pedro Santana and the Archbishop of Santo Domingo. The archbishop initially refused the oath of fealty, declaring he would rather accept exile than swear to a heretical constitution. Santana delivered him a passport, placed a government vessel at his disposal, and granted travel funds while insisting that the clergy remain separate from politics, prompting the ecclesiastic to submit to civil authority and swear fealty with ceremony on April 4.

records.full_text:
We have received files of El Progreso, published in Saint Domingo, extending up to the 1st of May. It seems that the Dominicans are making preparations for war, as it is feared that Soulouque might meditate an invasion of their territory. El Progreso says:—

Last week a vessel of war left our port for Azua, loaded with troops; and to-day another goes to the same destination, taking provisions for the army. The Dominican President had already left for that town, where he is organizing a powerful army, capable of supplying the northern frontiers with whatever may be necessary to repel an invasion. Up to the present, no hostile activity on the part of Hayti has been observed; but it is known that Soulouque has assembled a considerable force in the Canton of Maissade, and that a single caprice of the Emperor of Hayti, is sufficient to draw us into an unexpected conflict. Up to the present, the Dominicans have accepted the mediation of the three powers; but we want peace, not a truce, and if Hayti will not make peace, we feel confident that above all the conduct of the Liberator is guided by wisdom and prudence.

The most conclusive argument against force is force itself. We have, besides, an army in the field; and we should not, therefore, be surprised if our liberty is protected by our troops. In the mean time, a Spanish vessel of war, the Cortes, and an English vessel of war, the Cormorant, are in the Canton of Guayubin, as has been reported, to protect their respective subjects; but we are assured that, on the contrary, the intervention of the Spanish vessel, through its captain, has brought about a reconciliation between the two parties.

The Spanish brig of war, Veloz, under the command of Don Carlos Valcarcel, had arrived at Saint Domingo on the 26th of April, bringing on board the envoy of the President of the republic in the name of Her Catholic Majesty. On coming into port, the Veloz saluted the Dominican flag with twenty-one guns, which were returned by the fort. The Spanish captain and officers were received at the house of the President of the Republic with the highest honors, and were entertained at a banquet given in their honor.

On Sunday, the 17th of April, the ratification of the treaty of peace, navigation and commerce between France and the Dominican Republic was celebrated in Saint Domingo with great pomp. The day was announced by the firing of cannon and the ringing of the cathedral bells. Three high masses were celebrated in the cathedral, after each of which off went a broadside from the French vessel of war, Iphigenie, which was lying in port; after which the French flag was hoisted on the cathedral, and the French consul was received at the portal by the President of the Republic. In the evening a grand ball was given by the President, at which all the authorities, civil and military, were present. The festivities were concluded on the 18th, when the treaty was solemnly ratified with a salvo of twenty-one guns.

records.headline: From Santo Domingo.
records.summary_en: The *Port Gibson Reveille* reported the arrival of a Spanish brigantine under Don Carlos Valcarcel from Puerto Rico to congratulate the President of the Dominican Republic on behalf of her Catholic Majesty. Additionally, the newspaper covered the grand celebration in St. Domingo on Sunday, April 17, marking the ratification of a treaty between the French Empire and the Dominican Republic with music, fireworks, balloons representing friendly nations, and a solemn church service accompanied by military salutes.

El periódico reseñó asimismo las solemnidades cívicas celebradas en Santo Domingo el domingo 17 de abril para festejar la ratificación del tratado entre el Imperio francés y la República Dominicana, concurridas con acordes marciales, fuegos de artificio, globos alegóricos a potencias amigas y una misa de acción de gracias con salvas de ordenanza.

records.headline: In a congressional reply to President Baez, the Dominican Congress observes that his claim to leave the republic at peace
records.summary_en: In a congressional reply to President Baez, the Dominican Congress observes that his claim to leave the republic at peace with all the world except Haiti described precisely the state of the country when he entered the presidency. The Congress joins in joy at the solemn recognition of Dominican independence by England, France and Denmark and at the treaties of amity and commerce those powers had entered into with the republic.
records.summary_es: En una respuesta del Congreso al presidente Báez, el Congreso dominicano observa que su afirmación de dejar la república en paz con todo el mundo excepto Haití describía precisamente el estado del país cuando asumió la presidencia. El Congreso comparte la alegría por el solemne reconocimiento de la independencia dominicana por Inglaterra, Francia y Dinamarca y por los tratados de amistad y comercio que esas potencias habían celebrado con la república.

records.headline: The New York Herald publishes official documents brought to Boston
records.summary_en: The New York Herald publishes official documents brought to Boston from Santo Domingo aboard the schooner Arcturus. The papers include an executive decree issued under the national motto "God, Country and Liberty" by President Pedro Santana, General-in-Chief and Liberator of the Republic. The decree concerns offenses committed by Father Francisco Vionet, a Barcelona-born curate; while Santana affirms that such actions fall under ordinary judicial tribunals pursuant to the constitution and penal code, he defers to the Archbishop's request for executive clemency to avoid public scandal.
records.summary_es: El New York Herald publica documentos oficiales traídos a Boston desde Santo Domingo a bordo de la goleta Arcturus. Los papeles incluyen un decreto ejecutivo promulgado bajo el lema nacional «Dios, Patria y Libertad» por el presidente Pedro Santana, general en jefe y libertador de la República. El decreto se refiere a las faltas cometidas por el padre Francisco Vionet, cura oriundo de Barcelona; aunque Santana afirma que tales actos corresponden a los tribunales ordinarios conforme a la constitución y al código penal, acoge la solicitud del arzobispo de conceder clemencia ejecutiva para evitar el escándalo público.

records.headline: An article reprinted from the National Democrat in the Washington Sentinel highlights
records.summary_en: An article reprinted from the National Democrat in the Washington Sentinel highlights the geopolitical and commercial significance of Santo Domingo, situated at the nexus of major trade routes near Cuba and Jamaica. The piece rebukes the United States for maintaining an attitude of cruel indifference toward a country capable of providing immense wealth or serious political vexation. Describing the island as divided between a Black empire and a white republic, the article recounts how the Dominicans threw off Haitian oppression through heroic struggle. The author laments that Washington offered no assistance to the suffering republic during its contest for independence.
records.summary_es: Un artículo reproducido del National Democrat en el Washington Sentinel resalta la importancia geopolítica y comercial de Santo Domingo, situada en el nexo de las principales rutas comerciales cerca de Cuba y Jamaica. El escrito recrimina a los Estados Unidos por mantener una actitud de cruel indiferencia hacia un país capaz de proporcionar inmensas riquezas o graves complicaciones políticas. Al describir la isla como dividida entre un imperio negro y una república blanca, el artículo relata cómo los dominicanos se sacudieron la opresión haitiana mediante una lucha heroica. El autor lamenta que Washington no haya ofrecido auxilio a la sufrida república durante su contienda por la independencia.

records.headline: An editorial in the Daily Union highlights the ongoing dangers
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Daily Union highlights the ongoing dangers confronting the Dominican Republic from the neighboring Haitian empire. The paper asserts that European powers share an interest in aiding Haitian efforts to crush the Dominican republic and eliminate independent republican governance in the West Indies. Noting that the Dominican Republic is the only territory along this island perimeter aligned with American principles, the editorial argues that the safety and independence of "Dominica" represents a vital United States interest. The paper calls on Washington to offer protection, alliance, and formal recognition.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en el Daily Union destaca los continuos peligros que enfrenta la República Dominicana ante el vecino imperio haitiano. El diario sostiene que las potencias europeas tienen interés en respaldar los esfuerzos haitianos para aplastar a la república dominicana y eliminar el gobierno republicano independiente en las Antillas. Al advertir que la República Dominicana es el único territorio en ese perímetro insular afín a los principios estadounidenses, el editorial afirma que la seguridad y la independencia de «Dominica» representan un interés vital para los Estados Unidos. El periódico pide a Washington ofrecer protección, alianza y reconocimiento formal.

records.headline: The Richmond Enquirer quotes a New York Sun review of an article
records.summary_en: The Richmond Enquirer quotes a New York Sun review of an article in the New York paper La Verdad regarding the Dominican Republic. The piece contends that the United States government acts against its own interests by neglecting to cultivate a close alliance with its sister republic. According to the article, such an alliance would foster the extension of republican institutions throughout the island and thwart British-backed designs to "Africanize" the West Indian archipelago against the influence of the American republic.
records.summary_es: El Richmond Enquirer cita una reseña del New York Sun sobre un artículo publicado en el diario neoyorquino La Verdad en relación con la República Dominicana. El artículo sostiene que el gobierno de los Estados Unidos actúa en contra de sus propios intereses al descuidar el cultivo de una estrecha alianza con su república hermana. Según el texto, dicha alianza promovería la extensión de las instituciones republicanas por toda la isla y frustraría los planes auspiciados por los británicos para «africanizar» el archipiélago antillano en detrimento de la influencia de la república estadounidense.

records.headline: Reprinting an item from the New York Sun, the Weekly National Intelligencer notes
records.summary_en: Reprinting an item from the New York Sun, the Weekly National Intelligencer notes that a recent issue of La Verdad of New York contains an article examining the Republic of St. Domingo, its relations with the United States, and its position toward the Empire of Faustin I in Haiti. According to the report, the article argues that the U.S. government and people are neglecting their own interests by failing to foster their sister republic and form a closer alliance and community of interests with her. It points out that the rational result of such an alliance would be the extension of republican institutions over the Haitian portion of the island and the prevention of a British-protected scheme to "Africanize the Columbian Archipelago" as a bulwark against the spread of U.S. principles and institutions.
records.summary_es: Reproduciendo una nota del New York Sun, el Weekly National Intelligencer señala que un número reciente de La Verdad de Nueva York contiene un artículo que examina la República de Santo Domingo, sus relaciones con los Estados Unidos y su posición frente al Imperio de Faustin I en Haití. Según el informe, el artículo sostiene que el pueblo y el gobierno estadounidenses descuidan sus propios intereses al no fomentar a su república hermana ni procurar formar una alianza más estrecha y una comunidad de intereses con ella. Señala como resultado racional de dicha alianza la extensión de las instituciones republicanas sobre la parte haitiana de la isla y la prevención de un plan protegido por el gabinete británico para «africanizar el archipiélago colombino» como baluarte contra el avance de los principios e instituciones de los Estados Unidos.

It says the account ended with a truce said to be consolidating into peace.

Dice que el relato terminaba con una tregua que se consolidaba en paz.

records.headline: The New York Herald reports that after two French Haitians were expelled
records.summary_en: The New York Herald reports that after two French Haitians were expelled from the country, the French demanded that President General Santana dismiss his cabinet and appoint another more favorable to French interests. The article predicts that French intrigue may bring about Santana's downfall in January or February and reinstate ex-President Báez—whom it characterizes as thoroughly French in feeling and sentiment—as dictator. The paper asks whether the U.S. government will permit this violation of its professed principles and urges the cabinet in Washington to investigate and compel the French to desist if proved to be "filibustering with the Dominican republic." It adds that the greatest excitement prevailed in the City of St. Domingo on the 25th of the previous month.
records.summary_es: El New York Herald informa que, tras la expulsión de dos haitianos franceses del país, los franceses exigieron al presidente general Santana la destitución de su gabinete y el nombramiento de otro más acorde con los intereses franceses. El artículo pronostica que la intriga francesa podría provocar la caída de Santana en enero o febrero y restituir como dictador al expresidente Báez, a quien describe como completamente francés en sentimiento. El periódico pregunta si el gobierno de los Estados Unidos permitirá esta violación de sus principios profesados e insta al gabinete en Washington a investigar el asunto y obligar a los franceses a desistir si se demuestra que están «filibusteando con la República Dominicana». Añade que la mayor agitación reinaba en la ciudad de Santo Domingo el día 25 del mes anterior.

records.summary_en: A romantic history of Santo Domingo for American readers: Columbus and the first settlements, the massacres of the conquest era, and a recent fight in which Dominican horsemen under the white cross of Dominica repelled an attack by one of Soulouque's captains near the old chapel of Our Lady of Mercy.
records.summary_es: Una historia romántica de Santo Domingo para lectores estadounidenses: Colón y los primeros asentamientos, las masacres de la conquista y un combate reciente en que jinetes dominicanos, bajo la cruz blanca de Dominica, rechazaron el ataque de un capitán de Soulouque cerca de la antigua capilla de Nuestra Señora de la Merced.
records.passage: Still later, when Santana, the Liberator, unfurled the flag of Dominican independence, a party of negroes, led by one of Soulouque's black captains, attacked the neighboring village, with the war-cry of "death to the whites." This ominous cry, which has so often carried terror and destruction to the whites of eastern Hayti, sent the frightened inhabitants to the mountain dells for refuge, but as they fled they were met near the ruined church by a little band of horsemen, coming to their rescue. The young leader unfurled the white cross of Dominica under the light of their blazing homes, and rallied them to battle in their own defence. It was a deadly, desperate strife. They were not many, but they fought hand to hand with all the cherished bitterness of hostile races, until the morning — the glorious, gorgeous morning of the tropics — dawned on the field, and revealed the victory of the whites. Seventeen white men lay dead or wounded, but among them more than thrice their number of blacks, and they were dressed for burial, and the last rights were paid them close beside the ancient church of the palm grove, where the last princess of the red men had been treacherously slain by the Spaniards, where the children of the Spaniards had been savagely murdered by the Africans. There the children of the Africans had also paid the blood-penalty of their own and their father's deeds. This last act of this retributive drama of races is a late occurrence.
