records.headline: An editorial in the New York Herald argues that a reply in La Patrie fully
records.summary_en: An editorial in the New York Herald argues that a reply in La Patrie fully confirmed the impression that France contemplated serious steps against the independence of the Dominican Republic. According to the Herald, La Patrie passed over in silence the specific charges made by the Herald's correspondent and instead claimed that the inhabitants of St. Domingo had frequently demanded annexation to France or a French protectorate. The Herald counters that M. Mouttet conveniently omitted that those demands were made under the direct influence of ex-President Báez, a partisan of French interests who was subsequently expelled from the island for his anti-national tendencies. The editorial concludes that the object of the French hostile demonstration was to restore Báez and establish a French protectorate, which aroused indignation among the Dominican people.
records.summary_es: Un editorial del New York Herald sostiene que una respuesta publicada en La Patrie confirmó plenamente la impresión de que Francia contemplaba medidas graves contra la independencia de la República Dominicana. Según el Herald, La Patrie guardó silencio sobre las acusaciones específicas formuladas por el corresponsal del Herald y, en cambio, afirmó que los habitantes de Santo Domingo habían solicitado con frecuencia la anexión a Francia o un protectorado francés. El Herald replica que a M. Mouttet no le convino añadir que dichas demandas se hicieron bajo la influencia directa del expresidente Báez, partidario de los intereses franceses que posteriormente fue expulsado de la isla por sus tendencias antinacionales. El editorial concluye que el objeto de la demostración hostil francesa era restaurar a Báez y establecer un protectorado francés, lo cual despertó indignación entre el pueblo dominicano.

records.headline: Reporting from Santo Domingo newspaper files up to February 18
records.summary_en: Reporting from Santo Domingo newspaper files up to February 18, the New York Herald states that the Constituent Assembly was in session and spiritedly debating proposed constitutional amendments drafted by a select committee. Citing El Orden, the paper notes that Andrés Aybar, Alcalde of the capital, has undertaken vigorous municipal reforms in San Domingo, including the immediate construction of an extensive market house. Additionally, the Santo Domingo papers announce the death on January 23 of José Joaquín Delmonte at the age of eighty-four, noting that he devoted sixty-two years to public service and most recently served as President of the Supreme Court of Justice in the republic.
records.summary_es: Informando a partir de periódicos de Santo Domingo hasta el 18 de febrero, el New York Herald señala que la Asamblea Constituyente se encontraba en sesión y debatía animadamente varias enmiendas constitucionales propuestas y redactadas por una comisión selecta. Citando a El Orden, el diario indica que Andrés Aybar, alcalde de la capital, ha emprendido vigorosas reformas municipales en Santo Domingo, entre ellas la construcción inmediata de un amplio mercado. Asimismo, los periódicos anuncian el fallecimiento, el 23 de enero, de José Joaquín Delmonte a los ochenta y cuatro años de edad, destacando que dedicó sesenta y dos años al servicio público y que su último cargo fue el de presidente de la Suprema Corte de Justicia de la república.

records.summary_en: According to the *New-York daily tribune* on April 21, 1854, martial law was declared in Santiago following a conspiracy, with five ringleaders before the court and over forty persons under arrest. Meanwhile, the revision of the Dominican Constitution was completed, featuring an increased number of representatives and senators, the creation of a vice president, and changes reducing the naturalization time periods required for foreigners to become eligible as representatives and senators. Additionally, while the standard presidential and vice-presidential term was set at four years, actual President General Santana was granted two terms in office, allowing him to hold the chair until February 1861.
records.summary_es: Con arreglo al *New-York daily tribune* del 21 de abril de 1854, se declaró el estado de sitio en Santiago a raíz de una conspiración, encausándose ante los jueces a cinco cabecillas y permaneciendo más de cuarenta sujetos en prisión. Entre tanto, concluyó la reforma de la Constitución dominicana, elevándose la representación en el cuerpo legislativo con mayor número de diputados y senadores, estableciéndose la magistratura de vicepresidente y abreviándose los plazos de avecindamiento para que los forasteros optasen a ser elegidos representantes y senadores. Asimismo, fijándose en cuatro años el mandato ordinario del presidente y vicepresidente, al actual mandatario, general Santana, se le concedieron dos períodos sucesivos, autorizándosele a regir la presidencia hasta febrero de 1861.

records.headline: An editorial in the Washington Sentinel criticizes the failure of the United States
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Washington Sentinel criticizes the failure of the United States to recognize the independence of the Dominican Republic. Recounting twenty-two years of Haitian rule over the Spanish portion of the island of Santo Domingo, the paper states that the sons of the colonists in the plains of Seybo and Vega rose under Pedro Santana, fought three or four decisive battles, and drove Soulouque and his forces back to the west, where they have been kept for ten consecutive years. Having maintained the Dominican Republic under a liberal constitution, the Dominicans ask the United States for the moral aid of friendly recognition as what the paper calls the only free white self-governing American state in the West Indies. The editorial laments that after nine years this request remains unanswered, neglecting an opportunity to bring the republic into the American system as a center of resistance to the European policy of "Africanizing" the islands.
records.summary_es: Un editorial del Washington Sentinel critica la negativa de los Estados Unidos a reconocer la independencia de la República Dominicana. Al relatar veintidós años de dominio haitiano sobre la parte española de la isla de Santo Domingo, el periódico afirma que los hijos de los colonos en las llanuras de El Seibo y La Vega se levantaron bajo el mando de Pedro Santana, libraron tres o cuatro batallas decisivas y rechazaron a Soulouque y sus fuerzas hacia el oeste, donde han sido contenidos durante diez años consecutivos. Habiendo mantenido la República Dominicana bajo una constitución liberal, los dominicanos solicitan a los Estados Unidos el apoyo moral de un reconocimiento amistoso para lo que el diario denomina el único Estado americano libre, blanco y autónomo en las Antillas. El editorial lamenta que, al cabo de nueve años, esta solicitud siga sin respuesta, desaprovechando la oportunidad de integrar la república al sistema americano como núcleo de resistencia frente a la política europea de «africanizar» las islas.

records.headline: An editorial in the Washington Sentinel argues that the Dominicans
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Washington Sentinel argues that the Dominicans, having established their republic and defended their territory from the Haitian government at the west end of the island for ten years, are entitled to U.S. recognition by all rules of international comity. The paper contends that "Dominica" is already forced to contend with Haiti as directed by the diplomacy of France and England, and that U.S. passivity and refusal to distinguish the Dominican Republic from Haiti aids European aims in the West Indies. It concludes that the mere act of acknowledging the Dominican Republic and establishing diplomatic relations with her would save the country from European machinations and preserve a valuable state for the American system.
records.summary_es: Un editorial del Washington Sentinel sostiene que los dominicanos, tras haber establecido su república y defendido su territorio frente al gobierno haitiano en el extremo occidental de la isla durante diez años, tienen derecho al reconocimiento de los Estados Unidos según todas las normas de cortesía internacional. El periódico argumenta que «Dominica» ya se ve obligada a enfrentarse a Haití bajo la dirección de la diplomacia de Francia e Inglaterra, y que la pasividad estadounidense y su negativa a distinguir a la República Dominicana de Haití favorecen los propósitos europeos en las Antillas. Concluye que el solo acto de reconocer a la República Dominicana y establecer relaciones diplomáticas con ella salvaría al país de las maquinaciones de Europa y preservaría un Estado valioso para el sistema americano.

records.headline: Reprinting a New York Herald dispatch dated April 28 at the City of St. Domingo
records.summary_en: Reprinting a New York Herald dispatch dated April 28 at the City of St. Domingo, the Lynchburg Daily Virginian reports reliable news that Emperor Soulouque has forty thousand men ready to march into the Dominican Republic to exterminate the whites and mulattoes. According to the correspondent, the Dominicans are making active preparations to receive him, though it has been discovered that the cannonballs purchased for their warships are too large for the guns and that they lack both seamen and commanders. Nevertheless, the writer remarks that this makes no difference because the Dominicans rely on close combat against the Haitians and are always victorious.
records.summary_es: Reproduciendo un despacho del New York Herald del 28 de abril en la ciudad de Santo Domingo, el Lynchburg Daily Virginian informa de noticias fidedignas según las cuales el emperador Soulouque tiene listos cuarenta mil hombres para marchar hacia la República Dominicana a fin de exterminar a los blancos y mulatos. Según el corresponsal, los dominicanos realizan activos preparativos para recibirlo, aunque se ha descubierto que las balas compradas para sus buques de guerra son demasiado grandes para los cañones y que carecen tanto de marineros como de comandantes. No obstante, el autor señala que esto no importa porque los dominicanos confían en el combate cuerpo a cuerpo contra los haitianos y siempre resultan victoriosos.

records.headline: A contributor in the New-York Daily Tribune criticizes the Post
records.summary_en: A contributor in the New-York Daily Tribune criticizes the Post for treating the Dominican Republic—described as independent and self-sustaining for ten years—as revolted subjects of Haiti, and disputes the claim that "Dominica" is no less a Black government than Haiti or Liberia. The writer asserts that the President, the entire Cabinet, and all other high officials of the Dominican government whom the writer has met were white gentlemen, except for one naval officer of maternal Indigenous descent. The letter further contrasts the two nations, stating that the Dominicans maintain a liberal, progressive republic where foreigners may hold property and enjoy freedom of religious worship, whereas Haiti excludes white citizens under a harsh "Czarism." Finally, the writer denies that General Pierce or his administration have engaged in any intrigue regarding the young republic.
records.summary_es: Un colaborador del New-York Daily Tribune critica al Post por tratar a la República Dominicana —descrita como independiente y autosuficiente durante diez años— como súbditos sublevados de Haití, y refuta la afirmación de que «Dominica» no sea menos un gobierno negro que Haití o Liberia. El autor asegura que el presidente, todo el gabinete y todos los demás altos funcionarios del gobierno dominicano que ha conocido eran caballeros blancos, con la excepción de un oficial naval de ascendencia indígena por línea materna. Asimismo, la carta contrasta a ambas naciones, señalando que los dominicanos mantienen una república liberal y progresista donde los extranjeros pueden poseer propiedades y gozar de libertad de culto religioso, mientras que Haití excluye a los ciudadanos blancos bajo un severo «zarismo». Por último, el autor niega que el general Pierce o su administración hayan participado en intriga alguna respecto a la joven república.

records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* reported that a publication named the *Post* glossed over and justified the savage acts committed during Faustin Soulouque's invasion of the Dominican Republic, while suppressing his defeat at Las Carracas by General Santana. The *Post* criticized President Fillmore's dispatch of Mr. Walsh to prevent Soulouque from renewing attacks on Dominican territory and congratulated itself on publishing the affair to make the U.S. government appear to disadvantage.
records.summary_es: El *New York Herald* censuró que una publicación denominada el *Post* atenuara y justificara las crueldades perpetradas durante la invasión de Faustino Soulouque contra la República Dominicana, silenciando su aplastante descalabro en Las Carreras a manos del general Santana. El *Post* reprobaba el envío del comisionado Walsh por el presidente Fillmore para atajar nuevas agresiones de Soulouque sobre suelo dominicano, ufanándose de haber sacado a la luz los trámites para menoscabar la reputación del gobierno de Washington.

records.full_text:
TO THE EDITOR OF THE NEW YORK HERALD.

The Evening Post, in an article so maliciously and contemptibly false that it could not possibly be written by a gentleman, and to which no gentleman would condescend a written answer, accuses me of playing a very secondary part in what he calls the "St. Domingo intrigue." My whole course in the matter of a Dominican treaty, from the first moment of her revolution to and since annexation, will answer for me; nor did I ever speak or think of influencing any man's party or acting on any man's dictation.

By one accident, has happened one truth: I do feel a deep sympathy for the brave Dominicans, and I shall not be driven by the tricks of any anti-American clique, or partisan who prostitute their cause until the Dominican republic obtains its deserved and honored place in the family of free American States. I protest against the insolence of the Post in abandoning my principles whenever the popular tide sets against them, or fleeing my colors from newspaper warfare.

I could not descend to reply to the Post—for my way—but it is my duty as an American citizen to throw light on the subject of the Dominican treaty.

I charge the New York Evening Post with working—at standard prices—for His Imperial Majesty Faustin I., Emperor of Hayti, for the destruction of the white population of that island.

I charge it—in its capacity of organ and co-laborer of the imperial government of Faustin I.—with habitually garbling and suppressing the news from St. Domingo, for the purpose of keeping people from turning their attention and sympathy to that brave struggle of the Dominicans for liberty and self-government. It has aimed to sustain Hayti in its anti-American system for the exclusion of whites, and as such, has denied the right to carry into their territory an army of invasion for the purpose of destroying her sovereignty.

I charge it with asserting disgraceful ignorance or wilful falsehood, in asserting that the Dominican is not an independent state, and that there is not a negro in the Dominican territory, while the fact is that the number of pure black Haytien inhabitants in this small American State is smaller than of any other.

I charge it with attempting to deceive and mislead the American people by fabricating, under the form of Post editorials, the fabulous bulletins of Soulouque, written by his own tools; of glossing over the invasion of the Dominican republic in 1849; and of glossing over, and indirectly justifying, the burning of whole villages, and the indiscriminate slaughter of women, children, and even domestic animals, on his savage march. Faustin and the Post say he marched an army into the Spanish portion of the island, "with the intention of restoring the integrity of the republic." They suppress the history of Soulouque's humiliating defeat at Las Carracas, by a small force of Dominicans, and his retreat—or rather his covered retreat by stating that, "in consequence of the mutual distress of the troops, and the impossibility of getting food for his horses, he was obliged to return;" but "gave notice that he intended to renew hostilities the following year—1850"

The Post says, Mr. Pierce ought not to send Mr. Fillmore "to prevent Soulouque's executing his purpose of subduing Hispaniola to his government and territory," and is as indignant as his friend Faustin can be at Mr. Fillmore's threat to check these wholesale butcheries. It regrets that "this absurd pretension directly led to a second attempt by Soulouque with more respect than it deserved—for he did not make it until the Dominicans refused to give any pledges for the future;" and then this false organ of Hayti adds, "the President could not put it hard in so publishing the affair as to make it appear that the threats of the United States had any effect, for the simple reason that these things are taken from its own open and glorified in-structions to the French commander." This was a significant visit of one of the concern to Hayti! and the author of the article above quoted was sent to learn what reward for past service, or what pay for future exertion, was then arranged with Faustin.

Finally, I charge the Post with wilfully misrepresenting the Dominican government and people, in order to discourage the American government and people, in order to prevent a treaty between them... and turn it, if possible, into Haytien channels, to carry out their plan of Haytien policy, which is already enjoying the best of the St. Domingo trade, through secret pay with the Haytien government. This young, enlightened and pro-gressive people, with a debt of not a dollar in their treasury, has ably sustained its domestic government for ten years, and is as free to form alliance and make treaties with other nations as any nation on earth, and far more worthy of American sympathy.

I finally charge the Post with subterfuge in in-sinuating that the President is attempting by these in-trigues to frighten weaker children than itself—if it refers to the Dominican people as symptoms of new slave States and future annexations. I have had no interest, directly or indirectly, in the Dominican treaty, nothing to hide, deny or conceal in my plans, princi-ples or conduct.

Whatever I have done in the matter of Dominican independence, has been because I thought it right, necessary and beneficial to both countries; and while life lasts, my whole influence, so far as it extends, shall be used to preserve the white race from Haytien supremacy.

WILLIAM L. CAZNEAU.

records.headline: An editorial in the Washington Sentinel urges the United States
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Washington Sentinel urges the United States to recognize the independence of the Dominican Republic, emphasizing that San Domingo lies at America's doors and has established a form of government similar to that of the United States. The paper notes that the Dominican Republic invites commerce and emigration and is anxious to conclude commercial treaties that would benefit U.S. trade, whereas the refusal to grant recognition prevents both treaty-making and any effort to end the chronic hostilities on the island. Pointing out that the United States has refused to recognize the government of Haiti, the editorial asks why Washington should respect Haitian claims to Dominican territory. It concludes that only an act of Congress is needed for recognition and states that President Pierce takes a deep interest in the matter and would be pleased to sign such legislation.
records.summary_es: Un editorial del Washington Sentinel insta a los Estados Unidos a reconocer la independencia de la República Dominicana, destacando que Santo Domingo se encuentra a las puertas de los Estados Unidos y ha establecido una forma de gobierno similar a la estadounidense. El periódico señala que la República Dominicana invita al comercio y a la emigración y desea celebrar tratados comerciales muy beneficiosos para el intercambio estadounidense, mientras que la negativa a otorgar el reconocimiento impide tanto la firma de tratados como cualquier gestión para poner fin al estado crónico de hostilidades en la isla. Al señalar que los Estados Unidos se han negado a reconocer al gobierno de Haití, el editorial pregunta por qué Washington habría de respetar las pretensiones haitianas sobre el territorio ocupado por los dominicanos. Concluye que solo se necesita una ley del Congreso para el reconocimiento y afirma que el presidente Pierce siente un profundo interés en el asunto y firmaría con agrado dicha ley.

records.headline: A correspondence from the City of St. Domingo, published in the New York Herald
records.summary_en: A correspondence from the City of St. Domingo, published in the New York Herald and signed "Felix," dated May 16, 1854, reports that circumstances regarding the anticipated war with Haiti have altogether changed. According to the writer, five French warships and one English warship went to Port-au-Prince to keep Emperor Soulouque quiet, and the English warship Trincomalee also sailed from Jamaica to Port-au-Prince for the same purpose. The correspondent adds that Emperor Napoleon sent President Santana a splendid set of porcelain, which Santana accepted. Expressing suspicion about why the French and English are so attentive to the Dominican Republic, the writer concludes that whenever the United States wishes to possess the island, "American valor will take it with as much ease as you would a pinch of snuff."
records.summary_es: Una correspondencia desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo, firmada por «Felix» y fechada el 16 de mayo de 1854, publicada en el New York Herald, informa que la situación respecto a la guerra prevista con Haití ha cambiado por completo. Según el autor, cinco buques de guerra franceses y uno inglés se dirigieron a Puerto Príncipe para mantener tranquilo al emperador Soulouque, y el buque de guerra inglés Trincomalee también partió de Jamaica hacia Puerto Príncipe con el mismo propósito. El corresponsal añade que el emperador Napoleón envió como obsequio una espléndida vajilla de porcelana al presidente Santana, la cual este aceptó. Tras expresar sospechas sobre la gran atención que franceses e ingleses prestan a la República Dominicana, el autor concluye que el día en que los Estados Unidos deseen poseer la isla, el valor estadounidense la tomará con tanta facilidad como quien toma una pizca de rapé.

records.summary_en: The June 9, 1854 *New York Herald* reports that the Dominican people are brave, orderly, and progressive, having successfully sustained their independence since 1844 by winning every battle against the Haytiens despite great odds, such as at the battle of Las Carreras where Santana defeated Faustin. The article states that Haytien emissaries attempted to incite colored Dominicans to murder whites and believe false rumors that Americans were coming to enslave them. Furthermore, the newspaper criticizes an American journal (the *Post*) for presenting cases in a way that incites insurrection among blacks while defending Hayti's destructive actions.

records.full_text:
It would hardly seem possible to deny, in a formal manner, the ridiculous stories put in circulation by the New York Evening Post respecting Gen. Cazneau's mission last winter to St. Domingo. His honorable career as a public officer, his high standing in Texas as head of the State Department, attest his character and capacity in a sufficient manner; but the letter we give below is the most complete refutation that could be given to the unmerited attacks of the Evening Post. It tells its own story, and we think our New York contemporary will find it no easy matter to extricate itself from its false position—never so satisfactorily as Gen. Cazneau does his with the Dominican and the Dominican republic.

To the Editor of the Union:
The Evening Post persists in grossly misrepresenting the Dominican people, and even goes so far in its spirit of Haytien partisanship as to deny that I desire the white or mixed race to be dominant. It branded that article as "so malicious and false that it could not possibly be written by a gentleman;" and if that is what the editor of the Post calls an admission of the truth, he is welcome to all the benefit of it. I ask no authority for its assertions, and I most emphatically deny, so far as I am concerned, all knowledge, past or present, of any "conspiracy" or "design," on my part for the acquisition of Domingo.

I do know, however, that the people of the Dominican republic, are anxious for the recognition of their independence, and of public justice. It has a right to expect this from our government; and its recognition as an act of justice and public faith. It has a right to expect this from our government; and its recognition and application as will secure that promising young State from the aggressions of Hayti.

It is the duty of the United States government to carefully promote our commerce with all the Republics on this continent.

Our ships are in a position to do their carrying-trade, and we should encourage and facilitate them in every way for the requirements of their people. It is our interest to cherish the peace of the world, and expand our commerce with all the American States, for their wealth and strength contribute to our own. It is our duty to maintain our peace with all European powers, in opposition to the present and future pretensions of European discussion. This is the principle of the American Monroe doctrine. The recognition of Dominica has long been urged upon my friends the propriety of giving it our warmest support. Generals Cass, Douglas, Houston, Rusk, and many other distinguished members of both houses of Congress, have advocated it with success, and their authority should be as good authority with an enlightened people as that of the Evening Post.

"We infer," says the Post, coming at last to the real question, "that it is the intention of the Dominican party to claim that Dominicans and Hayti are two different races; and that it is the interest of the whites for which they contend."

This is precisely the issue; they are different races: Dominicans are white and mixed, the Haytiens are black; and I repeat, and, a white government. I repeat, Mr. Editor, what I said, that, "since the late peace congress, or the convention, that has just adjourned, who has no sympathy with the color of his line. Hayti is an intolerant, irresponsible, stubborn negro despotism, without a language, though their tongue assimilates to the French.

They are governed throughout by men of pure African race. In their wars, they are as merciless as savages; and it has been, on more than one occasion, their declared intention to wholly annihilate the white and mixed race on this island. The Post is extremely unfortunate in taking into its service "rights of Hayti," which the Post's editorials maintain in terms remarkably like the official bulletins of Soulouque.

The Dominican people, on the contrary, are brave, orderly, and peaceful. Their long conflict, "sustained by their own courage," is proved by the manner in which they have successfully maintained their independence since the expulsion of the Haytien government in 1844. They have been victorious in every battle with the Haytiens; and always against great odds. In the battle of Las Carreras, Faustin had five hundred men, (and three pieces of artillery,) killed; yet the Dominicans had the character and courage to cut off his retreat, taking several pieces of artillery. His retreat across the frontier was characterized by Haytien cruelties, by the sacrifice of blood and ashes, by the destruction of property and the cruel slaughter of women and children.

Haytien atrocities cause among the colored Dominicans that horror which I take to be common to their race, to torture and murder the whites in the interior districts. They were used until the Dominicans were compelled to make slaves of them—in the style of the Post planters, which they "succeeded in doing;" but the Dominican blacks were not ignorant enough to believe those white men were their enemies; and, if the Post's editorial does not cause distress, and should fail to shake them, American slavery would be more tolerable than the Haytien, which alarms and excites the blacks into insurrection, while it defends the "rights of Hayti," to make a general destruction of the white race.

The editor of the Post may keep his eyes on the white race of the world, but he cannot see that a white-black war in Dominica would not destroy the line of white people, as it does in some of our southern States—but it is surprising that he, on the contrary, insists that we are doing nothing to promote peace and harmony between the white and black populations.

I not only "pretend to believe," but positively assert, that there are African fringe in that brave soldier and patriot statesman, President Santana. Look at the president of Hayti, Faustin, and at President Santana, educated in Louisiana, and Senior Baez, a quadroon—and compare the former monster in the South upon that accomplished gentleman as a "full-blooded white man." The American consul, or commercial agent, at Santo Domingo may inform the Post whether he considers his father-in-law, the dignified Don Domingo de la Roca, a white man. He is the minister said to be now in charge of the government, while Santana heads the army. Baez was a quadroon, but he owed his short-lived elevation to European intrigues, which are always at work in the Antilles to elevate the African, and harass and subdue the white race. He attempted, with their aid, to fraternize with Hayti, and was banished from the country in consequence.

The editor of the Post probably met some of the Baez party last winter, in the select circles of the negro nobility, during his stay of about six months ago. This is very natural, considering some of his extraordinary information in regard to Santo Domingo; for example—"that there are not two hundred whites, all told, sailors and diplomats included," in the republic of Santo Domingo.

The editor of the Post informs his readers that he knew nothing about me six months ago. This is very natural, considering the difference in our tastes and associations; but there is no occasion for the rancorous violence he exhibits because I prefer the free, permanent and intelligent white society of Dominica to the attractions of his Haytien circle. He may don a coat of mail, if he choose, and present a breastwork to Hayti; but I did not thereupon write home slanderous attacks upon the character of a citizen who was doing no wrong to his family. Men do not engage in work like this. My own character is above the reach of those mischievous misrepresentations which are calculated to lead to the wholesale murder of the white race in the island of Santo Domingo.
WM. L. CAZNEAU.

In contrast, it describes the Dominican people as brave, orderly, and progressive, noting that they have been victorious in every battle against the Haitians since 1844, despite facing great odds such as at the battle of Las Carreras. Additionally, the article states that Haitian emissaries attempted to incite colored Dominicans last winter to murder whites in the interior districts by falsely claiming Americans were coming to enslave them.

Además, la nota expone que emisarios haitianos intentaron soliviantar el pasado invierno a los dominicanos de color para que asesinaran a los blancos en los cantones del interior, propalando la falsedad de que los estadounidenses venían a esclavizarlos.

records.full_text:
It was hardly worth the trouble to deny, in a formal manner, the ridiculous stories put in circulation by the New York Evening Post respecting Gen. Cazneau's business last winter in St. Domingo. His honorable career as a [illegible] of their people. It is our interest to cherish the power, production, and general welfare of all these American States, and build up a strength to contribute to our own. It is so much strength added to the American force, in opposition to the present and future pretensions of European dictation. This is the principle of the American system, or it has none. In accordance with that principle, I have been urging upon my friends the propriety of giving to the Dominican republic the encouragement of a friendly recognition, as long and as earnestly as I have opposed it in the service of the black Emperor Faustin Soulouque.

The only plan I have ever heard of, or advocated, in connection with Gen. Cazneau, or any successor of his in office, was to strengthen the country relation with all the Spanish American States, and to establish them where they did not exist, as in the case of Dominica. It was only on this principle of American policy, that the recognition of Dominica was discussed with Senators Rusk, Douglas, Mason, Slidell, and many other distinguished members of the Senate, prior to Gen. Cazneau's connection with them; and those gentlemen should be as little suspected of a scheme of "filibustering" as the allies of Faustin.

We infer, says the Post, coming at last to the real question, "that it is the intention of the Post's editorial friends to show that Dominica and Hayti are under the control of different races, and that it is the interest of the whites for which they show such an anxiety."

This is precisely the issue; they are different races. Dominica is governed by civilized white manners, with a democratic constitution, and, obedient to the laws of nations. There is not, to name one man, either in the cabinet, Congress, or the Dominican forces, that has a drop of African blood in his veins. Hayti is an ignorant, barbarous, stubborn negro despotism, without a legal code, and obedient to no laws, unanalogous to the French.

They are governed throughout by men of negro blood and negro ideas. In their wars, they are as merciless enemies to quadroons as to whites, for they audaciously proclaim their intention to wholly annihilate the white and mixed race on the island. This creed of extermination is the leading point in those "rights of Hayti," which the Post's editorials maintain in terms so remarkably like the official bulletins of Soulouque.

The Dominican people, on the contrary, are from Spanish stock, and their character is not "without character and courage," as the Post says. As a matter of history, having sustained themselves since the establishment of their republic, they have been victorious in every battle with the Haytians. Under Santana, as well as under Santana's predecessors—at the battle of Las Carreras, Faustin had five times their force, and yet victory was with the Dominicans. Have the Dominicans had the "character and courage" to put him to flight, with the loss of thousands of his troops? He escaped, and the frontier was characteristic of Haytian warfare, and marked by blood and ashes, by the destruction of property and the cruel slaughter of women and children.

Haytian emissaries came among the colored population in Dominica, and tried to set the country on fire, to incite them to rise and murder the whites in the interior districts. They asserted that the Americans were coming to make slaves of them—in the style of the Post's phraseology about "the extension of slavery;" but the Dominican blacks were not ignorant enough to believe these monstrous absurdities. Their prudence does not excuse, and should put to shame an American journal in continually presenting the case in a shape to alarm and excite the blacks into insurrection, while it defends the "rights of Hayti" to make a general destruction of the white race.

records.headline: In an editorial argument using the paper's period racial language, the writer recounts Dominican independence
records.summary_en: In an editorial argument using the paper's period racial language, the writer recounts Dominican independence, repeated Haitian attempts at reconquest repulsed through 1849, and a truce after Soulouque's rout by Santana. It argues the United States should protect the Dominican Republic and says France was intriguing for its conquest.
records.summary_es: En un argumento editorial que usa el lenguaje racial de la época del periódico, el autor relata la independencia dominicana, los repetidos intentos haitianos de reconquista rechazados hasta 1849 y una tregua tras la derrota de Soulouque por Santana. Sostiene que Estados Unidos debería proteger la República Dominicana y dice que Francia intrigaba para conquistarla.

records.headline: An editorial in the New-York Daily Tribune calls public attention
records.summary_en: An editorial in the New-York Daily Tribune calls public attention back to intelligence derived from the journals of St. Domingo City regarding General Cazneau's mission to the Dominican Republic. The paper states that Cazneau, the alleged U.S. Commissioner, is notoriously connected with a scheme for colonizing and annexing "Dominica," noting that when he sailed aboard the frigate Columbia, its avowed destination was Haiti at the other end of the island. Consequently, the Tribune argues that either Cazneau is falsely passing himself off as a U.S. Commissioner with a frigate aiding the deception, or the Executive under General Pierce and Mr. Marcy is carrying out a conspiracy against a weak neighbor to gratify "slave-drivers" who have long coveted the Dominican Republic.
records.summary_es: Un editorial del New-York Daily Tribune vuelve a llamar la atención del público sobre las noticias procedentes de los periódicos de la ciudad de Santo Domingo acerca de la misión del general Cazneau en la República Dominicana. El diario afirma que Cazneau, el supuesto comisionado estadounidense, está notoriamente vinculado con el plan de colonizar y anexar a «Dominica», y señala que cuando zarpó a bordo de la fragata Columbia, el propósito declarado del viaje era dirigirse a Haití, en el otro extremo de la misma isla. En consecuencia, el Tribune sostiene que o bien Cazneau se hace pasar allí por comisionado de los Estados Unidos sin autorización pero con una fragata que secunda el engaño, o bien el Ejecutivo bajo el general Pierce y el señor Marcy lleva adelante una conspiración contra un vecino débil para complacer a los esclavistas que desde hace mucho codician a la República Dominicana.

records.headline: An editorial in the Burlington Free Press warns of comprehensive schemes of pro-slavery
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Burlington Free Press warns of comprehensive schemes of pro-slavery expansion, noting alongside designs on Mexico, the African slave trade, and Brazil that a U.S. Senator has broached the recognition of the Dominican Republic with an ulterior view to its annexation. Although the paper acknowledges that some of these designs are still embryonic and not shared by judicious men of any section, it argues that their mere conception among men of eminent station should awaken public vigilance. Because American plans are executed with "the rapidity of magnetism," the editorial urges timely watchfulness against the earliest beginnings of such pro-slavery projects.
records.summary_es: Un editorial del Burlington Free Press advierte sobre amplios planes de expansión esclavista y señala, junto a proyectos relativos a México, el tráfico de esclavos africanos y Brasil, que un senador estadounidense ha planteado el reconocimiento de la República Dominicana con la mira ulterior de su anexión. Aunque el periódico reconoce que algunos de estos designios se encuentran aún en ciernes y no son compartidos por los hombres sensatos de ninguna región, sostiene que su sola concepción entre figuras de alta posición debe despertar la vigilancia pública. Dado que en la nación los planes se ejecutan con «la rapidez del magnetismo», el editorial insta a mantener una vigilancia oportuna frente a los primeros indicios de tales proyectos proesclavistas.

records.headline: "The Plot Against Dominica" heads a New-York Daily Tribune editorial
records.summary_en: "The Plot Against Dominica" heads a New-York Daily Tribune editorial recalling that more than three years earlier the paper first warned the American public of a conspiracy to acquire the eastern part of St. Domingo, aimed at the ultimate conquest and annexation of the island to the American confederation as two or more slave states. The article recounts the visit of a U.S. diplomat—whom President Báez described to France as having come as Chargé d'Affaires—whose public purpose never transpired. According to the Tribune, the real scope of his visit was revealed in certain "Propositions of Colonization" submitted by that diplomat and his father, General Duff Green, which offered money, one or two steamers, and regular postal communication with the United States in exchange for permission for the Greens and their associates to introduce colonists.
records.summary_es: Bajo el titular «El complot contra Dominica», un editorial del New-York Daily Tribune recuerda que hace más de tres años el periódico advirtió por primera vez al público estadounidense sobre la existencia de una conspiración para adquirir la parte oriental de Santo Domingo, con miras a la conquista definitiva y anexión de la isla a la confederación estadounidense en forma de dos o más Estados esclavistas. El artículo relata la visita de un diplomático estadounidense —de quien el presidente Báez escribió a Francia que había llegado como encargado de negocios— cuyo propósito público nunca trascendió. Según el Tribune, el verdadero alcance de su visita se manifestó claramente en ciertas «Proposiciones de Colonización» presentadas por dicho diplomático junto con su padre, el general Duff Green, las cuales ofrecían dinero, uno o dos vapores y comunicación postal regular con los Estados Unidos a cambio de que se permitiera a los Green y sus asociados introducir colonos.

records.headline: The New-York Daily Tribune continues its critique of pro-slavery
records.summary_en: The New-York Daily Tribune continues its critique of pro-slavery interest in the Dominican Republic, arguing that appeals made on behalf of the people of "Dominica" by those who prioritize racial complexion are hypocritical and driven by "motives worthy only of robbers and slave-drivers." The editorial contends that it is difficult to see how the U.S. government can recognize "Dominica" while refusing the same courtesy to Haiti and Liberia, asserting that neither of the latter countries is more under the control of men of Black blood or less worthy in the character and abilities of its administrators. The passage also references B. E. Green's mission to St. Domingo City as a commissioner sent by President Polk and the propositions offering the Dominican government a loan and American colonists to carry on mining, concluding that selective diplomatic recognition depends on whether Northern freemen are willing to be used to spread slavery.

records.headline: The Oxford Democrat warns against emerging schemes of pro-slavery
records.summary_en: The Oxford Democrat warns against emerging schemes of pro-slavery expansion, noting that alongside calls to withdraw the U.S. naval squadron from the African coast and reported overtures to Brazil for a southern slaveholding confederacy, a U.S. Senator has broached the recognition of the Dominican Republic with an ulterior view to its annexation. While observing that some of these designs remain in an early stage and are not supported by judicious men of any section, the editorial argues that their mere conception among prominent figures should serve as a warning and awaken public vigilance. Because American plans move rapidly from thought to action, the paper urges timely watchfulness against the earliest beginnings of such projects.
records.summary_es: El Oxford Democrat advierte contra los planes emergentes de expansión esclavista y señala que, junto con los llamados a retirar la escuadra naval estadounidense de la costa de África y las supuestas gestiones ante Brasil para establecer una confederación esclavista en el Sur, un senador estadounidense ha planteado el reconocimiento de la República Dominicana con el propósito ulterior de su anexión. Aunque observa que algunos de estos proyectos están aún en ciernes y no cuentan con el respaldo de los hombres sensatos de ninguna región, el editorial sostiene que su sola concepción entre figuras prominentes debe servir de advertencia y despertar la vigilancia pública. Dado que los planes estadounidenses pasan rápidamente de la idea al hecho, el periódico insta a mantener una vigilancia oportuna contra los primeros indicios de tales designios.

records.full_text:
From the Boston Commonwealth.
THE SLAVE POWER AND ST. DOMINGO.

Filibustering Manifest Destiny has proclaimed that the Slave Power must have ‘our Southern islands,’ and that the negroes of Cuba, Hayti, &c., must be doomed to perpetual slavery, and ‘kept at work under white republican masters.’ When this language was used in the Democratic Review, Hayti was named particularly, and it expressed no more than the Slave Power actually means and is now planning to accomplish. The purpose is to get possession of Hayti by means of filibusterism cunningly introduced into Dominica. One insidious attempt has been made upon Dominica, but failed. Duff Green was concerned in that affair, and his son was the agent employed in Dominica by our government. The conspirators sought to make an arrangement with the Dominican authorities, which should secure filibusters the privilege of ‘colonizing’ on that part of the island, with a separate and independent military organization of their own. Ostensibly, they were to be cutters of mahogony and dye woods, but really a filibustering army designed for the subjugation of the island when strong enough in numbers. But the Dominicans were suspicious, and the negotiation fell through.

Recently, Mrs. Cazneau, the ‘Cora Montgomery’ of some of the newspapers, and Gen. Cazneau, her husband, have been sent to Dominica to negotiate, plot, and intrigue, in behalf of this scheme of the Slave Power; and ‘Cora,’ it is said, has far more genius for the business than the General. It is reported that they have made some progress, that our Government will make a formal treaty with Dominica, and recognize its independence as a nation, and that the matter will soon be in shape to come before Congress. Of course, all this will not be done without such provisions in the treaty as will give our Slave Power that foothold in the island which it seeks. The whole purpose, on the part of our Government, is a filibustering invasion of both Dominica and Hayti. It means nothing else. It is seeking to execute that decree which says the African race in that island must be reduced to slavery, and ‘kept at work under white republican masters.’ If what is reported is true, (and it is fully credited by those likely to be best informed on the subject,) this is one of the next forms in which the slavery question is to be presented to the country, and the people should take it to their thoughts and feelings. The following statement in regard to this Cazneau treaty shows what is on foot:—

‘As far as could be collected from the first proceedings, the treaty is to have for one of its various ostensible objects, to stipulate for certain rights in the ports of the Republic, and especially in the spacious and secure bay of Samana, for the armed vessels of the United States, in case of war, and in time of peace, for the establishment of a kind of colonization, black or white, of individuals from the United States, in some part of the Dominican Republic.’

The Boston Post has already begun its defence of this villany, in a characteristic parrgraph of three or four lines, full of hypocritical wonder that anti-slavery men should put forth hostile criticism on the disposition of our government to recognize the independence of Dominica. Of course, that paper will never intimate to its readers, that, if this disposition of our Government were honest—if it is not, in fact, full of plotting piracy—it would also propose a recognition of the independence of Hayti and Liberia. There are more and stronger reasons for recognizing either of these gevernments than can be invented for this negotiation with Dominica. We have a large commerce with Hayti, and Liberia has grown up under American influences. Dominica is of little or no importance commercially, and would now be politically united with Hayti, if it had not rebelled and withdrawn, because that government proclaimed free toleration of all religious sects. The Dominicans have the religious training and bigotry of Spanish Catholics. They occupy what was the Spanish portion of the island, and the Haytiens that part which was held by the French. But they are all of African descent, and would constitute but one people, if not interfered with by the rascally intrigues of outsiders.

Our Slave Power has decided that it will injure the peculiar institution to allow the Dominicans and Haytiens, whose parents were slaves, to realize a prosperous and happy fortune. It will not do to let the world see them work out for themselves such a fortune; and, moreover, the slaveholders hope to prepare that island for annexation to the Union as a slave State. ‘Our Southern islands,’ they say; and how much that signifies!

records.headline: The Daily National Intelligencer reports news from St. Thomas
records.summary_en: The Daily National Intelligencer reports news from St. Thomas and states that U.S. diplomatic agents to the Dominican Republic have succeeded in their mission to secure the Bay of Samaná for a United States naval station. According to the report, President Santana is inclined to accept the friendship of the United States in the hope of finding a permanent barrier for the Dominicans against the ambition of the neighboring Haitian Emperor. The paper describes the Bay of Samaná, near the eastern end of the north side of the island, as one of the largest and most commodious harbors in the world, capable of accommodating the largest naval or merchant vessels and commanding both the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea more advantageously than any harbor in Cuba.
records.summary_es: El Daily National Intelligencer informa sobre noticias procedentes de San Tomás. Según éstas, los agentes diplomáticos de los Estados Unidos en la República Dominicana han tenido éxito en su misión de asegurar la bahía de Samaná para una estación naval estadounidense. Según el informe, el presidente Santana se inclina a aceptar la amistad de los Estados Unidos con la esperanza de encontrar en ella una barrera permanente para los dominicanos frente a la ambición del vecino emperador haitiano. El periódico describe la bahía de Samaná, situada en la costa norte cerca del extremo oriental de la isla, como uno de los puertos más grandes y cómodos del mundo, capaz de albergar a los mayores buques de guerra o mercantes y con dominio sobre el golfo de México y el mar Caribe en condiciones más ventajosas que cualquier puerto de Cuba.

records.summary_en: A letter in the New York Post says Soulouque, who was not worth a sous when chosen Emperor of Haiti, now owns property valued at $2,000,000. It lists six large distilleries with sugar plantations attached for the manufacture of tafia and rum, fifty to seventy stores and houses, mostly in Port-au-Prince, and a new plantation bought recently for $60,000 with the intention, it is said, of attempting the manufacture of sugar.
records.summary_es: Una carta en el New York Post dice que Soulouque, que no valía un sou cuando fue elegido emperador de Haití, posee ahora propiedades valoradas en 2.000.000 de dólares. Enumera seis grandes destilerías con plantaciones de azúcar anexas para fabricar tafía y ron, entre cincuenta y setenta tiendas y casas, en su mayoría en Puerto Príncipe, y una nueva plantación comprada recientemente por 60.000 dólares con la intención, se dice, de intentar fabricar azúcar.

records.headline: Reprinting an item from the New York Herald, the Cecil Whig notes
records.summary_en: Reprinting an item from the New York Herald, the Cecil Whig notes a rumor that the U.S. diplomatic emissaries have succeeded in their mission to the Dominican Republic and that the port of Samaná has been ceded to the United States. The article expresses skepticism and calls for more authentic evidence before giving the report credence, asking why the Dominicans would be in such a hurry to part with their best seaport when the United States has no particular claim on their regard. Instead, the paper suggests it is more likely that the envoys followed in the steps of Louis-Philippe and obtained from the Dominicans the same privileges previously granted to that monarch.

En cambio, el periódico sugiere que parece más probable que los enviados hayan seguido los pasos de Luis Felipe y obtenido de los dominicanos los mismos privilegios que fueron concedidos a dicho monarca.

According to the account, the bay's entrance on the Atlantic is about twenty-four miles wide, its waters extend fifty miles inland, and two mile-long islands—the Grand Levantados Keys, situated fifteen miles from Cape Raphael on the south and twelve miles from Cape Samaná on the north—break the force of the winds and waves to create a secure anchorage. North of the bay stretches the hilly Samaná peninsula, which varies from four to ten miles in width, while the Port of Samaná, reported to be ceded to the United States, is formed by a cove extending from the bay into the peninsula.

records.full_text:
Correspondence of the N. Y. Tribune.
Santiago, (Island of Hayti,) Sept. 14, 1854.
The Island of Hayti is divided nominally between two independent powers, the Dominican Republic at the east, which is under white preponderance, and the west, which is exclusively under the black. There is, however, a third district that differs in its moral elements almost from either. The rich district of the gold-teeming Cibao, and the fertile plain of the Vega is considered a part of the Dominican Republic, but its population are a distinct race and sympathize not entirely in accordance with those of the capital and extreme east of the Republic.

The Cibao district is not of Indian, as Eastern Hayti is white with a dash of African, and more than any other part of the island it cherishes an uncompromising hatred of the Haytians. In every quarter the inhabitants have stories of Haytian acts of cruelty to tell their children, and every family has its own tale of horrors about the Haytian invasions. They look upon even a peaceful presence and free intercourse with Hayti, lest it might lead, as it did once before, to a union of the whole island under a colored government. They openly declare themselves in favor of annexation to the United States, and have never ceased to demand white immigration. This district once memorialized the United States Government on the subject of receiving it into the Union, or making it a separate and neutral State, with ports entirely and forever open to our commerce, on condition of being protected from the all-destroying inroads of the Haytians. This memorial was buried, like Sir John Moore, in silence and darkness, without a word from the American press, but it awakened France and England to insist upon a peace between the belligerent parties.

Eastern Hayti has a large colored population, and the fusion of the races, with the final supremacy of the blacks, is fast approaching there; Santana, the Liberator, Generals Alfau and Contreras, are Dominican whites, and their death or another dash of their stamp could be out of the way; but Central Hayti would never consent.

The British Consul has more than once advised the Dominicans to strike the white cross and raise the Haytian tri-color, but President Santana was enraged at the counsel, and the Cibao said if it was attempted they would form a new State and call on the Americans to come with letters of marque and conquer Hayti on their own account.

You can understand, therefore, that the Island of Hayti is divided in two governments and three parties, and that each party textually demands its share of the territory, but the Haytians have two-thirds of the entire population—or 650,000 out of 800,000 inhabitants.

Eastern Hayti is so much under European influence that it can never be annexable under European policy, which is declared here without reserve, of uniting with Hayti, but for the central district, whose standard of political independence is high.

The geographical position of these districts is much against their independence, for they are between the two Haytis of Hayti on one side and European Hayti on the other, and it is only by a union with the United States would be reliable protection to the island, for the protection of an American State would unite its sections in a common sentiment, and settle it firmly in its place among the republic of nations. America ought to wish to see this island or any part of it annexed to the United States. It would be an immense field for our enterprising citizens, who would then have the monopoly of her trade, and entirely clothe this people with our manufactures.

A Commissioner from the United States is at St. Domingo City at this moment, negotiating a Treaty which will give our citizens the right to buy land and work mines, and all the rights and privileges of American citizens. This is the same as giving a new State to American enterprise, and we must hope that Gen. Cazneau will succeed in spite of all opposition from abroad; but Hayti is of all classes and colors, and in particular it opens a fine field for American enterprise, being of mixed blood. The laws and the constitution make no distinctions of colors, and the customs of society prefer the white race all to whom the white blood visibly preponderates.

If southern American protection would pass, for I have not met any one whose education and position would place him in the highest society if he were white, who would think of southern Americans keeping down the blacks here quite as positively as they are in the South.

Let the friends of the colored race try out the problem of its capacities on this friendly soil and under a favorable climate. There is nothing here, not even the prejudices of society to hinder their efforts. Land is cheap, fertile, the laws liberal, society kind, and the country very near to you. Send school books and teachers, and encourage the honest and industrious of the colored race of the Union to come here and show the world what they are worth. There will be order and safety so long as American results will be tangible facts, and we want some real solid facts to thicken all the froth of philanthropy with which the United States are simmering.
AMERICUS.

records.headline: In a letter to the editor of the New-York Daily Tribune dated
records.summary_en: In a letter to the editor of the New-York Daily Tribune dated New York, October 20, 1854, a writer signing as "G." calls attention to what he terms a gross error in a St. Domingo correspondent's letter dated Santiago, September 14. The correspondent had claimed that the British Consul had more than once advised the Dominicans to strike the white cross and raise the Haitian tricolor, enraging the Dominican President. Asserting personal acquaintance with Sir Robert Schomburgh, the British Consul at St. Domingo, the letter writer declares that this allegation is a complete mistake and that the consul's actual course throughout has been the reverse of what was attributed to him.

El corresponsal había afirmado que el cónsul británico había aconsejado más de una vez a los dominicanos arriar la cruz blanca e izar el tricolor haitiano, enfureciendo al presidente dominicano. records.headline: An editorial in the Worcester Daily Spy warns that while northern
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Worcester Daily Spy warns that while northern freemen remain indifferent to the question of human freedom, pro-slavery forces are advancing plans to extend American slavery. According to the paper, agents of President Franklin Pierce have obtained from the Dominican government the right to establish naval and military stations in the northern part of the island of St. Domingo, including the mineral-rich mountainous region of Samaná, along with privileges for Americans to mine and trade in the Dominican Republic without naturalization. The editorial argues that the partial cession of the department of Cibao in "Dominica" is intended to facilitate the conquest of Haiti, Cuba, and Central America on behalf of the "Slaveocracy."
records.summary_es: Un editorial del Worcester Daily Spy advierte que mientras los hombres libres del Norte permanecen indiferentes ante la cuestión de la libertad humana, las fuerzas esclavistas avanzan en sus planes para extender la esclavitud estadounidense. Según el periódico, los agentes del presidente Franklin Pierce han obtenido del gobierno dominicano el derecho de establecer estaciones navales y militares en la parte norte de la isla de Santo Domingo, incluida la región montañosa y rica en minerales de Samaná, junto con privilegios para que los estadounidenses exploten minas y comercien en la República Dominicana sin necesidad de naturalizarse. El editorial sostiene que la cesión parcial del departamento del Cibao en «Dominica» tiene el propósito de facilitar la conquista de Haití, Cuba y Centroamérica en beneficio de la «esclavocracia».

records.full_text:
VIRGINIA REINS.—The New York Tribune is a monomaniac on the Southern question. Not a paper comes from that office which does not bear its "testimony" against the "curse" of slavery. Greeley evidently thinks that the salvation of his soul depends upon blazing away at slavery in every number of his paper. He cannot eat, drink, or sleep, without slavery, emancipated negroes, blood, chains and lashes, before his eyes. Lately he is talking about Virginia ruins, and thus sesquipedally he discourseth:
'The ruins of Jamestown but typify the ruins of the whole State,' &c. This is the substance of the sneering article recorded. For example: Norfolk is a small village; Richmond, if not a ruin, is a place of very small importance, and has no human flesh. The fields of Virginia, too, are ruined, and the people, and tobacco-chewers, smoking, spitting have contributed to wear them out and drive the chivalry to other lands. The people, too, are intellectually ruined.'
In this elegant manner, the New York Express, thus handsomely raps the demented philosopher over the knuckles:
'The New York Tribune is mistaken! Norfolk is in a high state of prosperity. Richmond is as prosperous as any city in the Northern States.—There are some things in Virginia, however, of a higher science displayed on them, than any where in New York, negro-traders, tobacco juice, equal in our State. The people have an amount of brain and power we feel else, they would never have given us that class of statesmen who are living in the Northern States more than two-thirds of them (Everett and Fillmore) equal to Rives and Hunter. Bayly, a member from Accomac even, has more practical and actual power, from mind and experience, than any Northern State in the House of Representatives. The people of Virginia have their vices and their faults, but the breed of its mighty men is in some degree run out; but the State only needs manufacturing to become a great and ancient power. The vice of its system is, that it is not commercial and agricultural. The undistinguishing slanders upon the people of our own countrymen are simply disgusting.'
The New York Tribune may find a more inviting field for its philanthropy in the history of Hayti. The bravest of them provoked their savage masters to kill them at once, but some others were known to drag out their miserable lives under the whip like ill-treated slaves on the country patches of ten negroes. No negro was responsible by negro law, for the murder or maltreatment of even a mulatto, much less of a white person. The cruelties which the mixed bloods suffered in attempting to hide and protect some white families of San Christoval, are too horrible to be related. If the Tribune wants a field for its philanthropy, let it look to Hayti, and not to Virginia.

records.summary_en: The *New-York Daily Tribune* reported on Dominican resistance to Haitian control, noting that memories of severe mistreatment and violence during past Haitian rule deterred locals from favoring Haitian dominance. Despite rumors circulated that Americans intended to enslave the population, both white and mixed-race residents remained fearful of a Haitian return. The correspondent urged the United States to counter British diplomatic influence by officially recognizing the Dominican Republic.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Daily Tribune* dio cuenta de la irreductible resistencia dominicana a la hegemonía haitiana, observando que la memoria de atropellos y rigores padecidos durante el régimen anterior apartaba a los naturales de cualquier simpatía hacia el dominio haitiano. Pese a las patrañas propaladas de que los norteamericanos proyectaban esclavizar a la población, tanto los moradores blancos como los de color temían sobremanera la restauración del yugo haitiano. El corresponsal encarecía a Estados Unidos a contrarrestar la injerencia diplomática británica mediante el reconocimiento oficial de la República Dominicana.

records.headline: A correspondent reports that it is generally understood in both
records.summary_en: A correspondent reports that it is generally understood in both official circles and among the public that General Cazneau, the United States Commissioner accredited to the Dominican Republic, has secured for the United States the right to establish military and naval depots on the northern coast of the island. According to the writer, these depots are regarded as essential for acquiring Cuba and Puerto Rico by force of arms, after which Dominican territory would also be colonized and annexed to the Union as a slave state. The correspondent adds that the broader plan contemplates dividing Cuba into two states so that, together with St. Domingo and Puerto Rico, four additional slaveholding states would be added to the Union.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal informa que se da por sentado, tanto en los círculos oficiales como entre el público en general, que el general Cazneau, comisionado de los Estados Unidos acreditado ante la República Dominicana, ha asegurado para los Estados Unidos el derecho de establecer depósitos militares y navales en la costa norte de la isla. Según el autor, dichos depósitos se consideran esenciales para asegurar la adquisición de Cuba y Puerto Rico por la fuerza de las armas, tras lo cual el territorio dominicano también sería colonizado y anexado a la Unión como un estado esclavista. El corresponsal añade que el plan contempla dividir a Cuba en dos estados para que, junto con Santo Domingo y Puerto Rico, se sumen cuatro estados esclavistas adicionales a la Unión.

records.headline: Citing a Tribune correspondent writing from St. Thomas, the Perrysburg Journal reports
records.summary_en: Citing a Tribune correspondent writing from St. Thomas, the Perrysburg Journal reports that United States diplomatic agents Mr. and Mrs. Cazneau have succeeded in their mission to the Dominican Republic to secure the Bay of Samaná for a U.S. naval station. The report states that President Santana is inclined to accept American friendship in hopes of establishing a permanent barrier for "Dominica" against the ambitions of the Haitian Emperor. Located near the eastern end of the northern coast, Samaná Bay is described as one of the largest and most commodious harbors in the world, capable of receiving the largest naval or merchant vessels and commanding both the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea better than any harbor in Cuba.
records.summary_es: Citando a un corresponsal del Tribune que escribe desde San Tomás, el Perrysburg Journal informa que los agentes diplomáticos de los Estados Unidos, el señor y la señora Cazneau, han tenido éxito en su misión ante la República Dominicana para asegurar la bahía de Samaná como estación naval estadounidense. El informe señala que el presidente Santana se inclina a aceptar la amistad estadounidense con la esperanza de establecer una barrera permanente para «Dominica» frente a las ambiciones del emperador haitiano. Situada cerca del extremo oriental de la costa norte, la bahía de Samaná es descrita como uno de los puertos más grandes y cómodos del mundo, capaz de recibir a los mayores buques navales o mercantes y de dominar tanto el golfo de México como el mar Caribe mejor que cualquier puerto de Cuba.

records.headline: A correspondent in the New-York Daily Tribune quotes a skeptical statement
records.summary_en: A correspondent in the New-York Daily Tribune quotes a skeptical statement arguing that President Santana would not be so improvident as to dispose of so important a maritime position as the peninsula of Samaná on his own without first consulting the governments of France and England, which would undoubtedly use every means in their power to refuse their consent. Responding to that view, the Tribune writer asks by what right France or England should be consulted by independent St. Domingo regarding whether it chooses to transfer a portion of its territory to the United States. The writer contends that the United States might just as well demand to be consulted on the balance of power in Europe and offer unsolicited aid to Russia against England and France.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal en el New-York Daily Tribune cita una declaración escéptica según la cual el presidente Santana no sería tan imprudente como para disponer por sí solo de una posición marítima tan importante como la península de Samaná sin consultar primero a los gobiernos de Francia e Inglaterra, los cuales sin duda emplearían todos los medios a su alcance para negar su consentimiento. En respuesta a esa postura, el autor del Tribune pregunta con qué derecho Francia o Inglaterra habrían de ser consultadas por un Santo Domingo independiente acerca de si decide o no transferir una parte de su territorio a los Estados Unidos. El articulista sostiene que, con igual razón, los Estados Unidos podrían exigir ser consultados sobre el equilibrio de poder en Europa y prestar ayuda no solicitada a Rusia contra Inglaterra y Francia.

records.summary_en: Reprinting an item from the New York Herald titled "Annexation of Samana," the Nevada Journal notes rumors that Mr. and Mrs. Cazeneau have succeeded in their mission to the Dominican Republic and that the fine port of Samaná has been ceded to the United States. The paper asks for more authentic evidence before giving the report full credence, questioning why the Dominicans would be in such haste to part with their best seaport when the United States holds no special claim on their regard. Instead, the article suggests it is more likely that the American envoys have obtained from the Dominicans the same privileges previously granted to a French monarch.
records.summary_es: Reproduciendo una nota del New York Herald titulada «Anexión de Samaná», el Nevada Journal recoge los rumores de que el señor y la señora Cazeneau han tenido éxito en su misión ante la República Dominicana y de que el excelente puerto de Samaná ha sido cedido a los Estados Unidos. El periódico pide pruebas más auténticas antes de dar entero crédito a la noticia, cuestionando por qué los dominicanos tendrían tanta prisa en desprenderse de su mejor puerto marítimo cuando los Estados Unidos no tienen ningún derecho particular a su favor. En cambio, el artículo sugiere que es más probable que los enviados estadounidenses hayan obtenido de los dominicanos los mismos privilegios concedidos anteriormente a un monarca francés.

records.summary_en: An editorial charges that the United States has an agent in St. Domingo quietly securing a naval station in the Bay of Samana, valuable mines, and citizenship rights without naturalization, as preliminary steps toward annexation. It denounces the Dominican negotiation as a contrivance to extend slavery, and asks who would work the mines of sulphur, silver and gold and till the coffee lands offered at three dollars an acre.
records.summary_es: Un editorial denuncia que los Estados Unidos tienen un agente en Santo Domingo que discretamente está asegurando una estación naval en la bahía de Samana, minas valiosas y derechos de ciudadanía sin naturalización, como pasos preliminares hacia la anexión. Denuncia la negociación dominicana como un ardid para extender la esclavitud, y pregunta quiénes trabajarían las minas de azufre, plata y oro y cultivarían las tierras de café ofrecidas a tres dólares el acre.

records.headline: The paper's editorial denounces expeditions aimed at Haiti, posing rhetorical questions about whether regiments from the South
records.summary_en: The paper's editorial denounces expeditions aimed at Haiti, posing rhetorical questions about whether regiments from the South, trained to hunting and dogging fugitive slaves, will achieve what Bonaparte could not — the re-enslavement of Haiti. It asks whether America is to carry slavery's woes to every contiguous country and island of the continent.

Pregunta si Estados Unidos ha de llevar los males de la esclavitud a cada país e isla contiguos del continente.

records.headline: A letter from Santo Domingo printed by the paper claims that General Cazneau had succeeded in securing for the United States
records.summary_en: A letter from Santo Domingo printed by the paper claims that General Cazneau had succeeded in securing for the United States the right to establish military and naval depots on the north coast of the island. The letter further claims, as the writer's understanding of a plan, that Dominican territory would be colonized and annexed to the Union as a slave state, alongside Cuba divided into two states and Puerto Rico.
records.summary_es: Una carta desde Santo Domingo publicada por el periódico afirma que el general Cazneau había logrado asegurar para Estados Unidos el derecho de establecer depósitos militares y navales en la costa norte de la isla. La carta afirma además, como interpretación del escritor de un plan, que el territorio dominicano sería colonizado y anexado a la Unión como un estado esclavista, junto con Cuba dividida en dos estados y Puerto Rico.

records.headline: The paper asks why the president kept back the mission of Mrs. Cazneau
records.summary_en: The paper asks why the president kept back the mission of Mrs. Cazneau to the Dominican end of the island, saying it comprehended a project of moral and material aid to the Dominicans against the Haitian emperor. It argues the mission involved a contingency of war that required Congress's authority and that the House should call for her official correspondence.

Cazneau al extremo dominicano de la isla, diciendo que comprendía un proyecto de ayuda moral y material a los dominicanos contra el emperador haitiano. Sostiene que la misión implicaba una contingencia de guerra que requería la autoridad del Congreso y que la Cámara debería pedir su correspondencia oficial.

records.headline: The paper discusses Mrs. Cazneau's correspondence
records.summary_en: The paper discusses Mrs. Cazneau's correspondence and special mission to Dominica, undertaken after rumors of an intended invasion by Soulouque of the Spanish and mulatto republic. It says her plan is understood to be to turn the tables on him, put him down, re-establish slavery and annex the whole island to the United States, and that she is said to have already bought a seaport as a naval rendezvous for squatters and filibusteros under the original plan of General Duff Green.

Dice que se entiende que su plan es volver la situación contra él, derribarlo, restablecer la esclavitud y anexar toda la isla a los Estados Unidos, y que se dice que ya ha comprado un puerto marítimo como punto de reunión naval para ocupantes y filibusteros según el plan original del general Duff Green.

records.headline: The Tribune prints the Cazneau treaty of amity and commerce with the Dominican Republic in full and editorializes on its terms:
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints the Cazneau treaty of amity and commerce with the Dominican Republic in full and editorializes on its terms: the clause on consuls, the Dominican legislature's proposed amendment on the rights of its citizens, and the hitch that has stalled ratification.
