records.full_text:
THE UNITED STATES AND ST. DOMINGO.—MR. CAZNEAU AND THE TREATY—FRENCH INTERFERENCE—NEW SCHEME OF COLONIZATION—ALLIANCE BETWEEN NAPOLEON AND SOULOUQUE, &c., &c.

[From the National Democrate.]
Great events are about to come forth in this island in behalf of the children of Africa, and may God turn the result of the events alluded to in the United States to befriend our cause.

Louis Napoleon, the Emperor of France, of he highest rank among the sovereigns of the world, will not leave the whole island of Hayti under the just and vigorous sceptre of Faustin the First.

The Dominicans pretend to be a white population, and although there may be some who can show a clear skin, look at the characters, and try to find out their progenitors. If a man is so white that no one can perceive that he has African blood in his veins, then he may pass; but not else.

The Dominicans have, they say, made propositions to the French and English nations, and for the sale of St. Domingo to France, and Samana to England; but they cannot touch them; but these great European powers will never allow a single square inch of Hayti to be given up to the United States.

These powers have given full authority to their agent in St. Domingo to arrange for the return of the Dominican Republic—to the dominion of the empire. They will be allowed to retain the houses they really live in, but all the rest of the property will be restored to its original owners. The unoccupied land will be taken by the Dominican government, to be given to those who, for the offered terms, which our Emperor intends to make, shall come from France to populate the country.

This warm climate suits the African race, and there are no people under the sun so much indebted to us as those who have no house or home. To these the Emperor Faustin will give lands, and the great influence of their friends in the United States will help them to a noble existence.

It is said that the French Emperor will remit one million of francs from the French indemnity, which is to be employed in assisting ten thousand men of color to come to us from France. They will, by their intelligence, maintain the peace of the Haytian Empire, which is finally the only source of security to France for her indemnity, and that of Hayti itself.

There are at least fifty thousand small farms at St. Domingo, which could be divided among ten thousand families of color; but the Dominicans are not disposed to give them up. All will be offered to settlers of African blood from the United States, who wish to come to Hayti.

Our brethren in the United States may be certain of success. There is so much land in Hayti that thousands of smart settlers could come out to us from America, and clear up the country, and make it flourish.

Mr. Bigelow's letters about our Emperor are terribly exaggerated. He came here with his head full of ridiculous notions, directly from the United States, to write a book for the Emperor Faustin, and here his letters are coming out, of which he ought to be ashamed; for he has written what he can hardly read, and must have lately improved in his intellect if he can write so well. Mr. Bigelow should not set him up for the lawful lord of the whole island, when we are under the French rule. Faustin has the weakness of his race for fine clothes, and should not carry it to excess, though—which is the dominant language here—than is taught him by rote for scholastic occasions.

If this is the way our friends talk of us in France, we are not surprised that our enemies in America should speak ill of us; but as for Faustin, we can only say, if he does not know how to govern this island, we at least do not keep Bigelow's faith with us, it will all be ours again.
QUAROU.

THE FRENCH ACCOUNT.
We are in the reception of details of the famous mission of Mr. Cazneau at Santo Domingo, and of the negotiations carried on by this diplomatic pair, and of the present state of the Haytian question, which we hope will have the double merit of edifying and of interesting our readers. The correspondent to whom we are indebted for them might have added many others even more piquant. "A great deal might have been said," he writes us, "about Mr. Cazneau personally, the position which he has assumed since his arrival, and especially that of his eccentric half; their establishment in a sort of negro hut, covered with thatch, and other means of seeking popularity, not less singular, contrived by her; but I have endeavored to abstain from everything of a personal nature."

We therefore give the history of this conjugal mission, stripped of all accessories:—

Port au Prince, Domingo, Dec. 1, 1854.
The treaty concluded between the United States and the Dominican Republic, signed on the 7th of August, was printed and laid before the public on the 1st of November. It created here the greatest emotion. It was generally believed that Mr. Cazneau had failed in his mission as to Samana, threatened to return to Washington, and that Mr. Cazneau had taken his threat, he became resigned, and for the present, at least, gave up the Samana project, provided that he obtained a ceded tract. This article would have secured to the United States, under the name of a public naval depot, a tract of land on the Bay of Samana, for the purpose of a naval station, and given the United States jurisdiction over American citizens who should settle upon this tract.

This article of the treaty, which has been for so long a time so frequently mentioned by the attraction of the public, which Mr. Cazneau has so long tried to conceal, and which has spent all Mr. Cazneau's journey across a country not less famous for its iron than its copper, was the only point between this point and New York, the only one put forward to excite the vanity of the Americans, to awaken the attention of the English and French governments, and to make the latter believe that if the treaty was ratified, the independence of Santo Domingo from Hayti, Samana, as its position, threatens not only Hayti, but Cuba and the Spanish islands.

The Cazneau treaty, as signed, stipulates that the powers who shall have signed it within eighteen months, come immediately to secure that of his government, the second for six months, and the third for an indefinite period of delay. But Mr. Cazneau, who lacks a little of that energy of which he speaks, was afraid to send the treaty, such as it was signed, with the French modification to the United States Congress, for fear that it would be rejected, and he chose rather to consider the French text as having been accepted, as last, for the sake of getting his treaty passed. The treaty was signed on the 11th of November; but as it was first agreed upon, before the French modification was added, it aroused the fears of the English and French consuls of Santo Domingo, who dispatched a vessel of war to Port au Prince, and sent the English minister of the foreign affairs belonging to the French naval station of the Antilles, M. Raybaud. He arrived on the 15th at Santo Domingo, on board of a French brig of war, called the Le Yeketallow, and by his parasite, Angulo Guridi, a native of Santo Domingo, presented to the Dominican government the form of a protest, to the French and English consuls, against the treaty signed between the Dominican government and Mr. Cazneau, and threatening them with the arrival of the whole force of the French and English naval forces. To this message, marked by a humor quite in character with M. Raybaud, the Dominican ministers as brief as they were determined.

This energetic language was little favorable to the plans of M. Raybaud, and he was obliged to have recourse to intimidation to the people who were convinced that the treaty was signed, and he excited a strong movement of party on the soil of the offer, provided they submitted to Hayti. The French consul had even offered to pay the Dominicans, because of the color of nineteen-twentieths of the population, a sum of money which could scarcely be honorable to the country without real advantage, and they had declared that they would never unite with the United States because of their local laws and of their institution of slavery. He urged that if the treaty was signed, the white portion of the population exposed, whatever be their fortune and personal merit, to be expelled from the island. The threat of a treaty to the Dominican Congress cooled of wonderfully, and they refused to give their sanction to the modification in the hope of seeing this counter-movement subside. In this state of things, M. Raybaud, seeing the success which he desired, he sailed on the 23d of November a second time for Port au Prince, to get a temporary postponement. The government answered four days after, by a refusal to give a delay, saying that they would wait for no further negotiations, but that as soon as Mr. Cazneau should withdraw the treaty, it it was not ratified, they would invade Santo Domingo. They forbade this presentation at that time. Mr. Cazneau sent a copy of his treaty to Washington, but he has, as a man of color, as are also three out of his four ministers, signed the treaty, and if it is not ratified in eighteen months he would break off all correspondence. He has sent by a vessel belonging to his government, the steamer Metropolis, to his government for instructions. This is where matters stand now. St. Domingo has, and has completely, escaped from the clutches of the French consul; but more particularly of M. Maxime Raybaud, who has for four years used all his influence, that it should be attached to St. Domingo, on his way to Paris, where he was sent by Faustin; and from where M. Raybaud crossed to St. Domingo, with the idea of making it a Haytian province, or at least that he might quietly in the way of a truce, for a long period, between the two countries, which would finally result in a total submission. The establishment of a French naval station at Samana, at which the Haytian government would seem to be with and good cause, singularly alarmed.

The French consul, however, was mistaken as to the devotion of the Dominican Congress, which will give its sanction to the treaty, and Mr. Cazneau will sign within two days the between the readinigs. It is generally supposed that Mr. Cazneau will stay long enough to be able to dispose of such persuasive means, if necessary, as to make the Dominican Congress accede to his details; still it is impossible to discover any advantage to this position, except for the greater or less success of certain parties.

records.headline: The Alexandria Gazette reports a formal protest by General Cazneau
records.summary_en: The Alexandria Gazette reports a formal protest by General Cazneau, the United States Commissioner, to the French and English consuls at St. Domingo, noting that four French warships are currently in the port and an English fleet is shortly expected. In the protest, dated at St. Domingo on November 17, Cazneau declares that French and British agents, aided by a menacing display of armed force before the capital, have overawed and controlled the free action of the Dominican Republic in its relations with the United States. Protesting against this encroachment on the sovereign rights of an independent American power, he affirms the determined purpose of the United States to oppose any measure intended to subject an American nation to the arbitrary will of a foreign power, whether strong or weak among its sister republics.
records.summary_es: La Alexandria Gazette informa que el comisionado de los Estados Unidos, el general Cazneau, ha dirigido una enérgica protesta a los cónsules de Francia e Inglaterra en Santo Domingo, señalando que cuatro buques de guerra franceses se encuentran actualmente en el puerto y que se espera en breve la llegada de una flota inglesa. En la protesta, fechada en Santo Domingo el 17 de noviembre, Cazneau declara que los agentes franceses y británicos, apoyados por un despliegue amenazante de fuerza armada frente a la capital, han intimidado y controlado la libre acción de la República Dominicana en sus relaciones con los Estados Unidos. Al protestar contra esta usurpación de los derechos soberanos de una potencia americana independiente, reafirma el firme propósito de los Estados Unidos de oponerse a cualquier medida destinada a someter a una nación americana a la voluntad arbitraria de una potencia extranjera, sin hacer distinción entre las repúblicas hermanas fuertes y las débiles.

records.full_text:
Our St. Domingo Correspondence.
ST. DOMINGO, Nov. 24, 1854.
Antics of European Diplomacy on the Island—The European Consuls think St. Domingo is Sebastopol—Uncle Sam has his Laugh at them.

The mail packet from St. Thomas brought to St. Domingo on Sunday, 19th inst., news of the fall of Sebastopol. Fresh French and English forces, and great was the joy and loud the shouting thereat.

Mr. Maxime Raybaud, the French Charge d'Affaires at the Haytien court, came here to forbid any treaty whatever with the United States; for, he says "England and France will not permit." This is a simple falsehood, based a good deal like European encroachments on the independence of an American power; but of course it will appear all right to the Haytiens and the Spanish junkers of the Dominican States.

Monsieur Raybaud has lorded it largely over both the white and black governments on this island for some time past, threatening one with the other when he desired to bring it down. He feeds it, now using the seventy millions of francs claimed by his government from Hayti as a screw; now, when he professes a condescending friendship to the Dominicans, to put the Haytiens in the way of conquering this fine territory, in the hope that, after a while, both will be able to pay their debts to France. The Dominicans would rather make a free gift of their country to the United States.

These European Consuls will chafe mightily at seeing all their fine plans frustrated by this treaty with the United States.

But to return to the Sebastopol news: These French and English diplomats in their imagination forgot that Sebastopol was only one extreme corner of the Russian empire, and that it would take a hundred such victories to break down Nicholas, with his six-million subjects, and they carried themselves as if Russia was entirely at their feet.

At their command, the Comandante of St. Domingo was directed to raise the French and English flags to the highest place of honor, higher than a national flag. By some mistake, the officer raised the American flag higher, and had hardly got it hoisted, when in came a messenger in haste from Monsieur Raybaud, ordering down the American flag. The officer attempted to obey, but the obstinate flag took firm hold of the rope by the upper outside corner, and spread out in full size—refusing to come down—there to the confusion... for twenty minutes, our stars half covering the French and English flags, to the supreme anger of Monsieur Raybaud and the British Consul, Mr. Schomburgk, and the secret satisfaction of the Dominicans, who were delighted with this emblem of arrogance. They were compelled to lower all the flags before the stars and stripes could be taken off. Sebastopol was forgotten, and the flags had to be hoisted and saluted the following day.

Then they wrote such a brag story... these diplomatic gentlemen ... that, having disposed of Russia, "Our governments would now turn their attention to the United States."

Sunday was a great Dominican gala day. Some two thousand troops, in full uniform, received their banners and attended divine service. Monsieur Raybaud, taking advantage of the occasion, got a French priest to sing a Te Deum, and preach a sermon, explaining to the troops the glorious Christian victory; for, according to the Padre and this diplomat, the Turks must be super-excellent Christians. Oh, "what a great day for Santo Domingo!"

But the mail packet of the 6th comes in and says that all the news from Europe is false, that Sebastopol was not taken, and that the story of the glorious victory was a great hoax. The Consuls go about with long faces and a very downcast air.

You will know all about the fate of Sebastopol before us; but if it is not taken when this reach you, you may go to bed in peace, for Monsieur Raybaud does not intend taking the United States until Sebastopol is used up.
AN AMERICAN.

St. Domingo, Nov. 25, 1854.
Invasion of the Rights of an American Citizen by the Haytien Consul—Threats of Violence—Expression of American Sympathies—The Feeling of the Dominicans with the United States.

If the Dominicans have a party, and even a press, in the United States, they may seek to deny the facts I relate; but the person legally vested with the character of representative of France and Hayti at this capital, has forced the Dominican government to destroy the liberty of the press, and also prevented the treaty with the United States.

Allow me here to state some facts which will prove I am correct.

I saw in the NEW YORK HERALD of February last, an article containing a very exact description of the festivities of the sixth anniversary of the republic, French republic, with the context, and, on its site; point, Houston and Brasseur, my paper, El Orden. M. Raybaud made very haughty complaints that this was a disrespect to his imperial master, and that the article must be written by an American, because my paper was printed in the government printing office.

President Santana therefore withdrew the privilege, and stopped the Orden. I was ruined; but, feeling the injustice, submitted without murmur.

Again, in October last, I, with two of my Dominican friends, got up a paper called El Oasis, the prospectus of which, as we had not as yet the machinery necessary, we had permission to use the government type and press. No sooner had it appeared, than M. Raybaud again complained, with extreme reserve, in order that this French dictator should not be offended, President Santana again took away our freedom of speech—proposing to continue our editorial observations carefully and exclusively to Dominican affairs.

The treaty with the United States was at this time known to be on the carpet. It excited the enthusiasm of all patriotic Dominicans, but there were also the most violent and absurd slanders put in circulation respecting the object of the mission of General Cazneau—no less than the American government. No one pretends to doubt these vile slanders were prepared at the European Consulates, and were exciting panic among the Haytiens in the country.

The editors of the Fenix, in the simple desire to have the truth understood by the Dominican people, republished the articles from the NEW YORK HERALD, as being printed at the moment for the use of Congress. M. Raybaud came from Hayti to stop the treaty, and he pretended to find in those articles that the Dominican editor was an American paper, and must be stopped.

I happened to see the proofs as they first came from the type, and when he found the trespass... he inserted the word "Santo Domingo," with the headline "Santo Domingo and the United States," he republished the article without any comments, in order that these offensive truths could see the light. I enclose an exact copy of it to the editor of the NEW YORK HERALD, in order that the Americans may know in what manner French agents in Santo Domingo pretend to master American interests and the liberty of the press in St. Domingo.

The article was as follows:
"Our readers will find below the treaty of friendship, alliance and trade, concluded between the United States and the Dominican republic, which we have no doubt will be read with interest by every one of our citizens, not only for the interest it must inspire in the minds of all who sincerely desire a prosperous future for our country, but even more for its effect on the destiny of that interesting island. To those who are spectating this new tie of friendship which is to enlarge our commerce and increase the power and dignity of our country, it will be gratifying to know that it was produced in the atmosphere of suppositions, conjectures and fears which the allies were so anxious to spread over the zenith and scatter the clouds that float in space. No one knew the terms of the treaty until its final signature and general. The only difference is the article regarding Santo Domingo, which is now considered as mutual and general and unquestionable interest. Besides, the terms of this stipulation are equally high on both sides, and it will end by a treaty with the United States.

"The Haytiens, who are alike the enemies of the United States and the Dominican republic, have displayed and are displaying extraordinary alarm at the mission of General Cazneau, the American Plenipotentiary near this government. This is natural—a true treaty between the two republics would not agree with their hopes to make the passive attitude of the United States applicable to all the Spanish country around the gulf... No one can foresee the end of this drama; but there is no reasonable why one American State should not be the friend of another, they try to turn to tricks and falsehoods to prevent the realization of this friendship.

"The press of Hayti, directed by Frenchmen, spreads a fear that General Cazneau came here to exact some concessions in favor of the United States, and to ask a precedence. We can only laugh at these fables and fantasies. What can Hayti do to Santo Domingo? The Haytien press is a St. Domingo Columbia. We will not insult the United States so much as to believe that it would compromise its dignity by taking part in these petty internationalities. We believe, besides, that the Dominican republic, however weak, is strong enough to maintain itself now; for though small in power and population, God, the protector of justice, will save us from the Haytiens, and even in climate—our lack of strength and numbers.

"The editor of the Fenix has republished this article as an ultimatum messis, which we give to these false reports, that those who believe that the United States intends to compromise the independence or sovereignty of the Dominican republic, may see their error. Santo Domingo, if she was not independent, would choose of making this island what nature intended it should be—an asylum for European despotism; and if we believed there was in Samana the seeds of danger to Santo Domingo, we would be the first to oppose the mission of Commodore Perry, of the United States navy, who obtained that point. Is there a Dominican, we would ask, who does not see that foam with consternation and in a state of desperation, all those whose interests are opposed to the prosperity of our country? They see in the progress of the State most dreaded by Hayti. But we say to all these alarms, the treaty with the United States is concluded, and there is nothing in it incompatible with our national independence and sovereignty—so we may smile at all these Haytien reports.

"The treaty is now given to the public light, and we leave it to the judgment of our citizens, whether it is not one of the best steps which the government could have taken, and one which we have conceived for advancing the condition of the country, and one which will bring us fruit.

"It is no slight satisfaction to us, after having been President of the republic, to have effected this convention—and it is a still greater satisfaction when we think, and the great majority of the country is of the same opinion, that it will destroy forever the pretensions of the Cbao, who have thus declared themselves the enemies of our prosperity. So long live the friendship of the American Union a powerful support to our independence, and long live President Santana!

"This article, Mr. Editor, and this alone, was sufficient to cause the arrest of Mr. Guridi, and threatened, at the same time, the hopes of your friend and servant,
ANGULO GU RIDI.

records.full_text:
The Tribune professes to have news of what the "Two-horse Mission," as it calls it, to St. Domingo, up to the 20th. It says that Mr. Cazneau has failed in his mission, and, it is understood, is to be withdrawn, because, upon examination, it has been found that the present Government of St. Domingo shall have the same political and physical relations to the United States that the rest of the world has, namely, foreign, in consideration of the Americans being mostly white, and most of the Dominicans being mostly black.

The Tribune's cause of this "step backward" is reported to be the fact that "the Dominicans are mostly of African descent. It seems that the Government was entirely satisfied with Mr. Cazneau's standard of a white man; but it now turns out that, to speak correct, the President has become cognizant of the color of the nation, only some months since, that there is not a single man connected with the Dominican Government, from the highest to the lowest, who, if brought into United States, would not, by the rule of the State Department, be entitled to a passport, and, strictly speaking, incapable of holding office in a foreign country. It seems our neighbors have got their eyes open, and our Administration is not yet prepared to recognize the nationality of Hayti or St. Domingo, or to exchange with them the international courtesies of independent nations. The Administration, they say, are—they have perceived, though too late for their credit, that they can have no dealings with the Dominicans as an independent nationality. Now, as the Administration have been pleased to avail themselves thus far of our advice in this business, they will pardon us for making one more suggestion. There is but one honest way of acquiring title to any real estate on the Bay of Samana, and that is by negotiations with the Emperor of Hayti, for he is the sovereign of the whole island—the Dominican Government being revolutionary and properly non-extant. The negotiations would be very simple, and the terms very favorable; for all that would be the first step to be taken would be to acknowledge the nationality of the empire—a position so compunctious about which so much pother was made, when it was proposed to acknowledge Hayti, or send a Consul or Commercial Agent. The Emperor of Hayti would, no doubt, gladly send Ministers, or Charges, or Consuls, to the United States, to set off against our Minister, President Pierce, or any of his Cabinet. He is too chivalrous to insist on any difference of color of his representatives here or elsewhere.

It will be a hard case, we own, for the United States for commercial advantages, if we could have no treaty of reciprocity or of alliance or commerce with the island, now some fifty years known as the Empire of Hayti. It makes it worth our while to cultivate friendly relations with them, and there is nothing in the way of it but the foolish fear of offending the Dominicans; which, it seems, is now pretty much over, the nation becoming daily more and more ashamed.

Though the Tribune does not give the source of its information about the results of the "two-horse mission" to St. Domingo, we presume it is derived from one of the span, as we learn that they have recently returned to the United States, and their dissatisfaction with the reception of their bargain is now naturally finding its way into the public journals. Is it possible that one of these gentlemen, to wake up his resolution about the acknowledgment of the nationality of St. Domingo, which he offered, it is promised to wake it up the next day, and yet it has already slept nine months—an ominous number. Surely it is time something came of it.

records.headline: Pierce's Diplomacy in Dominica.
records.summary_en: According to *The Liberator*, Secretary Marcy withheld a treaty granting the United States a naval station at the Bay of Samaná from the Senate due to fears of abolition and amalgamation, and attempted to have the Ambassador take it back. To overcome legislative obstacles in Dominica to this plan, Mrs. Cazneau reportedly prepared a *coup d'état* to grant the President dictatorial powers. Additionally, Mr. Cazneau engaged in a protest-based correspondence with British and French Consuls regarding European interference, prompting non-conciliatory replies and the arrival of three French warships before the city.

records.full_text:
From the New York Tribune.
PIERCE'S DIPLOMACY IN DOMINICA.

We have received some curious and interesting intelligence of a late date from St. Domingo city. It seems that, by management, underhandedness, and the conjugal representations of Messrs. Pierce and Cazneau had, by some oversight, or possibly by design, succeeded in negotiating a treaty, concluded and signed on October 5, on the part of the United States and the Dominican Republic, by which all the privileges guaranteed to any white foreigner, including rights of property, &c., in any part of the Dominican Republic, are secured to the United States—or, rather, to the citizens of the United States (for the Dominican Government, by the last step of our diplomacy, expressly excludes colored people of the empire, or of both, we are not informed) was secured to us. In return, we grant to the Dominicans right in any part of the United States that we grant to any white foreigner. Along with this concession on our part, it is true that a naval station on the Bay of Samana is secured to us; but this was not enough to commend the treaty, and to allay the fears of abolition and amalgamation which it caused at once in the bosom of Mr. Marcy, who determined to withhold it from the Senate, and to have the Embassador attempt to take it back if possible.

It seems, however, that there are serious obstacles in St. Domingo to the accomplishment of this natural wish on the part of our cautious but innovating Secretary. These obstacles the daring mind of Mrs. Cazneau proposed to overcome in a manner which would do no discredit to any feminine author of modern times. If an absurd prejudice of color is in the way; very well, abolish it! This was done. A decree was passed by the President of the Republic with dictatorial powers, and a treaty is, accordingly, being prepared by the fertile mind of Mr. Marcy's female plenipotentiary.

By way, probably, of varying the labors of this state-craft, Mrs. Cazneau has also been engaged in a correspondence with the British and French Consuls, in which, by a method of argument based on the Monroe doctrine, we presume, against the interference of European powers, she combats the counter schemes of Dominica. Their replies are said to be in very lively language, not backing up our Envoy. About the same time, three French ships-of-war, (the frigate Penelope, the brig Oreste, and the steamer Caiman,) entered the harbor, as did a Spanish war-steamer, (Francisco de Asis,) staying all three weeks, during which period, some British men-of-war were daily expected. Still, Mrs. Cazneau held her ground, undismayed by iron-sides, and hoisted the star-spangled banner, as an indication of the presence of the American diplomatic representatives. And there we will take our leave of them for the present, congratulating Mr. Marcy upon the remarkable vigor displayed by his diplomatic agent, and especially on its unequalled brilliancy in St. Domingo.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
The Government Blockade by French and English War Steamers—The Disaffirmance of the Encroachment—Grand Political Stroke of the Associated Soulouque—Louis Napoleon and Padre Higue—How Santana Outwitted, and the Americans Hatted—The Treaty Negotiations and In and Out of Control—International Law—What will be done at Washington?

Our situation is rather novel and extraordinary here in Santo Domingo. The Dominican government is in a state of silent blockade by the naval forces of France and England. It is no doubt very convenient to blockade a seaport, but to blockade a government, to invest it, to subjugate the action of a nation by force, yet without war, is a refined diplomatic trick which the black emperor Soulouque has made the two great empires perform for his own private purposes, and is in a fair way to make them conquer the whites for him without costing him a dollar. Soulouque is not the thick-headed, thick-lipped, stupid negro Mr. Bigelow represents him. He is as black and cruel as his infernal majesty of still warmer regions, but he has also enough of his sharpness to keep the French and English war steamers doing his errands, and may shove them into a war with the United States for his own exclusive benefit.

When Ventura Baez was President of the republic, Soulouque had arranged with him to deliver Santo Domingo to Hayti, but the plot was discovered and Baez was exiled. In the project he was assisted by a French priest—that was a priest, named Elias, who, as the price of his treason, was to be made archbishop of the whole island. After the plot was discovered, the French priest was exiled with Baez, and, like him, went to France, and was made much of by Louis Napoleon, who gave him a large salary from the secret service fund, and the cross of the Legion of Honor. He was sent back to the West Indies, with a salary to act for the white government. The French Consul-General compelled the Dominican government to receive him, although they saw through his plot, which was a bitter pill for the whites with this Haytien priest. The moment he landed he commenced preaching a crusade against Santana and the Americans, and formed a party to bring back Baez, and raise the Haytien flag.

Santo Domingo contains only about 100,000 souls, less than a mile square (within the walls), and pretty much controlled by the negroes and foreign merchants. San Domingo is the key to the island. Soulouque hates the Americans, and are entirely devoted to France and England. The Dominican government deserves the sympathy of the world, for planting the flag of the white race, and for planting it forever under the guns of Hayti, and the Dominican people, who are almost all the solid respectable population throughout the country, are in favor of the Americans, but they are overawed by the priests, and by the action of the United States. They can see that Faustin I., under the cover of the French and English government dares not trust to the slow movements of American policy. It had hardly signed a treaty with the Dominican Republic when Santana discovered it, and, without calling it a blockade, they took positions to command the city, and stopped the treaty. Maxime Raybaud, the French Minister, went about the city from daybreak to midnight to see the President, and everything shows the most hostile and mischievous action with regard to the United States. The English Consul lackeys his steps with the most ludicrous servility. Between Raybaud, Segovia and Soulouque, Santana has an uneasy life. When Raybaud arrived, the Dominican Congress passed a law authorizing the President of ratifying the treaty, but the Councils ordered Santana not to sign it in consequence of having foreign steamers, and held it back. The Dominican Congress had been called together to ratify the treaty, but when they came, were told that France and England would bring Baez and a Haytien army upon them, and Raybaud and Segovia in a hurry to avoid taking up the treaty. Several members of Congress then wrote Santana, asking if he did not notice that him no free action could be expected of that state body while surrounded by foreign forces on land and sea. Seeing this, and that the Consuls had blockaded the city, Santana informed the Congress that he had resigned. On this, the two Consuls sent Santana word to the effect that his government was treating with the enemy, and that they could not submit to the dictation or interference of the diplomatic agents of Europe.

Santana's language is no doubt severe, but let us recall how large the Vance Congress had talked about Santana, and he may be excused for giving this insulting dictation might arouse it to deeds. They sent word to the Consuls to leave the city, and the bomb-ketch Fort Fanfarron—was coming here to do it if they did not move, Santana gave orders about the treaty. They directed Santana to put the treaty before them again, and on the 1st of December Santana sent it back to the Congress ratified.

Raybaud and Padre Elias had arranged it through Santana, that it should be stopped. A phrase most insulting to the United States was written on the margin of the printed treaty, in Raybaud's own hand, and sent to the members in Congress, who were to propose to Santana that, notwithstanding this most explicit, insulting act—if not slaughter—of the treaty, when all turned out white Santana gave up the country, that the American plenipotentiary had withdrawn it. When Santana sent it back to the Congress, the delegates were under European duress, and the United States can have no doubt that they have been blockaded. The whole community is in a fever of anxiety. Foreigners have sent petitions to Congress to go on and smother the treaty, as they say, for the peace of the country. They say that the American plenipotentiary can have no such power over Santana, when it is so far off, and here is the French. Congress can tell me that Raybaud found he could not bring Santana to his terms, he threatened to abandon Dominican executive and this tete de fer of an American plenipotentiary, he had best make a jump from the eagle's nest, on the heights of San Carlos, to preach in Hayti, and leave Santana in the lurch.

This was when it appears they made nothing out of it. General Cazneau came here on the 13th of July, not for hostility, per se, as one of the primary conditions of a recognition of the Dominican Republic, but to obtain a treaty, and there was no backsliding wanting on the part of Dominica, that granting the Consul an equal right with any other nation—and of all the rights of the signature, this was no longer the case—that in the annihilation of the commercial treaty, the American government, and of its power to render the proposed equivalent, that the treaty was lost, for Santana's contract was annihilated with them. He said he was authorized to treaty with an independent and sovereign republic, and not with France and England, and, there was no independent republic when it was unable to arrest the treaty or control its ratification, it became a nullity. When the American agent was contemplated, and had altogether ceased to exist as a government, Santana gave the answer to Raybaud's position, that his powers ended with the treaty, and the treaty was no longer binding, and that it was prevented that act until it was ratified by one of the parties—all according to the treaty, not only by words, but the treaty having changed conditions, through foreign interference, while still incomplete, was null, void, and of no effect.

Whether the American plenipotentiary will take Santana's part, only Gen. Cazneau's law. If this is true, it has upset the French and English plot, and turned the laugh off the Yankees in disgust, by freeing the Dominican Congress from foreign influence. The two agents look extremely perplexed in the face of the British Consul, and so sour and yellow as Raybaud is, they say he looks blue at this stroke. Now, what will Mr. Pierce do with this blockade? Will they send down ships and drop a bombshell on the foreign agents who have blockaded two great empires of France and England? If we thought you would take no notice of this, we would advise the American steam frigates and spite before this could come to your hands. It is black and cowardly in France and England to force the poor Uriah of Santana to do what they dare not do themselves, and the United States will be shameful if, after all their Baltimore speeches, they let a French and English squadron drive them away from Santo Domingo.
ESPERANZA.

records.full_text:
From the Courier des Etats-Unis.

We are in possession of details on the famous mission of Mr. and Mrs. Cazneau to St. Domingo, of the negotiation, broken off by a diplomatic pair, and of the present state of the Republic. If General Cazneau had only the double merit of edifying and of amusing our readers, the extraordinary mission which was granted to him might have added many pages to our comic papers. "A great deal might have been said," he writes us, "about Mr. Cazneau, personally; his mission, which he has assumed since his arrival, and especially that of his spouse; their daily life at General Cazneau's, in a sort of negro hut, covered with thatch, and their excess of artistic luxury, by no means singular, contrived by her; but I have endeavors to write history, and everything which might seem like personality."

We proceed to the history of this Dominican signal, stripped of all accessories:

ST. DOMINGO, Nov. 5, 1854.

The treaty concluded between the United States and the Dominican Republic, signed on the 5th of October, was printed and laid before the Congress on the 9th of October. This negotiation has been conducted with the greatest secrecy, General Santana himself failing in his designs on Samana, threatened with a siege by the English. As soon as notice was taken of his threat, he became resigned. In the site granted by Santana to the American mission, part of article 28th of his project is found. "The Dominican Republic grants to the United States, under the form of a twenty-nine years' lease, the port of Samana, for the purpose of a maritime establishment, and for the creation of a naval station over American colonists who should settle near this establishment.

The shores of this Bay of Samana, for some time past, as reported to Congress by the direction of the profile, are almost a desert, and are situated in the East, or rather by sea, making a journey across a country red less barren. The Dominican Government, in sacrificing a portion of its territory, to justify a demand so suspicious, would naturally awaken the attention of the English and French Governments, who alone, for several years, have effectually protected the Dominican Republic against an invasion from Hayti; Samana by its position threatens not only Porto Rico and Cuba, but also all the Antilles.

The Cazneau treaty, as signed, stipulates that the ratifications shall be exchanged at St. Domingo, within the period of ten months, or sooner if possible. But, to the great regret of the American negotiator should, therefore, have been made, because the Dominican Government, or rather the President, Santana, has refused to ratify it. Mr. Cazneau, who lacks a little of perfection in diplomatic matters, believed that he had only to have his treaty ratified here before its presentation to the Senate, and had no suspicion that it would carry miscarriage in St. Domingo during the interval. But the English and French agents exerted, for the sake of peace, an extra pressure on the President Santana. On the 13th of November; but as it was first proposed, Mr. Cazneau took to his bed, put on by his mettlesome yokefellow, and by his own orders, the American Consul, Mr. Schomburg, in Havana, addressed a letter, in the form of a protest against the interference of the French and English agents, of interfering in his affairs—exclusively American. The reply of the Dominican Government was not long coming; the French Consul, Mr. Raybaud, being present, the Dominican Government by a foreign naval officer, demanding an answer to the protest of Mr. Cazneau, threatening, an answer was returned, couched in words of strict compliance with international law.

Meanwhile, public opinion, quite favorable to the Treaty, took up the question, and it became decidedly hostile to it when the people understood that the Treaty granted a privilege almost sacred to the citizens of either party on the site of the navy yard, and an exemption from the local laws and customs, would be only a rule for the Dominican Republic, consisting of nineteen-twentieths of the population. People began to say that no treaty could be made to the country without real reciprocity, and that such reciprocity was impossible with the United States, because of their local laws and customs. They resented the exclusions, the contempt, and the insults, to which blacks and people of color were exposed, whatever be their fortune and personal merits.

Under these circumstances, the President sent the treaty to the Dominican Congress cooled down by these objections, which he urged it to adjourn the presentation, in the hope of seeing the text modified by Mr. Cazneau. His measures to effect this not having all the success which he desired, he sent on the 23d of November a very sharp note to the local Government, to compel this postponement. The Government answered, four days after, that it had only yielded to his importunity in presenting the Treaty to Congress immediately, and that, unless Mr. Cazneau should withdraw the treaty, it knew of no principle of international law which could forbid the presentation at that time. At the same time, it wrote a note to President Santana, who is a gentleman of color, requesting the withdrawal of the Treaty, which he regarded as another insult, and that he would take no part in the negotiation. He has sent, by a much better operator than Mr. Cazneau, Mr. Delmonte, to your Government, for instructions, and it is said, for full powers. General Santana, who has chased away the English and French agents, and who is well disposed towards your Government, and who has consulted, but more particularly of M. Raybaud, of France, and Mr. Schomburg, of England, has taken a fortnight's leave of absence, and not in his public character. Mr. Raybaud return to St. Domingo, with the idea of legalizing, merely as a friend, to protect the interests of his countrymen, or to trace, for a long period, between the two portions of the island. The draft of this treaty was not more than the imminence of an American establishment at Samana, which both the Haytien Government and people seem to regard as an act of hostility towards them.

The treaty will be submitted to-morrow to the consideration of the Dominican Congress, which will give its opinion after three readings, with which the laws of Santo Domingo require three readings. It is generally supposed that it will be rejected, unless Mr. Cazneau's text is changed to dispose of such persuasive means, if necessary, that the result on this subject no longer remains certain; still it is impossible to discover any trace of an understanding between the greater of the contracting parties. — X.

records.headline: Reprinting a January 3 article titled "The Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: Reprinting a January 3 article titled "The Dominican Republic and the United States," the New York Herald reports that the measure of annexing Santo Domingo does not find general approbation even in the United States and meets complete opposition in the place most interested in the question. To illustrate domestic opposition, the writer quotes a manifesto to the American people issued at a June 20 meeting in Washington chaired by Representative Solomon Foot of Vermont on behalf of members of Congress opposed to the Nebraska bill. That manifesto warns of "unmistakable indications" of a design to annex the eastern part of San Domingo, subjugate the entire island, and restore it to slavery, followed by an alliance with Brazil to extend slavery into the valley of the Amazon. The writer praises these words as coming from Americans moved by the natural rights of mankind rather than the desire for territorial aggrandizement prevailing in the Southern states.
records.summary_es: Al reproducir un artículo del 3 de enero titulado «La República Dominicana y los Estados Unidos», el New York Herald informa que la medida de anexar a Santo Domingo no cuenta con la aprobación general ni siquiera en los Estados Unidos y encuentra una oposición total en el lugar más interesado en la cuestión. Para ilustrar la oposición interna, el autor cita un manifiesto dirigido al pueblo estadounidense emitido en una reunión celebrada el 20 de junio en Washington bajo la presidencia del representante Solomon Foot, de Vermont, en nombre de los miembros del Congreso opuestos al proyecto de ley de Nebraska. Dicho manifiesto advierte sobre «indicios inequívocos» de un propósito de anexar la parte oriental de Santo Domingo, subyugar toda la isla y restituirla al dominio de la esclavitud, seguido de una alianza con Brasil para extender la esclavitud hacia el valle del Amazonas. El articulista elogia estas palabras por provenir de estadounidenses movidos por los derechos naturales de la humanidad y no por el afán de engrandecimiento territorial que prevalece en los estados del Sur.

records.headline: Continuing its report on the Dominican Republic, an article
records.summary_en: Continuing its report on the Dominican Republic, an article in the New York Herald observes that nine-tenths of Santo Domingo's population of about 140,000 are Black or people of color. The writer states that France has taken measures to counteract American propensities toward annexing West Indian colonies, while Spain has been awakened to the imminent danger threatening Cuba and Puerto Rico should Americans take possession of Samaná or any other locality in Santo Domingo. According to the dispatch, the French chargé d'affaires and consul general at Haiti arrived in the capital and worked in concert with the English consul to warn President Santana's administration of the danger of permitting Americans to settle at Samaná. His effort was backed by the arrival of a division of the French West Indies squadron consisting of a 40-gun frigate, the 20-gun l'Oreste, and the 6-gun steam sloop l'Ardent.

records.summary_en: A Dominican writes from Santo Domingo (Dec. 19, 1854) on the French and English consuls' seizure of his government: their written protest against the Cazneau treaty, the threat that Faustin would land Báez with an army, and Santana's silent resistance.

Presently the American plenipotentiary enters the palace, in his plain black suit, and passes quite calmly into the President's private cabinet, where he remained so late that an officer had to be sent to the St. Carlos, or Gonde gate, to order it kept open for General Cazneau (who lives in the country), to pass out after the interview. The morning after this conference, their consular majesties were notified that their objections to the American treaty must be put in writing. records.summary_en: According to the *Thibodaux Minerva* of February 10, 1855, the French and British consuls cautioned the Dominican government against allowing Americans to settle at Samana, a warning reinforced by the arrival of a French naval division under Captain Fournier. The newspaper also noted public speculation regarding this naval demonstration, anticipated arrivals of English and Spanish warships, and reported that the Spanish government intended to send an accredited agent to Santo Domingo.

El rotativo reflejaba las conjeturas populares ante semejante despliegue marítimo, la inminente llegada de unidades de guerra británicas y españolas, y la resolución de Madrid de comisionar a un representante acreditado ante Santo Domingo.

records.full_text: EUROPEAN INTERFERENCE AT ST. DOMINGO.—London news, says the Baltimore Sun, furnishes further evidence of the fact that the British and French consuls did interfere to prevent the adoption by the Dominican Government of a treaty with the United States. It is stated that in July last the British consul had with the President of the Dominican Republic, which it says 'may be taken as the first direct opposition of the British agents upon the Samana,' the direct opposition we suppose having been found unavailing. The French consul subsequently joined the British consul in impressing upon the Dominican Government the dangerous step of permitting the Americans to settle at Samana. The means which were taken to make this impression are very complacently dwelt upon as follows: 'Raybaud is renowned for the energetic manner with which he knows how to make a powerful impression upon such weak minds as those that compose President Santa Anna's administration, and in this position he was powerfully backed by the arrival of a division of the French squadron at the West Indies, consisting of the frigate Penelope, 40; l'Oreste, 20; and the steam sloop l'Ardent, 6, under the command of the Chef de Division, Capt. Fourier. The object of this demonstration is not yet known, and the surmises of the public are various. It is likewise rumored that one or more English men-of-war are daily expected to join the French division, while the arrival of a large Spanish war steamer is equally looked for. It has been subsequently reported from Porto Rico, that the Spanish Government intended to send an accredited agent to Santo Domingo.'

records.headline: The Western Democrat publishes a letter stating that the population of the Dominican Republic consists of whites
records.summary_en: The Western Democrat publishes a letter stating that the population of the Dominican Republic consists of whites, persons of mixed white and Indian blood, and mulattoes, similar to all the Spanish American republics, and noting that President Santana and his secretaries are white men. The writer remarks that the Dominican people have been misrepresented by some American newspapers and urges greater commercial and political interest in the country on the part of the people and government of the United States. Arguing that St. Domingo is much richer than Cuba, he cites its mines of silver, gold, coal, copper, and quicksilver, its ship timber, mahogany, and other precious woods, and declares that the Bay of Samaná is the key to the Caribbean Sea just as Cuba is the key to the Gulf of Mexico. The writer adds that he is not a Dominican, having been born in Puerto Rico, educated at Havana, and later naturalized in the United States.
records.summary_es: El Western Democrat publica una carta en la que se afirma que la población de la República Dominicana se compone de blancos, personas de sangre mestiza blanca e indígena, y mulatos, de manera similar a todas las repúblicas hispanoamericanas, y señala que el presidente Santana y sus secretarios son hombres blancos. El autor observa que el pueblo dominicano ha sido tergiversado por algunos periódicos estadounidenses e insta a que el pueblo y el gobierno de los Estados Unidos presten mayor interés comercial y político al país. Sosteniendo que Santo Domingo es mucho más rico que Cuba, destaca sus minas de plata, oro, carbón, cobre y azogue, sus maderas aptas para embarcaciones, la caoba y otras maderas preciosas, y declara que la bahía de Samaná es la llave del mar Caribe así como Cuba es la llave del golfo de México. El autor añade que no es dominicano, pues nació en Puerto Rico, se educó en La Habana y posteriormente se incorporó a los Estados Unidos.

records.headline: A brief notice in the Springfield Weekly Republican states that St. Domingo
records.summary_en: A brief notice in the Springfield Weekly Republican states that St. Domingo is in some respects preferable to Cuba and is much richer in natural resources. According to the paper, the island possesses mines of silver, gold, coal, copper, and quicksilver, along with various kinds of timber suitable for shipbuilding, mahogany, and other precious woods. The item concludes that if Cuba is the key to the Gulf of Mexico, the Bay of Samaná in the Dominican Republic is undoubtedly the key to the Caribbean Sea.

El artículo concluye que si Cuba es la llave del golfo de México, la bahía de Samaná en la República Dominicana es, sin duda, la llave del mar Caribe.

records.headline: Under the headline "The Dominican Republic," the Richmond Daily Dispatch reports
records.summary_en: Under the headline "The Dominican Republic," the Richmond Daily Dispatch reports that the country's population consists of whites, persons of mixed white and Indian blood, and mulattoes, corresponding to the population of the other Spanish American republics. Quoting a letter, the paper states that President Santana and his secretaries are white men and argues that Cuba is by no means preferable to the island of St. Domingo. Instead, the letter describes St. Domingo as much richer than Cuba, possessing silver, gold, coal, copper, and quicksilver mines as well as ship timber, mahogany, and other precious woods, while characterizing the Bay of Samaná in the Dominican Republic as the key to the Caribbean Sea.

Citando una carta, el periódico señala que el presidente Santana y sus secretarios son hombres blancos y sostiene que Cuba no es de ningún modo preferible a la isla de Santo Domingo. Por el contrario, la carta describe a Santo Domingo como mucho más rico que Cuba, dotado de minas de plata, oro, carbón, cobre y azogue, así como de maderas para embarcaciones, caoba y otras maderas preciosas, al tiempo que califica a la bahía de Samaná en la República Dominicana como la llave del mar Caribe.

records.headline: An article in the Green-Mountain Freeman reports that the American plenipotentiary in Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: An article in the Green-Mountain Freeman reports that the American plenipotentiary in Santo Domingo has openly hinted at the risk of filibustering expeditions like those that have threatened Cuba, suggesting that Greytown is not the only place Americans can lay in ashes and that the city of St. Domingo is within their reach. According to the paper, his countrymen immediately provoked a quarrel in the roadstead of St. Domingo, which quickly brought two British steam sloops, a French frigate, and two war brigs to the scene. The article adds that the Americans seek to establish a foothold at Samaná, where a watch is being maintained against invaders, and remarks that the Dominicans are likely aware that any invasion of their coasts will depend in part on the course of the war in the Crimea.
records.summary_es: Un artículo del Green-Mountain Freeman informa que el plenipotenciario estadounidense en Santo Domingo ha insinuado abiertamente el riesgo de expediciones filibusteras como las que han amenazado a Cuba, sugiriendo que Greytown no es el único lugar que los estadounidenses pueden reducir a cenizas y que la ciudad de Santo Domingo está a su alcance. Según el periódico, sus compatriotas provocaron de inmediato una disputa en la rada de Santo Domingo, lo que atrajo rápidamente al lugar a dos corbetas de vapor británicas, una fragata francesa y dos bergantines de guerra. El artículo añade que los estadounidenses desean establecer una posición en Samaná, donde se mantiene la vigilancia ante la llegada de invasores, y observa que los dominicanos probablemente saben que cualquier invasión de sus costas dependerá en parte del curso de la guerra en Crimea.

records.headline: A correspondent's letter from the City of Santo Domingo describes a military commission that sentenced General Pelletier
records.summary_en: A correspondent's letter from the City of Santo Domingo describes a military commission that sentenced General Pelletier, General Aybar, Francisco Ruiz and others accused of conspiracy to death, with others sentenced to expatriation, imprisonment or banishment. After the condemned men's children pleaded for grace, the prisoners were led to the execution ground on May 21, knelt while their sentence was read and faced the firing party, until General Santana cried halt and had a pardon for the three read aloud; Ruiz rose from his knees having lost his reason under the horror. The letter adds that the pardoned men received passports to leave the country and that upwards of fifty individuals were banished, including women and children and the sisters of ex-President Baez.
records.summary_es: La carta de un corresponsal desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo describe una comisión militar que condenó a muerte al general Pelletier, al general Aybar, a Francisco Ruiz y a otros acusados de conspiración, mientras otros fueron condenados a expatriación, prisión o destierro. Después de que los hijos de los condenados suplicaran gracia, los prisioneros fueron llevados al lugar de ejecución el 21 de mayo, se arrodillaron mientras se leía su sentencia y quedaron frente al pelotón de fusilamiento, hasta que el general Santana gritó alto e hizo leer en voz alta un indulto para los tres; Ruiz se levantó de rodillas habiendo perdido la razón por el horror. La carta añade que los indultados recibieron pasaportes para salir del país y que más de cincuenta personas fueron desterradas, incluidas mujeres y niños y las hermanas del expresidente Báez.

records.full_text:
The Pierce diplomacy, as such recognized through Europe and the United States, is winning for its originators and supporters a reputation which will be well remembered long after his Presidential term has expired.

The representative of the United States to Belgium was a studied deception, official and personal, with all the members of his Cabinet. Jealousy and suspicion, between member and member, were in part the natural consequences of this system of deceit, and this state of feeling was on the increase, until an explanation was forced, and the cause of the difficulty was traced to the treachery of the President.

This discovery was followed up by rumors of Cabinet dissensions, threats of exposure of the President's duplicity, and a general loss of confidence throughout the newspaper press and the public mind. Failing at home in character, Mr. Soulé, the Minister of the United States to Spain, was honored as the first upon whom the experiment was to be tried. His failure at Madrid, is the by-word of all diplomatic circles throughout Europe. Nor was to the United States the attainment of the object which was to have been the special feature of the mission. The representative of the United States fell at once in Spanish estimation; it created difficulties between the United States Minister and the court to which he was accredited, until finally discovering that the President's confidential diplomacy had been the main cause of the trouble, running as it did in opposition to instructions received from the State Department, he expressed a preference to do his duty to the United States, willing, for the reputation of his country, to suffer the blame of 'Pierce diplomacy,' rather than offer his sovereign a reason that details would have compromised or disgraced the head of the American republic.

If the first essay of General Pierce's new system of 'Pierce diplomacy' was suggested in the ever-memorable Ostend conference, it was as unfortunate in its intended continuation. This convention originated and its proceedings were dictated by President Pierce. The belligerent character given to it was a proposition from the intrigant, who through private influence obtained the position of Chairman of Foreign Relations, imagining that their publicity would add support to his reputation as a skilful diplomat. How stands the case? Upon the arrival of French steamers of war, who entered the Dominican harbor, after the convention at Ostend, the French and Spanish agents, and the Spanish and French flags were raised, and the Dominican Minister for Foreign Affairs, in a letter to our representative, by the French Minister for Foreign Affairs:—'Whether His Majesty should regard Santo Domingo as a Spanish or a French colony, is not yet decided;' and his 'reasons for asking the question were: First, the proceedings at the Ostend Convention, official transcripts of which had been placed before the United States Congress, and copies of which had been forwarded to the French Government by the President.' A reading of the Ostend documents will show how far the question, thus submitted, was an improper one.

The same attempt at secrecy of General Pierce has been felt, as well as in England, by the same species of confidence which our ministers have hitherto enjoyed. It would be difficult to credit this towards his subordinates, but it is nevertheless known and understood to have been the case. Nor is it to be regarded the humiliating abandonment of our claim for damages committed by the government at the Hague? Mr. Marcy writes one dispatch, and General Pierce writes another, for an immediate settlement of the amount specified. He does so; and by this means the rights of American citizens and assistance to her claims are made. Daily interviews with the ministry are asked for and obtained, and the threats of General Pierce made to bear upon the question at a specified moment, and the glad news is despatched to Washington that the business is settled. The new thought strikes the President, and no blame whatever is chargeable to the Hague government, for it was only following out General Pierce's suggestion. An enviable position truly for an American representative to be placed in. To the other States of Europe, to which we will return, after a visit to St. Domingo. A treaty with this government was well known to have been a favorite idea with General Pierce. Through the ability of his agent, Gen. Cazneau, a most liberal one was agreed upon, and to make it valid, a little formal ceremony was necessary. This treaty brought a protest from the British and French Ministers at Washington, which had the recognition of Mr. Pierce. The British and French agents, who entered the Dominican harbor, and the British and French flags were raised, and the Dominican Minister for Foreign Affairs, in a letter to our representative, by order of his government, stated that the treaty between St. Domingo and the United States was ratified. This flagrant interference was submitted to by our President, who acknowledged the propriety of the protest of the foreign representatives against a treaty with that government, and in part forcing our Minister to abandon the treaty altogether. We shall return to this subject at some future day, and the following somewhat interesting facts have been furnished us:—'Does General Pierce imagine that he has established a secret diplomacy?' I thought a brief history of this statesman's operations in that department of politics, might not be without its interest.

The second edition of Mr. Pierce's system of secret diplomacy, while on terms of amity and friendship with another nation, has been carried out by him, while such nations as may be waging war to their injury and detriment, are compelled to suffer, by the standard of right and wrong, and under the cover of the foreign policy of General Pierce. Judge for yourself of its truth and justice. Shortly after the departure of our government of the present war in the East it was understood that Mr. Belmont, who had returned home a very few weeks, had declared his sympathy with Russia, and was determined to assist Russia, even with the whole cabinet. Marcy, in his despatches to Mr. Belmont, instructed him to remain strictly neutral, to observe all proper respect for the subject, and condemned everything bearing upon it, which was strictly carried out by our Minister during the present war. Further than this Marcy could not go. But Gen. Pierce, in his private correspondence with Mr. Belmont, urged upon him to aid Russia to the utmost of his power, copies of which were given to scientific and worthy American, then in Europe, who transmitted them to the French Government. The result was that the Emperor, as a result of the war, which was strongly in favor of Russia, demanded an explanation from Mr. Belmont.

This confidence led to private correspondence, until Mr. Marcy, who had been kept in ignorance of all that had passed, was compelled to send one dispatch after another, giving whatever is of interest to our Minister at the Hague. Knowing these facts, instructions were sent to the Minister for Foreign Affairs at the Royal Court, and a more disgraceful diplomatic transaction has never taken place. It is probable that this discovery led to the resignation of Mr. Soulé, who was also a resident. It will be remembered that a week or two before the resignation of Mr. Soulé, a rumors prevailed throughout the United States, and at Washington of important despatches from our Minister at Madrid. A messenger arrived, and went directly to the President's house, who received them from the Minister, but instead of giving them to Mr. Marcy, he put them in his pocket and took them with him to his country residence. Mr. Marcy called for them, but could not get them. Enough was known, however, as to their contents, which he had broadly hinted at, instead of performing his duty as a public officer, he, like a southern statesman, the proposed personal friend of General Pierce, preferred to use the President as a channel of private interviews between our Minister and the Prudential government, which resulted in Mr. Marcy tendering his resignation, which Gen. Pierce refused to accept, and indirectly intimating that Prussia would be regarded as a neutral States in the event of French or English interference.

In connection with this subject, we would add, that our representative at Russia, dictated by President Pierce, without the knowledge of the Secretary of State, sent a dispatch to St. Petersburg, and in the opening notes, it was found that Austria had spoken insultingly of our President, and Mr. Pierce, through his private secretary, sent a note to our Minister at Russia to presume that no such communication would have been made by Austria, without his authority, and that an explanation must be demanded of Austria. Such was the position of the United States and Russia; and it is still better understood, that should any future belligerent action take place in carrying out the act of Congress relative to the building of six war steamers, which the navy will require, if required, every available aid from three of the European Powers will be placed at the disposal of Russia. President Pierce, foreseeing this state of things, and with the view of securing his election, has taken these means to accomplish it, and when these facts are made when it is known to that, produce so important an effect, in forcing upon the United States a violation of treaty stipulation with foreign governments?

The subject will be brought up at the next session of Congress, when it will be vain for General Pierce to try to screen himself, and he will be held responsible for his actions foreign from the moment of his inauguration.

records.full_text:
The anti-American journals of Europe have largely occupied themselves, in concert with their faithful allies—the disunion press of this country—in misrepresenting the motives and circumstances of the treaty which I had concluded with the Dominican republic, but which was afterwards set aside by the hostile interference of France and England. This was to be expected; for the enemies of American progress instinctively favor any attack on the internal peace or national greatness of our republic; and as naturally oppose whatever tends to give the United States pre-eminence over the European kingdoms of their idolatry.
If such a thing exists as an "American system of policy," the Dominican republic had the strongest claims on the friendly notice of our government, and, at the solicitation of many Spanish-American friends who felt the importance of the crisis, I caused those claims and the condition of that country to be laid before President Pierce at the commencement of his administration.
Its geographical vicinity and central position were urged in behalf of interests common to both nations, as well as its desirable harbors; its valuable products—exactly what our country does not produce, and must purchase; its wants—exactly what our people can supply on the best terms; its commanding situation at the intersection of the great and growing lines of American commerce; its free and liberal institutions; its expressed wish to enter into closer relations with its "great neighbor of the north; and, not least among those considerations, the significant fact—which no American patriot can, and which no American statesman will, overlook—that this neglected republic is the only territory in the whole circle of West India islands under American rule.
This solitary foothold of American nationality is struggling for life against the attempts of Solouque to reduce it to a negro despotism. He claims for the negroes, under the title they acquired by their former massacres of the whites, the right to hold the remnant of the race in subjection, and to blot out civil and religious liberty at their pleasure. France and England secretly foment these pretensions, and they are sustained, more or less openly, by the leading disunion journals in the United States.
The Dominicans asked nothing but to be left in the peaceful possession of their own patrimony, and to receive from the United States the moral aid of a national recognition and the encouragement of a fair reciprocal treaty. Their object was a stable and independent nationality, with free security of person, property and religion for all creeds, classes, and races; and to serve the Dominican people in this necessity was also the soundest course of policy for the United States.
In plain terms, these are the questions before us: Shall the entire West Indies, with their one hundred thousand square miles of territory, and their three millions of inhabitants, be wholly Africanized and made the instruments of European opposition to American progress, or shall we encourage the Dominican republic to maintain an independent nationality and become the nucleus of an American system in the Antilles? Shall the allied powers, who boast that their position at the gates of the Gulf of Mexico enables them "at any time to cut in twain the commerce between the Northern and Southern States" of the Union, be permitted to increase this power by new encroachments, to exclude us altogether, while they usurp Samana, the key of the Caribbean sea, as they have before usurped the control of San Juan, the invaluable inlet of the Nicaragua route, and the Ruatan archipelago, the general outpour of our isthmus transit to California, or shall we be allowed to obtain by fair negotiation one haven of refuge in our own American seas where we can treat guaranteed all the rights of trade, travel, and residence conceded to the citizens of the most favored nations, under the same universal and applicable conditions of obedience to the laws of the country while within their jurisdiction.
The wise liberality of the Dominican laws enabled me to engraft in the permanent conditions of amity perfect freedom and security of conscience, worship, and property; and this, with its eminent advantages of soil and climate, was so well calculated to invite American industry and capital to settle in the country and enhance its prosperity, not to excite the active opposition of the allies.
The governments of France and England injure their own people in obstructing the prosperity of the American republics, for we are their best customers. The richer we are, the more largely we shall buy of their fabrics, unless they drive us into tariffs of exclusion by way of reprisal for their attacks on our interests.
In this jealous dread of American progress, the agents of France and England conspired with the negro party, headed by Baez, the secret ally of Solouque, to excite a war of races. Their prospect was to murder the heads of the government, overthrow the constitutional republic, and establish a negro despotism on the ashes of the white race. I was told weeks beforehand the co-operation of a French and English squadron was promised, and it actually presented itself at the appointed time before the city of Santo Domingo, and at certain indicated points in the vicinity. But when the squadron arrived it found the Dominican government had already discovered and crushed the plan of revolution and massacre, and the French and English consuls had to content themselves for the present with using the squadron and their diplomatic flags to protect the conspirators from punishment. Their consulates were made the rendezvous and asylum of the negro leaders of the frustrated plot; and when the Dominican authorities demanded these notorious criminals for trial, the consuls replied with the same insolent contempt of the sovereign rights of the Dominican republic which they had displayed in the American negotiations—that the rebels were "under the protection of France and England, and none of them should be (and none of them were) punished."
Every intelligent observer is aware that not only in Santo Domingo, but at all the points commanding our coast and isthmus trade, these powers are usurping territory and extending their semi-colonies and contraband protectorates; but no President can put an end to European encroachment on our side of the Atlantic until he is sustained by a Congress that has the nerve and patriotism to plant itself on American principles.
England and France have violated the laws of neutrality towards us, and it would be no more than a just act of self-protection if Congress were to repeal the neutrality laws of 1818, so far as they apply to the encroaching powers, but not in any form to enlarge the safety of unoffending neighbors; or suspend them until the allies shall have evacuated their usurpations on American soil and sovereignty, and shall give better guarantees for the future than evasive diplomatic explanations.
WILLIAM L. CAZNEAU.

records.summary_en: A United States representative reported that Dominican officials expressed concern that both their legislative and executive powers were under European duress and asked if the U.S. would defend their negotiations from European dictation. While the representative expressed confidence in the U.S. Executive and noted that resisting European encroachment is a fundamental doctrine of the American system, they acknowledged that past passive behavior regarding England in Nicaragua and Honduras might mean the U.S. would remain passive regarding France colonizing the Bay of Samana. Despite the representative's efforts to encourage resistance, they admitted the Dominican government was pressed on all sides by France and England.
records.summary_es: Un enviado de Estados Unidos comunicó que las autoridades dominicanas exteriorizaron su zozobra de que tanto el poder legislativo como el ejecutivo se hallasen bajo coacción europea, indagando si Washington ampararía sus deliberaciones frente a imposiciones del Viejo Mundo. Aunque el comisionado manifestó confianza en el gobierno norteamericano y recordó que repeler intromisiones europeas era principio medular de la doctrina continental, admitió que la pasividad anterior frente a Inglaterra en Nicaragua y Honduras hacía temer una inacción semejante ante la colonización francesa de la bahía de Samaná. Pese a sus exhortaciones a la firmeza, reconoció que el régimen dominicano se encontraba acosado por doquier por Francia y Gran Bretaña.
