records.headline: Reprinting an item from the Chicago Press, the Canton Weekly Register explains
records.summary_en: Reprinting an item from the Chicago Press, the Canton Weekly Register explains that the eastern portion of the island, called "St. Domingo or Dominica," was settled by Spaniards, whereas the people of Haiti descend from slaves held by the French on the western coast. Although the Dominicans are described as nearly all of mixed blood, including "Gen. Santander," the paper states that they call themselves Spaniards, cling tenaciously to their separate independence, and rely on steep mountain barriers to defend their population of about 175,000 against a Haitian population more than double that size. The Register also cites advices brought to the Philadelphia Exchange by Captain Burnaby of the schooner Ellen, which left Port-au-Prince on January 1, confirming the complete defeat of Emperor Faustin's 30,000-man march against the eastern side of the island, with Haitian losses of 200 to 300 soldiers, many officers, munitions, provisions, and the Emperor's military chest.
records.summary_es: Al reproducir un artículo del Chicago Press, el Canton Weekly Register explica que la porción oriental de la isla, llamada «Santo Domingo o Dominica», fue colonizada originalmente por españoles, mientras que los habitantes de Haití descienden de los esclavos mantenidos por los franceses en la costa occidental. Aunque se describe a los dominicanos como casi todos de sangre mestiza, incluido el «general Santander», el periódico señala que se llaman a sí mismos españoles, se aferran con tenacidad a su independencia separada y cuentan con escarpadas barreras montañosas para defender a su población de unos 175,000 habitantes frente a una población haitiana que supera el doble de esa cifra. El Register cita además informes llevados al Philadelphia Exchange por el capitán Burnaby, de la goleta Ellen, que zarpó de Puerto Príncipe el 1 de enero, los cuales confirman la completa derrota de la marcha de 30,000 hombres del emperador Faustin contra la parte oriental de la isla, con bajas haitianas de entre 200 y 300 soldados, numerosos oficiales, municiones, provisiones y la caja militar del emperador.

records.headline: An editorial in the Athens Post argues that it is hopeless to sustain
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Athens Post argues that it is hopeless to sustain an independent Black government on the same island as one largely composed of the Caucasian race, dismissing a New York Post correspondent's account of the defeat of 18,000 Haitian troops by four hundred Dominicans with cannon as the work of a "negro sympathizer." Claiming that General Walker's power in Nicaragua is now an established fact that will soon produce a Central American confederation infused with American energy and institutions, the paper predicts that these influences will extend to "Dominica" and cover the island of San Domingo, converting it into a republic within that Central American constellation. The editorial adds that the Cuba question will be resolved by the same process unless peaceful annexation brings the island into the United States first, declaring that "Manifest destiny" points to a brilliant career for filibusterism.
records.summary_es: Un editorial del Athens Post sostiene que es inútil intentar mantener un gobierno negro independiente en la misma isla junto a otro compuesto en gran parte por la raza caucásica, y desestima el relato de un corresponsal del New York Post sobre la derrota de 18,000 soldados haitianos frente a cuatrocientos dominicanos con cañones por considerarlo obra de un «simpatizante de los negros». records.headline: Reviewing recent Dominican newspapers, the New York Herald notes
records.summary_en: Reviewing recent Dominican newspapers, the New York Herald notes a leading article describing the public enthusiasm and joy in the city of Santiago following the victory over the Haitians. A second article by a contributor discusses the Dominican-Haitian question and concludes that the Republic of St. Domingo will either see peace established through the mediation of French and British agents or refuse to lay down its arms until the Haitian forces are completely defeated. The papers also contain communications praising Dominican valor in the December battle, an address by the inhabitants of Santiago eulogizing General Domingo Mallol for his bravery during the recent campaign, and more than a page of official dispatches on the recently concluded war signed by Generals Juan L. F. Uldo and Domingo Mallol. The Herald remarks that although the press in "Dominica" is entirely free, it badly needs improvement and none of the journals list the names of their proprietors or editors.
records.summary_es: Al reseñar periódicos dominicanos recientes, el New York Herald destaca un artículo principal que describe el entusiasmo y el júbilo público en la ciudad de Santiago tras la victoria sobre los haitianos. Un segundo artículo de un colaborador analiza la cuestión dominico-haitiana y concluye que la República de Santo Domingo verá establecida la paz mediante la intervención de los agentes de Francia e Inglaterra o, de lo contrario, no depondrá las armas hasta haber derrotado por completo a las fuerzas haitianas. Los periódicos incluyen además comunicaciones que elogian el valor dominicano en la batalla de diciembre, un mensaje de los habitantes de Santiago en alabanza al general Domingo Mallol por su bravura durante la última campaña, y más de una página de despachos y documentos oficiales sobre la guerra recién terminada firmados por los generales Juan L. F. Uldo y Domingo Mallol. El Herald observa que, aunque la prensa en «Dominica» es completamente libre, necesita mejoras urgentes y ninguno de los periódicos mencionados indica los nombres de sus propietarios o editores.

records.summary_en: A correspondent provided a retrospective summary of the governors and policies on the island, noting that the Emperor depended on disaffected Dominicans during the late contest and rejected foreign dictation regarding his government. English and French interest in Faustin I. was suspected to stem from jealousy of United States progress, while Dominican authorities ratified a treaty with the United States identical to the one negotiated by Cazneau. Additionally, President Mota proclaimed a death decree against any outlaws or filibusters landing on the island—primarily targeting ex-President Baez, who was reportedly encouraged by France, England, and Spain—and the U.S. storeship *Supply* stopped at Kingston, Jamaica, carrying thirty-five animals from the Mediterranean.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal trazó una reseña retrospectiva de los mandatarios y de la política insular, haciendo notar que el emperador se apoyó en dominicanos desafectos durante la última contienda y rehusó directrices extranjeras sobre su administración. Se recelaba que el celo franco-británico en torno a Faustino I obedecía al desasosiego por el engrandecimiento de Estados Unidos, mientras las autoridades dominicanas convalidaban un tratado con Washington gemelo al negociado por Cazneau. Asimismo, el presidente Mota promulgó bando de pena de muerte contra facciosos o filibusteros que hollasen el territorio —apuntando principalmente al expresidente Báez, a quien alentaban presuntamente Francia, Inglaterra y España—, arribando entretanto a Kingston el transporte militar estadounidense *Supply* con treinta y cinco animales traídos del Mediterráneo.

records.summary_en: According to the *National Press of Dominica*, as reported by *The New York Herald* on May 2, 1856, General Regla Mota, Vice President and charged with the Executive power of the Republic of San Domingo, issued a decree targeting foreign schemes and potential understandings with Haytiens. records.full_text:
NEWSPAPER ACCOUNTS.
[From the St. Thomas Times, March 22.]
By the arrival of the English schooner Aldebaren, Captain Leverock, yesterday, from St. Domingo, we have received the following communication from that city:—
Her Britannic Majesty’s steam sloop Argus, Capt. Purvis, arrived here on Sunday afternoon from Port au Prince, bearing despatches from the agents of the mediating Powers, dated the 6th March. A council of ministers had taken place that morning at Port au Prince, at which her Britannic Majesty’s Consul General and the Gerent of the French Consul General had been present, but the results have not transpired. Commodore Kellet, who commands the squadron of English and French ships now assembled at Port au Prince, considered it requisite to despatch the Argus forthwith.

records.headline: An Anglo-Africa Contraband Treaty.
records.summary_en: According to the *New-York dispatch* on May 4, 1856, England and France previously forced the Dominican Republic to cancel the Laznean treaty and insisted that a black population representative be appointed to the government, resulting in the nomination of an educated negro named Bobadilla to the Council of State. To avoid difficulty with England, President Pierce instructed the U.S. Commercial Agent at St. Domingo to revise or renegotiate the treaty using Bobadilla, and this new treaty was reportedly in the hands of the President for submission to the Senate around May 8th or 9th. Additionally, the Secretary of the Navy informed the President of the Pacific Mail Steamship Company that the U.S. ship *Cyane* had been ordered to Aspinwall to investigate the robbery and outrage against American citizens at Panama.
records.summary_es: Según el *New-York dispatch* del 4 de mayo de 1856, Inglaterra y Francia habían compelido en su momento a la República Dominicana a revocar el tratado de Cazneau [citado como Laznean], reclamando que se nombrase en el gobierno a un representante de la población de color, lo que derivó en la incorporación de Bobadilla al Consejo de Estado. Para solventar diferendos con Londres, el presidente Pierce dio orden al agente comercial en Santo Domingo de renegociar el pacto recurriendo a Bobadilla, hallándose dicho flamante texto en manos del mandatario para su elevación al Senado hacia el 8 o 9 de mayo. El secretario de Marina participó por otra parte al presidente de la Pacific Mail Steamship Company que la corbeta *Cyane* recibió orden de zarpar hacia Colón para indagar atropellos cometidos contra norteamericanos en Panamá.

records.headline: General Quitman's speech, quoted by The Anti-Slavery Bugle
records.summary_en: General Quitman's speech, quoted by The Anti-Slavery Bugle, surveys Nicaragua, Cuba, and San Domingo, in which he characterizes the Haitian government as a "strange and grotesque power" under whose rule a strategic Caribbean island is relapsing into barbarism while supported by European influences in attempting to exterminate the "small white Dominican Republic" that still holds part of the island. Observing that the rest of "insular America" is European or African, Quitman warns American statesmen that a "world-startling drama" is approaching in which the development, greatness, and safety of the United States are deeply concerned. In commentary following the excerpt, the Bugle ridicules the phrase "Insular America" as alien to the history and traditions of the American people, contrasting it with the "Continental America" that resisted George III.
records.summary_es: El Anti-Slavery Bugle cita un discurso del general Quitman que examina a Nicaragua, Cuba y Santo Domingo, en el cual califica al gobierno haitiano como un «poder extraño y grotesco» bajo cuyo dominio una estratégica isla del Caribe está recayendo en la barbarie, sostenido por poderosas influencias europeas en sus intentos de exterminar a la «pequeña República Dominicana blanca» que aún conserva una parte de la isla. Observando que el resto de la «América insular» es europea o africana, Quitman advierte a los estadistas estadounidenses que se avecina un «drama que asombrará al mundo», en el que el desarrollo, la grandeza y la seguridad misma de los Estados Unidos están profundamente comprometidos. En un comentario posterior al extracto, el Bugle ridiculiza la expresión «América insular» por considerarla ajena a la historia y las ideas del pueblo estadounidense, contrastándola con la «América continental» que resistió a Jorge III.

records.headline: Beginning to see Their Danger.
records.summary_en: A letter dated August 3 from Port au Platt reported that St. Domingo city was in a state of revolution due to a treaty with Spain favoring Spanish descendants, which caused widespread excitement, the suspension of business, and the President and Cabinet's desire to resign. The Spanish Consul was attempting to block the ratification of an American treaty, liberals were anticipating the arrival of a United States war vessel, and a city editor had killed a Spaniard in a political dispute before fleeing. Additionally, the excerpt briefly notes a duel fought by Col. Munoz, the expected return of political exiles from Spain, dull trade and freights, American Consul George W. Kimball's presence in Massachusetts, and a volcanic eruption and earthquake on the island of Great Sangir in the Moluccas.
records.summary_es: Una epístola fechada el 3 de agosto desde Puerto Plata daba cuenta de que la capital dominicana se hallaba en plena efervescencia revolucionaria a causa de un tratado con España que beneficiaba a los descendientes hispanos, provocando honda consternación, paralización del comercio y la dimisión en masa del presidente y sus ministros. El cónsul español procuraba trabar la convalidación de un convenio con Estados Unidos, los liberales aguardaban el arribo de un buque de guerra norteamericano y el director de una gaceta ultimó a un peninsular en refriega política dándose a la fuga. La correspondencia alude por lo demás a un duelo del coronel Muñoz, al retorno previsto de desterrados desde España, al abatimiento mercantil y de fletes, a la estancia del cónsul estadounidense George W. Kimball en Massachusetts y a una erupción sísmica en la isla de Sangihe, en las Molucas.

Even the press is beginning to speak out. The recent coup d'etat in Spain for the overthrow of constitutional government is alarming, as it shows what may be done at any moment in England and in other countries. It is not certain, but the latest accounts, through government sources, make it appear that the despots of Spain have triumphed, over-throwing the constitutionalists and trampling upon this news there was a row by the people. According to the report, the treaty's seventh article favored Spanish descendants becoming Spanish citizens, prompting thousands to register with the Spanish Consuls to hoist the Spanish flag again, while the President and his cabinet wished to resign, tribunals closed, and business was suspended. Additionally, the letter stated that the Spanish Consul was actively working to prevent the ratification of the American treaty and opposing the American consul.

records.full_text:
I write you under circumstances very dull for this republic. We are on the eve of a political hurricane; and I use this Indian word in this case, because it means wind from the four points, and the revolution which we expect every moment, will come from four points, viz:—France, England, Hayti and Spain, all combined, all united in the execution of two ideas—either to put down the present administration and to bring in Baez as chief magistrate, because it committed the crime of concluding a treaty with the United States, or, if not possible, to destroy the Dominican nationality by means of another Soulouque invasion, helped by those three nations.

On the 6th of June last, Senor Segovia, the Spanish Charge d'Affaires in this republic, went back to the capital from Puerto Plata, via St. Thomas, and soon after it was rumored there, as well as here, that he had received from the Cabinet of Madrid, by the Spanish mail steamer touching at Puerto Rico, full, arbitrary powers to act against the republic, under any pretext, no matter how light, in order to carry on their combined opposition to the American treaty, and in every way to prevent its exchange. And at the same time, the Spaniards in that city commenced to boast that a Spanish fleet was coming, and that the treaty would not be consummated.

By article 7th of the Dominican-Spanish treaty it was agreed that those Spaniards who have resided in the republic, and obtained Dominican nationality would be able to become again Spanish subjects, in which case their sons of age would have the same right. Senor Segovia, making a very wrong use of that stipulation, began to admit in his books as Spaniards some Dominicans, enemies of Santana's administration and friends of Baez, merely because their ancestors were Spaniards, in which point of law the great majority of the country might likewise be considered Spanish. The government, foreseeing the fatal consequences of this violent misinterpretation of the article, opposed Senor Segovia's action, and he closed the register of Spaniards until the two contracting parties would agree on its proper interpretation. Consequently, the Dominican government appointed an Extraordinary Envoy and Minister Plenipotentiary to the Court of Madrid to settle the difficulty; and as, almost at the same time, the American treaty was ratified, the Charge went in a hurry to St. Thomas in a British steam frigate of war, from which visit to that island and St. Martin he returned last month. Now, since his arrival he has been working the propaganda in favor of the interpretation which he gives to the above article, and has been propagating through his agents, in the interior as well as in the capital, that he has authority to register as Spaniards all those who declare their wish to be, giving them to understand, giving them a guarantee that no one who has once been registered in his consular office will be compelled by the Dominican government to carry arms. Consequently, the more ignorant, just with a view to relieve themselves from the military service, are running daily to the Spanish consulate by hundreds, and registering themselves as subjects of her Catholic Majesty.

By such conduct as this, Senor Segovia beyond question tramples on Dominican rights and independence, for it is plain, according to international law, that he cannot proceed on the admission of Dominican citizens as Spaniards, unless the question previously agreed by mutual agreement between Spain and the young republic. And what is more alarming, is the fact that on the 26th June last, General Blasco de Garay and the brig Gravina, of the Spanish navy, arrived in San Domingo, and no doubt the Dominicans believe that the only solution for the friends of Dominican nationality from this dark situation, was that Santana left the capital on that same day, with one hundred cavalry, and that every day are entering, little by little, a great many infantry, without beating the drums, in order, it seems, not to alarm the public. The government is no doubt adopting some great measure to be ready at the moment when the conspiracy is to explode; but it is impossible to ascertain what they propose to do.

President Mota, his ministers, the Senators, and several generals, go every day, and often twice a day, to visit the Liberador, as he is the commander-in-chief of the army, and because his opinion is always heard with respect by the cabinet. Certainly, as a means of mortification, the produce of the public revenue in cash is scarce. But, according to the first circular of the Minister for Foreign Relations, the revenue was increasing, not being burdened with unnecessary expenses or onerous contracts, and the hope was indulged that within a short time it would be exempted from transitory drawbacks, brought on by deplorable errors and the recent unfortunate events.

records.summary_en: Based on a letter from the schooner *Marietta Smith* arriving from Port-au-Platt, *The Daily Union* reported on August 20, 1856, that a revolution had broken out in the capital of the Dominican Republic following a treaty with Old Spain. The treaty's 11th article allowed Spanish descendants to become Spanish citizens, leading thousands of citizens and soldiers to register with Spanish consuls, which caused the suspension of business, the closure of tribunals, and the intended resignation of the President and his cabinet. Additionally, a city newspaper editor shot a Spaniard in broad daylight over a political dispute and escaped, prompting the Spanish consul to offer a $5,000 reward for his capture.
records.summary_es: Con base en una epístola conducida por la goleta *Marietta Smith* desde Puerto Plata, *The Daily Union* dio a conocer el 20 de agosto de 1856 que una revolución estalló en la capital dominicana a raíz del tratado con España. La cláusula undécima facultaba a los descendientes de españoles a recobrar la nacionalidad de sus mayores, empujando a millares de ciudadanos y tropa a inscribirse ante los cónsules hispanos, lo que ocasionó el cese de transacciones, la clausura de audiencias judiciales y la dimisión del presidente y su ministerio. Un redactor periodístico hirió de muerte a tiros a un peninsular a plena luz del día por motivos de facción dándose a la fuga, ofreciendo el cónsul español 5.000 duros de recompensa por su captura.

records.summary_en: The *Houma Ceres* reported that Spanish agent Segovia, backed by Spanish naval vessels and French diplomatic support, forced the Dominican government to recall a treaty pending in Washington. Segovia compelled President Santana to resign in favor of Buenaventura Báez and replaced pro-American cabinet members with his own allies. The report warned that Segovia was registering Dominicans as Spanish subjects to bring the entire island under Spanish rule and exclude American influence.
records.summary_es: El *Houma Ceres* informó que el agente español Segovia, respaldado por buques de guerra hispanos y el concurso diplomático francés, forzó al gobierno dominicano a retirar un tratado pendiente de ratificación en Washington. Segovia conminó al presidente Santana a dimitir en favor de Buenaventura Báez y sustituyó a los secretarios proclives a Estados Unidos por adictos a su causa. La noticia alertaba de que Segovia matriculaba a ciudadanos dominicanos como súbditos de la corona española con la mira de reincorporar toda la isla a la dominación de España y proscribir el predicamento norteamericano.

records.headline: Addressing the Chairman, the speaker in a speech printed by The Daily National Intelligencer surveys
records.summary_en: Addressing the Chairman, the speaker in a speech printed by The Daily National Intelligencer surveys San Domingo and describes the power ruling the island as a "caricature of government" under whose sway an island holding the same strategic relation to the Caribbean Sea as Cuba holds to the Gulf of Mexico is rapidly relapsing into barbarism. The speaker asserts that this regime is sustained by powerful European influences in its efforts to exterminate the "small white Dominican republic" that still retains part of the island, while all the rest of insular America is European or African. Warning that a "world-startling drama" is about to unfold affecting the development, greatness, and safety of the United States, he calls on American statesmen to act boldly and vigorously to fulfill the nation's destiny.
records.summary_es: El Daily National Intelligencer publica un discurso en el que el orador, dirigiéndose al presidente de la sesión, examina la situación de Santo Domingo y describe al poder que domina la isla como una «caricatura de gobierno» bajo cuyo mando una isla que guarda con el mar Caribe la misma relación estratégica que Cuba con el golfo de México está recayendo rápidamente en la barbarie. El orador afirma que dicho régimen es sostenido por poderosas influencias europeas en sus intentos de exterminar a la «pequeña república dominicana blanca» que aún conserva una parte de la isla, mientras que todo el resto de la América insular es europea o africana. Advirtiendo que está por desarrollarse un «drama que asombrará al mundo» y que atañe al desarrollo, la grandeza y la seguridad misma de los Estados Unidos, exhorta a los estadistas estadounidenses a actuar con audacia y vigor para cumplir el destino asignado a su república.

records.full_text: INTERESTING FROM HAVANA.—The steamer Black Warrior, with Havana dates to the 16th instant, arrived at New York on Monday night. It was reported in Havana that a Spanish brig-of-war has 6,000 stand of arms on board, destined for the use of the Spanish faction against the Dominican republic, to be taken down in a few days by an officer of the Spanish army, and that the annexation of the west end will be insisted upon by the Spanish as another gem to the Spanish crown. Santa Anna is expected to arrive at Havana on his way to Spain. Gen. Concha issued an order suspending all action of Spain as soon as the expected orders to that effect arrive from Madrid.

records.headline: Citing the Havana correspondent of the New York Herald, the Alexandria Gazette reports
records.summary_en: Citing the Havana correspondent of the New York Herald, the Alexandria Gazette reports that the Spanish government is engaging in what it characterizes as wholesale filibustering. According to the report, Spanish naval expeditions were preparing to depart Havana for San Domingo City and Vera Cruz. One fleet was to be sent to assist a movement against the territorial integrity of the Dominican Republic, while the other was to be dispatched to support Spanish claims in Mexico.
records.summary_es: Citando al corresponsal en La Habana del New York Herald, la Alexandria Gazette informa que el gobierno español se está embarcando en lo que califica como filibusterismo a gran escala. Según el informe, se estaban preparando expediciones navales españolas para zarpar de La Habana hacia la ciudad de Santo Domingo y Veracruz. Una flota sería enviada para apoyar el movimiento contra la integridad de la República Dominicana, mientras que la otra sería despachada para respaldar las pretensiones del gobierno español en México.

records.full_text:
The U. S. mail steamship Black Warrior, Capt. J. W. Smith, arrived at her wharf Wednesday evening last, and brings the following late Havana news:
The Black Warrior reports that the Spanish brig-of-war Habanero, with six thousand stand of arms, had sailed from Havana to support the insurrectionists excited by the Spanish authorities against the liberty of the Dominican Republic.
Preparations for the armed invasion of Mexico were being actively made at Havana. The island is said to be perfectly tranquil and quiet.
The sugar crop will be very large. Exchange on London 10 per cent.; on New York 4 per cent. Freights low and inactive.
From a statement published by the Customs department, we learn that the revenue of the island for the first six months of the present year, up to the 1st of July last was $1,486,789 37, being an excess over the corresponding month of the previous year of $135,308 50. The increase came entirely from the export duties, as the revenue from marine customs fell off $24,306 31.
The Diario says that some imported fresh cows were attracting much attention in Havana. The editor of the Diario says that they have an abundance of beautiful wool, and that they give a milk which is destined to be very good, of the same flesh, by those who have tasted it. The animal is from Asia, he thought, and Europe, and it is hoped they will become acclimated in Cuba.
The papers from the interior of the island show great activity in the public mind relative to internal improvements. The Gaceta (official) is to be published in the direction of Santo Espiritu, and a movement is on foot to run another of the same from Trinidad, thus crossing the island. The Cienfuegos road is doing an excellent business.
The Hoja, of Sagua, states that the sugar crop will not be so early out as was anticipated, although the cane is very large and fine, from the backward state of the preparatory labors. In Sagua cleaning has been generally commenced between the 15th of October and the 1st of January.
The Diario de la Marina says that the Dutch ship Maria sailed hence on the twenty of March last bound to Havana, with three hundred and fifty laborers from the Holo islands, provinces of China, which is inhabited by a race of robust agriculturalists. It hopes that this will tend to convince, if the labors of these men are much needed by the fields of Cuba.

records.summary_en: Under the headline "Later from San Domingo — Martial Law in Dominica," the Richmond Daily Dispatch reports advices received via Havana from both portions of the island up to mid-January. In the Dominican Republic, the longstanding conflict between Santana and President Báez, described as representing Spanish and French ideas respectively, continued to distract the country throughout its territory. While Santana held his position firmly in the mountains of Neyba, martial law was proclaimed in the name of the President and Senate. From Haiti, the paper adds that the anniversary of Haitian independence was celebrated with addresses involving Emperor Soulouque, and that Augustin Soulfrant, Prince of Jacmel and Grand Marshal of the Empire, died on January 9.

records.full_text:
Collision of American and Dominican Vessels—Arrest of the American Captain—His Sentence and Abandonment of his Schooner—A Call on the United States Cabinet.

We have an excellent case on account of the interference of this government with us. They abuse the Yankees here with impunity, and this is an excellent chance for redress.

It appears that some seven weeks since the American schooner Charles Hill, Captain Smith, bound from Mayaguez for this port, during the night came in collision with the Dominican packet schooner and stove her bows. The American schooner came in here, and while ready for sea was refused a pass and the captain summoned to appear before a court. He was sentenced to pay the sum of $3,100 for "wilfully running into and damaging the Dominican packet."

Now, every one knows that the captain was right, being on the starboard tack and on a wind, whereas the other had his larboard tack aboard and from the wind; therefore he should have kept off and not crossed the bows of the Charles Hill. This any Marine Court would allow, and here he was condemned without a trial, and not being able to pay was sentenced to a year's imprisonment. He (Captain Smith,) has abandoned his vessel to the Dominican government, and looks at home for redress. It is one of the most urgent cases ever heard of, and a complete burglary and robbery on their part. They even now laugh at our threats. Only to think of it. A petty government like this. It is too bad. I am in hopes for a time to come to correct all.

We have received the Gaceta Oficial of Santo Domingo to May 4.

The American schooner Charles Hill, Captain Albert Smith, was seen in collision with the Dominican packet schooner named the Nineteenth of March; and the Charles Hill having run in at San Domingo was detained, and the captain sentenced to pay $3,100 for wilfully running into and damaging the Dominican packet. We find the following documents, in reference to the case, published under the head of "Official:"—

THE UNITED STATES COMMERCIAL AGENT TO THE MINISTER OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS.
UNITED STATES COMMERCIAL AGENCY,
CITY OF SAN DOMINGO, March 13, 1857.
SIR—You will find enclosed the protest of Mr. Albert Smith, Captain of the American schooner Charles Hill, against the Dominican authorities, who, under false pretexts,
way to proceedings for illegal and unjust detention. I am, sir, &c.,
JONATHAN ELLIOTT.
To the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Dominican Republic.

THE DOMINICA MINISTER OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS TO THE AMERICAN COMMERCIAL AGENT.
Mr. AGENT—My government has been ignorant of your protest and remarks on the proceedings of your function. Entrusted of interim to Mr. Jacob Pereyra on account of your late unwellness, and my government cannot in the official manner. Nevertheless, in receiving your note of the 13th, accompanied by the protest of Capt. Smith, I have brought it to the notice of the government, for the proceedings to which it may give rise.

It is useless for me to say that if the Captain had only availed himself of the means of conciliation to which he was invited, this affair, most probably (not that question would have had a solution as speedy as it would have been desirable), not being welcome to the cabinet, it became impossible to change the matter to our ordinary tribunals, to be decided on them in conformity with the laws.

I have to state that it would have been more decorous for him to show before the tribunal, which had charge of the matter, and if not pleased thereat, appealed to where the captain complains, that being impartially examined they would see whether to confirm it or [illegible]. I am, &c.
FELIX M. DELMONTE.
SAN DOMINGO, March 16, 1857.

THE UNITED STATES COMMERCIAL AGENT TO THE DOMINICAN MINISTER OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS.
SAN DOMINGO, March 20, 1857.
SEÑOR MINISTER—The tribunal of the first instance, of this city, having declared that the cause between Albert Smith of the American schooner Charles Hill, for injury done to the Dominican packet 19th of March, was an act of amounting, with cost, to some $3,160, and from which decision the Captain will not appeal.

I desire now to know, and beg of you to inform me, whether the American schooner Charles Hill and the crew will be detained, or be allowed to proceed on her trip, for the injury and loss of its owners, until such time as the captain shall have complied with the judgment, or until the same shall have been exacted?
JONATHAN ELLIOTT.

TO THE MINISTER OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS.
COMMERCIAL AGENCY OF THE UNITED STATES,
SAN DOMINGO, March 28, 1857.
SIR—I have the honor to acknowledge the receipt of your communication of this day's date, by which I understand that Capt. Smith will not avail himself of the resource of appeal from the sentence, which can be done without prejudice to the protest, or that of his crew, and that he does not fear to submit to the result.

I assure you that the government has no other action over matters submitted to the tribunals than the interest of having the laws fulfilled, or distributing justice impartially, without meddling in any manner in decrees or their execution. Therefore, the tribunal alone is able to answer the question submitted by you, in determing whether it will accept bail. I am, &c.    FELIX M. DELMONTE.
To the Commercial Agent of the United States.

THE COMMERCIAL AGENT DEMANDS RESTITUTION, ETC.
COMMERCIAL AGENCY OF THE UNITED STATES,
SAN DOMINGO, April 17, 1857.
SIR—It was brought to my notice yesterday that the crew of the Dominican packet, in the detention of Capt. Albert Smith, from the schooner Charles Hill, of Portsmouth, was to be condemned on the ground of having wilfully run into the packet on the night of the 13th of March; against which sentence and proceedings I solemnly protest it.

The accusation against the Captain for having wilfully injured the Dominican packet "19th of March" is untrue.

The schooner Charles Hill has been anchored here six weeks, and as it has not been copper fastened, it is so much injured that it will probably never leave this port.

Consequently, as commercial agent of the United States, I ask in the name and on the behalf of the owners or shippers of the said vessel the sum of $5,000 from the government of the Dominican republic, to be paid on or before the 23d inst., and also the freedom of the vessel and captain to depart freely on that day.

The undersigned regrets extremely the occurrence of this thing, and the delay which it has occasioned to him, and takes this occasion to express to the honorable Minister, &c.
JONATHAN ELLIOTT.

THE MINISTER'S REPLY.
Mr. AGENT—My government has read with extreme regret your note of 17th inst., substantially affirming that the proceeding against Captain Albert Smith, who through carelessness, inattention to rules and an accidental cause, ran into and injured the Dominican packet, is untrue, and that the damage and cost of the vessel is, in your judgment, equal to a loss of $500.

Regretting that after this communication the freedom of the vessel can be unreasonable without acknowledging a theory fatal to all nations—1st. That wrongs committed at sea do not constitute crime nor carry responsibility for the material consequences. 2d. That tribunals can have no jurisdiction to take cognizance of these acts.

Neither the fact itself nor the even given admit of discussion. If a stranger in the Dominican republic commits an act of hostility, it is the duty of the Dominican tribunals to judge and sentence him. If in other nations there is a jurisdiction to the republic, it must be denied to every government, and the right being denied, it is difficult to see where in the world to decide these controverses could possibly be found.

If the act had taken place on the coasts of the republic, it is clear that if the Dominican packet was the one that was injured, that the Dominican vessel was the one that suffered, and the injured party presented its foreign consul and in default of this the justice of the republic and in no other, and that the government in taking cognizance the question could not have intervened in the case.

To disregard, as Captain Smith has disregarded, the right of appeal—to resort to the extraordinary course of international resources—and that against the government which invited him several times to the frankest settlement, is to reveal the desire of recurring to force, and not to the means which universal reason has accepted and sanctioned. Such a fatal precedent being permitted, it would be impossible for the civil power to decide questions between two foreigners.

If the act in question had occurred between an American and an English vessel, the American Captain denying the jurisdiction, and the English captain demanding justice, how could he evade the international demand? In no way, because the one would be described as abuse of

records.full_text:
Seizure of the Sch. Chas. Hill at St. Domingo.

The case of the Sch. Chas. Hill, which was seized at San Domingo, by the San Dominican government, may seem to many of little importance compared with the great question that agitates the public: but small acts of injustice between governments often lead to the most fatal results, and we wish now, in the commencement, to give a fair statement of the whole affair.

The sch. Chas. Hill, of this port, according to the statement of the Captain, as represented in papers by the owners, and the protest by the Commercial Agent of the United States, Mr. Jonathan Elliott at Porto Rico, on the evening of the 5th of March, off the port of St. Domingo. Nothing of importance occurred until about 5 o'clock, A. M., of the 7th, it being quite dark at the time, when the schooner C. Hill, running down for St. Domingo on the starboard tack on board, heading N. W. and the wind N. E., was collided with by an unknown vessel, standing by the wind with the larboard tack on board. This unknown vessel proved to be a Dominican government vessel, bound from San Domingo for St. Thomas. In attempting to go to the windward of the Charles Hill she struck her, the latter went through her main sail about half way from the gaff down to the boom, and cut her larboard leech rope, and the topping lift not giving way, caused the vessel to come along side and do some damage to her rail. Capt. Smith hailed the commander of the Chas. Hill, ordered his mate to lower the larboard boat, while the Dominican officer of the other vessel came on board the schooner and let go the halliards of her foresail and jib, which injured their sails, and then took the vessel in tow, no person having been injured nor list been lost alone. The vessel reached St. Domingo... Capt. Smith, of the C. Hill, immediately continued his voyage to San Domingo, fitting for sea as best he could, and presuming no great injury was done to the vessel in collision.

First—The collision took place on the high seas some twelve miles from San Domingo, as appears from the chart and distance run, and also from the fact that he did not take a pilot on board until 10 o'clock, and did not arrive at San Domingo until 11 1-2, the distance of twelve miles from that point making his making more than 12 miles into port. On his arrival at St. Domingo, the Dominican government demanded the enormous sum of $3,200 as restitution for injuries to their vessel, and imprisoned Capt. Smith before their courts to answer the charges made against him. Capt. Smith denied the jurisdiction of the Dominican government, as neither government nor individuals can be held liable for collision on the high seas... with the advice of our Commercial Agent, Jonathan Elliott. Capt. Smith moreover demanded an investigation to present to the Dominican government, an international question and not one to be tried by a local court. The San Dominican court refused to abide by the arbitration of the commanders of a French and English man-of-war then in port. This the San Dominican government refused doing, and proceeded to provide counsel for Capt. Smith, who was then inside of prison, and after hearing the evidence of their own men, without the testimony of any of the crew of the sch. Hill, condemned the schooner, and fined her heavily. Meanwhile the vessel not being coppered, was greatly eaten by the worms in the harbor, and Capt. Smith was advised to deliver the vessel up to the Dominican government, under a protest. This he did, and returned secretly to our country, as he was himself detained under false charges by the San Dominican government.

We have but three points to make after this short statement of the affair, which has been endorsed as correct by our Commercial Agent, Mr. Elliott, and which is corroborated by the good character for veracity Capt. Smith bears. In the first place, the collision took place on the high seas more than 12 miles from land, and by an acknowledged maritime law no country has a right of jurisdiction more than three miles from land. The San Dominican government had, therefore, no right to try the Chas. Hill 12 miles at sea. In the second place the Dominican government could not try a case in which the vessel broke loose, there is every justice and reason demand that governments no more than individuals are not to suffer for collisions at the same time. The question for restitution was a pure international question of international law, and ought to was to be decided by arbitration or agreement.—Thirdly and finally, if the collision had not taken place on the high seas, and the Dominican government had rightful jurisdiction in all actions arising, except by law Dominican government could not, and by maritime law vessels on the starboard tack are not accountable for collisions with vessels on the larboard tack.

We leave the conclusions to be drawn from so simple a statement and text of the affair, and we trust that our government will not hesitate to defend its citizens against the aggressions of other powers.

A correspondent of the New York Herald writes from St. Domingo, May 10, regarding this matter of the affair:

"It has now been some seven weeks since the American schooner Charles Hill, Captain Smith, while on her passage to this port, was run into on a dark night came in collision with the Dominican packet Charles, belonging to President Baez. The American schooner came in here, and when ready for sea was seized, it is said, and the captain brought before a court. He was sentenced to pay the sum of $3,200 for damages, besides costs of court, amounting to several hundreds more.

Now, every one knows that the captain was right, as he was on the starboard tack, with the wind on his port side, the other had his larboard tack aboard and from the wind; besides the collision took place at sea, before he crossed the bows of the American. This any Master of a vessel knows. This sentence was rendered without a trial, and not being able to pay was sentenced to close confinement. The captain, Capt. Smith, has abandoned his vessel to the Dominican government, and has made his escape to the United States... It is a pity government like this. It is too bad. I hope our government will interfere."

In the Gaceta Oficial of Santo Domingo of May 1st, we find the official correspondence regarding the case, published under the head of "official:"

Commercial Agency of the United States of America.
San Domingo, April 20, 1857.
To the Minister of Foreign Affairs:
Sir—You will find herewith the protest of Mr. Abner Smith, Captain of the American schooner Charles Hill, against the Dominican authorities, on account of their taking possession of his vessel as a legal and unjust detention. I am, sir, &c.
JONATHAN ELLIOTT.

To the Commercial Agent of the United States of America:
Minister of Foreign Affairs,
San Domingo, April 20, 1857.
Mr. Agent—My government has been informed that Mr. Abner Smith, Captain of the American schooner Charles Hill, after having fulfilled the duties of your functions, entrusted an interim to Mr. Jonathan Elliott, Commercial Agent of the U. S., notified my government thereof in an official manner, and that the said Mr. Elliott, when Capt. Smith arrived, accompanied by the protest of Capt. Smith, I have to state that Mr. Elliott is not a Commercial Agent, proceedings to which it may give rise.
Seeing that Mr. Elliott is not a Commercial Agent, I only availed of himself of the means of conciliation which offered themselves, and that a friendly arrangement as speedy as it would have been peaceable, but being rejected by Mr. Elliott, my government has to submit the matter to the common tribunals, to be decided according to the laws of the country.
I also believe that it would have been more meet of Mr. Elliott to await, as it was his duty, who had charge of the matter, the illegal proceedings taken against Capt. Smith, than to express, before being impartially examined the might be redress for damages to the packet. Accept &c.
FELIX M. DELMONTE,
Minister of Foreign Affairs.
SAN DOMINGO, March 16, 1857.

The Dominican Minister of Foreign Affairs to the American Consul.
SAN DOMINGO, March 27, 1857.
Sir—I have received receipt of your official note of this day, in which, after mentioning that Capt. Smith will not avail himself of the court of appeal which the laws permit him to do, you ask to be informed whether the confiscation of the vessel will be prevented before the execution of the sentence of the tribunal of commerce.
I assure you that the government has no other intention than to leave the court to act without any interest of the laws having the facility, or distribution of justice in this case. The party who believes himself injured by the sentence of the tribunal may appeal to the tribunal above to answer the question asked by your note, which I cannot answer. Accept, &c., I am, &c., FELIX M. DELMONTE,
Minister of Foreign Affairs.

The Commercial Agent to the Minister of Foreign Affairs.
Commercial Agency United States, Restauration, etc.
SAN DOMINGO, April 21, 1857.
Sir—It was I ought to say, to my great regret that Mr. Abner Smith, captain of the American schooner Charles Hill, of Portsmouth, N. H., was sentenced on the 18th to two years imprisonment in the jail of this city, and to pay the damages done to the Dominican packet, and to pay the cost of court.
The accusation against the captain for having run into the San Dominican packet "19th of March" is irrational.
Capt. Smith has already been in jail for a week, his vessel line six weeks, and as it has not been coppered far from six weeks, and if it remains here long will be a large outlay to repair it.
The Commercial Agent, commercial agent of the United States, I ask in the name and on the behalf of our government, that the vessel Charles Hill, with all her cargo, now in possession of the Dominican republic, to be paid or secured before the 23d inst., and further to allow the captain, vessel and its crew to depart hence on that date.
Accept the assurances of the high consideration with which I have the honor to be your ob't serv't,
JONATHAN ELLIOTT.
To the honorable Minister, &c.

The Minister's Reply.
DOMINICAN REPUBLIC,
MINISTRY OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS,
SAN DOMINGO, April 21, 1857.
The undersigned Minister of Foreign Affairs has the honor to reply to your note of 21st inst., Mr. Agent, stating that Mr. Abner Smith, captain of the American schooner Charles Hill, has been sentenced to two years imprisonment by the tribunal of commerce of this city, which through wish-recklessness, negligence, or malice, he collided with the Dominican packet 19th of March, as also to pay the costs and damages, and the detention of the vessel until it is paid:
The undersigned is surprised at your note, after the explanation I had the honor to give you in my note of the 20th inst., relative to this affair.
Neither the fact itself nor the consequent detention—the one is a violation of maritime law, and the knowing a theory fatal to all nations, ie. That the captain is not accountable for his acts, neither can nor carry responsibility for the losses occasioned; nor the Dominican government prevent the execution of the sentence until the laws take their course.
If the captain or the agent does not even admit of an appeal, and the 2d contains the 1st, because in the court of appeal the sentence may be revoked, or the damages diminished, the Dominican government having no jurisdiction in the western world to decide upon this case, it belonging to the tribunals, and if it the fact had taken place on the coasts of the Dominican republic, the tribunals could not judge for the first time since the event, and the aggrieved party must apply to the courts for justice, and if the assertion that justice is in this republic and in no other, can it be stated that there is a denial of justice when the question to the tribunals has done no wrong to any one.
The Dominican government cannot admit that by the right of appeal—to resort to the tribunals—because by doing so it would violate the laws, and the act of the government which invited him several times to use his right of appeal, or to give security to carry the case to court, and no to the means which unitly—and no government would do so—unless a fatal precedent being permitted, it would be impossible for any nation to govern, or to protect the rights of its citizens.
If such a question had occurred between an American and an English vessel, the American government would not have allowed the English government to demand the delivery of the vessel, under a demand of internal way. In way, because the one party had not exhausted all the legal means, nor was it considered as abuse of power or the other a denial of justice.
The Dominican government, on the contrary, when demand is not founded on reason. The government can do no more than leave the tribunals to carry out justice, and to trust the intelligence and rectitude to decide the question according to law; and hopes that the Commercial Agent of the United States will see the justice of its method and just proceedings in the present affair.
SAN DOMINGO, APRIL 21, 1857.
FELIX M. DELMONTE.

records.full_text:
From the London Anti-Slavery Reporter.

The following remarks on Hayti are so pertinent, and contain so much information, which is not extensively circulated as our own columns.—They are from the pen of Mr. F. W. Chesson.

"Hayti is a country unfortunately but little known in England, and is generally associated with treatment not calculated to inspire much affection and respect. But while a retrospect of Haytian history may, to a great extent, justify this idea of the country, so far as the past is concerned, it by no means follows that this idea is applicable to the present state of affairs. On the contrary, we have great pleasure in stating that under the firm and enlightened rule of the Emperor Faustin, as well as from a widespread education, Hayti has entered upon an era of peace and prosperity, during which she has developed her resources, and which cannot fail to be of lasting benefit, and to constitute the chief glory and strength of a nation.

"Few Englishmen (so far as our knowledge extends) know much either about the geographical position of Hayti, or the character and condition of her people; and yet the communication between England and Hayti is very frequent, and they are engaged in a large and lucrative trade with us, to the extent of which her custom-house entries are able to testify. Hayti is second to no country in the world in the quality of her soil and the excellence of her produce. Her coffee, cocoa, sugar, indigo, and mahogany are world-famed; and we believe that in the matter of cotton particularly, there is a glorious probability of Hayti playing a very prominent part in removing the necessity for the almost exclusive use of slave-grown cotton which is now painfully imposed upon us.

"But Hayti possesses other claims upon our attention besides those which are yielded from the richness of her soil and the value of her natural products. In the artistic standard of her work, particularly in those which, like cabinet making, require skill, taste, and ingenuity, Hayti is second to no nation on earth. The following extract from an article on Haytian Industry, from the pen of a distinguished Haytian, M. Durvelas Durval, will afford our readers some idea of the progress in this respect which his country has already made:

"'At the exhibition, these products were made: formerly some coarse cotton stuffs, known by the name of 'manganes,' baggings, saddle-cloths, saddles, ropes of the palm tree, and baskets, and large wicker-work baskets; now cloths of fine cotton and gold thread of different shades, and the making of artificial flowers and fruits in wax, which occupy the delicate hands of our young city girls, tanning, although not of the most perfect kind, shoemaking, harness-making, hatmaking, goldsmithing and clockmaking, all afford products worthy of notice, and employ many excellent workmen. The tailor's art, practised by Haytians as well as foreign workmen, follows the European fashions.—But the business in which the improvement is most striking is cabinet-making. It is to some skilful German workmen we owe the formation of those brave and intelligent Haytian operatives, whose number is increasing every year; in our shops, and also under their own direction, after the European manner and in a highly finished style.

"'There is, indeed, no department of mechanics, agriculture, or art, for that matter, which the people of Hayti have not afforded a proof of their ability to keep pace with European civilization.

"'A Haytian friend of ours tells an amusing story of a French bishop who was appointed to a diocese in Hayti, and who went out to the country with the idea that he was going to labor among a people as barbarous as the negro tribes of Western Africa. What was his astonishment, on landing at Jacmel, to find himself surrounded by all the evidences of an advanced civilization, and welcomed by a society whose good breeding and polished manners rivalled the social habits of Paris or London! But the bishop would have felt little surprise at what he saw and heard if he had been acquainted with the history, throughout the country, of an admirable system of education, founded by Emperor Christophe, that so far back as 1815, King Christophe introduced the Lancasterian system into his dominions, under the supervision of a number of enlightened English teachers, whom he invited over for that purpose. The country is divided into sixty-five parishes, in each of which a public school is maintained by the State; while in Port-au-Prince, Cape Haytian, and Cayes, there are high schools, academies, colleges, schools of medicine, and other superior educational establishments, provided for by the liberality of the community. In the colleges the English language is taught; the value of this requirement being universally appreciated, especially by those who intend to engage in commercial pursuits. All the teachers are natives of the country, and many of them are men of high respectable ability and attainments. The Emperor himself gives the highest encouragement to the education of his people, and no man is more fully conscious of the fact, that education is the most powerful and effective means of increasing the happiness and promoting the best and most permanent interests of a nation, and securing the stability of the empire. Hence His Majesty takes such a warm, paternal interest in the principal schools, and endeavors, from time to time, to increase their efficiency and usefulness.

"'Of the literature of Hayti we will, at present, say little, although much might be written thereupon. Mr. Alphonse de Saint-Remy, and M. Madieu, by name, have acquired some celebrity—the former by his biographical works, and the latter by his poems. But we have now before us several newspapers published in Hayti, containing original articles—copies of which we have had the pleasure to receive—written with great ability and spirit, and instinct with a high tone of moral feeling.

"'American journalists have grossly calumniated Hayti, but never were the primary cause of her social and political degradation. The writers of America naturally regard her with an unfriendly eye, because Hayti is a practical protest against the system of negro Slavery, and a convincing evidence of the capacity of the African race. And while we are gratified to observe that the French government and nation are disposed to view Hayti with a friendly eye, yet we cannot but deplore the subtle efforts which have been made to incite feelings of hostility between the two nations, and which efforts were excited by the successful efforts she made to cast off her galling yoke.

"'As a consequence of the state of public opinion in America we find the pro-slavery press making insidious attempts to obtain such a footing in the hitherto ill-governed and disorganized Dominican Republic, as will enable them the more effectually to attack the independence of Hayti, through what is logically her weakest and most powerful section of the island. But we are glad to be able to state that General Santana, the President of the Dominican Republic, who, there is grave reason to believe, had availed himself of his elevated position to promote the intrigues of American agents, has been removed from office amid general expressions of satisfaction. His successor is M. Baez, a patriotic statesman, whom he banished on his elevation to power, and whose Presidentship says the Journal des Debats, 'was inaugurated by public rejoicings.' 'The people,' continues the same journal, 'repaired in a body to the residence of the Archbishop, the ex-President, General Reglamota, the Consuls of Spain, England, and France, where speeches were delivered in celebration of this joyous event.'

"'We earnestly wish that the Journal des Debats exhibited as intelligent an acquaintance with the State of Hayti as it does with that of St. Domingo; for the truth is the very reverse of what it states, and it has so misinterpreted the condition of the former country that the Baron Damien, the Haytian Minister at Paris, felt himself called upon to address a dignified reply to the statements of the French journalist. In his reply he uses language to the following purport:

"'"I beg you and the whole world to believe me when I declare that the Emperor of Hayti has no desire to see St. Domingo subject to him. She is a State duly organized, that requires no suggestion, but quietly and unremittingly exerting herself to take the rank which belongs to her among other nations of the world... Her government... Her sovereign... and every foreigner who visits our country is astonished at the progress... that the chief to whom it has confided its destinies is a ruler of extraordinary wisdom, and fully competent to fulfill his mission; that he has no desire to disturb the internal peace and prosperity of the country, and that he has nothing more at heart than to protect the rights and interests of all who are interested in the future of the Haytian nation. Under these circumstances, it is the conviction of our dignity as a nation, and with a sense of the duty which devolves upon us, we shall, with the blessing of the Almighty, keep strictly within our own border, maintaining a position which will constitute the best justification for our independence, and win the respect of every friend of humanity.'

"It is a pleasure for us to turn from the Journal des Debats, to a late issue of the organ of the French press, Le Courrier de Havre. In an article on Hayti, this journal remarks that Hayti is putting forth efforts to raise herself to an equality with other civilized nations, both as regards the richness of her soil and her geographical position, and the desire she has to secure a strong and stable government. The following extract from this article cannot fail to be interesting:

"'"The two allied nations, especially France and England, should keep up a good understanding with that empire and its government, and to respect its independence. They ought to consider Hayti as a free, sovereign, and independent State... with which European ideas are penetrating into... Hayti has been made a subject of mockery... which has been laughed at because people did not understand the true state of things. The inhabitants to constitute themselves into a nation... Imagine the feuds, the jealousies, and probably even the wars, which would arise if England were divided into two separate principalities, each maintaining a different form of government, and each maintaining a different system of legislation... But if Hayti made an attempt at imitation, it is ridiculous to laugh at. Ought the attempt at imitation to be treated with laughter? Is the effort to raise herself to a level with European civilization to be answered by the contact with civilization? To prosecute such a course would be as unjust as it is contrary to humanity. The slanderers of Hayti did not give her time to move; they have judged her prematurely, and without reason; they did not see that it would have been honorable in them to encourage these generous efforts instead of insanely abusing a people composed of men, former slaves, who became independent by their valor, and were left to themselves to create a nationality. The man, who better than all his predecessors, understood the future of his country, who he felt in himself the force and energy necessary to overwhelm anarchy, and to found a strong and stable government, is the Emperor Faustin I. In spite of reverses, he has been able to establish... without caring for obstacles, which he overcame with admirable firmness, laying the foundation of the groundwork upon which he is raising a monumental edifice which is to assure the destiny of his people.'

"We cannot but deplore as a calamity the continued disunion subsisting between Hayti and St. Domingo. The fact simply is, that the island ought not to be ruled by two distinct governments. Imagine the feuds, the jealousies, and probably even the wars, which would arise if England were divided into two separate principalities, each maintaining a different form of government, and each maintaining a different system of legislation. The state of the actual affair of affairs in the island of St. Domingo is the greater pity; because, a direct misfortune, it is that the isolation of the Dominican Republic, from its weakness and instability, has enabled foreign intrigue to aim successful blows at the independence of the whole country. The Haytian government may have erred in its mode of expression, but, in the case of Hayti, it becomes a distinct right, and we cannot but deplore, and shall not think that negro capacity for self-government will have been fairly tried, so long as the two States under one government would form a far more efficient guarantee of the political independence of the entire nation, and of the tri-color flag, than all the treaties and all the foreign engagements into which France and England might enter to protect them, or any fleet which they might make in the Gulf of Mexico or the Caribbean Sea.

"Postscript.—Since the foregoing was written, a suspension of hostilities between Hayti and St. Domingo has been agreed to."

records.headline: The Revolution in St. Domingo.
records.summary_en: A private letter published in the *Turks Island Standard* reports that a revolution has broken out in the Dominican Republic. According to the excerpt, the primary cause of the uprising was an attempt by the government to depreciate the paper currency or alter the rate of exchange by twenty percent, alongside grievances regarding the central government's appropriation of provincial resources. Additionally, the revolutionists' manifesto—modeled after the American Declaration of Independence—complains of oppressive administrations, despotism, violations of personal liberty, arbitrary arrests, and the suppression of the press.
records.summary_es: Una misiva particular divulgada en el *Turks Island Standard* expone el estallido de un alzamiento revolucionario en la República Dominicana. Según el relato, el detonante principal consistió en la pretensión oficial de devaluar el papel moneda o alterar en un veinte por ciento el tipo de cambio, aunada a los agravios por la incautación de recursos provinciales por el poder central. Se añade que el manifiesto de los sublevados —inspirado en el Acta de Independencia de Estados Unidos— denunciaba administraciones vejatorias, tiranía, conculcación de la libertad individual, prisiones arbitrarias y clausura de la imprenta.

records.full_text: THE REVOLUTION IN ST. DOMINGO.—A private letter, dated Porto Plata, July 20th, which is published in the Turks Island Standard of August 1st, gives the principal cause of the revolution which has recently broken out in the Dominican republic as an attempt made by the government to alter the present rate of exchange or to depreciate the value of the paper currency of the country some twenty per cent. Another rumor was to the effect that the authorities of the city of St. Domingo have been drawing upon the resources of the provinces, and appropriating them without allowing a reasonable proportion to be spent in improvement and for other purposes of a local nature. Other causes are also assigned. The manifesto of the revolutionists is very nicely copied after our own Declaration of Independence, stating the preliminary dogmas about the uses of government, the reserved rights of the governed, &c., precisely in the same style, and giving that body failures as a succession of devouring and rapacious administrations which have oppressed the republic and despoiled the people of property and happiness. The rebels charge that the paper currency has been, time and again, has been nothing but the means of giving improper aid and support to despotism and plunder. They allege financial distresses, destruction of personal liberty, the arbitrary arrest of citizens, tyrannical judgments, the destruction of the liberty of the press, and of the nation, and the dissolution of the national representative bodies by insidious and artful intrigues.

records.headline: The Revolution in St. Domingo.
records.summary_en: A vessel arriving in New York from Turk's Island reported that the revolution in St. Domingo was rapidly nearing its close, with the entire Republic—except for the city of St. Domingo—declaring for the new Government. An army of 8,000 revolutionists was encamped before the city walls, expecting the inhabitants to declare in their favor, while President Baez had retired to the fortress and Soulouque was reportedly assembling a force on the northern frontiers. The movement had thus far been accomplished without bloodshed or arrests, and a July 8 proclamation by the people of Cibao at Santiago detailed grievances against previous governments regarding personal liberty, the press, and national freedom.
records.summary_es: Un buque fondeado en Nueva York procedente de las islas Turcas participó que la revolución en Santo Domingo tocaba rápidamente a su término, habiéndose pronunciado toda la república —a excepción de la capital— en favor del nuevo régimen. Un ejército sitiador de 8.000 revolucionarios acampaba ante las murallas de la plaza aguardando que el vecindario se declarase de su parte, mientras el presidente Báez se acogió a la fortaleza y Soulouque concentraba tropas en la frontera septentrional. El alzamiento se consumó hasta entonces sin efusión de sangre ni prisiones, detallando una proclama del 8 de julio rubricada por los cibaeños en Santiago las vejaciones de gobiernos precedentes sobre las garantías ciudadanas, la imprenta y la soberanía patria.

The first of the series appeared in the Intelligencer of Thursday last; the second is given to-day.

THE REVOLUTION IN ST. DOMINGO.

A vessel arrived at New York from Turk’s Island brings some interesting details of the progress of the revolution in St. Domingo. The advices from Port-au-Platte are to the 17th ultimo. The revolution is said to be drawing rapidly to a close. With the exception of the city of St. Domingo, the whole of the Republic has declared in favor of the new order of things. Baez was still in the capital, but it was thought he could not hold out much longer. The revolutionary party have established a provisional government at Santiago, of which Gen. Jose Desiderio Valverde is President. The new government has issued a decree for the election of a convention to frame a new constitution. The revolutionists have also issued a decree opening all the ports of the Republic to the commerce of all nations. The revolutionary army is said to be well organized and well equipped. The people are said to be enthusiastic in favor of the revolution.

records.full_text: We have received files of the St. Christopher Gazette to the 28th ult., containing interesting details of the revolution now in progress in the Dominican republic of St. Domingo, to remove President Baez and restore Santana. The Baez party, being hard pressed, had formed an alliance with the Emperor Soulouque, who had despatched assistance to his ally. The Royal Standard of the 22d inst. says: By the sloop Seaflower, from Port Platta, we have advices from that place to the 17th instant. From a correspondent we learn that the revolution is gaining ground, and that the Baez party are losing their influence. The revolutionary party have possession of the whole of the Cibao, and have established a Provisional Government at Santiago, of which General Jose Desiderio Valverde is President. The city of St. Domingo is closely besieged by the revolutionary party, and it is expected that it will soon be in their possession. The Baez party have called in the assistance of the Haytiens, and it is said that Soulouque has sent them 1,500 men. This has caused much indignation among the Dominicans, and many of the Baez party have, in consequence, joined the revolutionists.

records.headline: The New York Herald reports news brought by the schooner Mary Jane
records.summary_en: The New York Herald reports news brought by the schooner Mary Jane from Puerto Plata, reprinting items from the Turks Islands Gazette of October 7, regarding hostilities in San Domingo. A translated September 17 bulletin from the official paper at Santo Domingo announces that the English schooner Merillen arrived from Samaná with dispatches from a government general reporting that his forces attacked and routed the Cibao garrison at Savannah la Mar, inflicting heavy losses in killed and wounded while suffering only one soldier wounded and a slight shoulder contusion to the general himself. The official bulletin hails this victory as proof that Providence protects the loyal armies from Mojarra to this latest engagement and adds that the northern flotilla opened fire on the 11th against a group of men assembled near Matanzas. The Turks Islands Gazette remarks that although civil war is raging in the Dominican Republic, it has not yet been able to ascertain the aims of the contending parties.
records.summary_es: Al reproducir notas de la Turks Islands Gazette del 7 de octubre, el New York Herald informa sobre las noticias llevadas desde Puerto Plata por la goleta Mary Jane acerca de las hostilidades en Santo Domingo. Un boletín traducido del 17 de septiembre del periódico oficial de la ciudad de Santo Domingo anuncia que la goleta inglesa Merillen llegó procedente de Samaná con despachos de un general del gobierno en los que informa haber atacado y derrotado a la guarnición cibaeña en Savannah la Mar, causando numerosas bajas entre muertos y heridos, mientras que sus tropas solo tuvieron un herido además de una leve contusión en el hombro sufrida por el propio general. El boletín oficial celebra este triunfo como prueba de que la Providencia protege a los ejércitos leales desde Mojarra hasta este último encuentro, y añade que la flotilla que opera en el norte abrió fuego el día 11 contra un grupo de hombres reunidos cerca de Matanzas. La Turks Islands Gazette observa que, aunque la guerra civil hace estragos en la República Dominicana, aún no ha podido determinar los objetivos de los bandos en pugna.

records.full_text:
News from Saint Domingo.
THE LIBERTY PARTY ORGANIZING A CONSTITUTION—
ELECTIONS ORDERED—SIEGE OF SAN DOMINGO CITY
—TWO WAR VESSELS AND A LARGE MORTAR WANTED
—BAEZ’S FRIENDS FALLING OFF—THE AMERICAN
SCHOONER CHARLES HILL.

The schooner City Belle, Captain Pendleton, arrived at this port yesterday from Port au Plata, with news dated at that place on 29th of October.

The authors of the revolution of the liberty party in the Dominican republic are fast organizing a new government very different from that of Senor Baez.

The election for the deputies of the nation was to take place on the 10th of November, and the members were to meet at the town of Moca on the 1st of December.

General Santana and several other valiant Generals were besieging the city of St. Domingo with a force of 8,000 men. The besiegers are very moderate in their fire against the city, as it was momentarily expected that Baez would be forced to capitulate. An expedition of 2,000 men strong were marching against Samana, the only place holding for Baez.

Business in Port au Plata and Santiago continued quite safe and easy, although all the military in the province of Cibao were under arms.

The Cibao government wish to purchase two small clipper schooners of 150 to 180 tons, to blockade the port of St. Domingo; vessels that are staunch and strong, that will be able to carry a twenty-four pounder upon a pivot, besides small guns of smaller calibre. There being no vessels in port suitable, any American speculator might find a good offer from the government, if quickly attended to, in Port au Plata.

News had reached Port au Plata that many of the first families had lately left the city of St. Domingo, besides natives that Baez has sent away.

The people and foreign residents were very much astonished that the American government did not send a vessel of war to St. Domingo, to demand satisfaction in the case of the American schooner Charles Hill, which was seized by Baez (valued at $10,000), and as yet not claimed by the American government. The American Consul at St. Domingo had sent all the documents relative to this affair in May last to Washington.

Fighting men, friends to the republic, would be well received. Arms and ammunition were in good demand, and they were in want of an 18-inch mortar, for which the highest rates would be paid.

records.summary_en: Dispatches from the South American naval station report that conditions in the Dominican Republic required the French admiral to intervene for the protection of French residents. Additionally, the Paris Moniteur issues a caution to emigrants, noting that after a group recently departed France for St. Domingo and another departure was announced, unfavorable accounts of the first settlers prompted advice that French colonists postpone establishing themselves in the republic.
records.summary_es: Despachos desde la estación naval de América del Sur informan que las condiciones en la República Dominicana obligaron al almirante francés a intervenir para la protección de los residentes franceses. Asimismo, el Moniteur de París emite una advertencia a los emigrantes, señalando que, tras la reciente partida de un grupo desde Francia hacia Santo Domingo y el anuncio de otra salida, los informes desfavorables sobre la situación de los primeros colonos aconsejan que los colonos franceses pospongan sus planes de establecerse en la república.

records.headline: The Tribune reprints a report from the Turks Islands Standard based
records.summary_en: The Tribune reprints a report from the Turks Islands Standard based on the arrival of the Dominican sloop Isabel from Puerto Plata. At the vessel's departure, the capital had not yet surrendered to the besieging army under General Santana, while General E. Puello commanded 1,500 men before Samaná against forces facing a shortage of provisions. Meanwhile, the mail schooner Nineteenth of March surrendered under a flag of truce with $22,000 Spanish in provisions, leading to the capture of President Baez's correspondence from Europe and St. Thomas, with private letters forwarded to British Consul Hood for delivery. The Isabel then embarked General F. Sosa and other refugees who had fled Baez's persecution to transport them to Puerto Plata.
records.summary_es: El Tribune reproduce un informe del Turks Islands Standard basado en la llegada de la balandra dominicana Isabel desde Puerto Plata. A la salida de la embarcación, aún no se sabía que la capital se hubiera rendido al ejército sitiador del general Santana, mientras que el general E. Puello comandaba 1,500 hombres frente a Samaná contra fuerzas que enfrentaban escasez de víveres. Entretanto, la goleta correo Diecinueve de Marzo se rindió bajo bandera de tregua con provisiones valoradas en 22,000 pesos fuertes españoles, lo que condujo a la captura de la correspondencia del presidente Báez desde Europa y Saint Thomas, enviándose las cartas privadas al cónsul británico Hood para su entrega. Posteriormente, la Isabel embarcó al general F. Sosa y a otros refugiados que habían huido de la persecución de Báez para trasladarlos a Puerto Plata.
