records.headline: Under the headline "Spain and the Dominican Republic," the Daily Whig of Richmond observes
records.summary_en: Under the headline "Spain and the Dominican Republic," the Daily Whig of Richmond observes that rumors concerning Spain's designs against the Dominican Republic (referred to as "the Republic of Dominica") draw attention to the military and naval strength of the Madrid government. Citing a statement from the New York World, the article notes that in 1860 the Spanish navy numbered 137 vessels—including 49 ships-of-war, war steamers, and other war vessels—in addition to smaller coast-service craft, three ships-of-the-line with 1,000-horse auxiliary steam-power on the stocks, and five steam frigates. The piece also points to the size of Spain's regular army organization, including 10 captain-generals and 148 major-generals, and reports that in Cuba Spain maintains eight regiments of veterans, one regiment of artillery, a brigade of five batteries, one company of workmen, two regiments of cavalry, one battalion of engineers, and a large militia force across the principal ports and towns.
records.summary_es: Bajo el titular «España y la República Dominicana», el Richmond Daily Whig observa que los rumores sobre los designios de España contra la República Dominicana (denominada «la República de Dominica») llaman la atención sobre la fuerza militar y naval del gobierno de Madrid. Citando un informe del New York World, el artículo señala que en 1860 la armada española contaba con 137 buques —incluidos 49 buques de guerra, vapores de guerra y otras embarcaciones bélicas—, además de embarcaciones menores para el servicio costero, tres navíos de línea con potencia auxiliar de vapor de 1,000 caballos en astillero y cinco fragatas de vapor. La nota también destaca la magnitud de la organización del ejército regular español, que incluye 10 capitanes generales y 148 mayores generales, e informa que en Cuba España mantiene ocho regimientos de veteranos, un regimiento de artillería, una brigada de cinco baterías, una compañía de obreros, dos regimientos de caballería, un batallón de ingenieros y una numerosa fuerza de milicia distribuida en los principales puertos y poblaciones.

records.headline: The Wilmington Journal comments on the reported intention of Spain
records.summary_en: The Wilmington Journal comments on the reported intention of Spain to reconquer the Dominican Republic, noting that it is a former Spanish colony whose independence the Spanish government has never formally acknowledged. The paper mocks a Dominican call to arms declaring that the inhabitants would "make a fight of giants which will astonish the whole world, and make the earth tremble under our feet," contrasting the boast with the republic's total population of 126,500. Despite denials by the Spanish minister, the article states that Spain genuinely appears to intend to assert authority over San Domingo, predicting that Spain will take the eastern part of the island, known as the Dominican Republic, while France will take the western part, known as the Republic of Haiti.
records.summary_es: El Wilmington Journal comenta la anunciada intención de España de reconquistar la República Dominicana, señalando que se trata de una antigua colonia española cuya independencia el gobierno español nunca ha reconocido formalmente. El periódico ironiza sobre un llamado a las armas dominicano que declara que sus habitantes harían «una lucha de gigantes que asombrará al mundo entero y hará temblar la tierra bajo nuestros pies», contrastando la proclama con la población total de la república de 126,500 habitantes. A pesar de los desmentidos del ministro español, el artículo afirma que España realmente parece tener la intención de imponer su autoridad sobre Santo Domingo, y predice que España tomará la parte oriental de la isla, conocida como la República Dominicana, mientras que Francia tomará la parte occidental, conocida como la República de Haití.

records.headline: A correspondent in the Orleans Independent Standard reports
records.summary_en: A correspondent in the Orleans Independent Standard reports that no more than eighty Spaniards in all arrived at St. Domingo, consisting of mechanics and three officials who immediately assumed duties as port collectors, which the writer states represents the entirety of the "emigration" sent to the Dominican Republic by Spain, alongside the customary influx of South American exiles fleeing revolutions in Venezuela and neighboring countries. According to the writer, President Santana's policy nevertheless enabled his opponents to unite behind the charge that he was "selling the country to the whites," and as early as the previous December revolutionary circulars and proclamations were in type in St. Domingo, with a copy of the proofs shown to an ambassador in Paris. Although that plot was suppressed and Báez remains in exile, the writer reports that growing opposition intrigues have led Santana to call for outside aid both to perpetuate his own government and to repay his loan.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal en el Orleans Independent Standard informa que no más de ochenta españoles en total llegaron a Santo Domingo, compuestos por mecánicos y tres funcionarios que asumieron de inmediato sus funciones como recaudadores en los puertos, lo cual, según el autor, representa toda la «emigración» enviada a la República Dominicana por España, junto con el habitual flujo de exiliados sudamericanos que huyen de las revoluciones en Venezuela y los países vecinos. Según el articulista, la política del presidente Santana dio sin embargo pie a que la oposición se uniera bajo la acusación de que estaba «vendiendo el país a los blancos», y ya en el mes de diciembre anterior había circulares y proclamas revolucionarias en imprenta en Santo Domingo, cuyas pruebas fueron mostradas a un embajador en París. Aunque ese proyecto fue sofocado y Báez permanece en el exilio, el autor informa que las crecientes intrigas de la oposición han llevado a Santana a pedir ayuda externa tanto para asegurar la perpetuidad de su propio gobierno como para pagar el empréstito.

records.summary_en: Following the 1844 secession of the Dominican Republic, two alternating political parties led by Santana and Baez emerged, representing reunion and independence policies respectively. Santana repeatedly and unsuccessfully sought to place the republic under the control of Spain, France, or Venezuela, and also failed in his efforts to induce white emigration from the United States.

records.headline: The Anti-Slavery Bugle reprints "The Dominican Republic," an article
records.summary_en: The Anti-Slavery Bugle reprints "The Dominican Republic," an article from the New-York Tribune, noting that for nearly seventy years the island of Haiti—formerly called Hispaniola and later St. Domingo—has been a theater of revolutions since the first African slave was brought there. Situated fifty-four miles from Cuba and once known as the "Garden of the Antilles," the island was divided almost equally at the outbreak of the French Revolution into a French and a Spanish colony. According to the article, the wealthy white slaveholding proprietors of the French colony initially embraced principles of liberty and equality for themselves, before those principles spread downward through society. The account adds that in 1791 the French National Assembly decreed civil freedom for persons of color born of free parents, that universal freedom was proclaimed to the slaves in 1793, and that the Spanish colony was subsequently ceded to France.
records.summary_es: Reproduciendo un artículo titulado «La República Dominicana» del New-York Tribune, el Anti-Slavery Bugle señala que durante casi setenta años la isla de Haití —antes llamada La Española y luego Santo Domingo— ha sido escenario de revoluciones desde que fue llevado allí el primer esclavo africano. Situada a cincuenta y cuatro millas de Cuba y conocida en otro tiempo como el «Jardín de las Antillas», la isla estaba dividida casi en partes iguales al estallar la Revolución Francesa en una colonia francesa y otra española. Según el artículo, los ricos propietarios blancos de esclavos de la colonia francesa abrazaron inicialmente los principios de libertad e igualdad para sí mismos, antes de que dichos principios penetraran hacia los estratos inferiores de la sociedad. El relato añade que en 1791 la Asamblea Nacional Francesa decretó la libertad civil para las personas de color nacidas de padres libres, que en 1793 se proclamó la libertad universal para los esclavos y que posteriormente la colonia española fue cedida a Francia.

records.headline: Following the closing lines of a proclamation dated Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: Following the closing lines of a proclamation dated Santo Domingo, March 10, 1861, and signed by Santana with cries of long live Doña Isabel II and liberty, The Daily Green Mountain Freeman presents an account of the Dominican portion of the island in view of intelligence that it has been re-annexed to Spain. The paper describes the island of Haiti as the largest, richest, and most important of the West India islands next to Cuba, noting that since its independence it has been divided into Haiti, a former French colony occupying about two-fifths of its area, and the "republic of Dominica" (the Dominican Republic), a former Spanish colony holding the remaining three-fifths. According to the report, the Dominican Republic has a population of about 105,000, roughly one-tenth of whom are white, and maintains an army of 20,000 men and a navy of seven small vessels. In 1852, its total exports—chiefly mahogany, ebony, and other precious woods—amounted to one and a half million dollars, while its imports, largely from the United States, totaled slightly more.
records.summary_es: Tras las líneas finales de una proclama fechada en Santo Domingo el 10 de marzo de 1861 y firmada por Santana con vivas a Doña Isabel II y a la libertad, The Daily Green Mountain Freeman presenta una reseña de la parte dominicana de la isla ante la noticia de que ha sido reanexada a España. El periódico describe la isla de Haití como la más grande, rica e importante de las Antillas después de Cuba, señalando que desde su independencia se ha dividido entre Haití, antigua colonia francesa que ocupa cerca de dos quintas partes de su superficie, y la llamada «república de Dominica» (la República Dominicana), antigua colonia española que posee las tres quintas partes restantes. Según el informe, la República Dominicana tiene una población de unos 105,000 habitantes, de los cuales aproximadamente una décima parte son blancos, y mantiene un ejército de 20,000 hombres y una armada de siete embarcaciones pequeñas. En 1852, sus exportaciones totales —principalmente caoba, ébano y otras maderas preciosas— ascendieron a un millón y medio de dólares, mientras que sus importaciones, procedentes en gran parte de los Estados Unidos, superaron ligeramente esa cifra.

records.headline: A correspondent in the Holmes County Republican reports that since
records.summary_en: A correspondent in the Holmes County Republican reports that since the independence of the Dominican Republic, two parties led respectively by Santana and Baez have divided and alternately governed the country under policies represented by the words "reunion" and "independence." Some years earlier, Santana borrowed a million dollars from Spain and, failing to repay the loan according to its terms, offered a mortgage on the custom houses, resulting in the arrival the previous summer of no more than eighty Spaniards at St. Domingo, including three officials who immediately assumed duties as port collectors while the rest were mechanics. According to the writer, that group constituted all the "emigration" Spain had sent to the Dominican Republic, and Santana's policy united the opposition against his government with accusations that he was selling the country to the whites. Although revolutionary circulars and proclamations were in type in St. Domingo as early as December and proofs were shown to the ambassador at Paris, the project was nipped in the bud, Baez remains in exile, and Santana has called for aid as opposition intrigues continue and increase.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del Holmes County Republican informa que, desde la independencia de la República Dominicana, dos partidos encabezados respectivamente por Santana y Báez han dividido y gobernado alternativamente el país bajo políticas representadas por las palabras «reunión» e «independencia». Algunos años atrás, Santana tomó prestado un millón de dólares de España y, al no poder pagarlo según los términos del préstamo, ofreció una hipoteca sobre las aduanas, lo que dio lugar a la llegada el verano anterior de no más de ochenta españoles a Santo Domingo, entre ellos tres funcionarios que asumieron de inmediato sus cargos como recaudadores en los puertos mientras que el resto eran mecánicos. Según el autor, ese grupo constituía toda la «emigración» enviada por España a la República Dominicana, y la política de Santana unió a la oposición contra su gobierno bajo la acusación de que estaba vendiendo el país a los blancos. Aunque ya en diciembre circulaban en imprenta proclamas y circulares revolucionarias en Santo Domingo cuyas pruebas fueron mostradas al embajador en París, el proyecto fue sofocado en ciernes, Báez permanece en el exilio y Santana ha solicitado ayuda ante el continuo aumento de las intrigas opositoras.

records.headline: The transfer was to be effected by a coup it main
records.summary_en: According to *The New York herald* on April 19, 1861, three members of the Dominican cabinet orchestrated a transfer of power to Spain through a coup, supported by secret agents landed from the war steamer *Don John de Austria* and Spanish vessels arriving from Cuba and Porto Rico with paid emigrants, arms, and soldiers. When local authorities questioned these arrivals, they were officially told that the soldiers came to help repel Haytian invasions and the emigrants to till the ground, explanations that the people eventually came to believe after several months passed without further movements.
records.summary_es: Según *The New York Herald* del 19 de abril de 1861, tres miembros del gabinete dominicano orquestaron la entrega del poder a España mediante un golpe de Estado, secundados por agentes secretos desembarcados del vapor de guerra *Don John de Austria* y por navíos españoles procedentes de Cuba y Puerto Rico con inmigrantes pagados, armas y tropas. Cuando las autoridades locales inquirieron sobre estos desembarcos, se les contestó oficialmente que la tropa llegaba para ayudar a rechazar invasiones haitianas y los colonos para labrar la tierra, explicaciones que la población terminó por creer al cabo de varios meses sin que se registraran nuevos movimientos.

records.headline: A correspondent in the New-York Dispatch laments what he calls
records.summary_en: A correspondent in the New-York Dispatch laments what he calls the funeral obsequies of the Dominican Republic, asserting that Spain has bought up and intimidated President Santana and the heads of the Dominican forces so that the Spanish flag of "blood and gold" now floats from the bastions of Santo Domingo. According to the writer, the only free and constitutional state in the West Indies was stifled on March 18, 1861, by a select corps of traitors backed by a force of Spanish soldiers and Spanish bribe-money. The correspondent states that the late President of the United States had been informed of the plan to end the Dominican Republic by high-ranking Cubans and must also have been apprised of it by his own envoys at Madrid and Santo Domingo, yet took no notice of it. Two years earlier, La Presse and La Patrie of Paris had published articles on suppressing the Dominican Republic as semi-official feelers to gauge international reaction to converting a free state on the borders of the American Union into a Spanish coolie colony, while the Spanish press began patronizing its former colony as rich in natural wealth but lacking the political strength required of a nation.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del New-York Dispatch lamenta lo que denomina las exequias fúnebres de la República Dominicana, afirmando que España ha comprado e intimidado al presidente Santana y a los jefes de las fuerzas dominicanas, de modo que la bandera española de «sangre y oro» ondea ahora en los bastiones de Santo Domingo. Según el autor, el único Estado libre y constitucional de las Antillas fue sofocado el 18 de marzo de 1861 por un grupo selecto de traidores respaldados por una fuerza de soldados españoles y dinero de sobornos españoles. El corresponsal señala que el anterior presidente de los Estados Unidos había sido informado del plan para poner fin a la República Dominicana por cubanos de alta posición y que también debió haber sido advertido por sus propios enviados en Madrid y Santo Domingo, pero no le prestó atención. Dos años antes, La Presse y La Patrie de París habían publicado artículos sobre la supresión de la República Dominicana como sondeos semioficiales para medir la reacción internacional ante la conversión de un Estado libre cercano a la Unión Americana en una colonia española de culíes, mientras la prensa española comenzaba a referirse con condescendencia a su antigua colonia como rica en recursos naturales pero carente de la fuerza política propia de una nación.

records.headline: Continuing its report on the Spanish takeover, a correspondent
records.summary_en: Continuing its report on the Spanish takeover, a correspondent signed "E. D." in the New-York Dispatch states that Spain had been secretly landing men and supplies for three weeks while the entire population was disarmed before anyone suspected the cause. In the towns of Neyba, Azua, and San Cristobal, single officers collected all weapons under the pretext of replacing them with a better class, and popular patriotic leaders were lured inside the walls of Santo Domingo and detained as prisoners. At six in the morning on the 18th, the President, the three members of his cabinet, and a half-dozen high officers who had managed the affair raised the Spanish flag over the forts and proclaimed Isabella II Queen of the Dominican territory. The correspondent reports that the people received the notification in silent consternation and that scarcely a single Dominican outside the paid officials responded to the Spaniards' shout of "long live the Queen," despite double pay and lavish promises distributed overnight to the garrison and police, adding that desperate resistance is expected in the interior even though Dominicans say Spain will send 20,000 soldiers to crush the republic.
records.summary_es: Continuando su informe sobre la toma de posesión española, un corresponsal que firma «E. D.» en el New-York Dispatch afirma que España había estado desembarcando hombres y suministros en secreto durante tres semanas mientras toda la población era desarmada antes de que nadie sospechara la causa. En los pueblos de Neyba, Azua y San Cristóbal, oficiales recogieron todas las armas con el pretexto de reemplazarlas por otras de mejor clase, y los líderes patrióticos más populares fueron atraídos mediante engaños dentro de las murallas de Santo Domingo, donde permanecen detenidos como prisioneros. A las seis de la mañana del día 18, el presidente, los tres miembros de su gabinete y media docena de altos oficiales que habían dirigido el asunto izaron la bandera española sobre los fuertes y proclamaron a Isabel II reina del territorio dominicano. El corresponsal informa que el pueblo recibió la notificación con silenciosa consternación y que apenas un solo dominicano fuera de los funcionarios a sueldo respondió al grito español de «viva la Reina», pese a la paga doble y las pródigas promesas distribuidas durante la noche a la guarnición y a la policía, añadiendo que se espera una resistencia desesperada en el interior aunque los dominicanos dicen que España enviará 20,000 soldados para destruir la república.

records.headline: The New-York Daily Tribune, commenting on United States relations
records.summary_en: The New-York Daily Tribune, commenting on United States relations with Spain, remarks that there remains the chance of a collision, or rather of a diplomatic coolness and alienation, resulting from Spain's recent "reannexation" of the Dominican Republic (referred to in the passage as "Dominica"). The editorial characterizes the Spanish move as a rapacious and foolish act, though not nearly so unjustifiable as the United States' own kindred appropriation of Texas. The paper argues that had the United States ever treated the Dominican Republic with common decency or formally recognized its existence, Washington might now with reason interpose an energetic protest against the new Spanish blunder. As matters stand, the Tribune asks how the United States can protest when "Dominica," so far as appears on the surface, has chosen to merge its independent existence into a return to colonial dependence on Spain.
records.summary_es: Al comentar las relaciones de los Estados Unidos con España, el New-York Daily Tribune señala que subsiste la posibilidad de un choque, o más bien de un enfriamiento y distanciamiento diplomático, como resultado de la reciente «reanexión» española de la República Dominicana (denominada en el pasaje «Dominica»). El editorial califica la medida española de acto rapaz y necio, aunque ni de lejos tan injustificable como la apropiación similar de Texas por parte de los propios Estados Unidos. El periódico sostiene que si los Estados Unidos hubieran tratado alguna vez a la República Dominicana con decencia elemental o hubieran reconocido formalmente su existencia, Washington podría ahora interponer con razón una enérgica protesta contra el nuevo desacierto español. Tal como están las cosas, el Tribune se pregunta cómo pueden protestar los Estados Unidos cuando «Dominica», por lo que aparenta en la superficie, ha optado por fundir su existencia independiente en un retorno a la dependencia colonial de España.

records.headline: Presenting a Spanish account of the annexation of St. Domingo
records.summary_en: Presenting a Spanish account of the annexation of St. Domingo, The New York Herald states that the United States had always been a powerful obstacle to Spain opening her arms to her former colony, as Spain knew that the North Americans wanted St. Domingo for themselves just as they wanted Cuba, and delayed acquiring the former so as not to imperil the latter. Meanwhile, the Dominicans endeavored to counteract North American influence by becoming increasingly Spanish, opposing the continuous drafts of workmen sent by New York filibusters by encouraging the immigration of Spanish colonists and artisans at great sacrifice and appointing to their reduced army all Spanish officers who wished to enter the republic's service. Perceiving this, the North Americans redoubled their efforts, with one of Walker's former lieutenants operating in St. Domingo in a semi-official character to organize and receive the workmen sent from New York and establishing supplementary operations in Samana and Puerto Plata. According to the writer, two events rapidly changed the situation, including the war sustained by Spain in Africa, which gave Spain a consideration in the eyes of the Dominicans and Haitians that it had formerly lacked when they supposed Spain too weak to counteract North American influence.
records.summary_es: Al presentar un relato español sobre la anexión de Santo Domingo, The New York Herald afirma que los Estados Unidos habían sido siempre un poderoso obstáculo para que España abriera los brazos a su antigua colonia, pues España sabía muy bien que los norteamericanos querían Santo Domingo para sí mismos tal como querían a Cuba, y demoró la adquisición de la primera para no poner en peligro la segunda. Entretanto, los dominicanos procuraron contrarrestar la influencia norteamericana volviéndose cada vez más españoles, oponiendo a los continuos envíos de trabajadores mandados por los filibusteros de Nueva York la inmigración de colonos y artesanos españoles, fomentada a costa de grandes sacrificios, así como el nombramiento en su reducido ejército de todos los oficiales españoles que desearan entrar al servicio de la república. Al percibir esto, los norteamericanos redoblaron sus esfuerzos, hallándose uno de los antiguos lugartenientes de Walker en Santo Domingo con carácter semioficial para organizar y recibir a los trabajadores enviados desde Nueva York y estableciendo operaciones auxiliares en Samaná y Puerto Plata. Según el autor, dos acontecimientos cambiaron rápidamente la situación, entre ellos la guerra sostenida por España en África, la cual revistió a España ante los ojos de dominicanos y haitianos de una consideración que antes no tenía cuando la suponían demasiado débil para contrarrestar la influencia norteamericana.

records.headline: The New York Herald reviews a newly published pamphlet titled
records.summary_en: The New York Herald reviews a newly published pamphlet titled "French and European Interests in St. Domingo," noting that its author examines the question not merely from a political point of view but from the standpoint of liberal and democratic principles. Quoting the pamphlet, the article states that if principles are not words devoid of meaning in Europe, Spain will not be permitted to consummate its attempt against the Dominican Republic, where the author says liberty has reigned since 1822, nor against the Republic of Haiti, where it has reigned since the beginning of the century. The pamphlet argues that the people of Haiti are called upon to resolve the great question of the extent to which the Black race is susceptible of progress and civilization, noting that philosophers and politicians of all countries study their course while populations of African blood throughout the New World turn their eyes toward them. According to the author, they stand in the Antilles as a beacon pointing the road of liberty to eight million Black people who still groan under the lash and the stick in the nineteenth century, which he presents as their title to the protection of civilized nations.

Citando el folleto, el artículo afirma que si los principios no son en Europa palabras vacías de sentido, no se permitirá a España consumar su intento contra la República Dominicana, donde según el autor reina la libertad desde 1822, ni contra la República de Haití, donde reina desde principios del siglo. El folleto sostiene que el pueblo de Haití está llamado a resolver el gran problema de saber hasta qué punto la raza negra es susceptible de progreso y civilización, apuntando que filósofos y políticos de todos los países estudian con solicitud sus distintas fases mientras las poblaciones de sangre africana esparcidas por el Nuevo Mundo vuelven sus ojos hacia ellos. Según el autor, parecen haber sido colocados en las Antillas como un faro para señalar el camino de la libertad a ocho millones de negros que en pleno siglo XIX aún gimen bajo el látigo y el garrote, lo cual constituye su título a la protección de las naciones civilizadas.

records.headline: The Daily Exchange reports that letters from Kingston, Jamaica
records.summary_en: The Daily Exchange reports that letters from Kingston, Jamaica, indicate that the recent annexation of St. Domingo to Spain has been received there with very great alarm. A public meeting was recently held in Jamaica to consider the subject and to memorialize the British Queen. Among the resolutions adopted was a declaration that the attempt at annexation without the approval and concurrence of the popular vote of the Dominican Republic is contrary to every sentiment of justice and right, involves a gross outrage upon popular liberty, violates the principle held sacred by leading European powers that a people have the inalienable right to settle their own form of government, and could not be consummated without reflecting disgrace upon the Spanish flag. According to the report, the resulting memorial to the Queen has received not less than 3,500 signatures, making it the most numerously signed petition forwarded from the island with the exception of one on behalf of the late Governor Sir Lionel Smith.
records.summary_es: The Daily Exchange informa que cartas procedentes de Kingston, Jamaica, indican que la reciente anexión de Santo Domingo a España ha sido recibida allí con grandísima alarma. Recientemente se celebró una asamblea pública en Jamaica para examinar el asunto y elevar un memorial a la reina británica. Entre las resoluciones aprobadas figuraba una declaración según la cual el intento de anexión sin la aprobación y concurrencia del voto popular de la República Dominicana es contrario a todo sentimiento de justicia y derecho, entraña un grave atropello contra la libertad popular, viola el principio tenido por sagrado por las principales potencias europeas de que es derecho inalienable de un pueblo establecer su propia forma de gobierno, y no podría consumarse sin arrojar deshonra sobre la bandera española. Según el informe, el memorial dirigido a la reina ha recibido no menos de 3,500 firmas, convirtiéndose en el más numeroso enviado desde la isla con excepción de uno en favor del difunto gobernador Sir Lionel Smith.

records.headline: Under the headline "Revolution in St. Domingo," The Daily Dispatch reports
records.summary_en: Under the headline "Revolution in St. Domingo," The Daily Dispatch reports advices received from St. Domingo up to June 9 stating that a fierce reactionary movement against the renewal of Spanish rule is progressing in the country. According to the report, General Santana had established a reign of terror in support of Queen Isabella's annexation project, but the Dominicans had taken up arms against him in Moca, the Cibao, Vega, and every important standpoint of the country. A reinforcement had been sent from Puerto Rico to the Spanish army, and it was believed that 20,000 soldiers would be required in order to sustain Santana and the Spanish Queen. The dispatch adds that a severe mortality existed in the Spanish regiments.
records.summary_es: Bajo el titular «Revolución en Santo Domingo», The Daily Dispatch informa sobre despachos recibidos de Santo Domingo hasta el 9 de junio según los cuales avanza en el país un feroz movimiento de reacción contra el restablecimiento del dominio español. De acuerdo con el informe, el general Santana había instaurado un verdadero régimen de terror en apoyo del proyecto de anexión de la reina Isabel, pero los dominicanos se habían levantado en armas contra él en Moca, el Cibao, La Vega y todos los puntos importantes del país. Se había enviado un refuerzo desde Puerto Rico al ejército español, y se estimaba que serían necesarios 20,000 soldados para sostener a Santana y a Su Majestad Católica. El despacho añade que existía una grave mortandad en los regimientos españoles.

records.headline: Reporting on congressional proceedings, the Daily National Intelligencer notes
records.summary_en: Reporting on congressional proceedings, the Daily National Intelligencer notes a message from the President of the United States stating, through the Secretary of State, that the Executive Department of the Government did not deem it advisable at that time to communicate the diplomatic correspondence that had taken place between the United States Government and that of Her Catholic Majesty of Spain touching the annexation of the Dominican Republic to Spain. Following the message, the House of Representatives adjourned until twelve o'clock the next day.

Tras el mensaje, la Cámara de Representantes levantó la sesión hasta las doce del día siguiente.

records.headline: In correspondence from Havana, the Daily Ohio Statesman reports
records.summary_en: In correspondence from Havana, the Daily Ohio Statesman reports that General Serrano returned in an unpleasant mood from his trip to St. Domingo, having found everything in great confusion there and convinced himself that the inhabitants are dissatisfied with the way in which they are to be governed. According to the report, when the Dominicans annexed themselves to Spain, they insisted on being considered Spaniards and governed by the laws of Spain, but instead the Constitution there, as in Cuba, is a dead letter; although there is no slavery, the Dominicans aspire to possess as much political freedom as Spaniards have in Spain. When Serrano arrived aboard the Isabel la Catolica and signal guns announced his approach while troops lined the streets and fort artillery prepared a grand salute, a signal from the steamer ordered the troops back to their garrisons and directed that no public demonstrations be made. Serrano landed around twelve o'clock, walked to the palace for ten minutes, and rode off on horseback with officers to the villa "Los Molinos," where his wife, the Condesa de San Antonio, was awaiting him.
records.summary_es: En una correspondencia desde La Habana, el Daily Ohio Statesman informa que el general Serrano regresó de mal humor de su viaje a Santo Domingo, tras haber encontrado todo en gran confusión allí y haberse convencido de que los habitantes no están satisfechos con la forma en que van a ser gobernados. Según el informe, cuando los dominicanos se anexaron a España insistieron en ser considerados españoles y gobernados por las leyes de España, pero en cambio la Constitución allí, al igual que en Cuba, es letra muerta; aunque no hay esclavitud, los dominicanos aspiran a poseer tanta libertad política como la que tienen los españoles en España. Cuando Serrano llegó a bordo del Isabel la Católica y los cañonazos de señal anunciaron su aproximación mientras las tropas bordeaban las calles y la artillería de los fuertes preparaba una gran salva, una señal desde el vapor ordenó a las tropas regresar a sus guarniciones y dispuso que no se hicieran manifestaciones públicas. Serrano desembarcó alrededor de las doce, caminó hasta el palacio donde permaneció diez minutos y partió de inmediato a caballo acompañado de algunos oficiales hacia la quinta «Los Molinos», donde lo aguardaba su esposa, la condesa de San Antonio.

records.headline: Publishing the provisions of a Spanish royal decree in its Havana
records.summary_en: Publishing the provisions of a Spanish royal decree in its Havana correspondence, The New York Herald outlines the judicial arrangements scheduled to take effect on the first day of the coming year in the annexed territory of St. Domingo. Under Articles 2 through 4 of the decree, criminal proceedings will be adjusted in conformity with the laws and practice before the tribunals of the Spanish peninsula, while the civil code, the laws emanating from the legitimate powers of the former Dominican Republic, and the traditions and customs admitted by the tribunals of the territory will continue to be observed and applied in the meantime, with common law governing whenever there is no precedent under those codes, laws, and traditions. The correspondent adds that by subsequent decrees the Queen appoints judges and executive officers for the Supreme Court to be established at St. Domingo city, noting that many of them are respectable citizens of the acquired territory in a measure calculated to strengthen the bonds of union with the crown.
records.summary_es: Al publicar las disposiciones de un real decreto español en su correspondencia de La Habana, The New York Herald expone las normas judiciales que entrarán en vigor el primer día del año entrante en el territorio anexado de Santo Domingo. Conforme a los artículos 2 a 4 del decreto, los procesos penales se ajustarán a las leyes y prácticas vigentes ante los tribunales de la península española, mientras que el código civil, las leyes emanadas de los poderes legítimos de la antigua República Dominicana y las tradiciones y costumbres admitidas por los tribunales del territorio seguirán observándose y aplicándose entretanto, rigiendo el derecho común cuando no exista precedente bajo dichos códigos, leyes y tradiciones. El corresponsal añade que, mediante decretos posteriores, la reina nombra jueces y funcionarios ejecutivos para la Corte Suprema que habrá de establecerse en la ciudad de Santo Domingo, señalando que muchos de ellos son ciudadanos respetables del territorio adquirido, en una medida destinada a estrechar los lazos de unión con la corona.

records.headline: The republic was virtually dead, and the island was openly presented
records.summary_en: According to a January 13 dispatch reported by *The New York Herald* correspondent in San Domingo, the Dominican Republic was virtually dead and openly presented to the world as a Spanish province ruled by General Santana as the commissioned Captain-General for Queen Isabella. Spain promised numerous reforms as part of its policy of absorption—including declaring Samana a free port, inviting universal emigration, reducing tariffs on foreign-imported goods, proclaiming full religious toleration, and abolishing slavery—while it was also thought Queen Isabella would invite President Lincoln to send surplus negroes and contrabands to San Domingo. Additionally, the city's streets were enlivened with foreign carriages, buggies, drays, and new toilets, and the new United States Consul had not held any official intercourse with the government.
records.summary_es: Según un despacho del 13 de enero remitido por el corresponsal de *The New York Herald* en Santo Domingo, la República Dominicana había prácticamente dejado de existir, mostrándose abiertamente al mundo como provincia española gobernada por el general Santana como capitán general comisionado de la reina Isabel. España prometía múltiples reformas como parte de su política de absorción —incluida la declaración de Samaná como puerto libre, la invitación a la inmigración general, la rebaja de aranceles a las importaciones foráneas, la proclamación de una entera libertad de cultos y la abolición formal de la esclavitud—, al tiempo que se suponía que la reina Isabel cursaría una invitación al presidente Lincoln para asentar en Santo Domingo a los libertos negros rescatados de la Confederación («contrabands»). Asimismo, las calles de la capital se veían animadas con carruajes, calesas y carretas foráneas y novedades en el vestir, mientras que el nuevo cónsul de los Estados Unidos se abstenía de mantener trato oficial alguno con las autoridades.

A government decree admits such material free of duty. Ship bread is also ordered for free entry into the ports. Copper ore taken from mines near St. Domingo City was found to be strongly impregnated with gold. The coal beds of Samana promised a rich return to experienced miners. Napoleon had not yet appointed a French Consul in the city, or committed himself in any recognition of the new rule of Spain. The American “contrabands” left on Mr. Lincoln’s hands after the war can be taken, it is said, to the extent of four millions, on the island. They would be set to work, and really develope the wealth of the country. There was no American vessel in port.

records.summary_en: On April 24, 1862, the Senate unanimously ratified the Seward-Lyons treaty for the suppression of the African slave trade and passed a bill recognizing Hayti and Liberia. Additionally, French Minister M. Mercier returned to Washington from Richmond, visited the State Department to confer with Secretary Seward, and stated that his visit to Richmond was not of political importance and that he had never heard of Dr. Lemoine prior to his arrival.

Además, el ministro francés M. Mercier regresó a Washington procedente de Richmond, acudió al Departamento de Estado para conferenciar con el secretario Seward y declaró que su visita a Richmond carecía de trascendencia política, asegurando que jamás había oído hablar del Dr. Lemoine con anterioridad a su llegada.

records.headline: A correspondent writing from St. Domingo City
records.summary_en: A correspondent writing from St. Domingo City on May 17 reports that Spain is making its mark under the new rule, silencing the remaining malcontents and welcoming foreign capital and labour. A railroad from Santiago to Angelina on the Yuna has been decided upon, giving the Vega Real valley an outlet to the Bay of Samana, an American company has proposed navigating the Yuna, and a new tariff cutting duties from thirty to twenty per cent is expected to take effect in July.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal que escribe desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo el 17 de mayo informa que España está dejando su huella bajo el nuevo régimen, silenciando a los descontentos que quedan y dando la bienvenida al capital y la mano de obra extranjeros. Se ha decidido construir un ferrocarril de Santiago a Angelina, sobre el Yuna, que dará salida al valle de la Vega Real hacia la bahía de Samaná, una compañía americana ha propuesto navegar el Yuna, y se espera que en julio entre en vigor un nuevo arancel que reduce los derechos del treinta al veinte por ciento.

records.headline: The wishes of the people were not consulted, and how large
records.summary_en: According to the *New-York daily tribune*, the Dominican Republic was unexpectedly annexed to Spain on March 12, 1861, through the treason of President Santana without consulting the public, and the annexation was formally accepted by the Queen of Spain on May 20, 1861. While resident Spaniards and their descendants favored the change, citizens of African or mixed descent opposed it and desired to retain a republican form of government. Cuban papers report that the national party subsequently made an attempt to regain their independence.
records.summary_es: Según el *New-York daily tribune*, la República Dominicana fue anexionada inesperadamente a España el 12 de marzo de 1861 debido a la traición del presidente Santana sin consultar a la ciudadanía, y dicha anexión fue aceptada formalmente por la reina de España el 20 de mayo de 1861. Aunque los españoles residentes y sus descendientes favorecieron el cambio, los ciudadanos de ascendencia africana o mestiza se opusieron y desearon conservar la forma de gobierno republicana. Los diarios cubanos señalan que el partido nacionalista intentó posteriormente recuperar la independencia.

records.headline: In correspondence from Havana, The New York Herald reports that the rebellion
records.summary_en: In correspondence from Havana, The New York Herald reports that the rebellion in St. Domingo still continues and that Spanish troops are being dispatched to Puerto Plata. According to the dispatch, the screw corvette Santa Lucia left Santiago again on the 4th with troops, and the Ulloa sailed from Nuevitas on the 7th with a battery of artillery in company with the Isabel la Catolica, which had put in from stress of weather. The report further states that 216 soldiers of the Second Battalion San Marcial were found in Haiti by the Haitian government, disarmed, and delivered to the Spanish Consul at Port-au-Prince, who has sent to General Dulce for a vessel to take them away. The Haitian steamer Esther arrived at Santiago on the 3d, supposedly carrying the Spanish consul's dispatches for General Dulce, while more troops are scheduled to leave on Monday and the militia is expected to be called out.
records.summary_es: En una correspondencia desde La Habana, The New York Herald informa que la rebelión en Santo Domingo aún continúa y que se están enviando tropas españolas a Puerto Plata. Según el despacho, la corbeta de hélice Santa Lucía volvió a zarpar de Santiago el día 4 con tropas, y el Ulloa salió de Nuevitas el día 7 con una batería de artillería en compañía del Isabel la Católica, que había arribado por mal tiempo. El informe señala además que 216 soldados del segundo batallón de San Marcial fueron hallados en Haití por el gobierno haitiano, desarmados y entregados al cónsul español en Puerto Príncipe, quien ha solicitado al general Dulce un buque para retirarlos. El vapor haitiano Esther llegó a Santiago el día 3, supuestamente con los despachos del cónsul español para el general Dulce, mientras se prevé la salida de más tropas el lunes y se supone que se convocará a la milicia.

records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that after President Santana betrayed the Dominican people by annexing them to Spain, the Dominicans launched a unanimous rebellion marked by fierce fighting and atrocities on both sides. Recent reports indicated that Spanish troops suffered heavy losses, including a division of 2,000 men that was forced to capitulate after Santiago was burned, while another division of 1,600 men was repulsed. Additionally, the town of San Carlos near Santo Domingo city was reportedly burned by the rebels.
records.summary_es: El diario informó que, luego de que el presidente Santana traicionara al pueblo dominicano anexionándolo a España, los dominicanos emprendieron una rebelión unánime caracterizada por encarnizados combates y atrocidades de ambos bandos. Informes recientes indicaban que las tropas españolas sufrieron severas bajas, incluida una división de 2.000 soldados obligada a capitular tras el incendio de Santiago, al tiempo que otra división de 1.600 hombres fue rechazada. Además, se comunicó que el poblado de San Carlos, cercano a la ciudad de Santo Domingo, fue incendiado por los insurrectos.

records.summary_en: According to the *Chicago Daily Tribune* of October 10, 1863, the Dominican people are fiercely rebelling against Spanish rule following President Santana's annexation of the country to Spain. The newspaper reports that Spanish forces have suffered significant defeats—including a routed division of 3,000 men with over 1,000 casualties and the capitulation and retreat from Santiago—amid a conflict marked by mutual atrocities and the burning of towns such as San Carlos. Additionally, while the Dominicans reportedly receive sympathy and support from neighboring islands and the Unitedest States, the article questions their capacity for self-government due to past deficiencies in vigor and cohesion.
records.summary_es: Según el *Chicago Daily Tribune* del 10 de octubre de 1863, el pueblo dominicano se subleva con ferocidad contra el dominio español tras la anexión del país a España efectuada por el presidente Santana. El periódico consigna que las tropas españolas han sufrido considerables reveses —entre ellos una división dispersada de 3.000 hombres con más de 1.000 bajas, así como la capitulación y evacuación de Santiago— en el curso de una contienda signada por atrocidades recíprocas y el incendio de poblaciones como San Carlos. Además, si bien se señala que los dominicanos reciben la simpatía y el respaldo de islas vecinas y de los Estados Unidos, el artículo pone en duda su capacidad de autogobierno debido a su pasada falta de vigor y cohesión.

records.headline: This report describes the burning of Santiago and Puerto Plata under the Spanish occupation: the whole population of Puerto Plata
records.summary_en: This report describes the burning of Santiago and Puerto Plata under the Spanish occupation: the whole population of Puerto Plata has fled to foreign countries, and thousands of foreigners and natives have sought refuge on St. Thomas, Curacao and Turks Island and in the United States. The whole consular body, including the United States commercial agent and the French and British vice consuls, was forcibly compelled to leave the country, leaving behind property that was wantonly destroyed, and the writer hopes their governments will claim indemnification from Spain for the heavy losses sustained.

records.summary_en: According to *The Lancaster gazette* on November 5, 1863, fighting and fires in the Dominican Republic resulted in the destruction of the Government House, the Roman Catholic Church, and the American and British Consuls' residences, the latter of whom arrived at Grand Turk. Reports indicated that the entire south side of the island was in actual rebellion with 40,000 Dominicans in the neighborhood, and that Spanish soldiers pillaged the town before 600 Spaniards sortied from the fort and drove the Dominicans away with the aid of the fort's guns. The resulting fires destroyed numerous stores and properties belonging to foreign merchants, with losses in Santiago and Port-au-Platte expected to reach several millions of dollars.
records.summary_es: Según *The Lancaster Gazette* del 5 de noviembre de 1863, los combates e incendios en la República Dominicana ocasionaron la destrucción de la Casa de Gobierno, la iglesia católica y las residencias de los cónsules británico y estadounidense, habiendo llegado este último a Gran Turca. Los informes indicaban que toda la vertiente sur del territorio se hallaba en rebelión abierta con unos 40.000 dominicanos en las proximidades, y que la soldadesca española saqueó la población antes de que 600 peninsulares salieran de la fortaleza y rechazaran a los dominicanos con el auxilio de los cañones del fuerte. Los incendios resultantes destruyeron numerosos comercios y propiedades de comerciantes extranjeros, previéndose pérdidas millonarias en Santiago y Puerto Plata.

records.summary_en: *The New York Herald* reported, based on accounts from Port-au-Prince, that Dominican insurgents had established a provisional government in Santiago and chosen a native leader to head the republic. Fierce fighting in Santiago between Dominican forces and the Spanish garrison resulted in hundreds of casualties, forcing Spanish ally General Santana to flee into the woods near Azua. The report observed that Dominican enthusiasm for Spanish rule had collapsed, forcing Madrid to send costly military reinforcements.

The transports of joy with which they received the tidings that Spain did not refuse to open her arms to her prodigal children, so long estranged from her, is only equalled by the enthusiasm of the Mexican people on learning that they are to have a descendant of Charles V. for their Emperor. What, then, can be the cause of the wonderful change which has come over St. Domingo? It is not asserted that the Spaniards have made a tyrannical use of the power which St. Domingo spontaneously placed in their hands, and she must have known what she was doing when she exchanged her condition as a free State for the honor of being ruled by a Spanish viceroy.

There is reason to suspect that after all the desire for annexation to the mother country was not so deep or so general as was supposed, and that the Spanish government was the dupe of a handful of malcontents and adventurers. records.summary_en: According to the newspaper excerpt, eight to ten thousand Dominicans were in arms against Spanish troops, having burned Santiago to dislodge the Spaniards, while Spaniards burned Puerto Plata to deny refuge to natives. Foreigners reportedly handled all the business for both sides and stood to be the only ones with money when the war ended. Additionally, a report at San Cristobal stated the United States consul had a document that would benefit the U.S., following a failed Spanish military movement where the occupying force turned back upon hearing the enemy was accumulating ahead.
records.summary_es: Según el extracto periodístico, entre ocho y diez mil dominicanos se encontraban en armas contra las tropas españolas tras haber incendiado Santiago para desalojar a los peninsulares, mientras que los españoles quemaron Puerto Plata para privar de refugio a los patriotas. Trascendió que los extranjeros canalizaban el comercio de ambos contendientes y apuntaban a ser los únicos beneficiados económicamente al concluir la guerra. Además, un informe de San Cristóbal señalaba que el cónsul de los Estados Unidos poseía un pliego favorable a su nación, tras un fallido repliegue militar español donde la fuerza expedicionaria retrocedió al conocerse la concentración de tropas enemigas al frente.

records.summary_en: A correspondent in The New York Herald states that after the country was handed over to Spain by a couple of Dominican leaders headed by General Santana, the people initially accepted the annexation quietly while hoping for the best, but have now risen in rebellion upon seeing that Spain is oppressing them. Disputing another writer's claims that the island's commerce has vastly improved since becoming a Spanish province and that real estate worth hundreds in Dominican times was worth thousands in Spanish times, the letter asserts that commerce has actually diminished over the last two years and that real estate values have shown no difference. Furthermore, the correspondent states that Spain merely exchanged the Dominican paper currency for its own paper without introducing the gold or silver promised at the time of annexation. Endorsing the remark that it is a paradox to say Spain has fattened upon the blood of the island, the writer asks whether the acknowledged fact that annexation has proved a bad speculation for Queen Isabella authorizes her government to act so shamefully and to destroy a town where the property of many foreigners as well as her own subjects is deposited.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal de The New York Herald afirma que, después de que el país fue entregado a España por un par de líderes dominicanos encabezados por el general Santana, el pueblo aceptó inicialmente la anexión en silencio esperando lo mejor, pero ahora se ha levantado en armas al ver que España lo oprime. Rebatiendo las afirmaciones de otro autor en el sentido de que el comercio de la isla ha mejorado enormemente desde que se convirtió en provincia española y de que los bienes raíces que valían cientos en tiempos dominicanos valían miles en tiempos españoles, la carta sostiene que el comercio en realidad ha disminuido en los últimos dos años y que el valor de los bienes raíces no ha registrado diferencia alguna. Además, el corresponsal señala que España simplemente cambió el papel moneda dominicano por su propio papel sin introducir el oro ni la plata prometidos en el momento de la anexión. Suscribiendo la observación de que es una paradoja decir que España ha engordado con la sangre de la isla, el autor pregunta si el hecho reconocido de que la anexión ha resultado ser una mala especulación para la reina Isabel autoriza a su gobierno a actuar tan vergonzosamente y a destruir una población donde se hallan depositadas las propiedades de muchos extranjeros además de las de sus propios súbditos.

records.headline: In The New York Herald, a pro-Spanish correspondent asserts
records.summary_en: In The New York Herald, a pro-Spanish correspondent asserts the absence of any well-founded complaint against Spanish rule in St. Domingo. The sole exception is the conduct of a single official who was summoned to answer charges and reportedly tried to kill himself on the passage. The writer claims that all the respectable, industrious, and wealthy people of the island have remained loyal to Spain, while characterizing the insurrectionists as the vagabond class, professional revolutionists, and idle wretches with nothing to lose. According to the letter, St. Thomas opposes Spanish rule in St. Domingo out of pecuniary interest, alleging that its population of Jewish shopkeepers formerly sold wares to the natives at enormous profits during the days of the Dominican Republic when others would not trade with them. The correspondent argues that when Spain came in to protect life and property, threw open the island to foreign enterprise, and proposed making Samana a free port, those merchants lost their market.
records.summary_es: En The New York Herald, un corresponsal proespañol sostiene la ausencia de toda queja bien fundada contra el dominio español en Santo Domingo. La única excepción es la conducta de un solo funcionario que fue citado a responder cargos y que según se dice intentó quitarse la vida durante la travesía. El autor afirma que todas las personas respetables, laboriosas y adineradas de la isla han permanecido leales a España, mientras califica a los insurrectos como la clase vagabunda, revolucionarios de oficio y miserables ociosos que no tienen nada que perder. Según la carta, Saint Thomas se opone al dominio español en Santo Domingo por interés pecuniario, alegando que su población de comerciantes judíos vendía anteriormente sus mercancías a los nativos con enormes ganancias en los días de la República Dominicana, cuando otros no se dignaban comerciar con ellos. El corresponsal argumenta que cuando España intervino para dar protección a la vida y la propiedad, abrió la isla a la empresa extranjera y propuso convertir a Samaná en puerto libre, dichos comerciantes perdieron su mercado.

records.headline: The New York Herald reports that St. Domingo advices to the Turks Island Standard represent
records.summary_en: The New York Herald reports that St. Domingo advices to the Turks Island Standard represent the Spaniards as making little progress against the Dominicans. According to the dispatch, the town of Samana had been plundered by the Spaniards, and the Wesleyan Mission House and chapel had been burned. Meanwhile, the merchants of St. Thomas have closed all accounts with Puerto Rico, Haiti, and Cuba, refusing to transact any further business with those places except for cash. The report concludes by noting that Spanish forces under their commander were completely surrounded by the Dominicans at Bani, and that the Dominicans have erected a battery commanding the entrance to the harbor of Porto Platte.
records.summary_es: The New York Herald informa que las noticias de Santo Domingo recibidas por el Turks Island Standard presentan a los españoles logrando muy pocos avances frente a los dominicanos. Según el despacho, el pueblo de Samaná había sido saqueado por los españoles, y la casa de la Misión Wesleyana y su capilla habían sido incendiadas. Entretanto, los comerciantes de Saint Thomas han cerrado todas las cuentas con Puerto Rico, Haití y Cuba, y no realizarán más negocios con esas plazas sino al contado. El informe concluye señalando que las fuerzas españolas bajo su comandante se hallaban completamente rodeadas por los dominicanos en Baní, y que los dominicanos han levantado una batería que domina la entrada del puerto de Puerto Plata.

records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that Dominicans captured Spanish supplies and a field piece at Yabacoa, while Spanish forces under Santana remained unable to move forward near San Guino due to reinforcements of 700 men being offset by over 700 sick in camp. Additionally, a severe battle occurred on December 20th at Puerto Plata, resulting in the defeat of the Spaniards, who lost 100 out of 600 men and a cannon to the gallantly fighting Dominicans. The *Standard* characterized the contest as unprofitable and dishonorable for Spain, noting that the Spaniards only hold the ground they stand on, while a separate weather report from Toronto noted a fierce snowstorm stopping railroad trains.

Además, el 20 de diciembre se libró una cruenta batalla en Puerto Plata que concluyó con la derrota de los españoles, quienes perdieron 100 de sus 600 efectivos y un cañón ante el denodado arrojo dominicano. El *Standard* describió la lucha como estéril y deshonrosa para España, señalando que los españoles solo dominan el terreno que pisan, al tiempo que un parte meteorológico independiente desde Toronto daba cuenta de una feroz tormenta de nieve que paralizó los trenes.

records.headline: Reporting on the war in St. Domingo, the Cleveland Morning Leader states
records.summary_en: Reporting on the war in St. Domingo, the Cleveland Morning Leader states that the Dominicans still hold St. Christobal, preventing all communication with Spanish-occupied places, and have captured some 2,000 Spaniards, 300 rifles, 4,000 rounds of cartridges, and a field piece at the army supply depot at Yaba Coa. While the Spaniards are strengthening the fortifications of St. Domingo with two redoubts and two native regiments have been ordered there, the Spanish commander near San Girno, despite recently receiving 1,500 reinforcements, has more than 700 sick in his camp, is unable to move his army forward, and remains in a critical position. On December 20, a severe battle took place at Puerto Plata in which the Dominicans fought with great gallantry, captured a cannon, and defeated the Spaniards with a loss of 150 out of 600 men. Summarizing the situation, the Standard remarks that the sooner Spain withdraws from these dishonorable and unprofitable contests the better, as the Spaniards are masters only of the ground they stand upon and will acquire only a cemetery rather than vanquish the Dominicans.
records.summary_es: Al informar sobre la guerra en Santo Domingo, el Cleveland Morning Leader señala que los dominicanos aún mantienen San Cristóbal, impidiendo toda comunicación con los lugares ocupados por los españoles, y que han capturado a unos 2,000 españoles, 300 rifles, 4,000 cartuchos y una pieza de campaña en el depósito de suministros del ejército en Yabacoa. Mientras los españoles refuerzan las fortificaciones de Santo Domingo con dos reductos y se ha ordenado el envío de dos regimientos nativos, el comandante español cerca de San Girno, pese a haber recibido recientemente 1,500 hombres de refuerzo, tiene más de 700 enfermos en su campamento, no puede hacer avanzar su ejército y se encuentra en una posición crítica. El 20 de diciembre tuvo lugar un recio combate en Puerto Plata en el que los dominicanos lucharon con gran valentía, capturaron un cañón y derrotaron a los españoles, quienes sufrieron 150 bajas de un total de 600 hombres. En un resumen de la situación, el Standard observa que cuanto antes se retire España de estas contiendas deshonrosas e infructuosas será mejor, pues los españoles solo son dueños del terreno que pisan y, en vez de vencer a los dominicanos, solo adquirirán un cementerio.

records.summary_en: According to the newspaper, a leader deceived the Dominican people by inviting in Spanish forces under the guise of assistance and instruction, subsequently collecting their arms, declaring the Republic extinct, and proclaiming the Queen of Spain as ruler. After being oppressed by Spanish officials and failing twice in armed resistance, the Dominicans achieved victory on their third attempt, restoring their free constitution while retreating Spanish forces burned towns in vengeance. The report notes that the Spanish navy subsequently maintained a strict blockade of most of the seaboard with six thousand Spanish soldiers.
records.summary_es: Según el periódico, un caudillo engañó al pueblo dominicano llamando a las fuerzas españolas con el pretexto de ayuda e instrucción militar, para luego confiscarles el armamento, declarar extinguida la República y proclamar soberana a la reina de España. Tras padecer la opresión de los funcionarios coloniales y sucumbir en dos tentativas armadas, los dominicanos alcanzaron la victoria en su tercer alzamiento, restableciendo su constitución libre mientras las tropas españolas en retirada quemaban poblados por venganza. El informe agrega que la escuadra española impuso subsiguientemente un riguroso bloqueo sobre la mayor parte del litoral apoyada por seis mil soldados peninsulares.

records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* reported that Spanish power in America has proven contemptible in the St. Domingo war, as Spain has been unable to overcome the resistance of the islanders after much effort. The article noted that a Madrid paper urged the Spanish government to relinquish the hopeless attempt and be content with holding only the three towns of St. Domingo, Samana, and Puerto Plata, noting the struggle has brought debt and no credit to Spain.

El artículo apuntó que un diario de Madrid exhortó al gobierno español a desistir de esa empresa infructuosa y a conformarse con retener únicamente las tres plazas de Santo Domingo, Samaná y Puerto Plata, haciendo notar que la contienda solo ha traído deudas y ningún crédito a la corona española.

records.full_text:
ENGLAND’S RECOGNITION OF THE DOMINICANS.
[From the Madrid Epoca, Dec. 18.]
In consequence of the effect produced upon the public mind by this announcement, Sir John Crampton, the English Ambassador at this Court, felt bound to request explanations from his government upon a matter in which he was without official instructions. Earl Russell lost no time in replying, and his despatch reached the English representatives yesterday evening, at the same time that the First Secretary of State received the despatches from our Minister Plenipotentiary in London, previously announced by telegraph to the Spanish Cabinet. These despatches contained ample details of all that had occurred. On account of certain questions arising from events that have taken place in consequence of the blockade of the Dominican coasts by the Spanish squadron, the English government considered it necessary to take the opinion of the legal advisers of the crown, following its practice in all matters of this kind. Their opinion was favorable in a certain manner to the recognition of the Dominicans as belligerents—Spain being bound, according to their view, by the maritime law laid down in the treaty of Paris, to maintain a real and effective blockade of all the points of the island where she undertook to prevent the entry of supplies destined for the rebels. Earl Russell communicated this opinion to our representative in London, who in his turn considered it urgently necessary to acquaint the Spanish government with the same. Hence the origin of a news which, having come to the knowledge of the telegraphic agents of various periodicals in this city, was transmitted by them with the urgency which its importance dictated, although the want of the details above mentioned caused some exaggeration in their communications. The reply of Earl Russell to the English Ambassador could not be expressed in more satisfactory terms. The English Minister confirmed the explanations given by Senor Comyn, and, wishing to afford a proof of the friendly attitude of England in questions so greatly affecting the prestige of our country, he authorized the English Ambassador to acquaint the Spanish Cabinet with his determination to indefinitely postpone any act which might be considered hostile, or as tending to exercise any sort of influence in the settlement of our internal affairs. We, who cannot be accused of being ardent admirers of the English policy, have satisfaction in declaring that its conduct in the present circumstances has been worthy of a great Power, and therefore merits our most sincere eulogies.

records.summary_en: A letter from Florence, printed in the Tribune, reports that the government of Spain has acknowledged that the annexation of San Domingo in 1861 was a mistake. The heroic resistance of the Dominicans, the writer says, has shown clearly that they do not want Spanish rule, and Spain, having no intention of making conquests, gives up the sovereignty it bought from Santana and withdraws its troops. The letter hails the outcome as another great triumph of the republican form of government, and of the colored population of the country it calls Dominica, which has conquered its independence against the power that once held nearly all America.

records.headline: An editorial headed "St. Domingo" argues that Spain's attempt
records.summary_en: An editorial headed "St. Domingo" argues that Spain's attempt to recover Dominica has ended in confusion and failure. It recounts that the island stood divided between Dominica and Hayti, that the Haytian government ruled the whole island from 1822 until the Dominicans threw off its authority and formed a republic of their own, and that Spain, which obtained possession again in 1861, met an insurrection it never overcame and now withdraws after heavy losses in men and money. The paper offers the episode as a warning on the unwisdom and injustice of the original sale of the country to Spain.

records.summary_en: According to *The New York Herald* on April 30, 1865, European monarchies were described as quaking with fear over the growing strength of the United States and its potential impact on Spanish possessions like Cuba and Porto Rico. The article specifically cited a fearful argument presented by the "Conqueror of Africa," which claimed the United States planned to send thousands of freed colored people to St. Domingo to form a negro nationality and army to ultimately attack and destroy Cuba. The newspaper dismissed this theory as a "raving of an imagination entirely possessed by fear," asserting that no dilatory measures would be needed if the United States truly intended to conquer European possessions.

records.headline: Advices from San Domingo to April 9 announce that the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: Advices from San Domingo to April 9 announce that the Dominican Republic has been completely re-established. The sessions of the National Convention came to an end in late March, and a decree of amnesty was published, with exceptions that include the high functionaries who took part in the intrigues that produced the annexation, the officers and soldiers who fought under the Spanish flag, and the public writers who opposed the restoration in the newspapers. A Spanish steamer had arrived with the order from Madrid for the evacuation, and the Spanish troops left the island on March 30.
records.summary_es: Noticias de Santo Domingo hasta el 9 de abril anuncian que la República Dominicana ha sido completamente restablecida. Las sesiones de la Convención Nacional concluyeron a fines de marzo, y se publicó un decreto de amnistía con excepciones que incluyen a los altos funcionarios que participaron en las intrigas que produjeron la anexión, a los oficiales y soldados que lucharon bajo la bandera española y a los escritores públicos que se opusieron a la restauración en los periódicos. Un vapor español había llegado con la orden de Madrid para la evacuación, y las tropas españolas salieron de la isla el 30 de marzo.

records.headline: An editorial sets out the geography and population of the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: An editorial sets out the geography and population of the Dominican Republic and the failure of Spain's attempt to hold the country. The republic occupies the eastern and larger portion of the island, some 17,500 square miles, with a population estimated at between 120,000 and 200,000. Since the summer of 1863 the Spaniards have been confined to a few seaport towns, and the paper argues that Spain, whose bill before the Cortes admits that the inhabitants were unanimously opposed to her government, is now compelled to withdraw her troops and recognize the independence of the republic.
records.summary_es: Un editorial expone la geografía y la población de la República Dominicana y el fracaso del intento de España de retener el país. La república ocupa la porción oriental y mayor de la isla, unas 17,500 millas cuadradas, con una población estimada entre 120,000 y 200,000 habitantes. Desde el verano de 1863 los españoles han estado confinados a unos pocos puertos, y el periódico sostiene que España, cuyo proyecto ante las Cortes admite que los habitantes se opusieron unánimemente a su gobierno, se ve ahora obligada a retirar sus tropas y reconocer la independencia de la república.

records.headline: Advices from San Domingo announce the re-establishment of the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: Advices from San Domingo announce the re-establishment of the Dominican Republic and the departure of the Spanish troops from the island. The National Convention ended its sessions in late March and published a decree of amnesty that excepts, among others, the high functionaries implicated in the intrigues of the annexation, the soldiers who fought against their country under the Spanish flag, and the writers who opposed the restoration in the press. A Spanish steamer brought the order from Madrid for a total evacuation, and the troops embarked on March 30.
records.summary_es: Noticias de Santo Domingo anuncian el restablecimiento de la República Dominicana y la salida de las tropas españolas de la isla. La Convención Nacional terminó sus sesiones a fines de marzo y publicó un decreto de amnistía que exceptúa, entre otros, a los altos funcionarios implicados en las intrigas de la anexión, a los soldados que lucharon contra su país bajo la bandera española y a los escritores que se opusieron a la restauración en la prensa. Un vapor español trajo la orden de Madrid para la evacuación total, y las tropas embarcaron el 30 de marzo.

records.headline: An editorial traces the political history of Santo Domingo in defense of the principle
records.summary_en: An editorial traces the political history of Santo Domingo in defense of the principle that all races have equal rights before the law. It recalls the fall of President Boyer, the separation of the Dominican Republic in 1844, and some fifteen years of Haitian attacks that the Dominicans always defeated. The writer holds that if the Dominicans remain true to themselves and to their principles of liberty and equality, they will be secure in their independence forever.
records.summary_es: Un editorial recorre la historia política de Santo Domingo en defensa del principio de que todas las razas tienen iguales derechos ante la ley. Recuerda la caída del presidente Boyer, la separación de la República Dominicana en 1844 y unos quince años de ataques haitianos que los dominicanos siempre derrotaron. El autor sostiene que si los dominicanos se mantienen fieles a sí mismos y a sus principios de libertad e igualdad, estarán seguros en su independencia para siempre.

records.headline: An editorial hails the triumph of the Dominican Republic over Spain
records.summary_en: An editorial hails the triumph of the Dominican Republic over Spain as the most mortifying rebuke yet given to the schemes of European conquest in America. It describes the republic as occupying the eastern part of the island, some 17,500 square miles with a population put at between 120,000 and 200,000, recalls that Santana sold San Domingo to Spain, and notes that the Spaniards, confined since 1863 to a few seaport towns, have been compelled to withdraw and to recognize the independence of the country.

records.headline: The Dominican government refuses to sanction the acknowledgment
records.summary_en: The Dominican government refuses to sanction the acknowledgment Spain demands in return for its withdrawal from the island. Spain asks the republic to admit that she took possession at the spontaneous desire of the people, that her conduct while there was grandly generous, and that she leaves entirely of her own free will. Rather than sign such an admission, the government faces the blockade General Gandara has declared on all the coasts and harbors of the republic, while his officers talk in the streets of San Domingo of laying the city in ashes.
records.summary_es: El gobierno dominicano se niega a sancionar el reconocimiento que España exige a cambio de su retirada de la isla. España pide que la república admita que tomó posesión por deseo espontáneo del pueblo, que su conducta allí fue grandemente generosa y que se marcha enteramente por su propia voluntad. Antes que firmar tal admisión, el gobierno afronta el bloqueo que el general Gándara ha declarado sobre todas las costas y puertos de la república, mientras sus oficiales hablan en las calles de Santo Domingo de reducir la ciudad a cenizas.

records.summary_en: Intelligence from the Dominican Republic, whose official documents have been laid before the State Department, reports that by the act of the Spanish Cortes of May 1, 1865, the military occupation of the island was formally abandoned. The paper calls the attempt to convert an American state into a European colony a terrible failure, defeated by the brave and unceasing resistance of the Dominicans, and says Spain leaves San Domingo, as she left her other American colonies, because it was beyond her power to stay. As a last shot in the magazine, General Gandara demands from the republic a false and self-accusing acknowledgment that Spain came at the people's desire and behaved with generosity while there.

records.summary_en: According to the *New-York Daily Tribune* of August 22, 1865, the *Boletin Oficial* of Santiago reported on July 7 that departing Spanish troops were taking Dominican cannon and property, while a few Spanish troops still lingered in St. Domingo because Gen. Gándara and the Dominicans had not agreed on a final evacuation treaty. The Dominican government rejected a drafted treaty because Gándara's preferred language made the agreement appear to be a Spanish concession rather than a surrender, and Gándara subsequently refused to receive new commissioners unless they confirmed the objectionable treaty. Consequently, the Dominican government officially expressed its determination not to yield, signifying that the war had not ceased.
records.summary_es: Según el *New-York Daily Tribune* del 22 de agosto de 1865, el *Boletín Oficial* de Santiago denunció el 7 de julio que las tropas españolas en retirada se llevaban cañones y propiedades dominicanas, quedando aún remanentes peninsulares en Santo Domingo debido a desacuerdos entre el general Gándara y los dominicanos sobre el tratado definitivo de evacuación. El gobierno dominicano rechazó el borrador del convenio porque los términos exigidos por Gándara hacían figurar el acuerdo como una concesión graciosa de España y no como una capitulación en regla, negándose luego Gándara a recibir nuevos comisionados si no convalidaban dicho documento objetado. Por consiguiente, el gobierno dominicano ratificó oficialmente su firme decisión de no transigir, lo que evidenciaba que las hostilidades no habían concluido.
