records.summary_en: Under the head of Santo Domingo, the Avis reports intelligence received by the Solent from the Dominican Republic: by the Spanish steamer Pelayo came passenger Mr. John P. O'Sullivan, to enter into a convention with the authorities for the establishment of a line of steamers to run between New York and New Orleans, and the various ports of the Dominican Republic. This gentleman, the paper says, has filled several high diplomatic posts under the American government, and is accompanied by General Cazneau, who for some time was a resident of St. Croix. Mr. David Cohen, Postmaster-General and acting British consul at St. Domingo, was named by the government as a special commissioner to treat, and settle matters with, the American gentleman.
records.summary_es: Bajo el encabezado de Santo Domingo, el Avis informa de noticias recibidas por el Solent desde la República Dominicana: en el vapor español Pelayo llegó como pasajero el señor John P. O'Sullivan, para celebrar un convenio con las autoridades para el establecimiento de una línea de vapores que correría entre Nueva York y Nueva Orleans y los distintos puertos de la República Dominicana. Este caballero, dice el periódico, ha ocupado varios altos cargos diplomáticos bajo el gobierno estadounidense, y viene acompañado del general Cazneau, que durante algún tiempo fue residente de Santa Cruz. El señor David Cohen, administrador general de Correos y cónsul británico en funciones en Santo Domingo, fue nombrado por el gobierno comisionado especial para tratar y arreglar los asuntos con el caballero estadounidense.

records.headline: The Tribune reprints a Washington story from the Boston Post
records.summary_en: The Tribune reprints a Washington story from the Boston Post on the proposed Samana purchase: Mr. Seward's star is again in the ascendant, and the United States is likely to become the owner of the Bay of Samana, the purchase of which Frederick Seward failed to accomplish during his secret mission to the island of St. Domingo last winter. The difficulty in his way, the story says, was the exhibition of too great an anxiety to purchase, which induced Cabral, then at the head of the Dominican government, to become exorbitant, hoping thereby to get vast wealth with which to leave the island. Buenaventura Báez was called to the presidency of the republic in 1865, but Cabral succeeded in holding on until the spring of the present year, when he was driven from the country and Báez regularly installed in office; Báez is described as highly educated and immensely wealthy, most of his wealth invested in France, where he has spent many years of his life. He has just communicated to Secretary Seward his desire to transfer the Bay of Samana to the United States on Mr. Seward's own terms, provided these terms shall stipulate for a lease only and not for an actual sale of the property — Báez proposing to respect the bitter prejudices existing among the Dominicans against selling territory by leasing the bay for ninety-nine years to the United States.

records.headline: The Herald prints the prospectus of the Samana Bay Company
records.summary_en: The Herald prints the prospectus of the Samana Bay Company, published in New York for private circulation only. The passage opens in the middle of the Samaná affair, with word that Báez's own party is determined not to let him consummate anything of the kind. An opportunity is now being presented, the prospectus says, through the confidential agent of the Dominican Republic in New York, to secure a lease of the bay and peninsula of Samana, with all the eminent domain, rights and prerogatives of sovereignty now held and enjoyed by the republic, for a period of twenty years, paying for the same the sum of one hundred thousand dollars in gold annually in advance — it being understood that at the expiration of that period, or on the payment of the whole amount of the lease, to wit, two million dollars, the territory shall be finally transferred in fee and become the absolute property of the company. During the period of the lease the company will enjoy all privileges and immunities of sovereignty under the joint protection of the republics of St. Domingo and the United States; and in furtherance of the scheme the company proposes to raise at once the sum of one hundred thousand dollars in gold, and despatch its agent therewith to St. Domingo to tender the same to the Dominican authorities as the first instalment under the lease, and receive from them a formal ratification of the terms and conditions of the contract entered into with the Dominican agent in New York.

records.headline: In an editorial on the new political combinations now germinating
records.summary_en: In an editorial on the new political combinations now germinating in the countries south of the United States, the Ledger treats the Dominican Republic as an element in the complication: there the anti-Spanish party is on the eve of triumph over the government of President Báez, and the island, lying as it does between the Spanish islands of Cuba and Porto Rico, possesses ready means of danger to the Spanish forces which promise to be brought into play at an early day. In Mexico the question is already put forward as one of annexation of Cuba to the Mexican republic, the editorial says, while among the Dominicans, at home and in the revolutionary service in Cuba, it assumes the form of a West Indian confederation. No word of annexation to the United States is breathed by the Cuban revolutionists, and thus far President Céspedes seems to have carefully abstained from sending an authorized agent to Washington — a reserve the editorial traces to the opinion prevalent in Cuba that in former efforts to attain independence, whenever Cubans have confided their hopes and views to members of the Washington cabinet, from Fillmore's time down to that of Buchanan, they have been betrayed to the Spanish government. Whether the new combinations will crystallize into something effective and tangible, the Ledger concludes, yet remains to be seen.
records.summary_es: En un editorial sobre las nuevas combinaciones políticas que ahora germinan en los países al sur de los Estados Unidos, el Ledger trata a la República Dominicana como un elemento de la complicación: allí el partido antiespañol está en vísperas de triunfar sobre el gobierno del presidente Báez, y la isla, situada como está entre las islas españolas de Cuba y Puerto Rico, posee medios prontos de peligro para las fuerzas españolas que prometen entrar en juego en fecha temprana. En México la cuestión ya se plantea como la anexión de Cuba a la república mexicana, dice el editorial, mientras que entre los dominicanos, en el país y en el servicio revolucionario en Cuba, asume la forma de una confederación de las Indias Occidentales. Los revolucionarios cubanos no pronuncian palabra alguna de anexión a los Estados Unidos, y hasta ahora el presidente Céspedes parece haberse abstenido cuidadosamente de enviar un agente autorizado a Washington, reserva que el editorial atribuye a la opinión prevaleciente en Cuba de que en anteriores esfuerzos por alcanzar la independencia, cada vez que los cubanos han confiado sus esperanzas y pareceres a miembros del gabinete de Washington, desde los tiempos de Fillmore hasta Buchanan, han sido traicionados ante el gobierno español. Si las nuevas combinaciones cristalizarán en algo efectivo y tangible, concluye el Ledger, aún está por verse.

records.summary_en: The *Worcester Daily Spy* reported that the island of St. Domingo is divided between the Dominican Republic, where Spaniards and their descendants rule, and Hayti, where negroes hold all governmental power. According to the newspaper's correspondent, the natives of both parts are entirely opposed to the United States obtaining a foothold on the island, and the Dominicans are described as demoralized, heavily armed, and consumed by rapid political revolutions, judicial murders, and private assassinations. Although overtures have been made regarding the sale of Samana to the United States despite local hostility toward foreigners, it is stated that any such treaty would likely be abrogated by the Dominicans if purchased.
records.summary_es: El *Worcester Daily Spy* refirió que la isla de Santo Domingo se halla dividida entre la República Dominicana, donde gobiernan los españoles y sus descendientes, y Haití, donde los negros retienen todo el poder político. Según el corresponsal del rotativo, los naturales de ambas partes se oponen tenazmente a que los Estados Unidos sienten pie en la isla, describiéndose a los dominicanos como desmoralizados, fuertemente pertrechados y consumidos por vertiginosas revoluciones políticas, ajusticiamientos judiciales y homicidios privados. Si bien se habían entablado propuestas para la venta de Samaná a los Estados Unidos a pesar de la hostilidad local hacia los extranjeros, se advertía que cualquier tratado de compra probablemente sería revocado por los dominicanos con posterioridad.

records.summary_en: The Spy reports that the proposition for the annexation of the Dominican Republic to the United States is to be renewed at once in Congress. It was defeated in the House on Monday by an immense majority, the report says, but since then official facts have come to the knowledge of the government which the advocates of such an acquisition declare will change the situation. Parties professing to represent that republic say that the people there are willing to come over on almost any terms, making a gift to the United States of property which Mr. Seward, six months ago, was willing to pay millions for.

Personas que dicen representar a esa república aseguran que el pueblo de allí está dispuesto a incorporarse casi en cualquier término, haciendo donación a los Estados Unidos de propiedades por las que el señor Seward, hace seis meses, estaba dispuesto a pagar millones.

records.headline: Under the head 'What San Domingo Is,' the Spy describes the island of San Domingo
records.summary_en: Under the head 'What San Domingo Is,' the Spy describes the island of San Domingo and its resources. It has an area, with the smaller ones under its jurisdiction, of about 30,000 square miles, and is in extent about the size of Scotland. Every product of tropical and temperate climes can be grown there; it is known to be enormously rich in mineral wealth — for many years, while under the dominion of Spain, its annual tribute from the gold mines, consisting of one-fourth of the product, was about $5,000,000 — and in timber it is exceedingly rich, having every variety of cabinet woods; the flora includes the most valuable medicinal plants known to man. The Dominican territory could sustain in comfort at least ten million inhabitants, probably twice as many; there is an abundant water power; and it is geographically in the very centre of the Antilles. Commercially speaking, its position is worth everything to us, the writer says: we acquire Samana, one of the only half dozen harbors in the world in which the Great Eastern can ride, and secure the key and controlling position in the Gulf. The outlines given are, in the writer's judgment, what seems now the most honest in effort and most promising in result of all annexation schemes lately had before the public.
records.summary_es: Bajo el encabezado «Lo que es Santo Domingo», el Spy describe la isla de Santo Domingo y sus recursos. Tiene una superficie, con las islas menores bajo su jurisdicción, de unas 30.000 millas cuadradas, y en extensión es comparable a Escocia. Allí puede cultivarse todo producto de climas tropicales y templados; es conocida por su enorme riqueza mineral — durante muchos años, bajo el dominio de España, su tributo anual de las minas de oro, consistente en la cuarta parte del producto, fue de unos $5.000.000 — y en maderas es sumamente rica, con toda variedad de maderas preciosas; su flora incluye las plantas medicinales más valiosas que conoce el hombre. El territorio dominicano podría sostener con comodidad al menos a diez millones de habitantes, probablemente al doble; hay abundante fuerza hidráulica; y se halla geográficamente en el centro mismo de las Antillas. Comercialmente hablando, su posición lo vale todo para nosotros, dice el autor: adquirimos Samaná, uno de los escasos seis puertos del mundo en los que puede flotar el Great Eastern, y aseguramos la posición clave y dominante en el Golfo. Las líneas expuestas son, a juicio del autor, lo que parece ahora el esfuerzo más honesto y el resultado más prometedor de todos los planes de anexión presentados últimamente ante el público.

records.headline: An editorial in the Crescent argues for American expansion in the West Indies.
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Crescent argues for American expansion in the West Indies. It is intimated, the editorial says, that evidence may be produced to show that the populations of the most desirable of the West India islands, including Cuba and Porto Rico, are eager to solve the troublesome and at present gloomy problem of their destiny by annexation to the United States, and it dwells on the richness of the island of St. Domingo in mineral and agricultural resources. It is not to be supposed, the Crescent argues, that if the Dominican republic were annexed, Hayti would be content to remain, or would in any case long remain, outside of American jurisdiction. Dominica occupies the larger part of the territory, and contains the greater portion of the population, of the island of St. Domingo, of which the whole area is 28,000 square miles and the whole population 1,250,000; next to Cuba in point of population, this island is also, next to Cuba, the most beautiful and productive of the West Indies. And the value to American commerce of the trade which would be developed by the opening of this island to American enterprise by annexation is only less, the editorial says, than that which would result from the annexation of Cuba. The Crescent has no idea that any definite programme for these ends will be carried in the present Congress, but it expects that the subject will be a subject of increasing agitation during the incoming administration.
records.summary_es: Un editorial del Crescent defiende la expansión estadounidense en las Indias Occidentales. records.headline: An item in the National Republican, beginning in mid-argument
records.summary_en: An item in the National Republican, beginning in mid-argument, denies the report that advices have been received from the highest official sources that President Báez and the Dominican people would accept unconditional annexation: no such proposition, it says, has been made. The mission of Mr. Angenard is a plain one, the item continues, with which he alone is entrusted, and its object is sought to be attained by none of the dubious ways of diplomacy; it is free from disguise or concealment, and is in no wise, directly or indirectly, connected with any of the speculations with which efforts are made to associate it. The envoy says the interference of any one with his purpose is wholly unwarranted, and as damaging as it is manifestly indelicate and improper. But it is asserted by several prominent Congressmen, the item adds, that the commission now here treating for an annexation of San Domingo are humbugs, and are in the interest of Dominicans and Americans who wish annexation in order to make money out of it.

La misión del señor Angenard es sencilla, continúa la nota, confiada a él únicamente, y su objeto se busca alcanzar por ninguna de las vías dudosas de la diplomacia; está libre de disfraz u ocultamiento, y no está conectada en modo alguno, directa ni indirectamente, con ninguna de las especulaciones con las que se intenta asociarla. records.headline: A letter to the editor attacks Secretary of State Seward's shifting plans for St. Domingo
records.summary_en: A letter to the editor attacks Secretary of State Seward's shifting plans for St. Domingo, arguing that whether the form is intervention, a protectorate or annexation, the result would be enormous wealth for certain private individuals. The writer says President Baez, entrenched in his capital with civil wars to look after and exiles including Cabral returning, proposes through Seward to transfer to the United States the parts of his country over which he has no control.
records.summary_es: Una carta al editor ataca los cambiantes planes del secretario de Estado Seward para Santo Domingo, argumentando que, ya sea bajo la forma de intervención, de protectorado o de anexión, el resultado sería una riqueza enorme para ciertos particulares. El autor dice que el presidente Báez, atrincherado en su capital con guerras civiles que atender y exiliados como Cabral de regreso, propone por medio de Seward transferir a los Estados Unidos las partes de su país sobre las que no tiene ningún control.

When one form of action is ignominiously defeated in the House, he has substantially the same thing (at least so far as the interests of private parties are concerned) proposed in another shape. It makes little difference to him whether it is intervention, a protectorate," or annexation," which finally succeeds. records.headline: An editorial in the Tribune opens in mid-argument against the cession of St. Domingo
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Tribune opens in mid-argument against the cession of St. Domingo to the United States, holding that the beleaguered chief who pretends to cede the island has no more power to transfer it than Queen Isabella has at this moment to transfer Spain, and that the scheme would thus compel them to conquer the island. In the mean time, the editorial says, there is the 'Samana Bay Company' and the 'Alta Vela Guano Company,' rich and powerful in both countries: while the ceding and giving away is going on, land grants, gold mines, and guano islands may be made over to these gentlemen under the seal of the nation, and the President, too, his country being so ungrateful, might seek an honest recompense for all his toils by becoming a partner in the speculations of these good people. Besides all this, one of the conditions of the transfer is understood to be, as international law requires, that the United States shall pay the public debt of St. Domingo, and so soon as the former is made liable, the gentlemen of the ring will turn up with certificates of indebtedness. When the vaunted evidence of the willingness of the people of St. Domingo to be annexed comes to be produced, the Tribune predicts, it will likely be found to consist of nothing but the mutual assurances of these high contracting parties — of the waning President and 'his friends' on the one hand, and of the waning Secretary of State on the other.
records.summary_es: Un editorial del Tribune se abre a mitad de la argumentación contra la cesión de Santo Domingo a los Estados Unidos, sosteniendo que el asediado caudillo que pretende ceder la isla no tiene más poder para transferirla que el que tiene en este momento la reina Isabel para transferir España, y que el plan obligaría así a conquistar la isla. Mientras tanto, dice el editorial, están la «Compañía de la Bahía de Samaná» y la «Compañía del Guano de Alta Vela», ricas y poderosas en ambos países: mientras sigue la cesión y la entrega, podrán hacerse a estos caballeros, bajo el sello de la nación, traspasos de concesiones de tierras, minas de oro e islas de guano, y el propio presidente, su país siéndole tan ingrato, podría buscar una honesta recompensa por todos sus trabajos haciéndose socio de las especulaciones de esta buena gente. Además de todo esto, se entiende que una de las condiciones de la transferencia es, como exige el derecho internacional, que los Estados Unidos paguen la deuda pública de Santo Domingo, y en cuanto aquel quede obligado, los caballeros de la camarilla aparecerán con certificados de deuda. Cuando se presente la tan pregonada evidencia de la disposición del pueblo de Santo Domingo a ser anexado, predice el Tribune, probablemente se encontrará que consiste únicamente en las mutuas seguridades de estas altas partes contratantes: del presidente en decadencia y «sus amigos», por una parte, y del secretario de Estado en decadencia, por la otra.

records.headline: A Washington letter attacks Secretary Seward's scheme for St. Domingo
records.summary_en: A Washington letter attacks Secretary Seward's scheme for St. Domingo, which shifted within weeks from a protectorate to annexation with no explanation offered for either. The writer argues that President Baez, entrenched in his capital with several civil wars to look after, has no more right to give his country to the United States than Seward would have to give the United States to Great Britain, and warns that the Samana Bay Company and the Alta Vela Guano Company would gain land, mines and guano while the United States took on the Dominican public debt.
records.summary_es: Una carta desde Washington ataca el plan del secretario Seward para Santo Domingo, que en pocas semanas pasó de un protectorado a la anexión sin que se ofreciera explicación alguna de ninguno de los dos. El autor sostiene que el presidente Báez, atrincherado en su capital con varias guerras civiles que atender, no tiene más derecho a entregar su país a los Estados Unidos que el que tendría Seward de entregar los Estados Unidos a Gran Bretaña, y advierte que la Samana Bay Company y la Alta Vela Guano Company ganarían tierras, minas y guano mientras los Estados Unidos asumían la deuda pública dominicana.

records.headline: A letter printed in the Herald gives an account, beginning in mid-course
records.summary_en: A letter printed in the Herald gives an account, beginning in mid-course, of Secretary Seward's Caribbean diplomacy: kings, who were disposed to negotiate for a free and neutral port at Samaná as a great steam centre, he made a dash for St. Thomas: he would have bought Samana also, but until the Dominican President was reduced to extremity he dared not attempt the dismemberment of the republic. That failed, the letter continues, and we now hear of annexation. Báez has purposely secured his loan in such a way as to keep up his government for two years, and by the end of that term he trusts to the development of the mining and industrial interests of the country for maintaining it without sacrificing Samana. The idea of annexation failed to alarm the people, the letter says, because it came in the form of a fraternal invitation, highly flattering to their self-respect, and if the project is followed up in that guise there will be no opposition worth mentioning to the measure. The country is quiet, though many arrests were made after the Seibo fiasco, and some twenty persons are held for examination on a charge of conspiracy; it is said that henceforth such attempts will be treated with the utmost rigor of the law, but before this system is put into effect Báez will proclaim a general amnesty, and only those who renew seditious efforts are to suffer the death penalty. The roads are bad beyond description; and before signing the drafts for the first $200,000 instalment of the loan, two engineers, brought from Europe for the purpose, made a scientific reconnaissance of the gold districts, to see whether there was sufficient promise of mineral wealth to secure the payment.
records.summary_es: Una carta publicada en el Herald ofrece un relato, que comienza a mitad de su curso, de la diplomacia caribeña del secretario Seward: reyes que estaban dispuestos a negociar un puerto libre y neutral en Samaná como gran centro de vapores, él se lanzó sobre Santo Tomás: también habría comprado Samaná, pero hasta que el presidente dominicano no se viera reducido al extremo, no se atrevía a intentar el desmembramiento de la república. Aquello fracasó, continúa la carta, y ahora oímos hablar de anexión. Báez ha asegurado su empréstito deliberadamente de manera que su gobierno se mantenga dos años, y al final de ese plazo confía en el desarrollo de los intereses mineros e industriales del país para sostenerlo sin sacrificar Samaná. La idea de la anexión no alarmó al pueblo, dice la carta, porque vino en forma de una invitación fraternal, muy halagadora para su amor propio, y si el proyecto se sigue en esa forma no habrá oposición digna de mención a la medida. El país está tranquilo, aunque se hicieron muchos arrestos tras el fiasco de Seibo y unas veinte personas están detenidas para ser examinadas por un cargo de conspiración; se dice que en adelante tales intentos serán tratados con el máximo rigor de la ley, pero antes de que este sistema entre en vigor Báez proclamará una amnistía general, y solo quienes renueven los esfuerzos sediciosos sufrirán la pena de muerte. records.headline: An editorial in the Herald lays down conditions for annexation
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Herald lays down conditions for annexation: if they mean business in this annexation scheme, the annexationists must discuss the affair at home and show that a valid majority of the people of the Dominican Republic desire the step to be taken: when this is done the Dominican government can make its application, and it will be considered without fear or favor. The Dominican Republic will be the great gainer by the step if it is ever taken, the editorial says, and we have no need to pay a high price for a very small article. As for Samaná, it has been in the market for sale under every administration St. Domingo has had since it separated from Hayti, and has not found a purchaser, and it has been before the world for settlement and population ever since Columbus struck the New World, in 1492, and its pestilential shores are as solitary now as they were three hundred and fifty years ago. Let the Dominican spoilsmen agitate at home, the editorial concludes: they can get nothing out of the United States Treasury under the new regime of honesty that rules there.

La República Dominicana será la gran beneficiada por el paso, si alguna vez se da, dice el editorial, y no tenemos necesidad de pagar un precio alto por un artículo muy pequeño. En cuanto a Samaná, ha estado en venta bajo todas las administraciones que Santo Domingo ha tenido desde que se separó de Haití, y no ha encontrado comprador, y ha estado ante el mundo para su población y colonización desde que Colón llegó al Nuevo Mundo en 1492, y sus costas pestilentes están tan desiertas ahora como hace trescientos cincuenta años. Que los expoliadores dominicanos agiten en su país, concluye el editorial: no sacarán nada del Tesoro de los Estados Unidos bajo el nuevo régimen de honestidad que allí impera.

records.summary_en: The Herald prints what it says may be relied upon as exact and authentic — in point of fact, in sense and letter, the translation of Mr. Fabens' last official instructions. Báez so firmly believes that his views are also the accepted views in Congress, and he so firmly believes that they are also the accepted views of President Grant, that he has instructed Minister Fabens to confer with the incoming Secretary of State at as early a day as possible on the subject, and to take an early occasion to manifest to President Grant personally, and without the slightest reserve, the actual situation of the Dominican Republic, and to solicit the co-operation of the Washington Cabinet in the policy of creating a free and neutral centre of commerce in the Antilles. This knowledge, the Herald says, was imparted to the French, Italian and Danish consuls, if not officially at least distinctly, from the lips of the Dominican Secretary of State, in the course of a long conversation respecting various incorrect reports of revolutionary movements under the Ogandos, Marcos Adón and Luperón, which had never had existence, and from that the Secretary slid adroitly to the contradictory statements about the sale of Samana. 'None of you, Messieurs les Consuls, believe that there is any question of dismembering the republic,' said the Minister, with some warmth; 'and it is scarcely a secret from any of you that liberal propositions have been made to us to declare Samana a free and neutral port.' Such a measure, the French Consul replied, should command the sympathies of every maritime power.

records.headline: Under the head 'St. Domingo,' a Herald letter from St. Domingo
records.summary_en: Under the head 'St. Domingo,' a Herald letter from St. Domingo City, March 18, 1869, reports the anxiety of the Dominicans for annexation and the liabilities and assets of the republic. Mr. J. W. Fabens, Dominican envoy to the United States, left for Washington on the 11th instant: he carries with him a complete official exhibit of the industrial, financial and political situation of the republic. The debt, foreign and domestic, including the paper currency in circulation, figures at less than $1,000,000, while the schedule of public property to be transferred to the United States, including forts, arsenals, barracks, custom houses, vessels and munitions of war, is estimated at not less than a sum many times larger. Manifestoes have been received from Santiago de los Caballeros, Seibo and other points declaring for annexation, and clothing President Báez with full power to act. The State geological survey, under Professor William M. Gabb, of Philadelphia, is progressing; rich gold veins have been discovered. The country was never more quiet. Luperón's steamer Telégrafo has succeeded in reaching St. Marc, Hayti, where she is offered for sale, as Luperón has run out of funds.
records.summary_es: Bajo el encabezado «Santo Domingo», una carta del Herald desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo, del 18 de marzo de 1869, informa de la ansiedad de los dominicanos por la anexión y de los pasivos y activos de la república. El señor J. W. Fabens, enviado dominicano a los Estados Unidos, partió hacia Washington el día 11: lleva consigo una exposición oficial completa de la situación industrial, financiera y política de la república. La deuda, externa e interna, incluida la moneda de papel en circulación, asciende a menos de $1.000.000, mientras que el inventario de la propiedad pública que se transferiría a los Estados Unidos, incluidos fuertes, arsenales, cuarteles, aduanas, buques y pertrechos de guerra, se estima en no menos de una suma muchas veces mayor. Se han recibido manifiestos de Santiago de los Caballeros, Seibo y otros puntos declarándose por la anexión y confiriendo al presidente Báez plenos poderes para actuar. El reconocimiento geológico del Estado, bajo la dirección del profesor William M. Gabb, de Filadelfia, está en curso; se han descubierto ricas vetas de oro. El país nunca ha estado más tranquilo. El vapor Telégrafo, de Luperón, ha logrado llegar a Saint-Marc, Haití, donde se ofrece en venta, pues Luperón se ha quedado sin fondos.

records.headline: A further Herald account, in a passage that opens in mid-discussion of the Cabinet
records.summary_en: A further Herald account, in a passage that opens in mid-discussion of the Cabinet, relates that it is known to everybody in St. Domingo that Minister Fabens was instructed to obtain the co-operation of the United States in making Samana a great commercial centre, and the Dominican Cabinet seems perfectly satisfied with his course. He had written for certain official statistics to lay before the American people, but not receiving them in season, he came on in person and found them just ready to be forwarded to him. The papers thus prepared are in singular contradiction, the account says, to the estimate of the public debt made by Mr. Angenard: he estimated it at from $12,000,000 to $16,000,000, while it is in fact less than $1,000,000, and even if the French loan is accepted it will still be under that figure, and the republic has ten times that value in the public domain and gold fields, which are not burdened as yet by a single dollar of debt. There is not probably a single state in all America so free from debt and so rich in the means of securing her creditors as the Dominican Republic. Her whole revenue is some hundreds of thousands of dollars per annum, of which $400,000 is derived from her custom house receipts; these would inure to the United States Treasury in the event of annexation, but the Dominicans would have the desired equivalent in peace, protection, the development of her means and a vast enhancement of general prosperity.
records.summary_es: Un relato adicional del Herald, en un pasaje que se abre en mitad de la discusión sobre el gabinete, cuenta que es conocido por todos en Santo Domingo que el ministro Fabens recibió instrucciones de obtener la cooperación de los Estados Unidos para hacer de Samaná un gran centro comercial, y que el gabinete dominicano parece perfectamente satisfecho con su actuación. Había pedido ciertas estadísticas oficiales para presentarlas ante el pueblo estadounidense, pero al no recibirlas a tiempo, vino en persona y las encontró ya listas para serle enviadas. Los documentos así preparados están en singular contradicción, dice el relato, con la estimación de la deuda pública hecha por el señor Angenard: él la estimó entre $12.000.000 y $16.000.000, mientras que en realidad es de menos de $1.000.000, y aun si se acepta el empréstito francés seguirá por debajo de esa cifra, y la república posee diez veces ese valor en el dominio público y los campos de oro, que aún no están gravados por un solo dólar de deuda. Probablemente no hay un solo estado en toda América tan libre de deudas y tan rico en medios de asegurar a sus acreedores como la República Dominicana. Sus rentas totales ascienden a algunos cientos de miles de dólares al año, de los cuales $400.000 proceden de los ingresos de sus aduanas; estas pasarían al Tesoro de los Estados Unidos en caso de anexión, pero los dominicanos tendrían el equivalente deseado en paz, protección, el desarrollo de sus recursos y un vasto aumento de la prosperidad general.

records.headline: A letter printed in the Telegraph argues the case of the Galvanic
records.summary_en: A letter printed in the Telegraph argues the case of the Galvanic, a British vessel seized by Spain while bound from Nassau to Puerto Plata, in the Dominican Republic. An English possession with an English light-house upon it lay considerably north of the place of capture, the letter says, and far beyond Cuban waters; her papers were all in order, regularly made out for Puerto Plata, in the Dominican Republic; no arms were found on board, and if her passengers were Cubans, none had up to the time of the capture of the vessel engaged in acts of hostility against the Spanish government — and even if they had, the captain of the Galvanic had an unquestionable right to take them on board of his vessel, and carry them from Nassau to Puerto Plata. The trial of the captain and crew of the vessel the British representative justly deems of no weight, and farcical: the men were shown no justice or fairness, were denied all kind of assistance and defense, and were not even allowed to communicate in their emergencies with their Consul, and have the benefit of his presence during their trial. In view of the facts of the case, the demands of the British representative are therefore, the letter says, for rights and justice and not favors and concessions: they require that the Galvanic, a British vessel taken in British waters, be returned to her owners, and her captain, crew, and passengers set at liberty, and that damages be paid by the Spanish government. With such wide difference and discrepancies in the views of the British and Spanish authorities as to this case, the letter asks, may it not be well said to be fraught with perils to the peaceful relations of Great Britain and Spain?
records.summary_es: Una carta publicada en el Telegraph defiende el caso del Galvanic, buque británico apresado por España cuando se dirigía de Nasáu a Puerto Plata, en la República Dominicana. Una posesión inglesa con un faro inglés sobre ella quedaba considerablemente al norte del lugar de la captura, dice la carta, y muy fuera de las aguas cubanas; sus documentos estaban todos en regla, extendidos regularmente para Puerto Plata, en la República Dominicana; no se encontraron armas a bordo, y si sus pasajeros eran cubanos, ninguno había participado hasta el momento de la captura del buque en actos de hostilidad contra el gobierno español, y aun si lo hubieran hecho, el capitán del Galvanic tenía un derecho incuestionable de llevarlos a bordo de su buque y transportarlos desde Nasáu hasta Puerto Plata. El juicio del capitán y la tripulación del buque, el representante británico lo considera con justicia de ningún peso, y una farsa: a los hombres no se les mostró justicia ni equidad, se les negó toda clase de asistencia y defensa, y ni siquiera se les permitió comunicarse en sus emergencias con su cónsul ni contar con el beneficio de su presencia durante el juicio. En vista de los hechos del caso, las demandas del representante británico son, por tanto, dice la carta, de derechos y justicia y no de favores ni concesiones: exigen que el Galvanic, buque británico apresado en aguas británicas, sea devuelto a sus dueños, que su capitán, tripulación y pasajeros sean puestos en libertad, y que el gobierno español pague daños y perjuicios. Con tan amplia diferencia y discrepancias en los criterios de las autoridades británicas y españolas sobre este caso, pregunta la carta, ¿no puede decirse con razón que está cargado de peligros para las relaciones pacíficas entre Gran Bretaña y España?

records.headline: The Herald speculates, in an editorial extract that begins in mid-argument
records.summary_en: The Herald speculates, in an editorial extract that begins in mid-argument, that the annexation of the Antilles may be defeated by means of St. Domingo: if the cable should suddenly flash the intelligence that Napoleon III had forestalled the cabinets by recognizing in Cuba a whole people struggling for their existence as a distinct nationality, and asking Spain to grant them the political boon of independence, Spain and the Cubans alike would be apt to heed the advice of so strong a mediator, and in advance of this the Dominican republic will have learned exactly what it has to expect from the United States. France, the writer adds, will not waste much diplomacy to rescue Cuba from Spain if the island is given over to the United States; and Báez himself is very dubious on the subject of annexation, doubting much whether Congress will authorize the Executive to proceed immediately. That failing, the extract turns to a counter-plan of ports at Samaná and Monte Cristi, where the window breaks off.
records.summary_es: El Herald especula, en un extracto editorial que comienza a mitad de un argumento, que la anexión de las Antillas podría ser derrotada por medio de Santo Domingo: si el cable transmitiera de pronto la noticia de que Napoleón III se había adelantado a los gabinetes reconociendo en Cuba a todo un pueblo que lucha por su existencia como nacionalidad distinta y pidiendo a España que le concediera el don político de la independencia, tanto España como los cubanos se inclinarían a atender el consejo de tan fuerte mediador, y antes de ello la República Dominicana ya habría sabido exactamente qué debe esperar de los Estados Unidos. Francia, añade el autor, no gastará mucha diplomacia en rescatar a Cuba de España si la isla pasa a los Estados Unidos; y el propio Báez se muestra muy dudoso sobre el tema de la anexión, pues duda mucho que el Congreso autorice al Ejecutivo a proceder de inmediato. Fracasado eso, el extracto pasa a un plan alternativo de puertos en Samaná y Monte Cristi, donde la ventana se interrumpe.

records.summary_en: *The New York Herald* reported that Dominican envoy Pujol sought to offer Samaná or Manzanillo to the United States as a naval station, even as a free gift without requiring prior formal recognition. However, Secretary of State Seward, reportedly influenced by the Spanish minister, refused to grant Pujol an interview or acknowledge the Dominican Republic. The paper criticized the State Department for repeatedly disregarding strategic American opportunities in Samaná to accommodate Spanish interests.
records.summary_es: *The New York Herald* informó que el comisionado dominicano Pujol intentó ceder Samaná o Manzanillo a los Estados Unidos como estación naval, ofreciéndola incluso a título gratuito sin condicionarla al previo reconocimiento diplomático. No obstante, el secretario de Estado Seward, supuestamente influenciado por el ministro de España, se rehusó a conceder una audiencia a Pujol y a reconocer a la República Dominicana. El diario censuró al Departamento de Estado por desaprovechar reiteradamente ventajas estratégicas estadounidenses en Samaná en deferencia a los intereses españoles.

records.headline: A letter from the island reports that the cattle-stealing raids of the border
records.summary_en: A letter from the island reports that the cattle-stealing raids of the border Cacos, which give great trouble to the Dominican authorities, are magnified in the reports at Jacmel into regular battles in which the Cacos, like the Spaniards in Cuba, always claim to be splendidly victorious; several of the thieves have been taken, tried and shot by order of the general of the frontier, and even such cases are reported as important military movements by both parties. A conspiracy attempted in Santiago de los Caballeros at the close of Easter week, whose object was to depose Báez and unite with the Cacos of Hayti, was discovered and the plotters arrested, though that is not the popular idea of that section. Business is very good in the interior but continues dull at St. Domingo; there are no American vessels in port, but the W. D. Forrest is daily looked for from New York with a party of gentlemen who propose forming a commercial establishment at Monte Cristi, having a concession for making a wagon road from La Vega to Manzanillo Bay. It is one of the first buildings of prospective annexation, the writer says, and others are preparing to follow; the desire of annexation, or union with the Americans, as the country people describe it, is spreading daily.
records.summary_es: Una carta desde la isla informa de que las correrías de robo de ganado de los cacos fronterizos, que causan grandes dificultades a las autoridades dominicanas, se magnifican en los informes de Jacmel hasta convertirlas en batallas regulares en las que los cacos, como los españoles en Cuba, siempre proclaman haber salido espléndidamente victoriosos; varios de los ladrones han sido capturados, juzgados y fusilados por orden del general de la frontera, y aun casos como esos se reportan como importantes movimientos militares por ambas partes. Una conspiración intentada en Santiago de los Caballeros al cierre de la semana de Pascua, cuyo objeto era deponer a Báez y unirse con los cacos de Haití, fue descubierta y los conspiradores arrestados, aunque esa no es la idea popular de esa comarca. El comercio es muy bueno en el interior, pero sigue flojo en Santo Domingo; no hay buques estadounidenses en puerto, pero se espera a diario el W. D. Forrest, procedente de Nueva York, con un grupo de caballeros que se proponen formar un establecimiento comercial en Monte Cristi, con una concesión para construir un camino de carretas desde La Vega hasta la bahía de Manzanillo. Es uno de los primeros edificios de la anexión en perspectiva, dice el corresponsal, y otros se preparan a seguir; el deseo de anexión, o unión con los americanos, como lo describe la gente del campo, se extiende a diario.

records.headline: The Phoenix reprints from the Philadelphia Inquirer the report
records.summary_en: The Phoenix reprints from the Philadelphia Inquirer the report that Luperón and Adon have marched over the borders of Hayti, with their Caco allies, to invade the Dominican territory. Their force is some 500 men, quite an army in that country, and they rally upon the old cry, the overthrow of Báez and resistance to American annexation. The writer declares the war now one of races, the Cacos, in conjunction with the opponents of Presidents Salnave and Báez, making a final effort to get rid of all white residents, either by murder or by rendering the country too hot to hold them; but the chances are all against their success, the better classes of the population being in arms against them. It is evident, the item argues, that a majority of the people of Dominica desire annexation to this country, a desire manifested everywhere on the island but especially in the cities, from which the annexation movement is gaining daily strength; and unquestionably the time will arrive when a firm and sound American policy shall dictate the annexation not only of Dominica, but of the other West Indian islands.
records.summary_es: El Phoenix reproduce del Philadelphia Inquirer un informe según el cual Luperón y Adon han cruzado las fronteras de Haití, con sus aliados cacos, para invadir el territorio dominicano. Su fuerza es de unos 500 hombres, todo un ejército en ese país, y se agrupan bajo el viejo grito de la caída de Báez y la resistencia a la anexión estadounidense. El autor declara que la guerra es ahora una guerra de razas, y que los cacos, en conjunción con los opositores de los presidentes Salnave y Báez, hacen un esfuerzo final por deshacerse de todos los residentes blancos, ya por el asesinato, ya haciendo el país inhabitable para ellos; pero todas las probabilidades están en contra de su éxito, pues las clases más acomodadas de la población están en armas contra ellos. Es evidente, sostiene la nota, que una mayoría del pueblo de Dominica desea la anexión a este país, deseo que se manifiesta en toda la isla, pero especialmente en las ciudades, desde donde el movimiento anexionista gana fuerza a diario; e incuestionablemente llegará el momento en que una política estadounidense firme y sensata dicte la anexión no solo de Dominica, sino también de las demás islas de las Indias Occidentales.

records.headline: Writing from St. Domingo under date of April 20, a Herald correspondent
records.summary_en: Writing from St. Domingo under date of April 20, a Herald correspondent reports that after two fruitless attempts he has at last tracked up the mining pioneers to their working places. The heavy rains had continued six weeks later than usual this year, destroying half of the coffee crop and obstructing business by making the roads nearly impassable for bringing in products for exportation. There is but one way of travelling in the Dominican republic, he explains: on horseback, taking along a burden animal to carry hammocks, blankets and provisions for the trip; so equipped, with a native guide, three of the party started for a week's excursion, riding out through the suburb of San Carlos, which, according to tradition, occupies the site of the Sacred Palm Groves of the gentle tribes of Ozama, exterminated by the Spanish discoverers. For twelve miles they rode along a level road generally bordered by trees or thickets; for that distance from St. Domingo the Spanish forces made a complete desolation during their late occupation, dwellings, fences and fruit trees destroyed, and the extract ends as the riders near the city walls.
records.summary_es: Escribiendo desde Santo Domingo con fecha 20 de abril, un corresponsal del Herald informa de que tras dos intentos infructuosos por fin ha localizado a los pioneros mineros en sus lugares de trabajo. Las fuertes lluvias se habían prolongado este año seis semanas más de lo usual, destruyendo la mitad de la cosecha de café y obstruyendo el comercio al volver los caminos casi intransitables para sacar los productos de exportación. Solo hay una manera de viajar en la República Dominicana, explica: a caballo, llevando un animal de carga para las hamacas, las mantas y las provisiones del viaje; equipados así, con un guía nativo, tres del grupo partieron para una excursión de una semana, saliendo por el arrabal de San Carlos, que, según la tradición, ocupa el sitio de los Sagrados Palmares de las pacíficas tribus del Ozama, exterminadas por los descubridores españoles. Recorrieron doce millas por un camino llano bordeado generalmente de árboles o matorrales; en esa distancia desde Santo Domingo las fuerzas españolas hicieron una desolación completa durante su reciente ocupación, destruyendo viviendas, cercas y árboles frutales, y el extracto termina cuando los jinetes se acercan a las murallas de la ciudad.

records.headline: A New York letter in the Telegraph says there is no truth at all
records.summary_en: A New York letter in the Telegraph says there is no truth at all in the rumors started by sensational papers in regard to the Perit or the Arago: the Perit has sailed for Kingston, Jamaica, and upon her return will be placed on the St. Domingo line. The letter adds that Messrs. Spofford, Tileston & Co. are about starting a new West India line of steamers, the pioneer vessel of which, the Tybee, is advertised to sail June 2; the points embraced in the route are Samaná, Port-au-Prince, and, in fact, all the ports of any note in the Dominican republic. The days of departure are not as yet determined upon, but will be designated before another week has elapsed. The remainder of the letter turns to New York concert and theatre news.

records.headline: The Herald surveys the suitors pulling their wires round Secretary Fish
records.summary_en: The Herald surveys the suitors pulling their wires round Secretary Fish from every side of the American Mediterranean: President Céspedes and the Spanish Minister at Washington; President Báez and the agents of Cabral, who is said to be again afoot in St. Domingo; Salnave, and General Domingue, of Southern Hayti; and others whose schemes are less prominently developed as yet. Among all the contestants, the editorial says, the only apparent ground for stability of rule is found in the recognition by and active sympathy of the United States; popular sympathy and the national interest combine on one side, and the stipulations of the neutrality laws are appealed to on the other. If the present complications in the American Mediterranean are forced or even allowed to develop in a manner antagonistic to the permanent interests of the United States, the administration will lose its hold on the respect of the country and acquire a merited weight of popular obloquy. The extract ends in mid-discussion of the difficulties added by the Cabinet's past use of the neutrality laws.
records.summary_es: El Herald pasa revista a los pretendientes que mueven sus hilos en torno al secretario Fish desde todos los lados del Mediterráneo americano: el presidente Céspedes y el ministro español en Washington; el presidente Báez y los agentes de Cabral, de quien se dice que anda de nuevo en campaña en Santo Domingo; Salnave, y el general Domingue, del sur de Haití; y otros cuyos planes están aún menos desarrollados públicamente. Entre todos los contendientes, dice el editorial, el único fundamento aparente de estabilidad en el poder se halla en el reconocimiento y la simpatía activa de los Estados Unidos; la simpatía popular y el interés nacional se combinan de un lado, y del otro se apela a las estipulaciones de las leyes de neutralidad. Si las actuales complicaciones en el Mediterráneo americano se fuerzan o siquiera se dejan desarrollar de manera antagónica a los intereses permanentes de los Estados Unidos, la administración perderá el respeto del país y cargará con un merecido peso de oprobio popular. El extracto termina en mitad de la discusión sobre las dificultades añadidas por el uso que el Gabinete ha hecho en el pasado de las leyes de neutralidad.

records.summary_en: Based on the provided excerpt, the newspaper reported that the Dominican Republic's paper currency was overprinted by various chiefs and ultimately repudiated, leaving the masses with a deep aversion to government money. An attempted revolution in January to redeem a currency issue with silver failed to attract even 200 people. Additionally, General Cabral entered the Dominican territory and remained in the border belt without advancing further or being driven out, with conflicting reports claiming minor skirmishes resulting in fewer than a dozen casualties on either side up to May 5.

Una tentativa insurreccional en enero para rescatar una emisión fiduciaria en plata no logró concitar la adhesión ni de 200 hombres. Asimismo, el general Cabral incursionó en territorio dominicano manteniéndose en la franja fronteriza sin conseguir avanzar más ni ser desalojado, con partes contradictorios que reportaban escaramuzas aisladas que no alcanzaban la docena de bajas en ningún bando hasta el 5 de mayo.

records.full_text:
ST. DOMINGO.

Condition of the Country—Disappearance of the Paper Currency—Manoeuvres of Cabral—The Annexation Feeling—Trade with Europe.

ST. DOMINGO, May 20, 1869.

I complained in my last—of the 12th instant or thereabouts—that the rains were over due, but had not come. Since then they have been up to their duty. Nearly every day or night we have had at least one lively shower, and the crops and pastures are smiling gratefully in return. The roads will not improve as kindly as the vegetation, however, though a courier from the confines of Hayti, whom I caught on the wing, says they are in fine order from here to Azua. This courier brings letters worth reading, not from their intrinsic importance nor their literary value, but for their curiously confused statements. One minister writes that his "government" will unite with that of the Dominican republic in raising the flag of the United States if President Baez will share with his neighbor the loan he has lately obtained from England. Another of the ministers expresses his "loyal desire for a lasting peace with our Dominican brothers" but there can be no peace so long as the "evil disposed traitors of Santiago and Porto Plata are plotting to sell their country to the Yankees." So he proposes to use a just portion of the English loan to extinguish the Cabral-Cacos and establish a peaceful and united government over the whole island. These are not official letters—else I might have missed the pleasure of reading them—but the private communication of views to be acted upon in case the Dominican President should entertain them. The point of the joke is that "this government" was not yet in existence, but proposed to organize very soon—that is, early in May. The chiefs of this coming government had, it would seem, either failed to compare notes, or agreed to disagree. There were more letters by this courier, but one and all ignored Salnave, and all admitted that the sinews of war are sadly wanting in Hayti.

The issue of paper money, which has hitherto been the main element of revolution making, is played out. Dominican paper currency has entirely disappeared, after going down to a thousand for one under the last months of Cabral, and Haytien paper is now more than two hundred for one, and getting rapidly worse on the frontier.

This paper currency is the key to the whole situation—and all the situations—on this island. The various chiefs printed it off by wholesale and sold it to the merchants, who paid half or two-thirds of their duties with it, besides using it to buy produce. The soldiers received their pay in it, and everybody received it at some rate or other until the country was so overflooded with it that the traders would not receive it at any price. For a time each successful chief would try the virtues of a special issue, to be taken in preference at the Custom Houses, but one and all were finally overdone and repudiated. Thus the masses—on whom the evils of depreciation always fell most severely—have conceived a deep rooted aversion to government currency. The promise to redeem with silver the Cabral issue was the staple of the Seybo attempt at revolution about the beginning of January, but even that bait did not bring out 200 people, and the affair was snuffed out in a week.

General Cabral entered the Dominican territory nearly three months ago, and has been left in the possession of the depopulated border belt; but he neither gets further into the country nor is driven entirely out of it. Letters from both sides have quietly slipped into this city, each claiming to have had skirmishes (they call them battles), in which each asserts itself signally victorious; but the value of their victories may be estimated from this fact—not a dozen men have been killed or taken on either side up to May 3, the very last date of reliable accounts.

The news that Congress adjourned without inviting the Dominican republic to enter the Union was a great disappointment here. Any number of American flags had been found, or made, to be in readiness to flaunt on the arrival of the first United States ship-of-war. The people have so generally made up their minds to it that you will hear them talking of "our starry flag," "our beautiful money," and "our nice flour." United States quarters and dimes circulate largely in all the West India islands since the use of paper has made them scarce at home, and they are favorite "mediums"—they mean and make good their say.

Yesterday, the 19th, a schooner came in from Porto Rico overloaded with a live freight of Dominicans expelled from that Spanish colony by the orders of the home government. It was probably a necessary precaution, as not one of them could be trusted since the revolution in Cuba. Fifty-five—counting babies sixty—persons came over with their little all by this small craft, which they clubbed their meagre means to charter, and others are to follow as soon as they can find the means. They made a melancholy show, being mostly of the poorest class who had enlisted in the Spanish army during the period of occupation at St. Domingo. This arrival and the theatre are the chief excitements of the hour. I repeat that there is not, nor has there been, the least shade of public excitement here about the border movements. No one believes there will anything come of it, and if there should no one would care except the officials who are marched out.

Business is more animated with Europe, for 70,000 ceroons of superior tobacco are on the lists of sale and shipment, principally on German account, and none or next to none for the United States. All its value comes back in European goods. Even loaf sugar, which its nearer neighbors ought to supply, comes from France, and such articles as calicoes, sheetings and other cotton fabrics, are almost never seen here of United States manufacture. The only American cottons I have seen in the country were a few bales of sheetings, imported by Leyba & Co., and a bale of Merrimac calico, consigned to Read & Ricart, to try the market. While there are three vessels loading on the coast for England there is but one small craft taking in cargo for Boston. This is all wrong, for the United States ought to supply every yard of cotton goods used on this island, and would so do if affairs were rightly managed.

The news from the north side shows the tobacco crop to be larger than any previous year. It is estimated that not less than 120,000 ceroons of tobacco will be exported from Porto Plata this season.

Professor Gabb, State geologist, goes to New York by this steamer. The Professor is very reticent as to the result of his preliminary labors, but there is a certain twinkle in his eye that betokens inward satisfaction.

records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported on conditions in Santo Domingo, noting strong popular sentiment in favor of annexation to the United States, favorable reports on mineral wealth by State Geologist Professor Gabb, and a record tobacco crop. The paper also reported that many Dominicans were departing to assist Cuban insurgents against Spain. While initial reports claimed former President Cabral's rebellion had failed, subsequent dispatches indicated Cabral had defeated government forces in several southern towns, prompting President Báez to concentrate his troops at Azua.

records.full_text:
THE FIRE AT PUERTO PLATA—INCORRECT NEWS BY THE HAVANA CABLE—THE COUNTRY QUIET—DOMINICAN VOLUNTEERS FOR THE CUBAN ARMY—STRONG FEELING IN FAVOR OF ANNEXATION TO THE UNITED STATES.

By the arrival at this port yesterday of the schooner Charles Albert, from Puerto Plata, in 10 days, we have advices from Santo Domingo to the 27th ultimo.

The news received here from Havana by Cable, and published last Sunday, of a great fire having occurred at Puerto Plata, burning down the Custom-House at that place and many other buildings, whereby several of the merchants had been ruined, is totally incorrect. A fire did take place on the 26th May in the town, but only one building was destroyed by it, and beyond a scorching of the walls of the Custom-House from the flames of the burning building, that edifice sustained no damage. The sufferers from the fire are foreign merchants, Messrs. Hamburger and Meyer, and they are losers to the extent of $10,000, no part of which was covered by insurance.

The country was quiet. Ex-President Cabral was somewhere on the Haytian frontier, but all his efforts to provoke a revolutionary movement for the overthrow of Baez had signally failed, and he was no longer feared by the Government.

Numbers of Dominicans had left for Cuba to aid the insurgents in their struggle for independence, and many more were preparing to leave to join the patriot ranks. The Dominicans have not forgotten Spain's attempt to subjugate and enslave them six years ago, and the Cubans may expect to find them warm friends and sturdy allies.

The desire for annexation to the United States was stronger than ever, and regret is very generally expressed that the American Congress should have delayed action in the matter. The people were all looking hopefully to the time when the Stars and Stripes will be floating over the island.

Prof. Gabb, the State Geologist, had left for New-York, after having made an extensive survey of the copper regions, and the gold yielding districts. His report was looked for with much anxiety.

The crop of tobacco this year was the largest that has ever been gathered in Santo Domingo, and a brisk time in business was anticipated.

records.headline: The Telegraph recounts how the steamship Tybee came to be searched
records.summary_en: The Telegraph recounts how the steamship Tybee came to be searched at New York. The West Indies line was advertised by the firm of Spofford, Tileston & Co., No. 29 Broadway; the pioneer vessel was to be the first-class steamship Tybee, which the advertisement stated would leave Pier No. 4, North River, on Wednesday evening, going first to St. Thomas, proceeding thence to Santo Domingo City, Samaná, and Puerto Plata, and returning from the last-named place to New York. The vessel was advertised as for freight and passengers, and a notice on the steamship bulletin board at the General Post Office stated that a mail would be despatched by the Tybee. Subsequently the time for the sailing of the vessel was changed to Saturday, the 6th of June, at 8 o'clock, but the arrangements for her departure not having been completed by that time, she was further delayed till yesterday at noon. Meantime, suspicion having been aroused that the Tybee was intended to play the same role as the Perit, representations were made to Mr. Grinnell by the Spanish Consul in this city to the effect that the vessel's real destination was the Island of Cuba, whither she was about to convey munitions of war for the use of the insurgents, besides two hundred and fifty American volunteers for the Cuban army; in support of this it was stated that the Tybee had shipped several cases containing rifles. Acting upon this information, Collector Grinnell gave orders that the Tybee should be searched, and the extract ends as the search began yesterday forenoon.
records.summary_es: El Telegraph relata cómo el vapor Tybee llegó a ser registrado en Nueva York. La línea de las Indias Occidentales fue anunciada por la firma de Spofford, Tileston & Co., n.º 29 de Broadway; el buque pionero sería el vapor de primera clase Tybee, que según el anuncio saldría del Muelle n.º 4, North River, el miércoles por la noche, yendo primero a Santo Tomás, procediendo de allí a la ciudad de Santo Domingo, Samaná y Puerto Plata, y regresando desde este último lugar a Nueva York. El buque se anunciaba para carga y pasajeros, y un aviso en el tablón de vapores de la Oficina General de Correos indicaba que se despacharía correspondencia por el Tybee. Posteriormente la hora de salida del buque se cambió al sábado 6 de junio, a las 8 de la noche, pero, no habiéndose completado los arreglos de su partida para entonces, se retrasó aún más hasta ayer al mediodía. Entretanto, habiéndose despertado la sospecha de que el Tybee estaba destinado a desempeñar el mismo papel que el Perit, el cónsul español en esta ciudad hizo representaciones al señor Grinnell en el sentido de que el verdadero destino del buque era la isla de Cuba, adonde se disponía a llevar municiones de guerra para uso de los insurgentes, además de doscientos cincuenta voluntarios estadounidenses para el ejército cubano; en apoyo de esto se afirmó que el Tybee había embarcado varias cajas que contenían rifles. Actuando sobre esta información, el administrador de aduanas Grinnell dio órdenes de que el Tybee fuera registrado, y el extracto termina cuando el registro comenzaba ayer por la mañana.

records.summary_en: In the conclusion of the Tybee report, it is said that the vessel will be allowed to proceed on her voyage to-day. The Telegraph's reporter visited the Tybee last evening and found her ready for sea, the only addition made to her equipment after the visit of the customs officers being a 12-pounder, which had been taken on board, he was informed, not for warlike purposes, but for firing the signal gun usually discharged by steamers in leaving port. The captain of the Tybee ridiculed the charge brought against his vessel by the Spanish Consul, pointing to the fact that among the passengers going out to St. Domingo in her is a Commissioner from the United States Government to the Dominican republic.

records.summary_en: The Herald, in an editorial extract that begins in mid-discussion with a Mr. Hunt, who has orders to proceed to the Dominican republic and report upon its condition at an early day, and whether he has higher secret instructions the paper is not informed, surveys the new movements and combinations which are going on in the Antilles: Cuba is convulsed with the questions of revolution, independence and annexation; in St. Domingo a policy of seeking admission to the Union has been discussed by President Báez, which has awakened efforts against him by Cabral, his former antagonist; in Hayti General Domingue, who is making a powerful resistance to Salnave, months ago wrote to Secretary Seward, seeking a protectorate for the territory he ruled; in Porto Rico a violent explosion against the Spanish rule is only kept down by a force of bayonets; and in Jamaica the British government is exhibiting a sudden energy in restoring the harbor of Kingston. This movement, the editorial says, is an important one in many respects, and if the administration contemplates aright the combinations going on in the Antilles it may be productive in the highest degree of good to American political and material interests.

records.headline: The Herald argues, in a companion editorial extract, that under a late policy
records.summary_en: The Herald argues, in a companion editorial extract, that under a late policy all that was required was that an agent should present himself with a bag of gold in one hand and the American flag in the other, and that he had only to hoist the one as soon as the other had been accepted. In the pursuit of this petty and mischievous policy, it says, a signal rebuke was received from the Dominican republic in the Samaná question, and from the Senate of the United States in that of St. Thomas; both were merited, for the principles on which the course was founded were of the meanest and most contemptible kind. Questions of national importance merit a higher and a nobler style of treatment. Fifty years ago a policy was announced by President Monroe which acquired an extended influence in American politics and European cabinets, because it expressed the sentiment of the American people; during two generations that policy has been the pole star of national development on this continent, and it was adapted to its era and has consummated its work. It is no longer a question of founding new colonies or extending European influence over old ones; the colonies have become nations, and national development has brought new needs and new demands, and the extract ends as it turns to the desire developing in the countries south of the United States from their failure to attain the same prosperity.
records.summary_es: El Herald argumenta, en un extracto editorial complementario, que todo lo que se requería bajo una política reciente era que un agente se presentara con una bolsa de oro en una mano y la bandera estadounidense en la otra, y que solo tenía que izar la una tan pronto como la otra hubiera sido aceptada. En la prosecución de esta política mezquina y perniciosa, dice, se recibió una señalada reprensión de la República Dominicana en la cuestión de Samaná, y del Senado de los Estados Unidos en la de Santo Tomás; ambas fueron merecidas, pues los principios en que se fundaba ese proceder eran de la clase más ruin y despreciable. Las cuestiones de importancia nacional merecen un trato de estilo más elevado y noble. Hace cincuenta años un presidente, Monroe, anunció una política que adquirió una extensa influencia en la política estadounidense y en los gabinetes europeos, porque expresaba el sentimiento del pueblo estadounidense; durante dos generaciones esa política ha sido la estrella polar del desarrollo nacional en este continente, y estaba adaptada a su época y ha consumado su obra. Ya no se trata de fundar nuevas colonias ni de extender la influencia europea sobre las antiguas; las colonias se han convertido en naciones, y el desarrollo nacional ha traído nuevas necesidades y nuevas demandas, y el extracto termina cuando pasa al deseo que se desarrolla en los países al sur de los Estados Unidos por su fracaso en alcanzar la misma prosperidad.

records.headline: The Herald argues, in an editorial extract, that the islands of the Archipelago
records.summary_en: The Herald argues, in an editorial extract, that the islands of the Archipelago are to-day in a crisis of great political changes, the incipient point of which lies in the abolition of African slavery by the United States: Cuba is undergoing an armed revolution, with emancipation and annexation inscribed upon its banner; the Dominican republic is agitated with the proposition of a peaceful admission to the American Union; Hayti is divided into three hostile camps, in one of which at least the idea of an American protectorate is entertained; and Porto Rico is reported to have caught the fire in a way which greatly alarms the colonial officers of the Spanish monarchy. The various parties involved in all these movements have their active partisans in this country, who are engaged in pushing their respective views in every feasible way: the co-operation of the press is assiduously sought, diplomatic and extra-diplomatic communications are pressed upon the government and the people, arms and munitions of war are pushed forward through every possible channel, and steamers are being built, chartered or purchased and prepared for naval armament in behalf of several of the combatants. So numerous are these operations, and so conflicting is the information in regard to them which is laid before the administration, the extract ends, that the government thus far has not been able to convict or even detain those engaged in them.

records.full_text:
ST. DOMINGO.

LUPERON DECLARED A PIRATE—FAVORABLE REPORTS OF BAEZ.

ST. DOMINGO, June 20, via HAVANA, June 29.—The Dominican Senate has declared Gen. Luperon and the crew of the steamer Telegrafo pirates. The people of Puerto Plata and Samana refused to receive Luperon, who has issued a proclamation of rebellion.

The Dominican troops remain faithful to President Baez. The Boletin Official reports that the Provinces of Cibas, Seybro, and Samana are tranquil. More troops are needed, but large numbers of citizens are offering their services to defend the frontier.

BOMBARDMENT OF PUERTO PLATTE—FAILURE OF THE ATTACK.

We are in receipt of advices from Puerto Platte to the 8th inst. Gen. Luperon, who is acting in concert with ex-President Cabral for the overthrow of the Baez government, had carried out the threat made by him some time back, of bombarding Puerto Platte. He went from St. Marc in the steamer Telegrafo (formerly the blockade runner Little Bee), which he now owns, appearing off the harbor of Puerto Platte on the 2d inst. The steamer immediately opened fire upon the town, and kept it up in an intermittent sort of way for six days, but she was at so great a distance from the town, and the shots were so badly aimed that no damage was done to the place, no property destroyed, and no lives lost. Owing to the position taken up by the Telegrafo the forts could not possibly reply to her fire, and as she maintained that position during the whole of the bombardment, the Dominicans had no chance of getting a shot at her. On the morning of the 8th inst. she ceased firing and shortly afterward steamed away in a westerly direction—it was supposed for St. Marc. Luperon had expected that his arrival before Puerto Platte in this vessel would have been the signal for a revolutionary uprising in the town and surrounding country, but in this he was disappointed.

Intelligence had been received at Puerto Platte that Cabral had commenced active military operations in the south-western part of the Dominican territory. It was understood that Luperon should operate in the north, while Cabral should confine himself to the south, it being hoped that by thus compelling Baez to divide his forces a more easy conquest would be gained over him by the revolutionary chiefs.

Trade was brisk at Puerto Platte, and American provisions were plentiful, especially flour. American lumber was also in good supply.

records.headline: The Herald's correspondent, writing with the Tybee expedition
records.summary_en: The Herald's correspondent, writing with the Tybee expedition, opens mid-narrative with the steamer taking on board for transportation about forty soldiers designed to reinforce the patriotic inhabitants who had already turned their town against Luperón and driven him back from it. Gregorio Luperón is an outlaw from St. Domingo, in consequence of his turbulent conduct and his repeated and fruitless attempts at raising an insurrection; under any other than the humane administration of Báez, the writer says, the renegade would have been executed. Going to St. Thomas, with the assistance of parties leagued with him through large promises of lands and other advantages, he secured a steamer in which he succeeded in reaching Samaná bay; without any shadow of belligerent rights, under various flags, he assumed the privilege of attacking a legitimate government and interfering with rightful trade, and the steamer Telégrafo bore the American flag when she set out on her piratical cruise. After passing over the bar at the mouth of the Ozama the Tybee took in tow the Alta Gracia, eighty tons, an armed schooner belonging to the Dominican republic; the Capotillo, eighty tons, also an armed sister schooner, had been sent ahead the night before, both having in view an attack upon the pirate at Samaná. The extract ends as the Tybee overtook the Capotillo and fastened her on behind the Alta Gracia.

records.summary_en: The Herald's account of the Tybee's cruise observes that the country, drained while under Spanish dominion, misgovernment and oppression, might with fair investment of the means of developing the country and liberal business relations anticipate a vastly increased return; the ruins of ancient palaces and the decayed splendor of her towns in themselves bring vividly to the imagination the days of Spanish opulence in St. Domingo, and it is necessary to go no further than the crumbling ruins of the early Spanish cities to satisfy the most obtuse mind of the hidden resources of the island. In view of the much sought for political relations on the part of Báez's government and the tendency of American enterprise in this direction, the house of Spofford, Tileston & Co. have taken the initiatory step toward realizing the benefits of the large trade destined to spring up between St. Domingo and the United States: the fast propeller Tybee was fitted up for a special cruise of exploration to the ports of St. Domingo city, Samaná bay and Puerto Plata. After a good run of six days and twenty-two hours the steamer reached St. Thomas, where it was proposed to spend about twelve hours in order to reach port by daylight; the extract ends in the description of the approach to the island.

records.headline: A correspondent of the steamer Tybee, writing from Santo Domingo City on June 22, 1869, describes five lively days
records.summary_en: A correspondent of the steamer Tybee, writing from Santo Domingo City on June 22, 1869, describes five lively days loading an assorted cargo of exports and visiting the capital, which he calls the oldest city in the western hemisphere, its site selected by Christopher Columbus. He describes the old walls and fortifications, the chapel built by Columbus and his sundial, the first cathedral with its gilded high altar and silver furnishings, and the many ancient Spanish buildings still in use, in a city whose population is now about half the 20,000 it once held.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del vapor Tybee, que escribe desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo el 22 de junio de 1869, describe cinco días animados cargando un surtido cargamento de exportaciones y visitando la capital, a la que llama la ciudad más antigua del hemisferio occidental, cuyo sitio fue escogido por Cristóbal Colón. Describe las viejas murallas y fortificaciones, la capilla construida por Colón y su reloj de sol, la primera catedral con su altar mayor dorado y sus enseres de plata, y los muchos edificios españoles antiguos todavía en uso, en una ciudad cuya población es ahora cerca de la mitad de los 20,000 habitantes que tuvo una vez.

St. Domingo, June 22, 1869.
