records.headline: In the Herald's account of the Tybee party's entertainment at St. Domingo
records.summary_en: In the Herald's account of the Tybee party's entertainment at St. Domingo, the dinner was an elegant affair and heartily enjoyed by all the party. During the course of the entertainment Mr. Fabens, prefacing his remarks with a few appropriate expressions, proposed the health of the President of the Dominican Republic, which was drank standing. After a few moments President Báez rose and thanked Mr. Fabens and the party for their kind sentiments: there was a spirit of more than friendship existing between St. Domingo and the United States, and he hoped this would increase; he felt honored with the entertainment and proposed the health of the President of the United States, which was also drank standing. President Báez was then compelled to leave the table sooner than courtesy would seem to demand, owing to the severe pain he was suffering in the head from a renewed attack of neuralgia. The letter goes on to complain of the uncertainty of the mails between this city and the United States: letters written in March last via Havana had just reached the city upon the party's arrival, and letters sent in advance to announce the proposed departure of the Tybee had not been received; the Spanish steamers run semi-monthly, alternating on their way to Havana between this city and Puerto Plata, and returning on the same schedule to St. Thomas.

records.full_text:
REVOLUTIONISTS AFLOAT.

The Crusading Steamer Telegrafo—Sailing Under American, Spanish, Haytien and Venezuelan Colors—Her Official Status—Declared a Pirate by the Dominican Republic.

We gave yesterday in our St. Domingo correspondence a full account of the attack of the crusading steamer Telegrafo upon the settlement at Samaná, with a narrative of the detention by the crusader of the American steamer Hero, of New York, and of an unknown schooner during the action. It seems the Telegrafo had been purchased by some of the partisans of Cabral, who are exiles from the Dominican republic, and cleared from St. Thomas under the United States flag, with a sea letter from the American Consul. During her cruise she successively hoisted the Spanish and Haytien flags, and at the attack on Puerto Plata flew the Venezuelan ensign. In the fight at Samaná bay it is not stated that she used any colors. The following official documents proclaim her status and designs:—

ST. THOMAS, March 16, 1869.
Hon. J. W. FABENS, Envoy of the Dominican Republic to the United States of America, St. Thomas:—
SIR—In reply to your note of yesterday, asking information relative to the movements of the steamer Telegrafo, which sailed recently from this port under the American flag, I have to certify that the said steamer, when under the Haytien flag, had been detained here on the 10th February last at my request, made to the local Governor, in consequence of information having reached me to the effect that General Luperon, a Dominican exile, with an armed expedition, contemplated embarking on her to instigate a rebellion against the government of the Dominican republic. The Governor having required of the consignee a declaration under oath and guarantee that no armed force or arms or munitions of war should be landed at any part of the coast of St. Domingo, which declaration the consignee having declined to make, had ordered a search of the vessel to be made, when arms and munitions were found; and after my repeated requests and ultimate protests made to the Governor General of the Danish islands, the same were landed and deposited in the fort on the 15th and 16th ult.

On the 18th ult., at half-past three o'clock P. M., the Telegrafo hoisted the American flag, and having previously taken on board General Luperon, with several of his followers, sailed from this port at four o'clock P. M., having cleared at the Custom House for Jamaica.

Official information has since been received here that the said steamer had reached Turk's Island on the 21st ultimo, and there taken on board certain Dominican refugees, proceeding thence to St. Marc, Hayti, en route for which place she had appeared off Porto Plata, firing a few blank shots. She was at last advices, dated 25th ultimo, at St. Marc, with Luperon and his party on board. Apprehensions are still entertained that the said Luperon contemplates a descent on the Dominican coast, with the intention of operating against the actual government of St. Domingo.

I have the honor to be, sir, your obedient servant,
H. VICTORIA.

The Baez government, fully advised of Luperon's movements, have issued a decree, accompanied by an official detail of the piratical operations of the craft, and of which the following is a translation:—

[Official.]
SENATORIAL COUNCIL OF THE DOMINICAN REPUBLIC—ORDINARY LEGISLATIVE SESSION.

Inasmuch as the executive power, through the organ of the Citizen Minister of the Interior, has presented to this high body divers authenticated documents concerning the exile Gregorio Luperon, accompanied by other rebels like himself, now infesting the coast of the Dominican republic on board an armed steamer, from whose top flies the national ensign;

Whereas the steamer Telegrafo (Telegraph), which is commanded by the rebel Gregorio Luperon, hoisted successively in the harbor of St. Thomas the national colors of Spain and Hayti, which fact was registered by the local authorities at the instance of the Dominican Consul, and information thereof sent to the fort of the said island, which contains the armament, and her sailing was delayed for lack of papers confirming her claimed nationality;

Whereas by means of misrepresentation she obtained from the United States Consul in St. Thomas a sea letter for the said steamer, upon which she hoisted the flag of the Union and departed immediately from the above port, directing her course to Puerto Plata, where she communicated with the shore and secured a discharge for the coast, with the same colors, retiring then to St. Marc, an insurrectionary point in the Haytien republic, where she remained no little time;

Whereas that on the 1st day of June she appeared in front of Puerto Plata, hoisting the Venezuelan flag, under the protection of which and with a signal of distress she asked a pilot, which was granted, according to custom;

Whereas that she received the pilot and took him prisoner and used the vessel of the port to send a demand to surrender—an ultimatum of unusual arrogance—alarming the place by the resolution threats to open fire, which threats were subsequently put into execution under the Dominican flag;

Whereas that on the 8th day of the same month she was vigorously repulsed by the loyal population and authorities of the place, made a dash upon Samaná, impudently opened fire, effected a landing and performed acts of vandalism, and having been repulsed unanimously by the heroic population;

Whereas that when an armed vessel traverses the seas without a register and documents of nationality, or sails without recognized belligerent rights, only accredited as such under the supreme jurisdiction and authority of the nation to which it is supposed to belong, and shall be competent to certify its nationality;

Whereas that if these vessels of war legally armed can use foreign flags as signals it is not permitted to declare a flag false, nor under cover of these to perform acts of infidelity and felony, in which case it is made a very grave insult to the nation whose nationality she usurps;

Whereas, lastly, that the clandestine character of the sailing of the vessel above alluded to, its successive nationalities, the acts of savage vandalism committed by her crew, her visit to the coasts and demanding the surrender of the port, and using for her purposes a foreign flag whose incursions as traitors and depredators all prove evidently that she is a pirate and should be treated as such; in consideration of the above principles of constitutional law we urgently decree:—

ARTICLE 1. The steamer Telegraph, its chief, Gregorio Luperon, and the people who accompany him are declared pirates.

ART. 2. All vessels of war are fully authorized to give chase and pursue her and to act with respect to her chief, troops and crew according to the invariable and universal international law.

ART. 3. This decree will be sent to the executive authority for its promulgation and constitutional enforcement.

Given in the chamber of the Senate Council of St. Domingo on the 18th day of June, in the year 1869, in the twenty-sixth year of the independence, sixth year of the restoration and second year of the regeneration.

By the President of the Senate.
JACINTO DE LA CONCHO.
GERARDO BOBADILLA, Secretary.

Executed, published and circulated in the territories of the republic for its punctual observance.
Given in St. Domingo the 19th day of June, 1869, twenty-sixth year of the independence, sixth of the restoration, second of the regeneration.
BUENAVENTURA BAEZ.
Countersigned—JOSE HUNGRIA, Minister of War and Marine; M. MA. GAUTIER, Minister of Foreign Affairs.

records.full_text:
MOVEMENTS OF THE STEAMER TELEGRAFO—THE REVOLUTIONISTS AND THE SAMANA QUESTION—STEAM COMMUNICATION WITH NEW-YORK.

BARRAHANO, July 9.—Shortly after the fight in the Bay of Samana, between the steamer Telegrafo and the two armed schooners, which were towed down thither from Santo Domingo City by the New-York steamer Tybee, Gen. Luperon left Samana in the Telegraph for this place. The schooners were both disabled in the fight, but Luperon did not venture to follow them when they withdrew. It is said that his sudden departure from Samana was owing to the fear that Baez might make another and more formidable attack. From the fact that the schooners was towed to Samana by an American steamer, with Gen. Hongripa, the Dominican War Minister, on board, and the further fact that the same steamer landed a quantity of arms and ammunition at Fort Cacao for Baez, Luperon and his officers were led to believe that the Americans were about to assist Baez in fighting the revolutionists, and they concluded that the most prudent course under the circumstances was to get away. On the way to Barrahano the Telegrafo captured five sloops, a schooner, and three open boats, all Dominican, which were brought hither as prizes and delivered to Cabral, as well as the arms and ammunition on board the steamer. The Telegrafo then left for Turks Island, from whence she was to proceed to St. Marc, but her route is uncertain, and where she will turn up remains to be seen. It is said that Luperon's presence here just now was not desired by Cabral and the other leaders of the revolution.

While he was at Samana Luperon organized a provisional Government, and addressed a circular dispatch to the agents in foreign countries of the revolutionary party, apprizing them of the fact. In the circular he instructs them to take pains to let it be distinctly understood abroad that the revolutionists have possession of the important Bay of Samana, henceforth separated from the power and control of Baez, and that consequently all treaties and contracts which may have been made, or may hereafter be made, relative to the cession or the sale of said Bay, will be regarded and treated as null and void and of no effect, the Dominican people protesting, as they will ever protest, against any act violating the integrity of the national territory.

The Samana question is producing a crop of trouble for President Baez, who, it is said, considers that the precipitate action of Col. Fabens at Washington, relative to annexation, has done the Dominican Government more harm than good. The revolutionists are gaining ground.

Baez is very anxious to have regular steam communication between New-York and Santo Domingo, and has himself written to a New-York mercantile firm, offering every facility and encouragement for the establishment of a line of steamers between the two places.

records.headline: The Herald estimates that in the Dominican republic one-tenth of the population
records.summary_en: The Herald estimates that in the Dominican republic one-tenth of the population is white, while the remainder represent every shade of color peculiar to a mixed race, and observes that as neither of these republics seems satisfied with the occupation which a war with the other affords, an insurrection by some rival claimant for civic and military rule is frequently going on besides. This is the purport of its latest advices from the town of St. Domingo, which represent the insurgents as at present besieging the town of Azua, while President Báez is hurrying up troops to the relief of the garrison. This President Báez, it remarks, has had more ups and downs in life than can be met with in the history of any politician living out of the happy family of Spanish speaking republics. St. Domingo or Hayti, for the island is known by both names, is the Hispaniola of Columbus, celebrated in American history; it is rich beyond estimation in mines of gold, silver and lead, but these mineral resources, although known to exist, are still in a great measure undeveloped; the interior of the island consists of a mountain range covered with magnificent tropical forests, and the plains that stretch from thence to the sea are of amazing fertility. The extract ends as it asks what this island might become if under a firm government.
records.summary_es: El Herald estima que en la República Dominicana una décima parte de la población es blanca, mientras el resto representa todos los matices de color propios de una raza mezclada, y observa que, como ninguna de estas repúblicas parece satisfecha con la ocupación que les brinda una guerra con la otra, con frecuencia hay además una insurrección de algún pretendiente rival al mando civil y militar. Tal es el sentido de sus últimas noticias desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo, que representan a los insurgentes sitiando actualmente la ciudad de Azua, mientras el presidente Báez apresura tropas en auxilio de la guarnición. Este presidente Báez, comenta, ha tenido más altibajos en la vida que los que pueden hallarse en la historia de cualquier político vivo fuera de la feliz familia de las repúblicas de habla española. Santo Domingo o Haití, pues la isla es conocida por ambos nombres, es la Hispaniola de Colón, célebre en la historia americana; es rica más allá de toda estimación en minas de oro, plata y plomo, pero estos recursos minerales, aunque se sabe que existen, están aún en gran medida sin explotar; el interior de la isla consiste en una cordillera cubierta de magníficos bosques tropicales, y las llanuras que se extienden desde allí hasta el mar son de una fertilidad asombrosa. El extracto termina cuando pregunta qué podría llegar a ser esta isla bajo un gobierno firme.

records.headline: The Herald's correspondent writes that his preceding despatch
records.summary_en: The Herald's correspondent writes that his preceding despatch gives details of the brilliant little engagement between the Dominican war schooners Capotillo and Alta Gracia and the pirate Telégrafo, and the defeat of the latter. At the same time he has been able, through actual observation and from various sources, to obtain much information respecting this magnificent bay. The pirate, lying far in the bay, succeeded in reaching that part stretching from the headlands at the entrance to the Cayo Levantado; this portion constitutes the main bay, and in event of the United States becoming the fortunate possessor of this powerful and convenient naval station, would form the anchorage of the fleet, and the islands and the adjoining shores the sites of the government fortifications, docks, warehouses, magazines, workshops and other necessary buildings and improvements. Standing in a northwesterly direction from Cape Engaño, the most eastern point of the island of St. Domingo, and passing Cape Raphael, distance about fifty miles, he arrived off the entrance to the Bay of Samaná. The coast is bold, and in many places rises perpendicularly out of the sea; the approach is well defined by high headlands on the coast and mountain ranges, prolific with vegetation, in the interior. On the north side the conical crest of Azúcar de Pilón, or Sugar Loaf Mountain, nearly 2,000 feet in height, and La Montaña del Diablo, with an altitude of 1,500 feet, form excellent landmarks to the approaching navigator.
records.summary_es: El corresponsal del Herald escribe que su despacho precedente da detalles del brillante pequeño combate entre las goletas de guerra dominicanas Capotillo y Alta Gracia y el pirata Telégrafo, y de la derrota de este último. Al mismo tiempo ha podido obtener, por observación directa y de diversas fuentes, mucha información sobre esta magnífica bahía. El pirata, echado muy adentro de la bahía, logró llegar a la parte que se extiende desde los promontorios de la entrada hasta el Cayo Levantado; esta porción constituye la bahía principal y, en caso de que los Estados Unidos llegaran a ser los afortunados poseedores de esta poderosa y conveniente estación naval, formaría el fondeadero de la flota, y las islas y las costas adyacentes, los sitios de las fortificaciones, muelles, almacenes, polvorines, talleres y demás construcciones y mejoras necesarias del gobierno. Poniéndose en dirección noroeste desde el Cabo Engaño, el punto más oriental de la isla de Santo Domingo, y pasando el Cabo Rafael, a una distancia de unas cincuenta millas, llegó frente a la entrada de la bahía de Samaná. La costa es escarpada y en muchos lugares se alza perpendicularmente del mar; la aproximación está bien definida por altos promontorios en la costa y cordilleras, prolíficas en vegetación, en el interior. Del lado norte, la cresta cónica del Azúcar de Pilón, o Monte Pan de Azúcar, de cerca de 2.000 pies de altura, y La Montaña del Diablo, con una altitud de 1.500 pies, forman excelentes puntos de referencia para el navegante que se aproxima.

records.headline: Continuing his description of Samaná, the Herald's correspondent
records.summary_en: Continuing his description of Samaná, the Herald's correspondent describes the bay and peninsula as an easily accessible and commodious station on the island of St. Domingo, certainly the central point at which all the advantages of a position in the tropical regions are to be realized. Its contiguity to the United States and other points of significance may be judged by the following table of distances: from Samaná to New York 1,600 miles; from Samaná to Porto Rico, western end, 80; from Samaná to Turks Island 165; from Samaná to Puerto Plata, St. Domingo, 110; from Samaná to island of Saona 100; from Samaná to St. Domingo city the figure is not legible in the passage; from Samaná to the Spanish Main 600; from Samaná to Aspinwall 1,000; from Samaná to Key West, Florida, 800; and from the northwest end of St. Domingo island to Cuba 60. It will be seen that steamers stationed in the bay would have convenient access to all the surrounding islands and coasts, and for purposes of trade or as a coaling station the position is admirable. The coal mines of Samaná are as yet undeveloped, and therefore nothing can be said of their probable utility, though with such flattering indications it is encouraging that this valuable material will be found in quantity and quality to answer every purpose. The correspondent has already alluded to the unexampled fertility of the adjacent country, its excellent building material of limestone and sandstone, its valuable and inexhaustible forests of wood for cabinet and domestic uses and shipbuilding, its streams of pure water, its vegetable productions and its animal life.

records.headline: A special report from St. Domingo describes
records.summary_en: A special report from St. Domingo describes Samana Bay in detail, calling it a powerful and convenient naval station if the United States becomes its possessor. It traces the bay's entrance, headlands, landmarks such as Sugar Loaf Mountain, its channels and reefs, and its inner anchorage where a fleet, fortifications, docks and warehouses could be placed.
records.summary_es: Un informe especial desde Santo Domingo describe en detalle la Bahía de Samaná, llamándola una estación naval poderosa y conveniente si los Estados Unidos llegan a poseerla. Traza la entrada de la bahía, sus cabos, puntos de referencia como la montaña Pan de Azúcar, sus canales y arrecifes, y su fondeadero interior, donde podrían colocarse una flota, fortificaciones, muelles y almacenes.
records.passage: sheet of water is well encircled by land and perfectly protected. Between Cape Samana on the north and Cape Raphael on the south the mouth measures twenty-one miles north, west three-fourths north, reckoned from Cape Raphael. From this line, including the inner harbor, as we may term it, the bay extends thirty miles to the mouth of the Yuna river. This stream is one of the largest on the island of St. Domingo and enters the bay at the extreme western shore. The breadth of the bay about midway its depth from the towns of Samana on its northern to Savannah la Mar on its southern shore is eight miles. Ten miles west of Cape Raphael, near Punta Jicaco, begins a reef which stretches northwestward to a number of islets or rocks, called Cayo Pascual, Levantado and Carenero, better known as the Samana Cays. This reef protects the basin of the bay against the heavy seas which otherwise a gale from the north and east would send into it. The passage for the entrance and exit of vessels is thus contracted to one [illegible] between Punta Cacao and Cayo Pascual. In the middle of this channel is a small reef, marked on the charts and called Jean Bart, having three and three-fourths fathoms, or twenty-four feet, of water. This could be indicated by a buoy. At other points not less than six fathoms, or thirty-six feet, of water is found, while a channel exists, well defined on the charts, showing nowhere less than eight fathoms, or forty-eight feet. records.headline: This special report, datelined St. Domingo
records.summary_en: This special report, datelined St. Domingo, July 12, 1869, presents Samana Bay as an American Gibraltar of the Antilles and describes its history, geography and importance to the United States. It recounts a fight in the bay between the Dominican war schooners Capotilla and Alta Gracia and the craft Telegrafo, and then surveys the bay's entrance, headlands, channels and islands, and the Yuna river, which enters the bay at its western end and is one of the largest rivers on the island.
records.summary_es: Este reportaje especial, fechado en Santo Domingo el 12 de julio de 1869, presenta la bahía de Samaná como un Gibraltar americano de las Antillas y describe su historia, su geografía y su importancia para los Estados Unidos. Relata un combate en la bahía entre las goletas de guerra dominicanas Capotilla y Alta Gracia y la embarcación Telégrafo, y luego describe la entrada de la bahía, sus cabos, canales e islas, y el río Yuna, que desemboca en la bahía en su extremo occidental y es uno de los ríos más grandes de la isla.
records.passage: strong. Boats formerly ascended the river some miles. The stream is navigable inside the bars for boats drawing four to five feet of water as far as the junction of the Yuna. The Yuna, with a large population on its banks, would prove a valuable tributary of supplies by native craft to a population on the shores of Samana. The stream, with its branches, courses [illegible] the most fertile valleys in the world, and also [illegible] the mineral districts of Maimon and the pine forests of the Cibao. In 1807 the trade of the greater portion of the valley, which stretches from the Bay of Samana to Cotuy on the Yuna and Conception on the [illegible], averaging eight miles in width, was carried on by native canoes of about two tons burden. A railroad is in contemplation from the head of the bay to the towns of Conception and Santiago, which will go far to open the country. Towards the southward from the Yuna are the anchorages of Barranca Chica and Barranca Grande, both anchorages not now used. The Naranjo river here enters the Bay of Samana, passing under a hill of calcareous rock, through which it has forced an outlet. The central chain of mountains traversing the peninsula of Samana from west to east in its geographical formation consists principally of mountain limestone, schistose rocks, with veins of calcareous spar and sandstone. Quartz occurs frequently, and at the eastern end of the peninsula there is found an abundance of mica slates. A large quantity of fossil shells in great variety are met with.

records.headline: A special report dated July 12, 1869 calls Samana Bay the American Gibraltar of the Antilles and describes it in detail:
records.summary_en: A special report dated July 12, 1869 calls Samana Bay the American Gibraltar of the Antilles and describes it in detail: a mouth twenty-one miles wide between Cape Samana and Cape Raphael, a reach of thirty miles to the mouth of the Yuna River, and sheltering cays and reefs. It also recounts the defeat of Luperon's vessel Telegrafo by the Dominican war schooners Capotillo and Alta Gracia, and presents the bay as the anchorage and fortified naval station the United States would gain by possessing it.
records.summary_es: Un reportaje especial fechado el 12 de julio de 1869 llama a la bahía de Samana el Gibraltar americano de las Antillas y la describe en detalle: una boca de veintiún millas de ancho entre el cabo Samana y el cabo Raphael, una extensión de treinta millas hasta la desembocadura del río Yuna, y cayos y arrecifes que la protegen. También relata la derrota del buque Telegrafo de Luperon por las goletas de guerra dominicanas Capotillo y Alta Gracia, y presenta la bahía como el fondeadero y la estación naval fortificada que los Estados Unidos ganarían al poseerla.
records.passage: The information I have derived from Mr. [Fennell?], commence at a point called Los [illegible], about ten miles to the westward of the town of Santa Barbara, and crops out at intervals as far as Las [illegible], at the head of the bay, and it is thought extends [illegible] the mountains separating La Vega Real from the sea. The soil of the peninsula of Samana, like all other portions of the island of St. Domingo, is highly productive. Its principal woods are extensive forests of mahogany, espinello, caya, carina and other cabinet woods; roble and [illegible] wood, suitable for shipbuilding; capa, valuable for bottoms of vessels, and lignumvitae. The soil and climate have also produced indigo, cacao, cotton and coffee. The present inhabitants are satisfied with cultivating yams, Indian corn and fruits, chiefly bananas, plantains, pineapples, oranges, mangoes, alligator pears and cocoanuts, while from the jungle and the forest they gather, as the cravings of taste may dictate, other fruits in endless variety and inexhaustible abundance. The bay of Samana abounds with fish, which is an important article of diet with the people on its shores. In spring whales visit the adjacent sea. Near the mouth of the Yuna river oysters are found in large quantities. Aquatic birds visit the bay in great numbers, chiefly flamingoes, spoonbills, scarlet ibis, snipe and many other varieties. records.headline: The Herald's correspondent reports the commerce of the bay of Samaná
records.summary_en: The Herald's correspondent reports the commerce of the bay of Samaná with Turk's Island, shipping provisions to that barren spot, and receiving in return quantities of salt. The small town of Santa Barbara is situated on the slopes bordering a small bight on the north side of the bay, about six miles northwest of Cayo Levantado; it was founded in 1750 by Don Francisco Rubio y Peñaranda, then Governor of St. Domingo. On the southern shore, near the mouth of the Yuna, is the village of Savanna La Mar, containing a few hundred inhabitants. The bay of Samaná was one of the earliest attractions in the physical features of ancient Hispaniola, and its convenience of geographical position from a strategic point of view, and the accommodations afforded by its well sheltered and placid waters, have associated it with all the warlike operations of the Antilles. After his discovery of the country, which he named Hispaniola, now St. Domingo, Columbus set out on his return to old Spain; in January 1493 he passed a high headland, which he named Cabo del Enamorado, the Lover's Cape, now Cape Cabron; further eastward he saw another headland, now Cape Samaná, which formed the most eastern point of the peninsula of the same name, where the extract ends.
records.summary_es: El corresponsal del Herald informa de que el comercio de la bahía de Samaná es con la isla Turca, embarcando provisiones hacia ese lugar estéril y recibiendo a cambio cantidades de sal. El pequeño pueblo de Santa Bárbara está situado en las laderas que bordean una pequeña ensenada del lado norte de la bahía, a unas seis millas al noroeste del Cayo Levantado. Fue fundado en 1750 por don Francisco Rubio y Peñaranda, a la sazón gobernador de Santo Domingo. En la costa sur, cerca de la desembocadura del Yuna, está el pueblo de Sabana de la Mar, que contiene unos pocos cientos de habitantes. La bahía de Samaná fue uno de los primeros atractivos en los rasgos físicos de la antigua Hispaniola, y su conveniente posición geográfica desde el punto de vista estratégico, y las facilidades que ofrecen sus aguas bien abrigadas y plácidas, la han asociado con todas las operaciones bélicas de las Antillas. Tras su descubrimiento del país, al que llamó Hispaniola, hoy Santo Domingo, Colón emprendió su regreso a la vieja España; en enero de 1493 pasó un alto promontorio, al que llamó Cabo del Enamorado, ahora Cabo Cabrón; más hacia el este vio otro promontorio, hoy Cabo Samaná, que formaba el punto más oriental de la península del mismo nombre, donde termina el extracto.

records.headline: A Herald survey of the island's intended road and railway lines
records.summary_en: A Herald survey of the island's intended road and railway lines recalls that, on the first inception of the idea, a correspondent of the paper traversed one of the great lines in question, from St. Domingo westward to the bay of Ocoa, and crossed the entire island from sea to sea to determine where the truth lay between the extremely contradictory reports sent to the Northern press. An English company, the survey reports, has secured a charter for a line of railway from Monte Cristi up through the length of the great tobacco region, by La Vega and Santiago, to the foot of the first spurs of the Abao, the "Gold Mountains" of Indian name — about 150 miles, or half the entire distance to the city of St. Domingo on the south coast; the second 150 miles cross some rugged mountain spurs, but offer no such difficulties as were conquered on more than one Pennsylvania railroad. This first great trunk line of 300 miles crosses the island from the best port on the northwest to St. Domingo, and from Santiago it is to send down lines to Puerto Plata, a short but terrible road of sixty miles, and to Samaná, where the window breaks off.

records.full_text:
ST. DOMINGO.

Across the Island—La Vega Real—Beautiful Savannas—Arrival at Cotuy—Crossing the Isabella—Arrival at the Republican Capital—Natural Resources of the Island.

ST. DOMINGO, W. I., July 8, 1869.
A journey from Santiago de los Caballeros to this city, completing the trip across the island of St. Domingo, is one of those experiences which might be considered agreeable in retrospect, but would not, under ordinary circumstances, bear repetition with any degree of complacency in the same person.

There is no doubt that the geologist and mineralogist would find in St. Domingo a fine field of study and exploration; but they should be men of means or represent some legitimate society of science interested in developing the resources of a country for the benefit it may be to mankind and the promotion of science, not companies formed for speculation and continually grumbling, while their employés on various pretences are clipped of their hard earned pittance. But, whatever may be said of her undeveloped mineral resources, it is certain the greatest and surest wealth of St. Domingo is in her fertile soil, her valuable forests, her beautiful rivers. The various productions find upon her mountain sides and rolling savannas a congenial soil, properly cultivated and with population to increase the area subject to the industry of man, would prove more valuable than all the mines of the Jaina and the Cibao. What St. Domingo needs is a quiet government, emigration and the implements of agriculture, and the time will be short when her fertile valleys and luxuriant mountains will teem with a numerous people enjoying all the comforts, luxuries and works of public enterprise which affluence can bestow.

records.headline: Continuing his account of St. Domingo, a Herald correspondent
records.summary_en: Continuing his account of St. Domingo, a Herald correspondent lists the island's strong places as the paper prints them: the fort of San Luis at Santiago de los Caballeros, the castle of San Felipe at Puerto Plata, the fort of San Francisco at Monte Cristi, the fort of Santa Barbara at Samaná and another fort at the same place, whose name is not legible in the passage; the custom houses at St. Domingo and its dependencies and at Samaná; the ports of St. Domingo, Azua, Samaná and Puerto Plata, licensed for commerce with foreigners; and numerous other ports and bays that could be used, among them Monte Cristi, Barahona, Las Calderas, La Romana and Manzanillo. The concessions granted by the government, he continues, are for a geological survey of the island; a steam line between New York and New Orleans and the ports of the island; the right to ship guano from Alta Vela; the right to build a railroad from Monte Cristi to Santiago, or from Santiago to the Yuna river, with a grant of land; the right to build a wagon road from Santiago to the coast; and a steamship line from the island to New York. The value of St. Domingo to the United States would unquestionably be incalculable, he writes, but the country, however willing it may be to become part of the North American confederation, is certainly at present in no condition to assume the important duties which attach to such relations, its institutions being entirely unknown to the people; it would therefore first be a wise policy to give them time to become familiar with them, where the window ends.

records.headline: Writing from Porto Plata on September 6, 1869, the correspondent recalls that Columbus founded Isabella, the first European town
records.summary_en: Writing from Porto Plata on September 6, 1869, the correspondent recalls that Columbus founded Isabella, the first European town in the New World, near here, and that only ruins remain where it stood. He describes a country whose trade has been almost annihilated, with Porto Plata and St. Domingo City as its principal outlets and small trade also at Azua and Samana, and reports an unusually large tobacco crop, estimated at 100,000 quintals for export, shipped almost exclusively to Hamburg, with talk of a railroad from Santiago to carry it to the sea.
records.summary_es: Escribiendo desde Puerto Plata el 6 de septiembre de 1869, el corresponsal recuerda que Colón fundó cerca de aquí La Isabela, la primera ciudad europea del Nuevo Mundo, y que solo quedan ruinas donde estuvo. Describe un país cuyo comercio ha sido casi aniquilado, con Puerto Plata y la ciudad de Santo Domingo como sus principales salidas y un pequeño comercio también en Azua y Samaná, e informa de una cosecha de tabaco inusualmente grande, estimada en 100.000 quintales para la exportación, embarcada casi exclusivamente a Hamburgo, mientras se habla de un ferrocarril desde Santiago para llevarla al mar.
records.passage: of a primitive and feeble effort at agriculture satisfy the small demands for money. PORTO PLATA AND THE OPEN PORTS. The result of this condition of things is almost an entire annihilation of trade. This port and St. Domingo City are the only two principal outlets to the island. A very small trade is accomplished also at the open ports of Azua and Samana. Porto Plata is now the only port on the northern side of the island, and the proceeds of the Custom House here are the main source of revenue to the government. The town itself is small and very uninviting; it has a small harbor well protected by reefs; a vessel anchors some distance from the shore: all cargo is put on board the vessels or taken off by lighters, which cannot themselves approach the shore within fifty yards, owing to the shallowness of the water on the beach which sweeps in front of the town. The shippers have a very novel mode of conveying cargo from shore to lighters and vice versa. This is done by means of carts drawn into the water a sufficient depth by bullocks which are manoeuvred by ropes passing through the cartilage of the nose. All this trouble, inconvenience and expense could be saved by a pier run out to a sufficient depth of water to allow vessels to lie alongside. Although Porto Plata is one of the early towns of the Island the Spaniards, upon being driven out of the country, completely destroyed it. records.headline: In a statistical account of the Dominican republic's commerce
records.summary_en: In a statistical account of the Dominican republic's commerce that begins in mid-item, the Herald reports that American vessels freighted on the island and five British vessels also loaded; the value of the importation of provisions, flour and petroleum from the United States under the British flag was $40,000, and during the year 162 vessels, including those carrying the Dominican flag, arrived at St. Domingo, with a total of 12,203 tons. Its table for the year ending June 30 — the year itself is not legible in the passage — gives Puerto Plata exports of $696,463 against imports of $354,808, and totals of $788,838 in exports with an excess of exports of $53,471; several of the table's other figures are not legible in the passage and are not stated here. In the same year, the item adds, seven American vessels arrived in port with cargoes valued at $22,600; and during the quarter ending March 31, 1869, two American vessels arrived from St. Thomas in ballast and four British vessels from Boston, with cargoes valued at $20,000, the exports by the two American vessels being valued at $19,364 and by three British vessels at $14,855. The production of the island by the hand of man is small, the Herald continues, and the foreign trade is also limited, owing to the smallness of the population, which numbers not more than 200,000 souls; the territory under the jurisdiction of the Dominican republic embraces about two-thirds of the island of St. Domingo, or nearly 20,000 square miles.

Su tabla para el año terminado el 30 de junio — el año mismo no es legible en el pasaje — da para Puerto Plata exportaciones de $696.463 frente a importaciones de $354.808, y totales de $788.838 en exportaciones con un excedente de exportaciones de $53.471; varias de las demás cifras de la tabla no son legibles en el pasaje y no se consignan aquí. En el mismo año, añade la nota, llegaron a puerto siete buques estadounidenses con cargamentos valorados en $22.600; y durante el trimestre terminado el 31 de marzo de 1869, llegaron dos buques estadounidenses desde Santo Tomás en lastre y cuatro buques británicos desde Boston, con cargamentos valorados en $20.000, valorándose las exportaciones de los dos buques estadounidenses en $19.364 y las de tres buques británicos en $14.855. La producción de la isla por mano del hombre es pequeña, continúa el Herald, y el comercio exterior también es limitado, debido a la escasa población, que no pasa de 200.000 almas; el territorio bajo la jurisdicción de la República Dominicana abarca unas dos terceras partes de la isla de Santo Domingo, o cerca de 20.000 millas cuadradas.

records.headline: A letter from St. Domingo dated
records.summary_en: A letter from St. Domingo dated October 8, 1869 says the summary of Dominican feeling on annexation is 'ready and eager,' but that a painful fear lingers that Congress might refuse to receive the country. If Dominicans offered their country and were turned away, the writer warns, Baez and his party would be swept from power, so the invitation, he argues, must come from the United States.
records.summary_es: Una carta de Santo Domingo fechada el 8 de octubre de 1869 dice que el sentimiento dominicano sobre la anexión se resume en estar 'listos y deseosos', pero que persiste el temor doloroso de que el Congreso pudiera negarse a recibir al país. Si los dominicanos ofrecieran su país y fueran rechazados, advierte el autor, Báez y su partido serían barridos del poder, por lo que la invitación, sostiene, debe venir de los Estados Unidos.

records.headline: The dispatch gives the case of Mr. Davis
records.summary_en: The dispatch gives the case of Mr. Davis Hatch, a United States citizen who was living at Barahona as agent of a New York company interested in working salt mines. When government troops evacuated the port at the end of August, Hatch was taken with them to Azua and arrested, then brought to the capital and held in close confinement, then taken back to Azua, tried by court martial and sentenced to be shot. A messenger was at once sent back to Azua with a pardon for Hatch, and the dispatch says the anxiety of five days of suspense had a severe effect on his mind and health.
records.summary_es: El despacho expone el caso del señor Davis Hatch, ciudadano de los Estados Unidos que vivía en Barahona como agente de una compañía de Nueva York interesada en explotar minas de sal. Cuando las tropas del gobierno evacuaron el puerto a finales de agosto, Hatch fue llevado con ellos a Azua y arrestado, luego trasladado a la capital y mantenido en estricto confinamiento, y después devuelto a Azua, juzgado por un consejo de guerra y condenado a ser fusilado. De inmediato se envió un mensajero de regreso a Azua con un indulto para Hatch, y el despacho dice que la angustia de cinco días de suspense tuvo un efecto grave en su mente y su salud.

records.headline: In an editorial fragment that begins in mid-argument, the Herald argues
records.summary_en: In an editorial fragment that begins in mid-argument, the Herald argues for the bay of Manzanillo as the site for an American naval station: Monte Cristi and the noble bay of Manzanillo are on the dividing line, it argues, and the presence of a United States steamer would protect both governments in the act of transition; President Grant has it in his power to accept the use of a naval station at Manzanillo, which is peculiarly safe from hurricanes, is about as central as Samaná, and is the key to the great agricultural and mining regions of the east and the mountains of Cibao. The Stars of the Union, the paper continues, would not float a month over a naval station at Manzanillo before the chief provinces of the Dominican republic would openly declare for annexation, and the nearest half of the republic of Hayti would lose no time in profiting by the example; while these sections were passing a brief period of preparation under a provisional government as a Territory of the United States, the window ends. The fragment's Haytian half concerns the friends of Salnave, president of that division, against the partisans of Pimentel, who assert that their chief would put the question to a vote any day a United States agent will call to salute his flag and recognize his government.

Las estrellas de la Unión, continúa el periódico, no flotarían un mes sobre una estación naval en Manzanillo sin que las provincias principales de la República Dominicana se declararan abiertamente por la anexión, y la mitad más cercana de la república de Haití no perdería tiempo en aprovechar el ejemplo; mientras estas secciones pasaban un breve período de preparación bajo un gobierno provisional como Territorio de los Estados Unidos, termina la ventana. records.headline: In a historical essay on the island's two republics, the Herald explains
records.summary_en: In a historical essay on the island's two republics, the Herald explains that the republic of Hayti, which comprises the western third of the island, that being the area of the ancient French colony, displaced the name of St. Domingo for the more distinctive and historic appellation of Hayti, by which the natives introduced their island to Columbus. This uniformity of name between the island as a whole and the separate government of the western portion, the essay observes, often leads careless inquirers into confounding the Dominican republic with that of Hayti, though there is a wide difference between them: the Dominicans are Spanish in language, customs and habits of thought, though more democratic in sentiment and more tolerant in religion than the corresponding social levels usually found in the mother country. The Dominican republic, it adds, was the first American state which made the absolute equality of all races before the law a fundamental principle of its constitution, where the window ends. Of Hayti itself the essay recounts that its French section was the scene of the first successful struggle of the black race for political equality with the whites, and that the newly emancipated slaves discarded the colonial name of St. Domingo and restored the one known to the red race.
records.summary_es: En un ensayo histórico sobre las dos repúblicas de la isla, el Herald explica que la república de Haití, que comprende el tercio occidental de la isla, siendo esa el área de la antigua colonia francesa, desplazó el nombre de Santo Domingo por el apelativo más distintivo e histórico de Haití, con el que los nativos presentaron su isla a Colón. Esta uniformidad de nombre entre la isla en su conjunto y el gobierno separado de la porción occidental, observa el ensayo, lleva a menudo a los indagadores descuidados a confundir la República Dominicana con la de Haití, aunque hay una amplia diferencia entre ellas: los dominicanos son españoles en lengua, costumbres y hábitos de pensamiento, aunque más democráticos en sentimiento y más tolerantes en religión que los niveles sociales correspondientes que suelen hallarse en la madre patria. La República Dominicana, añade, fue el primer estado americano que hizo de la igualdad absoluta de todas las razas ante la ley un principio fundamental de su constitución, donde termina la ventana. De Haití mismo el ensayo relata que su sección francesa fue el escenario de la primera lucha exitosa de la raza negra por la igualdad política con los blancos, y que los esclavos recién emancipados desecharon el nombre colonial de Santo Domingo y restauraron el conocido por la raza indígena.

records.headline: Traordinary preparations now going on in the 'navy yards arc not
records.summary_en: According to the *Nashville Union and American*, extraordinary preparations in navy yards were reported to be for guarding the annexation of the Dominican Republic to the United States rather than for war with Spain over Cuba. The article stated that General Babcock, a confidential officer on Grant's staff, had settled the annexation conditions with San Domingo authorities, and the treaty—modeled after the Texas annexation—would be submitted to the Senate. Additionally, warships were sent to West Indies ports at President Baez's request to be present when the U.S. flag was hoisted, with opposition anticipated only from a revolutionary faction aided by Cabral.
records.summary_es: Según el *Nashville Union and American*, los extraordinarios aprestos en los astilleros navales respondían al propósito de asegurar la anexión de la República Dominicana a los Estados Unidos antes que a un conflicto armado con España a causa de Cuba. El artículo exponía que el general Babcock, edecán de confianza en el estado mayor de Grant, había acordado las cláusulas de anexión con las autoridades dominicanas, previéndose remitir al Senado el tratado —calcado del modelo de incorporación de Texas—. Se agregó asimismo que varios buques de guerra zarparon hacia las Antillas a requerimiento del presidente Báez para asistir al acto de izamiento del pabellón estadounidense, aguardándose resistencia tan solo de la facción rebelde auxiliada por Cabral.

records.full_text: THE New York Sun has discovered something out of which to manufacture a sensation. That paper says, editorially, in its issue of the 11th inst., that the extraordinary preparations now going on in the navy yards are not in expectation of war with Spain about Cuba, but simply to keep guard over the annexation of the Dominican Republic to the United States. The conditions of annexation have been fully settled between Gen. Babcock, confidential officer of Grant's staff, and the authorities of San Domingo. The treaty is similar to that for the annexation of Texas, and will be laid before the Senate when Congress opens. All members of the Dominican government and leading men among the people are anxious for annexation, and the approval of the Senate is confidently expected. The ships of war now going to the West Indies are sent at the request of President Baez and his advisers, so that there may be one or more in each port when the United States flag is hoisted. No trouble is expected from the people generally, and the only opposition would be from a revolutionary faction aided by Cabral. This may be something more than a mere sensation.

records.headline: A Washington letter in the Herald recounts the earlier course of the St. Domingo
records.summary_en: A Washington letter in the Herald recounts the earlier course of the St. Domingo negotiations, in which the annexation was on the eve of completion in 1865, having been wisely and prudently negotiated by Mr. J. Somers Smith, United States Commercial Agent at St. Domingo City; Mr. Frederick Seward was sent out in a United States war vessel with the necessary power and funds to arrange the preliminaries of the acquisition, but that gentleman made himself so absolutely offensive to Báez and his Cabinet that these gentlemen summarily declined to consider any of the propositions he had to lay before them. It is considered here, the letter continues, that the course being pursued in the negotiation is hardly that which should be adopted between two independent nations engaged in a matter of so great moment to both; it is thought that General Báez should send a commissioner to Washington to be a party to the negotiation here and to witness the ratification of the treaty — such gentlemen as the Minister of War, without doubt the most popular man on the island; the Minister of Justice, conversant with our language; and Gautier, Minister of Foreign Affairs, a gentleman of culture — where the window breaks off in the middle of the list. The St. Domingo question, the letter indicates, is now in a fair way of speedy and practical solution, both in the hands of the United States government and in the administration of Báez.
records.summary_es: Una carta de un corresponsal en Washington publicada en el Herald relata el curso anterior de las negociaciones de Santo Domingo: la anexión estuvo en vísperas de completarse en 1865, habiendo sido negociada sabia y prudentemente por el Sr. J. Somers Smith, agente comercial de los Estados Unidos en la ciudad de Santo Domingo; el Sr. Frederick Seward fue enviado en un buque de guerra estadounidense con los poderes y fondos necesarios para arreglar los preliminares de la adquisición, pero ese caballero se hizo tan absolutamente ofensivo para Báez y su gabinete que estos caballeros declinaron sumariamente considerar ninguna de las proposiciones que él tenía que presentarles. Se considera aquí, continúa la carta, que el curso que se sigue en la negociación apenas es el que debería adoptarse entre dos naciones independientes empeñadas en un asunto de tan gran momento para ambas; se piensa que el general Báez debería enviar un comisionado a Washington para ser parte de la negociación aquí y presenciar la ratificación del tratado — caballeros tales como el ministro de Guerra, sin duda el hombre más popular de la isla; el ministro de Justicia, conocedor de nuestro idioma; y Gautier, ministro de Relaciones Exteriores, un caballero de cultura — donde la ventana se interrumpe en mitad de la lista. La cuestión de Santo Domingo, indica la carta, está ahora en vías de una solución rápida y práctica, tanto en manos del gobierno de los Estados Unidos como en la administración de Báez.

records.headline: A descriptive item on the island in the Marshall County Republican reports
records.summary_en: A descriptive item on the island in the Marshall County Republican reports that the imports to the United States for 1868 were valued at 760,000 from Hayti and $33,000 from San Domingo, the principal articles being raw cotton, sugar, coffee, dye woods, gum arabic, hides and cocoa. San Domingo is divided into five provinces; there is an army of 20,000 troops of all arms, and a small navy; the language of the people is Spanish, and the religion Roman Catholic; the government is that of a president, with a Congress consisting of two branches. Hayti and Dominica were several times united, the item recounts, but were divided by revolution, and the country has been for twenty years in a state of chronic revolution, the Dominicans having long since concluded that there can be no peace until they are taken under the flag of the United States; for several years they have proposed to cede the Bay of Samana to the United States, and now offer the whole republic. The other part of the island, the Republic of Hayti, contains 10,000 square miles and a population of 600,000; in considering the question of the acquisition of Dominica, the item concludes, it is necessary to consider also the probable acquisition of Hayti, where the window ends.

Haití y Dominica estuvieron varias veces unidas, relata la nota, pero se dividieron por revolución, y el país ha estado durante veinte años en un estado de revolución crónica, habiendo concluido los dominicanos desde hace tiempo que no puede haber paz hasta ser tomados bajo la bandera de los Estados Unidos; durante varios años han propuesto ceder la bahía de Samaná a los Estados Unidos, y ahora ofrecen la república entera. records.headline: In an editorial on the annexation of St. Domingo, the Herald argues
records.summary_en: In an editorial on the annexation of St. Domingo, the Herald argues from the letter it published yesterday from its Washington correspondent that the St. Domingo question, both in the hands of the United States government and in the administration of Baez, at the head of affairs in the Dominican republic, is in a fair way towards a speedy and practical solution. The project of annexation, the editorial continues, has long been entertained by the two contending parties in that republic, and the small faction of Cabral revolutionists who oppose it would doubtless favor it, as they favored it when in power a few years ago, if they were now in power. The people generally are reported to be well disposed to the step: President Baez was assured during last summer that the inhabitants of Porto Plata, Santiago, Lavega and Cotuy are agreed on this point. Baez, of course, could not with propriety initiate this annexation scheme any more than he could consent to the leasing of the Bay of Samana or to the plan of a protectorate to be exercised by the United States government, unless that government, as well as his own people, were unquestionably willing and ready to accomplish it; and without entering into the details of the preliminary negotiations which have from time to time been informally conducted between the two independent governments, the editorial expresses the opinion that it is now highly probable — where the window breaks off in mid-sentence, the editorial continuing beyond it.

El proyecto de anexión, continúa el editorial, ha sido acariciado durante mucho tiempo por los dos partidos contendientes en esa república, y la pequeña facción de revolucionarios de Cabral que se le opone sin duda lo favorecería, como lo favoreció cuando estuvo en el poder hace unos años, si estuviera ahora en el poder. Se informa que el pueblo en general está bien dispuesto hacia la medida: el presidente Báez recibió seguridades el verano pasado de que los habitantes de Puerto Plata, Santiago, La Vega y Cotuy están de acuerdo en este punto. records.headline: In a later window of the same Herald editorial on annexation
records.summary_en: In a later window of the same Herald editorial on annexation, the paper argues that the abolition of slavery in the United States and the establishment of civil and political equality have removed certain objections which used to stand in the way of annexation, and there will be no difficulty on this score in governing Dominica and Hayti as territories until they shall have ripened into States. It will not be long, the editorial continues, before American capital, which has already turned its eye towards the incalculable, undeveloped resources of this beautiful and fertile island, and American enterprise, which has established Dominican banking, railway and steamship companies — in fact, actually laying the egg out of which annexation seems about to be hatched — and, in due time, emigration from the United States, from Europe and, perhaps, from China, will redeem the island of St. Domingo from revolutionary chaos and open multiplied markets to its increased productions. Moreover, the annexation of St. Domingo carries the consideration that Cuba is within but a few hours' sail of the waters in which a really formidable American fleet is now being gathered; whatever may be the upshot of the Cuban insurrectionary movement, the editorial concludes by asking how long it will be before all the West India islands shall form the encircling belt of the Gulf of Mexico as an inland lake of the United States — this is merely a question of time.
records.summary_es: En una ventana posterior del mismo editorial del Herald sobre la anexión, el periódico argumenta que la abolición de la esclavitud en los Estados Unidos y el establecimiento de la igualdad civil y política han eliminado ciertas objeciones que solían interponerse a la anexión, y no habrá dificultad en este punto para gobernar a Dominica y Haití como territorios hasta que hayan madurado como estados. No pasará mucho tiempo, continúa el editorial, antes de que el capital estadounidense, que ya ha vuelto su mirada hacia los incalculables y no explotados recursos de esta hermosa y fértil isla, y la empresa estadounidense, que ha establecido compañías dominicanas de banca, ferrocarriles y vapores — de hecho, poniendo realmente el huevo del que la anexión parece a punto de salir — y, a su debido tiempo, la emigración desde los Estados Unidos, desde Europa y, tal vez, desde China, rediman a la isla de Santo Domingo del caos revolucionario y abran mercados multiplicados a sus aumentadas producciones. Además, la anexión de Santo Domingo conlleva la consideración de que Cuba está a solo unas horas de navegación de las aguas en las que ahora se está reuniendo una flota estadounidense realmente formidable; cualquiera que sea el desenlace del movimiento insurreccional cubano, el editorial concluye preguntando cuánto pasará antes de que todas las islas de las Indias Occidentales formen el cinturón que rodea el golfo de México como un lago interior de los Estados Unidos: es meramente una cuestión de tiempo.

records.headline: In a narrative of the annexation negotiations that begins in mid-item
records.summary_en: In a narrative of the annexation negotiations that begins in mid-item, the Tribune relates that Mr. Seward was pleased at the prospect of having the great Bay of Samana for the United States, and supposed that its acquisition would be pregnant of good results; the people of Santo Domingo did not relish the project and were at one time on the point of driving Baez out of power, and he deemed it the more prudent course to suspend for a season all negotiations. But as soon as General Grant was introduced to power, Mr. O'Sullivan began to work again, and in a short time has encouraged President Baez to perfect a scheme for the annexation of the island. The people of San Domingo have, on divers occasions of late years, manifested, in a remarkable degree, their love of liberty and independence: they resisted the last invasion of Spain for two years, until, in fact, the Spanish Treasury became poorer by some twenty-four millions and 15,000 of the soldiers of the Peninsula had died of disease and in battle; the natives, it is said, fought like heroes, and, on one occasion, 5,000 Spanish troops were terribly harassed by about 50 Dominicans. The Government of Spain became so hard pressed for money that they were compelled to appeal to the liberality of the rich men of Havana, where the window ends.
records.summary_es: En un relato de las negociaciones de anexión que comienza a mitad de la nota, el Tribune relata que el Sr. Seward estaba complacido ante la perspectiva de tener la gran bahía de Samaná para los Estados Unidos, y suponía que su adquisición estaría preñada de buenos resultados; el pueblo de Santo Domingo no gustó del proyecto y estuvo en un momento a punto de expulsar a Báez del poder, y él juzgó más prudente suspender por una temporada todas las negociaciones. Pero tan pronto como el general Grant asumió el poder, el Sr. O'Sullivan comenzó a trabajar de nuevo, y en poco tiempo ha animado al presidente Báez a perfeccionar un esquema para la anexión de la isla. El pueblo de Santo Domingo ha, en diversas ocasiones de los últimos años, manifestado, en grado notable, su amor a la libertad y la independencia: resistieron la última invasión de España durante dos años, hasta que, de hecho, el tesoro español quedó más pobre por unos veinticuatro millones y 15.000 de los soldados de la Península habían muerto de enfermedad y en batalla; se dice que los nativos pelearon como héroes, y, en una ocasión, 5.000 tropas españolas fueron terriblemente acosadas por unos 50 dominicanos. El gobierno de España llegó a estar tan apremiado de dinero que se vieron obligados a apelar a la liberalidad de los hombres ricos de La Habana, donde termina la ventana.

records.headline: The Evening Telegraph reprints a Havana despatch: all the Dominican leaders
records.summary_en: The Evening Telegraph reprints a Havana despatch: all the Dominican leaders are anxious for annexation to the United States in consideration of a reasonable amount of money. Baez, Pimentel, and Cabral, however much they may disagree on other points, are united on this, and the only question is which shall get the money: Baez is the constitutional President of the republic, and it is stated that he is ready to open negotiations whenever the Congress of the United States shall make the necessary appropriations; his rivals, however, are equally well disposed, the partisans of Pimentel scattering among the people handbills favoring annexation with the United States, and Cabral hoping to be in power when the bargain is concluded, so that he may get the money. In Hayti, the despatch adds, the only opponents to selling out to the United States are parties under European influence, while Salnave and Saget, the rival Presidents, both are willing and anxious to dispose of their claims; the entire island, it is said, can be purchased for $2,000,000, where the window ends. The despatch is set against Spain's refusal to sell Cuba, which the paper says we really have a longing for, on any terms.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de La Habana reimpreso en el Evening Telegraph informa de que todos los líderes dominicanos están ansiosos por la anexión a los Estados Unidos a cambio de una cantidad razonable de dinero. Báez, Pimentel y Cabral, por mucho que discrepen en otros puntos, están unidos en esto, y la única cuestión es cuál ha de recibir el dinero: Báez es el presidente constitucional de la república, y se afirma que está listo para abrir negociaciones cuando el Congreso de los Estados Unidos haga las asignaciones necesarias; sus rivales, sin embargo, están igualmente bien dispuestos, con los partidarios de Pimentel repartiendo entre el pueblo hojas sueltas a favor de la anexión con los Estados Unidos, y Cabral esperando estar en el poder cuando se concluya el trato, para poder recibir él el dinero. En Haití, añade el despacho, los únicos opositores a venderse a los Estados Unidos son partidos bajo influencia europea, mientras que Salnave y Saget, los presidentes rivales, están ambos dispuestos y ansiosos por vender sus derechos; se dice que la isla entera puede comprarse por $2.000.000, donde termina la ventana. El despacho se contrapone a la negativa de España a vender Cuba, la cual, dice el periódico, deseamos realmente, en cualquier término.

records.headline: The Herald prints a letter received at Havana from St. Domingo
records.summary_en: The Herald prints a letter received at Havana from St. Domingo, dated the 10th, showing that all the Dominican leaders, including Baez, Pimental and Cabral, are pledged to the annexation of the island to the United States. President Baez is ready to open negotiations when assured that the Congress of the United States is ready to make the necessary appropriation to meet the requirements of the occasion; the people of St. Domingo are opposed to the dismemberment of the republic, and favor the annexation of the country in its entirety. The partisans of Pimental are scattering handbills throughout the island favoring the project of annexation, and the only opposition exhibited is that derived from European sources. The republic of Hayti is following suit as regards annexation, the letter adds, and Salnave and Saget are loud in its favor; it is said the entire island can be purchased by the United States for $2,000,000, the same figure other papers of the week printed for the same report.
records.summary_es: El Herald imprime una carta recibida en La Habana desde Santo Domingo, fechada el día 10, que muestra que todos los líderes dominicanos, incluidos Báez, Pimental y Cabral, están comprometidos con la anexión de la isla a los Estados Unidos. El presidente Báez está listo para abrir negociaciones cuando tenga la seguridad de que el Congreso de los Estados Unidos está listo para hacer la asignación necesaria para cubrir las exigencias de la ocasión; el pueblo de Santo Domingo se opone a la desmembración de la república, y favorece la anexión del país en su totalidad. Los partidarios de Pimental reparten hojas sueltas por toda la isla a favor del proyecto de anexión, y la única oposición manifestada es la derivada de fuentes europeas. La república de Haití sigue el ejemplo en cuanto a la anexión, añade la carta, y Salnave y Saget se pronuncian ruidosamente a su favor; se dice que la isla entera puede ser comprada por los Estados Unidos por $2.000.000, cifra que es la misma impresa para el mismo informe en otros periódicos de la semana.

We shall not in the least degree be surprised, the editorial continues, if before the expiration of six months the annexation of the magnificent island of St. Domingo, or Hayti, shall be an accomplished fact. The recent departure of General Babcock, accompanied by General Rufus Ingalls, on board the United States steamer Albany, from New York, bound for the island with instructions from President Grant regarding the course he shall pursue in the pending negotiations of our government with President Baez, of the Dominican republic, assures us of the energetic prosecution of the purpose; and within the same period we look first for the independence of Cuba, and secondly for an application from the republic, a la Texas, for admission into the Union, which will not be denied, where the window ends.

records.full_text:
ST. DOMINGO.

The steamer Tybee, Captain Delanoy, from St. Domingo the 16th and Porto Plata the 19th, arrived here yesterday. She brings letters and papers up to date of sailing. The compliments of the purser are acknowledged.

Political Affairs—The Position of President Baez—What Is Thought of Annexation—European Influence at Work.

ST. DOMINGO, Nov. 16, 1869.
There is a party here so deeply implicated in the interior complication of the Dominican republic and so well situated to convey false statements to the foreign press that it is nearly impossible for the simple truth to obtain a hearing. For example, it went from here, on "consular" authority and endorsement, that the important and central town of Santiago had declared against Baez and that this government was on the eve of downfall. Your correspondent happened to be in company with the very general who was named as the leader of this fictitious revolution, and at that very date he was on his way to this city with a committee of the leading men of La Vega, Santiago and Puerte Plata, who came to this city to congratulate President Baez on the advance of public industry "which had resulted from the perfect tranquillity which for two years has reigned throughout the country." "We do not count the Caco guerillas on the frontier as a serious disturbance of the public peace." General Luccano went on to say although the labors and the vigilance demanded for their repression has caused the government some inconvenience, as everywhere in the great body of our territory enterprise has taken root and the general products of the country largely increased.

Speaking of enterprises, the proposal for introducing 2,000 German emigrants in the coffee and mining regions is not yet acted upon, but it most probably will be, as it is believed that M. Landais, the French Consul, gives it his warm though secret support, and he is a strong man with the Baez Cabinet, and is also a man of liberal ideas. It is reported, or rather whispered cautiously inside the consular ring, that Mr. Martin Hood, the former British Consul here, is to be sent back "to cure the Dominicans of the annexation fever." He is and was of old very obnoxious to the whole Baez party, for various personal as well as political reasons, and some members of the Senate have advised the President in advance not to receive him officially.

Major K. H. Perry, the newly appointed United States Consul, arrived in the Tybee last week, and raises his flag to-day. He was warmly welcomed by Baez.

I have heretofore attempted to explain the curious triangular antagonism of Baez, Cabral and Pimentel, each of whom accuses the other of an "intrigue to dismember the republic by selling its most precious section"—the peninsula of Samaná—to the United States, and all of whom are, more or less, openly working and praying for annexation.

The proposition of the English Company for a free port at Manzanilla with all the public lands within ten leagues of it for colonization, is probably a movement to head off annexation. The proposal is to establish the Germans, "or other European immigrants" in parties of thirty families, in a continuous chain of settlements, giving to each man a three acre block in the village or a twenty acre farm in its vicinity. These villages, beginning at their fine seaport of Manzanilla and taking in some sites with fine water power for manufacturing purposes, would extend to the old gold mines of San Rafael, which the French and Spanish governments agreed should be closed about a century ago. The promoters of this colonization project forget that German immigrants to America are almost invariably intensely loyal to the land of their adoption and would be more likely to swell than to oppose the vote for annexation. They also forget when debating on the "unwieldy expansion" of the United States—a favorite European phrase—that the telegraph and railways have compacted our national limits into much firmer and more manageable bounds than the Union exhibited at the beginning of this century, before either Florida or the States of the lower Mississippi were added to the old thirteen. Baez himself put it rather neatly at the introduction of the new United States Consul, Major Perry, to the Ministers and consular corps, at the President's morning reception. "San Francisco is now very much nearer the government at Washington," he observed, "than Mobile or New Orleans was forty years past, and all these islands are within easier reach of the commerce (he did not say arms, but he thought it) of all its seaboard States than those of the Atlantic with those of the Gulf of Mexico or either of them with the States of the Pacific."

This remark shows that Baez has looked at the map and reflected upon the beauties of a free exchange of products.

The Tybee takes on 3,000 bales of tobacco in transit for Europe, that is if the horrible roads will allow of getting down to port in time.

The London Alta Vela Company have made their arrangements for taking out from 1,000 to 5,000 tons of guano per month. The works started by the Baltimore firm, which Spain turned adrift so unceremoniously, come in very nicely for the London company. It pays a royalty of five dollars per ton on all the guano exported, and the magnitude of its arrangements is the best proof of the value of the American discovery. There can be no mistake about it, for, as I wrote you at the time, Mr. Lawson, one of the present owners, made a careful exploration of the island, accompanied by a chemist and other guano savans, with laborers and all other appliances for a thorough examination. On this he offers a royalty of one pound per ton and takes the island.

It is hardly worth the space to say that for the last six weeks the Cacos have had an uncomfortable time on the Dominican frontier. Two of their officers—Curiel and Volla—have been captured, and their great Dominican leader, the brave but misguided General Cabral, narrowly escaped by leaving his horse and throwing himself down an almost impracticable ravine.

These border raids are amplified into undue importance by the St. Thomas and Jamaica press, out of spite for Baez's supposed intention to cede Samaná to the United States for a naval station, which, of course, is regarded as the entering wedge of annexation.

No American vessel in port except the steamer Tybee. Europe does all the business here.

records.summary_en: Under the heading "Dominica," the Chicago Tribune writes that the departure of General Babcock for San Domingo, with sealed instructions from the President, in response to the proposition of President Baez to submit the question of annexation to the people of the Dominican Republic, indicates a belief on the part of our administration that a thirty-eighth star is soon to be added to the National cluster. The Dominican Republic, comprising the eastern three-fifths of the island, has maintained during nearly its whole history a separate political existence, whether as colony or republic, owing to its original settlement by the Spanish, while the remainder of the island was French; its area is stated in the passage in a comparison — about half as large as the State of Indiana, and more than twice the size of Massachusetts — the square mileage itself not being legible. Its population numbers 140,000, of whom one-tenth are whites and the rest are of African descent and mixed; the country is chiefly valuable for magnificent mountain forests of cabinet woods, ebony, mahogany, and live-oak. Its constitution as a republic was modelled upon that of the United States; it abolished slavery on achieving independence, and has never made any political distinction on account of color. Secret negotiations for the cession of the island to the United States were made during Pierce's administration, with Santana, the predecessor of Baez; indeed, the dissatisfaction with Santana, fomented — where the window breaks off.

records.headline: In the Chicago Tribune's long descriptive feature, Port au Prince
records.summary_en: In the Chicago Tribune's long descriptive feature, Port au Prince, sometimes called Port Republican, stands at the hinge of two bays, and Baez's capital, the city of Santo Domingo, is on the south side. Yet, while Dominica is the more eligible and open country and far larger than its mountain rival, Hayti has as many people as New Jersey, while Dominica has no more than Rhode Island, the writer observing that the cause of this difference lies in the superior energy and fecundity of the French race, as the passage puts it. Under the heading "Dominica and its people," the feature relates that the eastern, superior, and yet weaker half of the island contains the historical relics: the first colony founded in the New World was Isabella, on its north coast, near the present town of Puerto Plata, founded by Columbus himself; his brother, Bartholomew Columbus, founded the city of Santo Domingo in 1494, as the passage dates it; Columbus' son Diego built the cathedral here. It rose into importance and riches long prior to the greater conquests of Spain; here Cortez was a notary before he dreamed of Mexico; the Spanish made the island the key to the whole of their possessions in the New World, and it entered upon a wonderful career of gold and silver mining, stock raising, sugar and coffee growing, and commerce. The original people, called the Caribs, were all killed off speedily, and this prosperity only ceased when Peru and greater conquests on the mainland were achieved, where the window ends.
records.summary_es: En un extenso reportaje descriptivo, el Chicago Tribune sitúa a Puerto Príncipe, a veces llamado Puerto Republicano, en la bisagra de las dos bahías de la isla, y la capital de Báez, la ciudad de Santo Domingo, en el lado sur. Sin embargo, mientras Dominica es el país más elegible y abierto y mucho más grande que su rival montañoso, Haití tiene tanta gente como Nueva Jersey, mientras que Dominica no tiene más que Rhode Island, observando el autor que la causa de esta diferencia radica en la energía superior y la fecundidad de la raza francesa, según lo expresa el pasaje. Bajo el encabezado «Dominica y su pueblo», el reportaje relata que la mitad oriental, superior y sin embargo más débil de la isla contiene las reliquias históricas: la primera colonia fundada en el Nuevo Mundo fue Isabella, en su costa norte, cerca de la actual ciudad de Puerto Plata, fundada por el propio Colón; su hermano, Bartolomé Colón, fundó la ciudad de Santo Domingo en 1494, según lo fecha el pasaje; Diego, hijo de Colón, construyó aquí la catedral. Surgió en importancia y riquezas mucho antes que las mayores conquistas de España; aquí Cortés fue notario antes de soñar con México; los españoles hicieron de la isla la llave de todas sus posesiones en el Nuevo Mundo, y entró en una maravillosa carrera de minería de oro y plata, cría de ganado, cultivo de azúcar y café, y comercio. El pueblo original, llamados los caribes, fueron todos extinguidos rápidamente, y esta prosperidad solo cesó cuando se lograron el Perú y mayores conquistas en el continente, donde termina la ventana.
