records.headline: The Chicago Tribune's descriptive feature continues: Puerto Plata
records.summary_en: The Chicago Tribune's descriptive feature continues: Puerto Plata is the chief place of resort for American vessels, for we do the majority of the trade both for Hayti and Dominica. The cattle of Dominica are celebrated; its mahogany and sandal wood are the best in the tropics; many American colored men have settled in this republic, and, but for the civil war, none would ever have quitted it. The bay of Samana, the feature continues, is the outlet of the Yuna River, and is fifty miles long and from fifteen to twenty miles wide; the ocean entrance to it is only a mile wide, and is commanded by an old fort, while high mountains enclose both shores. Twenty-five miles up the bay, upon an inlet to the north, is the town of Samana, the inlet very deep and almost land-locked; the bay has been compared both to the Bay of Naples and to the Chesapeake, to the former for its dazzling tropical and mountain scenery, to the latter for its innumerable wild fowl. This bay has been pronounced the key to the Gulf of Mexico; fine beds of coal surround it, and navigators say that the future route to Darien and Mexico will be by the Mona Passage, just outside of Samana. Samana town, the passage adds, is no town at all, a mere semi-detached peninsula with town vestiges upon it, and the site is swampy; Bonaparte planned a city near Samana, to be called Napoleon, and had the site surveyed. The window ends as the feature turns toward Hayti, mid-sentence: while the State of Dominica contains all the most ancient and hallowed relics of St. Domingo, Hayti —
records.summary_es: Continuando su reportaje descriptivo, el Chicago Tribune escribe que Puerto Plata es el principal lugar de frecuentación de los buques estadounidenses, pues hacemos la mayoría del comercio tanto para Haití como para Dominica. El ganado de Dominica es célebre; su caoba y su madera de sándalo son las mejores de los trópicos; muchos hombres estadounidenses de color se han establecido en esta república, y, de no ser por la guerra civil, ninguno la habría abandonado jamás. La bahía de Samaná, continúa el reportaje, es la desembocadura del río Yuna, y tiene cincuenta millas de largo y de quince a veinte millas de ancho; la entrada oceánica a ella tiene solo una milla de ancho, y está dominada por un viejo fuerte, mientras que altas montañas encierran ambas orillas. A veinticinco millas bahía arriba, sobre una ensenada al norte, está el pueblo de Samaná, con la ensenada muy profunda y casi cerrada por tierra; la bahía ha sido comparada tanto con la bahía de Nápoles como con la de Chesapeake, con la primera por su deslumbrante paisaje tropical y montañoso, y con la segunda por sus innumerables aves silvestres. Esta bahía ha sido pronunciada la llave del golfo de México; finas capas de carbón la rodean, y los navegantes dicen que la ruta futura a Darién y México será por el paso de la Mona, justo fuera de Samaná. El pueblo de Samaná, añade el pasaje, no es pueblo en absoluto, una mera península semidesprendida con vestigios de pueblo sobre ella, y el sitio es pantanoso; Bonaparte planeó una ciudad cerca de Samaná, que se llamaría Napoleón, y mandó reconocer el sitio. La ventana termina cuando el reportaje se vuelve hacia Haití, a mitad de frase: mientras el Estado de Dominica contiene todas las reliquias más antiguas y veneradas de Santo Domingo, Haití —

records.headline: An unnamed speaker tells the Chicago Tribune, in its final window
records.summary_en: An unnamed speaker tells the Chicago Tribune, in its final window, that "we have been besieged from the Spanish end of the island these four or five years, to annex Domingo, bodily, and twice or thrice during the same period we have been asked to extend our protectorate over Hayti." Baez has offered to use the whole influence of his party to make the United States proprietors of Dominica, accepting it as a territory of the United States, to be, in course of time, a candidate for admission into the Union as a State, and for no other price than the assumption of its small debt; this offer is open to us at present. With a foothold established there, the Haytian end of the island would be soon anxious for annexation, and Salnave would be only too glad to be the instrument of consigning Hayti to a place among the United States. Asked whether there is any party in either end of St. Domingo violently opposed to annexation, the speaker answers: none; the Jacmel party of Hayti have been, at times, incensed with us for permitting our Consuls and Agents to take sides with Salnave, and we have reason to believe that the enemies of Baez are the enemies of the United States; but everybody in St. Domingo who owns a foot of land wants us to come. The offer, the speaker adds, is not entirely from the natives: there are many Americans, with large interests, in both republics — merchants, planters, and lumber-sawyers — whose property would appreciate immensely if the United States shielded the land, where the window ends.

records.headline: In a historical sketch of the Dominican leaders, the Herald relates
records.summary_en: In a historical sketch of the Dominican leaders, the Herald relates that Pimentel, Provisional President in the war of deliverance, deputed Don Pablo Pujol to Washington to proffer a naval station at Samaná, and that Mr. Seward would not receive Pujol, nor recognize the restored Dominican republic even as a belligerent. Cabral, who had shared the struggle with Pimentel, is the sketch's Putnam of Dominican history, as Báez is its Talleyrand; the window traces his breach with Pimentel, his entry into St. Domingo city with the title of Protector when the Spaniards retired to their ships, his resignation in favor of Báez in 1866 and his later succession to the presidency, and breaks off in mid-sentence as it turns to the Samaná offer he was induced to accept at a price.
records.summary_es: En un bosquejo histórico de los líderes dominicanos, el Herald relata que Pimentel, presidente provisional en la guerra de liberación, comisionó a don Pablo Pujol a Washington para ofrecer una estación naval en Samaná, y que el Sr. Seward no quiso recibir a Pujol ni reconocer a la restaurada república dominicana ni siquiera como beligerante. Cabral, que había compartido la lucha con Pimentel, es en el bosquejo el Putnam de la historia dominicana, como Báez es su Talleyrand; la ventana sigue su ruptura con Pimentel, su entrada en la ciudad de Santo Domingo con el título de Protector cuando los españoles se retiraron a sus barcos, su renuncia a favor de Báez en 1866 y su posterior sucesión en la presidencia, y se interrumpe a mitad de frase cuando pasa a la oferta de Samaná que se le indujo a aceptar a un precio.

records.headline: A United States Navy lieutenant writing from the island reports that he has travelled some two hundred miles since
records.summary_en: A United States Navy lieutenant writing from the island reports that he has travelled some two hundred miles since leaving Santo Domingo, crossing the mountains and now working on the northern side under his instructions, keeping a full journal of what he has seen. He says that wherever he went he received the kindest attention, even in the mountains, and that he might have travelled with any amount of money without fear of being molested, though he also saw misery and destitution that would make the heart ache; the island's resources, he writes, are inexhaustible and want only population and a more industrious people to develop them.
records.summary_es: Un teniente de la Marina de los Estados Unidos que escribe desde la isla informa que ha viajado unas doscientas millas desde que salió de Santo Domingo, cruzando las montañas y trabajando ahora en el lado norte según sus instrucciones, llevando un diario completo de lo que ha visto. Dice que dondequiera que fue recibió la atención más amable, incluso en las montañas, y que podría haber viajado con cualquier cantidad de dinero sin temor de ser molestado, aunque también vio una miseria y una indigencia que daban dolor al corazón; los recursos de la isla, escribe, son inagotables y solo necesitan población y un pueblo más industrioso para desarrollarlos.

records.headline: A special despatch reports that the United States steamer Albany sailed
records.summary_en: A special despatch reports that the United States steamer Albany sailed for Santo Domingo on Wednesday afternoon carrying three commissioners who go to take formal possession of Samaná Bay as an American station; the Albany was loaded with heavy ordnance for coast fortifications, and will take nearly a regiment of infantry and a company of artillery at the Dry Tortugas. The sending of the commissioners, the despatch adds, is looked upon as paving the way for the annexation of the Dominican Republic, the negotiations entered into last August having progressed so far as to substantially provide that San Domingo shall be annexed as a State, without going into Territorial form.
records.summary_es: Un despacho especial informa que el vapor estadounidense Albany zarpó hacia Santo Domingo el miércoles por la tarde con tres comisionados que van a tomar posesión formal de la bahía de Samaná como estación americana; el Albany iba cargado de artillería pesada para fortificaciones costeras, y recogerá en las Dry Tortugas casi un regimiento de infantería y una compañía de artillería. El envío de los comisionados, añade el despacho, se considera el paso que abre el camino a la anexión de la República Dominicana, pues las negociaciones entabladas en agosto pasado han avanzado hasta el punto de disponer sustancialmente que Santo Domingo sea anexado como Estado, sin pasar por la forma territorial.

records.headline: The President's views come in a Herald account that begins in mid-item
records.summary_en: The President's views come in a Herald account that begins in mid-item with the choice between the sale of Samaná and a lease of it for from fifty to one hundred years. The President does not think an immediate acquisition of St. Domingo desirable, for various reasons, among them the great difference in the habits and tastes of the people of that country and our own. Under a trial lease of the bay for a term of years, he believes, the Dominicans would within three or four years be so convinced of the superiority of the American style of government that they would be not only willing but clamorous for annexation, which would then follow. The account adds that the lease, with the possession of the entire Dominican portion of the island in prospect, meets with great favor in official circles, and that the bay of Samaná commands one of the main avenues between the Atlantic Ocean and the Caribbean Sea; the window ends in mid-sentence on the peninsula's valuable woods and its vein of coal.
records.summary_es: Las opiniones del Presidente vienen en un relato del Herald que comienza a mitad de un artículo con la elección entre la venta de Samaná y su arrendamiento por un período de cincuenta a cien años. El Presidente no considera deseable una adquisición inmediata de Santo Domingo, por varias razones, entre ellas la gran diferencia de hábitos y gustos entre el pueblo de ese país y el nuestro. Con un arrendamiento de prueba de la bahía por un término de años, cree, los dominicanos quedarían en tres o cuatro años tan convencidos de la superioridad del estilo de gobierno americano que no solo estarían dispuestos a la anexión, sino que la reclamarían, y esta seguiría entonces. El relato añade que el arrendamiento, con la posesión de toda la porción dominicana de la isla en perspectiva, goza de gran favor en los círculos oficiales, y que la bahía de Samaná domina una de las principales avenidas entre el océano Atlántico y el mar Caribe; la ventana termina a mitad de frase con los valiosos bosques de la península y su veta de carbón.

records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* argued that if the United States desires Samaná or any part of St. Domingo, it should simply purchase the territory to avoid future disputes, while criticizing the current government's policy as timid and narrow-minded. The newspaper also questioned whether the administration's sudden emphasis on the importance of the Bay of Samaná was a subterfuge designed to cover up its weak policy regarding Cuba.
records.summary_es: *The New York Herald* sostuvo que, si los Estados Unidos ambicionan la bahía de Samaná o cualquier otra comarca de Santo Domingo, debieran comprar llanamente el territorio para prevenir futuros litigios, fustigando la conducta del actual gabinete estadounidense como pusilánime y estrecha de miras. El diario cuestionó además si el súbito interés de la administración por la bahía de Samaná constituía un subterfugio para encubrir su endeble ejecutoria frente a la cuestión cubana.

records.full_text:
Policy of the Administration in the West Indies.

We published yesterday a glowing account of the reported lease of the Bay of Samana, island of St. Domingo, by the United States government, which was communicated to us, and also a letter from Washington of the same tenor, announcing the arrival at New York of General Babcock and the Dominican Commission on board the United States steamer Albany, for the purpose of negotiating a fifty years' lease with our government for the Bay of Samana. There is some discrepancy between the two statements. One has it that the bargain has been completed, and that the United States flag now floats over that portion of the Dominican territory; while the other says the Commission has arrived for the purpose of negotiating a lease. Then, again, it is stated the territory embraces an area of two thousand five hundred square miles; when it appears from a reliable communication from our correspondent at Samana that it is only estimated at two hundred and twenty-five to two hundred and forty square miles—that is, the length is about thirty miles and the breadth eight miles, including the islands along the coast.

It is particularly worthy of notice, too, that in the same paper in which these statements appear, that is, in our issue of yesterday, was published the news of St. Domingo having negotiated a loan with British capitalists, for seven hundred and fifty-seven thousand pounds sterling, on the condition that St. Domingo hypothecates the entire proceeds of receipts from imports and exports at the ports of St. Domingo and Puerto Plata, as well as the royalties from the working and export of guano from the island of Alta Vela, and in addition to the revenues arising from coal and other minerals, and mahogany and other woods, from the peninsula of Samana. If this be true the cunning Dominicans are playing a nice game with both the United States and the British, and all on this strip of territory called Samana, with its bays, harbors and islands. If they would only sell out some other, or some of the same privileges to France, Spain and other European countries, it would make as nice a muddle in the future as any one could wish to see. This Samana business has all the appearance of a big job or, may be, a number of jobs.

But why lease the Bay of Samana at all? Why give a hundred and fifty thousand dollars in gold a year for fifty or a hundred years for a lease? It may be said, and indeed it is said, this is only an entering wedge for the ultimate acquisition of Samana or the whole island. What a miserable policy for a mighty republic like this to enter upon! What wretched peddling! It is utterly unworthy any great nation, and particularly the United States, which is the dominating Power of this hemisphere. If we want Samana, or any part of the island of St. Domingo, let us buy it and have no further trouble about the matter, or any possible dispute hereafter. Our government appears to be the tool of any insignificant ruler or country or clique of speculators. It seems incapable of a comprehensive policy, of acting with foresight with regard to the future or of appreciating the commanding position this republic holds over all questions pertaining to the countries of America. Its peddling, narrow-minded and timid course is enough to make every American citizen feel ashamed of his government.

The most curious and significant thing about this Samana business is that the administration, or rather the Secretary of State, appears very desirous of making a great fuss about it just now, and of representing that leased possession as more important than the island of Cuba. If we relied upon the glowing accounts given of the Bay of Samana and the official action so far concerning it, we might suppose it the most valuable possession in the Antilles. Indeed, it has been stated that this bay would be of more advantage to the United States than the annexation of Cuba. Is this absurd statement another dodge to cover up the weakness and miserable policy of the administration relative to Cuba? Does the government suppose it can blind the American people by any such wretched subterfuge? Yes, let us have the Bay of Samana; but let us get it in a proper way; let us buy it, and not pay tribute to a few negroes or mulattoes for permission to use it. Yes, let us have the whole island if that suits our policy and it can be made useful. We go as far as the farthest in our desire to extend the area and usefulness of our country. But let it be remembered that St. Domingo is sparsely settled by little more than a hundred thousand negroes and mulattoes, while Cuba has a million and a half inhabitants, and out of that number seven or eight hundred thousand of the white European race. Let it be remembered that the island of St. Domingo is desolated and produces little, while Cuba is one of the most, if not the most, productive country on the globe. The Bay of Samana may be a fine harbor, and may prove of value to us; but it lies on the eastern and outer verge of the whole of the West Indies, and is almost fifteen hundred miles from the nearest point of the United States. Cuba has many as fine or finer harbors, and some of them are almost within sight of the United States. The whole island stretches along and faces our border. It commands the entrance to the Gulf of Mexico; it dominates the channel of Yucatan, which connects the gulf with the Caribbean Sea, and it controls the windward passage at the east end, and consequently nearly all the navigation of the West Indian group. The idea of comparing the value of Samana with Cuba is simply ridiculous. Cuba, for its productions and trade, and from its important position, geographically considered, is worth far more to the United States than the whole of the rest of the West Indies put together. So much, then, for the speculative and glowing accounts of Samana and the supremely absurd comparison of it with the rich and highly important island of Cuba.

In connection with this subject it will not be out of place to notice the peculiar position the administration occupies at present on the Cuban question. Looking at the refusal of the Secretary of State to give Congress the information asked for about Cuba, we are compelled to infer that negotiations are still going on or have been revived with Spain for the cession of the island. The conduct of Mr. Fish cannot be accounted for on any other ground. We hope it may be so, and that the terrible, bloody drama and work of devastation now going on in Cuba may be soon stopped. Of course our government is honest in the matter, should we be right in this supposition. But is Spain honest? Are not Prim and his associates humbugging our Minister at Madrid and our weak Secretary of State? Do they not still cling to the hope of crushing the Cubans, and that by temporizing with the United States? And then, if successful, would they not tell their faithful ally that, the trouble being over, Spanish honor and pride would forbid any further negotiation for the cession of Cuba? In short, would they not laugh at us for our folly, and should we not have to coolly pocket the insult? Mr. Fish may have confidence in his Spanish friends, but we have not. We hope Congress, therefore, will stand no nonsense or unnecessary palaver, but will bring this question to a practical issue at once, and that in favor of Cuban independence and annexation.

records.summary_en: Writing from Havana, a correspondent reports that the Stars and Stripes were flying over Samana Bay in token of United States possession, and then surveys the new acquisition in detail. He describes the bay's deep, sheltered coves, the port of Cacao, the old careening place used by pirates, the inlet once chosen for a United States naval station, and the town of Santa Barbara, capital of the peninsula.

records.summary_en: Writing from Havana on December 18, the correspondent describes Samana Bay after the Stars and Stripes were raised over it, having entered the bay aboard the United States steamer Albany, whose Captain Balch planted the flag. He surveys the bay's deep sheltered coves, among them Cacao and the Carenero, the inner inlet General McClellan had selected for a United States naval station, and the town of Santa Barbara, the capital of the peninsula, with its cottages set among fruit trees along the shore.

Recorre las ensenadas profundas y abrigadas de la bahía, entre ellas Cacao y el Carenero, la ensenada interior que el general McClellan había escogido para una estación naval de los Estados Unidos, y el pueblo de Santa Bárbara, la capital de la península, con sus casas entre árboles frutales a lo largo de la costa.

records.headline: The Evansville Journal's account, beginning in mid-report, states
records.summary_en: The Evansville Journal's account, beginning in mid-report, states that when the matter was satisfactorily settled and the agreed payment made, the Albany, with the commissioners and one of President Báez's staff, sailed to the Bay of Samaná to take formal possession of the waters and peninsula in the name of the United States, and that on the 6th of December the United States flag was hoisted on the island of Corenero, in the bay, amidst general joy on the part of the inhabitants. The lease of Samaná is already stated for fifty years, at $130,000 in gold per annum, and the Journal notes the heavy freight the hold of the Albany contained. The same column carries the Herald's report that the government of St. Domingo has negotiated a loan for nearly $4,000,000 in gold, for the repayment of which the revenues of the ports of St. Domingo and Puerto Plata, to the amount of $53,000 per annum, and the royalties produced from the export of guano from the island of Alta Vela, and the duties from coal and mahogany from the peninsula of Samaná are pledged.

El arrendamiento de Samaná se fija ya en cincuenta años, a $130,000 en oro por año, y el Journal señala la pesada carga que contenía la bodega del Albany. La misma columna trae el informe del Herald de que el gobierno de Santo Domingo ha negociado un empréstito de casi $4,000,000 en oro, para cuyo pago están pignorados los ingresos de los puertos de Santo Domingo y Puerto Plata, hasta la suma de $53,000 por año, y las regalías producidas por la exportación de guano de la isla de Alta Vela, y los derechos sobre el carbón y la caoba de la península de Samaná.

records.headline: The closing window of the Herald's long essay on the island
records.summary_en: The closing window of the Herald's long essay on the island gives the terms on which, it says, the United States is to assume the possession of the Dominican republic: a Territorial government identical with the other Territorial governments within the jurisdiction of the United States, the Dominican people first deciding by vote to allow such possession, the United States assuming the public debt and other obligations of the Dominican government, amounting to one million dollars, and paying for their State property one million dollars more. The essay recalls that our government sent out commissioners in July last, who returned in October expressing their belief that the Dominicans are desirous of annexation and that the island is worth possessing, and predicts that, 'Dominica once a Territory of the United States, Hayti will soon seek our protection,' Salnave already looking with favor upon annexation and having several times sought the protection of the American flag, while the newly accredited Minister from Hayti, General Alexander Tate, is said to favor annexation — the man who, in 1861, offered his services to Mr. Lincoln to aid in the organization of colored troops. The window ends in mid-sentence, on the peace that possession will bring 'to a people long distracted.'

records.summary_en: The window opens with the closing lines of the Herald's sketch of the Samaná peninsula and turns to 'The St. Domingo Loan': a flysheet containing an exposition and a condemnation of the loan recently entered into by the government of St. Domingo has been extensively circulated in St. Domingo city and other towns of the republic, and the Herald prints a liberal translation of the document. The flysheet states that English papers contain an account of the negotiation of a loan between this republic and British bankers of the nominal value of £767,700 sterling, on the basis of seventy pounds per cent discount, six per cent annual interest for the capital and four per cent for the liquidation of the loan, the whole to be paid in twenty-five years, the guarantees being the hypothecation of the entries of certain custom houses and the exportation dues of the guano of Alta Vela, the coal mines and mahogany of Samaná and the other mines of the republic, on condition that the loan be applied to the construction of railroads and the improvement of the highways generally. records.headline: The Herald announces that the United States steamer Albany arrived
records.summary_en: The Herald announces that the United States steamer Albany arrived on Sunday last, with the three commissioners on board, direct from the island of St. Domingo, and set the Samaná matter at rest, enabling it to announce that the Bay of Samaná had become American territory and that the American flag waved over our first foothold in the Antilles; from the fact of our having at length planted the United States flag in Dominica and having taken formal possession of the Bay of Samaná, a sketch of the Dominican republic follows. The sketch describes the republic as the eastern portion of the island of Hayti, comprising nearly three-fifths of the island, its name derived from the ancient Spanish appellation of the island, San Domingo; its area is estimated at 17,600 square miles, and its population at about 180,000, of whom one-tenth claim to be whites and the rest are of African descent or of mixed African and European, and it records that the Dominican republic was the first American State which made the absolute equality of all races before the law a fundamental portion of its constitutional existence. The boundary between it and the Haytien republic is traced from the mouth of the river Massacre, on the north coast, to the river Anses-à-Pitre, or Pedernales, on the south; the window ends as the sketch turns to the mountain ranges of the interior.

records.full_text:
FIRST NEGOTIATIONS FOR THE CESSION OF SAMANA.

Samana, however, is no new love of the American government, for not less than fifteen years ago, when Franklin Pierce was President and Wm. L. Marcy was Secretary of State, an energetic effort was made to obtain its bay and peninsula. In June, 1854, almost directly after he had returned from surveying the Western section of the proposed Northern Pacific Railroad, in Washington Territory, General (then Captain) George B. McClellan was entrusted by our government with a mission that demanded much discretion and a considerable knowledge of naval and military requirements. This important duty was the undertaking of a secret expedition to the West Indies with the object of selecting a convenient harbor and a suitable coaling station for the vessels of the United States navy cruising in the neighborhood of those islands and passing into the Gulf of Mexico. He sailed in the United States frigate Columbia, first to St. Domingo and then to other islands in the vicinity, and returned home in September with a vast amount of information of considerable importance, and with a large number of maps and sketches of the places visited. The result of Captain McClellan's inquiries was the selection for the proposed station and harbor of the bay and peninsula of Samana, the advantages of which were set forth in two reports—one on the harbor and its defences and the other descriptive of the island—but neither of which have been given to the public, doubtless owing to the secret nature of the expedition. Negotiations were at once opened with the government of St. Domingo and every endeavor made to obtain the cession of the bay and peninsula to the United States, but without terminating in the desired acquisition, owing, it was supposed at the time, to the jealousy of the European Powers and their influence upon the Dominican government. If we are to take the remarks of the London Times as any guidance to the action of the Powers of Europe at the present day, we may anticipate a more favorable issue to the present negotiations. In fact, the government of St. Domingo have now agreed, while before they refused, to cede the desired territory, which is one step in advance of the previous negotiations; but an attempt may yet be made to prevent the ratification of the treaty by that republic, should it pass the ordeal of the United States Senate.

TERMS OF THE CONTRACT.

The provisions of the contract for the leasing of the Bay of Samana to the United States are, so far as at present known, to be as follows:—The lease is to run for a term of fifty years, and the United States to pay to the Dominican government the annual rental of $150,000 in gold. The first year's rent has been paid down. In addition to the annual rent, President Baez, it is said, is to receive the sum of $50,000 annually. To say the least of it this reads somewhat strange and requires some explanation. Apart from the money supplied by the United States, $80,000 worth of arms and munitions of war have been placed at the disposal of the republic of St. Domingo. This amount, however, is to be deducted from future appropriations. Such, in brief, are the reported terms upon which the United States has acquired this magnificent harbor, which has been pronounced by Admiral Porter as "the finest naval station in the world." It is not a little remarkable that the transfer of the Bay of Samana was made on the anniversary of the first landing of Columbus, which took place on the 6th day of December, 1492. Three hundred and seventy-seven years have passed over since the famous Genoese made the discovery of the fruitful island of Hispaniola, and where for centuries waved the proud flag of Spain the banner of a nation then unknown now floats in triumph.

records.headline: The report sets out Admiral Porter's opinion of Samana Bay, calling its position beside the Mona Passage of vast
records.summary_en: The report sets out Admiral Porter's opinion of Samana Bay, calling its position beside the Mona Passage of vast importance to the United States, since the power holding it could command the commerce of any nation it was at war with. Porter is quoted praising the bay as the best harbor in the West Indies, with timber, iron, coal and copper for shipbuilding, and the article adds similar English and French opinions, including Sir R. Schomburgk's description of Samana as one of the principal keys to the Isthmus of Central America and the Gulf of Mexico.
records.summary_es: El informe expone la opinión del almirante Porter sobre la bahía de Samaná, calificando su posición junto al Paso de la Mona de enorme importancia para los Estados Unidos, ya que la potencia que la poseyera podría dominar el comercio de cualquier nación con la que estuviera en guerra. Se cita a Porter elogiando la bahía como el mejor puerto de las Indias Occidentales, con madera, hierro, carbón y cobre para la construcción naval, y el artículo añade opiniones similares inglesas y francesas, incluida la descripción de Sir R. Schomburgk de Samaná como una de las principales llaves del istmo de América Central y del golfo de México.
records.passage: by the mainland. Is about thirty-three miles long and eight broad. The Yuna, the largest river in the country, flows into it at its western end. The harbor is considered to be one of the finest in the world, and its position, both in a naval and military point of view, is of the highest importance. ADMIRAL PORTER'S OPINION OF SAMANA. As the geographical position of Samana Bay is of vast importance to the United States, in case it should be placed at the disposition of such a Power as France, I deem it worthy of a passing notice. Situated close to the highway of all vessels coming from Europe (the Mona passage) and of most of the vessels from the United States bound to the West Indies, the Power that owned it could command the commerce of any nation with whom they were at war. It contains within itself all the requisites for shipbuilding—the finest timber, iron, coal and copper—and, no doubt, a good geological survey would develop resources in minerals yet unthought of. The bay and harbor are the best in the whole West Indies, and is capable, I am told, of containing the combined fleets of Europe and rendering them perfectly secure against the most destructive tempests. Very great numbers of whales find refuge here in the large bay, where they increase and multiply because not pursued, the government having prohibited all vessels from taking whales in those waters. One American alone has been allowed to fish there, and the government, I think, could be induced to extend the permission to other citizens.

records.headline: Since the acquisition of Samana by the United States government was announced, many have contended it is only the preliminary move
records.summary_en: Since the acquisition of Samana by the United States government was announced, many have contended it is only the preliminary move toward possession of the whole island, and the paper's correspondents report that Dominicans themselves favor annexation. Before leaving office Secretary Seward had received President Baez's proposition for an American protectorate, which a House committee majority favored but which was defeated in Congress for lack of information about Dominican affairs, and New York business men are now discussing Samana's commercial value under a fifty years' lease, with a bank, lumber companies and coal and copper mines already being talked of.
records.summary_es: Desde que se anunció la adquisición de Samaná por el gobierno de los Estados Unidos, muchos han sostenido que es solo el paso preliminar hacia la posesión de toda la isla, y los corresponsales del periódico informan que los propios dominicanos favorecen la anexión. Antes de dejar el cargo, el secretario Seward había recibido la proposición del presidente Báez de un protectorado estadounidense, que la mayoría de una comisión de la Cámara favoreció pero que fue derrotada en el Congreso por falta de información sobre los asuntos dominicanos, y los hombres de negocios de Nueva York discuten ahora el valor comercial de Samaná bajo un arrendamiento de cincuenta años, hablándose ya de un banco, compañías madereras y minas de carbón y cobre.

'We thought there were two parties to that arrangement,' the paper remarks, 'or would Mr. Baez prefer to annex the United States to San Domingo?... We hope for the best, but do not wish to acquire San Domingo by small craft or sharp practice. Our national mortification would be great if we had helped an unscrupulous ruler to a trick, and got tricked ourselves. We must soon know the truth of San Domingo.'

records.headline: A Havana despatch of December 23 reports that the news of the lease of the Bay of Samaná
records.summary_en: A Havana despatch of December 23 reports that the news of the lease of the Bay of Samaná to the United States causes intense excitement among the people of St. Domingo, and that the revolutionists are making efforts to overthrow Báez before the American Congress can ratify the arrangement for the lease. The despatch, printed under the heading 'Affairs in St. Domingo,' adds that Báez's troops have taken a place printed as 'Carle Volta,' and two of Cabral's Generals, who were captured, were immediately executed. The same column's Hayti news, dated to the 6th instant, reports that Salnave now only holds the city of Port-au-Prince; that the revolutionary President, Saget, has informed the foreign representatives at the capital that five war vessels are coaling at St. Marc for the purpose of proceeding to bombard Port-au-Prince, the land forces to attack the city simultaneously with the fleet; that Salnave has threatened to burn Port-au-Prince before he will surrender; and that one dollar in gold was worth four thousand dollars in Haytien currency.

records.headline: A description of the Bay of Samaná, whose opening lines are cut
records.summary_en: A description of the Bay of Samaná, whose opening lines are cut in the window, gives the bay as eight miles broad and receiving at its west end the Yuna, the largest river in the Dominican Republic; it forms one of the finest harbors in the world, and may be regarded as a most important maritime position in reference to the trade of the Gulf of Mexico and the inter-oceanic routes across Central America, in both a commercial and a military point of view. On the north shore is the small town of Santa Bárbara, which lies in a land-locked bay and has natural facilities for repairing vessels, a dilapidated Roman Catholic church, a neat Wesleyan chapel and a custom house; the peninsula of Samaná is thirty-two miles long, its highest peak, Sugar Loaf Hill, 1,936 feet, and Devil's Hill 1,309 feet above the level of the sea, its soil extremely fertile and to a great extent covered with timber suited both for ship-building and cabinet-work, and containing gold, copper and bituminous coal, its population at the last census 1,721. The news of the occupation of Samaná by the United States, the description closes, created great excitement among the people of San Domingo, and the revolutionary party were making redoubled efforts to drive out Báez, who had effected the negotiations and declares that he will annex the whole republic to the United States if he is forced to that alternative.

En la costa norte está el pequeño pueblo de Santa Bárbara, situado en una bahía cerrada por tierra, con facilidades naturales para reparar embarcaciones, una iglesia católica romana en ruinas, una pulcra capilla wesleyana y una aduana; la península de Samaná tiene treinta y dos millas de longitud, su pico más alto, Sugar Loaf Hill, de 1,936 pies, y Devil's Hill de 1,309 pies sobre el nivel del mar, su suelo extremadamente fértil y cubierto en gran parte de maderas aptas tanto para la construcción naval como para la ebanistería, y con oro, cobre y carbón bituminoso, y su población en el último censo de 1,721 habitantes. La noticia de la ocupación de Samaná por los Estados Unidos, cierra la descripción, creó una gran agitación entre el pueblo de Santo Domingo, y el partido revolucionario redoblaba sus esfuerzos por expulsar a Báez, que había efectuado las negociaciones y declara que anexará toda la república a los Estados Unidos si se ve forzado a esa alternativa.

records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* warned that using violence against San Domingo would provoke widespread alarm and hatred throughout South America. records.full_text:
WHAT THE DOMINICANS SAY.

At date of St. Domingo, December 6, a Committee of Dominicans write to us as follows:

The world will see with scandal Gen. Grant pursuing his plans with regard to this island. The world, as well as Gen. Grant and his Yankees, ought to know that in the list of Dominican restorers are not to be found the names of Baez, Gautier, Felix Delmonte, nor any of those who form this band of traitors. These men—the Spaniards of yesterday—know that it will not be possible for them to continue in the government of this country, and for that reason they are negotiating it. President Grant does not know—cannot know what is passing here. Daily are being executed honorable Dominicans, in witness of which we refer to the Government’s official gazette, and to any stranger—and even to any honest Yankee—not to such corrupt speculators as Cazneau and Fabens. Gen. Grant intends well to the Dominican Republic, and if the Congress and Senate participate in his intention, why do they not wait for the resolution of the present question by the free act of the Dominicans themselves? A violence done to San Domingo will raise a cry of alarm which will resound in all South America, and with that cry will arise a hatred equal to that which Spain will ever deserve.

records.headline: The islands of the Gulf have no destiny beyoud the folds
records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported on January 13, 1870, that while the islands of the Gulf and San Domingo naturally gravitated toward the United States through trade and statesmanship, immediate annexation might be fraught with peril, though leasing Samana Bay remained a good idea. The article noted that the U.S. government might encounter competing claims or leases regarding Samana Bay, highlighting a "sharp colored American" mariner who bought land there five years prior and now owns a considerable portion of the available water frontage, coal lands, and valuable property where a naval station would likely be located.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* expuso el 13 de enero de 1870 que, si bien las islas del golfo y Santo Domingo gravitaban de forma natural hacia los Estados Unidos por imperativos mercantiles y geopolíticos, una anexión inmediata entrañaba graves riesgos, considerándose no obstante acertado el arrendamiento de la bahía de Samaná. El escrito prevenía que el gobierno estadounidense podría afrontar títulos contrapuestos o derechos de arriendo en la zona, destacando a un «sagaz marino estadounidense de color» que adquirió tierras allí un lustro antes y retenía una porción considerable de la ribera marítima, terrenos carboníferos y valiosas heredades donde previsiblemente se asentaría el apostadero naval.

records.full_text:
HOW ANNEXATION WILL BE REGARDED BY THE DOMINICANS.

Within two or three days past, the writer has conversed at length with a gentlemen of the highest character and intelligence, thoroughly acquainted with the condition of both San Domingo and Hayti, and having the best possible means of understanding "the situation." I propose to state some of his views, and preliminary thereto desire to say that my informant is most heartily in sympathy with all honest and equitable efforts at increasing the friendly influence of the United States in the islands of the Gulf, in fact, with all other American peoples. He regards this Government and people as altogether derelict, not only in neighborly duty, but in that careful selfishness which is as usually deemed sagacious among nations as among individuals. He also declares his conviction—and as a native of one of the Antillean islands, he has the right to speak—that the only possible future for these communities lies through complete friendship with the Great Republic, and a control obtained over them by virtue of the energizing and educational influences of our civilization. In this manner he would pave the way to unity with us. Absorption, attraction of gravitation would be either of them a better word than annexation to describe the means by which my West Indian friend would have us obtain control of all the fair islands of the Caribbean Sea.

From this standpoint he regards favorably a proposition to lease Samana Bay from Baez, or to obtain privileges from Hayti at the Mole St. Nicholas. Any treaty looking to direct annexation he would now regard as sure to produce trouble—and that, too, of a character that must not be underrated.

The direct reasons given for this view are simple and plain. Distrust of all white races is yet a marked attribute, not of the Haytians only, but the Dominicans also. Perhaps with the latter it is not as distinct a sentiment, but the late attempt of Spain revived and strengthened it. Certainly in Hayti the jealousy of the white man is a fact that must be considered, for it is duly and sedulously fostered by ambitious demagogues. In both Republics the mass of the people are very ignorant, and the intelligence of our great progress in vindicating "all rights for all men," has found its way slowly among them. The presence at Port-au-Prince of Minister Bassett, a gentleman possessed of healthy and honest brown skin, is a visible sign of the change which has been made. Still it is by no means a sufficient proof to them that annexation would not mean evil. The men of Hayti and San Domingo are a proud people. Our negroes, even the best of them, fail to exhibit the pride which is a natural inheritance of those who fought against such terrible odds for personal freedom.

In San Domingo, my informant believes that Baez's annexation policy will prove his own overthrow. Even the Samana lease may do it. If we consummate the lease however, the money necessarily expended in preparing the proposed station, and the labor that would be employed, in less than two years would have a marked impression on the people. Prosperity, coming through this means, would rapidly build a bridge for annexation. The petty chieftains would not oppose the United States; on the contrary, seeing that colored men among us had equal rights, their ambition would be fed by the larger fires which flame upon our altar-stones. After two years, occupation of Samana Bay might ensue; peaceful annexation of all San Domingo. It is not at all probable that such would be the case now. My informant declares—and he knows the island and people thoroughly—that if Cabral and Luperon should be able to organize anything like a successful revolt in consequence of an annexation policy, it would take 25,000 men to hold the country and five years' time to conquer it. A thousand men, determined, well equipped and led, might force their way across the island, but except as to the ground which they held by their presence, and perhaps the seacoast, they would have gained nothing. The interior of the island is mountainous, and very easily defensible.

THE DOMINICAN LEADERS.

Gen. Baez is a man of ability and European training. As a politician he is shrewder, craftier perhaps, abler certainly, than his opponents. He is very nearly a statesman, and would make a very respectable Senator from the new State of San Domingo, which is probably a not ill-defined hope in his mind. Like the leaders in both the island Republics, he is counted cruel and unscrupulous. Baez was Salnave's friend through all his earlier struggles, and if the indomitable Haytian has escaped, as is supposed, from Port-au-Prince, he may yet get aid enough from Baez to stir up renewed disorder.

Cabral and Luperon are men of lower type than Baez. Neither as soldiers nor politicians have they proved themselves his equals, and yet with such a possible grievance as the transfer of territory and nationality, Cabral is especially capable of making formidable use of the feelings that may easily be aroused. These facts and suggestions are presented as showing difficulties uppermost in my informant's mind; which, in his judgment, ought and may be avoided, by not pressing annexation to a direct issue at the present time.

The United States cannot yet assume the role of benefactor and guardian among the dark-skinned communities in the Gulf. Distrust is the penalty we have yet to pay for Slavery. The educated understand, but the masses fear. It must come to them in a beneficent way, restoring prosperity through trade, &c. The islands of the Gulf have no destiny beyond the folds of our flag, but by decent statesmanship and a little nursing they will come, but will not be forced. The tree would perhaps need vigorous shaking now; later, the fruit would fall ripe into our laps.

What is said of San Domingo is in large degree applicable to Hayti—only more so. Two years of reciprocity and commercial activity would settle this question in Hayti. The conclusion is reached that annexation may and probably will at this time be fraught with peril. The leasing of the Samana Bay, apart from this condition, is a good thing to do.

records.summary_en: The Tribune warns, in an editorial paragraph, that the Dominica news it has lately published makes it tolerably clear that, in case of the annexation of any part of that Republic, we shall have a good deal of fighting on hand, which will probably last for some time. In considering the negotiations for the leasing of the Bay of Samaná, or any of the other negotiations with President Báez, it would be well for Congress to bear this fact in mind: 'We can, of course, whip the Dominicans, or any other enemy who rises to fight us; but still, fighting cannot be called a matter of economy or pleasure.'

records.full_text:
The San Domingo Property.

While Mr Sumner's committee is considering the San Domingo annexation treaty, a hundred editors and correspondents are exploring for all the facts that can be got at about the undivided half of a great island which will come to us if the treaty is ratified. The extent of the Dominican part of Hayti is uncertain, but cannot well be less than 20,000 square miles. The population is a mixture of Spanish, Indian, negro and French, and the whole number is not more than 150,000. They are now, as usual, in a state of inactive revolution against the nominal government, which is made up of President Baez, a Castilian, his secretary of state, M. M. Gautier, who was his commissioner in conducting the negotiations, Attorney-General Felix Del Monte, Secretary of War and Marine Hungria, and Secretary of the Treasury Curiel. These officers are all white, being either of Castilian or French descent. There is also a supreme court, of which Señor Tejera, a pure Castilian, is chief justice. The republic is divided into seven provinces, each of which has a representative in the Senate, which is the only legislative body, and meets regularly once a year for legislative business. The Senate is understood to be with Baez in his wish to transfer the country to us, but there is a party headed by two generals, Cabral and Luperol, who are bitter against annexation.

A document protesting against it has found signers in Curacoa, St Thomas, Venezuela, Turks Island, and those few parts of the Dominican republic which are in the hands of the revolutionary party. The Dominicans who have been expelled from the country, and the partisans of Cabral and Luperol have signed it, wherever they may happen to be. They call themselves the "constitutional party," and denounce Baez for his cruelties toward them. His success, they say, is owing to American intervention, which alone could have prevented the triumph of Cabral and Luperol, and that, as a consequence of this intervention, there are more than 200 prisoners in the jails, some of whom are dying of hunger, and others are being destroyed by reason of terrible sufferings. Moreover, Baez is engaged in shooting a large number of friends of the constitution, because they are opposed to the projects of an unfaithful executive. Sustained by the government at Washington, which has remitted him arms, and sent a steamer to cruise in Dominican waters for his aid and support in case of emergency, Baez has thus been kept in power against the will of the people, and now proposes to trade them off to the United States. They declare that they will resist annexation to the death, etc., etc. Their leader, Cabral, is on the Haytian frontier, with a few hundred men, principally Cacos from Hayti. The town of Jabon, captured some time back by these insurgents, had been retaken by the government troops, of which a force sufficiently numerous to keep Cabral and his adherents effectually in check, holds possession of that part of the country. Luperol is at Turks Island, awaiting the issue of the Haytian war. A perfect understanding is said to exist between him and the revolutionary leaders in Hayti, who have promised that as soon as they succeed in overthrowing Salnave, they will place all their resources, including their war vessels, at the service of Cabral and Luperol, to be employed against President Baez. The latter, nothing daunted, has issued a proclamation, directing the commandants of the several districts to make arrangements for submitting the treaty to a popular vote. The feeling in the city of San Domingo, in Porto Platte, in Santiago, and in all the towns, is strongly in favor of annexation; but not in the country districts, the rural population being generally under the impression that the Americans are coming to take possession of all the good things of the land, and make serfs of the natives.

This feeling among the Dominicans is probably due in part to the fact that they are not to come into the Union as a state, but under territorial government. Their first proposition was for admission as a state, and the admission of Texas was cited as a precedent, but while Gen Babcock did not then have power to fix any conditions, he was invested with a general discretion which authorized him to inform Baez that this was out of the question. Knowing this, and hearing, perhaps, of the combinations forming in New York and Washington to make money out of the material riches of the island, it is no wonder that the Dominicans feel jealous about it. Moreover, they are mostly very ignorant, and have an unreasonable jealousy of all foreigners. The more intelligent, however, know the advantage of being under the protection of a strong government, and probably the vote will show a majority for annexation. There is little distinction of caste, color or religion among the people. Baez's chief of staff, Guielermo, is a colored man, and so is the collector of the port of San Domingo. The Catholic church prevails, though other denominations are tolerated. At San Domingo there has been a Methodist chapel for twenty-four years, and on Samana bay among the blacks, there is a Methodist church of several hundred members. There is little either of religion or morals among the population, of whatever church they profess to be. The condition of their paper currency is as bad as their morals. About two millions were issued some years since, but it soon became uncurrent, and the merchants and dealers repudiated it by fixing its rate of redemption at $400 of paper for one in gold. Subsequently this rate was ratified by legislative action, and a large amount of the money, which was printed on ordinary printing presses, was burned in the public square of San Domingo City. The revenues of the republic have been wholly derived from export and import duties. The export duties, however, are very small and are levied on sugar, coffee, rice, salt, hides, mahogany, logwood, "lignum vitæ," tobacco, etc. They have no system of internal or property taxation. Their import duties are also very light, and our government will have several blessings to confer upon their new children in the shape of internal taxation, high tariffs, and a small army of office-holders. The few soldiers of the Dominican army have just been furnished with new uniforms and rifles, both secured from the United States as part of the consideration for the lease of the bay of Samana. Col J, W. Fabins is in Samana in charge of the American flag there, which is duly raised every morning; another American is there looking after railroad matters, and ready to begin building a line into the interior as soon as the treaty is ratified. We trust there will be no haste about this, for there is no reason why we should spring a trap on anybody in San Domingo.

records.headline: A letter from San Domingo printed by the Tribune reports that the sensation
records.summary_en: A letter from San Domingo printed by the Tribune reports that the sensation produced throughout the whole extent of the Island by the arrival of a commission charged with unfolding the United States flag at Samaná has been extraordinary, and that President Báez has been forced to declare that the Stars and Stripes should not be placed upon other soil than two small keys of the bay, which would serve the Americans for deposits of coal. All the inhabitants in the interior, who suffered so much from Spanish domination, consider intervention in the affairs of this country, no matter whence it may come, as a real calamity; among the different populations, as also in the principal towns, there are only a few merchants or business men who favor an alienation of territory, and these have an interest in the speculation, while all the remainder of the people, and even many foreigners, as is the case particularly in Puerto Plata, are privately or openly opposed to the sale of Samaná. One fact will enable the reader to form an idea of the great opposition to the annexation scheme: the Senate is composed of men wholly devoted to the service of Báez — as, for example, his brother Carlos — but even this Senate vacillates when it sees the agitation which reigns throughout the Republic, and does not know whether or not to give its approbation to the President's now favorite project; the Government's attempt to make believe that this agitation is produced by English gold is, the letter says, clearly a falsehood. The window ends in mid-sentence, on the English Consul, Mr. Leon.
records.summary_es: Una carta de Santo Domingo publicada por el Tribune informa que la sensación producida en toda la extensión de la isla por la llegada de una comisión encargada de desplegar la bandera de los Estados Unidos en Samaná ha sido extraordinaria, y que el presidente Báez se ha visto forzado a declarar que la bandera de las barras y estrellas no se colocaría en otro suelo que dos pequeños cayos de la bahía, que servirían a los americanos como depósitos de carbón. Todos los habitantes del interior, que tanto sufrieron bajo la dominación española, consideran la intervención en los asuntos de este país, venga de donde venga, como una verdadera calamidad; entre las distintas poblaciones, como también en las principales ciudades, solo hay unos pocos comerciantes u hombres de negocios que favorecen la enajenación de territorio, y estos tienen interés en la especulación, mientras todo el resto del pueblo, e incluso muchos extranjeros, como es el caso particularmente en Puerto Plata, se oponen en privado o abiertamente a la venta de Samaná. Un hecho permitirá al lector formarse una idea de la gran oposición al plan de anexión: el Senado está compuesto por hombres enteramente devotos al servicio de Báez —como, por ejemplo, su hermano Carlos—, pero incluso este Senado vacila cuando ve la agitación que reina en toda la República, y no sabe si dar o no su aprobación al proyecto favorito actual del Presidente; el intento del Gobierno de hacer creer que esta agitación es producida por el oro inglés es, dice la carta, claramente una falsedad. La ventana termina a mitad de frase, con el cónsul inglés, el Sr. León.

records.headline: The Tribune directs its readers to correspondence from San Domingo
records.summary_en: The Tribune directs its readers to correspondence from San Domingo and Washington which it prints elsewhere, giving a number of important phases of the Dominican question: those who seek enlightenment as to the reputation of Mr. Báez as a trader in concessions, or to the antecedents of Cabral on the proposition to lease Samaná, may have it for the reading. The most striking point of our correspondence, however, is the hitherto unregarded fact that San Salvador, no less than San Domingo, has been an applicant for annexation: in 1822 the Salvadorian Congress declared for incorporation with the United States, and in 1849 Commissioners of Nicaragua and Honduras also offered the cession of these territories to the United States.
records.summary_es: El Tribune remite a sus lectores a la correspondencia de Santo Domingo y Washington que publica en otra parte, que ofrece varios aspectos importantes de la cuestión dominicana: quienes busquen ilustración sobre la reputación del Sr. Báez como negociante de concesiones, o sobre los antecedentes de Cabral en la proposición de arrendar Samaná, podrán encontrarla con la lectura. El punto más llamativo de nuestra correspondencia, sin embargo, es el hecho hasta ahora inadvertido de que San Salvador, no menos que Santo Domingo, ha sido solicitante de la anexión: en 1822 el Congreso salvadoreño declaró a favor de la incorporación a los Estados Unidos, y en 1849 comisionados de Nicaragua y Honduras también ofrecieron la cesión de estos territorios a los Estados Unidos.

records.summary_en: The paper narrates Haitian revolutionary troops pursuing former leader Salnave as he tried to reach Barahona in the Dominican Republic, with Cabral moving to cut him off. records.full_text:
ANNEXATION IN SAN DOMINGO.

THE UNPOPULARITY OF BAEZ—HIS ATTITUDE TOWARD THE HAYTIANS—THE CLERGY OPPOSED TO HIM—HIS NEGOTIATIONS—ANOTHER GENERAL PRONOUNCED.

SAN DOMINGO, Jan. 13.—President Baez, seeing that his troops are deserting him and going over to the standard of Cabral, has announced in flattering terms to his employés, both civil and military, that they will continue to hold their present positions and draw large salaries from the United States as soon as the annexation project shall have been consummated. To Baez it is perhaps a matter of indifference whether he leaves his country under a load of compromises, or whether the United States shall so complicate their bargain with him that they will be obliged at last to retire discreditably from San Domingo, or endeavor to subjugate the restless Dominicans. But Baez will know how to profit by the dislike which his countrymen feel toward foreign domination. Since the fall of Salnave (who cannot hereafter demand of Baez the $25,000 he lent him to oppose the cession of Samana at a former day) Baez has caused the circulation of the report that the revolutionists under the command of Cabral and Pimentel are Cacos from Hayti. He urges that all Dominicans should rise up against this Haytian invasion, ignoring the fact that Haytian soldiers led by a Haytian general entered the capital with him as part of his own army. Does he not remember Gen. Barriere, whose men marched into the city of Domingo, shouting "Down with Cabral—away with the Ojos-Azules!" (blue-eyes, meaning Yankees.)

It has been said that the Dominican clergy are in favor of Baez. This is not true. The Vicar is a foreigner, while among the exiles figure the most venerable priests, as, for example, Father F. A. Merino, the most talented man, perhaps, in the Republic. He is the Archbishop-elect. Other reverend exiles are noteworthy. Father Gutierrez, a man 70 years of age, is distinguished in the province of Seybo as "the father of the poor." Father Figari, aged 60 years, an American citizen, has his house at Higney, where it is called "the house of charity." Father Pinelli, the curé of Santiago de los Caballeros; Father Richardo, the curé of the Cathedral Church of Santo Domingo City; Father Moya, curé of La Vega, who died in banishment, have been always opposed to Baez. Receiving no support from the natives toward carrying out his projects, Baez looked abroad for encouragement. Of all the clergy only Father Bougement sustained him, and he is a Belgian.

records.headline: News brought by steamer reports that the planned occupation of the Bay of Samana by the United States is stirring
records.summary_en: News brought by steamer reports that the planned occupation of the Bay of Samana by the United States is stirring strong feeling in Haiti, where the provisional government of Saget, friendly to Cabral, is expected to help him defeat Baez's cession of the bay and where a clash with the United States is feared possible. The item also prints Saget's address to the Haitians, appealing to them to preserve public order, repair their losses under peace, and rebuild their democratic institutions while guarding against tyranny.
records.summary_es: Las noticias traídas por vapor informan que la ocupación planeada de la bahía de Samana por los Estados Unidos está provocando fuertes sentimientos en Haití, donde se espera que el gobierno provisional de Saget, amigo de Cabral, lo ayude a derrotar la cesión de la bahía por parte de Baez y donde se teme un posible enfrentamiento con los Estados Unidos. La nota también reproduce el discurso de Saget a los haitianos, en el que les pide preservar el orden público, reparar sus pérdidas bajo la paz y reconstruir sus instituciones democráticas protegiéndose contra la tiranía.

records.headline: Despatches printed by the Tribune report, from Havana, February 5
records.summary_en: Despatches printed by the Tribune report, from Havana, February 5, the latest intelligence from San Domingo: Cabral has issued a new protest against the occupation of Samaná by the United States; forty-five of the inhabitants of the capital who supported the protest have been banished by President Báez; the revolutionists, headed by Pimentel, are marching northwest, and they have captured Guayubín; and General Luperón has passed through St. Thomas en route to Jamaica. Official advices received at Washington, February 6, add that the Haytian Government has offered to assist the revolutionists in the former Republic, but that the Administration attaches no importance to the information.
records.summary_es: Despachos publicados por el Tribune informan, desde La Habana, el 5 de febrero, las últimas noticias de Santo Domingo: Cabral ha emitido una nueva protesta contra la ocupación de Samaná por los Estados Unidos; cuarenta y cinco de los habitantes de la capital que apoyaron la protesta han sido desterrados por el presidente Báez; los revolucionarios, encabezados por Pimentel, marchan hacia el noroeste, y han capturado Guayubín; y el general Luperón ha pasado por Santo Tomás en ruta hacia Jamaica. Avisos oficiales recibidos en Washington, el 6 de febrero, añaden que el gobierno haitiano ha ofrecido ayudar a los revolucionarios en la antigua República, pero que la Administración no concede importancia a la información.

records.headline: The Tribune's narrative of Báez's career: Pimentel elected President
records.summary_en: The Tribune's narrative of Báez's career: Pimentel elected President, then forced to give way to Cabral when a pronunciamiento broke out in San Domingo City on the 4th of August, Cabral being commissioned Protector of the Republic; Báez presented himself as a candidate in the following December and, though not a military hero and notwithstanding that his sympathies and support were given to the Spaniards during their invasion of the island, by his tact and consummate management defeated Cabral and became President; Pimentel and Cabral entered his Cabinet, but in 1866 a revolution headed by Pimentel drove him out of San Domingo, and another revolution the same year brought him back into power; Cabral succeeded him, but in the latter part of 1867 the office was again vacated, and after Cabral and his Cabinet fled at night from the capital, Báez was formally proclaimed President in 1868; Cabral remained in the field, with Polanco, Luperón, Moreno, Castillo, Ogando and Adó, opposed to the President with arms or otherwise, and Salnave lent Báez a helping hand in those trying times, without which he could never have maintained his position — the window closing mid-sentence, on the President's notoriety for shrewdness.

records.headline: Under the heading 'Movements of Mr. Seward,' the Intelligencer reports
records.summary_en: Under the heading 'Movements of Mr. Seward,' the Intelligencer reports letters just received from the ex-Secretary, now at Havana, stating that he proposes, as soon as the situation in Hayti will permit, to visit that country and, after a short sojourn there, to proceed to San Domingo, where he intends to remain until April, thus avoiding the severe March weather at his home in New York State; it is believed that Seward's presence in the Dominican Republic will assist materially in settling the unsatisfactory condition of affairs that appears to prevail in the republic, the result of the attempt to carry into effect the cession of that country to the United States, and his health is much improved.

Following Fabens's return to Washington around April 1, Baez, his Ministers, and the Consulting Committee of the Senate made a loan contract on May 1st, which was printed in the Government journal on September 29, 1869, nearly five months later.

records.full_text:
Pursuant to the request of the Chairman of Foreign Affairs, Mr. Seward dispatched Mr. Fabens to San Domingo with the view of obtaining all such information as was suggested in the letter of Gen. Banks. Especially was he directed to look into the condition of the debt of the Republic. Fabens remained two days in San Domingo City, and immediately returned to Washington, bringing the statement that the debt of San Domingo was only $600,000 (or, perhaps, a few thousand more), but he had no information to communicate to the Secretary of State respecting grants, concessions, and franchises. Fabens was himself at that time supposed to be interested in grants and franchises.

Fabens returned to Washington about the 1st of April, and we find Baez, his Ministers, and the Consulting Committee of the Senate making a loan on the first day of May following. The contract for the loan was made. It was first printed in the Government journal on the 29th of September, 1869, nearly five months after it had been made, and has only quite recently become known, as that journal has only a privileged circulation.

records.headline: A Santo Domingo letter of February 9 describes the change in the city
records.summary_en: A Santo Domingo letter of February 9 describes the change in the city in the two months since his arrival: a place that had seemed antediluvian, its commerce an occasional schooner from Curacao or St. Thomas and its shopkeepers lounging in hammocks behind their counters, now wears an air of improvement — the Ozama River filled with ships of all sizes, four merchantmen dropping down together, the wharves piled with barrels of flour, cords of logwood and sacks of coffee and sugar, the Custom House officers as busy as bees and the merchants standing upright and making their stores attractive; the transformation has been effected by the rumor of annexation and the presence of a few live Yankees, and one party of capitalists has organized a bank.

records.summary_en: The Herald's St. Domingo despatch, via Havana, March 1, reports the official declaration in favor of annexation: the government officially invited a general vote on the measure, and the result, as recorded in the capital, shows an overwhelming majority in the affirmative; Santiago, La Vega and Azua led the demand for admission to the Union, and nowhere was there any opposition; the Council of Ministers places the public debt at less than $1,500,000, and the American war vessel Swatara, Commander Allen, arrived at the port in time to witness the people's enthusiasm on the vote.

records.headline: A Herald editorial on its special telegram from St. Domingo
records.summary_en: A Herald editorial on its special telegram from St. Domingo city, via Havana, announces that the Dominican republic has formally declared in favor of annexation to the United States, the vote of the people taken by order of the government having resulted in an overwhelming majority with opposition nowhere visible; having thus obtained the almost unanimous consent of the masses, the Herald argues, no obstacle will present itself to the early gaining of a permanent foothold in the West Indies, calls St. Domingo in every respect a desirable acquisition for its commanding position in the Antilles, its naval advantages, fertile soil, minerals and fine climate, and holds that nothing now remains but the formal ratification by the Senate of the pending treaties — adding that President Grant takes a deep interest in the movement.
records.summary_es: Un editorial del Herald sobre su telegrama especial desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo, vía La Habana, anuncia que la República Dominicana se ha declarado formalmente a favor de la anexión a los Estados Unidos, habiendo resultado la votación del pueblo, realizada por orden del gobierno, en una abrumadora mayoría sin oposición visible en ningún lugar; obtenido así el consentimiento casi unánime de las masas, argumenta el Herald, ningún obstáculo se presentará para ganar pronto un punto de apoyo permanente en las Indias Occidentales, califica a Santo Domingo como una adquisición deseable en todo sentido por su posición dominante en las Antillas, sus ventajas navales, su suelo fértil, sus minerales y su clima agradable, y sostiene que ya solo resta la ratificación formal por el Senado de los tratados pendientes — añadiendo que el presidente Grant tiene un profundo interés en el movimiento.

records.summary_en: A St. Domingo despatch of February 20, via Havana, March 1, announces that the Dominican Republic has formally declared for annexation to the United States: the vote, which was officially proposed by the government, has been taken and, as recorded there, shows an overwhelming majority in favor; the towns of Santiago, La Vega and Azua led the demand for admission to the Union, and nowhere was there any visible opposition; the United States steamer Swatara, Captain Allen, arrived just in time to hear the vote declared.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de Santo Domingo del 20 de febrero, vía La Habana, 1 de marzo, anuncia que la República Dominicana se ha declarado formalmente por la anexión a los Estados Unidos: la votación, propuesta oficialmente por el gobierno, se ha realizado y, según se registró allí, muestra una abrumadora mayoría a favor; las ciudades de Santiago, La Vega y Azua encabezaron la demanda de admisión a la Unión, y en ningún lugar hubo oposición visible; el vapor estadounidense Swatara, al mando del capitán Allen, llegó justo a tiempo para escuchar la declaración del voto.

records.headline: The Gazette reports that Rear Admiral Porter, commanding the United States fleet
records.summary_en: The Gazette reports that Rear Admiral Porter, commanding the United States fleet in the West Indies, has written to the Navy Department — his name is printed 'Roar Admiral Poor' — that he warned the Haytian government it must not interfere with affairs in San Domingo, on the other side of the island, while negotiations are pending for the annexation of the Dominican Republic to the United States; the Haytian President, it adds, made an abrupt reply to the menace and is represented to have been greatly offended.
records.summary_es: La Gazette informa que el contralmirante Porter, al mando de la flota de los Estados Unidos en las Indias Occidentales, ha escrito al Departamento de Marina — su nombre viene impreso «Roar Admiral Poor» — que advirtió al gobierno haitiano que no debe interferir en los asuntos de Santo Domingo, al otro lado de la isla, mientras están pendientes las negociaciones para la anexión de la República Dominicana a los Estados Unidos; el presidente haitiano, añade, dio una respuesta abrupta a la amenaza y, según se le representa, quedó muy ofendido.

records.headline: This history of the Dominican Republic recounts how Santana negotiated a treaty with General Cazneau, President Pierce's
records.summary_en: This history of the Dominican Republic recounts how Santana negotiated a treaty with General Cazneau, President Pierce's agent, on October 6, 1854, whose secret stipulations are believed to have provided for ceding the Bay of Samana to the United States, though it was never ratified. It follows Santana's deposition in 1856, Baez's second term and expulsion in 1858, the Spanish invasion and the two-year war that ended with Spain's defeat and withdrawal, and the rapid succession of Salcedo, Espaillet, Polanco, Pimentel, Cabral and Guillermo that followed.
records.summary_es: Esta historia de la República Dominicana relata cómo Santana negoció un tratado con el general Cazneau, agente del presidente Pierce, el 6 de octubre de 1854, cuyas estipulaciones secretas, según se cree, contemplaban la cesión de la bahía de Samaná a los Estados Unidos, aunque nunca fue ratificado. Sigue con la deposición de Santana en 1856, el segundo gobierno de Báez y su expulsión en 1858, la invasión española y la guerra de dos años que terminó con la derrota y retirada de España, y la rápida sucesión de Salcedo, Espaillat, Polanco, Pimentel, Cabral y Guillermo que vino después.

records.headline: This history of Samana Bay recounts how the natives called the land Samana, how their cacique Cayacoa visited
records.summary_en: This history of Samana Bay recounts how the natives called the land Samana, how their cacique Cayacoa visited Columbus's ship, and how Columbus christened the bay De las Flechas after a skirmish there. It also tells how the English pirate Jack Banister, at the close of the seventeenth century, placed his guns on one of the cays and with 200 men beat off two English frigates, killing more than 120 of the assailants, an engagement that gave the islets the name Banister's Cays.
records.summary_es: Esta historia de la bahía de Samaná cuenta cómo los naturales llamaban Samaná a la tierra, cómo su cacique Cayacoa visitó la nave de Colón y cómo Colón bautizó la bahía De las Flechas tras una escaramuza en el lugar. Cuenta también cómo el pirata inglés Jack Banister, a fines del siglo XVII, colocó sus cañones en uno de los cayos y con 200 hombres rechazó a dos fragatas inglesas, matando a más de 120 de los asaltantes, un combate que dio a los islotes el nombre de Banister's Cays.

The natives called the land Samana, and Columbus christened the bay De las Flechas, in consequence of the skirmish. After remaining four days the Spaniards sailed upon their homeward voyage to Portugal, which they reached in nine more than six weeks. Reefs, islets, and rocks form natural defenses to the entrance of the bay, and are so situated that, if properly fortified, any hostile vessel that attempted to enter might be placed under a destructive cross fire. The favorable situation of some of these islets or cays for preventing the approach of an enemy was signally proved at the close of the seventeenth century, by that noted English pirate, Jack Banister, who, with his bold buccaneers, at that time infested the neighborhood. He had just arrived at [Samana?], accompanied by another vessel commanded by a Frenchman named Lagarde, when the commanders of two English frigates, hearing that Banister was anchored there, prepared to enter the bay. The pirate immediately caused the guns of his vessel to be placed ashore upon one of the cays, and defended the entrance with his own crew and that of the French vessel, consisting of 200 men. so effectively that more than 120 of the assailants were killed and the frigates forced to retire. Meanwhile, the antagonists of President Baez, led by Luperon and Cabral, issued violent protests against the Samana scheme in December 1869.
