records.full_text:
Senate · Washington, Jan. 10, 1871

When Mr. Trumbull concluded his remarks, Mr. Morton moved to take up the Senate Dominican joint resolutions as returned from the House, with an amendment providing that nothing contained in them shall be held, understood or construed as committing Congress to the policy of the annexation of the said republic of Dominica.

Mr. Sumner asked whether the Senator was aware that there would be some discussion. He submitted whether the consideration of the amendment could be proceeded with except by unanimous consent.

The Vice President replied that he was not aware of any rule which would prevent it from being taken up, except the pendency of the present bill.

Mr. Morton's motion was then agreed to, yeas 26, nays 16.

The House amendment to the Senate resolution was read, when Mr. Morton moved that the Senate concur.

Mr. Sumner asked for the yeas and nays. He knew not if Senators were aware of the painful news received since the debate on this subject, showing more than ever why we should hesitate in this business. It might be remembered that he protested against the whole measure as involving a bloody lawsuit. As prudent citizens we should not buy a lawsuit, especially one flowing with blood. Since the last discussion a proclamation of General Cabral had been received. He held in his hand an original copy in Spanish, printed on the island, against the usurper Baez, who, he had once said, was retained in power by the republic of the United States, a republic standing before the world to maintain the power of a pretender. Truly a sad part for a republic to play. The proclamation commenced with the words “God, country and liberty,” and was signed “Cabral, General of a division of the army,” in which he states “that the South was still in arms; that lately the enemy was beaten and routed; that reinforcements had reached the advanced posts, and without waiting for the infantry he vigorously attacked and defeated the foe,” &c. The proclamation is dated November 15, 1870. Mr. Sumner asked whether he was wrong when he called this a bloody lawsuit? This opened a melancholy picture; it was a picture of civil war. Here was a chief in the mountains, and another chief on the seashore, the latter sustained in power by the United States, and we were asked to proceed still further in this business. Better say with Macbeth, “I'll proceed no further in this business.” When this subject was formerly before the Senate he (Mr. Sumner) discussed the character of the President's Message as a menace to the people of Hayti. He did not then so soon anticipate a report from that republic; he did not at that time know how promptly he would be confirmed in his fears. He had before him a paper which, for its news, had not its superior in the country, the New York Herald. It was a paper known to be in no respect in sympathy with him or his conclusions. He thought proper to present this paper, bearing date January 5, 1871, as it gave news direct from Hayti. The letter is dated “Port au Prince, December 22, 1870,” with the heading:

Hayti—How the Haytiens receive the annexation news—Intense excitement on receipt of President Grant's Message—A guerilla warfare to be carried on—The Haytiens will fight to the death in support of their independence, and they threaten to burn the towns and then to take to the mountains—Demands on the government.

Mr. Sumner said that Senators smiled. He read it from an important newspaper, differing from him in sentiment. It did not seem unnatural that there was in the human heart a love of independence. When our independence is assailed we are aroused. He could not complain of the humble Haytiens, because their independence is assailed. It was a painful matter to think that this great country of ours, which should be a benediction, should become a terror and violence.

Mr. Pomeroy asked the Senator to yield the floor, so that he might suggest, by unanimous consent, that a vote be taken at two or three o'clock to-morrow.

Mr. Morton asked whether it would not be better to take a recess until this evening.

Mr. Sumner wished to offer an amendment to the resolution by adding at the end that the commissioners shall inquire specially of the alleged pendency of civil war in Dominica, the extent of the territory occupied by the respective parties; also the relations existing between Dominica and Hayti, and the claims of the latter on the former, and if there is a war or a menace of war between these countries.

Mr. Wilson wanted to adjourn and take up the subject to-morrow.

Mr. Trumbull hoped there would be no more excitement. If they should go into discussion now the session would be protracted. It would be better for them all to adjourn until to-morrow, and resume the matter at one o'clock. There was at this moment no attempt to prevent the action of the Senate. Should such an attempt be made to-morrow he trusted that every Senator would sit it out. He should not expect any Senator to try to prolong the proceedings.

Mr. Conkling asked Mr. Trumbull whether, after the measure had been once fully debated in the Senate and came back with an amendment tending to dilute it, an intention to reopen the whole subject afforded evidence to his mind of a factious opposition and a desire to delay and procrastinate.

Mr. Trumbull replied he never entered into an enterprise of that kind. He hoped the time would never come when he would enter into a factious opposition.

Mr. Stewart remarked that on a former occasion he stayed there all night; if he remembered correctly, the Senator relieved himself by going home. If this thing was to be repeated he would rather stay here to-night than any other night.

Mr. Warner sincerely trusted that no difficulty would arise. He thought the friends of the resolution would be glad to agree that the vote on the question should be taken at three or four o'clock to-morrow.

Mr. Pomeroy said he should be glad if the Senate by unanimous consent would agree to vote on the question to-morrow at four o'clock.

Mr. Saulsbury objected to the introduction, in effect, of the previous question by fixing an hour for the termination of the debate and taking a vote. Heretofore discussion was freely allowed. There never had been a more serious and important question than this. For the first time the Senator from Massachusetts is right. (Laughter.) He hoped the Senate would therefore allow the fullest discussion.

The Senate agreed to close the discussion at four o'clock to-morrow, when, at a quarter to five o'clock, an adjournment took place.

House of Representatives · Washington, Jan. 10, 1871

St. Domingo

The House resumed the consideration of the joint resolution for the appointment of commissioners to Dominica.

Mr. Willard (rep.) of Vt., a member of the Committee on Foreign Affairs, explained why he was found voting yesterday with so few of his republican colleagues against taking the resolution from the Speaker's table. He was opposed to the acquisition of the republic of Dominica by treaty or by joint resolution, and therefore he was opposed to taking any step looking to that acquisition. He was unwilling to authorize the friends of acquisition in working this machinery in aid of their scheme. It was charged, and not denied, that the commission was to return to Washington in time for Congress to act on its report at this session. What opportunity, then, would the Commission have for obtaining the information directed? Were the commissioners to inquire only from Fabens or Baez or Cazneau, or were they to traverse the republic and ascertain facts for themselves? If the latter they would require not two weeks, but six months or a year. The scope of the investigation was so broad that the idea that the commission was to bring back any plausible information was absurd. It was impossible for the commissioners to report anything from their own observation, but a report would be made and would be given to the country as the report of the commissioners.

Mr. Cox (dem.) of N.Y. opposed the joint resolution. After discussing the details of the measure he said the proviso of Mr. Ambler may not pass. It is sugar-coating. This measure is a pretence for information. It is annexation, in fact. If annexation is accomplished there is no need of this commission. If it is not to be accomplished what need is there, then? The information is already here, all we want. It was sent in last night late. Let us print and read what we have. It is voluminous; but does it give the list of grants and jobs attached to the treaty? I assert there is such a list; it was not sent to the Senate. It was called for by a resolution I drew last session. The annexation will be that of husks. The kernels are already gone to private parties. What do you want the annexation for—a port for commerce? Had you not better first revive commerce? How our phantom ships and ghostly steamers will sail into Samana! Oh, but it is Manifest Destiny! Democrats are invited to our old policy and charged with inconsistency by those who always opposed us. So you radicals are copying the despised democracy, are you? Is Saul also among the prophets? Remember that no one but Prince Arthur could wield the prince's magic sword. I am not against this scheme because it adds territory, but because it is a private, wicked scheme. Jefferson was for extended empire, but, as he said, “with self-government.” We are departing in many ways from the Jeffersonian standard and policies. I find but one precedent for this, and that hardly analogous. Not the Puritan way of taking the land of the Pequods, but Joshua sending spies to go over Jordan and search out the land. They went into Jericho and kept bad company. Is Baez your Rahab? I do not object because the territory is not coterminous. It is as near as California was. And because we swallow 200,000 colored people, after taking in 4,000,000, we can digest a few. The man who swallowed a pumpkin worried down a peach. I oppose the scheme because it is a specious, prearranged, corrupt job, and no commission can deodorize its putrescence. It is not to be compared to the achievements of the democracy in their expanding policy. When the democracy obtain power they will take care of the Monroe doctrine and territorial expansion.

Mr. Hoar (rep.) of Mass. explained the reasons which led him to differ from the majority of his colleagues. He did not concur in the idea that respect for the President of the United States required them to support this measure. The Committee on Foreign Affairs had refused to report a proposition for the appointment of commissioners to form a treaty, but instead of that had reported a proposition for the perpetration of a farce as great as had ever been enacted on such a subject. He was not willing to annex to a self-governing republic an island which would be filled with the scum of the tropics, the adventurers of all lands, who would come to influence the government of this country. In eleven States there was a rebellious element striking hands with Tammany Hall and striving to obtain possession of the government for the next four years. He was not willing to do anything to add to that danger.

Mr. Stevenson (rep.) of Ohio spoke in favor of the acquisition of Dominica and of its admission as one of the Territories of the Union. He did not want any information about the island. He found it crystallized in books. He found the island was rich in mines of gold and silver, copper, iron and coal. He found that it was rich in bays and harbors, one of which was the key of the Gulf. He found that the climate, though tropical, was less unwholesome than elsewhere in the West Indies. Its soil was exceedingly fertile, producing sugar, coffee, cotton and tropical fruits, and he found that its political constitution was modelled after that of the United States.

Mr. Voorhees (dem.) of Ind. sent to the Clerk's desk and had read a telegraphic despatch, stating that the Senate of Indiana had just passed a joint resolution instructing the Senators and requesting the Representatives from that State to vote against the annexation of St. Domingo. (Laughter.)

Mr. Orth (rep.) of Ind. remarked that those who knew how the democratic party in Indiana had obtained control of the Senate would not be surprised at the action of that body.

Mr. Potter (dem.) of N.Y. spoke against the acquisition of Dominica.

Mr. Swann (dem.) of Md., a member of the Committee on Foreign Affairs, also spoke against the joint resolution. He regarded the vote about to be taken as one involving important and vital issues. They all knew that before the making of the treaty oppressed Cuba was knocking at the doors of the American republic, but that the President of the United States, by his power and influence, defeated the proposition of the Committee on Foreign Affairs in aid of Cuba. He would not assail the President of the United States, but he would ask why did the President manifest such interest in this matter? Why did they see Senators and Cabinet officers lobbying in the House in favor of this measure? If the Postmaster General had no more influence in the House than he had in his own State of Maryland he should have been kept in his department attending to its business, which was sadly in need of attention, instead of coming to the House to try to influence its legislation.

Mr. Fitch (rep.) of Nev. said that he should vote for the pending resolution and against the eviscerating amendment of the gentleman from Ohio (Mr. Ambler). He should vote for it because he believed it would be followed by the annexation of Dominica, and then of Hayti and Cuba. He should have preferred to vote directly for a joint resolution of annexation.

Mr. Ela (rep.) of N.H. opposed the joint resolution as one tending to entangling alliances with a foreign people having no common interest with the people of the United States, who have already in their midst enough of conflicting elements. It meant the expenditure of vast sums of money for fortifications, navy yards and ships-of-war. He believed that the policy would end in disaster, and therefore he opposed it.

Mr. Farnsworth (rep.) of Ill. declared that he was opposed to the annexation of Dominica; that his constituents were opposed to it, and that, in his belief, nine-tenths of the constituents of every member were opposed to it. He was not so much of a manifest destiny man as his friend from Nevada (Mr. Fitch). He believed that the wings of the American Eagle might be spread too much, to the injury of that national bird. He would rather wait and people the territory already possessed. He would rather wait until Nevada got some population. (Laughter.) If the amendment offered by Mr. Ambler was agreed to he would vote for the joint resolution; but otherwise he would vote against it.

Mr. Butler (rep.) of Mass. sustained the joint resolution, and opposed the amendment of Mr. Ambler as only tending to produce delay, and thus kill the investigation.

Mr. Ambler (rep.) of Ohio denied having offered the amendment with any such intention.

Mr. Butler accepted the statement, but always attributed to a man's act its natural consequences.

Mr. Dawes (rep.) of Mass. asked him if the subject would not stand debate.

Mr. Butler replied that it would stand debate even from the false friend of the party. He had heard many painful things, but none more painful than the telegraphic despatch from Indiana, not that the Senate, organized through fraud, should send such a message, but that it should have been sent to the honored and revered Senator from Massachusetts (Mr. Sumner).

Since he's misnamed the Morning Star,
Nor man nor fiend hath fallen so far.

Mr. Voorhees remarked that a majority of republicans had been elected to the Indiana Senate, but that enough of them had been disgusted by the course of the party in Congress to induce them to vote as they did.

Mr. Butler went on to say that the political party which would set itself up against annexation of territory would come to naught. It was the doctrine of Jefferson, of Jackson, of Polk and of every democratic administration, and had now come to be accepted as the doctrine of the country.

Mr. Bingham (rep.) of Ohio sustained the joint resolution and opposed Mr. Ambler's resolution as unnecessary and only tending to promote delay. He pointed with pride to the vast acquisition of territory by this government in the past, and to the emigration from the north of Europe promoted by that territorial expansion. He was for an honorable acquisition of Dominica if it could be made and it were for the interest of the people, and it was to ascertain the facts that these commissioners were to be sent out. The only way to obtain knowledge of the facts was by inquiry. The resolution proposed an inquiry. He was for the resolution without the amendment.

At the conclusion of Mr. Bingham's remarks Mr. Garfield (rep.) of Ohio proposed a further extension of fifteen minutes of the time allowed for discussion.

Mr. Butler objected.

Mr. Garfield: Listen to the gentleman who cracks a whip objecting to debate! (Excitement.)

Mr. Butler: And listen to the man whose back smarts! (Laughter.)

Mr. Garfield: The gentleman's lash can hurt nothing but the cause in which he wields it.

Mr. Morgan (dem.) of Ohio: The House is under the domination of a whip-cracker.

Mr. Shanks (rep.) of Ind. supported the resolution as one which proposed to obtain information which would show the false position in which its opponents placed themselves and which would furnish an answer to the Senator from Indiana.

Mr. Poland (rep.) of Vt. also supported the resolution and opposed the amendment.

Mr. Kellogg (rep.) of Conn. said he would vote for the resolution and against the amendment.

The discussion was closed by Mr. Orth in support of the resolution. He declared that nothing could be discovered in the resolution, when honestly examined, which could deter any member, much less a member of his own side of the House, from giving it his support. It contained but the single proposition that the President of the United States, a man in whom a large majority of the House had confidence, should appoint three commissioners to proceed to the island of St. Domingo, and there acquire certain information to be laid before the American Congress and the American people. He knew nothing about the character of those commissioners, but he entertained no doubt as to the result of their report on the acquisition of that island. There was nothing in the resolution which committed the government to the rejection or acceptance of the report. If he had been honored by a seat in the next Congress he would not consider himself bound to vote for the adoption of the report which the commission would make to the next Congress, for he had no hope that the commission could proceed to its destination and accomplish its object in time for action at this Congress. He opposed the amendment offered by Mr. Ambler as one which would only cause delay and reopen in the Senate a quarrel which no friend of the union and harmony of the republican party would desire to see reopened. The adoption of the resolution, pure and simple, was due to the President, who had been unjustly assailed by political enemies and by political friends.

Mr. Brooks (dem.) of N.Y. asked Mr. Orth to allow him to offer an amendment that the Commissioners be appointed by the Speaker of the House and the President of the Senate.

Mr. Orth declined to do so.

Mr. Brooks reminded him of his promise to allow it to be offered at some time during the session.

Mr. Orth replied that the promise meant at some time during the present session. (Laughter.)

The House then proceeded to vote on Mr. Ambler's amendment, declaring that nothing in the resolution was to be construed as committing the government to the annexation of Dominica.

The amendment was agreed to, yeas 106, nays 76.

The joint resolution as amended was then passed, yeas 123, nays 63. The democrats voted solidly in the negative, and the following named republicans also voted no: Messrs. Beatty, Boyd, Finkelnburg, Hoar, Peters and Willard.

The joint resolution goes back to the Senate for action on the amendment.

records.headline: A Washington article traces the money behind the Samana lease to a West India fund obtained by Thaddeus Stevens
records.summary_en: A Washington article traces the money behind the Samana lease to a West India fund obtained by Thaddeus Stevens, saying Seward took $100,000 of it on his West Indies trip and General Babcock took the balance of $150,000, with which he leased the Bay of Samana. With that fund now exhausted, the article says, Senators friendly to the administration asked Representative Dawes to bring in a bill appropriating $150,000 for the payment now due to Fabens, but Dawes refused because there is no law for it, and Senator Sumner is quoted as saying the whole proceeding is without a shadow of law.
records.summary_es: Un artículo de Washington atribuye el dinero del arrendamiento de Samaná a un fondo para las Indias Occidentales obtenido por Thaddeus Stevens, y dice que Seward se llevó 100.000 dólares de ese fondo en su viaje a las Indias Occidentales y que el general Babcock se llevó el resto, 150.000 dólares, con los que arrendó la bahía de Samaná. Agotado ya ese fondo, dice el artículo, senadores afines a la administración pidieron al representante Dawes que presentara un proyecto para asignar 150.000 dólares para el pago que ahora se debe a Fabens, pero Dawes se negó porque no existe ley que lo autorice, y se cita al senador Sumner diciendo que todo el procedimiento carece de la menor base legal.
records.passage: appropriated, and soon after Seward, with his son and Admiral Porter, started for the West Indies. They took with them $100,000 out of Thad's West India fund, and spent the most of it. As is well known, this trip did not result in anything. When General Babcock went to St. Domingo he took the balance of this Seward -Stevens fund, 150,000, with which he leased the Bay of Samana. This fund is now exhausted, so that Envoy Fabens will not be able to collect his rent from that source. It is stated that a couple of Senators, friends of the administration, visited Mr. Dawes, chairman of the House Committee on Appropriations, and requested him to bring in a bill appropriating [illegible] for the payment now due. Dawes, who is a very careful fellow, and who does not seem to be aware of the existence of the "extra article" of the treaty, positively refused to comply with the request, for the reason, as he alleged, that there is no law for it. He told the Senators that he could only make appropriations which are authorized by law. Should Mr. Dawes adhere to his determination it is difficult to see where Mr. Fabens will get his rent. It might be taken out of the State Department Secret Service fund, but of late years this fund has been limited. Last year it was cut down from [illegible] to [illegible]. This year Judge Kelsey, who has charge of the Diplomatic and Consular appropriation bill, says he intends to keep it down to $100,000. This will not be sufficient for the payment of Mr. Fabens little bill. Senator Sumner

records.headline: This pro-annexation Herald editorial takes up both ends of the island
records.summary_en: This pro-annexation Herald editorial takes up both ends of the island, Dominica the Spanish and Hayti the French, and declines to repeat the financial, commercial, political and military reasons of President Grant's annual message: annexation, it says, is no new idea, for twenty-six or twenty-seven years ago John C. Calhoun was mixed up with intrigues for the island's acquisition in the interest of Southern African slavery. In the last year of the French dominion, it recalls, the Haytian end exported 47,500,000 pounds of clayed sugars, nearly 77,000,000 pounds of coffee and 7,000,000 pounds of cotton; as in St. Domingo African slavery was first established on American soil, so there it was first abolished in a deluge of blood. The material advantages of possessing the island are clear enough, the editorial says, provided its colored freemen can be brought to work; it puts the population of Dominica at about 140,000 and of Hayti at 575,000 — the window closing mid-sentence on the scheme of annexation.
records.summary_es: Este editorial anexionista del Herald aborda ambos extremos de la isla, Dominica la española y Haití la francesa, y se abstiene de repetir las razones financieras, comerciales, políticas y militares del mensaje anual del presidente Grant: la anexión, dice, no es una idea nueva, pues hace veintiséis o veintisiete años John C. Calhoun estuvo mezclado en intrigas para la adquisición de la isla en interés de la esclavitud africana del Sur. En el último año de la dominación francesa, recuerda, el extremo haitiano exportó 47,500,000 libras de azúcares mascabados, casi 77,000,000 libras de café y 7,000,000 libras de algodón; así como en Santo Domingo se estableció por primera vez la esclavitud africana en suelo americano, allí también fue abolida por primera vez en un diluvio de sangre. Las ventajas materiales de poseer la isla son bastante claras, dice el editorial, siempre que sus libertos de color puedan ser llevados a trabajar; estima la población de Dominica en unos 140,000 y la de Haití en 575,000: la ventana se cierra a mitad de una frase sobre el plan de anexión.

records.headline: The Senate resumed debate on the resolution for a commission to visit San Domingo, with Mr. Sumner proposing
records.summary_en: The Senate resumed debate on the resolution for a commission to visit San Domingo, with Mr. Sumner proposing that the commissioners inquire especially into the alleged civil war in Dominica, the territory held by the opposing parties, and the republic's relations with Hayti. Senator Schurz spoke at length in determined hostility to annexation, while Senators Stewart, Morton and Yates argued for expansion, Morton reporting that the leader Cabral favored annexation as an independent question but opposed it under Baez.
records.summary_es: El Senado reanudó el debate sobre la resolución para que una comisión visitara Santo Domingo, y el Sr. Sumner propuso que los comisionados investigaran especialmente la supuesta guerra civil en Dominica, el territorio ocupado por las partes en pugna, y las relaciones de la república con Haití. El senador Schurz habló extensamente con hostilidad decidida hacia la anexión, mientras los senadores Stewart, Morton y Yates argumentaron a favor de la expansión, y Morton informó que el caudillo Cabral favorecía la anexión como cuestión independiente pero se oponía a ella bajo Báez.
records.passage: the question being upon Mr. Sumner's motion to amend the House amendment by adding thereto, "and the Commissioners shall inquire especially into the alleged pendency of civil war in Dominica, and state the territory occupied by the opposing parties: also, relations to the existing Government of Dominica, and the neighboring Republic of Hayti, and pendency of any claim, territorial or pecuniarily, by the latter or the former, and whether any war now exists, or is menaced between these two governments." Mr. SAULSBURY moved as a farther amendment to add, and providing farther that Benj. F. [Curtis?], Millard Fillmore, and General W. T. Sherman act as Commissioners." Mr. STEWART took the floor in favor of the resolution. He argued that the farther territorial expansion of this country was a part of its manifest destiny, and a necessary incident to its growth in wealth and power. records.summary_en: The paper reports Senate debate on the Dominican annexation inquiry, in which amendments by Senator Sumner, including withdrawing U.S. naval forces from Dominican territory before the commission began its investigation, were rejected. Other rejected amendments concerned whether a Dominican government was authorized to treat for annexation and whether the Dominican constitution forbade ceding territory.

Otras enmiendas rechazadas trataban de si un gobierno dominicano estaba autorizado a negociar la anexión y de si la constitución dominicana prohibía ceder territorio.

records.headline: Under the rubric 'Commission of 1871,' the Tribune prints a geographical and historical account of the island
records.summary_en: Under the rubric 'Commission of 1871,' the Tribune prints a geographical and historical account of the island, in a window opening mid-argument: the island of Hayti, or San Domingo, lies between Cuba on the north-west, Porto Rico on the south-east and Jamaica on the south-west, with an area of 27,000 square miles and a population of 703,500; San Domingo proper, or the Dominican Republic, has an area of 17,500 square miles and a population of 136,800, according to the Geographisches Jahrbuch — the two republics so connected, the article says, that in discussing the one it is almost discussing the other. The island was called Hayti, the Highland Country, by the natives, and Hispaniola, or Española, and also San Domingo, by the Spaniards; its bold coast is a succession of rugged limestone mountains, and three great ranges traverse it from west to east, the highest summit of the central range rising 7,200 feet. The island was discovered by Columbus in 1492, and the Spaniards established their first permanent settlement on its northern coast — the window closing as it turns to their disappointment in the yield of gold.
records.summary_es: Bajo la rúbrica «Commission of 1871», el Tribune publica una descripción geográfica e histórica de la isla, en una ventana que se abre a mitad de un argumento: la isla de Haití, o Santo Domingo, se encuentra entre Cuba al noroeste, Puerto Rico al sureste y Jamaica al suroeste, con una superficie de 27,000 millas cuadradas y una población de 703,500; Santo Domingo propiamente dicho, o la República Dominicana, tiene una superficie de 17,500 millas cuadradas y una población de 136,800, según el Geographisches Jahrbuch: las dos repúblicas están tan conectadas, dice el artículo, que al discutir la una es casi discutir la otra. La isla era llamada Haití, el País de las Alturas, por los nativos, e Hispaniola, o Española, y también Santo Domingo, por los españoles; su costa audaz es una sucesión de montañas escarpadas de piedra caliza, y tres grandes cordilleras la atraviesan de oeste a este, con la cumbre más alta de la cordillera central elevándose 7,200 pies. La isla fue descubierta por Colón en 1492, y los españoles establecieron su primer asentamiento permanente en su costa norte: la ventana se cierra cuando pasa a su decepción con el rendimiento del oro.

records.full_text:
Misrule and oppressive taxation brought about the revolution of 1863, the restoration of the republic in 1865, and of Baez as President, but no cessation of the intrigues of Cabral, who, though much inferior in intelligence to Baez, who was educated in Paris, has many partisans in the interior, the principal strength of Baez being at the capital and the large seaports.

San Domingo is one of the richest in natural resources of the West India Islands, though thus far little has been done to develop them, notwithstanding the unusual mildness of its tropical climate and its many fine harbors. The soil is generally fertile in the highest degree, the soil of the mountain slopes being almost as fertile as that of the plains and valleys. The south part of the island is intersected and watered by many rivers, which not only increase the natural productiveness of the soil, but afford a means of communication with the interior districts.

records.headline: A letter from S. M. Boom protests
records.summary_en: A letter from S. M. Boom protests President Grant's Dominican annexation measure, arguing it was pressed by presidential patronage against the wishes and judgment of Republican newspapers and the mass of the people. Boom calls the commission sent to San Domingo a whitewashing effort and protests the measure as fraught with evil, and only evil, to the party and to the country.

Boom califica la comisión enviada a San Domingo de esfuerzo de encubrimiento y protesta contra la medida por estar cargada de mal, y solo mal, para el partido y para el país.

records.headline: A Washington despatch reports the commission's delayed sailing
records.summary_en: A Washington despatch reports the commission's delayed sailing: because of the delay in forming it, the expedition will not sail until Tuesday; the commission as now formed is generally spoken of with favor: Dr. Samuel G. Howe is named as a well-known philanthropist, and the Hon. Andrew White, a member of the commission, arrived to-day and had a pleasant interview with the President, who told him he was earnestly anxious to have everything probed to the bottom, wanted all villainy exposed if any could be found, and special search made for those lots on Samaná bay said to be marked 'Grant, Babcock & Co.' At the request of the Commissioner of Agriculture, the despatch adds, the President has authorized him to send a botanical department with the commissioners to San Domingo, to collect seeds, plants and minerals, and to study the nature of its climate and its adaptability for plantations, cinchona for quinine, the price of labor, and other objects connected with his department.

records.headline: The Santo Domingo commissioners mustered in strong force at the Astor House
records.summary_en: The Santo Domingo commissioners mustered in strong force at the Astor House yesterday, the Herald reports under the head 'The Commission in New York,' with their secretaries, interpreters, stenographers and representatives of the press: Ex-Senator Wade and Professor White arrived early in the morning, accompanied by Secretary Burton and Assistant Secretary Fred Douglass, and Commissioner Howe later in the day; Secretary Robeson, General Porter, the President's secretary and Commodore Alden, Chief of the Bureau of Navigation, had also come on from Washington to speed the parting commissioners and superintend the arrangements on board the Tennessee, which is to convey the three commissioners, the two secretaries, two stenographers and the press representatives — General Sigel and Fred Douglass, Jr., also accompanying the expedition. A meeting announced for the afternoon, to examine the credentials of the journalists to be granted passage, waited until evening for the last of them to appear; and it remains uncertain, the Herald says, whether the Tennessee can accommodate the whole party, a second vessel of war to be detailed if necessary — the window closing mid-sentence on the method of the investigation.
records.summary_es: Los comisionados de Santo Domingo se reunieron ayer en gran número en el Astor House, informa el Herald bajo el encabezado «The Commission in New York», con sus secretarios, intérpretes, taquígrafos y representantes de la prensa: el ex senador Wade y el profesor White llegaron temprano en la mañana, acompañados por el secretario Burton y el secretario adjunto Fred Douglass, y el comisionado Howe más tarde en el día; el secretario Robeson, el general Porter, el secretario del Presidente y el comodoro Alden, jefe de la Oficina de Navegación, habían venido también de Washington para despedir a los comisionados y supervisar los preparativos a bordo del Tennessee, que ha de conducir a los tres comisionados, los dos secretarios, dos taquígrafos y los representantes de la prensa: el general Sigel y Fred Douglass, Jr., acompañan también la expedición. records.headline: The Herald reprints testimony summed up in six points on Dominica
records.summary_en: The Herald reprints testimony summed up in six points on Dominica, the Spanish portion of St. Domingo: first, that it was thinly populated — the estimates varied widely, their endpoints not legible in this printing, and those who appeared to have the best opportunities for correct information fixed the number at less than 200,000; second, that its soil was rich, of a productive power beyond any corresponding extent of Cuba; third, that its actual production was greatly diminished by the disturbed state of its civil and political society, caused partly by the Spanish invasion, partly by the character of the population, and largely by the aggressive policy of the neighboring republic of Hayti; fourth, that all parties with equal unanimity sought refuge in a more intimate connection with the United States, regarded as the natural protector of republican institutions in the Western Hemisphere; fifth, that to this end all desired to lease the bay and peninsula of Samaná to the United States for a naval station, as a first step toward ultimate annexation; and sixth, that the bay of Samaná was the key to the Mona Channel, the 'Gate to the Caribbean Sea and the Isthmus of Panama.'
records.summary_es: El Herald reproduce un testimonio resumido en seis puntos sobre Dominica, la parte española de Santo Domingo: primero, que estaba escasamente poblada —las estimaciones variaron ampliamente, sus extremos no legibles en esta impresión, y quienes parecían haber tenido las mejores oportunidades de información correcta fijaron el número en menos de 200,000—; segundo, que su suelo era rico, de un poder productivo superior a cualquier extensión correspondiente de Cuba; tercero, que su producción real estaba muy disminuida por el estado perturbado de su sociedad civil y política, causado en parte por la invasión española, en parte por el carácter de la población, y en gran medida por la política agresiva de la vecina república de Haití; cuarto, que todos los partidos con igual unanimidad buscaban refugio en una conexión más íntima con los Estados Unidos, considerados el protector natural de las instituciones republicanas en el Hemisferio Occidental; quinto, que con ese fin todos deseaban arrendar la bahía y la península de Samaná a los Estados Unidos como estación naval, como primer paso hacia la anexión definitiva; y sexto, que la bahía de Samaná era la llave del canal de la Mona, la «Puerta al mar Caribe y al istmo de Panamá».

records.headline: The Tribune prints Mr. Fabens telling a story against himself
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints Mr. Fabens telling a story against himself — a stranger denouncing 'Fabens' to him as the wretch at the bottom of the San Domingo job, and opening his eyes when told, 'I am that Fabens exactly' — and then answering questions about the debt of the Dominican Republic: it was, he alleged, a very small debt, a part owing to Hayti, a part to a celebrated banking house of Curaçao, described as the Rothschilds of the West Indies, and besides some debt owing to Peabody & Company in London. The two marplots in the whole business, he said, were St. John, a British consul, and a former Spanish consul at San Domingo city, who had brought about the Spanish occupation: the Spaniard opposes the annexation of San Domingo by the Americans because Spain had failed in it, and St. John's conduct he attributed to the general cussedness of the British character in any matter of territorial emulation. Saget, the present usurper of Hayti in Fabens's word, he described with racial contempt, while Salnave, who had been killed at Cape Haytien, he called a hero; Saget, he said, had Salnave's body dragged behind an ox cart before the American consul's residence, where the wife and family of the dead President remained, as a token of his contempt of the United States.
records.summary_es: El Tribune publica al Sr. Fabens relatando una anécdota en su contra —un desconocido que le denunciaba a «Fabens» como el miserable que estaba en el fondo del asunto de Santo Domingo, y a quien se le abrieron los ojos cuando se le dijo: «Yo soy exactamente ese Fabens»— y respondiendo luego preguntas sobre la deuda de la República Dominicana: era, alegó, una deuda muy pequeña, una parte debida a Haití, otra parte a una célebre casa bancaria de Curazao, descrita como los Rothschild de las Indias Occidentales, y además alguna deuda debida a Peabody & Company en Londres. Los dos entorpecedores de todo el asunto, dijo, eran St. John, un cónsul británico, y un antiguo cónsul español en la ciudad de Santo Domingo, que habían provocado la ocupación española: el español se opone a la anexión de Santo Domingo por los americanos porque España fracasó en ella, y la conducta de St. John la atribuyó a la general maldad del carácter británico en cualquier asunto de emulación territorial. A Saget, el actual usurpador de Haití en la palabra de Fabens, lo describió con desprecio racial, mientras que a Salnave, que había sido muerto en Cabo Haitiano, lo llamó un héroe; Saget, dijo, hizo arrastrar el cuerpo de Salnave detrás de una carreta de bueyes ante la residencia del cónsul americano, donde permanecían la esposa y la familia del presidente muerto, como muestra de su desprecio hacia los Estados Unidos.

records.headline: The Tribune reprints the report of an Assistant Secretary of State
records.summary_en: The Tribune reprints the report of an Assistant Secretary of State on an earlier Samaná negotiation: the Dominican government, he reported, said it could not consent to an absolute sale of territory without violating an express provision of the constitution of the Dominican Republic just adopted, and that it would be inconvenient to await amendments to the constitution; it proposed instead a lease of Cayo Levantado, which commands the entrance of the bay of Samaná, with the use of the adjacent waters and certain specified privileges on the mainland and the peninsula. This, the Assistant Secretary said, would not answer the purpose of the United States: he declined to entertain the proposition, stating frankly that the United States wanted no place at all unless it was one it should have absolute control over while it owned it, large enough for its use, and one it could hold, fortify and maintain against all enemies; and he reported as the result of all the discussions that it was impracticable to conclude any arrangement at that time on the basis of the Department's instructions, the Dominican government offering only such privileges as it needs no treaty to obtain in any part of the civilized world — space for yards, wharves and buildings, to be paid for with United States money but not to be under its flag or protected by its guns — the window closing mid-sentence on the project's commendation by leading minds.
records.summary_es: El Tribune reproduce el informe de un subsecretario de Estado sobre una negociación anterior de Samaná: el gobierno dominicano, informó, dijo que no podía consentir en una venta absoluta de territorio sin violar una disposición expresa de la constitución de la República Dominicana recién adoptada, y que sería inconveniente esperar enmiendas a la constitución; propuso en cambio un arrendamiento de Cayo Levantado, que domina la entrada de la bahía de Samaná, con el uso de las aguas adyacentes y ciertos privilegios especificados en tierra firme y en la península. Esto, dijo el subsecretario, no respondería al propósito de los Estados Unidos: declinó aceptar la proposición, declarando francamente que los Estados Unidos no querían lugar alguno a menos que fuera uno sobre el que tuvieran control absoluto mientras lo poseyeran, suficientemente grande para su uso, y que pudieran ocupar, fortificar y mantener contra todos los enemigos; e informó como resultado de todas las discusiones que era impracticable concluir arreglo alguno en aquel tiempo sobre la base de las instrucciones del Departamento, ofreciendo el gobierno dominicano solo los privilegios que no necesita tratado alguno para obtenerse en cualquier parte del mundo civilizado —espacio para astilleros, muelles y edificios, a pagarse con dinero de los Estados Unidos pero sin estar bajo su bandera ni protegido por sus cañones—: la ventana se cierra a mitad de una frase sobre la recomendación del proyecto por las mentes principales.

records.headline: Mr. Somers Smith's letters to the Department, reprinted by the Tribune
records.summary_en: Mr. Somers Smith's letters to the Department, reprinted by the Tribune, open on December 9, 1868: he wrote that he had had repeated interviews for the past fortnight with President Báez — General Luperón had protested against any kind of arrangement between the United States and the Dominican Republic, and had written to President Salnave saying it was necessary to forbid all negotiations, to protect the negroes, 'the only caste that must govern this island'; Salnave refused to agree with him, and sent Mr. Báez the communication of General Luperón; General Pimentel had likewise protested; and the only true government that possesses power and popularity, and wishes to be under the protection of the United States, is that of Mr. Báez. On December 10 he wrote that Mr. Delmonte had called, at the special instance of the President, to inform him that Báez had addressed letters to the different authorities throughout the republic on the question of seeking the protection of the United States, and had received replies from all quarters affirming that such measure is most highly approved of, and is very popular in all parts of the country; and on December 19 he wrote again, that Báez is well aware that the Congress of the United States may not be inclined to bring about the annexation of any state or country by an act of war — the window closing inside the third letter.

El 10 de diciembre escribió que el Sr. Delmonte había acudido, por instancia especial del Presidente, para informarle de que Báez había dirigido cartas a las diferentes autoridades de toda la república sobre la cuestión de buscar la protección de los Estados Unidos, y había recibido respuestas de todas partes afirmando que tal medida es muy altamente aprobada, y es muy popular en todas las partes del país; y el 19 de diciembre escribió de nuevo, que Báez es bien consciente de que el Congreso de los Estados Unidos puede no estar inclinado a realizar la anexión de ningún estado o país mediante un acto de guerra: la ventana se cierra dentro de la tercera carta.

records.headline: The United States steamer Tennessee's sailing with the San Domingo commission
records.summary_en: The United States steamer Tennessee's sailing with the San Domingo commission is reported in the Dispatch's telegraphic briefs: the Tennessee sailed from New York on the afternoon of January 17 with the commission on board, and while proceeding down the harbor the commission organized, and resolved to proceed directly to San Domingo city, touching at the bay of Samaná only if the captain should think it advisable — their reason for going to the capital first being to show a proper respect for the authorities of the country.

records.headline: The News reprints two San Domingo items: a statement of position
records.summary_en: The News reprints two San Domingo items: a statement of position introduced as the Tribune's, and a special telegram on the commission's personnel. The first, from a writer of little previous interest in the question, holds that honest men and good patriots may fairly differ, and that the primary question is one of fact — do the people of the Dominican Republic really desire annexation to the United States? If they do, the writer inclines to receive them into the Union; if they do not, he strongly objects to annexing them by force, wanting no acquisitions of territory whose people prefer to keep apart; and he has heartily supported Senator Morton's proposition, because its adoption seemed calculated to shed light on the vital question. The second reports the commission now complete: Mr. Wade is to be chairman, and Professor Andrew White, of Cornell University, and Dr. Samuel G. Howe, of Boston, are the other members; Dr. Howe was notified by telegraph to-day of his appointment and directed, in case of acceptance, to repair to New York in time to sail on Tuesday, and it is understood he has since notified the President of his acceptance; General Sigel had accepted a place with the commission but has since given it up, for reasons not given — the window closing inside the item.

records.headline: A correspondent who travelled extensively through the island reports that in Santiago, Puerto Plata, La Vega
records.summary_en: A correspondent who travelled extensively through the island reports that in Santiago, Puerto Plata, La Vega, Macoris and Moca the universal sentiment was in favour of annexation, with people heartily tired of war and the better class of merchants and property holders enthusiastically endorsing President Baez and his policy. He reports that the election at Azua resulted in an unprecedented majority in favour of annexation, and denies the charge that grants had been given to those sent to negotiate the treaty. A further dispatch adds that news of the appointment of a United States commission was generally favourably received at St. Domingo.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal que viajó extensamente por la isla informa que en Santiago, Puerto Plata, La Vega, Macorís y Moca el sentimiento universal era favorable a la anexión, con un pueblo muy cansado de la guerra y la clase alta de comerciantes y propietarios apoyando con entusiasmo al presidente Báez y su política. Informa que la elección en Azua dio una mayoría sin precedentes a favor de la anexión, y niega la acusación de que se hubieran dado concesiones a los enviados a negociar el tratado. Otro despacho añade que la noticia del nombramiento de una comisión de los Estados Unidos fue recibida en general favorablemente en Santo Domingo.
records.passage: lar inquiries as to the sentiments of all classes on the subject. In the towns of Santiago, Puerta Plata, La Vega. Macoris and Moca the universal sentiment expressed was in favor of the measure. The people are heartily sick and tired of war, and look to annexation as the sound way to put a stop to such petty factions as that now held by Cabral. All the better class of merchants and property holders are enthusiastic in their endorsement of President Baez and his policy, and esteem him as a statesman and a patriot. The election at Azua resulted in an UNPRECEDENTED MAJORITY IN FAVOR OF ANNEXATION. and their voice was re-echoed all over the island. As to the charge that the [illegible] here to negotiate the treaty were interested in plantations, and that grants had been given them, it is like the balance of the Senator's statements? simply untrue. Your correspondent has had access to the records in the Department of the Interior, and knows that no grant ever has been given or offered to further this or any similar movement. He has, further, in the official handwriting of Minister Delmont, a specific denial of the charges made. This fact will be shown conclusively to the new Commission coming on its arrival. It is to be hoped in the future those opposing the proposed annexation will deal in facts, and not risk their reputations, as the Hon. Senator from Massachusetts has done, by making assertions unbecoming and unmanly.

records.headline: The Herald presents a legend from the childhood of President Báez.
records.summary_en: The Herald presents a legend from the childhood of President Báez. It recounts that upon his baptism as Bonaventura, his father was so moved by a dream that his son would deliver his people that he built a church to commemorate it. The paper observes that the fulfillment of the dream is well known to the people of the country it calls Dominica, where Báez has proven himself a statesman and patriot. A separate dispatch from Santo Domingo dated January 10 reports that news of the appointment of a United States commission was received favorably and with enthusiasm, though public improvements remain halted awaiting congressional action. It adds that agents of German, English, and American capitalists are investigating investment opportunities in anticipation of annexation, while Cabral continues depredations and writes proclamations without confronting Báez's troops.
records.summary_es: El Herald presenta una leyenda de la infancia del presidente Báez. Relata que, tras su bautismo con el nombre de Buenaventura, su padre quedó tan impresionado por un sueño según el cual su hijo sería el libertador de su pueblo que construyó una iglesia para conmemorarlo. El periódico observa que el cumplimiento de ese sueño es bien conocido para el pueblo del país que llama Dominica, donde Báez ha demostrado ser un estadista y patriota. Un despacho por separado desde Santo Domingo fechado el 10 de enero informa que la noticia del nombramiento de una comisión de los Estados Unidos fue recibida favorablemente y con entusiasmo, aunque las mejoras públicas permanecen paralizadas a la espera de la acción del Congreso estadounidense. Añade que agentes de capitalistas alemanes, ingleses y estadounidenses investigan oportunidades de inversión a la espera de la anexión, mientras Cabral continúa sus depredaciones y redacta proclamas sin enfrentarse a las tropas de Báez.

records.full_text:
I have not ascertained satisfactorily what is the situation here, but I will briefly state my belief on the subject.

President Baez, as a statesman and patriot, sincerely desires the annexation of Dominica to America. Delay in accomplishing this is attended by financial trouble, anxiety and risk of insurrection. There is a very rich and large extent of valley country on the western frontier of Dominica, watered by the affluents of the Artibonite, containing some small towns, bearing Spanish names, but of which the Dominicans have not had the complete possession. It is here that Cabral operates with a small predatory party, which President Baez believes is procured and supported by Hayti. Cabral is now at San Juan, say forty miles east of the boundary line between Dominica and Hayti, according to the treaty between Spain and France, with his followers, variable in numbers, but always small, whence he makes raids and retreats as occasion requires. His last operation, noised about as a movement to defeat annexation, was very insignificant and amounted to a few persons killed, wounded and captured by his followers. At Azua and at the posts on several roads leading westward from it the Dominicans have some 1,000 or 1,500 troops. These seem to be in position for defence against incursion from without or insurrection from within. They appear to form the main organization of troops, though there are some troops here and in other places. Though the ordinary expenses of the military, which is the chief administration, are estimated at about $7,000 monthly, the revenue is so small and the paper money of the country is of so little value that the employés of the government have been a long time unpaid, and measures are now proposed looking to treating the paper money like our Continental currency and the French assignats, and providing for receiving some real money for duties wherewith to carry on the government.

records.headline: The Herald's correspondent reports that a British flying squadron
records.summary_en: The Herald's correspondent reports that a British flying squadron has been ordered to rendezvous at Kingston, Jamaica, alongside other British naval movements in the region. The correspondent visited the USS Severn, flagship of the West India squadron, whose admiral reported that the Dominicans are unanimous in favor of annexation. The dispatch attributes the British naval precautions to London's apprehension over expanding United States influence and territorial foothold in the West Indies should Santo Domingo be annexed. It also notes that Admiral S. P. Lee, commanding the North Atlantic Squadron, was entertained at dinner by the Governor of Jamaica.
records.summary_es: El corresponsal del Herald informa que un escuadrón volante británico ha recibido órdenes de concentrarse en Kingston, Jamaica, junto con otros movimientos navales británicos en la región. El corresponsal visitó el buque estadounidense Severn, nave capitana del escuadrón de las Antillas, cuyo almirante informó que los dominicanos son unánimes a favor de la anexión. El despacho atribuye las precauciones navales británicas al recelo de Londres ante la expansión de la influencia y la presencia territorial de los Estados Unidos en las Antillas si se anexa Santo Domingo. También señala que el almirante S. P. Lee, al mando del Escuadrón del Atlántico Norte, fue agasajado en una cena por el gobernador de Jamaica.

records.headline: A published list of inquiries signed 'Bache' outlines the subjects of investigation
records.summary_en: A published list of inquiries signed 'Bache' outlines the subjects of investigation concerning the Dominican Republic. The questions propose examining the physical, moral, and intellectual condition of the Dominicans, their wealth and industrial capacity, and the country's agricultural, forest, marine, and mineral resources. They further call for investigating the climate, soil, harbors, public debt, foreign treaties, and the names of individuals holding territorial grants and concessions. The writer also asks about the meteorological character of the country it calls Dominica, including its exposure to hurricanes and earthquakes, and concludes by asking on what terms the Dominican government desires annexation to the United States.
records.summary_es: Una lista publicada de interrogantes firmada por «Bache» detalla los temas de investigación relativos a la República Dominicana. Las preguntas plantean examinar la condición física, moral e intelectual de los dominicanos, su riqueza y capacidad industrial, así como los recursos agrícolas, forestales, marinos y minerales del país. Piden además indagar sobre el clima, el suelo, los puertos, la deuda pública, los tratados extranjeros y los nombres de las personas que poseen concesiones y mercedes territoriales. El autor pregunta asimismo sobre el carácter meteorológico del país que denomina Dominica, incluyendo su exposición a huracanes y terremotos, y concluye indagando bajo qué términos desea el gobierno dominicano la anexión a los Estados Unidos.

records.headline: Andrew D. White
records.summary_en: Andrew D. White, a member of the San Domingo Commission, had a very agreeable interview with President Grant, who told him he was anxious to have everything thoroughly sifted. The President remarked with a broad smile that he wanted all villainy exposed if any could be found, especially those lots on Samana Bay said to be marked Grant, Babcock and others, and said he was open to conviction against the policy of annexation.
records.summary_es: Andrew D. White, miembro de la Comisión de Santo Domingo, tuvo una entrevista muy agradable con el presidente Grant, quien le dijo que deseaba que todo se investigara a fondo. El presidente comentó con una amplia sonrisa que quería que se expusiera toda villanía si se encontraba alguna, especialmente aquellos lotes en la bahía de Samana que se dice están marcados Grant, Babcock y otros, y dijo que estaba abierto a ser convencido en contra de la política de anexión.

records.headline: The Reporter notes a common mistake in referring to the country
records.summary_en: The Reporter notes a common mistake in referring to the country sought by the United States as 'Dominica.' The paper clarifies that the proper geographical designation is San Domingo and that the formal name of the nation is the Dominican Republic. It explains that the island of Dominica belongs to the British, situated in the Leeward group twenty-two miles north of Martinique and fully five hundred miles east of San Domingo, with another island of that name located in the Marquesas group of the South Pacific.
records.summary_es: El Reporter señala un error muy común al denominar «Dominica» al país al que aspiran los Estados Unidos. El periódico aclara que la designación geográfica correcta es Santo Domingo y que el nombre formal de la nación es República Dominicana. Explica que la isla de Dominica pertenece a los británicos, situada en el grupo de Sotavento a veintidós millas al norte de Martinica y a más de quinientas millas al este de Santo Domingo, y que existe otra isla con ese mismo nombre ubicada en el grupo de las Marquesas en el Pacífico Sur.

records.headline: An article in the Telegraph reviews the historical prosperity
records.summary_en: An article in the Telegraph reviews the historical prosperity and current agricultural potential of the island. It recounts that prior to the revolution of 1789–1790 San Domingo was the wealthiest colonial possession in the Americas, with prosperous French and Spanish sections exporting sugar, coffee, tobacco, and cocoa. Turning to the present, the paper asserts that the territory belonging to the Dominican Republic could support five million people, yet trade remains depressed and the people of Dominica lack even basic implements. It states there is not a single iron plow or sawmill within the republic, despite rich exports of mahogany, lignum-vitae, logwood, and other valuable timbers.
records.summary_es: Un artículo en el Telegraph examina la prosperidad histórica y el potencial agrícola actual de la isla. Recuerda que con anterioridad a la revolución de 1789-1790 Santo Domingo fue la posesión colonial más rica de las Américas, con partes francesa y española prósperas que exportaban azúcar, café, tabaco y cacao. Al abordar el presente, el periódico afirma que el territorio perteneciente a la República Dominicana podría sostener a cinco millones de habitantes, pero el comercio sigue deprimido y la población de Dominica carece incluso de herramientas básicas. Afirma que no existe un solo arado de hierro ni aserradero dentro de la república, a pesar de sus ricas exportaciones de caoba, guayacán, campeche y otras maderas preciosas.

records.headline: The Manchester Journal details the agricultural, forest, and mineral
records.summary_en: The Manchester Journal details the agricultural, forest, and mineral wealth of Santo Domingo. It reports that Dominican tobacco is exported in large quantities to Bremen and Hamburg, with the best quality grown on the great plain near La Vega, marketed in Santiago, and transported across the mountains to Puerto Plata for shipment. The article also notes extensive forests of superior mahogany, logwood, oak, ebony, and mountain pine suitable for shipbuilding, alongside abundant crops of plantains, fruits, and spices. In addition, it describes diverse mineral resources, including deposits of gold, silver, copper, iron, platinum, quicksilver, marble, and rock salt.
records.summary_es: El Manchester Journal detalla la riqueza agrícola, forestal y mineral de Santo Domingo. Informa que el tabaco dominicano se exporta en grandes cantidades hacia Bremen y Hamburgo, cultivándose la mejor calidad en la gran llanura cerca de La Vega, comercializándose en Santiago y transportándose a través de las montañas hasta Puerto Plata para su embarque. El artículo destaca además extensos bosques de caoba superior, campeche, roble, ébano y pino de montaña adecuado para la construcción naval, junto con abundantes cosechas de plátanos, frutas y especias. Asimismo, describe diversos recursos minerales, entre ellos yacimientos de oro, plata, cobre, hierro, platino, azogue, mármol y sal de roca.

records.headline: The Yorkville Enquirer sketches the Dominican Republic's geography
records.summary_en: The Yorkville Enquirer sketches the Dominican Republic's geography and history, noting that it comprises nearly three-fifths of the island, with an area of about 17,500 square miles and a population of roughly 136,000, of whom one-tenth claim to be white. The paper recounts early settlement from Columbus's first colony at Isabela and the founding of Santo Domingo in 1496, followed by French settlement in the west. It states that the whole island was reunited under President Boyer in 1822, until the inhabitants of the eastern part rose against the Haitians and established the independent Dominican Republic in 1844. The article contrasts this with the western section, describing Hayti as historically the richer and more populous portion, which once supplied Europe with half its sugar.
records.summary_es: El Yorkville Enquirer esboza la geografía y la historia de la República Dominicana, y señala que abarca casi tres quintas partes de la isla, con una superficie de unas 17,500 millas cuadradas y una población de aproximadamente 136,000 habitantes, de los cuales una décima parte afirma ser blanca. El periódico relata los primeros asentamientos desde la colonia inicial de Colón en La Isabela y la fundación de Santo Domingo en 1496, seguidos por el establecimiento francés en el oeste. Afirma que toda la isla fue reunificada bajo el presidente Boyer en 1822, hasta que los habitantes de la parte oriental se levantaron contra los haitianos y establecieron la República Dominicana independiente en 1844. El artículo contrasta esto con la sección occidental, describiendo a Haití como la porción históricamente más rica y poblada, que en el pasado abasteció a Europa con la mitad de su azúcar.

records.headline: The Tribune reports that Dominican insurgents under Cabral and other leaders
records.summary_en: The Tribune reports that Dominican insurgents under Cabral and other leaders are determined to challenge the United States protectorate over the Báez government, declaring themselves ready to engage American gunboats. General Pimentel landed near Monte Cristi with 500 Dominicans from St. Thomas and Turks Island, equipped from El Seibo, and is threatening Puerto Plata, while Cabral marches toward Azua. The dispatch notes that Santiago de los Caballeros is set to join the uprising, naming prominent figures of the restoration struggle, including Luperón and Sánchez, among the rebel leaders. It adds that while the insurgent forces are prepared to resist vigorously, the forces of Pimentel and El Seibo are expected to make overtures to the visiting United States commissioners.
records.summary_es: El Tribune informa que los insurgentes dominicanos bajo el mando de Cabral y otros caudillos están decididos a desafiar el protectorado de los Estados Unidos sobre el gobierno de Báez, y se declaran dispuestos a enfrentarse a las cañoneras estadounidenses. El general Pimentel desembarcó cerca de Montecristi con 500 dominicanos procedentes de Santo Tomás y las Islas Turcas, pertrechados desde El Seibo, y amenaza Puerto Plata, mientras Cabral marcha hacia Azua. El despacho señala que Santiago de los Caballeros se apresta a sumarse al levantamiento, y menciona entre los jefes rebeldes a destacadas figuras de la gesta de la Restauración, como Luperón y Sánchez. Añade que, aunque las fuerzas insurgentes están dispuestas a ofrecer una enérgica resistencia, se prevé que las tropas de Pimentel y de El Seibo presenten propuestas a los comisionados estadounidenses que visitan el país.

records.summary_en: The editorial argues that Dominican annexation, if accomplished at all, should be accomplished honorably, and that it cannot be while the U.S. fleet lies in the waters of Santo Domingo after threats conveyed to the president of the Haitian republic by the American minister and admiral. It calls the recall of the ships the first necessity of the situation and says an admiral who threatened to open fire on the Haitian chief should be called before a court of inquiry, as that was an act of war Congress had not declared.

records.headline: The Chicago Tribune analyzes the absence of news from the frigate
records.summary_en: The Chicago Tribune analyzes the absence of news from the frigate Tennessee, which departed carrying the United States commissioners to Santo Domingo. The paper explains that the vessel faced head winds, sluggish engines, and a limited twelve-day coal supply, leading its commander to rely largely on sail. Calculating the 1,600-mile voyage from New York to Samaná Bay, along with intended stops at Samaná and Santo Domingo City and transit to Havana, the article estimates that at least twenty-two days would be required before reports could reach the United States. It concludes that there is no real foundation for the prevailing rumors of disaster, and notes that officials in Washington remain confident of the expedition's safety.
records.summary_es: El Chicago Tribune analiza la falta de noticias sobre la fragata Tennessee, que zarpó con los comisionados estadounidenses rumbo a Santo Domingo. El periódico explica que la nave enfrentó vientos contrarios, un rendimiento deficiente de sus máquinas y un suministro de carbón limitado a doce días, lo que llevó a su comandante a navegar principalmente a vela. Al calcular la travesía de 1,600 millas desde Nueva York hasta la bahía de Samaná, junto con las escalas previstas en Samaná y la ciudad de Santo Domingo y el traslado a La Habana, el artículo estima que se requerirían al menos veintidós días para recibir informes en los Estados Unidos. Concluye que no existen motivos reales para los rumores de siniestro y señala que los funcionarios en Washington confían en la seguridad de la expedición.

records.headline: The Evening Telegraph publishes an explanation discounting concerns
records.summary_en: The Evening Telegraph publishes an explanation discounting concerns over the lack of intelligence from the frigate Tennessee and the Dominican commission. It notes that the commissioners had not decided whether to sail directly to Santo Domingo City or visit Samaná Bay first, which would alter the eight-to-ten-day sailing schedule. The report stresses that no regular commercial or telegraphic communication exists at this season from Dominican ports to points linked to the United States, and that no news should be expected until the steamer Tybee returns to New York in about ten days. It reassures the public by describing the Tennessee as a staunch, newly built vessel of nearly three thousand tons, fully capable of weathering the voyage.
records.summary_es: El Evening Telegraph publica una explicación para disipar la inquietud por la falta de noticias de la fragata Tennessee y de la comisión para Santo Domingo. Señala que los comisionados no habían resuelto si navegarían directamente a la ciudad de Santo Domingo o si visitarían primero la bahía de Samaná, lo que modificaría el tiempo de navegación estimado de ocho a diez días. Tranquiliza al público describiendo al Tennessee como un buque nuevo, sólido y de casi tres mil toneladas, plenamente capacitado para la travesía.

records.headline: A satirical squib in The Spirit of Democracy pretends to anticipate
records.summary_en: A satirical squib in The Spirit of Democracy pretends to anticipate the findings of the Dominican commission report while it is still in the pocket of commissioner Wade at Samaná Bay. The paper mockingly predicts the commission will report that the Dominican Republic is the original Garden of Eden with modern improvements, and that its inhabitants possess such moral and intellectual perfection that they seemingly escaped the fall of man. It further lampoons annexation arguments by suggesting that the United States cannot pay its debts, earn a living, or keep out of the poorhouse without annexing San Domingo.
records.summary_es: Una nota satírica en The Spirit of Democracy finge anticipar las conclusiones del informe de la comisión dominicana mientras este aún permanece en el bolsillo del comisionado Wade en la bahía de Samaná. El periódico predice en tono de burla que la comisión dictaminará que la República Dominicana es el Jardín del Edén original con mejoras modernas, y que sus habitantes poseen tal perfección moral e intelectual que aparentemente escaparon a la caída del hombre. Satiriza además los argumentos anexionistas al sugerir que los Estados Unidos no podrán pagar sus deudas, ganarse el sustento ni evitar la bancarrota sin la anexión de Santo Domingo.

records.headline: An official dispatch in The Portland Daily Press gives assurance of no alarm
records.summary_en: An official dispatch in The Portland Daily Press gives assurance of no alarm regarding the frigate Tennessee and the Dominican commission. The dispatch states that the vessel's route between Santo Domingo City and Samaná Bay remained undecided at departure, making the exact duration of the voyage variable beyond the baseline of eight to ten days under steam. It emphasizes that no regular telegraphic or shipping channels connect Dominican ports to points in contact with the United States at this season, meaning news cannot be expected until the steamer Tybee arrives in New York in about ten days. The statement adds that the Tennessee is a staunch vessel of nearly 3,000 tons, larger than any American warship in the West Indies.
records.summary_es: El Portland Daily Press publica un despacho oficial con respecto a la fragata Tennessee y a la comisión dominicana. El despacho explica que no debe cundir la alarma. El despacho indica que la ruta del buque entre la ciudad de Santo Domingo y la bahía de Samaná no estaba decidida al momento de zarpar, lo que hacía variable la duración de la travesía más allá de los ocho a diez días normales a vapor. Subraya que en esta temporada no existen canales telegráficos ni marítimos regulares que comuniquen los puertos dominicanos con puntos en contacto con los Estados Unidos, por lo que no pueden esperarse noticias hasta que el vapor Tybee arribe a Nueva York en unos diez días. La declaración añade que el Tennessee es un navío sólido de casi 3,000 toneladas, más grande que cualquier buque de guerra estadounidense en las Antillas.

records.headline: Commander John Irwin reports how, at President Baez's request, he sent Lieutenant Commander McCook and the Nantasket
records.summary_en: Commander John Irwin reports how, at President Baez's request, he sent Lieutenant Commander McCook and the Nantasket to Azua, where partisans of Cabral, accompanied by Haitians, were causing trouble, and then to Puerto Plata when Baez warned that Luperon's partisans, aided by men from Turks Island, intended to seize that place. He adds that Baez later reported Cabral moving on Azua with a force of Haitians and Dominicans, countenanced by the Haitian government, and asked him to carry dispatches to St. Thomas for the American government.
records.summary_es: El comandante John Irwin relata cómo, a petición del presidente Báez, envió al teniente comandante McCook y al Nantasket a Azua, donde los partidarios de Cabral, acompañados de haitianos, estaban causando problemas, y luego a Puerto Plata cuando Báez advirtió que los partidarios de Luperón, ayudados por hombres de las islas Turcas, pretendían apoderarse de ese lugar. Añade que Báez informó después que Cabral avanzaba sobre Azua con una fuerza de haitianos y dominicanos, con el respaldo del gobierno haitiano, y le pidió llevar despachos a St. Thomas para el gobierno estadounidense.

records.headline: The Weekly Ottumwa Courier prints an authoritative statement
records.summary_en: The Weekly Ottumwa Courier prints an authoritative statement on the frigate Tennessee, dispelling rumors concerning its safety. It explains that whether the commissioners proceeded directly to Santo Domingo City or stopped first at Samaná Bay, the voyage would require eight to ten days under steam, with additional time for any port call. The paper underscores that there are no regular winter communication lines connecting Dominican ports to telegraphic centers, so that news should not be anticipated until the steamer Tybee reaches New York in about ten days. It assures readers of the vessel's seaworthiness, describing the Tennessee as a newly built ship of nearly 3,000 tons, larger than any other in the West India squadron and commanded by an experienced officer.
records.summary_es: El Weekly Ottumwa Courier publica una declaración oficial sobre la fragata Tennessee, para disipar los rumores sobre su seguridad. Explica que, ya fuera que los comisionados se dirigieran directamente a la ciudad de Santo Domingo o hicieran escala previa en la bahía de Samaná, el viaje requeriría de ocho a diez días a vapor, con tiempo adicional por cualquier parada en puerto. El periódico subraya que no existen líneas regulares de comunicación invernal que conecten los puertos dominicanos con centros telegráficos, por lo que no deben anticiparse noticias hasta que el vapor Tybee llegue a Nueva York en unos diez días. Asegura a los lectores la navegabilidad del buque, describiendo al Tennessee como una nave de reciente construcción de casi 3,000 toneladas, más grande que cualquier otra en el escuadrón de las Antillas y comandada por un oficial experimentado.

records.headline: The New National Era publishes official naval correspondence
records.summary_en: The New National Era publishes official naval correspondence, outlining United States operations in Dominican waters. The instructions direct American naval commanders to secure United States authority at Samaná Bay and the capital, ordering them to capture or destroy any Haitian ships that might attack the Dominicans. The paper notes exchanges between Admiral Poor and Haitian officials regarding these orders, as well as an instance where President Báez requested an American warship to carry mails to St. Thomas. A concluding dispatch from Admiral Lee, dated January 16 at Santo Domingo, reports that he ordered the Swatara to provision at Samaná, directed the Nantasket from Puerto Plata to assist the arriving commission, and designated the commander of the Yantic as senior officer.
records.summary_es: El New National Era publica correspondencia naval oficial, que detalla las operaciones de los Estados Unidos en aguas dominicanas. Las instrucciones ordenan a los comandantes navales estadounidenses asegurar la autoridad norteamericana en la bahía de Samaná y en la capital, disponiendo capturar o destruir cualquier buque haitiano que ataque a los dominicanos. El periódico da cuenta de intercambios entre el almirante Poor y funcionarios haitianos sobre estas órdenes, así como de una ocasión en que el presidente Báez solicitó un buque de guerra estadounidense para transportar correspondencia a Santo Tomás. Un despacho final del almirante Lee, fechado el 16 de enero en Santo Domingo, informa que ordenó a la Swatara abastecerse en Samaná, envió al Nantasket desde Puerto Plata para asistir a la comisión entrante y designó al comandante del Yantic como oficial superior.
