records.headline: Why no dispatches have arrived from the frigate Tennessee is explained
records.summary_en: Why no dispatches have arrived from the frigate Tennessee is explained in an authoritative statement reprinted by The Emporia News. It points out that the vessel's destination remained uncertain between Santo Domingo City and Samaná Bay, with direct sailing estimated at eight to ten days under steam. The report notes that no regular winter lines of communication link Dominican ports to points with telegraphic service to the United States, meaning no intelligence should be anticipated until the steamer Tybee returns to New York. It adds that the Tennessee is a new, strongly constructed vessel—given here as nearly 300 tons burden—larger than any ship in the West India squadron and proven staunch in rough seas.
records.summary_es: The Emporia News reproduce una declaración oficial sobre la fragata Tennessee. La declaración explica por qué no han llegado despachos de la fragata. Señala que el destino del buque permanecía indeciso entre la ciudad de Santo Domingo y la bahía de Samaná, estimándose la navegación directa entre ocho y diez días a vapor. El informe destaca que en invierno no existen líneas regulares de comunicación que enlacen los puertos dominicanos con puntos provistos de servicio telegráfico a los Estados Unidos, por lo que no debe anticiparse información hasta el retorno del vapor Tybee a Nueva York. Añade que el Tennessee es un navío nuevo y de construcción sólida —registrado aquí como de casi 300 toneladas de carga—, mayor que cualquier barco del escuadrón de las Antillas y probado como resistente en mares agitados.

records.headline: The lack of communication from the frigate Tennessee is explained
records.summary_en: The lack of communication from the frigate Tennessee is explained in an official report carried by The New Orleans Republican. It states that the commissioners had not determined whether to land first at Santo Domingo City or visit Samaná Bay or another northern Dominican port, an itinerary that would extend the baseline voyage of eight to ten days. Because no regular communication exists during this season between Dominican ports and telegraph stations, the dispatch notes that intelligence cannot reasonably be expected until the return of the steamer Tybee to New York in roughly ten days. It reassures the public by describing the Tennessee as a staunch ship of nearly three thousand tons burden, launched since the close of the war and larger than any American vessel in the West Indies.
records.summary_es: El New Orleans Republican publica un informe oficial sobre la fragata Tennessee. El informe explica la falta de comunicación de la fragata. Señala que los comisionados no habían determinado si desembarcarían primero en la ciudad de Santo Domingo o si visitarían la bahía de Samaná u otro puerto del norte dominicano, itinerario que prolongaría la travesía estimada de ocho a diez días. Dado que durante esta época no existe comunicación regular entre los puertos dominicanos y las estaciones telegráficas, el despacho indica que razonablemente no pueden esperarse noticias hasta el regreso del vapor Tybee a Nueva York en unos diez días. Tranquiliza al público describiendo al Tennessee como un barco resistente de casi tres mil toneladas de porte, botado tras el fin de la guerra y más grande que cualquier buque estadounidense en las Antillas.

records.headline: The Chicago Tribune recalls a previous naval mission to examine
records.summary_en: The Chicago Tribune recalls a previous naval mission to examine public sentiment regarding annexation across all ports of the Dominican Republic. It recounts that the USS Nipsic lost her screw propeller three days out and had to put into Port-au-Prince, Haiti, under sail, leading Commander Selfridge to report that strong trade winds and currents made it impossible for a sailing vessel to beat to windward and forced him to abandon his Dominican orders. The paper suggests that if the frigate Tennessee suffered an engine breakdown in these same waters, she would face similar navigation difficulties, though it maintains there is still no evidence that any accident has occurred.
records.summary_es: El Chicago Tribune recuerda una misión naval previa destinada a examinar el sentimiento público hacia la anexión en todos los puertos de la República Dominicana. Relata que el buque estadounidense Nipsic perdió su hélice propulsora a los tres días de navegación y tuvo que arribar a vela a Puerto Príncipe, Haití, lo que llevó al comandante Selfridge a informar que los fuertes vientos alisios y las corrientes hacían imposible que un velero navegara contra el viento, obligándolo a abandonar sus órdenes respecto a Santo Domingo. El periódico sugiere que, de haber sufrido la fragata Tennessee una avería en sus máquinas en esas mismas aguas, enfrentaría dificultades de navegación semejantes, aunque sostiene que aún no existe prueba de que haya ocurrido accidente alguno.

records.headline: In a review of recent magazine literature, the New-York Tribune notices
records.summary_en: In a review of recent magazine literature, the New-York Tribune notices 'My Mission to San Domingo,' an article by Robert M. Walsh published in a monthly periodical. The review states that the work recounts Walsh's experiences as a special agent of the United States government sent to cooperate with British and French commissioners in negotiating peace between the Dominican Republic and the Empire of Hayti. While noting that the article presents many interesting observations on the social condition of the island, the paper criticizes the author's tone as too flippant for so serious a subject, marked by occasional touches of Wall Street slang.
records.summary_es: En una reseña de literatura periódica reciente, el New-York Tribune comenta «My Mission to San Domingo», artículo de Robert M. Walsh publicado en una revista mensual. La reseña señala que la obra relata las vivencias de Walsh como agente especial del gobierno de los Estados Unidos enviado a cooperar con comisionados británicos y franceses para negociar la paz entre la República Dominicana y el Imperio de Haití. Si bien destaca que el artículo aporta numerosas observaciones de interés sobre la condición social de la isla, el periódico censura el tono del autor por considerarlo demasiado frívolo para un tema tan serio, con ocasionales dejes de la jerga de Wall Street.

records.headline: A letter describes the annexation commissioners' planned route through Azua and the north side of the island
records.summary_en: A letter describes the annexation commissioners' planned route through Azua and the north side of the island, probably stopping at Port-au-Prince and Puerto Plata, and lists the questions regarded as most important, including whether a war with Haiti would soon follow annexation and whether the U.S. treasury could stand the required appropriation. It expects the commission's report to give a favorable summing up of the island's material resources and a strong commendation of Samana as a naval station.

Espera que el informe de la comisión haga un balance favorable de los recursos materiales de la isla y una firme recomendación de Samaná como estación naval.

records.headline: A correspondent of the New Orleans Republican describes the northern
records.summary_en: A correspondent of the New Orleans Republican describes the northern approach to the island, remarking that while the land remains uncultivated owing to Haitian incursions over the past half century, its picturesque beauty enchanted voyagers long at sea. The dispatch recalls Columbus’s first sight of the island and compares the harbor of Cape François with those of St. Nicolas and Samaná. It notes that Cape François sits at the western end of the great Vega Real, a fertile plain extending far into the Spanish or Santo Domingo part of the island. The writer highlights a historical tie to Louisiana, recalling that explorer Iberville organized naval operations there after establishing French settlements under Sauville and Bienville.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del New Orleans Republican describe la aproximación a la isla desde el norte y señala que, aunque la tierra permanece inculta debido a las incursiones haitianas durante el último medio siglo, su pintoresca belleza cautivó a los viajeros tras una larga travesía marítima. El despacho recuerda la primera impresión de Colón al avistar la isla y compara el puerto de Cabo Francés con los de San Nicolás y Samaná. Observa que Cabo Francés se ubica en el extremo occidental de la gran Vega Real, fértil llanura que se adentra profundamente en la parte española o de Santo Domingo. El autor resalta un lazo histórico con Luisiana al recordar que el explorador Iberville organizó allí operaciones navales tras establecer los primeros asentamientos franceses dirigidos por Sauville y Bienville.

records.headline: Writing from aboard the frigate Tennessee at sea, a special
records.summary_en: Writing from aboard the frigate Tennessee at sea, a special correspondent of the Herald assesses the political stakes surrounding the commission sent to Santo Domingo. The correspondent argues that President Grant has staked his administration and West Indian policy on annexation, meaning the expedition's outcome may make or unmake his presidency. If the commissioners and the journalists accompanying them report favorably on the territory, annexation would satisfy the American desire for expansion and bolster Grant's re-election prospects. Conversely, should the commission or the press report unfavorably, the scheme could collapse and strengthen the formidable opposition already mounted against the administration in Congress.
records.summary_es: Desde la fragata Tennessee en alta mar, un corresponsal especial del Herald evalúa la trascendencia política que rodea a la comisión enviada a Santo Domingo. El corresponsal sostiene que el presidente Grant ha apostado su administración y su política hacia las Antillas a la anexión, por lo que el resultado de la expedición podría consagrar o arruinar su presidencia. Si los comisionados y los periodistas que los acompañan emiten un informe favorable sobre el territorio, la anexión satisfaría el anhelo estadounidense de expansión y fortalecería las perspectivas de reelección de Grant. Por el contrario, si la comisión o la prensa informan desfavorablemente, el proyecto podría fracasar y robustecer la formidable oposición ya entablada contra la administración en el Congreso.

records.headline: A Herald dispatch from Samana reports local claims that there is no sickness there worth speaking about, while
records.summary_en: A Herald dispatch from Samana reports local claims that there is no sickness there worth speaking about, while cautioning that the people have every motive to make a favorable impression on the Commission. The writer finds the climate agreeable and the breezes on the bay balmy, the soil rich and the vegetation luxuriant with palms and coconut groves, but notes that little is raised for market except a few oranges and coconuts, and that improving the country is above all a question of labor.
records.summary_es: Un despacho del Herald desde Samaná recoge las afirmaciones locales de que allí no hay enfermedades de las que valga la pena hablar, advirtiendo a la vez que la gente tiene todos los motivos para causar una impresión favorable a la Comisión. El autor encuentra el clima agradable y las brisas de la bahía templadas, el suelo rico y la vegetación exuberante con palmeras y cocotales, pero señala que poco se cultiva para el mercado salvo unas cuantas naranjas y cocos, y que mejorar el país es ante todo una cuestión de mano de obra.

records.headline: The Herald profiles the leadership of the Dominican commission
records.summary_en: The Herald profiles the leadership of the Dominican commission under a display heading surveying the geography of Santo Domingo. The correspondent characterizes former Senator Benjamin F. Wade, the president of the commission, as an honest investigator who nonetheless believes firmly in manifest destiny and the eventual union of all North American lands with the United States. Noting Wade's longstanding support for Cuban independence and its ultimate incorporation into the Union, the dispatch considers him General Grant’s ideal choice to head the mission and command the confidence of Congress. It introduces Andrew D. White as another commissioner, describing him as a learned university president free from political prejudice against annexation.
records.summary_es: Bajo un encabezado ilustrado que examina la geografía de Santo Domingo, el Herald traza una semblanza del liderazgo de la comisión dominicana. El corresponsal caracteriza al expresidente del Senado Benjamin F. Wade, presidente de la comisión, como un investigador íntegro que, no obstante, cree con firmeza en el destino manifiesto y en la unión final de todas las tierras norteamericanas con los Estados Unidos. Al recordar el respaldo constante de Wade a la independencia de Cuba y a su eventual incorporación a la Unión, el despacho lo considera la elección ideal del general Grant para encabezar la misión y concitar la confianza del Congreso. Presenta además a Andrew D. White como otro de los comisionados, describiéndolo como un erudito presidente universitario exento de prejuicios políticos contra la anexión.

records.headline: The Herald analyzes appointments to the Dominican commission
records.summary_en: The Herald analyzes appointments to the Dominican commission and the political and racial strategy behind them. The correspondent describes the inclusion of a colored father and son in an official role on the commission as an adroit stroke of policy designed to satisfy domestic radicals and propitiate the colored citizens of the Dominican Republic. By displaying Black officials on an equality with distinguished white commissioners and naval officers, the paper argues that Dominicans will see proof of equal rights under the American flag and be encouraged to accept annexation. It observes that such integration illustrates the profound social revolution experienced by the United States over the previous decade, before noting the inclusion of German-American figures such as General Franz Sigel.
records.summary_es: El Herald analiza la estrategia política y racial tras las designaciones en la comisión para Santo Domingo. El corresponsal califica la inclusión de un padre e hijo de color con carácter oficial en la comisión como una hábil maniobra destinada a satisfacer a los radicales en el país y a ganarse a los ciudadanos de color de la República Dominicana. El periódico sostiene que, al mostrar a funcionarios negros en pie de igualdad con distinguidos comisionados y oficiales navales blancos, los dominicanos verán una prueba de igualdad de derechos bajo la bandera estadounidense y se sentirán inclinados a aceptar la anexión. Observa que dicha integración ilustra la profunda revolución social experimentada por los Estados Unidos durante la última década, antes de señalar la presencia de personalidades germano-estadounidenses como el general Franz Sigel.

records.headline: A Herald dispatch dated January 21 from aboard the frigate Tennessee announces
records.summary_en: A Herald dispatch dated January 21 from aboard the frigate Tennessee announces the arrival of the United States commissioners at Samaná Bay following a seven-day voyage. The correspondent reports a smooth passage without storms, noting that the ship relied on favorable winds and auxiliary steam, which was limited to four or five miles an hour because one boiler had been removed. Captain Temple is commended for his skillful navigation and courteous care of the expedition's members. Describing Samaná Bay, the dispatch notes its bold shoreline, deep entrance waters, and the small settlement of Santa Bárbara de Samaná, which it describes as an impoverished village of two to three hundred inhabitants situated on an inner bay inaccessible to large warships.
records.summary_es: Un despacho del Herald fechado el 21 de enero a bordo de la fragata Tennessee anuncia la llegada de los comisionados estadounidenses a la bahía de Samaná tras una travesía de siete días. El corresponsal informa de un viaje tranquilo y sin tormentas, señalando que el buque aprovechó vientos favorables y vapor auxiliar, limitado a cuatro o cinco millas por hora debido a que se le había desmontado una de las calderas. Se elogia al capitán Temple por su diestra navegación y sus esmeradas atenciones hacia los miembros de la expedición. Al describir la bahía de Samaná, el despacho destaca sus costas escarpadas, las aguas profundas en la entrada y el pequeño poblado de Santa Bárbara de Samaná, al que describe como una aldea modesta de doscientos a trescientos habitantes ubicada en una rada interior inaccesible para buques de guerra de gran calado.

records.headline: The dispatch reports that the officials at Samana pray for annexation, and explains that Colonel Abreu, whom the commissioners
records.summary_en: The dispatch reports that the officials at Samana pray for annexation, and explains that Colonel Abreu, whom the commissioners had honoured as the chief man there, is only the special agent and military commander of the Dominican government, while the governor of this section is General Acosta. The commission, with its geologists, botanists, naturalists and correspondents, has been sending parties out to explore the country bordering the bay and up to the mouths of the Yuna River, and going ashore daily to talk with the people and examine their plantations.
records.summary_es: El despacho informa que los funcionarios de Samaná ruegan por la anexión, y explica que el coronel Abreu, a quien los comisionados habían honrado como el hombre principal del lugar, es solo el agente especial y comandante militar del gobierno dominicano, mientras que el gobernador de esta sección es el general Acosta. La comisión, con sus geólogos, botánicos, naturalistas y corresponsales, ha estado enviando grupos a explorar el país que bordea la bahía y hasta las bocas del río Yuna, y desembarcando a diario para hablar con la gente y examinar sus plantaciones.

records.headline: A Herald correspondent reports arriving at St. Domingo City
records.summary_en: A Herald correspondent reports arriving at St. Domingo City on February 3 after a thirty-five hours' passage from Samana, and describes the so-called harbor as a poor roadstead the Tennessee could not leave, where vessels roll heavily even in a light land breeze. In the morning the ship fired a salute of twenty-one guns, which the Dominican fort returned, and the correspondent describes St. Domingo as a quaint, ancient and dilapidated town of seven or eight thousand inhabitants, the oldest place built by Europeans in America.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del Herald informa de su llegada a la ciudad de Santo Domingo el 3 de febrero tras una travesía de treinta y cinco horas desde Samaná, y describe el llamado puerto como una mala rada que la Tennessee no podía abandonar, donde los buques se balancean pesadamente aun con una ligera brisa de tierra. Por la mañana el buque disparó una salva de veintiún cañonazos, que el fuerte dominicano devolvió, y el corresponsal describe Santo Domingo como una ciudad pintoresca, antigua y derruida de siete u ocho mil habitantes, el lugar más antiguo construido por europeos en América.

records.headline: The Tennessee arrived at Santo Domingo from Samana, a few hours after the Nantasket, and the United States commissioners
records.summary_en: The Tennessee arrived at Santo Domingo from Samana, a few hours after the Nantasket, and the United States commissioners came ashore. The dispatch recounts how President Baez's offer of an unoccupied palace for the commissioners was declined by their secretaries, who instead rented a smaller house belonging to Baez and then had to ask him for cots and other necessities, while the correspondents accepted the palace. That day the commission paid a formal visit to Baez, presenting President Grant's autograph letter, and Baez replied that he desired a closer union of the two republics and offered every facility for inquiry, including hearing opponents of annexation.
records.summary_es: El Tennessee llegó a Santo Domingo desde Samaná, pocas horas después del Nantasket, y los comisionados de los Estados Unidos bajaron a tierra. El despacho cuenta cómo el ofrecimiento del presidente Báez de un palacio desocupado para los comisionados fue rechazado por los secretarios de estos, que en su lugar alquilaron una casa más pequeña perteneciente a Báez y luego tuvieron que pedirle catres y otros artículos necesarios, mientras que los corresponsales sí aceptaron el palacio. Ese día la comisión hizo una visita formal a Báez, presentándole la carta autógrafa del presidente Grant, y Báez respondió que deseaba una unión más estrecha de las dos repúblicas y ofreció todas las facilidades para la investigación, incluida la de escuchar a los opositores de la anexión.

M., having been preceded a few hours by the Nantasket. The Commissioners sent for the American Consul, Dr. Ames, to come on board, and this morning they all came ashore. A MISUNDERSTANDING. An unpleasant incident has occurred, which shows either great ignorance and mismanagement on the part of those who conduct matters for the Commissioners or else great cowardice on their part. The messengers who came across country from Samana, after presenting their despatches to President Baez, received from him an offer of an unoccupied palace for the accommodation of the Commissioners and suite. This offer was not to include provisioning them, but simply to afford them proper accommodations. As it was extended through courtesy, and as quarters for such a large party were difficult to be obtained, the offer was accepted on behalf of the Commissioners. When the latter arrived, however, their private secretaries in their wisdom deemed that public opinion in the United States would frown upon such an undemocratic proceeding, and vetoed the whole arrangement. Wise philosophers! They declined the kind offer and hired, for a small price, a smaller house, which, however, belongs to President Baez as his private property; and then, not being able otherwise to procure cots and many other necessary articles, they were compelled finally to ask President Baez to furnish them. records.headline: An editorial in the Chicago Tribune discusses the investigations of the United States Commissioners
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Chicago Tribune discusses the investigations of the United States Commissioners in the Dominican Republic. The paper observes that the Commissioners will hardly determine whether the population genuinely favors annexation until completing their tour of the interior, while noting their inquiries into whether Dominicans will accept American internal revenue laws. It reports that fortifying Samaná is estimated to equal the cost of fortifications around New York, and dismisses the island's mountain scenery as of little value to productive industry. Presuming that Dominicans desire annexation mainly because the Haitians oppose it, the paper cites President Báez's assertion that Cabral's band consists of predatory Haitians operating near the border, and notes that the Commission is inquiring whether annexing Dominica will ultimately require the purchase or conquest of Haiti.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en el Chicago Tribune comenta las investigaciones de los comisionados de los Estados Unidos en la República Dominicana. El periódico observa que los comisionados difícilmente determinarán si la población favorece genuinamente la anexión hasta que concluyan su recorrido por el interior, al tiempo que señala sus indagaciones sobre si los dominicanos aceptarán las leyes estadounidenses de rentas internas. Informa que se estima que fortificar Samaná igualaría el costo de las fortificaciones alrededor de Nueva York, y desestima el paisaje montañoso de la isla como de escaso valor para la industria productiva. Al presumir que los dominicanos desean la anexión principalmente porque los haitianos se oponen a ella, el periódico cita la afirmación del presidente Báez de que la banda de Cabral está compuesta por haitianos depredadores que operan cerca de la frontera, y señala que la comisión averigua si la anexión de Dominica requerirá en última instancia la compra o conquista de Haití.

records.headline: A dispatch in the Chicago Tribune reports that President Grant received
records.summary_en: A dispatch in the Chicago Tribune reports that President Grant received congratulations in Washington following the safe arrival of the frigate Tennessee in the Dominican Republic. The paper reprints a New-York Tribune correspondence dated Samaná Bay, January 27, describing the voyage of the vessel conveying the annexation Commissioners. The correspondent recounts that after fine initial weather, the ship encountered heavy seas and persistent discomfort off Cape Hatteras. Although the vessel made a moderately quick passage using both steam and sail, the writer notes that its machinery suffered from serious defects, contrasting its poor performance under steam with its faultless sailing qualities before sighting land on the morning of January 24 amid blistering heat.
records.summary_es: Un despacho en el Chicago Tribune informa que el presidente Grant recibió felicitaciones en Washington tras la llegada segura de la fragata Tennessee a la República Dominicana. El periódico reproduce una correspondencia del New-York Tribune fechada en la bahía de Samaná el 27 de enero, que describe la travesía del buque que transportaba a los comisionados de la anexión. El corresponsal relata que, tras un buen clima inicial, el barco encontró mares agitados y persistentes incomodidades frente al cabo Hatteras. Aunque el buque realizó una travesía moderadamente rápida utilizando vapor y velas, el autor señala que su maquinaria sufría de graves defectos, contrastando su deficiente desempeño a vapor con sus impecables cualidades de navegación a vela antes de avistar tierra la mañana del 24 de enero en medio de un calor abrasador.

records.headline: A Santo Domingo dispatch says President Baez emphatically denies reports that he intended to leave the country, and that because of reported
records.summary_en: A Santo Domingo dispatch says President Baez emphatically denies reports that he intended to leave the country, and that because of reported troubles at Azua the United States steamer Nantasket would probably sail for that port. The commission had a long interview with Baez and his cabinet, and Baez offered guides, interpreters and, if needed, a guard, and agreed to grant safe conduct to the city even to Cabral or any of his partisans whom the commission wished to consult.

records.headline: A correspondent for the New-York Tribune reports on agricultural
records.summary_en: A correspondent for the New-York Tribune reports on agricultural practices and tobacco culture in the Dominican Republic. The dispatch notes that local sugarcane remains strong and healthy for decades with minimal cultivation, while plows remain entirely unheard of in the area. The writer pronounces the tobacco grown near Samaná far superior to American varieties, judging a one-cent Samaná cigar superior to cigars selling for ten or fifteen cents in New York, and notes that local smoking tobacco brings twenty cents a pound compared to $1.50 or $2.00 in the United States. He adds that local inhabitants of both sexes frequently chew tobacco and share cigars socially from person to person, considering it wasteful to smoke an entire cigar alone.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del New-York Tribune informa sobre las prácticas agrícolas y el cultivo del tabaco en la República Dominicana. El despacho señala que la caña de azúcar local se mantiene vigorosa y saludable durante décadas con un cultivo mínimo, mientras que los arados son completamente desconocidos en la zona. El autor califica el tabaco cultivado cerca de Samaná como muy superior a las variedades estadounidenses, juzgando que un cigarro de un centavo de Samaná es mejor que los cigarros que se venden por diez o quince centavos en Nueva York, y señala que el tabaco para fumar local cuesta veinte centavos la libra frente a $1.50 o $2.00 en los Estados Unidos. Agrega que los habitantes locales de ambos sexos mastican tabaco con frecuencia y comparten los cigarros socialmente de persona a persona, considerando un despilfarro fumar un cigarro entero en solitario.

records.headline: A correspondent for the New-York Tribune reports on Dominican
records.summary_en: A correspondent for the New-York Tribune reports on Dominican public opinion regarding annexation, stating that Captain McCook found the inland town of Baní, with its 1,800 inhabitants, largely in favor of the measure. According to the dispatch, annexationist sentiment prevailed generally across the country except at Puerto Plata, where English and German merchants feared their commercial interests would suffer. The writer observes that residents around Samaná hold an abiding faith that annexation will make them wealthy, causing land prices to rise so high that no land can be purchased within five miles of the town. Under the heading "The Government," the report states that local magistrates disregard established legal codes, administering summary justice according to their own crude concepts of equity.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del New-York Tribune informa sobre la opinión pública dominicana respecto a la anexión, señalando que el capitán McCook encontró que el poblado interior de Baní, con sus 1,800 habitantes, está ampliamente a favor de la medida. Según el despacho, el sentimiento anexionista prevalecía en general en todo el país, excepto en Puerto Plata, donde los comerciantes ingleses y alemanes temían que sus intereses comerciales se vieran afectados. El autor observa que los habitantes de los alrededores de Samaná mantienen una fe inquebrantable en que la anexión los enriquecerá, provocando que los precios de la tierra suban tanto que no se puede adquirir ninguna parcela a menos de cinco millas del pueblo. Bajo el título «El Gobierno», el informe señala que los magistrados locales ignoran los códigos legales establecidos y administran justicia sumaria según sus propias nociones rudimentarias de equidad.

records.headline: The New-York Tribune's correspondent reports from Samaná on the activities of the United States Commission
records.summary_en: The New-York Tribune's correspondent reports from Samaná on the activities of the United States Commission to Santo Domingo. The dispatch states that on the morning of January 26, the Commissioners sent Captain Henry Wade, son of Commission President Benjamin F. Wade, overland with journalists on an eighty-mile journey to deliver an official communication to President Báez in Santo Domingo City. It reports that the Commissioners toured Samaná and its surrounding district in person, taking shorthand testimony from prominent local residents for submission to President Grant. Among those examined were Provincial Governor José Silvano Acosta, military commandant Enrique Abren, local magistrate Eugenio García, council member Benito García, and planter Benjamin Burr.
records.summary_es: El corresponsal del New-York Tribune informa desde Samaná sobre las actividades de la comisión de los Estados Unidos en Santo Domingo. El despacho señala que la mañana del 26 de enero los comisionados enviaron al capitán Henry Wade, hijo del presidente de la comisión Benjamin F. Wade, por tierra junto a varios periodistas en un viaje de unas ochenta millas para entregar una comunicación oficial al presidente Báez en la ciudad de Santo Domingo. Informa que los comisionados recorrieron personalmente Samaná y su distrito circundante, tomando testimonios taquigráficos de destacados residentes locales para presentarlos al presidente Grant. Entre los examinados figuraron el gobernador provincial José Silvano Acosta, el comandante militar Enrique Abren, el magistrado local Eugenio García, el miembro del concejo Benito García y el hacendado Benjamin Burr.

records.headline: An editorial in The New York Herald announces the safe arrival of the frigate
records.summary_en: An editorial in The New York Herald announces the safe arrival of the frigate Tennessee at Samaná Bay, Santo Domingo, on January 24, following a seven-day voyage from New York with all on board reported well. The paper denounces rival journals for fabricating sensational rumors questioning the vessel's seaworthiness or reporting it lost at sea. It asserts that the Herald never entertained any doubt regarding the ship's safety, having consistently maintained that the Commissioners had arrived at their destination to inspect the country and enjoy the tropical scenery. The editors declare satisfaction that their steady reporting allayed public anxiety, claiming that the paper's statements can always be relied upon as factual.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en The New York Herald anuncia la llegada segura de la fragata Tennessee a la bahía de Samaná, Santo Domingo, el 24 de enero, tras una travesía de siete días desde Nueva York con todos a bordo en buen estado. El periódico denuncia a los diarios rivales por inventar rumores sensacionalistas que cuestionaban las condiciones de navegación del buque o lo daban por perdido en el mar. Afirma que el Herald nunca albergó duda alguna sobre la seguridad del barco, habiendo sostenido constantemente que los comisionados habían llegado a su destino para inspeccionar el país y disfrutar del paisaje tropical. Los editores manifiestan satisfacción de que sus continuas informaciones calmaran la inquietud pública, asegurando que siempre se puede confiar en la veracidad de las afirmaciones del periódico.

A Tribune correspondent's account of Santa Barbara de Samana follows, describing a poor village of 80 or 90 bamboo and palm-thatched buildings along half a mile of shore, with about 250 inhabitants in the village and about 3,000 on the whole peninsula, a majority of the villagers speaking English.

Sigue el relato de un corresponsal de la Tribune sobre Santa Bárbara de Samaná, que describe un pueblo pobre de 80 o 90 edificios de bambú y techo de palma a lo largo de media milla de costa, con unos 250 habitantes en el pueblo y unos 3.000 en toda la península, hablando inglés la mayoría de los vecinos.

During the stay of the commission at Samana Bay the Tribune correspondent wrote as follows: Samana is a poor little dirty place enough, for all its romantic and picturesque appearance. It is built in a random haphazard sort of way along half-a-mile of curving shore at the foot of a ridge of high wooded hills, and what with its rambling lanes and grotesque huts, I think it is one of the most absurd places I ever saw. There are [illegible] or [illegible] buildings, all told, consisting for the most part of a light framework of scantlings brought from the States, and clapboarded with bamboos split in half and pressed flat by piling stones upon them while wet. The rude planking made in this primitive manner is from four to six inches wide and a half a quarter of an inch thick. Paint is almost unknown, but most of the huts are whitewashed. The roofing is of cocoa leaves bound together with vines. The flooring, when there is any, which is not often, consists of rough-hewn wood, or bark, or boughs, or the same leaves that are used for thatch. records.headline: A Tribune correspondent describes the San Domingo expedition's voyage to Samana Bay: charming weather for two days
records.summary_en: A Tribune correspondent describes the San Domingo expedition's voyage to Samana Bay: charming weather for two days, then stormy seas from the latitude of Hatteras onward, until land was sighted on the morning of January 24. Rounding Cape Cabron and entering the bay, the party saw the roofs of Santa Barbara de Samana, palm tops, green hills and small farm patches, and dropped anchor in the outer harbor at two o'clock that afternoon.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del Tribune describe el viaje de la expedición a Santo Domingo hasta la bahía de Samaná: tiempo encantador durante dos días y luego mares tormentosos desde la latitud de Hatteras en adelante, hasta que se avistó tierra en la mañana del 24 de enero. Al doblar el Cabo Cabrón y entrar en la bahía, el grupo vio los techos de Santa Bárbara de Samaná, las copas de las palmas, las colinas verdes y pequeños pedazos de tierra cultivada, y echó el ancla en el puerto exterior a las dos de esa tarde.

Writing in the Bay of Samana, on January 27, the Tribune correspondent says: We had charming weather for the first two days out cold, indeed, but bright and clear, with fresh and favoring winds, and every prospect of a pleasant voyage. But toward evening of the second day, in the rough latitude of Hatteras, our troubles began, and from that time until we neared our destination we experienced abundant discomfort and many stormy seas, though without any specially severe test of the seagoing qualities of the frigate. Using generally both steam and sails, we have made a moderately quick passage; but the behavior of the vessel under steam is far from satisfactory, and the machinery is found to be full of serious defects. As a sailer, however, the ship is pronounced faultless. We had been out of sight of land six days and a half, when on the morning of the 24th we heard from the look-out in the maintop the welcome cry of "Land ho!" and the passengers rushed upon deck. Thick clouds hung heavily over a dark line about two points off our starboard bow, hardly discernible at first; but as we came nearer we gradually traced the outline of the mountain range which stretched westward to the mainland from Cape Cabron at the extremity of the peninsula of Samana. The ship anchored in the outer harbor about two miles from the village, where the American flag floated over the property leased by the United States and the steamer Nantasket lay, and the commissioners landed to visit the local authorities.

El barco ancló en el puerto exterior, a unas dos millas del pueblo, donde la bandera americana ondeaba sobre la propiedad arrendada por los Estados Unidos y se encontraba el vapor Nantasket, y los comisionados desembarcaron para visitar a las autoridades locales.

Behind this mountain barrier and opening to the east lies the bay to which we were bound. The morning was the hottest we had yet felt. A burning sun blistered the deck. The brass work of the frigate glowed like fire, and the waters glittered like burnished metal under the blazing heavens. There was hardly a breath of air, and as we steamed through the calm sea the sails hung useless from the yards. Long before noon the whole country around the mouth of the bay was distinctly visible in outline. There were the hills rising abruptly close to the shore, the palisade-like rocks almost surrounding the peninsula, the irregular and picturesque profile of the range stretching back as far as the eye could reach. We could discover no table-land; we saw no beach; and at first there was no sign of life except in the waters, from which a flying fish darted now and then; nor was there much appearance of vegetation. records.headline: The correspondent describes sailing into Samana Bay on the 24th, rounding Cape Cabron to find Santa Barbara de
records.summary_en: The correspondent describes sailing into Samana Bay on the 24th, rounding Cape Cabron to find Santa Barbara de Samana coming into view, and anchoring in the outer harbour near the United States steamer Nantasket, with the American flag flying over the property leased by the United States. Ashore the next day, the party inspected the town's few public buildings, its Catholic church, a Methodist church being built, and schools whose pupils include descendants of the coloured colony sent here from Philadelphia, whose textbooks are all in English.

Al día siguiente en tierra, el grupo inspeccionó los pocos edificios públicos del pueblo, su iglesia católica, una iglesia metodista en construcción, y escuelas cuyos alumnos incluyen descendientes de la colonia de color enviada aquí desde Filadelfia, cuyos libros de texto están todos en inglés.
records.passage: It was not until we had rounded Cape Cabron and entered the mouth of the bay that the dingy aspect of the landscape changed, and we realized something of that tropical luxuriance and freshness upon which travellers have loved to dilate. In the distance, we soon descried, peeping above the horizon, the roofs of Santa Barbara de Samana, and little by little the whole scene broke upon us in its delicious beauty. One by one appeared the spreading tops of the palms. The brown hue of the hills changed to the most brilliant shades of green, their sides showed here and there a little patch of farm-land shut in by waving forest, and over all the country was a mantle of that soft, beautiful verdure which we never see at home except after the showers of early summer. We could appreciate now the rapture with which Columbus (and we were sailing so they say in the very track of the discoverer) painted the beauties of this island paradise. Close to the shore, in a little gully through which a stream of water ran singing to the sea, stood a hut, with round thatched roof and a single window looking out upon the ocean. Waving palms shaded it in front and rear; blooming hills sheltered it from the winds, and close by was a huge ragged rock against which the lazy surf beat perpetual music. This perfect picture was succeeded by views of larger houses, with patches of cleared land and groves of cocoonuts and bananas. records.headline: A correspondent at Samana describes landing with the commissioners and inspecting the town's public buildings
records.summary_en: A correspondent at Samana describes landing with the commissioners and inspecting the town's public buildings, including its Catholic church, a Methodist church being built, and its schools, where the textbooks are all in English and published in Philadelphia. He also describes the barefoot, half-clad troops guarding the jail, their varied knives, swords and muskets, and a village where more than half of the eighty houses are in some way devoted to trade.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal en Samaná describe el desembarco con los comisionados y la inspección de los edificios públicos del pueblo, incluidos su iglesia católica, una iglesia metodista en construcción y sus escuelas, donde los libros de texto están todos en inglés y publicados en Filadelfia. También describe a las tropas descalzas y semivestidas que guardan la cárcel, con sus variados cuchillos, espadas y mosquetes, y un pueblo donde más de la mitad de las ochenta casas se dedican de algún modo al comercio.

Later in the day the commissioners landed for a visit to the local authorities, and these latter distinguished officials hastened to return the compliment. It was not until the morning of the 25th that the rest of the party went ashore. SCENES AT SAMANA. After giving the description of the town, already published by us, the correspondent continues: We pushed our way through the lazy, grinning, good-natured crowd, and made an inspection of the public buildings of Samana. It did not take us long, for there are none at all except two churches and a calaboose and, perhaps, I should add a couple of school houses. The Catholic church is a rude structure, much larger than the inhabitants seem to require, and full of the oddest images dressed in quaint, not to say grotesque, habiliments. We tried to converse with the priest, but he spoke none of the three languages at the command of our party, so we gave it up. We afterwards learned that he was an Italian. A Methodist church is building under the auspices of the English Mission Society, and the British flag is displayed on the unfinished edifice as well as on the residence of the minister. The Rev. Joseph James is a colored man of ordinary intelligence, and has a congregation including about three hundred communicants, mostly descendants of the colored colony sent here from Philadelphia in [illegible]. records.headline: The Evening Telegraph reprints a report from a New-York Tribune correspondent
records.summary_en: The Evening Telegraph reprints a report from a New-York Tribune correspondent concerning agricultural conditions and public health in the Dominican Republic. The dispatch notes that local sugarcane grows vigorously without replanting, plows are unknown, and Samaná tobacco sells locally for twenty cents a pound compared to $1.50 or $2.00 in the United States. Under the heading "The Climate of Samana," the writer reports inquiries indicating that Santo Domingo is as healthy as any southern American state. Citing data gathered by Professor Newcomb from municipal officials and clergy, the report states that the Samaná peninsula, with an estimated population of about 8,000, recorded seventeen deaths and over 600 births during the preceding year, despite possessing neither a doctor nor a pharmacy.
records.summary_es: The Evening Telegraph reproduce un informe de un corresponsal del New-York Tribune relativo a las condiciones agrícolas y la salud pública en la República Dominicana. El despacho señala que la caña de azúcar local crece con vigor sin necesidad de replantar, los arados son desconocidos y el tabaco de Samaná se vende localmente a veinte centavos la libra frente a $1.50 o $2.00 en los Estados Unidos. Bajo el título «El clima de Samaná», el autor informa sobre indagaciones que indican que Santo Domingo es tan saludable como cualquier estado del sur estadounidense. Al citar datos recopilados por el profesor Newcomb ante funcionarios municipales y clérigos, el informe afirma que la península de Samaná, con una población estimada en unos 8,000 habitantes, registró diecisiete defunciones y más de 600 nacimientos durante el año anterior, a pesar de no contar con médicos ni farmacias.

records.headline: A dispatch from Samana reports that small parties of the scientific corps will be sent into the country in various directions
records.summary_en: A dispatch from Samana reports that small parties of the scientific corps will be sent into the country in various directions, and that those who examined the place as a naval station agreed the harbor where the coaling station stands should be obtained by the United States Government by lease or purchase. It says the commission hopes to start home soon after March 1, with no case of illness in the party.

Dice que la comisión espera partir de regreso poco después del 1 de marzo, sin ningún caso de enfermedad en el grupo.

records.summary_en: Under the printed heading "Safety of the Steamer Tennessee," the Green-Mountain Freeman reports that the vessel conveying the San Domingo Commission arrived safely at its destination on February 2 with all passengers in good health. The dispatch explains that the ship experienced a six-day detention at Samaná Bay owing to inadequate coaling facilities. According to the report, the Commissioners found the inhabitants of the peninsula generally in favor of annexation and determined that no United States official held any private land interest around the harbor. However, it notes that Fabena and associates, along with O. Sullivan, hold a perpetual lease at a nominal price on nearly all available deep-water frontage in Samaná harbor, while finding no valuable minerals in that area.

El despacho explica que el barco sufrió una demora de seis días en la bahía de Samaná debido a la falta de instalaciones para el suministro de carbón. Según el informe, los comisionados encontraron a los habitantes de la península generalmente a favor de la anexión y determinaron que ningún funcionario de los Estados Unidos poseía intereses privados en tierras alrededor del puerto. No obstante, señala que Fabena y sus asociados, junto con O. records.headline: An article in The Central Presbyterian describes the physical and political geography of the island of Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: An article in The Central Presbyterian describes the physical and political geography of the island of Santo Domingo in relation to President Grant's annexation policy. The paper emphasizes that the island is divided between two distinct republics: Haiti in the western two-fifths and the Dominican Republic in the eastern three-fifths. It stresses that President Grant proposes to annex the Dominican Republic rather than the entire island, noting that the question involves incorporating a distinct nationality. Demographically, the article estimates the Dominican population at 150,000 to 200,000, reporting that no more than one-tenth are white, that the remainder are Spanish-speaking persons of color, and that the population is predominantly Roman Catholic.
records.summary_es: Un artículo en The Central Presbyterian describe la geografía física y política de la isla de Santo Domingo en relación con la política de anexión del presidente Grant. El periódico destaca que la isla está dividida entre dos repúblicas distintas: Haití en las dos quintas partes occidentales y la República Dominicana en las tres quintas partes orientales. Subraya que el presidente Grant propone anexionar la República Dominicana y no la totalidad de la isla, señalando que la cuestión implica la incorporación de una nacionalidad diferenciada. Demográficamente, el artículo estima la población dominicana entre 150,000 y 200,000 habitantes, informando que no más de una décima parte son blancos, que el resto son personas de color hispanohablantes y que la población es predominantemente católica.

He describes the town's 80 or 90 buildings, its roughly 500 inhabitants, including descendants of Black colonists sent from Pennsylvania, Maryland and Delaware by the American Colonization Society in 1824, and a village sustained by local traffic from occasional vessels.

[FROM OUR SPECIAL CORRESPONDENT] On Board THE TENNESSEE, Samana Bay, Jan. 30.—Samana is, without doubt, the most fortunate starting point for any exploring expedition. One cannot help accumulating a fund of enthusiasm which may help him endure possible future hardships and disappointments. He who has glowing views of annexation feels them confirmed, while the anti-annexationist is content to have his pet arguments overthrown by such a pleasant refutation. Far out at sea the rough outline of the yellowish mountains disappoints and prepares one for a rocky, barren coast but, as you approach, the somber mountains gradually disappear, and ranges of low hills, covered with the densest vegetation, come in sight. A week before we had been in New York, with cold and sleet and leafless trees; now we were warm with linen clothes, and the hills before us were covered with a mass of trees and vines, green beyond all description, a clear, fresh color, such as the woods with us have in Spring after a shower. records.headline: The New-York Tribune outlines the specific investigative tasks
records.summary_en: The New-York Tribune outlines the specific investigative tasks assigned to specialists accompanying the United States Commission to Santo Domingo. The report notes that practical farmer Mr. Jacobs was asked to examine agriculture in the Yuna valley, Professor Newcomb to report on sanitary conditions at Samaná, Frederick Douglass to investigate the English-speaking colored emigrants on the peninsula, and General Sigel to report on military defenses. Under the heading "Santo Domingo: The Work of the Commission," the paper lists formal inquiries framed for the investigation concerning religion, schools, land distribution, and local sentiment regarding annexation to the United States. The inquiries also ask residents for their views on their former union with Spain and on a potential union of the republics of Hayti and Dominica under a single government, including whether desire for annexation stems from fear of Haytian subjugation.
records.summary_es: El New-York Tribune detalla las tareas de investigación específicas asignadas a los especialistas que acompañaban a la comisión de los Estados Unidos en Santo Domingo. El informe señala que se pidió al agricultor práctico Sr. Jacobs que examinara la agricultura en el valle del Yuna, al profesor Newcomb que informara sobre las condiciones sanitarias en Samaná, a Frederick Douglass que investigara a los emigrantes de color de habla inglesa en la península y al general Sigel que evaluara las defensas militares. Bajo el título «Santo Domingo: El trabajo de la comisión», el periódico enumera las preguntas formales formuladas para la indagación sobre religión, escuelas, distribución de la tierra y el sentimiento local respecto a la anexión a los Estados Unidos. Las preguntas también consultan a los residentes sobre sus opiniones acerca de su antigua unión con España y sobre una posible unión de las repúblicas de Haití y Dominica bajo un solo gobierno, incluyendo si el deseo de anexión se deriva del temor a la subyugación haitiana.

records.headline: The commissioners made an excursion to the plantation of Mrs. Dichmain
records.summary_en: The commissioners made an excursion to the plantation of Mrs. Dichmain, about two miles from Samana, where they drank fresh coconut milk and saw a primitive sugar mill turned by two bulls, with the juice boiled nearby into coarse brown sugar. Mrs. Dichmain, who has lived 42 years in Santo Domingo and has 15 children and 50 grandchildren, farms 100 acres producing bananas, pineapples, sugar, coffee and chocolate, and she told the visitors she was most decidedly in favor of annexation, longing intensely for quiet and order.
records.summary_es: Los comisionados hicieron una excursión a la plantación de la señora Dichmain, a unas dos millas de Samaná, donde bebieron leche fresca de coco y vieron un primitivo molino de azúcar movido por dos bueyes, con el jugo hervido cerca de allí hasta convertirlo en azúcar moreno grueso. La señora Dichmain, que lleva 42 años viviendo en Santo Domingo y tiene 15 hijos y 50 nietos, cultiva 100 acres que producen plátanos, piñas, azúcar, café y chocolate, y dijo a los visitantes que estaba decididamente a favor de la anexión, pues anhelaba intensamente la tranquilidad y el orden.

records.headline: An editorial in the Burlington Weekly Free Press discusses early reports
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Burlington Weekly Free Press discusses early reports from correspondents accompanying the San Domingo Commission. The paper notes that while correspondents describe the country's natural richness as beyond question, they find the harbors of Samaná Bay and Santo Domingo too shallow to accommodate the frigate Tennessee or first-class warships, while characterizing the population as lacking energy. It reports that the primary problems under review include the difficulty of assimilating a mixed population, uncertainty whether Dominicans would accept American taxation, the risk of a subsequent war with Hayti, and the substantial cost annexation would impose on the United States Treasury. The editorial adds that initial findings appear likely to vindicate President Grant's motives and show his connection to the treaty was strictly official.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en el Burlington Weekly Free Press comenta los primeros informes de los corresponsales que acompañaban a la comisión de Santo Domingo. El periódico señala que, aunque los corresponsales describen la riqueza natural del país como incuestionable, consideran que los puertos de la bahía de Samaná y de Santo Domingo son demasiado poco profundos para dar cabida a la fragata Tennessee o a buques de guerra de primer orden, a la vez que caracterizan a la población como carente de energía. Informa que los principales problemas bajo análisis incluyen la dificultad de asimilar a una población mixta, la incertidumbre sobre si los dominicanos aceptarían los impuestos estadounidenses, el riesgo de una guerra posterior con Haití y el costo sustancial que la anexión impondría al Tesoro de los Estados Unidos. El editorial añade que los hallazgos iniciales parecen respaldar los motivos del presidente Grant y demostrar que su vínculo con el tratado fue estrictamente oficial.

records.headline: In Santo Domingo, the New York Herald's correspondent reports
records.summary_en: In Santo Domingo, the New York Herald's correspondent reports on the itinerary of the United States Commission, estimating that the frigate Tennessee will return to the United States by late March or early April. The correspondent expresses concern that the Commission's report will consist of an overwhelming volume of unimportant details and one-sided Dominican testimony. According to the dispatch, after remaining nearly three weeks in Santo Domingo City, the Commission plans to travel to Azua to inspect the district and seek an interview with insurgent chief Cabral, before sailing to Port-au-Prince to assess whether the Haitians would be peaceful neighbors in the event of annexation. Under the heading "Departure of Parties for the Interior," the writer notes that two groups departed for the interior, including a scientific party under Professor Blake traveling overland to Puerto Plata.

El corresponsal expresa su preocupación de que el informe de la comisión consista en un volumen abrumador de detalles intrascendentes y testimonios dominicanos parcializados. Según el despacho, tras permanecer casi tres semanas en la ciudad de Santo Domingo, la comisión planea viajar a Azua para inspeccionar el distrito e intentar entrevistarse con el jefe insurgente Cabral, antes de navegar hacia Puerto Príncipe para evaluar si los haitianos serían vecinos pacíficos en caso de anexión. Bajo el título «Salida de comisiones hacia el interior», el autor señala que dos grupos partieron hacia el interior, entre ellos una comisión científica bajo la dirección del profesor Blake que viajaba por tierra hacia Puerto Plata.

records.headline: The New York Herald's correspondent in Santo Domingo City reports
records.summary_en: The New York Herald's correspondent in Santo Domingo City reports skeptically on Dominican mineral wealth, attributing glowing accounts to annexationist partisans of President Báez. In a letter dated February 13 under the heading "The Fabens-Sullivan-Holliday Job," the writer asserts that earlier waterfront concessions granted to Joseph W. Fabens and Judge Sullivan at Samaná are minor compared to larger speculative grants. He reports that under the Survey and Geological Exploration Grant, now controlled by the St. Domingo Company of New York and Ben Holladay, one-fifth of all public lands in the Dominican Republic was conceded to Fabens. The dispatch cites Article 5 of the concession contract, which President Báez delivered directly to the correspondent to establish the terms of the agreement.
records.summary_es: El corresponsal de The New York Herald en la ciudad de Santo Domingo informa con escepticismo sobre la riqueza mineral dominicana, atribuyendo las descripciones entusiastas a partidarios anexionistas del presidente Báez. En una carta fechada el 13 de febrero bajo el título «El negociado de Fabens, Sullivan y Holliday», el autor afirma que las concesiones anteriores sobre la ribera de Samaná otorgadas a Joseph W. Fabens y al juez Sullivan son insignificantes en comparación con adjudicaciones especulativas mayores. Informa que, bajo la concesión de exploración geológica y agrimensura, controlada actualmente por la St. Domingo Company de Nueva York y Ben Holladay, se otorgó a Fabens una quinta parte de todas las tierras públicas de la República Dominicana. El despacho cita el artículo 5 del contrato de concesión, que el presidente Báez entregó directamente al corresponsal para corroborar los términos del acuerdo.

records.headline: The Herald's correspondent reports that the evidence taken at Samana, and his own dealings with the people, show a majority
records.summary_en: The Herald's correspondent reports that the evidence taken at Samana, and his own dealings with the people, show a majority in favor of annexation to the United States, which they expect would bring peace and security to a productive country left desolate by constant revolutions. He identifies the opposition as the Cabralists, who largely object only out of hostility to Baez, foreign merchants fearing the loss of their monopoly, and a limited anti-American feeling, while the Catholic clergy decline to express any opinion and some intelligent Dominicans fear their race would be swamped by a superior one.
records.summary_es: El corresponsal del Herald informa que las declaraciones recogidas en Samaná, y su propio trato con la gente, muestran una mayoría a favor de la anexión a los Estados Unidos, de la que esperan que traiga paz y seguridad a un país productivo dejado desolado por las constantes revoluciones. Identifica a la oposición como los cabralistas, que en gran parte objetan solo por hostilidad hacia Báez, los comerciantes extranjeros que temen perder su monopolio y un limitado sentimiento antiestadounidense, mientras que el clero católico se niega a expresar opinión alguna y algunos dominicanos ilustrados temen que su raza quede ahogada por una superior.

records.headline: A correspondent quartered in St. Domingo City describes
records.summary_en: A correspondent quartered in St. Domingo City describes the so-called Palace, the former palace of the Spanish Captain Generals, where several of the visiting party are lodged, and a superstition that no president can reside there and leave it alive, which has kept President Baez and other presidents from living there. He also describes the city as a fortified place of about five thousand people, with walls, a ditch and guarded gates, narrow streets and mostly one-story houses.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal alojado en la ciudad de Santo Domingo describe el llamado Palacio, antiguo palacio de los Capitanes Generales españoles, donde se hospedan varios de los visitantes, y una superstición según la cual ningún presidente puede residir allí y salir con vida, lo que ha impedido que el presidente Báez y otros presidentes vivan en él. También describe la ciudad como una plaza fortificada de unos cinco mil habitantes, con murallas, un foso y puertas custodiadas, calles estrechas y casas en su mayoría de un piso.
records.passage: religion and religious orders the Spaniards brought with them. THE THEATRE. One of the largest convent churches is the theatre now, though, as might be supposed, it is little used. No European or American stars are likely to come here, nor even fourth-rate actors. THE PALACE. The best building, perhaps, in St. Domingo, is the so-called Palace, where several of our party are quartered. It was the viceregal Palace of the Spanish Captain Generals. It is not so old as some of the other buildings, and until a recent period was kept in order. It has the luxury of glass windows, which no other building I have seen has, and the floors are of coarse marble laid in squares. There was no furniture in it, and those of the Tennessee party who took quarters there had to provide themselves with stretchers to sleep on and such other things as they needed. This palace was offered by the government to the Commissioners for their accommodation while here; but the offer was declined, because it was thought such regal style would sound badly at home and because the Commissioners did not wish to accept any favor from the government.

records.headline: A fragment opening a dispatch in the Public Ledger urges the expulsion of President Báez
records.summary_en: A fragment opening a dispatch in the Public Ledger urges the expulsion of President Báez from Dominica, to prevent the country from being sold as merchandise. Reporting from Santo Domingo under a February 13 dateline, the paper states that the United States Commissioners have been in the capital eleven days and will likely remain another week, predicting the steamer Tennessee will not return before late March or early April. It reports that two parties departed for the interior: a scientific expedition headed by Professor Blake traveling across the island to Puerto Plata via La Vega and Santiago, and a second group composed of correspondents and General Sigel sent to Azua to open communication with Cabral. The dispatch notes that Cabral is positioned in the mountains eighty miles from Azua with a small force, and that Báez sent troops to oppose him.
records.summary_es: Un despacho en el Public Ledger comienza con un fragmento que insta a la expulsión del presidente Báez de Dominica, para evitar que el país sea vendido como mercancía. Al informar desde Santo Domingo bajo una fecha del 13 de febrero, el diario indica que los comisionados de los Estados Unidos llevan once días en la capital y probablemente permanecerán una semana más, pronosticando que el vapor Tennessee no regresará antes de finales de marzo o principios de abril. Informa que dos comisiones partieron hacia el interior: una expedición científica encabezada por el profesor Blake que cruza la isla hacia Puerto Plata vía La Vega y Santiago, y un segundo grupo compuesto por corresponsales y el general Sigel enviado a Azua para abrir comunicaciones con Cabral. El despacho añade que Cabral se encuentra en las montañas a ochenta millas de Azua con una fuerza reducida, y que Báez envió tropas para enfrentarlo.

records.headline: A correspondent for the Springfield Weekly Republican reports
records.summary_en: A correspondent for the Springfield Weekly Republican reports on economic and religious conditions on the Samaná peninsula. The dispatch observes that daily wages for common labor have risen from 30 to 50 cents in trade to $1.00 or $1.25 in cash since annexation was first discussed, while timber and mahogany along the Yuna River offer substantial commercial prospects. Under the heading "Religion and Education," the report states that over two-thirds of the inhabitants are Catholic and fewer than one hundred are Protestant. It notes that the Catholic pastor ministers to about 2,000 souls on the peninsula and at Sabana de la Mar, while a Methodist congregation led by pastor Jacob James counts 250 communicants representing roughly 500 African-American residents descended from immigrants sent to the island in 1824 by the American Colonization Society.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del Springfield Weekly Republican informa sobre las condiciones económicas y religiosas en la península de Samaná. El despacho observa que los jornales del trabajo común aumentaron de 30 a 50 centavos en mercancías a $1.00 o $1.25 en efectivo desde que se empezó a hablar de la anexión, mientras que la madera y la caoba a lo largo del río Yuna ofrecen importantes perspectivas comerciales. Bajo el título «Religión y educación», el informe señala que más de dos tercios de los habitantes son católicos y menos de cien son protestantes. Hace constar que el párroco católico atiende a unas 2,000 almas en la península y en Sabana de la Mar, mientras que una congregación metodista liderada por el pastor Jacob James cuenta con 250 comulgantes que representan a unos 500 residentes afroamericanos descendientes de inmigrantes enviados a la isla en 1824 por la Sociedad Americana de Colonización.

records.headline: A section of the commissioners' report describes life on the Samana peninsula, where the only schools the party
records.summary_en: A section of the commissioners' report describes life on the Samana peninsula, where the only schools the party could hear of included a small private school of not more than 20 pupils, started by the late Rev. Dr. Judd and now kept by his son at a dollar a month in tuition. It notes that the Methodists, whose meeting house was burned by the Spanish troops in 1863, are building a new one to hold 500 persons, that settlers of American descent are regarded as the foremost men in the settlement, and that farming is done on small plots of three to five acres with heavy hoes, picks and machetes rather than ploughs.
records.summary_es: Una sección del informe de los comisionados describe la vida en la península de Samaná, donde las únicas escuelas de las que el grupo pudo tener noticia incluían una pequeña escuela privada de no más de 20 alumnos, fundada por el difunto reverendo Dr. Judd y ahora a cargo de su hijo, con una matrícula de un dólar al mes. Señala que los metodistas, cuya casa de reunión fue quemada por las tropas españolas en 1863, están construyendo una nueva con capacidad para 500 personas, que los pobladores de ascendencia estadounidense son considerados los hombres más destacados del asentamiento y que la agricultura se hace en pequeñas parcelas de tres a cinco acres con azadas pesadas, picos y machetes en vez de arados.

records.headline: A correspondent for the Springfield Weekly Republican describes
records.summary_en: A correspondent for the Springfield Weekly Republican describes the arrival of the United States annexation Commissioners at Santo Domingo City in a letter dated February 4, 1871. Following a rough voyage from Samaná on January 30, the party anchored offshore amid heavy Caribbean swells that made remaining aboard ship intolerable. The dispatch states that although President Báez and his cabinet prepared the former government palace for their reception, the Commissioners declined the accommodation in order to reside in rented quarters at their own expense, adhering to republican simplicity. The delegation subsequently leased a vacant house belonging to President Báez for forty dollars a month, the identical rate paid by its previous tenant.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del Springfield Weekly Republican describe la llegada de los comisionados de anexión de los Estados Unidos a la ciudad de Santo Domingo en una carta fechada el 4 de febrero de 1871. Tras una difícil travesía desde Samaná el 30 de enero, la comitiva fondeó frente a la costa en medio de un fuerte oleaje en el Caribe que hacía intolerable permanecer a bordo del barco. El despacho indica que, aunque el presidente Báez y su gabinete acondicionaron el antiguo palacio de gobierno para su recepción, los comisionados declinaron el alojamiento para hospedarse en una vivienda alquilada a sus propias expensas, manteniendo la sencillez republicana. La delegación arrendó posteriormente una casa desocupada propiedad del presidente Báez por cuarenta dólares al mes, la misma tarifa pagada por su inquilino anterior.

records.headline: A dispatch from Santo Domingo City dated February 11 reports that the United States commission had met, exchanged
records.summary_en: A dispatch from Santo Domingo City dated February 11 reports that the United States commission had met, exchanged views, and decided to make its full field of inquiry wider than first expected, naming the middle of April for its arrival in Washington. Expeditions were out across the island: Professors Blake and Crane on their way to Puerto Plata, Professor Ward exploring, parties gone to Azua and to examine the copper region, and others making botanical and medical researches, while the second payment for Samana had not been made, leaving Baez embarrassed and nearly all his officers without pay.

records.headline: The Chicago Tribune reports that the second payment due for the lease of Samaná
records.summary_en: The Chicago Tribune reports that the second payment due for the lease of Samaná has not been made, a fact to which President Báez called the attention of the visiting United States Commission. The item explains that this perceived breach of faith seriously embarrassed Báez's government and left nearly all his public officials without pay, leading the Commissioners to conclude decidedly that the money should be paid immediately. The dispatch also recounts a novel legal occurrence in Santo Domingo, where an American was admitted to plead as principal counsel before the Supreme Court for the first time in its history. Colonel William McMichael of Philadelphia, an officer accompanying the Commission, undertook the case at the request of an American resident and won it.
records.summary_es: El Chicago Tribune informa que no se ha efectuado el segundo pago correspondiente al arrendamiento de Samaná, hecho sobre el que el presidente Báez llamó la atención de la comisión visitante de los Estados Unidos. La nota explica que este percibido incumplimiento de compromiso perjudicó gravemente al gobierno de Báez y dejó a casi todos sus funcionarios públicos sin cobrar sus sueldos, lo que llevó a los comisionados a opinar de manera decidida que el dinero debe pagarse de inmediato. El despacho relata además un suceso jurídico inédito en Santo Domingo, donde un estadounidense fue admitido para litigar como abogado principal ante la Corte Suprema por primera vez en su historia. El coronel William McMichael de Filadelfia, un oficial que acompañaba a la comisión, asumió el caso a solicitud de un residente estadounidense y lo ganó.

records.headline: The United States Commission's travel itinerary is outlined
records.summary_en: The United States Commission's travel itinerary is outlined in a dispatch in The Evening Telegraph, noting planned journeys to Samaná, Puerto Plata, and Santiago—described as the largest and richest interior city in the Republic—before visiting Cap-Haïtien and Port-au-Prince to consult Haitian authorities. Under the heading "No Formal Statement of Indebtedness," the correspondent reports that the Dominican government has not yet submitted an official statement of its liabilities to the Commission, though public lands are estimated at 11,000 square miles, or 8,000 under a liberal recognition of private titles. The dispatch adds that the Vicar Apostolic informed the Commissioners that the Catholic Church expects to retain undisturbed all its existing properties and buildings, while asserting no claim to Church lands confiscated under President Boyer.
records.summary_es: Un despacho en The Evening Telegraph describe el itinerario de viaje de la comisión de los Estados Unidos, señalando los recorridos previstos a Samaná, Puerto Plata y Santiago —descrita como la ciudad interior más grande y rica de la República— antes de visitar Cabo Haitiano y Puerto Príncipe para consultar a las autoridades haitianas. Bajo el título «Ninguna declaración formal de deuda», el corresponsal informa que el gobierno dominicano aún no ha presentado una relación oficial de sus obligaciones a la comisión, si bien se estiman las tierras públicas en 11,000 millas cuadradas, u 8,000 si se realiza un reconocimiento generoso de títulos privados. El despacho añade que el vicario apostólico informó a los comisionados que la Iglesia católica espera conservar sin perturbaciones todas sus propiedades y edificios actuales, al tiempo que no reclamará las tierras de la Iglesia confiscadas bajo el régimen del presidente Boyer.

records.headline: The Union Democrat reports that President Báez and his cabinet
records.summary_en: The Union Democrat reports that President Báez and his cabinet cordially welcomed the United States Commission to Santo Domingo, assuring the delegates that peace and political stability would follow annexation. Báez asserted that the Dominican people were unanimous for union, claimed that insurgent general José María Cabral commanded only Haitians, and alleged that Haiti was actively staging border incursions to influence the American visitors. According to the dispatch, Báez urged the Commissioners to examine all classes of inhabitants, promised every facility, and agreed to issue safe-conduct passes for Cabral and his officers to meet the Commission in person. The paper notes that the Commissioners found no evidence of civil disturbance, reported the crews of visiting American warships in good health, and learned that Dominican authorities were preparing a popular vote on annexation.
records.summary_es: The Union Democrat informa que el presidente Báez y su gabinete dieron una cordial bienvenida a la comisión de los Estados Unidos en Santo Domingo, asegurando a los delegados que la paz y la estabilidad política se consolidarían tras la anexión. Báez sostuvo que el pueblo dominicano apoyaba unánimemente la unión, afirmó que el general insurgente José María Cabral solo comandaba a haitianos y aseguró que Haití organizaba activamente incursiones fronterizas para influir sobre los visitantes estadounidenses. Según el despacho, Báez instó a los comisionados a interrogar a todas las clases sociales, prometió brindar todas las facilidades y acordó emitir salvoconductos para que Cabral y sus oficiales se entrevistaran personalmente con la comisión. El periódico destaca que los comisionados no encontraron indicios de alteración del orden público, informaron que las tripulaciones de los buques de guerra estadounidenses gozaban de buena salud y supieron que las autoridades dominicanas preparaban una votación popular sobre la anexión.

records.headline: The Worcester Daily Spy prints an excerpt from an address delivered
records.summary_en: The Worcester Daily Spy prints an excerpt from an address delivered in the Dominican Republic by an American Commissioner responding to an evening serenade. The speaker remarks that while residents have spoken to him of the convulsions, civil wars, and oppressions under which they suffer, his own senses have been overwhelmed by the natural beauty and agreeable atmosphere of the island. He praises the enchanting scenery, mild temperature, luscious fruits, and welcoming music, humorously noting that his senses have been won over in favor of the country. Concluding his remarks, the speaker states that while he cannot disclose what official advice he will offer regarding the annexation of the Dominican Republic, he feels personally inclined to annex himself and his family to the island.
records.summary_es: El Worcester Daily Spy publica un extracto del discurso pronunciado en la República Dominicana por un comisionado estadounidense en respuesta a una serenata nocturna. El orador comenta que, si bien los habitantes le han hablado de las convulsiones, guerras civiles y opresiones que padecen, sus propios sentidos han quedado cautivados por la belleza natural y el clima agradable de la isla. Elogia el paisaje encantador, la temperatura templada, las frutas exquisitas y la acogedora música, señalando con humor que sus sentidos han sido conquistados a favor del país. Al concluir sus palabras, el orador manifiesta que, aunque no puede revelar qué recomendación oficial ofrecerá respecto a la anexión de la República Dominicana, se siente personalmente tentado a anexarse a sí mismo y a su familia a la isla.
