records.headline: A dispatch from Port-au-Prince in the New National Era reports
records.summary_en: A dispatch from Port-au-Prince in the New National Era reports that the San Domingo Commission arrived from Azua on March 2 in excellent health, awaiting Commissioner White's arrival from Puerto Plata aboard the Nantasket alongside two scientific expeditions under Professors Blake and Ward. The correspondent notes that questions of public debt and the disputed boundary remain foremost, with Haitians opposing annexation though receiving the commissioners civilly. Reports questioning the seaworthiness of the Tennessee were met with indignation, with the party expecting to reach home between late March and April 1. In addition, Commissioner Wade is preparing a preliminary report and a letter to the President to be dispatched to New York aboard the steamer Port-au-Prince.
records.summary_es: Un despacho desde Puerto Príncipe publicado en el New National Era informa que la Comisión de Santo Domingo llegó desde Azua el 2 de marzo en excelente estado de salud, a la espera de la llegada del comisionado White desde Puerto Plata a bordo del Nantasket junto con dos expediciones científicas bajo los profesores Blake y Ward. El corresponsal señala que las cuestiones de la deuda pública y la frontera disputada siguen siendo primordiales, con los haitianos opuestos a la anexión aunque recibieron cortésmente a los comisionados. Los informes que ponían en duda las condiciones de navegación del Tennessee fueron recibidos con indignación, esperando la comitiva llegar a casa entre finales de marzo y el 1 de abril. Además, el comisionado Wade prepara un informe preliminar y una carta para el presidente que se enviarán a Nueva York en el vapor Port-au-Prince.

records.headline: A correspondent of the Boston Advertiser who accompanied the commissioners writes that its last days at the capital
records.summary_en: A correspondent of the Boston Advertiser who accompanied the commissioners writes that its last days at the capital were spent ascertaining the full extent of San Domingo's debt and the concessions made to private individuals, and that although the authorities insisted a million and a half dollars would discharge the entire public debt, a list of pending claims prepared after persistent effort made the debt much larger. He reports that under the terms Baez was willing to offer, the public lands not already disposed of were to be held to settle the claims, and that Baez had staged the show of support for annexation, with societies coming at his request and men who declared for the project in public giving strong reasons against it in private.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del Boston Advertiser que acompañó a los comisionados escribe que sus últimos días en la capital se dedicaron a averiguar la magnitud completa de la deuda de Santo Domingo y las concesiones hechas a particulares, y que aunque las autoridades insistían en que un millón y medio de dólares saldaría toda la deuda pública, una lista de reclamaciones pendientes preparada tras un esfuerzo persistente hizo la deuda mucho mayor. Informa que, según los términos que Báez estaba dispuesto a ofrecer, las tierras públicas aún no enajenadas quedarían afectas al pago de las reclamaciones, y que Báez había montado la demostración de apoyo a la anexión, con sociedades que acudían a petición suya y hombres que en público se declaraban por el proyecto y en privado daban fuertes razones en contra.

Here they will await the arrival of Mr. White, who came across by land from San Domingo to Puerto Plata. The harmony which marked the first week of the work at the capital was unfortunately almost entirely destroyed toward the close of the stay there; and this, of course, detracted much from the efficiency of the inquiry and the value of the results. records.headline: In a letter from Azua, W. G. Temple asks
records.summary_en: In a letter from Azua, W. G. Temple asks Commissioner B. F. Wade to withhold consent to a proposed expedition and to ask President Baez to forbid the gentlemen's passage through his lines. The correspondence adds that a new plan had been devised since arriving at Azua: Dr. Howe questioned prisoners and deserters from Cabral's force and, with Baez's consent, sent one prisoner back to the mountains with a letter to the revolutionary chieftain requesting a conference on Haitian territory, the messenger to receive three Spanish doubloons on his return.
records.summary_es: En una carta desde Azua, W. G. Temple pide al comisionado B. F. Wade que niegue su consentimiento a una expedición propuesta y que solicite al presidente Báez que prohíba el paso de esos caballeros a través de sus líneas. La correspondencia añade que desde la llegada a Azua se había ideado un nuevo plan: el Dr. Howe interrogó a prisioneros y desertores de la fuerza de Cabral y, con el consentimiento de Báez, envió a uno de los prisioneros de vuelta a las montañas con una carta para el jefe revolucionario solicitando una conferencia en territorio haitiano, y el mensajero recibiría tres doblones españoles a su regreso.

records.headline: A correspondent's travel account in the Springfield Weekly Republican describes
records.summary_en: A correspondent's travel account in the Springfield Weekly Republican describes an excursion departing Santo Domingo City, accompanied by Mr. Blackwell of the Journal, a native packer, and a local guide named Peter Bennett. The writer portrays Bennett as a well-known resident of Calle de San Francisco who manufactures inexpensive cigars and speaks a St. Thomas dialect. Mounted on small native horses weighing four to six hundred pounds and carrying several days' provisions, the travelers crossed the Ozama River by rope ferry, ascended past the suburb of Pajarito at the capital's original site, and entered upon the broad road through the forest toward the Great Savana and the Llanos.
records.summary_es: Una crónica de viaje de un corresponsal en el Springfield Weekly Republican describe una excursión que partió de la ciudad de Santo Domingo, acompañada por el señor Blackwell del Journal, un arriero nativo y un guía local llamado Peter Bennett. El redactor retrata a Bennett como un conocido vecino de la calle de San Francisco que fabrica cigarros económicos y habla un dialecto de St. Thomas. Montados en pequeños caballos nativos de cuatrocientas a seiscientas libras y con provisiones para varios días, los viajeros cruzaron el río Ozama en un transbordador de cuerda, ascendieron junto al suburbio de Pajarito en el sitio original de la capital y se adentraron en el ancho camino a través del bosque hacia la Gran Sabana y los Llanos.

records.headline: An article in the Springfield Weekly Republican outlines the four
records.summary_en: An article in the Springfield Weekly Republican outlines the four senatorial districts of the Dominican Republic—El Seibo, Santo Domingo, Azua, and Cibao—estimating the republic's total population at 130,000, with Cibao containing 70,000 residents and Azua bordering the Haitian frontier where Cabral maintains a revolt against Báez. The piece reviews the travels of the U.S. commissioners during their investigation of less than four weeks, noting that all visited the capital and Samaná, while Wade and Howe explored Azua, Howe alone visited El Seibo, and White crossed Cibao to Puerto Plata. The paper credits the factual accuracy of their inquiry, but contends that Commissioner Wade was committed in advance to annexation, whereas Dr. Howe and Mr. White were initially inclined toward a protectorate.
records.summary_es: Un artículo en el Springfield Weekly Republican describe los cuatro distritos senatoriales de la República Dominicana —El Seibo, Santo Domingo, Azua y el Cibao—, estimando la población total de la república en 130,000 habitantes, con 70,000 residentes en el Cibao y con Azua limitando con la frontera haitiana donde Cabral mantiene una revuelta contra Báez. El texto reseña los viajes de los comisionados estadounidenses durante su investigación de menos de cuatro semanas, señalando que todos visitaron la capital y Samaná, mientras que Wade y Howe exploraron Azua, Howe visitó en solitario El Seibo y White cruzó el Cibao hasta Puerto Plata. El periódico da crédito a la exactitud fáctica de su indagación, pero sostiene que el comisionado Wade estaba comprometido de antemano con la anexión, mientras que el Dr. Howe y el señor White se inclinaban inicialmente hacia un protectorado.

records.headline: An article in the Springfield Weekly Republican reviews official
records.summary_en: An article in the Springfield Weekly Republican reviews official communications demonstrating United States naval protection of President Báez's government in Santo Domingo. It cites warnings from naval officers and U.S. Consul Gautier stating that any outside interference would be considered an act of hostility against the American flag and that force would be used if necessary to protect the Dominican regime. The paper also quotes Minister Bassett urging the Haitian government to observe strict neutrality regarding Dominican internal affairs. The Republican observes that Haitian authorities responded with guarded courtesy, avoiding overt resentment while practically yielding to American demands.
records.summary_es: Un artículo en el Springfield Weekly Republican examina comunicaciones oficiales que demuestran la protección naval de los Estados Unidos al gobierno del presidente Báez en Santo Domingo. Cita advertencias de oficiales navales y del cónsul estadounidense Gautier afirmando que cualquier interferencia externa sería considerada un acto de hostilidad contra la bandera norteamericana y que se emplearía la fuerza de ser necesario para proteger al régimen dominicano. El periódico cita asimismo al ministro Bassett instando al gobierno haitiano a mantener una estricta neutralidad respecto a los asuntos internos dominicanos. El Republican observa que las autoridades haitianas respondieron con cautelosa cortesía, evitando un resentimiento abierto mientras cedían en la práctica ante las exigencias estadounidenses.

records.headline: In the Worcester Daily Spy, a correspondent outlines the nepotism of President Báez's administration.
records.summary_en: In the Worcester Daily Spy, a correspondent outlines the nepotism of President Báez's administration. It reports that his brother-in-law Gautier directs the cabinet, his brothers hold provincial governorships and military commands, and his sons serve as vice president and custom house collector. The dispatch notes that Commissioner Wade characterized the Dominican government after three weeks of study as an absolute military despotism in practice. While most citizens testifying before the commission publicly favored annexation, the correspondent reveals that many concealed their true sentiments out of fear of Báez, with several confidential witnesses expressing firm opposition on the belief that a peaceful change could not endure.
records.summary_es: La carta de un corresponsal en el Worcester Daily Spy describe el nepotismo de la administración del presidente Báez. Informa que su cuñado Gautier dirige el gabinete, sus hermanos ostentan gobernaciones provinciales y mandos militares, y sus hijos se desempeñan como vicepresidente y recaudador de aduanas. El despacho señala que el comisionado Wade definió al gobierno dominicano, tras tres semanas de estudio, como un despotismo militar absoluto en la práctica. Aunque la mayoría de los ciudadanos que testificaron ante la comisión apoyaron públicamente la anexión, el corresponsal revela que muchos ocultaron su sentir verdadero por temor a Báez, expresando varios testigos confidenciales una firme oposición bajo la convicción de que un cambio pacífico no podría perdurar.

records.headline: An editorial in the Springfield Weekly Republican reports the arrival
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Springfield Weekly Republican reports the arrival at the Florida Keys of the returning expedition of over thirty commissioners, secretaries, and correspondents, with only three or four members declaring against annexation. The paper highlights disagreements within the commission itself, observing that Commissioner Wade was eager to return promptly to urge Congress to annex the Dominicans, having repeatedly assured President Grant of a favorable report. In contrast, Dr. Howe and Mr. White refused to hurry, insisting on a comprehensive investigation rather than merely endorsing executive wishes, with White collecting scientific information and specimens for his university.
records.summary_es: Un editorial del Springfield Weekly Republican informa del regreso de la expedición, integrada por más de treinta comisionados, secretarios y corresponsales, que ha llegado a los cayos de Florida, con solo tres o cuatro miembros manifestándose en contra de la anexión. El periódico resalta las discrepancias dentro de la propia comisión, observando que el comisionado Wade estaba ansioso por regresar con prontitud para instar al Congreso a anexar a los dominicanos, habiendo asegurado reiteradamente al presidente Grant un informe favorable. En contraste, el Dr. Howe y el señor White rehusaron apresurarse, insistiendo en una investigación exhaustiva en lugar de limitarse a refrendar los deseos del ejecutivo, mientras White recolectaba información y especímenes científicos para su universidad.

records.headline: The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer prints resolutions introduced
records.summary_en: The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer prints resolutions introduced in the Senate concerning the deployment of the United States Navy off the coasts of St. Domingo during annexation negotiations. The preamble declares that negotiations for territorial acquisition with a smaller people should be free from the menace of superior force, recalling Spain's boast that its 1861 re-incorporation of Dominica occurred without the presence of a Spanish warship or soldier. The resolution urges that United States naval forces be withdrawn from Dominican coasts while negotiations are pending, asserting that republican institutions must respect the sovereign equality of all nations under international law.
records.summary_es: The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer publica resoluciones presentadas en el Senado respecto al despliegue de la Armada de los Estados Unidos frente a las costas de Santo Domingo durante las negociaciones de anexión. El preámbulo declara que las negociaciones para la adquisición territorial con un pueblo más pequeño deben estar exentas de la amenaza de una fuerza superior, recordando la afirmación de España de que su reincorporación de Dominica en 1861 se produjo sin la presencia de buques de guerra ni soldados españoles. La resolución insta a retirar las fuerzas navales de los Estados Unidos de las costas dominicanas mientras las negociaciones estén pendientes, afirmando que las instituciones republicanas deben respetar la igualdad soberana de todas las naciones conforme al derecho internacional.

records.headline: The New York Herald publishes an address sent to Senator Charles Sumner
records.summary_en: The New York Herald publishes an address sent to Senator Charles Sumner by Dominican exiles residing in Aguadilla, Puerto Rico, which accompanied a formal protest against annexation that Sumner was ruled out of order when attempting to present to the Senate. The paper remarks that the document presents a powerful argument from Dominican refugees, demonstrating that citizens of Dominica are far from unanimous in supporting annexation. Writing in defense of Dominican liberty and independence, the exiles submit an authoritative statement on conditions under General Báez, affirming that their representation reflects patriotic duty rather than personal animosity.
records.summary_es: El New York Herald publica una comunicación dirigida al senador Charles Sumner por exiliados dominicanos residentes en Aguadilla, Puerto Rico, la cual acompañaba una protesta formal contra la anexión que Sumner intentó presentar en el Senado antes de que fuera declarada fuera de orden. El periódico señala que el documento ofrece un argumento contundente por parte de refugiados dominicanos, demostrando que los ciudadanos de Dominica están lejos de apoyar unánimemente la anexión. Al escribir en defensa de la libertad y la independencia dominicanas, los exiliados presentan una exposición autorizada sobre las condiciones bajo el general Báez, afirmando que su representación responde al deber patriótico y no a la animosidad personal.

records.headline: In a Senate speech published in the Evening Star, Senator Charles Sumner reviews
records.summary_en: In a Senate speech published in the Evening Star, Senator Charles Sumner reviews Dominican political history, stating that while he always wished to extend assistance to Dominica, he never encouraged armed uprisings. Sumner recounts that when President Cabral sought American aid and offered a lease of Samaná Bay to resolve financial embarrassments, Báez denounced the proposal, secured military assistance from Haitian ruler Salnave, and forced Cabral to capitulate on February 8. Following his takeover, an unelected convention nominated Báez as dictator, an appointment he modified to 'Grand Citizen' with unlimited powers while imprisoning, exiling, and executing opponents. Sumner charges that Báez subsequently pursued the annexation scheme out of personal greed.
records.summary_es: En un discurso en el Senado publicado en el Evening Star, el senador Charles Sumner repasa la historia política dominicana, afirmando que si bien siempre deseó brindar asistencia a Dominica, nunca alentó insurrecciones armadas. Sumner relata que cuando el presidente Cabral buscó ayuda estadounidense y ofreció el arrendamiento de la bahía de Samaná para resolver sus apuros financieros, Báez denunció la propuesta, obtuvo apoyo militar del gobernante haitiano Salnave y obligó a Cabral a capitular el 8 de febrero. Tras su toma del poder, una convención no electa designó a Báez dictador, nombramiento que este modificó al de «Gran Ciudadano» con poderes ilimitados, mientras encarcelaba, desterraba y ejecutaba a sus adversarios. Sumner acusa a Báez de haber impulsado posteriormente el plan de anexión movido por la codicia personal.

records.headline: Senator Sumner argued, in the paper's account, that Baez was maintained in power by the U.S. Navy
records.summary_en: Senator Sumner argued, in the paper's account, that Baez was maintained in power by the U.S. Navy to enable him to carry out the sale of his country, and that the neighboring republic of Haiti was violently menaced in breach of public law. Sumner contended that the promise to employ the war powers without the authority of Congress was void, since the Constitution gives Congress the power to declare war.

Sumner afirmó que la promesa de emplear los poderes de guerra sin la autoridad del Congreso era nula, ya que la Constitución otorga al Congreso el poder de declarar la guerra.

records.headline: The Evening Telegraph publishes an address quoting naval orders
records.summary_en: The Evening Telegraph publishes an address quoting naval orders issued to Rear-Admiral Poor directing warships to Port-au-Prince and Dominica. The dispatch instructs the admiral to inform Haitian authorities that the United States is determined to protect the Dominican government with all its power, and to capture or destroy any Haitian vessels that attack the Dominicans. The orders further direct naval commanders to secure American authority at Samaná Bay and Santo Domingo City while protecting the Báez administration. The accompanying commentary condemns these instructions as warlike and dangerous, contending that establishing United States authority in Dominican harbors amounts to military occupation.
records.summary_es: The Evening Telegraph publica un discurso que cita órdenes navales emitidas al contraalmirante Poor para enviar buques de guerra a Puerto Príncipe y a Dominica. El despacho instruye al almirante a informar a las autoridades haitianas de que los Estados Unidos están decididos a proteger al gobierno dominicano con todo su poderío, y a capturar o destruir cualquier barco haitiano que ataque a los dominicanos. Las órdenes encomiendan además a los comandantes navales afianzar la autoridad estadounidense en la bahía de Samaná y en la ciudad de Santo Domingo mientras protegen a la administración de Báez. El comentario adjunto condena estas instrucciones por belicistas y peligrosas, sosteniendo que implantar la autoridad de los Estados Unidos en puertos dominicanos equivale a una ocupación militar.

records.headline: A Senate speech charges that Baez was sustained in power by the United States Navy while the annexation voting
records.summary_en: A Senate speech charges that Baez was sustained in power by the United States Navy while the annexation voting proceeded, citing a dispatch of March 19, 1870 placing the Severn at Santo Domingo, the Swatara sent to Samana, the Nantasket to Puerto Plata and the Yantic in the river, and an official's sworn testimony that the navy's acts were protecting Baez from the citizens of St. Domingo. It also tells how the American citizen Davis Hatch was arrested on a trumped-up charge and, even after his formal pardon, kept in prison at the instance of Cazneau and with Fabens's connivance to prevent his opposition to the treaty, as a Dominican minister's note admitted his imprisonment was only to prevent his hostile action in New York.
records.summary_es: Un discurso en el Senado acusa que Baez fue sostenido en el poder por la Marina de los Estados Unidos mientras se realizaba la votación sobre la anexión, citando un despacho del 19 de marzo de 1870 que situaba al Severn en Santo Domingo, al Swatara enviado a Samana, al Nantasket a Puerto Plata y al Yantic en el río, y el testimonio jurado de un funcionario de que los actos de la Marina protegían a Baez de los ciudadanos de Santo Domingo. También relata cómo el ciudadano americano Davis Hatch fue arrestado con un cargo inventado y, aun después de su perdón formal, mantenido en prisión a instancias de Cazneau y con la complicidad de Fabens para impedir su oposición al tratado, pues una nota de un ministro dominicano admitió que su encarcelamiento era solo para impedir su acción hostil en Nueva York.

records.headline: A Washington report in the Alexandria Gazette describes the Senate debate
records.summary_en: A Washington report in the Alexandria Gazette describes the Senate debate on President Grant's Dominican policy, noting that Senator Charles Sumner concluded his speech by appealing to the President to abandon annexation and help reconcile Haiti and Dominica. Senator Morton replied, arguing that Sumner's sole aim was to accuse the President of crimes and assist the Democratic party. The dispatch reports that an immense audience filled the Senate chamber to hear Sumner, repeatedly applauding his speech until the Vice President threatened to clear the galleries, while Sumner also rebuked fellow senators for interrupting his remarks.
records.summary_es: Una crónica desde Washington en la Alexandria Gazette describe el debate en el Senado sobre la política dominicana del presidente Grant, señalando que el senador Charles Sumner concluyó su discurso apelando al presidente a abandonar la anexión y contribuir a conciliar a Haití y Dominica. El senador Morton respondió sosteniendo que el único objetivo de Sumner era acusar al presidente de crímenes y beneficiar al Partido Demócrata. El despacho informa que una concurrencia inmensa llenó la sala del Senado para escuchar a Sumner, aplaudiendo reiteradamente su intervención hasta que el vicepresidente amenazó con desalojar las tribunas, al tiempo que Sumner también reprendió a senadores colegas por interrumpir sus palabras.

records.headline: The article reprints a letter from Captain Temple of the Tennessee, written at Azua Bay on February 11, 1871
records.summary_en: The article reprints a letter from Captain Temple of the Tennessee, written at Azua Bay on February 11, 1871, warning Commissioner Wade that members of the Santo Domingo expedition who were about to travel overland toward Port-au-Prince would be placing themselves in the position of spies. Temple argues that because President Grant has ordered the American navy to protect the Baez government against any demonstration by Haiti or Cabral, Cabral would be justified in treating the travelers as spies liable to a drum-head court martial, and he asks Wade to refuse his consent to the trip and to ask President Baez to forbid their passage through his lines.
records.summary_es: El artículo reproduce una carta del capitán Temple, del Tennessee, escrita en la bahía de Azua el 11 de febrero de 1871, en la que advierte al comisionado Wade que los miembros de la expedición de Santo Domingo que estaban a punto de viajar por tierra hacia Puerto Príncipe se colocarían en la posición de espías. Temple sostiene que, como el presidente Grant ha ordenado a la marina americana proteger al gobierno de Báez contra cualquier demostración de Haití o de Cabral, Cabral estaría justificado en tratar a los viajeros como espías sujetos a un consejo de guerra sumario, y pide a Wade que niegue su consentimiento al viaje y que solicite al presidente Báez que prohíba su paso por sus líneas.

records.headline: The editorial accuses the United States of keeping Baez in power, occupying Dominican harbors with warships, and sending
records.summary_en: The editorial accuses the United States of keeping Baez in power, occupying Dominican harbors with warships, and sending warships including the monitor Dictator to menace Haiti. It cites Minister Bassett's February 17, 1870 notice informing the Haitian government that the United States asked and expected it to observe strict neutrality regarding Dominican internal affairs.

Cita el aviso del ministro Bassett del 17 de febrero de 1870, en el que informaba al gobierno haitiano de que Estados Unidos pedía y esperaba que observara una estricta neutralidad respecto a los asuntos internos dominicanos.

records.headline: In a Senate speech published in The Portland Daily Press, Senator Charles Sumner examines
records.summary_en: In a Senate speech published in The Portland Daily Press, Senator Charles Sumner examines executive correspondence regarding the deployment of American warships to the Dominican Republic in 1869. Quoting instructions from the State Department, Sumner emphasizes that the administration ordered a man-of-war to visit Dominican ports to investigate views on annexation and the lease of Samaná Bay before receiving any invitation from the Dominican people. He cites a naval order of June 29, 1869, directing the warship Nipsic to visit every Dominican harbor, arguing that the administration relied on naval force as its primary instrument from the very beginning of negotiations.
records.summary_es: En un discurso en el Senado publicado en The Portland Daily Press, el senador Charles Sumner examina la correspondencia ejecutiva relativa al despliegue de buques de guerra estadounidenses en la República Dominicana en 1869. Citando instrucciones del Departamento de Estado, Sumner subraya que la administración ordenó a un buque de guerra visitar los puertos dominicanos para investigar las opiniones sobre la anexión y el arrendamiento de la bahía de Samaná antes de recibir invitación alguna del pueblo dominicano. Cita una orden naval del 29 de junio de 1869 que instruía al buque de guerra Nipsic a visitar todos los puertos dominicanos, sosteniendo que la administración se apoyó en la fuerza naval como su instrumento principal desde el comienzo mismo de las negociaciones.

records.headline: Continuing his Senate speech in The Portland Daily Press, Senator Charles Sumner examines
records.summary_en: Continuing his Senate speech in The Portland Daily Press, Senator Charles Sumner examines the diplomatic mission of General Babcock to Santo Domingo under instructions dated July 15, 1869. He highlights orders issued on the same day by the Secretary of the Navy instructing Commander Owen of the warship Seminole to remain on the Dominican coast and furnish Babcock with 'the moral support of your guns.' Sumner denounces this instruction as an executive usurpation and the first overt act of war, arguing that deploying naval artillery to influence diplomatic inquiries represented lawless military coercion rather than lawful negotiation.
records.summary_es: Al continuar su discurso en el Senado publicado en The Portland Daily Press, el senador Charles Sumner examina la misión diplomática del general Babcock a Santo Domingo conforme a las instrucciones del 15 de julio de 1869. Destaca las órdenes emitidas ese mismo día por el secretario de la Armada que instruían al comandante Owen del buque de guerra Seminole a permanecer en la costa dominicana y proporcionar a Babcock «el apoyo moral de sus cañones». Sumner denuncia esta orden como una usurpación del poder ejecutivo y el primer acto manifiesto de guerra, argumentando que el despliegue de artillería naval para incidir en indagaciones diplomáticas representaba una coerción militar arbitraria en lugar de una negociación legítima.

records.headline: A Washington dispatch to the New-York Tribune traces the return
records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch to the New-York Tribune traces the return voyage of the San Domingo expedition aboard the Tennessee via Key West and Charleston, noting that the party arrived in Washington by steamer from Aquia Creek. The correspondent reports that the commissioners plan to call upon President Grant once Mr. Wade's health permits, with their report virtually finished and expected to be submitted within days. The writer discounts rumors that the administration intends to abandon the Santo Domingo project to unify the Republican party, attributing such speculation to remarks by Senator Morton and reiterating that the commissioners remain unanimously in favor of annexation.
records.summary_es: Un despacho desde Washington para el New-York Tribune detalla la travesía de regreso de la expedición de Santo Domingo a bordo del Tennessee pasando por Cayo Hueso y Charleston, señalando que la comitiva arribó a Washington en vapor desde Aquia Creek. El corresponsal informa que los comisionados planean presentarse ante el presidente Grant una vez que la salud del señor Wade lo permita, encontrándose su informe prácticamente concluido y listo para entregarse en cuestión de días. El autor desestima los rumores de que la administración planee abandonar el proyecto de Santo Domingo para unificar al Partido Republicano, atribuyendo tales conjeturas a declaraciones del senador Morton y reiterando que los comisionados continúan unánimemente a favor de la anexión.

records.headline: A Senate speech reported in The New York Herald denounces the Grant administration
records.summary_en: A Senate speech reported in The New York Herald denounces the Grant administration for employing naval warships to sustain President Báez in power during the negotiation of annexation treaties with Santo Domingo. Citing an official report of March 13, 1870, the speaker points out that American warships including the Severn, Swatara, Nantasket, and Yantic were stationed in Dominican ports to enforce order while voting on the treaty was underway. He further cites sworn testimony before the Senate committee on the Davis Hatch case, which acknowledged that American naval vessels had been actively engaged in protecting Báez against his own citizens.
records.summary_es: Un discurso en el Senado reseñado en The New York Herald denuncia a la administración de Grant por emplear buques de guerra para sostener al presidente Báez en el poder durante la negociación de los tratados de anexión con Santo Domingo. Citando un informe oficial del 13 de marzo de 1870, el orador señala que buques estadounidenses como el Severn, el Swatara, el Nantasket y el Yantic estuvieron desplegados en puertos dominicanos para imponer el orden mientras se realizaba la votación sobre el tratado. Cita además testimonios bajo juramento ante el comité del Senado sobre el caso de Davis Hatch, los cuales reconocieron que las naves de guerra norteamericanas estuvieron activamente dedicadas a proteger a Báez frente a sus propios ciudadanos.

records.headline: An article in the Herald examines an official Spanish dispatch
records.summary_en: An article in the Herald examines an official Spanish dispatch from November 1861 outlining the government's stance toward the annexation of Santo Domingo. According to the dispatch, the primary and indispensable condition required by Spain was that the reincorporation be the unanimous, spontaneous, and explicit expression of the will of the Dominicans. The Spanish government insisted that the events in Dominica were not the work of Spanish emigrants or authorities in Havana, asserting that neither a Spanish soldier nor a Spanish vessel was on the coast when reunion was proclaimed. The Herald observes the energy with which the Spanish minister sought to exclude any suspicion of force or foreign interference in the annexation.
records.summary_es: Un artículo en el Herald examina un despacho oficial español de noviembre de 1861 que describe la postura del gobierno respecto a la anexión de Santo Domingo. Según el despacho, la condición primordial e indispensable exigida por España era que la reincorporación fuera la expresión unánime, espontánea y explícita de la voluntad de los dominicanos. El gobierno español insistió en que los acontecimientos en Dominica no fueron obra de emigrantes españoles ni de las autoridades de La Habana, afirmando que ningún soldado ni buque español se encontraba en la costa cuando se proclamó la reunión. El Herald observa la firmeza con la que el ministro español procuró excluir toda sospecha de fuerza o injerencia extranjera en la anexión.

records.headline: In a Senate speech, Mr. Sumner recounts
records.summary_en: In a Senate speech, Mr. Sumner recounts how Cabral became president by a direct vote of the people, how the exiled Baez came to Washington seeking money and arms and got no encouragement, and how Cabral, pressed by financial difficulties, offered a lease of the Bay of Samana. He says Baez then denounced the sale of his country, organized a hostile force with the help of Salnave of Haiti, forced Cabral's capitulation on February 8, 1868, and was named dictator by an appointed convention, after which treaties were signed to sell the country for $1,500,000 and lease Samana Bay for $150,000 a year, with the United States Navy used to keep Baez in power.
records.summary_es: En un discurso en el Senado, el señor Sumner relata cómo Cabral llegó a la presidencia por voto directo del pueblo, cómo el exiliado Baez fue a Washington en busca de dinero y armas y no recibió apoyo, y cómo Cabral, presionado por dificultades financieras, ofreció el arrendamiento de la bahía de Samana. Dice que Baez denunció entonces la venta de su país, organizó una fuerza hostil con ayuda de Salnave de Haití, forzó la capitulación de Cabral el 8 de febrero de 1868 y fue nombrado dictador por una convención designada, tras lo cual se firmaron tratados para vender el país por $1,500,000 y arrendar la bahía de Samana por $150,000 al año, con la Marina de los Estados Unidos empleada para mantener a Baez en el poder.

records.headline: An editorial in the Tribune argues that even if the commissioners
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Tribune argues that even if the commissioners report favorably on Santo Domingo, the main question for the United States remains undecided. Even if the Dominican Republic's debt is under $2,000,000, its resources vast, and its people desirous of annexation, the paper contends that the acquisition offers little benefit to an already land-rich nation. Instead, it asserts that holding a tropical outpost would heighten the hazards and expenses of war, requiring the United States to double its naval armaments. Furthermore, the Tribune warns that annexation would inevitably demand heavy expenditures for coast surveys, lighthouses, harbor improvements, and fortifications at Samaná and other points, alongside guarding an exposed inland frontier.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en el Tribune sostiene que, aun si los comisionados presentan un informe favorable sobre Santo Domingo, la cuestión principal para los Estados Unidos sigue sin resolverse. Incluso si la deuda de la República Dominicana es inferior a $2,000,000, sus recursos vastos y su pueblo favorable a la anexión, el periódico afirma que la adquisición ofrece escaso beneficio a una nación que ya abunda en tierras. En cambio, asevera que retener un puesto de avanzada tropical aumentaría los peligros y gastos de guerra, obligando a los Estados Unidos a duplicar sus armamentos navales. Además, el Tribune advierte que la anexión exigiría inevitablemente cuantiosos desembolsos para levantamientos costeros, faros, mejoras de puertos y fortificaciones en Samaná y otros puntos, además de resguardar una frontera interior expuesta.

records.headline: The Spy prints an extract from Secretary of the Navy George M. Robeson's letter
records.summary_en: The Spy prints an extract from Secretary of the Navy George M. Robeson's letter to Admiral Lee explaining executive policy toward the Dominican Republic. Robeson writes that while the right of revolution against constituted authority belongs to every people, the existing government remains the legal representative of the nation until overthrown. He argues that insurgents have no right under international law to treat agents of foreign nations as enemies while they act in accordance with existing laws. Robeson asserts that the United States has not taken part in internal Dominican conflicts, emphasizing the President's constitutional authority to negotiate treaties and noting congressional appropriations made to acquire a naval station at Samaná.
records.summary_es: El Spy publica un extracto de la carta del secretario de la Armada, George M. Robeson, al almirante Lee en la que explica la política del ejecutivo hacia la República Dominicana. Robeson escribe que, si bien el derecho de revolución contra la autoridad constituida pertenece a todo pueblo, el gobierno existente sigue siendo el representante legal de la nación hasta ser derrocado. Sostiene que los insurgentes no tienen derecho, según el derecho internacional, a tratar a los agentes de naciones extranjeras como enemigos mientras actúen conforme a las leyes vigentes. Robeson afirma que los Estados Unidos no han intervenido en los conflictos internos dominicanos, destacando la autoridad constitucional del presidente para negociar tratados y señalando las asignaciones del Congreso para adquirir una estación naval en Samaná.

records.headline: An editorial item in The Sun examines Dominican tobacco cultivation
records.summary_en: An editorial item in The Sun examines Dominican tobacco cultivation, reporting that production over the last five years has averaged about 100,000 bales of 100 pounds each, equal to about 30,000 cases of seed leaf. The average cost price at Puerto Plata is reported at about ten cents per pound, with capacity for hundreds of thousands of bales under proper cultivation. Citing a Tribune article, the paper notes that Santo Domingo tobacco was prized for cigar wrappers, but trade declined because it could not compete against duty-free leaf from Connecticut and Pennsylvania. The Sun remarks that if Santo Domingo is annexed, its tobacco will enter free, predicting that Connecticut growers will hardly view Grant's annexation project with complacency.
records.summary_es: Una nota editorial en The Sun examina el cultivo del tabaco dominicano, informando que la producción en los últimos cinco años ha promediado unos 100,000 fardos de 100 libras cada uno, equivalente a unas 30,000 cajas de hoja para siembra. El precio de costo promedio en Puerto Plata se sitúa en unos diez centavos por libra, con capacidad para producir cientos de miles de fardos bajo un cultivo adecuado. Citando un artículo del Tribune, el diario señala que el tabaco de Santo Domingo era muy apreciado para capas de cigarros, pero el comercio decayó por no poder competir con la hoja libre de impuestos de Connecticut y Pensilvania. The Sun advierte que si Santo Domingo es anexionado, su tabaco entrará libre de aranceles, augurando que los cultivadores de Connecticut difícilmente verán con complacencia el proyecto de anexión de Grant.

records.headline: The Tribune publishes an extract from Senator Charles Sumner's speech
records.summary_en: The Tribune publishes an extract from Senator Charles Sumner's speech citing official dispatches from U.S. Commercial Agent Raymond H. Perry in Santo Domingo to show executive intervention. In a dispatch dated January 20, 1870, Perry reported that the warship Nantasket was visiting Puerto Plata and Samaná Bay, stating that Báez needed a man-of-war before public opinion on annexation was expressed. Sumner argues that Báez urgently requested naval forces because he feared the Dominican people would pronounce for his overthrow rather than for annexation. Sumner also cites a February 8, 1870 dispatch in which Perry reported that Báez complained daily that the United States had failed to fulfill its promise to send warships to the coast.
records.summary_es: El Tribune publica un extracto del discurso del senador Charles Sumner en el que cita despachos oficiales del agente comercial estadounidense Raymond H. Perry en Santo Domingo para demostrar la intervención del ejecutivo. En un despacho fechado el 20 de enero de 1870, Perry informó que el buque de guerra Nantasket visitaba Puerto Plata y la bahía de Samaná, señalando que Báez necesitaba un buque de guerra antes de que se expresara la opinión pública sobre la anexión. Sumner sostiene que Báez pedía con urgencia fuerzas navales porque temía que el pueblo dominicano se pronunciara por su derrocamiento en lugar de la anexión. Sumner cita también un despacho del 8 de febrero de 1870 en el que Perry informó que Báez se quejaba a diario de que los Estados Unidos no habían cumplido su promesa de enviar buques de guerra a la costa.

records.headline: This account of Dominican history relates that after Baez was overthrown, General Jose Maria Cabral became lawful president
records.summary_en: This account of Dominican history relates that after Baez was overthrown, General Jose Maria Cabral became lawful president by the direct vote of the people in September 1866, the first time a question had been submitted to a direct vote in the country's history, and that peace ensued. It says Cabral, embarrassed by financial difficulties, turned to the United States offering a lease of the bay of Samana, while the exiled Baez denounced the sale of his country, organised a hostile force with the help of Salnave of Hayti, and compelled Cabral's capitulation on February 8, 1868, after which a convention named Baez Grand Citizen with unlimited powers and his enemies were exiled or executed.
records.summary_es: Este relato de la historia dominicana cuenta que, tras la caída de Báez, el general José María Cabral llegó a ser presidente legítimo por el voto directo del pueblo en septiembre de 1866, la primera vez que una cuestión se sometía al voto directo en la historia del país, y que sobrevino la paz. Dice que Cabral, agobiado por dificultades financieras, se dirigió a los Estados Unidos ofreciendo el arrendamiento de la bahía de Samaná, mientras Báez, desde el exilio, denunciaba la venta de su patria, organizaba una fuerza hostil con la ayuda de Salnave, de Haití, y obligaba a Cabral a capitular el 8 de febrero de 1868, tras lo cual una convención nombró a Báez Gran Ciudadano con poderes ilimitados y sus enemigos fueron exiliados o ejecutados.
records.passage: also manifesto of Cabral, assigning at still greater length reasons for the overthrow of Baez, and holding him up as the enemy of peace and union; also a manifesto by the Triumvirate, constituting the Provisional Government, declaring his infractions of the Constitution; also a manifesto from the General in command of the City of Santo Domingo, where, after denouncing the misdeeds of one man, it says, "this man, this monster, this speculator, this tyrant is Buenaventura Baez." Soon after the disappearance of Baez, his rival became lawful President by the direct vote of the people, according to the requirement of the Constitution. Different numbers of the official journal now before me contain the election returns in September, 1866, where the name of Gen. José Maria Cabral appears at the head of the poll. This is memorable as the first time in the history of Dominica when a question was submitted to the direct vote of the people. By that direct vote Cabral became President, and peace ensued. Since then there has been no election, so that this was last as well as first. During his enforced exile Baez found his way to Washington. Mr. Seward declined to see him, but referred him to me. records.headline: The Chicago Tribune prints an extract from Secretary of the Navy Robeson's letter
records.summary_en: The Chicago Tribune prints an extract from Secretary of the Navy Robeson's letter explaining the administration's actions regarding the Dominican Republic. The letter asserts that the right of revolution does not empower insurgents to treat agents of foreign nations as enemies while they act under existing laws. Robeson states that neither the United States nor its executive has taken part in internal Dominican conflicts. He argues that the President holds the constitutional authority to initiate treaties, and that Congress appropriated funds in 1866 to lease or purchase territory on the island of San Domingo. Robeson maintains that the bay and peninsula of Samaná were deemed most suitable for a naval station, justifying the negotiation of treaties for cession and annexation.
records.summary_es: El Chicago Tribune publica un extracto de la carta del secretario de la Armada Robeson en la que explica las acciones del gobierno respecto a la República Dominicana. La carta asevera que el derecho de revolución no faculta a los insurgentes para tratar a los agentes de naciones extranjeras como enemigos mientras actúen bajo las leyes vigentes. Robeson declara que ni los Estados Unidos ni su ejecutivo han intervenido en los conflictos internos dominicanos. Sostiene que el presidente posee la facultad constitucional para iniciar tratados y que el Congreso asignó fondos en 1866 para arrendar o comprar territorio en la isla de Santo Domingo. Robeson mantiene que la bahía y península de Samaná se consideraron las más adecuadas para una estación naval, justificando la negociación de tratados de cesión y anexión.

records.headline: A Washington dispatch in the Daily Kennebec Journal reports
records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch in the Daily Kennebec Journal reports that Senate discussion of the San Domingo question drew a large crowd to the galleries, attracting House members after adjournment to hear General Carl Schurz. Schurz, standing near Senator Sumner and receiving frequent suggestions from him, was announced to speak the next day in criticism of Secretary Robeson's March 21 letter to Admiral Lee. The dispatch further notes that the San Domingo Commissioners have agreed upon their report, with the exception of the subjects of public health and the debts of the Dominican Republic. It adds that the commissioners may not be ready to submit their findings until Thursday.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de Washington en el Daily Kennebec Journal informa que el debate en el Senado sobre la cuestión de Santo Domingo atrajo a una multitud a las galerías, congregando a miembros de la Cámara tras el receso para escuchar al general Carl Schurz. Schurz, ubicado cerca del senador Sumner y recibiendo constantes sugerencias suyas, fue anunciado para hablar al día siguiente criticando la carta del 21 de marzo del secretario Robeson al almirante Lee. El despacho señala además que los comisionados de Santo Domingo han acordado su informe, a excepción de los temas de salud pública y la deuda de la República Dominicana. Añade que los comisionados tal vez no estén listos para presentar sus conclusiones hasta el jueves.

records.headline: Senator Morton's reply to Sumner: the commission could not negotiate, Haiti itself assured Minister Bassett it would not interfere
records.summary_en: Senator Morton's reply to Sumner: the commission could not negotiate, Haiti itself assured Minister Bassett it would not interfere with the Dominicans' free will, and the United States merely warned Haiti - which had given Cabral passage and war vessels - not to make war during the negotiations.

records.passage: Mr. Morton then had read by the Secretary a dispatch to United States Minister Bassett, from the Haytien Secretary of Foreign Affairs, assuring him that Hayti had no disposition or desire to interfere with the free will of the Dominicans. As a further reply to Mr. Sumner, he reminded the Senator, as evidence, that the Administration had not proposed to take any immediate action upon annexation; that Commission had no authority to negotiate a treaty, and that no one went with them who could take a single step in that direction. The Haytien Government, in violation of the law of nations, had given free passage across its territory to Cabral, and had furnished him with war vessels to attack Dominica, and the United States had merely notified Hayti that while our negotiations were pending with Dominica we would not allow him to make war on the island. This the United States had an undoubted right to do, because our Government had information of organizations on foot in Hayti to defeat annexation. No one need tell him (Morton) that the Senator from Massachusetts was a friend of liberty or the colored man when he so industriously spent his time in an effort to put the Democratic party in power, for to destroy the President is to destroy the great party of which he is the head (applause), and we know the terrible effect upon the liberties of this country if the Democratic party comes into power.

records.headline: The Kentucky Gazette reports that Secretary of the Navy Robeson addressed
records.summary_en: The Kentucky Gazette reports that Secretary of the Navy Robeson addressed a letter to Rear-Admiral Lee defending the administration's naval posture toward Haiti during the San Domingo negotiations. Robeson maintained that in executing United States policy, not a single shot had been fired nor had any armed men landed in hostility on the island of San Domingo. He insisted that the government had neither interfered in the internal conflicts of the Dominican Republic nor coerced any foreign power. Instead, Robeson explained that the administration simply announced its intention to protect its acquired interests in the republic against external attacks until the annexation treaties were decided, thereby preserving its right of pre-emption.
records.summary_es: The Kentucky Gazette informa que el secretario de la Armada Robeson dirigió una carta al contraalmirante Lee defendiendo la postura naval del gobierno frente a Haití durante las negociaciones sobre Santo Domingo. Robeson sostuvo que, al ejecutar la política de los Estados Unidos, no se había efectuado un solo disparo ni desembarcado hombres armados en actitud hostil en la isla de Santo Domingo. Insistió en que el gobierno no había intervenido en los conflictos internos de la República Dominicana ni coaccionado a ninguna potencia extranjera. Por el contrario, Robeson explicó que la administración simplemente anunció su intención de proteger contra ataques externos los intereses adquiridos en la república hasta que se resolvieran los tratados de anexión, preservando así su derecho de prelación.

records.headline: The Evening Telegraph prints a Washington report headed 'Cabral
records.summary_en: The Evening Telegraph prints a Washington report headed 'Cabral Goes Back on His Friend Sumner,' citing a letter from General José María Cabral obtained by the San Domingo Commission in Port-au-Prince. The correspondent writes that Cabral's authentic letter upsets Senator Charles Sumner's calculations regarding Santo Domingo. In the letter, addressed to the President of the United States Senate on February 18, 1871, Cabral refers to Sumner's December 21, 1870 speech. Cabral quotes Sumner's assertion that Cabral's actual policy was to reunite the two governments of Dominica and Haiti as they existed before 1844, a claim Cabral seeks to correct.
records.summary_es: The Evening Telegraph publica un informe de Washington titulado «Cabral le da la espalda a su amigo Sumner», citando una carta del general José María Cabral obtenida por la comisión de Santo Domingo en Puerto Príncipe. El corresponsal escribe que la auténtica carta de Cabral desbarata los cálculos del senador Charles Sumner respecto a Santo Domingo. En la misiva, dirigida al presidente del Senado de los Estados Unidos el 18 de febrero de 1871, Cabral hace referencia al discurso pronunciado por Sumner el 21 de diciembre de 1870. Cabral cita la aseveración de Sumner de que su verdadera política era reunir nuevamente los dos gobiernos de Dominica y Haití como estaban antes de 1844, afirmación que Cabral busca rectificar.

Bajo el título «Reconstruyendo su informe», una breve nota aparte indica que los comisionados han acordado los aspectos principales de su informe, excepto en lo relativo a la salud y la deuda de la República Dominicana. Añade que, debido a estos temas pendientes, es posible que los comisionados no puedan entregar su informe definitivo hasta el jueves.

records.headline: A Washington dispatch in the Worcester Daily Spy recounts Senate debate
records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch in the Worcester Daily Spy recounts Senate debate following Charles Sumner's speech against the administration. Senator Oliver P. Morton argued that the executive had not violated international law, maintaining that Haiti had routinely breached the law of nations in its relations with Dominica by permitting its territory to serve as a base for hostile incursions and supplying domestic insurgents with money and weapons. Morton asserted that American naval intervention to protect San Domingo from Haitian hostility during pending treaty negotiations was an exercise of legitimate rights under international law. The correspondent adds that Senator Howe of Wisconsin subsequently attacked Sumner with great intensity, comparing his course to historical party apostates.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de Washington en el Worcester Daily Spy reseña el debate en el Senado tras el discurso de Charles Sumner contra el gobierno. El senador Oliver P. Morton sostuvo que el ejecutivo no había violado el derecho internacional, afirmando que Haití había infringido sistemáticamente el derecho de gentes en sus relaciones con Dominica al permitir que su territorio sirviera de base para incursiones hostiles y al suministrar dinero y armas a los insurgentes locales. Morton aseveró que la intervención naval estadounidense para proteger a Santo Domingo de la hostilidad haitiana durante las negociaciones del tratado constituía un ejercicio de derechos legítimos bajo el derecho internacional. El corresponsal añade que el senador Howe de Wisconsin atacó luego a Sumner con notable vehemencia, comparando su conducta con la de conocidos apóstatas de la historia.

records.headline: A Senate report in the Portland Daily Press covers Carl Schurz's response
records.summary_en: A Senate report in the Portland Daily Press covers Carl Schurz's response to Senator Frelinghuysen regarding Secretary Robeson's dispatch to Admiral Lee. Schurz condemned as brazen Robeson's assertion that the Executive had not taken part in internal Dominican affairs, citing naval orders under which American commanders at Dominica protected President Báez against both Haiti and his own citizens. Schurz stated that a United States warship carried Báez's troops from Azua to Santo Domingo, and that the Tennessee conveyed Báez and his staff so he could direct his forces. Schurz further charged that Báez's troops carried the American flag against Cabral to deceive opponents, and noted that rockets were supplied to Báez during a threatened attack by Luperón.
records.summary_es: Una crónica del Senado en el Portland Daily Press cubre la respuesta de Carl Schurz al senador Frelinghuysen respecto al despacho del secretario Robeson al almirante Lee. records.summary_en: The New York Herald reports on Senator Carl Schurz's speech challenging Secretary Robeson's dispatch to Admiral Lee, which Senator Frelinghuysen had introduced. Schurz denounced Robeson's claim that the executive had refrained from participating in Dominican internal affairs, contending it contradicted official Navy Department orders. Under those orders, Schurz argued, naval commanders at Dominica intervened to uphold Báez against both Haiti and domestic opposition. He cited evidence that an American war vessel transported Báez's troops from Azua to Santo Domingo, that the Tennessee carried Báez and his staff to command military operations, and that Dominican government forces carried the United States flag against Cabral to deceive insurgents into believing they faced American soldiers.

Chronological Epitome.

1795—By the treaty of Basle, the Spanish portion of Santo Domingo is ceded to France.

1798—Hedouville lands at French Cape, and sends Toussaint L'Ouverture, an emancipated slave, to France. On the 8th of May, the English leave the island, and civil war between Toussaint L'Ouverture and Rigaud.

1802—The French squadron, under Leclerc, arrives at Port au Prince in February; takes the Cape and burns the town, Dessalines opposing. A truce concluded May 1st.

records.headline: The Worcester Daily Spy prints a report of Senator Carl Schurz's Senate speech
records.summary_en: The Worcester Daily Spy prints a report of Senator Carl Schurz's Senate speech condemning American naval intervention in the Dominican Republic. Schurz argued that Secretary Robeson's denial of executive interference was refuted by instructions under which naval officers at Dominica upheld Báez against Haiti and his own people. He highlighted instances where a U.S. warship carried Báez's troops from Azua to Santo Domingo, the Tennessee transported Báez and his staff, and Dominican troops flew the American flag against Cabral's forces. Schurz further recounted that when Luperón threatened Báez's faction, rockets were supplied from the warship Congress to summon aid; when one was fired, an armed boatload of sailors immediately put off toward shore.
records.summary_es: El Worcester Daily Spy publica una crónica del discurso del senador Carl Schurz en el Senado en el que condena la intervención naval estadounidense en la República Dominicana. Schurz sostuvo que la negativa del secretario Robeson sobre una injerencia del ejecutivo quedaba desmentida por las instrucciones bajo las cuales los oficiales navales en Dominica respaldaron a Báez frente a Haití y su propio pueblo. Destacó casos en que un buque de guerra estadounidense trasladó tropas de Báez de Azua a Santo Domingo, el Tennessee transportó a Báez y a su estado mayor, y las tropas dominicanas enarbolaron la bandera estadounidense frente a las fuerzas de Cabral. Schurz relató además que cuando Luperón amenazó a la facción de Báez, se suministraron cohetes desde el buque de guerra Congress para pedir auxilio; al dispararse uno, un bote con marineros armados zarpó de inmediato hacia la orilla.

records.headline: An editorial in the New-York Tribune examines the Dominican border
records.summary_en: An editorial in the New-York Tribune examines the Dominican border conflict, describing an ill-defined boundary and disputed territory between the Dominican Republic and Haiti. The paper notes that the entire island was originally Spanish and had previously been united, in the paper's phrasing, under Haitian rule for a few years half a century earlier. It reports that José María Cabral, operating in the debatable border region with quiet backing from Haitian men and munitions, seeks to overthrow President Buenaventura Báez by appealing to Dominican patriotism against annexation. The Tribune defends President Grant's directive providing moral naval support to Báez, arguing it simply warns Haiti and Cabral not to subvert the Dominican government by force while treaty negotiations remain pending.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en el New-York Tribune examina el conflicto fronterizo dominicano, describiendo un límite impreciso y un territorio en disputa entre la República Dominicana y Haití. El periódico señala que toda la isla fue originalmente española y había estado previamente unida, según la formulación del diario, bajo dominio haitiano durante algunos años medio siglo antes. Informa que José María Cabral, operando en la zona fronteriza disputada con el respaldo encubierto de hombres y pertrechos haitianos, procura derrocar al presidente Buenaventura Báez apelando al patriotismo dominicano contra la anexión. El Tribune defiende la disposición del presidente Grant de brindar apoyo naval moral a Báez, argumentando que simplemente advierte a Haití y a Cabral que no derroquen por la fuerza al gobierno dominicano mientras las negociaciones del tratado sigan pendientes.

records.headline: The Rutland Weekly Herald comments editorially on the removal of Charles Sumner
records.summary_en: The Rutland Weekly Herald comments editorially on the removal of Charles Sumner from the chairmanship of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations. The Herald expresses skepticism that Sumner's displacement will result in the annexation of San Domingo or damage foreign relations, asserting that other able senators can adequately fill the position. Citing the Montpelier Freeman, the paper dismisses predictions of party rupture, noting that whether the action is viewed as an administration victory regarding the Santo Domingo annexation scheme or prompted by other motives, it need not disturb Republican harmony. The Freeman emphasizes that although Vermont's two senators took opposing stances, no division within the state's party will follow.
records.summary_es: El Rutland Weekly Herald comenta en su editorial sobre la destitución de Charles Sumner de la presidencia del Comité de Relaciones Exteriores del Senado. El Herald manifiesta su escepticismo de que el relevo de Sumner conduzca a la anexión de Santo Domingo o perjudique las relaciones exteriores, afirmando que otros senadores competentes pueden ocupar adecuadamente el cargo. Citando al Montpelier Freeman, el periódico descarta los pronósticos de una ruptura partidaria, señalando que, ya sea vista la medida como una victoria de la administración respecto al plan de anexión de Santo Domingo o motivada por otras razones, no tiene por qué perturbar la concordia republicana. El Freeman recalca que, aun cuando los dos senadores de Vermont adoptaron posturas opuestas, no se derivará división alguna dentro del partido en el estado.

records.headline: The Daily Kennebec Journal prints an extract from Secretary of the Navy Robeson's official
records.summary_en: The Daily Kennebec Journal prints an extract from Secretary of the Navy Robeson's official letter defending executive actions concerning the Dominican Republic. Robeson states that the Republic of San Domingo, with its advantageous position, natural wealth, and friendly population, was deemed highly desirable for American commerce and naval stations at Samaná. He maintains that the President held the constitutional power to initiate and negotiate treaties for the cession of Samaná and annexation with the established de facto and de jure Dominican government. While acknowledging that these treaties remained subject to ratification by the Senate and the Dominican people, Robeson argues that the Executive had a clear duty to protect this newly acquired interest against foreign interference.
records.summary_es: El Daily Kennebec Journal publica un extracto de la carta oficial del secretario de la Armada Robeson en defensa de las acciones del ejecutivo relativas a la República Dominicana. Robeson manifiesta que la República de Santo Domingo, con su ventajosa posición, riqueza natural y población amistosa, se consideraba muy conveniente para el comercio estadounidense y para estaciones navales en Samaná. Sostiene que el presidente poseía la facultad constitucional para iniciar y negociar tratados de cesión de Samaná y de anexión con el gobierno dominicano establecido de facto y de jure. Si bien reconoce que dichos tratados estaban sujetos a la ratificación del Senado y del pueblo dominicano, Robeson afirma que el ejecutivo tenía el claro deber de proteger este interés recién adquirido frente a cualquier injerencia extranjera.

records.headline: The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer reprints a New York Times dispatch
records.summary_en: The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer reprints a New York Times dispatch, under the heading 'Fred Douglass' Views on San Domingo and Sumner,' reporting an audience between Frederick Douglass and President Grant, attended by Secretary Robeson and Attorney General Akerman. When questioned by the President, Douglass reported his impressions of Dominica and Haiti, describing the Dominicans as far superior to the Haitians and characterizing Haiti's government as an oppressive despotism devoid of republicanism. Douglass expressed regret over Senator Charles Sumner's opposition, hoping the forthcoming commissioners' report would convince him to change his views. Douglass stated that if Sumner continued his resistance, he would consider him 'the worst foe the colored race has on this continent,' while affirming his own support for annexation.
records.summary_es: Bajo el título «Opiniones de Fred Douglass sobre Santo Domingo y Sumner», el Wheeling Daily Intelligencer reproduce un despacho del New York Times que informa sobre una audiencia entre Frederick Douglass y el presidente Grant, en presencia del secretario Robeson y el fiscal general Akerman. Al ser consultado por el presidente, Douglass transmitió sus impresiones sobre Dominica y Haití, calificando a los dominicanos de muy superiores a los haitianos y describiendo el gobierno de Haití como un despotismo opresivo carente de republicanismo. Douglass lamentó la oposición del senador Charles Sumner, esperando que el próximo informe de los comisionados lo indujera a rectificar su postura. Douglass declaró que si Sumner persistía en su resistencia, lo consideraría «el peor enemigo que tiene la raza de color en este continente», reafirmando su propio respaldo a la anexión.

records.headline: The Springfield Weekly Republican prints an extract from Secretary of the Navy Robeson's official
records.summary_en: The Springfield Weekly Republican prints an extract from Secretary of the Navy Robeson's official letter to Rear-Admiral Lee. Robeson addresses a published letter concerning the San Domingo Commission, warning that it misleads the public and authorities of San Domingo regarding the spirit of executive orders to naval vessels. He rejects the premise that anyone connected with the commission captured within rebel lines could be treated as a spy on the theory that the United States had chosen to intervene in Dominican domestic conflicts. Robeson terms this assertion unfounded in fact and law, insisting that the United States was dealing with the regularly constituted government of the Dominican Republic in accordance with international law.
records.summary_es: El Springfield Weekly Republican publica un extracto de la carta oficial del secretario de la Armada Robeson dirigida al contraalmirante Lee. Robeson se refiere a una carta divulgada relativa a la comisión de Santo Domingo, advirtiendo que induce a error al público y a las autoridades de Santo Domingo sobre el verdadero sentido de las órdenes del ejecutivo a los buques navales. Rechaza la premisa de que cualquier persona vinculada a la comisión capturada tras las líneas rebeldes pudiera ser tratada como espía bajo la teoría de que los Estados Unidos habían resuelto intervenir en los conflictos internos dominicanos. Robeson califica dicha aseveración de infundada en los hechos y en el derecho, insistiendo en que los Estados Unidos trataban con el gobierno legítimamente constituido de la República Dominicana conforme al derecho internacional.

records.headline: A Herald letter from aboard the frigate Tennessee, off Port-au-Prince on March 1871, describes the Santo Domingo Commission's return
records.summary_en: A Herald letter from aboard the frigate Tennessee, off Port-au-Prince on March 1871, describes the Santo Domingo Commission's return journey, with the steamer Nantasket arriving from Puerto Plata bringing Professor White and the parties who had rendezvoused there after traversing the country. The commissioners are shown quarreling over the journey home: Ben Wade wants to make the most direct course home now that their business is done and their report almost completed, while Dr. Howe and Professor White outvote him, to the general dissatisfaction of everyone on board, and the letter doubts the three will even settle on a joint report.
records.summary_es: Una carta del Herald desde a bordo de la fragata Tennessee, frente a Puerto Príncipe en marzo de 1871, describe el viaje de regreso de la Comisión de Santo Domingo, con la llegada del vapor Nantasket desde Puerto Plata trayendo al profesor White y a los grupos que se habían reunido allí tras recorrer el país. Los comisionados aparecen discutiendo sobre el regreso: Ben Wade quiere tomar el rumbo más directo a casa ahora que su trabajo está hecho y su informe casi terminado, mientras el doctor Howe y el profesor White lo superan en votos, para disgusto general de todos a bordo, y la carta duda que los tres lleguen siquiera a acordar un informe conjunto.

records.headline: In a letter from his headquarters dated March 5, 1871, General Jose Maria Cabral tells the United States
records.summary_en: In a letter from his headquarters dated March 5, 1871, General Jose Maria Cabral tells the United States Commissioners, Wade, White and Howe, that he has no power to enter into any negotiations on the annexation of his country, that he has protested against it and that his people have been protesting with arms in their hands for more than a year. He invites the Commissioners to visit the people and his headquarters, but White and Howe reply that a visit is not convenient for the present, while Mr. Wade declines to sign the reply; the correspondent adds that Cabral in fact holds only a small strip of mountainous land along the Neyba River.
records.summary_es: En una carta desde su cuartel general fechada el 5 de marzo de 1871, el general José María Cabral dice a los comisionados de los Estados Unidos, Wade, White y Howe, que no tiene poder para entrar en ninguna negociación sobre la anexión de su país, que ha protestado contra ella y que su pueblo lleva más de un año protestando con las armas en la mano. Invita a los comisionados a visitar al pueblo y su cuartel general, pero White y Howe responden que la visita no es conveniente por el momento, mientras el señor Wade se niega a firmar la respuesta; el corresponsal añade que Cabral en realidad solo ocupa una pequeña franja de tierra montañosa a lo largo del río Neyba.
records.passage: GENERAL HEADQUARTERS, [illegible], March [illegible], 1871. To Señors Benjamin B. Wade, Andrew D. White and Samuel G. Howe, members of the Commission of the United States: GENTLEMEN: I have read the contents of your communication, dated on the 21st of the past month, with an additional note dated on the 28th of the same month in Azua, and have duly countered them. But not having any power to enter into any class of negotiations, or to treat in any way as to the annexation of my country, and having protested in the month of March past in behalf of the people and the army which I have the honor to govern, it appears to me altogether useless to be interviewed as to the subject which you propose to me. records.headline: The New York Herald prints a formal letter from General José María Cabral addressed
records.summary_en: The New York Herald prints a formal letter from General José María Cabral addressed to the President of the United States Senate. Cabral protests a statement made in Senator Charles Sumner's December 21, 1870 speech, which attributed to Cabral a policy of reuniting the two governments of Dominica and Haiti as they existed prior to 1844. Cabral denies that he or his party pursues such a policy, declaring that his protest fulfills a sacred duty as party leader to reflect the true stance of his associates. The passage also includes a subsequent shipboard report describing the commissioners' voyage from Port-au-Prince to Kingston, noting that the departure was reached as a compromise with Commissioner Ben Wade.
records.summary_es: El New York Herald publica una carta oficial del general José María Cabral dirigida al presidente del Senado de los Estados Unidos. Cabral protesta contra una afirmación hecha en el discurso del senador Charles Sumner del 21 de diciembre de 1870, en la cual se atribuía a Cabral la intención de unificar los dos gobiernos de Dominica y Haití como estaban organizados antes de 1844. Cabral niega que él o su partido sostengan semejante política, declarando que su protesta cumple con el deber sagrado de líder partidario al reflejar la verdadera posición de sus correligionarios. El pasaje incluye además una crónica posterior a bordo que describe el viaje de los comisionados desde Puerto Príncipe hasta Kingston, señalando que la partida se acordó como una fórmula de compromiso con el comisionado Ben Wade.

records.headline: An editorial paragraph in The Sun discusses Washington dispatches
records.summary_en: An editorial paragraph in The Sun discusses Washington dispatches reporting Commissioner Ben Wade's view that Congress must act immediately on the annexation of Santo Domingo. Wade reportedly argued that unless annexation is promptly agreed upon, President Buenaventura Báez will be unable to maintain power and will be overthrown by revolution. The Sun mocks this assertion, contrasting it with Wade's claims that Dominicans enthusiastically favor annexation, asking how the public could despise Báez if they adore the measure he embodies. The paper concludes that the United States would do best to leave Báez and the Dominicans to paddle their own canoe, along with General Grant and his speculative associates.
records.summary_es: Una nota editorial en The Sun analiza los despachos de Washington que informan sobre la opinión del comisionado Ben Wade de que el Congreso debe actuar de inmediato sobre la anexión de Santo Domingo. Según los informes, Wade sostuvo que, a menos que se apruebe prontamente la anexión, el presidente Buenaventura Báez no podrá sostenerse en el poder y será derrocado por una revolución. The Sun ridiculiza esta afirmación, contrastándola con las declaraciones de Wade de que los dominicanos apoyan con entusiasmo la anexión, y preguntando cómo el pueblo podría rechazar a Báez si idolatra la medida que él personifica. El periódico concluye que lo mejor para los Estados Unidos sería dejar a Báez y a los dominicanos remar su propia canoa, junto con el general Grant y sus allegados especuladores.

records.headline: A Washington letter in the Pawtucket Gazette and Chronicle criticizes
records.summary_en: A Washington letter in the Pawtucket Gazette and Chronicle criticizes Senator Charles Sumner for delivering his speech before the San Domingo Commission made its report. The correspondent argues that candor, patriotism, and gratitude toward President Grant should have restrained Sumner from weakening the administration while it struggled with southern disturbances. Under the heading 'The San Domingo Commission,' the letter reports that the commissioners arrived in Washington the previous evening by rail directly from Charleston. The correspondent notes that while no official results of their visit to the Dominican Republic have been made public, reports circulating in the press indicate that the forthcoming commission report will be favorable.
records.summary_es: Una carta de Washington en el Pawtucket Gazette and Chronicle critica al senador Charles Sumner por pronunciar su discurso antes de que la comisión de Santo Domingo presentara su informe. El corresponsal sostiene que la franqueza, el patriotismo y la gratitud hacia el presidente Grant debieron frenar a Sumner de debilitar al gobierno mientras enfrentaba disturbios en el sur. Bajo el título «La comisión de Santo Domingo», la carta informa que los comisionados llegaron a Washington la noche anterior por ferrocarril directamente desde Charleston. El corresponsal señala que, aunque no se ha hecho público ningún resultado oficial de su visita a la República Dominicana, los informes que circulan en la prensa indican que el próximo informe de la comisión será favorable.

records.headline: The Springfield Weekly Republican publishes an excerpt from Senator Charles Sumner's speech
records.summary_en: The Springfield Weekly Republican publishes an excerpt from Senator Charles Sumner's speech recounting Dominican political history. Sumner relates that José María Cabral attained the presidency through direct popular vote, and that during Báez's exile in Washington, Secretary Seward referred Báez to Sumner. Sumner states that Báez visited his residence seeking money and arms to overthrow the Dominican government, but received no encouragement, though Sumner expressed his hope that America would assist Dominica. He explains that when Cabral later offered to lease Samaná Bay to relieve financial distress, Báez denounced the proposal as a sale of his country, but subsequently organized a force backed by President Salnave of Haiti that forced Cabral's capitulation on February 8, 1868.
records.summary_es: El Springfield Weekly Republican publica un extracto del discurso del senador Charles Sumner en el que repasa la historia política dominicana. Sumner relata que José María Cabral alcanzó la presidencia mediante el voto popular directo y que, durante el exilio de Báez en Washington, el secretario Seward remitió a Báez ante Sumner. Sumner señala que Báez visitó su casa en busca de dinero y armas para derrocar al gobierno dominicano, sin obtener apoyo alguno, aunque Sumner expresó su deseo de que los Estados Unidos ayudaran a Dominica. Explica que cuando Cabral ofreció más tarde arrendar la bahía de Samaná para aliviar dificultades financieras, Báez denunció la propuesta como una venta de su patria, pero luego organizó una fuerza respaldada por el presidente Salnave de Haití que forzó la capitulación de Cabral el 8 de febrero de 1868.

records.headline: The paper reports Senator Sumner repeating his allegations that Báez was maintained in power by the U.S. Navy
records.summary_en: The paper reports Senator Sumner repeating his allegations that Báez was maintained in power by the U.S. Navy to carry out the sale of his country and that Haiti was menaced by an American admiral to assure that sale, both of which he called breaches of public law. Sumner said he now presented the charges on documentary evidence from government officers.

Sumner dijo que ahora presentaba los cargos con pruebas documentales de oficiales del gobierno.
