records.headline: An article cites dispatches from Commercial Agent Perry at Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: An article cites dispatches from Commercial Agent Perry at Santo Domingo to argue that President Buenaventura Báez was kept in power only by United States naval force. In a dispatch dated January 20, 1870, Perry reported that the warship Nantasket was visiting Puerto Plata and Samaná Bay in Dominica, noting that American naval protection was urgently needed before public opinion on annexation was expressed. The writer asserts that Báez actually feared the Dominican people would pronounce for his overthrow without warships present. Dispatches from February 8 and February 20 further report that Báez complained daily of delays in sending warships and warned that if American ships were withdrawn, he could not maintain his government in the Dominican Republic.
records.summary_es: Un artículo cita despachos del agente comercial Perry en Santo Domingo para sostener que el presidente Buenaventura Báez se mantenía en el poder únicamente por la fuerza naval de los Estados Unidos. En un despacho fechado el 20 de enero de 1870, Perry informó que el buque de guerra Nantasket visitaba Puerto Plata y la bahía de Samaná en Dominica, señalando que la protección naval estadounidense era sumamente necesaria antes de que se expresara públicamente la opinión sobre la anexión. El articulista afirma que Báez en realidad temía que el pueblo dominicano se pronunciara por su derrocamiento si no había buques de guerra presentes. Los despachos del 8 y 20 de febrero informan además que Báez se quejaba a diario de los retrasos en el envío de buques de guerra y advertía que, si se retiraban los barcos estadounidenses, no podría sostener su gobierno en la República Dominicana.

records.summary_en: A letter of Capt. Temple published in New York reveals that President Grant had ordered the navy to protect the government of Baez against any demonstrations by Haiti, the paper reports. Official correspondence also published confirms it and shows that Admiral Porter and Minister Bassett had notified the Haitian government of the executive's order.

La correspondencia oficial también publicada lo confirma y muestra que el almirante Porter y el ministro Bassett habían notificado al gobierno haitiano la orden del ejecutivo.

records.headline: Under the heading "Dominica," the paper reports that the report of the San Domingo Commissioners
records.summary_en: Under the heading "Dominica," the paper reports that the report of the San Domingo Commissioners is nearly completed. According to the summary of its findings, the Dominican government was found in full operation, with President Báez in peaceable possession of the entire country except along the Haitian border. The report states that Báez enjoys the respect of the great majority of the population and that the president, cabinet, legislature, and judiciary all favor relinquishing their power to the United States. It adds that years of commotion have paralyzed industry and left the Dominican Republic unable to pay its expenses, while an insurgent leader holds only three or four mountain villages and Luperon stirs disturbances in the north.

records.headline: A correspondent recounts arriving at Samaná aboard the steamer
records.summary_en: A correspondent recounts arriving at Samaná aboard the steamer Tybee, noting that officers boarded from naval vessels in the bay and passengers landed at a dock built by Spofford Brothers near Santa Barbara. After departing Samaná in the afternoon, the writer arrived off Santo Domingo City the following night and entered the capital early the next morning. The correspondent reports being presented to President Buenaventura Báez and his brother Damien, the governor of Santo Domingo City, describing both as refined gentlemen who offered saddle-horses for the visitor's use. The letter describes warm summer weather, abundant tropical fruits, and plans to write further once rested and acclimated.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal relata su llegada a Samaná a bordo del vapor Tybee, señalando que los oficiales abordaron desde los buques de guerra en la bahía y que los pasajeros desembarcaron en un muelle construido por Spofford Brothers cerca de Santa Bárbara. Tras partir de Samaná por la tarde, el autor llegó frente a la ciudad de Santo Domingo la noche siguiente y entró a la capital temprano a la mañana siguiente. El corresponsal informa haber sido presentado al presidente Buenaventura Báez y a su hermano Damián, gobernador de la ciudad de Santo Domingo, describiendo a ambos como caballeros refinados que pusieron caballos de montar a su disposición. La carta describe el clima veraniego, las abundantes frutas tropicales y los planes de escribir con mayor detalle una vez que haya descansado y se haya aclimatado.

records.full_text:
ST. DOMINGO REPORT.

The report of the Santo Domingo commissioners was read in the Cabinet meeting to-day, and will probably be submitted to Congress on Monday. It will be accompanied by a brief message from the President, in which, it is reported, he will inform Congress that while their official report is merely confined to answering the inquiries proposed by Congress, he has, nevertheless, been informed by them that they are in favor of the immediate annexation of Santo Domingo. It remains to be seen whether the President thus proposes to travel outside of the official record. If so, his only excuse will be the opinion expressed to him by the commissioners that Baez's condition is such that the annexation question must necessarily be disposed of at the earliest practicable moment. Several Republican Senators favor disposing of the question by passing a resolution now declaring Congress opposed to annexation, and thus obviate the negotiation and subsequent discussion of a new treaty. A Republican Senator has prepared such a resolution, and is only awaiting events before offering it.

records.headline: An article reviews the Dominican rebellion led by Cabral against Spain
records.summary_en: An article reviews the Dominican rebellion led by Cabral against Spain and the political upheavals in Dominica that followed it. It recounts that after the Spanish withdrawal, Cabral served as protector before Báez was restored to power, only for another revolution to reinstate Cabral, who then offered the United States a lease of Samaná Bay. Following another convention, Báez assumed executive power while Cabral withdrew to the interior to wage war, prompting Báez to seek foreign protectorate aid after European powers refused his half of the island. The paper sharply criticizes the Grant administration for sending an inexperienced young officer to negotiate with Báez, and condemns the American promoter Cazneau for securing lucrative concessions in the Dominican Republic while remaining disloyal to the United States.
records.summary_es: Un artículo examina la rebelión dominicana encabezada por Cabral contra España y las convulsiones políticas que la siguieron en Dominica. Relata que, tras la retirada española, Cabral fungió como protector antes de que Báez fuera restablecido en el poder, solo para que otra revolución reinstalara a Cabral, quien luego ofreció a los Estados Unidos el arrendamiento de la bahía de Samaná. Tras una nueva convención, Báez asumió el poder ejecutivo mientras Cabral se retiraba al interior para hacer la guerra, lo que llevó a Báez a buscar ayuda extranjera después de que las potencias europeas rechazaran su mitad de la isla. El periódico critica severamente al gobierno de Grant por enviar a un joven oficial inexperto a negociar con Báez, y condena al promotor estadounidense Cazneau por asegurarse lucrativas concesiones en la República Dominicana mientras se mostraba desleal a los Estados Unidos.

records.passage: THE SANTO DOMINGO REPORT NOT READY YET — NO DISAGREEMENT AMONG THE COMMISSIONERS — SPECULATIONS CONCERNING THE PRESIDENT'S INTENTIONS — THE NEW-YORK APPOINTMENTS. [BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.] WASHINGTON, Monday, April 3, 1871. The Santo Domingo report is not yet finished, but those who have been most familiar with the views of the Commissioners believe that there is not the slightest variation in the general views of the members, and that the report, when finally finished and signed, will be as favorable to annexation as the first report prepared by Mr. Wade. The report which will be presented to the President will be more full in details, will embrace more subjects, and give more space to discussion of the subjects laid down in the resolutions of Congress than the report which was first considered. It seemed doubtful yesterday that the Commissioners were in full accord, but the intimate friends of all the Commissioners say that there will be no disagreement, and that the report will be mainly straightforward and emphatic, and not meaningless recital of what was seen and heard by Commissioners in making their investigation. One of the Commissioners says that any one who reads the report cannot be in doubt as to the opinions and views of the members. The report is now [finishing?], and a meeting of Commissioners to-morrow will determine the whole subject. A sufficient number of clerks are now engaged in arranging the documentary evidence and testimony of witnesses, which the investigation elicited, and all the documents and testimony, enough to make a large book, will be ready for the printer by time the report shall be handed in.

The Dominican minister reports that the country remains entirely tranquil and is increasingly eager for annexation to the United States to be speedily accomplished. Quoting the letter directly, the dispatch notes that the writer sees annexation as the only salvation against the insidious intrigues of Haiti, and announces that President Báez has returned to the capital after routing Cabral at Azua.

Citando directamente la carta, el despacho señala que el autor considera la anexión como la única salvación frente a las insidiosas intrigas de Haití, y anuncia que el presidente Báez ha regresado a la capital tras derrotar a Cabral en Azua.

records.passage: be agreed to by Baez. Mr. Sumner was unwilling, however, to consent to annexation on any terms, and gave Fabens his reasons. During the conversation, Mr. Sumner asked Fabens if he thought that annexation would stop with Santo Domingo. "Oh, no!" replied the Dominican Envoy, "you must have Hayti too." And is that all, continued the Senator. Fabens thought that we could not stop with Hayti, but must, in the nature of things, finally absorb Porto Rico, Jamaica, Cuba, the Windward Islands, and, indeed, all of the West Indies. Mr. Sumner then called the attention of Fabens to the fact that the treaty involved not only the question of the annexation of the little republic of Santo Domingo, but an entirely new foreign policy for the United States. He professed his friendship for the people of the island, and his willingness to aid them by every means in his power; but while he doubted that Santo Domingo would in the end gain by annexation, he was sure that the United States would lose. Mr. Sumner believes that the West India Islands are destined to be the home of the black race. In proof of this he points to the fact that in almost every instance the blacks have increased there much more rapidly than the whites, so that in some of the islands the white population is not more than 25 per cent of the whole, while in many others it is less than 50 per cent. records.headline: Reprinting an editorial from the New York World, the paper denounces
records.summary_en: Reprinting an editorial from the New York World, the paper denounces conditions in Santo Domingo, asserting that paper currency has collapsed to where $1,000 is needed to buy a pound of tea and claiming the country had three revolutions and 4,000 major generals in five years. The piece claims that Commissioners Benjamin Wade, Dr. Howe, and Frederick Douglass regard the situation as a failure, pointing to widespread ignorance and asserting that the populace does not understand republican government. It cites an unnamed gentleman with the Commission who saw no improvement since visiting thirty years earlier, judging the Haitians to be better and wiser. The excerpt concludes that the Commission will nonetheless urge annexation to please President Grant.
records.summary_es: Al reproducir un editorial del New York World, el periódico denuncia las condiciones en Santo Domingo, afirmando que su moneda de papel ha colapsado hasta el punto de requerirse 1,000 dólares para comprar una libra de té, y alegando que el país tuvo tres revoluciones y 4,000 mayores generales en cinco años. El artículo afirma que los comisionados Benjamin Wade, el Dr. Howe y Frederick Douglass consideran la situación un fracaso, señalando una ignorancia generalizada y asegurando que la población no comprende el gobierno republicano. Cita a un caballero no identificado vinculado a la Comisión que no vio mejora alguna desde que la visitó treinta años antes, considerando a los haitianos más capaces y prudentes. El extracto concluye que, pese a todo, la Comisión instará a la anexión para complacer al presidente Grant.

records.summary_en: Quoting the New York Herald, the paper characterizes President Grant's message accompanying the San Domingo commissioners' report as the most significant document submitted. The Herald describes the message as a straightforward review of the administration's actions regarding Santo Domingo, praising Grant for disavowing any intention to enforce his annexation policy against the will of the Dominican people.

El Herald describe el mensaje como un examen directo de las acciones del gobierno con respecto a Santo Domingo, elogiando a Grant por renunciar a cualquier intención de imponer su política de anexión contra la voluntad del pueblo dominicano.

The report says earlier accounts of coal nearby are not confirmed by the expedition's geologists, calls the bay the natural outlet of the rich La Vega plain, and notes that the Yuna river can be navigated by light-draught vessels and that a railroad along its valley would face no heavy grades or large rivers.

records.headline: The paper publishes an excerpt from the San Domingo Commission's report
records.summary_en: The paper publishes an excerpt from the San Domingo Commission's report reviewing the career and legitimacy of President Buenaventura Báez. The report notes that Báez presided over Congress following the overthrow of Haitian rule and that his initial term was the only one in Dominican history to complete its full constitutional period before Gen. Pedro Santana succeeded him in 1853. Following subsequent upheavals and Spanish rule, Báez was repeatedly recalled to establish provisional authority, once on the invitation of a delegation including Gen. Cabral. The Commissioners find that in his third year of office, Báez has maintained as much liberty as circumstances allowed, with no rival holding a superior title to power.
records.summary_es: El periódico publica un extracto del informe de la Comisión de Santo Domingo que examina la trayectoria y legitimidad del presidente Buenaventura Báez. El informe señala que Báez presidió el Congreso tras el derrocamiento del dominio haitiano y que su período inicial fue el único en la historia dominicana en cumplir todo su mandato constitucional antes de que el general Pedro Santana lo sucediera en 1853. Tras los trastornos subsiguientes y la dominación española, Báez fue llamado repetidamente para establecer una autoridad provisional, en una ocasión por invitación de una delegación que incluía al general Cabral. Los comisionados determinan que, en su tercer año de mandato, Báez ha mantenido tanta libertad como permitían las circunstancias, sin que ningún rival ostente un derecho superior al poder.

records.headline: The Commission reports finding extensive evidence that insurgent
records.summary_en: The Commission reports finding extensive evidence that insurgent forces under Cabral received direct assistance from Haiti, citing examinations of Haitian prisoners captured with Haitian-stamped muskets. Near Manzanillo Bay, insurgent leader Luperón commands a small guerrilla band described by local witnesses as having only the strength of a desperado. According to the Commissioners, both movements would have collapsed without foreign intriguers and the support of Haiti, a nation with nearly five times the population and revenue of the Dominican Republic. The report adds that internal instability is compounded by long-standing regional jealousy between the northern provinces, including Santiago and Puerto Plata, and the southern district.
records.summary_es: La Comisión informa haber hallado amplias pruebas de que las fuerzas insurgentes dirigidas por Cabral recibieron auxilio directo de Haití, citando interrogatorios a prisioneros haitianos capturados con fusiles que llevaban el cuño haitiano. Cerca de la bahía de Manzanillo, el líder insurgente Luperón comanda una pequeña partida guerrillera calificada por testigos locales de poseer solo la fuerza de un forajido. De acuerdo con los comisionados, ambos movimientos habrían fracasado sin la ayuda de intrigantes extranjeros y el respaldo de Haití, país que cuenta con casi cinco veces la población y los ingresos de la República Dominicana. El informe agrega que la inestabilidad interna se agrava por el arraigado recelo regional entre las provincias del norte, incluidas Santiago y Puerto Plata, y el distrito sur.

records.headline: Under the heading "The Bay of Samana," the Commission's report
records.summary_en: Under the heading "The Bay of Samana," the Commission's report surveys the harbors of the Dominican Republic, noting that while Ocoa and Manzanillo accommodate large vessels, neither possesses major military significance. The report singles out Samaná Bay as the most important harbor in the West Indies, describing it as thirty miles long by ten miles wide and capable of sheltering the largest naval fleets. Citing a survey by General McClellan, the Commissioners state that simple fortifications at the bay's entrance and at Port Jackson would provide complete defense. They add that the bay commands the Mona Passage and would acquire immense strategic value upon the opening of a canal route across the Isthmus of Darien.
records.summary_es: Bajo el subtítulo «La bahía de Samaná», el informe de la Comisión examina los puertos de la República Dominicana y señala que, aunque Ocoa y Manzanillo admiten embarcaciones de gran calado, ninguno posee gran importancia militar. El informe destaca la bahía de Samaná como el puerto más importante de las Antillas, describiéndola con una extensión de treinta millas de largo por diez de ancho y capacidad para albergar las mayores flotas navales. Citando un estudio del general McClellan, los comisionados señalan que fortificaciones sencillas en la entrada de la bahía y en Port Jackson bastarían para defenderla por completo. Añaden que la bahía domina el paso de la Mona y adquiriría un inmenso valor estratégico si se abre una ruta canalera a través del istmo de Darién.

records.headline: The Commission's report details trade routes from Samaná Bay
records.summary_en: The Commission's report details trade routes from Samaná Bay. It observes that the Yuna River could accommodate light-draft steamers and that the surrounding valley offers favorable conditions and abundant timber for a railroad. While at the capital, the Commissioners learned that although the United States had continuously occupied Samaná Bay as a naval station, its rental payments were in default for more than a year. Under the heading "Public Debt," the report outlines an exhaustive inquiry into the liabilities of the Dominican Republic. The Commissioners collected data from public financial records, interviewed official custodians, examined private claimants, and received detailed itemized claims from the Dominican Senate and President Báez.
records.summary_es: El informe de la Comisión detalla las rutas comerciales desde la bahía de Samaná. Observa que el río Yuna podría admitir vapores de poco calado y que el valle circundante ofrece condiciones propicias y abundante madera para un ferrocarril. Estando en la capital, los comisionados se enteraron de que, si bien los Estados Unidos habían ocupado de forma continua la bahía de Samaná como estación naval, el pago del alquiler presentaba un retraso de más de un año. Bajo el subtítulo «Deuda pública», el informe expone una minuciosa investigación sobre las obligaciones financieras de la República Dominicana. Los comisionados recopilaron datos de los registros contables oficiales, entrevistaron a funcionarios encargados, examinaron a reclamantes privados y recibieron listas detalladas de reclamaciones del Senado dominicano y del presidente Báez.

records.headline: The Commission reports that it examined the originals of the annexation treaty and the Samana lease in the archives of the Dominican Government
records.summary_en: The Commission reports that it examined the originals of the annexation treaty and the Samana lease in the archives of the Dominican Government in Santo Domingo City, in the presence of the President and his Cabinet on February 18, 1871, and found no particle of evidence of any secret clause or concession favoring any United States official. President Baez told the commissioners his government was willing to stand by the 1869 treaty, but asked whether the Samana rent for the nearly two years of delay might fairly be paid without deduction, and he agreed to modify the treaty to devote one-fifth of the public lands to common schools if the United States would add land for colleges of agriculture, mining and engineering.
records.summary_es: La Comisión informa que examinó los originales del tratado de anexión y del arrendamiento de Samaná en los archivos del Gobierno dominicano en la ciudad de Santo Domingo, en presencia del Presidente y su Gabinete el 18 de febrero de 1871, y no encontró ni la menor evidencia de cláusula secreta o concesión alguna en favor de ningún funcionario de los Estados Unidos. El presidente Báez dijo a los comisionados que su gobierno estaba dispuesto a mantener el tratado de 1869, pero preguntó si no sería justo que la renta de Samaná por los casi dos años de demora se pagara sin deducción, y aceptó modificar el tratado para dedicar una quinta parte de las tierras públicas a escuelas comunes si los Estados Unidos añadían tierras para colegios de agricultura, minería e ingeniería.

records.headline: The Herald publishes an extract detailing mining concessions
records.summary_en: The Herald publishes an extract detailing mining concessions and land grants made to foreign individuals, from the report of the San Domingo Commission and corporations. The list enumerates rights to copper and coal deposits in San Cristóbal and Samaná, including concessions awarded to William L. Cazneau, Cambiaso and Company, and the San Domingo Company. The Commissioners affirm that the Dominican government has made no grant or concession of public land to any foreign government other than the United States. In addition to national concessions, the report notes municipal grants made to American citizens in the village of Santa Bárbara on Samaná Bay, including a waterfront parcel granted to J. P. O'Sullivan.
records.summary_es: El Herald publica un extracto del informe de la Comisión de Santo Domingo, que detalla las concesiones mineras y de tierras otorgadas a personas y corporaciones extranjeras. La lista enumera derechos sobre yacimientos de cobre y carbón en San Cristóbal y Samaná, incluidas concesiones otorgadas a William L. Cazneau, Cambiaso y Compañía, y la San Domingo Company. Los comisionados afirman que el gobierno dominicano no ha otorgado ninguna cesión ni concesión de tierras públicas a ningún gobierno extranjero con excepción de los Estados Unidos. Además de las concesiones nacionales, el informe menciona cesiones municipales otorgadas a ciudadanos estadounidenses en la villa de Santa Bárbara en la bahía de Samaná, incluida una parcela frente al mar concedida a J. P. O'Sullivan.

records.headline: Under the heading "St. Domingo," the Herald reports Havana telegraphic
records.summary_en: Under the heading "St. Domingo," the Herald reports Havana telegraphic dispatches describing recent clashes between Dominican government forces under President Báez and insurgents commanded by Cabral and Luperón. The dispatches state that the insurgent forces were defeated in two separate engagements, though casualties and prisoner counts were apparently light. The paper notes that the insurgents likely lost their entire cavalry force, with fourteen horses captured in the first action and fifteen in the second. Approximately eight hundred men and ten general officers participated in the initial encounter, though the Herald observes that these government victories provide no guarantee of lasting peace.
records.summary_es: Bajo el título «Santo Domingo», el Herald informa sobre despachos telegráficos desde La Habana que describen recientes enfrentamientos entre las fuerzas del gobierno dominicano bajo el presidente Báez y los insurgentes comandados por Cabral y Luperón. Los despachos indican que las tropas insurgentes fueron derrotadas en dos combates distintos, aunque el número de bajas y prisioneros aparentemente no fue elevado. El periódico señala que los insurgentes probablemente perdieron toda su caballería, habiéndose capturado catorce caballos en la primera acción y quince en la segunda. Alrededor de ochocientos hombres y diez oficiales generales participaron en el choque inicial, aunque el Herald advierte que estas victorias gubernamentales no ofrecen garantía alguna de una paz duradera.

records.summary_en: A summary of the Santo Domingo commissioners' report describes the island as one of the most fertile regions on earth, producing all tropical fruits and vegetables as well as commercial staples, with general health and longevity equal to or greater than in the United States. The commissioners state that acquiring Samana Bay would give the United States a powerful military and naval station, and the report, which also gives the total of the Dominican government's debt and claims, was transmitted by the President to Congress.

records.headline: Under the heading "San Domingo: The Annexation Fever," dispatches
records.summary_en: Under the heading "San Domingo: The Annexation Fever," dispatches report that President Grant transmitted the report of the San Domingo Commissioners to Congress just before the House adjourned. A telegram from St. Thomas dated April 1 announces that President Báez has defeated Cabral's forces near Azua, while Luperón's troops are reported to be advancing in the northern provinces. The dispatch notes that the Dominican public remains anxious for a final resolution of the annexation question. A dispatch from Havana adds that intense public excitement over the American annexation project persists in neighboring Haiti, though that country otherwise remains quiet.
records.summary_es: Bajo el título «Santo Domingo: La fiebre de la anexión», los despachos informan que el presidente Grant transmitió el informe de los comisionados de Santo Domingo al Congreso poco antes de que la Cámara levantara la sesión. Un telegrama de Saint Thomas, fechado el 1 de abril, comunica que el presidente Báez derrotó a las fuerzas de Cabral cerca de Azua, mientras se reporta que las tropas de Luperón avanzan en las provincias del norte. El despacho señala que el público dominicano sigue ansioso por una resolución definitiva de la cuestión de la anexión. Por su parte, un despacho de La Habana añade que persiste una intensa agitación pública sobre el proyecto de anexión estadounidense en el vecino Haití, aunque ese país por lo demás permanece tranquilo.

records.headline: An excerpt from the report of the San Domingo Commission estimates
records.summary_en: An excerpt from the report of the San Domingo Commission estimates the population of the republic at 150,000, of whom more than nineteen-twentieths are native Dominicans, noting that white blood largely preponderates. The report surveys the country's mineral wealth, finding abundant iron ore, moderately rich copper deposits, extensive salt beds near Neyba, and coal in Samaná and Puerto Plata, though of inferior quality to Pennsylvania coal. The Commissioners divide the territory into five classes of land, including rich mountain valleys, pasture prairies, and the fertile agricultural plains of La Vega. They conclude that almost the entire country is cultivable and exceptionally fertile, observing that sugar cane yields fifteen annual cuttings from a single root.
records.summary_es: Un extracto del informe de la Comisión de Santo Domingo estima la población de la república en 150,000 habitantes, de los cuales más de diecinueve vigésimos son dominicanos nativos, señalando que la sangre blanca predomina ampliamente. El informe examina las riquezas minerales del país, destacando abundantes minerales de hierro, depósitos de cobre de regular riqueza, extensos yacimientos de sal cerca de Neyba y carbón en Samaná y Puerto Plata, aunque de calidad inferior al carbón de Pensilvania. Los comisionados dividen las tierras en cinco clases, entre ellas fértiles valles montañosos, llanuras de pastoreo y las ricas tierras agrícolas de La Vega. Concluyen que casi todo el territorio es cultivable y sumamente fértil, observando que la caña de azúcar produce quince cortes anuales a partir de una misma raíz.

The Commissioners concluded that Dominican independence has never been a reality and that union as a State is the republic's only chance to secure its freedom and independence, though they made no formal recommendation on whether to adopt that course.

Los comisionados concluyeron que la independencia dominicana nunca había sido una realidad y que la incorporación como Estado de la Unión constituía la única vía para afianzar sus libertades e independencia, aun cuando se abstuvieron de formular una recomendación explícita sobre dicho camino.

records.full_text:
FINANCIAL.

The Commissioners made a thorough and careful examination of the debt of San Domingo, and find the sum total of all debts and outstanding claims against the Republic to be $1,565,831. The receipts of the government for 1870 were $772,684, of which $728,605 was from customs and $35,466 from taxes. The Commissioners lay great stress on their efforts to get the exact state of the debt of the Dominican Republic, and believe their conclusions substantially correct. San Domingo is not believed to be liable for any of the indemnity exacted by France from Hayti, and the Commission is assured that no obligation or negotiations have been entered into with any country except the United States.

The extent of undisputed Dominican territory is 22,512 square miles. The portion which formerly involved a dispute with Hayti being 1000 square miles. The Commissioners present a full statement of all the grants and concessions of public lands and franchise, and declare that after the most searching and complete investigation they were unable to find any grant or concession in any form or manner to any U. S. official, either in connection with the negotiation or preparation of the treaty.

records.headline: The St. Cloud Journal notes that Senator Charles Sumner's speech
records.summary_en: The St. Cloud Journal notes that Senator Charles Sumner's speech against Dominican annexation was, in the view of leading newspapers, injudicious, delivered before the San Domingo Commissioners submitted their report. It quotes the New York Tribune, which argues that Sumner erred by speaking before Commissioners Wade, White, and Howe concluded their municipal inquiries across the Dominican Republic, adding that Sumner holds no superiority in honesty or information over the commissioners. The paper also quotes the New York Times, which asserts that Sumner's facts fail to warrant his conclusions and cannot sustain his charge of usurpation against President Grant.
records.summary_es: El St. Cloud Journal señala que destacados periódicos consideran imprudente el discurso del senador Charles Sumner contra la anexión dominicana, pronunciado antes de que los comisionados de Santo Domingo presentaran su informe. Cita al New York Tribune, que sostiene que Sumner se equivocó al hablar antes de que los comisionados Wade, White y Howe concluyeran sus investigaciones municipales en casi toda la República Dominicana, añadiendo que Sumner no aventaja a los comisionados en honradez ni en información. El diario cita también al New York Times, el cual afirma que los datos expuestos por Sumner apenas justifican sus conclusiones y fracasan por completo en fundamentar su acusación de usurpación contra el presidente Grant.

records.headline: An excerpt from the report of the San Domingo Commission characterizes
records.summary_en: An excerpt from the report of the San Domingo Commission characterizes the insurgent band under Luperón as a small guerrilla force possessing only the strength of a desperado. The Commissioners state that Dominican insurgent leaders would have been suppressed long ago without foreign intrigue and the armed backing of Haiti, which possesses nearly three times the population and revenue of the Dominican Republic. Under the heading "Causes of Disturbance," the report explains that internal strife is further aggravated by intense provincial rivalry between the northern and southern regions. It contrasts the thriving northern commercial centers of Puerto Plata and Santiago with the historic capital of Santo Domingo in the south.
records.summary_es: Un extracto del informe de la Comisión de Santo Domingo califica la partida insurgente de Luperón como una pequeña fuerza guerrillera que solo posee la fuerza de un forajido. Los comisionados afirman que los líderes insurgentes dominicanos habrían sido reprimidos hace mucho tiempo de no ser por las intrigas extranjeras y el respaldo armado de Haití, país que cuenta con casi tres veces la población y los ingresos de la República Dominicana. Bajo el subtítulo «Causas de los disturbios», el informe explica que las contiendas internas se ven agravadas además por una marcada rivalidad provincial entre las regiones del norte y del sur. Contrasta los prósperos centros comerciales norteños de Puerto Plata y Santiago con la histórica capital de Santo Domingo en el sur.

records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that Haytian and Dominican forces have alternately occupied disputed territory, with Haytiens holding practical control of San Rafael, San Miguel, and Los Caobas, while the Benica valley and Neiba district were overrun by both governments. It also noted a map issued by private parties—based on a Haytian report from President Geffrard's time—detailing a boundary line from Monte Cristi to the south shore, which the publication dismissed as preposterous. Furthermore, a member of the Commission recently found Monte Cristi inhabited by a Spanish-speaking people under Dominican authorities with no awareness of any outside claim since 1814.
records.summary_es: El periódico expuso que las fuerzas dominicanas y haitianas habían ocupado de forma intermitente comarcas limítrofes en litigio, reteniendo los haitianos el control material de San Rafael, San Miguel y Las Caobas, en tanto que el valle de Bánica [Benica] y el distrito de Neiba eran recorridos por destacamentos de ambos bandos. Mencionó asimismo un mapa impreso por particulares —fundado en una memoria haitiana de tiempos del presidente Geffrard— que trazaba una línea divisoria desde Montecristi hasta la costa sur, lindero que la publicación desestimó por absurdo. Además, un miembro de la comisión comprobó recientemente que Montecristi se hallaba habitado por gentes de habla hispana sujetas a las autoridades dominicanas, ajenas a reclamación extranjera alguna desde 1814.

records.full_text:
...sequent treaties, all of which refer to it as the undisputed boundary. It is doubly important in the history of the island. It marks the separation of different languages, different national traditions and characteristics, different modes of dividing and surveying the soil, different peoples. In 1821 the people of what is now the Dominican Republic threw off the Spanish yoke and proclaimed a republic. At this time the boundary was not disputed, and the republic included all the Spanish part of the island, or, in other words, was along the line of 1777.

In 1822 the Haytien President Boyer acquired possession of the whole island, and it remained under one government until the revolution of 1844 resulted in the expulsion of the Haytien rulers and the re-establishment of the independence of the Dominican Republic throughout the Dominican or Spanish speaking portion of the island, except a few interior valleys on the Dominican side of the line, in some of which there has been an almost constant struggle. Since that time the Haytien and Dominican forces alternately held all the disputed territory. Of this disputed territory the Haytiens have held practically constant possession of the towns of San Rafael, San Miguel, and Las Caobas.

The Banica valley east of these, with Banica as its principal town, and the Nezba valley to the south, have been alternately overrun by both governments. The attention of the Commission has been drawn to a map issued by private parties in our own country, claiming to be based on a Haytien report made on this subject in President Geffrard's time. The boundary given by this map from a point just east of Monte Cristi, on the north shore of the island, in a nearly north and south line to a point on the south shore nearly opposite the island of Alta Vela.

Whether the Commission be right or wrong in judging that any infringement on Dominican territory has been based on usurpation, and is therefore null, the claim to any such line as that above indicated must seem preposterous to any one conversant with Dominican or Haytien affairs. The town of Monte Cristi, which by that map is placed under Haytien control, was at a recent visit by a member of the commission found to be inhabited by a Spanish-speaking people, with Dominican authorities, and no one seemed to be at all aware that it had been claimed since 1844 by any other government than Dominica.

As to the Banica valley and the other valleys thus claimed, the people are Dominicans, and from all that could be learned have never considered themselves otherwise. The Commission also made inquiries regarding the foundation of the Haytien claims outside of 1775, both of intelligent persons living in Hayti and of the Haytien ex-President Geffrard, now an exile in Jamaica, but from neither source could they obtain any direct presumptive evidence for the Haytien claim.

records.headline: An installment of the San Domingo Commission report in the Tribune describes
records.summary_en: An installment of the San Domingo Commission report in the Tribune describes the agricultural and social condition of the Dominican people. The report notes that pineapples flourish widely and that wheat grows in the high valley of Constanza, yet observes that underdeveloped agriculture forces reliance on imported French sugar, Danish butter, and American condensed milk. Turning to education and civic life, the Commissioners note that only one small, poorly equipped printing office operates in the capital, though teachers report good native ability among students. Under the heading "General Political Capacity," the report judges the populace to be by no means hopeless, emphasizing that generations without slavery or caste divisions have fostered self-reliance, industry, and capable patriotic leaders.
records.summary_es: Una entrega del informe de la Comisión de Santo Domingo en el Tribune describe la situación agrícola y social del pueblo dominicano. El informe señala que las piñas prosperan ampliamente y que el trigo crece en el alto valle de Constanza, aunque observa que el subdesarrollo agrícola obliga a depender de azúcar francés, mantequilla danesa y leche condensada estadounidense importadas. En cuanto a la educación y la vida cívica, los comisionados indican que solo funciona una imprenta pequeña y mal equipada en la capital, si bien los maestros informan de una buena capacidad innata en los estudiantes. Bajo el subtítulo «Capacidad política general», el informe considera que el pueblo no es en modo alguno desesperanzador, destacando que generaciones sin esclavitud ni castas han fomentado la dignidad, el trabajo y líderes patriotas capaces.

records.headline: The Commissioners' report describes St. Domingo's forests
records.summary_en: The Commissioners' report describes St. Domingo's forests as its most striking feature, with palms near the coast and mahogany, satinwood, Dominican oak, pitch pine, lignum vitae, logwood and other valuable woods inland. It says wide forests in the interior remain untouched for lack of roads, that large mahogany logs are left to decay by the roadside within thirty miles of the principal northern seaport, and that no sawmill was found in the country.
records.summary_es: El informe de los Comisionados describe los bosques de Santo Domingo como su rasgo más llamativo, con palmas cerca de la costa y caoba, palo satín, roble dominicano, pino resinoso, guayacán, campeche y otras maderas valiosas en el interior. Dice que amplios bosques del interior permanecen intactos por falta de caminos, que grandes troncos de caoba se dejan pudrir junto a los caminos a menos de treinta millas del principal puerto del norte, y que no se encontró ningún aserradero en el país.

The testimony of the head of a thrifty New England family, who had resided in the neighborhood of Samana Bay nearly two years, was to the effect that there was as little difficulty in keeping a house clear from troublesome insects, as in our Northern States. products [illegible] The most striking characteristic of St. Domingo, at first sight, is the wonderful luxuriance of its forests. In many parts, and especially in the neighborhood of the Bay of Samana, although there are abrupt ridges, perpendicular cliffs and bold headlands, no bare rocks can be seen, being hidden by a mass of strong vegetation. But on close observation another and not less striking characteristic is revealed: an astonishing variety in forest products. The cause of this variety is to be found, doubtless, in the great difference in elevation of the surface exposure and character of the soil. Near the coast various species of palm are abundant, and very valuable in constructing such houses as have been generally found best suited to the climate. On the mountain slopes, at different heights, grow in abundance both the choicest cabinet woods, as mahogany, satinwood, &c., and a great variety of timber especially valuable in housebuilding. The roble, or Dominican oak, and a hard pitch pine were found in abundance in various parts of the country. In the more dry districts flourish several valuable woods, the best known of which, perhaps, is the lignum vitae, of which the quantity is very great. records.headline: An excerpt from the report of the San Domingo Commission in the Herald reviews
records.summary_en: An excerpt from the report of the San Domingo Commission in the Herald reviews the political leadership of President Buenaventura Báez. The Commissioners state that a large majority of the Dominican people esteem Báez for his administrative capacity, regarding him as the sole leader capable of maintaining national unity against internal discord and external threats. The report recounts that following the overthrow of Haitian rule, Báez presided over the constituent congress and was elected president in 1849, presiding over the only administration in Dominican history to serve out its complete constitutional term. After Gen. Pedro Santana succeeded him in 1853, recurrent civil turmoil and Spanish annexation followed, during which Báez was repeatedly summoned from exile to re-establish provisional government.
records.summary_es: Un extracto del informe de la Comisión de Santo Domingo publicado en el Herald examina el liderazgo político del presidente Buenaventura Báez. Los comisionados afirman que una gran mayoría del pueblo dominicano aprecia a Báez por su capacidad administrativa, considerándolo el único líder capaz de preservar la unidad nacional frente a las discordias internas y las amenazas externas. El informe relata que, tras la expulsión del dominio haitiano, Báez presidió el congreso constituyente y fue elegido presidente en 1849, encabezando la única administración en la historia dominicana que completó todo su período constitucional. Después de que el general Pedro Santana lo sucediera en 1853, sobrevinieron recurrentes disturbios civiles y la anexión española, durante los cuales Báez fue convocado reiteradamente desde el exilio para restablecer el gobierno provisional.

records.headline: Border rebellions and foreign interference in Dominican affairs
records.summary_en: Border rebellions and foreign interference in Dominican affairs are addressed in an extract of the Commission's report printed by the Herald. The Commissioners confirm government charges that insurgent forces received arms and troops through Haiti, citing depositions and the examination of Haitian prisoners carrying muskets with Haitian government stamps. The report characterizes Luperón's force near Manzanillo Bay as a small guerrilla band lacking broad support, asserting that neither Cabral nor Luperón could have sustained their resistance without foreign intriguers and the active backing of Haiti. Under the heading "Causes of Disturbance," the Commissioners add that regional jealousy between the northern and southern provinces has further weakened national cohesion.
records.summary_es: El Herald publica un extracto del informe de la Comisión sobre las rebeliones fronterizas, que aborda la injerencia extranjera en los asuntos dominicanos. Los comisionados confirman las acusaciones gubernamentales de que las fuerzas insurgentes recibieron armas y tropas a través de Haití, citando declaraciones y el interrogatorio de prisioneros haitianos que portaban fusiles con el sello del gobierno haitiano. El informe califica la fuerza de Luperón cerca de la bahía de Manzanillo como una pequeña partida guerrillera carente de apoyo amplio, afirmando que ni Cabral ni Luperón habrían sostenido su resistencia sin intrigantes extranjeros y el respaldo activo de Haití. Bajo el subtítulo «Causas de los disturbios», los comisionados agregan que el recelo regional entre las provincias del norte y del sur ha debilitado aún más la cohesión nacional.

records.headline: The United States Commissioners report that of the great bays of Samana, Azua and Manzanilla, which admit vessels of the largest
records.summary_en: The United States Commissioners report that of the great bays of Samana, Azua and Manzanilla, which admit vessels of the largest draft, only Samana has importance from a military point of view, and that its acquisition would give the United States a powerful military and naval station and the site of an important commercial city. The report also sets out the Dominican government's debt and obligations in detail, along with its receipts for 1870, while noting that the statement includes much the Dominican government itself believes to be partially or wholly groundless.
records.summary_es: Los comisionados de los Estados Unidos informan que de las grandes bahías de Samaná, Azua y Manzanillo, que admiten buques del mayor calado, solo Samaná tiene importancia desde el punto de vista militar, y que su adquisición daría a los Estados Unidos una poderosa estación militar y naval y el sitio de una importante ciudad comercial. El informe expone también en detalle la deuda y las obligaciones del gobierno dominicano, junto con sus ingresos de 1870, señalando que la relación incluye mucho que el propio gobierno dominicano cree parcial o totalmente infundado.

records.summary_en: According to the newspaper, Dominican authorities informed the Commissioners that their current administration has had no diplomatic representation, treaties, or engagements with any government except the United States. The Commissioners also found that undisputed Dominican territory spans 22,212 square miles, with about 1,000 square miles formerly involved in disputes with Hayti. Additionally, after examining government and municipal grants, including records in Samana, the Commissioners found no truth to rumors that land concessions or grants had been made to officials of the Government or the United States during the negotiation of the 1869 annexation treaty.
records.summary_es: Según el diario, las autoridades dominicanas manifestaron a los comisionados que la administración en funciones carecía de representaciones diplomáticas, alianzas o compromisos con nación alguna fuera de los Estados Unidos. Los comisionados determinaron igualmente que el territorio dominicano incontestado comprendía 22.212 millas cuadradas, con cerca de 1.000 millas cuadradas sujetas antiguamente a diferendos con Haití. Asimismo, tras registrar los archivos oficiales y municipales, incluidos los protocolos de Samaná, la comisión constató la total falsedad de las imputaciones sobre concesiones de tierras otorgadas a dignatarios del gobierno dominicano o de los Estados Unidos durante la negociación del tratado de anexión de 1869.

records.full_text:
The following statement of receipts for 1870 is here presented, in order to give, as far as possible, a complete view of the financial condition of the Dominican Republic: Resume of the income of the Government for 1870: First, Customs receipts, tonnage, $2,730,660; entrance fees, $147,995; light houses, $67,901; anchorage, $196,995; pilotage, $142,827; lighterage, $21,800; interpreter, $646 26; signal men, $59,410; quarantine, $48,016; wharfage, $679,888; recargo municipal, $110,586; recargo for steamer, $588,614; water, $24,100; impost dues, $691,393 64; export dues, $71,419 20; coast fees, $7,511 11.

The Commissioners believe that the statement of the public debt given above includes all the indebtedness or obligations for which the Dominican Republic is in any degree liable, as well as that which it considers valid and binding, as that which it regards as unfounded or overstated by the claimants. Throughout the inquiry it was urged upon the Dominican authorities that every claim known to exist, of whatever character, should be exhibited to the Commission, whose object was not to determine the precise amount that was justly due and binding, but to get at the bottom and find the utmost limit of their obligations, and setting forth everything for which the Government could under any circumstances be made liable. The above account contains much that the Dominican Government believes to be partially or wholly groundless, and some which upon the inspection will appear questionable. Among the pending claims is one of President Baez for the destruction of property. It is alleged by the claimant that the Spanish Government recognized this claim as valid, and ordered an examination to fix the amount, but the Commission can in not understand how this claim could be valid against the Dominican Government.

A question has been raised in our country whether the Government and people of the Dominican Republic, having once been under the rule of Haytiens, might not be liable for a portion of the indemnity exacted for France from Hayti, for the estates of French families which had been confiscated by the Haytiens during the revolution of 1791. The Commission made inquiries on the subject of the Dominican Government, and also in Hayti, and they could not learn that the Haytien Government had ever made this claim upon the Dominican Republic, and they think that if made it would be wholly without foundation.

The Commissioners were informed by the Dominican authorities that the present administration of the Government has not had diplomatic representation or made treaties or engagements with any other government except the United States. An enumeration of the treaties made during the previous history of the Republic of France, Great Britain, and other powers, will be found in Ex. Doc. 17, Forty-first Congress, second session. They are mostly treaties of navigation and commerce, and contain no unusual provision requiring notice here.

The extent of undisputed Dominican territory is 22,212 square miles, the portion of which has been formerly involved in dispute with Hayti being about 1,000 square miles.

records.headline: A special correspondent describes the history and commercial vitality of Santiago de
records.summary_en: A special correspondent describes the history and commercial vitality of Santiago de los Caballeros, noting that after repeated destruction by French forces, Haitian invasions, the 1842 earthquake, and fires during the 1864 restoration war against Spain, the town was substantially rebuilt. The writer highlights the enterprise of its residents, observing that Santiago now boasts the finest shops in the Dominican Republic and bustling streets filled with pack trains transporting coffee and tobacco from Moca and La Vega to Puerto Plata. The letter reports that local merchants maintain commercial ties across the interior but remain financially dependent on trading houses in St. Thomas and Hamburg, where most purchases and exports are concentrated.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal especial describe la historia y la vitalidad comercial de Santiago de los Caballeros, destacando que, tras repetidas destrucciones a manos de tropas francesas, invasiones haitianas, el terremoto de 1842 y los incendios de la guerra restauradora contra España en 1864, la ciudad fue reconstruida sólidamente. El autor resalta la iniciativa de sus pobladores y observa que Santiago cuenta hoy con los mejores comercios de la República Dominicana y calles concurridas por recuas que transportan café y tabaco desde Moca y La Vega hacia Puerto Plata. La carta informa que los comerciantes locales mantienen vínculos mercantiles en todo el interior, pero dependen financieramente de las casas comerciales de Saint Thomas y Hamburgo, donde se concentran la mayoría de sus compras y exportaciones.

records.headline: A correspondent travelling with the Commission reports being repeatedly
records.summary_en: A correspondent travelling with the Commission reports being repeatedly urged that, following annexation, the United States should organize Dominican men into a paid uniform militia capable of maintaining domestic order without foreign troops. Small American garrisons at Puerto Plata, Samaná, and Azua were considered sufficient additions to such a local force. The writer notes that in Santiago and across the country, most landowners and educated residents favor annexation to secure stability. Upon reaching Puerto Plata, described as the republic's primary commercial port and chief center of unrest, the party rendezvoused with Commissioner White and sailed on March 5th aboard the warship Nantasket for Port-au-Prince to rejoin their colleagues.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal que viajaba con la Comisión relata que le sugirieron reiteradamente que, tras la anexión, los Estados Unidos deberían organizar a los dominicanos en una milicia remunerada y uniformada, capaz de mantener el orden interno sin tropas extranjeras. Se consideraba que bastaría añadir pequeñas guarniciones estadounidenses en Puerto Plata, Samaná y Azua a dicha fuerza local. El autor señala que en Santiago y en todo el país, la mayoría de los terratenientes y ciudadanos educados apoyan la anexión para asegurar la estabilidad. Al llegar a Puerto Plata, descrita como el principal puerto comercial y foco de disturbios de la república, la comitiva se reunió con el comisionado White y zarpó el 5 de marzo en el buque de guerra Nantasket rumbo a Puerto Príncipe para unirse a sus colegas.

records.headline: A published joint resolution details the scope of inquiry for the commissioners
records.summary_en: A published joint resolution details the scope of inquiry for the commissioners appointed to examine conditions in the Dominican Republic. It directs them to investigate meteorological phenomena, public debt whether funded or unadjusted, foreign treaties, territorial boundaries, and concession grants, as well as the terms under which the Dominican government may desire annexation as a United States territory. The commissioners are instructed to report to the President for transmittal to Congress, serving without compensation beyond expenses. The resolution specifies that nothing contained within it shall be construed as committing Congress to annexing the territory of the republic of Dominica.
records.summary_es: Una resolución conjunta publicada detalla el alcance de la investigación para los comisionados designados para examinar las condiciones en la República Dominicana. Les ordena investigar los fenómenos meteorológicos, la deuda pública ya sea consolidada o no liquidada, los tratados extranjeros, los límites territoriales y las concesiones otorgadas, así como los términos bajo los cuales el gobierno dominicano pueda desear la anexión como territorio de los Estados Unidos. Se instruye a los comisionados a informar al presidente para su remisión al Congreso, prestando sus servicios sin más compensación que sus gastos. La resolución especifica que nada de lo contenido en ella se interpretará como un compromiso del Congreso con la anexión del territorio de dicha república de Dominica.

records.headline: The Springfield Weekly Republican prints findings from the San Domingo commission
records.summary_en: The Springfield Weekly Republican prints findings from the San Domingo commission report regarding local governance, the Spanish occupation, and annexation sentiment. The commissioners report that difficulties in local self-government would disappear under connection with a strong nation, noting that many town councils remain efficient and capable. Under the heading 'The Spanish Occupation,' the report finds that the 1861 annexation was consummated by fraud and proved oppressive, threatening Freemasonry and risking the return of slavery until popular revolt forced Spanish troops into unhealthy coastal strongholds, where between 6,000 and 8,000 of Spain's 35,000 soldiers died of disease or deserted. The commissioners add that desire for annexation to the United States was found to be widespread and ardently shared by colonies of colored immigrants from the United States.
records.summary_es: El Springfield Weekly Republican publica conclusiones del informe de la comisión de Santo Domingo relativas a la gobernanza local, la ocupación española y el sentimiento hacia la anexión. Los comisionados informan que las dificultades en el autogobierno local desaparecerían bajo la conexión con una nación fuerte, señalando que muchos ayuntamientos siguen siendo eficientes y capaces. Bajo el título «The Spanish Occupation», el informe determina que la anexión de 1861 se consumó mediante fraude y resultó opresiva, amenazando a la masonería y arriesgando el restablecimiento de la esclavitud hasta que la sublevación popular obligó a las tropas españolas a retirarse a fortalezas costeras insalubres, donde entre 6,000 y 8,000 de los 35,000 soldados de España murieron por enfermedades o desertaron. Los comisionados añaden que encontraron un deseo generalizado de anexión a los Estados Unidos, compartido fervientemente por las colonias de inmigrantes de color procedentes de dicho país.

records.headline: The Springfield Weekly Republican publishes extracts from the commission
records.summary_en: The Springfield Weekly Republican publishes extracts from the commission report assessing the character of the Dominican people and the mineral resources of the republic. The commissioners favorably regard the political capacity of the population, citing their proverbial shrewdness, the absence of slavery or caste distinctions, and the courage shown in past struggles, while noting that only one small printing office exists in the country. They estimate the population at 150,000, over nineteen-twentieths of whom are native Dominicans, reporting that white blood largely preponderates. Under the heading 'Minerals of the Country,' expedition geologists report extensive deposits of iron ore, accessible copper beds, gold regions, petroleum, and valuable rock salt near Neyba, while finding that coal reported at Samaná and Puerto Plata is only low-value lignite.
records.summary_es: El Springfield Weekly Republican publica extractos del informe de la comisión que evalúan el carácter del pueblo dominicano y los recursos minerales de la república. Los comisionados valoran favorablemente la capacidad política de la población, citando su proverbial agudeza, la ausencia de esclavitud o distinciones de casta y el valor demostrado en luchas pasadas, al tiempo que señalan que en el país solo existe una pequeña imprenta. Estiman la población en 150,000 habitantes, de los cuales más de diecinueve vigésimos son dominicanos nativos, e informan que la sangre blanca prepondera ampliamente. Bajo el encabezado «Minerals of the Country», los geólogos de la expedición informan sobre extensos yacimientos de mineral de hierro, vetas de cobre accesibles, regiones auríferas, petróleo y valiosa sal gema cerca de Neyba, determinando que el carbón reportado en Samaná y Puerto Plata es únicamente lignito de escaso valor.

records.headline: An editorial in the Register contends that the commission report
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Register contends that the commission report presents nothing new regarding Santo Domingo, remarking that the public already knows its mixed population has alternated between internal conflicts and wars with Haiti. The paper asserts that the so-called President of Dominica desires to sell out to President Grant, who is reported to be anxious to complete the purchase. It concludes that the Senate's course remains to be seen, while claiming evidence shows President Grant regrets introducing the measure and would gladly escape the consequences of his folly.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en el Register sostiene que el informe de la comisión no presenta nada nuevo sobre Santo Domingo, señalando que el público ya sabe que su población mixta se ha debatido entre conflictos internos y guerras con Haití. El periódico afirma que el supuesto presidente de Dominica desea venderse al presidente Grant, de quien se informa que está ansioso por concretar la compra. Concluye que el proceder del Senado aún está por verse, al tiempo que afirma que existen pruebas de que el presidente Grant lamenta haber presentado la medida y escaparía con gusto de las consecuencias de su insensatez.

records.headline: In a Senate speech against annexing San Domingo, Mr. Morrill argues
records.summary_en: In a Senate speech against annexing San Domingo, Mr. Morrill argues that the Bay of Samana would be a source of weakness rather than a defensive point, and that the Dominican people would prove a serious political, moral and financial encumbrance. He says Dominican commerce has steadily declined, the island would yield no revenue, and the United States would have to pay for a civil service, a permanent naval squadron, regiments of soldiers, harbors and railroads, while placing little reliance on claims that Dominicans favor annexation.
records.summary_es: En un discurso en el Senado contra la anexión de Santo Domingo, el señor Morrill sostiene que la bahía de Samana sería una fuente de debilidad y no un punto defensivo, y que el pueblo dominicano resultaría una carga política, moral y financiera seria. Dice que el comercio dominicano ha disminuido constantemente, que la isla no produciría ingresos y que los Estados Unidos tendrían que pagar una administración civil, una escuadra naval permanente, regimientos de soldados, puertos y ferrocarriles, mientras da poco crédito a las afirmaciones de que los dominicanos favorecen la anexión.

records.headline: The Tribune publishes Senator Justin S. Morrill of Vermont's Senate speech
records.summary_en: The Tribune publishes Senator Justin S. Morrill of Vermont's Senate speech opposing President Grant's Santo Domingo annexation policy. Senator Morrill states that although he differs sharply with the administration on the policy, he freely accords President Grant the credit of being actuated by pure motives and disclaims any intent to assault his personal reputation. He criticizes the commissioners' report, arguing they praised the climate merely because a five-week stay caused them no harm, commended the soil simply for producing bananas and pineapples not grown in northern states, and treated mineral resources slightingly.
records.summary_es: El Tribune publica el discurso en el Senado del senador Justin S. Morrill de Vermont, en oposición a la política de anexión de Santo Domingo del presidente Grant. El senador Morrill manifiesta que, aunque difiere profundamente de la administración en cuanto a esta política, le reconoce plenamente al presidente Grant el mérito de haber actuado con intenciones puras y rechaza cualquier propósito de atacar su reputación personal. Critica el informe de los comisionados, sosteniendo que elogiaron el clima meramente porque una estancia de cinco semanas no les causó daño, alabaron el suelo simplemente por producir plátanos y piñas que no se cultivan en los estados del norte, y trataron los recursos minerales con ligereza.

records.headline: Senator Morrill, speaking on President Grant's Santo Domingo policy, treats the commissioners' report with open
records.summary_en: Senator Morrill, speaking on President Grant's Santo Domingo policy, treats the commissioners' report with open skepticism, saying they praised the soil for producing bananas and pine-apples and were despondent about finding coal at Samana, where there is only a poor show of lignite. Their report, he argues, will be found neither more exhaustive nor more trustworthy than the works of impartial travelers who spent far more time on the island, and will be chiefly valuable for vindicating the personal integrity of the President and of the officer charged with negotiating the defeated treaty.
records.summary_es: El senador Morrill, hablando sobre la política del presidente Grant hacia Santo Domingo, trata el informe de los comisionados con abierto escepticismo, diciendo que alabaron el suelo por producir bananas y piñas y que se mostraron desalentados por encontrar carbón en Samaná, donde solo hay una pobre muestra de lignito. Su informe, sostiene, no resultará ni más exhaustivo ni más digno de confianza que las obras de viajeros imparciales que pasaron mucho más tiempo en la isla, y será valioso sobre todo para vindicar la integridad personal del Presidente y la del oficial encargado de negociar el tratado derrotado.

records.headline: Commissioners reported the Dominican republic was disturbed by insurrectionary leaders, Haitians and political intriguers
records.summary_en: Commissioners reported the Dominican republic was disturbed by insurrectionary leaders, Haitians and political intriguers made active by fear of U.S. annexation, and that President Báez had the respect of a great majority of Dominicans. They recount his 1848 election after the expulsion of Haitian power and say the republic under him enjoyed as much liberty and more tranquility than predecessors allowed.

Relatan su elección de 1848 tras la expulsión del poder haitiano y dicen que la república bajo su gobierno disfrutó tanta libertad y más tranquilidad que la permitida por sus predecesores.

records.headline: A Washington dispatch to the American Press Association reports
records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch to the American Press Association reports that the secretary of the San Domingo commission received a letter dated March 30 from the Dominican Republic's Secretary of War. The Dominican official states that the country is completely tranquil and increasingly anxious for speedy annexation to the United States as its only salvation against the intrigues of Haiti. He further reports that President Báez has returned to Santo Domingo from Azua after routing Cabral, leaving that district peaceful and in the best of order.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de Washington para la American Press Association informa que el secretario de la comisión de Santo Domingo recibió una carta con fecha del 30 de marzo del ministro de Guerra de la República Dominicana. El funcionario dominicano manifiesta que el país se encuentra en completa tranquilidad y cada vez más ansioso por una rápida anexión a los Estados Unidos como su única salvación frente a las intrigas de Haití. Informa además que el presidente Báez regresó a Santo Domingo desde Azua tras derrotar a Cabral, dejando esa comarca en paz y en el mejor orden.

records.headline: An article in The Evening Telegraph acknowledges Senator Sumner
records.summary_en: An article in The Evening Telegraph acknowledges Senator Sumner as a sincere and honest friend of the colored race, but criticizes his opposition to the annexation of Santo Domingo. The writer argues that Sumner's stance is unfortunate and injurious to the colored inhabitants of Santo Domingo and potentially disastrous for black Americans. The piece maintains that Sumner's resistance divides the Republican party, encourages the notion that no further members of the colored race should be incorporated into the United States, and plays directly into the hands of the Democratic party.
records.summary_es: Un artículo en The Evening Telegraph reconoce al senador Sumner como un amigo sincero y honesto de la raza de color, pero critica su oposición a la anexión de Santo Domingo. El articulista sostiene que la postura de Sumner es lamentable y perjudicial para los habitantes de color de Santo Domingo y potencialmente desastrosa para los afroamericanos. El texto afirma que la resistencia de Sumner divide al Partido Republicano, fomenta la idea de que no se deben incorporar más personas de la raza de color a los Estados Unidos y favorece directamente los intereses del Partido Demócrata.

records.headline: A commentary in the Grant County Herald disputes the idea that Senator Sumner
records.summary_en: A commentary in the Grant County Herald disputes the idea that Senator Sumner was dropped from the Committee on Foreign Relations because of his opposition to annexing Santo Domingo. The writer argues that it is far from certain that a Senate majority favors acquiring Santo Domingo, insisting that no effort was made to displace Sumner on that account and that his Dominican views were never urged against him. The article notes that Sumner had opposed annexation long before December without losing his post, adding that other senators who opposed annexation with equal determination remained entirely unmolested.
records.summary_es: Un comentario en el Grant County Herald refuta la idea de que el senador Sumner fuera apartado de la Comisión de Relaciones Exteriores debido a su oposición a la anexión de Santo Domingo. El autor sostiene que dista mucho de ser seguro que una mayoría del Senado favorezca la adquisición de Santo Domingo, e insiste en que no se hizo ningún intento de desplazar a Sumner por ese motivo y que sus opiniones sobre la cuestión dominicana nunca se esgrimieron en su contra. El artículo señala que Sumner se había opuesto a la anexión mucho antes de diciembre sin perder su cargo, y añade que otros senadores que se opusieron a la anexión con igual determinación no fueron molestados en absoluto.

records.headline: The Western Reserve Chronicle publishes President Grant's transmittal
records.summary_en: The Western Reserve Chronicle publishes President Grant's transmittal message and the opening section of the San Domingo commission report. The commissioners state that they traversed the Dominican Republic in several directions, either in person or through agents, spending several weeks at the capital conferring daily with President Báez and reviewing official records while taking testimony. The report describes the Dominican government as theoretically a constitutional republic with executive, legislative, and judicial branches. It outlines the six-year terms of the president and vice president, their ineligibility for immediate re-election, the composition of the Council of State, and the structure of the Senate.
records.summary_es: El Western Reserve Chronicle publica el mensaje de remisión del presidente Grant y la sección inicial del informe de la comisión de Santo Domingo. Los comisionados manifiestan que recorrieron la República Dominicana en varias direcciones, ya sea en persona o mediante comisionados, pasando varias semanas en la capital conferenciando diariamente con el presidente Báez y examinando registros oficiales a la vez que tomaban testimonios. El informe describe el gobierno dominicano como teóricamente una república constitucional con poderes ejecutivo, legislativo y judicial. Detalla los mandatos de seis años del presidente y vicepresidente, su inelegibilidad para la reelección inmediata, la integración del Consejo de Estado y la estructura del Senado.

records.summary_en: More of the commissioners' report: the Dominican frame of government, Báez in full possession save the Haitian border, the people's familiarity with the annexation question, and the vast, under-produced resources of one of the most fertile regions on earth.

These are incited to be active at this time by fear of annexation to the United States. From all the Commissioners could ascertain, President Baez has the respect of a great majority of the Dominican people for his administrative ability, and strong attachment to many leading men who regard him as the only statesman among them who can hold the nation against domestic factions and foreign foes. The Commissioners do not find that there is any opponent to the present administration of the Republic, who has now or who ever had any claim to the chief magistracy by a title superior to the present incumbent. Whatever technical defects there might have been in his original title to the office, it was confirmed by national convention, and ratified by the assent and support of the people. The frequency of civil commotion during a long period, and consequent insecurity of property, have paralyzed industry and discouraged accumulation, and so impoverished the country that for the last two years the financial resources of the Government have been inadequate to pay expenses. The insurrections which still exist are led by Cabral and Luperon. The former of these is universally conceded to be the more important, but neither has a distinct flag or a regularly organized army. records.headline: An editorial in the Green-Mountain Freeman discusses President Grant's transmittal of the San Domingo commission
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Green-Mountain Freeman discusses President Grant's transmittal of the San Domingo commission report to Congress, arguing that the commission was devised to aid annexationists and added nothing new to public knowledge. Summarizing the findings, the paper observes that the commissioners describe the government of the republic of Dominica as republican, a fact already well established. The editorial points out that President Báez obtained power through irregular usurpation rather than election, criticizing the commissioners for defending his coup on the claim that he is superior to his predecessor, an assertion the paper dismisses as biased information coming from Báez himself.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en el Green-Mountain Freeman analiza la remisión al Congreso del informe de la comisión de Santo Domingo por parte del presidente Grant, argumentando que la comisión se ideó para favorecer a los anexionistas y no añadió nada nuevo al conocimiento público. Al resumir los hallazgos, el periódico observa que los comisionados describen el gobierno de la república de Dominica como republicano, un hecho que ya era bien conocido. El editorial señala que el presidente Báez llegó al poder mediante una usurpación irregular y no por elección, y critica a los comisionados por defender su golpe bajo el argumento de que es superior a su predecesor, afirmación que el periódico descarta como información parcial procedente del propio Báez.

records.headline: The New National Era prints an excerpt from the San Domingo commission
records.summary_en: The New National Era prints an excerpt from the San Domingo commission report examining the bays and harbors of the Dominican Republic. The report notes that while most harbors admit only light-draft craft, the three great bays of Samaná, Ocoa, and Manzanillo accommodate the largest vessels. The commissioners highlight the Bay of Samaná, describing it as thirty miles long, ten miles wide, sheltered by mountains, and capable of holding large fleets. They emphasize that its narrow entrance is easily fortified and commands the Mona Passage to the Gulf of Mexico, concluding that its strategic value as a naval coaling station cannot be overrated and that a great commercial center would flourish there under a secure government.
records.summary_es: El New National Era publica un extracto del informe de la comisión de Santo Domingo que examina las bahías y puertos de la República Dominicana. El informe señala que, si bien la mayoría de los puertos solo admiten embarcaciones de poco calado, las tres grandes bahías de Samaná, Ocoa y Manzanillo dan cabida a los buques más grandes. Los comisionados destacan la bahía de Samaná, describiéndola como de treinta millas de largo por diez millas de ancho, resguardada por montañas y con capacidad para albergar grandes flotas. Subrayan que su estrecha entrada es fácilmente fortificable y domina el canal de la Mona hacia el golfo de México, concluyendo que su valor estratégico como estación naval de carbonero no puede sobreestimarse y que un gran centro comercial prosperaría allí bajo un gobierno seguro.

It notes that a geological survey funded by New York capitalists under Professor Gabb is currently underway, with reports and contracts submitted to the commission. The report details specific grants, including a steamship concession to R. M. Funkhouser giving five percent of customs dues, guano rights at Alto Velo to Edward H. Hartmont, and railroad concessions granted to Fred H. Fischer, Felix Montecatini, and Julian Grangerard. Other concessions listed include telegraph rights to Levi Hollingsworth, salt-works leases at Baní and Beata Island, and an immigration and colonization grant to W. L. Cazneau.
