records.headline: A correspondence from Santo Domingo in the Worcester Daily Spy reports
records.summary_en: A correspondence from Santo Domingo in the Worcester Daily Spy reports that Spanish, English, and French are spoken in the Dominican Republic, describing the local Spanish as a harsh-sounding patois. The writer notes that formal marriages are rare, though couples live together, raise large families, and generally maintain fidelity. This domestic arrangement is not viewed unfavorably, a tolerance the writer attributes to universal poverty, although priests once prompted a wave of church weddings by invoking prophecies of an impending earthquake and tidal wave. The national religion is Roman Catholic, while Black American residents maintain their Methodism, and nightly processions carrying effigies of Christ mark Holy Week.
records.summary_es: Una correspondencia desde Santo Domingo en el Worcester Daily Spy informa que en la República Dominicana se hablan español, inglés y francés, calificando el español local de patois de sonido áspero. El autor señala que los matrimonios formales son infrecuentes, aunque las parejas conviven, crían familias numerosas y generalmente guardan fidelidad. Esta convivencia no se juzga con malos ojos, tolerancia que el autor atribuye a la pobreza generalizada, si bien los sacerdotes lograron en una ocasión una oleada de bodas eclesiásticas valiéndose de profecías sobre un terremoto y maremoto inminentes. La religión nacional es la católica romana, mientras que los residentes negros estadounidenses conservan su metodismo, y procesiones nocturnas con efigies de Cristo conmemoran la Semana Santa.

records.headline: A letter from Santo Domingo in the Worcester Daily Spy reports
records.summary_en: A letter from Santo Domingo in the Worcester Daily Spy reports that President Báez, upon taking power, granted poor inhabitants parcels on ruined church lands to erect dwellings, requiring only an annual payment of four dollars to the national church. The writer describes the tropical climate as consistently tempered by daytime sea breezes and evening mountain winds, with annual temperatures fluctuating by no more than ten to fifteen degrees, and praises the remarkable productivity of the soil. The correspondent also provides a personal portrait of President Buenaventura Báez, describing him as a pleasant, European-educated leader of about sixty years of age, of medium height and mixed Spanish and African descent, whose physical features lean more toward the Spanish type.
records.summary_es: Una carta desde Santo Domingo en el Worcester Daily Spy relata que el presidente Báez, al asumir el poder, otorgó a habitantes pobres parcelas en terrenos de ruinas eclesiásticas para levantar viviendas, exigiendo únicamente un pago anual de cuatro dólares a la iglesia nacional. El autor describe el clima tropical como constantemente templado por brisas marinas diurnas y vientos montañosos nocturnos, con temperaturas anuales que fluctúan no más de diez a quince grados, y elogia la notable fertilidad del suelo. El corresponsal ofrece asimismo un retrato personal del presidente Buenaventura Báez, describiéndolo como un mandatario agradable, educado en Europa, de unos sesenta años de edad, estatura mediana y ascendencia mixta española y africana, cuyos rasgos físicos se inclinan más hacia el tipo español.

records.headline: Official congressional proceedings in the Gold Hill Daily News publish
records.summary_en: Official congressional proceedings in the Gold Hill Daily News publish the instructions for commissioners tasked with examining the Dominican Republic. The resolution directs inquiry into public debt, existing treaties, territorial limits, foreign concessions and franchises, and the conditions on which the Dominican government might seek incorporation into the United States as a territory. Section 2 instructs the commissioners to report their findings to the President for presentation to Congress. Section 3 provides that the commissioners shall serve without salary beyond necessary expenses, while affirming that nothing in the resolution commits Congress to the policy of annexing the territory of the republic of Dominica.
records.summary_es: Actas oficiales del Congreso en el Gold Hill Daily News publican las instrucciones para los comisionados encargados de examinar la República Dominicana. La resolución ordena indagar sobre la deuda pública, los tratados vigentes, los límites territoriales, las concesiones y franquicias a extranjeros, y las condiciones en que el gobierno dominicano pudiera pretender incorporarse a los Estados Unidos como territorio. La sección 2 instruye a los comisionados a remitir sus conclusiones al presidente para su presentación al Congreso. La sección 3 dispone que los comisionados presten servicios sin salario fuera de los gastos necesarios, afirmando al mismo tiempo que nada en la resolución compromete al Congreso con la política de anexar el territorio de la república de Dominica.

records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that the Dominican Republic possesses highly productive agricultural lands capable of yielding sugar-cane, tobacco, tropical fruits, and dyes with less labor than Louisiana beet sugar lands. It described the island as the gateway to the Caribbean Sea and noted that its sparse population is industrious, free of caste, and anxious to join their fortunes with the United States. Additionally, the excerpt detailed England's strategic military positions and island holdings around Cuba, the Gulf of Mexico, and the Caribbean Sea.
records.summary_es: El periódico refirió que la República Dominicana cuenta con terrenos agrícolas altamente ubérrimos capaces de producir caña de azúcar, tabaco, frutos tropicales y tintes con menor faena que las tierras remolacheras de Luisiana. Describió a la isla como la llave de acceso al mar Caribe y ponderó a su escasa población como laboriosa, exenta de prejuicios de casta y ansiosa por enlazar su destino al de los Estados Unidos. El texto desgranó además las posiciones militares estratégicas y las posesiones insulares que Inglaterra mantenía en torno a Cuba, el golfo de México y el mar Caribe.

records.full_text: San Domingo is admitted to be an island of great fertility. That part of it known as the State of San Domingo contains an area of 20,000 square miles, or 12,800,000 acres. Much of this is now covered with the most valuable timbers known to commerce, at an elevation above the diseases incident to a tropical climate, and is capable of producing, when cleared of its native forest, one thousand five hundred pounds of coffee per acre. The valleys and lowlands are of great productiveness, the sugar-cane requiring resetting only once in twenty years, and producing to the acre, with much less labor, nearly double that of the best sugar lands of Louisiana.

records.summary_en: The Gold Hill Daily News prints the text of a congressional resolution directing an investigation of Dominican conditions by appointed commissioners. The resolution specifies that the inquiry encompass government debts and liabilities, treaties with foreign powers, boundaries, grants or concessions, and the terms on which the Dominican government desires annexation to the United States. The commissioners are instructed to deliver their report to the President as soon as convenient for submission to Congress. Section 3 stipulates that the commissioners shall serve without pay apart from expenses, and adds an explicit proviso that nothing in the resolution commits Congress to annexing the territory of the republic of Dominica.

Se ordena a los comisionados entregar su informe al presidente tan pronto como sea conveniente para su envío al Congreso. La sección 3 estipula que los comisionados sirvan sin remuneración aparte de los gastos, y añade una salvedad explícita de que nada en la resolución compromete al Congreso a anexar el territorio de la república de Dominica.

records.headline: An article headed "African Giants at War" in the New National Era notes
records.summary_en: An article headed "African Giants at War" in the New National Era notes that Frederick Douglass continues to advocate the annexation of Santo Domingo in the paper's pages, while the Rev. Henry Highland Garnet opposes the policy from the pulpit of Shiloh church in New York City. The writer regrets seeing both prominent Black leaders in public conflict, but criticizes Douglass for accepting an appointment as a mere attaché on the Santo Domingo commission after being spoken of as a commissioner or secretary. The piece contends that Black Americans felt their dignity compromised by Douglass accepting an undefined subordinate post on a commission where Black national interests were at stake.
records.summary_es: Un artículo titulado «African Giants at War» en el New National Era observa que Frederick Douglass continúa defendiendo la anexión de Santo Domingo en las páginas del periódico, mientras que el reverendo Henry Highland Garnet se opone a dicha política desde el púlpito de la iglesia de Shiloh en la ciudad de Nueva York. El autor lamenta ver a ambos destacados líderes negros en conflicto público, pero critica a Douglass por aceptar el nombramiento de simple agregado en la comisión de Santo Domingo tras haberse barajado su nombre como comisionado o secretario. El artículo sostiene que los negros estadounidenses sintieron comprometida su dignidad al ver a Douglass aceptar un puesto subordinado e indefinido en una comisión donde estaban en juego los intereses nacionales de los negros.

records.headline: Letters of General Luperon from Capotillo in early 1871 report him organizing a small force for a campaign in the Cibao
records.summary_en: Letters of General Luperon from Capotillo in early 1871 report him organizing a small force for a campaign in the Cibao, with anti-annexation propaganda very active around Guayabin and Monte Cristi and word that the American flag has been raised at Monte Cristi. He writes that Cabral could send him no men from the south, that he will make his sortie with only forty or fifty officers, and he urgently asks for at least fifty thousand chassepot cartridges; a Santo Domingo letter adds that Luperon was later defeated and his secretary, General Manuel Rodriguez Objio, captured and shot.
records.summary_es: Cartas del general Luperon desde Capotillo a principios de 1871 lo muestran organizando una pequeña fuerza para una campaña en el Cibao, con una propaganda contra la anexión muy activa alrededor de Guayabin y Monte Cristi y la noticia de que la bandera americana ha sido izada en Monte Cristi. Escribe que Cabral no pudo enviarle hombres desde el sur, que hará su salida con solo cuarenta o cincuenta oficiales, y pide con urgencia al menos cincuenta mil cartuchos para fusiles chassepot; una carta de Santo Domingo añade que Luperon fue derrotado después y que su secretario, el general Manuel Rodriguez Objio, fue capturado y fusilado.

Un extracto de una carta de Santo Domingo dice que Cabral era derrotado repetidamente cuando se movía en la frontera sur.

records.headline: A paragraph from a Santo Domingo letter explains why General Manuel Rodriguez Objio, secretary to a defeated leader
records.summary_en: A paragraph from a Santo Domingo letter explains why General Manuel Rodriguez Objio, secretary to a defeated leader, was shot after being taken prisoner. It says he was condemned under decrees of the Senate, that he had surrendered the town of Puerto Plata, which he governed for Baez, to Luperon, and that he had ordered the murder of Jose Bariento, a father of a family who was tied to a tree and shot at more than fifty times.

records.headline: The Gold Hill Daily News publishes the joint resolution for an investigation
records.summary_en: The Gold Hill Daily News publishes the joint resolution for an investigation into the condition of the Dominican Republic. The measure instructs commissioners to examine Dominican public debts, foreign treaties, territorial limits, private concessions, and the terms under which the Dominican government desires annexation to the United States as a territory. Section 2 directs the commission to report to the President as soon as convenient, so that he may lay the report before Congress. Section 3 provides that the commissioners serve without pay beyond expenses, while stipulating that nothing in the resolution commits Congress to the policy of annexing the territory of the republic of Dominica.
records.summary_es: El Gold Hill Daily News publica la resolución conjunta que ordena una investigación sobre la situación de la República Dominicana. La medida instruye a los comisionados examinar las deudas públicas dominicanas, los tratados con el exterior, los límites territoriales, las concesiones privadas y los términos bajo los cuales el gobierno dominicano desea la anexión a los Estados Unidos como territorio. La sección 2 ordena a la comisión rendir informe al presidente tan pronto como sea conveniente, a fin de que este lo someta al Congreso. La sección 3 dispone que los comisionados presten servicios sin remuneración fuera de los gastos, estipulando que nada en la resolución compromete al Congreso con la política de anexar el territorio de la república de Dominica.

records.headline: A series of political resolutions published in The Stark County Democrat denounces
records.summary_en: A series of political resolutions published in The Stark County Democrat denounces lawless conspiracies and declares earnest opposition to the proposed annexation of the Dominican Republic. The resolution grounds its opposition partly on what it characterizes as the mongrel population of the country and their unfitness for American citizenship, but emphasizes primarily the corrupt motives behind the measure's inception and the reprehensible means used to pursue it. The accompanying resolutions reject repudiation of the national debt and advocate payment of public liabilities in lawful money.
records.summary_es: Una serie de resoluciones políticas publicadas en The Stark County Democrat denuncia las conspiraciones contra la ley y manifiesta una enérgica oposición a la propuesta de anexión de la República Dominicana. La resolución fundamenta su rechazo en parte en lo que califica como la población mestiza del país y su falta de aptitud para la ciudadanía estadounidense, pero recalca primordialmente los motivos corruptos en el origen de la medida y los medios censurables empleados para impulsarla. Las resoluciones que la acompañan rechazan el repudio de la deuda nacional y propugnan el pago de las obligaciones públicas en moneda de curso legal.

records.headline: The Tama County Republican publishes the platform resolutions of the Iowa Democratic
records.summary_en: The Tama County Republican publishes the platform resolutions of the Iowa Democratic convention, including a resolution expressing earnest opposition to the proposed annexation of the Dominican Republic. The platform bases its resistance partly on the character of what it describes as a mongrel population unfit for American citizenship, but more especially on the corrupt motives behind the project's inception and the reprehensible means employed to achieve it. Additional resolutions condemn federal intervention in state affairs without local request, attack protective tariffs as legalized plundering, and denounce federal extravagance and land grants to railroad monopolies.
records.summary_es: El Tama County Republican publica las resoluciones de la plataforma de la convención demócrata de Iowa, incluida una resolución que expresa una decidida oposición a la propuesta de anexión de la República Dominicana. La plataforma fundamenta su rechazo en parte en el carácter de lo que describe como una población mestiza no apta para la ciudadanía estadounidense, pero más especialmente en los motivos corruptos en el origen del proyecto y los medios reprochables empleados para consumarlo. Otras resoluciones condenan la intervención federal en asuntos estatales sin previa solicitud local, atacan los aranceles proteccionistas calificándolos de expoliación legalizada y denuncian el despilfarro federal y la concesión de tierras a monopolios ferroviarios.

records.headline: Official enactments printed in the Gold Hill Daily News include
records.summary_en: Official enactments printed in the Gold Hill Daily News include the joint resolution establishing a commission of inquiry for the Dominican Republic. The commissioners are directed to examine Dominican meteorological phenomena, public debts and obligations, international treaties, boundary lines, land grants and concessions, and the terms on which the Dominican government desires annexation to the United States as a territory. Section 2 directs the commission to report to the President as soon as convenient for submission to Congress. Section 3 allows only expense reimbursement for the commissioners, while specifying that nothing in the resolution commits Congress to the policy of annexing the territory of the republic of Dominica.
records.summary_es: Disposiciones oficiales publicadas en el Gold Hill Daily News incluyen la resolución conjunta que establece una comisión investigadora para la República Dominicana. Se ordena a los comisionados examinar los fenómenos meteorológicos dominicanos, las deudas y obligaciones públicas, los tratados internacionales, las líneas fronterizas, las mercedes y concesiones de tierras, y los términos en que el gobierno dominicano desea la anexión a los Estados Unidos como territorio. La sección 2 dispone que la comisión rinda informe al presidente tan pronto como sea conveniente para su presentación al Congreso. La sección 3 permite únicamente el reembolso de gastos a los comisionados, especificando que nada en la resolución compromete al Congreso con la política de anexar el territorio de la república de Dominica.

records.headline: A speech printed in the New Orleans Republican defends President Grant's administration
records.summary_en: A speech printed in the New Orleans Republican defends President Grant's administration and reviews the Democratic Party's stance toward Dominican annexation. The speaker notes that Grant referred the San Domingo question to the people, and recites the Iowa Democratic convention's resolution opposing annexation on racial grounds and allegations of administrative corruption. The speaker argues that while Democrats abuse Grant in extravagant terms, they favor annexation in principle and would make it their first major policy under a Democratic presidency, observing that Eastern Democrats openly support annexation while Western Democrats merely feign opposition.
records.summary_es: Un discurso publicado en el New Orleans Republican defiende la administración del presidente Grant y examina la postura del Partido Demócrata hacia la anexión dominicana. El orador señala que Grant remitió la cuestión de Santo Domingo al pueblo, y cita la resolución de la convención demócrata de Iowa que rechazó la anexión por motivos raciales y alegaciones de corrupción administrativa. El orador sostiene que, aunque los demócratas atacan a Grant en términos extravagantes, favorecen la anexión en principio y la convertirían en su primera gran medida bajo una presidencia demócrata, señalando que los demócratas del este apoyan abiertamente la anexión mientras que los del oeste solo fingen oponerse.

records.headline: An article in the New National Era laments the political paralysis
records.summary_en: An article in the New National Era laments the political paralysis surrounding Dominican annexation, asserting that Republicans avoid the question to preserve party harmony while Democrats wait to claim credit for annexing the island themselves. The writer states that the Dominican people, having looked upon annexation as salvation from the feuds of rival chiefs and foreign invasion, are left bitterly disappointed and despairing. Comparing their abandonment to that of the mountaineers of Crete, the author hopes that Santo Domingo, with its rich natural resources and geographical advantages, will be spared from becoming a foreign colony or falling into civil war and Haytian subjugation until American public opinion grants their petition for the protection of United States laws.
records.summary_es: Un artículo en el New National Era lamenta la parálisis política en torno a la anexión dominicana, afirmando que los republicanos eluden el asunto para conservar la armonía de su partido mientras los demócratas esperan adjudicarse el mérito de anexar la isla ellos mismos. El autor expone que el pueblo dominicano, tras haber considerado la anexión como la salvación frente a las pugnas de caudillos rivales y las invasiones extranjeras, queda amargamente defraudado y desesperanzado. Comparando su abandono con el de los montañeses de Creta, el autor confía en que Santo Domingo, con sus ricos recursos naturales y sus ventajas geográficas, se libre de convertirse en colonia extranjera o caer en la guerra civil y la subyugación haitiana hasta que la opinión pública estadounidense conceda su petición de acogerse a la protección de las leyes de los Estados Unidos.

records.headline: An editorial in the Chicago Tribune reports that ex-President
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Chicago Tribune reports that ex-President Cabral and the anti-Báez party have organized a provisional government at Las Matas and prepared an attack on Báez's forces assembled at Azua. The paper denounces reports that the United States war steamer Nantucket left Samaná to cruise near Azua and co-operate by sea with Báez, declaring that such naval interference constitutes an act of war initiated without congressional approval. Calling the administration's support for Báez a wretched speculation, the editorial insists that American naval forces be recalled from Dominican waters so that Báez and the Dominican people may settle their affairs themselves.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en el Chicago Tribune informa que el expresidente Cabral y el partido contrario a Báez han organizado un gobierno provisional en Las Matas y preparado un ataque contra las fuerzas de Báez reunidas en Azua. El periódico denuncia los informes de que el vapor de guerra estadounidense Nantucket partió de Samaná para patrullar cerca de Azua y cooperar por mar con Báez, declarando que semejante interferencia naval constituye un acto de guerra iniciado sin la aprobación del Congreso. Tras calificar el respaldo gubernamental a Báez como una especulación miserable, el editorial insiste en que las fuerzas navales estadounidenses sean retiradas de las aguas dominicanas para que Báez y el pueblo dominicano resuelvan sus asuntos por sí mismos.

records.headline: An editorial notice in The Daily State Journal commends an article
records.summary_en: An editorial notice in The Daily State Journal commends an article by Dr. Howe reprinted on the paper's third page as a clear, frank, and explicit explanation of United States relations with the Dominican Republic. The paper asserts that the article exposes widely circulated falsehoods and will reinforce the convictions of those supporting the annexation of San Domingo to the United States. It adds that opponents who believed they could easily brush aside the annexation issue have overrated their capacity to do so.
records.summary_es: Una nota editorial en The Daily State Journal elogia un artículo del doctor Howe reproducido en la tercera página del diario, calificándolo de explicación clara, franca y explícita sobre las relaciones de los Estados Unidos con la República Dominicana. El periódico afirma que el artículo desenmascara falsedades ampliamente difundidas y reforzará las convicciones de quienes apoyan la anexión de Santo Domingo a los Estados Unidos. Agrega que los adversarios que creyeron poder desestimar con facilidad el asunto de la anexión han sobrestimado su capacidad para lograrlo.

records.headline: A defense published in the New Orleans Republican refutes criticisms
records.summary_en: A defense published in the New Orleans Republican refutes criticisms directed at Buenaventura Báez, rejecting claims by James Redpath and American editors who characterize him as a runaway barber or a traitor selling his country. The writer states that Báez comes from an ancient, wealthy family in the Azua district of San Domingo, describing him as a cultivated, courteous gentleman respected by his neighbors and regarded abroad as a skillful diplomat who was made a Mariscal de Campo in Spain. The author notes that when the Dominicans revolted against Spanish rule, Báez refused an offer to command a Spanish army against his native land. Serving in the fourth year of his third presidential term, Báez is reported to live plainly while maintaining an unusual degree of peace and order.
records.summary_es: Una defensa publicada en el New Orleans Republican refuta las críticas dirigidas contra Buenaventura Báez, rechazando las acusaciones de James Redpath y de directores de periódicos estadounidenses que lo califican de barbero prófugo o traidor que vende su patria. El autor afirma que Báez desciende de una antigua y acaudalada familia del distrito de Azua en Santo Domingo, describiéndolo como un caballero culto y cortés, respetado por sus vecinos y considerado en el exterior como un hábil diplomático a quien se confirió el grado de mariscal de campo en España. El autor destaca que, cuando los dominicanos se rebelaron contra el dominio español, Báez rechazó la oferta de comandar un ejército español contra su tierra natal. Al cumplir el cuarto año de su tercer mandato presidencial, se informa que Báez vive con sencillez y mantiene un grado extraordinario de paz y orden.

records.headline: The Gold Hill Daily News prints the congressional resolution
records.summary_en: The Gold Hill Daily News prints the congressional resolution outlining the inquiries assigned to commissioners appointed to examine the Dominican Republic. The measure instructs the commissioners to report on meteorological phenomena, public debts, foreign treaties, territorial limits, private concessions, and the terms desired by the Dominican government for becoming a territory of the United States. Section 2 requires the commission to report as soon as convenient to the President, who will transmit the document to Congress. Section 3 provides that the commissioners serve without pay beyond actual expenses, concluding with a proviso that the resolution does not commit Congress to annexing the territory of the republic of Dominica.
records.summary_es: El Gold Hill Daily News publica la resolución del Congreso que detalla las investigaciones asignadas a los comisionados designados para examinar la República Dominicana. La medida instruye a los comisionados a informar sobre fenómenos meteorológicos, deudas públicas, tratados extranjeros, límites territoriales, concesiones privadas y los términos deseados por el gobierno dominicano para convertirse en territorio de los Estados Unidos. La sección 2 exige que la comisión rinda informe tan pronto como sea conveniente al presidente, quien remitirá el documento al Congreso. La sección 3 establece que los comisionados presten servicios sin remuneración fuera de los gastos efectivos, concluyendo con una salvedad de que la resolución no compromete al Congreso a anexar el territorio de la república de Dominica.

records.headline: A correspondence in the New National Era argues that the annexation of Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: A correspondence in the New National Era argues that the annexation of Santo Domingo will eliminate the market monopoly enjoyed by Cuba and Puerto Rico in the United States, forcing those Spanish colonies to seek admission into the American Union. The writer contends that annexation would put an end to the open slave markets in Havana, where enslaved people are currently bought and sold for $800 to $1,000 each. The correspondent warns that slaveholders maintain these prices only out of apprehension over Dominican annexation, predicting that if the prospect is abandoned, prices will rise to $1,500 and the African slave trade will revive. Characterizing the recent Spanish emancipation law as an unenforced farce, the letter insists that only the annexation of St. Domingo can fulfill the hopes of opponents of slavery.
records.summary_es: Una correspondencia en el New National Era sostiene que la anexión de Santo Domingo eliminará el monopolio de mercado del que disfrutan Cuba y Puerto Rico en los Estados Unidos, obligando a esas colonias españolas a solicitar su ingreso en la Unión Americana. El autor afirma que la anexión pondría fin a los mercados abiertos de esclavos en La Habana, donde actualmente se compran y venden personas cautivas por entre 800 y 1,000 dólares cada una. El corresponsal advierte que los hacendados mantienen estos precios únicamente por temor a la anexión dominicana, pronosticando que, si se abandona esa posibilidad, los precios subirán a 1,500 dólares y resurgirá la trata con África. Tras calificar la reciente ley de emancipación española de farsa no aplicada, la carta insiste en que solo la anexión de Santo Domingo puede hacer realidad las aspiraciones de quienes se oponen a la esclavitud.

records.headline: The paper reports the statement that President Grant does not intend
records.summary_en: The paper reports the statement that President Grant does not intend in his forthcoming message to recommend further measures for the annexation of Santo Domingo, barring unanticipated events. While the President's personal views remain unchanged, he adheres to the position of his previous message to Congress and will not depart from that policy or assume responsibilities transferred to the legislature. The administration is doing nothing regarding the Santo Domingo question, leaving agents still working for annexation to proceed at their own risk without official encouragement.

Aunque las opiniones personales del presidente permanecen sin cambios, se adhiere a la postura de su mensaje anterior al Congreso y no se apartará de dicha política ni asumirá responsabilidades transferidas al poder legislativo. La administración no está haciendo nada respecto a la cuestión de Santo Domingo, dejando que los agentes que aún trabajan a favor de la anexión continúen sus labores por su propia cuenta y riesgo, sin estímulo oficial.

records.passage: HONORS TO PRESIDENT BAEZ. Baez started out upon the journey, from which he has just returned, accompanied only by Gautier, Delmonto, Curiel, and a colonel of cavalry. He went unarmed — a thing said to be before unknown in his history. A few days ago, the Commandante Macoris became intoxicated, abused his office and his people, was removed, and undertook to rebel against his successor. He was captured and put in prison. This was said to be a new revolution, and was reported to Gen. Camenero as such. The General, with 60 men, went to Macoris, but the man had been captured before he reached there, and was lodged in the old castle in this city. Gen. Camenero has just told me that the only foundation for the story was, that a mob was raised to punish the man for abusing his wife. The German war steamer Gazelle, Capt. Avent, was here some 10 days ago, and remained several days. Thirty-five of the officers came up into the city, and had a jolly time. The captain gave a dinner on board of his ship to foreign representatives, and prominent merchants of the place. He gave a toast to the Dominican Government — the Governor being present — and remarked that he hoped they would be able to sustain themselves, and the principles they had avowed before the world. He had hoped to set forth his views more fully to the Government, but as the President was absent he would reserve further remarks till the return. He was going to Hayti, and would return in a few days, when he hoped to see the President, and more fully make known the object of his visit. T

records.full_text:
THE CASE OF THE STEAMER TELEGRAFO.
HER UNJUST SEIZURE FOR PIRACY—A MEASURE INSTIGATED BY THE UNITED STATES GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE THE ANNEXATION SCHEME.
To the Editor of The Tribune.
SIR: The connection of the steamer Telegrafo with the wicked and cruel attempt of a few speculators to get possession of the Dominican part of San Domingo is familiar to all who have taken an interest in the subject. The English Court of Chancery having now confirmed the decision of the Admiralty Court of Tortola, given in May, 1870, this case becomes one of great interest to us by the action of our Government in seizing her on the alleged ground of her being a pirate; and this case acquires additional interest in the fact that the high Courts of the British Empire have decided a claim against a British subject, and in favor of a citizen of the United States, Mr. George A. Philips, (of the firm of George A. Philips & Co. of St. Thomas,) formerly of Collins of New-York, to whom a jury of merchants awarded £18,000 indemnity for the seizure and illegal sale of the Telegrafo, of which he was the owner. The history of this remarkable case is as follows:

The Telegrafo was chartered in St. Thomas, in May 1869 by Dominican exiles. The vessel was to carry the American flag, and was to be employed against the usurper Baez in the waters of the Dominican Republic. She proceeded to the British Island of Inagua, where she was put under the British flag, armed and fitted as a vessel of war. Thence she proceeded to Santo Domingo.

records.headline: In a letter reprinted from the Woman's Journal, Julia Ward Howe describes
records.summary_en: In a letter reprinted from the Woman's Journal, Julia Ward Howe describes her arrival and experiences at Puerto Plata on Sunday, February 20, 1872. She recounts attending morning services at the local Wesleyan chapel, noting that it was the sole church in the town where the English language was employed. She depicts the modest wooden chapel, resembling a New England schoolhouse, and praises the decorum and neat attire of the racially diverse congregation, observing women in folded turbans and summer bonnets listening with earnest attention.
records.summary_es: En una carta reproducida del Woman's Journal, Julia Ward Howe describe su llegada y experiencias en Puerto Plata el domingo 20 de febrero de 1872. Relata haber asistido a los servicios matutinos en la capilla wesleyana local, destacando que era la única iglesia del pueblo donde se utilizaba el idioma inglés. Describe la modesta capilla de madera, semejante a una escuela rural de Nueva Inglaterra, y elogia el decoro y la pulcra vestimenta de la congregación racialmente diversa, observando a mujeres con turbantes doblados y sombreros de verano que escuchaban con atenta devoción.

records.headline: Mrs. Howe's correspondence continues with the voyage from Puerto Plata
records.summary_en: Mrs. Howe's correspondence continues with the voyage from Puerto Plata to Samaná Bay aboard the steamer Tybee. She relates conversations with fellow passengers, including a Cuban refugee who recounted hardships suffered under Spanish forces during the revolution, including the loss of her property and an epidemic among refugees on interior plantations. Upon reaching Samaná, Howe praises the natural harbor and describes the small port town of Santa Bárbara. She notes that the Tybee was welcomed with intense relief, as delays in its sailing from New York had driven rice to forty cents per pound at Puerto Plata and sparked fears that the vessel had met disaster.
records.summary_es: La correspondencia de la señora Howe continúa con la travesía desde Puerto Plata hasta la bahía de Samaná a bordo del vapor Tybee. Relata conversaciones con otros pasajeros, entre ellos una refugiada cubana que refirió las privaciones sufridas bajo las fuerzas españolas durante la revolución, incluyendo la pérdida de sus bienes y una epidemia entre los refugiados en las plantaciones del interior. Al llegar a Samaná, Howe elogia el puerto natural y describe el pequeño poblado de Santa Bárbara. Señala que el Tybee fue recibido con inmenso alivio, ya que los retrasos de su salida desde Nueva York habían elevado el precio del arroz a cuarenta centavos por libra en Puerto Plata y desatado temores de que el buque hubiera sufrido un desastre.

HAYTI.
—
Another of our Consuls in Trouble.
NEW YORK, April 13.—Haytien advices report the arrest and imprisonment of the American Consul at Port au Prince, because of his having given protection to Gen. Batellia, insurrectionary leader who escaped the custody of the guard and sought refuge in the Consul's office while on his way to be imprisoned. The Consul has conferred with Minister Bassett on the subject, who, it is understood, will apply to the Haytien government for redress.

Threat of War with San Domingo.
PORT AU PRINCE, April 13.—The invasion from Monte Christo consisted of 200 men. Eight Haytiens, five Dominicans, and one Frenchman were captured and executed. It is reliably reported that the Haytien Government will probably declare war against Baez, who is charged with an attempt to overthrow President Saget.

records.full_text:
And yet, again: Here at Santo Domingo City other popular ideas, propagated by Congressional speeches, are found to have no basis save in the distempered imaginations of political leaders.

How often have our people been assured that our Executive was guilty of maintaining a fleet in these waters, at vast expense, without necessity, and "solely to maintain a usurper in power!"

How confidently, how earnestly, how frequently have our orators asserted that the Baez administration was kept in power mainly by our naval forces, and that it could not stand a day after their withdrawal!

How have our orators thundered against this abuse of national power, this degrading service of our navy; and how have weak-kneed Republicans shaken their heads in disapproval of the supposed error and wrong! But what is the truth about it? We must have a squadron in the West Indies. The Dominican ports are capacious and convenient, and thither our ships frequently resort. But at this time there is not one of our war vessels in Dominican waters! The last one, the "Nantasket," sailed away some time ago, to return no one knows exactly when. But yet President Baez has not fallen nor fled! He sits more firm in the saddle than ever, and his administration has the confidence and the almost unanimous support of the people!

History will show, what all in these regions admit, that the moral effect of the presence of our fleet in Dominican and Haytian waters has been blessed indeed, because it has helped greatly to deter fillibusters, and to maintain peace and order.

records.full_text:
On his return to Washington the young man who had assumed to be "Aid-de-Camp of His Excellency General Ulysses S. Grant," and had bound the President to become a lobbyist for a wretched usurpation, instead of being disavowed and reprimanded, was sent back to the usurper with instructions to negotiate two treaties—one for the annexation of the half island of Dominica, and the other for the lease of the Bay of Samana. By the constitution of the United States ambassadors and other public ministers are appointed by the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate; but our aid-de-camp had no such commission. Presidential prerogative empowered him. Nor was naval force wanting. With three war ships at his disposal, he entered upon negotiation with Baez and obtained the two treaties. Naturally force was needed to keep the usurper in power while he sold his country, and naturally such a mission required a Presidential aid-de-camp unknown to constitution or law rather than a civilian duly appointed according to law.

On other occasions it has been my solemn duty to expose the outrages which attended this dark business, where at each step we are brought face to face with Presidential pretensions—first in the seizure of the war powers of the Government, as if he were a Caesar; forcibly intervening in Dominica and menacing war upon Hayti, all of which is proved by the official reports of the State Department and Navy Department, being nothing less than war by kingly prerogative in defiance of that distinctive principle of republican government first embodied in our Constitution, which places the war powers under the safeguard of the legislative branch, making any attempt by the President to declare war an undoubted usurpation.

records.full_text:
THE DOMINICAN TREATY.
Let us examine the evidence, and, first of all, take up the charges and evidence against him. The Santo Domingo Treaty, unlike going to Long Branch, smoking a cigar, or riding in a palace-car, was a piece of public business, and is, therefore, a topic not forbidden or unworthy. His guilt and his innocence in this respect can all be briefly stated.

The Monroe doctrine is one of the traditions of our country, and of both political parties. The Monroe doctrine means opposition to acquisitions on this continent by European powers. When President Grant came in no such question was pending, but such a question soon arose. An agent from the Dominican Republic presented himself to the President, saying that the people of Dominica, few in numbers, but rich in one of the most fertile isles of any sea, lying close to our shores, desired to come under the American flag; and that, failing this, that they would look to a European alliance. The President made no reply, and afterward a second agent appeared, repeating these statements, with glowing accounts of the fertility and resources of the Island of Santo Domingo.

Gen. McClellan, Admiral Porter, Commissioner Fabens and others had previously examined and reported upon the island, and had strongly stated its advantages as a coaling station, a naval station, a military key to the Gulf of Mexico, and as an area prolific in coffee, sugar cane, rice, dye-stuffs, mahogany, and other valuable woods, and in other products of the tropics, besides coal, copper, gold and salt.

records.headline: A report summarizes ten charges brought against President Grant's administration
records.summary_en: A report summarizes ten charges brought against President Grant's administration in a political speech comparing him with Horace Greeley. The third charge denounces Grant's negotiations for the annexation of the Dominican Republic without a minister approved by the Senate, along with his undignified lobbying of senators to secure ratification of the treaty. The indictment further condemns Grant for appointing unqualified cabinet members and relatives, forcing the resignation of Interior Secretary Cox, improperly enforcing congressional enforcement acts with troops, and mismanaging foreign relations.
records.summary_es: Un informe resume diez acusaciones formuladas contra la administración del presidente Grant en un discurso político que lo compara con Horace Greeley. La tercera acusación denuncia las negociaciones de Grant para la anexión de la República Dominicana sin un ministro aprobado por el Senado, así como su cabildeo indigno con senadores para lograr la ratificación del tratado. El pliego condena además a Grant por nombrar ministros del gabinete y parientes no cualificados, forzar la renuncia del secretario del Interior Cox, aplicar indebidamente las leyes de ejecución mediante el ejército y gestionar deficientemente las relaciones exteriores.

records.headline: An extract from a published statement by a senator responds
records.summary_en: An extract from a published statement by a senator responds to accusations by President Grant that his opposition to the administration was driven by denied patronage. The writer maintains that patronage was actively employed by the White House to promote the annexation of the Dominican Republic among members of Congress. He states that while the Santo Domingo treaty was pending, two gentlemen intimately connected with the administration separately approached him, offering him whatever patronage he desired if he would support the project. The author notes that after being taunted on the Senate floor, he asked one of those emissaries whether the patronage offer had been authorized by the President.
records.summary_es: Un extracto de una declaración publicada de un senador responde a las acusaciones del presidente Grant de que su oposición al gobierno fue motivada por la denegación de cargos y prebendas. El autor sostiene que la Casa Blanca empleó activamente el clientelismo político para promover la anexión de la República Dominicana entre los miembros del Congreso. Afirma que mientras el tratado de Santo Domingo estaba pendiente, dos caballeros estrechamente vinculados a la administración se le acercaron por separado, ofreciéndole todo el patronazgo que deseara a cambio de su apoyo al proyecto. Furthermore, the report claimed that Grant acted as a lobbyist to fulfill this agreement and ordered the United States Navy to attack anyone threatening the rule of the Dominican ruler, Baez.

El texto añadía que Grant operó como un gestor de antesala para cumplir dicho compromiso y dio órdenes a la armada de los Estados Unidos de atacar a cualquiera que amenazase la permanencia en el poder del mandatario dominicano, Báez.

records.full_text: Soon after his accession to power, he gave his mind, not to the great problems the solution of which the people so anxiously looked for, but to a project of his own—the acquisition of Santo Domingo. A subject of such importance as the incorporation with our political system of a tropical country with an utterly heterogeneous people, called for the most careful and earnest consideration. It is believed that the Secretary of State did not favor the scheme, and the State Department, whose office it is to conduct all the diplomatic affairs of the Government, was unceremoniously set aside. The President commenced a personal negotiation with Baez, the ruler of Santo Domingo, which he intrusted to one of his young aides de camp, whose zeal he had reason to believe equal to his own. The extraordinary character of this proceeding did not trouble him. He wanted to have the thing done; and to do it, an aide de camp was better than a Secretary of State. The aide de camp made a sort of a personal treaty between the two potentates, in which the President was pledged to propose to the favor of Congress for the scheme of the lobby at once. This disgraceful engagement would have revolted the sensibilities of any President having the dignity of his high office and the honor of the nation at heart.

records.headline: A correspondent defends President Grant against charges of racial
records.summary_en: A correspondent defends President Grant against charges of racial prejudice regarding the Santo Domingo Commission's return to Washington. The writer explains that the official duties of Frederick Douglass and General Sigel terminated immediately upon submitting their respective reports on American colored emigrants in the Dominican Republic and the fortification of Samaná Bay. Both men departed that night to reunite with their families, while the commissioners remained and were invited to dine with President Grant after paying their respects. The author argues that had Douglass been present he would certainly have been invited, asserting that Grant had completely rejected color prejudice in his treatment of Douglass.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal defiende al presidente Grant contra acusaciones de prejuicio racial tras el regreso de la Comisión de Santo Domingo a Washington. El autor explica que las funciones oficiales de Frederick Douglass y del general Sigel terminaron de inmediato al entregar sus respectivos informes sobre los emigrantes de color estadounidenses en la República Dominicana y sobre la fortificación de la bahía de Samaná. Ambos partieron esa misma noche para reunirse con sus familias, mientras que los comisionados permanecieron y fueron invitados a cenar con el presidente Grant tras presentarle sus respetos. El autor sostiene que de haber estado presente Douglass habría sido invitado sin duda, afirmando que Grant había desechado por completo el prejuicio racial en su trato hacia él.

records.headline: An article in the Free Press recounts ten charges leveled against President Grant during
records.summary_en: An article in the Free Press recounts ten charges leveled against President Grant during the presidential contest between Grant and Horace Greeley. Among the specific indictments, the third charge attacks Grant's negotiations for the annexation of the Dominican Republic, asserting that no minister was approved by the Senate and that Grant engaged in improper lobbying to secure ratification. The remaining charges accuse Grant of nepotism, appointing unqualified cabinet secretaries, forcing the removal of Interior Secretary Cox, using troops to carry out the enforcement acts, and mismanaging American foreign policy.
records.summary_es: Un artículo en el Free Press relata diez acusaciones formuladas contra el presidente Grant durante la contienda electoral entre Grant y Horace Greeley. Entre los cargos específicos, la tercera acusación ataca las negociaciones de Grant para la anexión de la República Dominicana, afirmando que ningún ministro fue aprobado por el Senado y que Grant recurrió a un cabildeo impropio para asegurar la ratificación. Los cargos restantes acusan a Grant de nepotismo, de nombrar ministros sin cualificaciones, de forzar la destitución del secretario del Interior Cox, de utilizar tropas para ejecutar las leyes de coerción y de gestionar deficientemente la política exterior estadounidense.

records.summary_en: Based on the provided excerpt, the newspaper reported that Hayti has historically acted as a bully and a constant threat to the progress and independence of Dominica, treating it as its lawful prey while possessing a much larger population. The publication defended U.S. actions regarding San Domingo—asserting it was under U.S. protection and duty-bound to prevent outside pressure—while accusing the Haytien government of aiding opponents of the legal executive of San Domingo, including Cabral, with men-of-war, arms, and mountaineer forces. Additionally, it recounted that an American admiral in the Gulf sailed to Port-au-Prince to quietly inform the Haytien minister of state about pending negotiations involving San Domingo.

El rotativo defendió la conducta de los Estados Unidos con respecto a Santo Domingo —sosteniendo que se hallaba bajo amparo estadounidense y en el deber de atajar coacciones foráneas—, inculpando a la vez al gobierno haitiano de secundar a los enemigos del gobernante constitucional dominicano, en especial a Cabral, facilitándoles buques de guerra, armamento y combatientes monteros. Añadió que un almirante estadounidense en el Golfo fondeó en Puerto Príncipe para advertir discretamente al ministro de Estado haitiano acerca de las negociaciones pendientes relativas a Santo Domingo.

Fabre Geffrard and Salnave were the only Haytien executives who had not sought to embroil or invade the feebler republic. Four times the Haytiens have swept over the Dominican territory. Hayti is nearly all black, made up of slaves from over sixty African tribes, whose descendants have nobly, and savagely, too, fought and won their personal freedom and national independence. But, though they may be honored in this, there’s nothing in their history for sixty years past to go in ecstacies over. When Mr. Sumner says we bullied them, San Domingo was, in diplomatic usage, under our protection. We had the right, and it was our duty, to prevent outside pressure. records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that Hayti repeatedly sought to subjugate Santo Domingo, whose government eventually appealed to the United States for protection amidst an imminent crisis. In response, the U.S. administration notified Haytian authorities that, pending a decision by Congress on the preliminary annexation treaty, any foreign invasion of Dominican territory would be considered an unfriendly act toward the United States. The author defended this action as a necessary duty in the interest of peace and humanity rather than a violation of international law.

Como réplica, la administración de Washington notificó a las autoridades haitianas que, mientras el Congreso deliberase sobre las bases del tratado de anexión, toda invasión foránea al territorio dominicano se consideraría un acto hostil hacia los Estados Unidos. El autor justificó dicho proceder como una obligación ineludible en aras de la paz y de la humanidad, y no como una transgresión del derecho internacional.

The alleged outrage upon Hayti occurred as follows: No sooner was it known that a negotiation for annexation was pending than preparations were made by the Haytian authorities to invade their feeble neighbor, instigated to this course by the diplomatic representatives of certain European Powers, who were jealous of American supremacy. Hayti, which comprises less than one-third of the island, (10,000 square miles,) has repeatedly sought to subjugate the whole (32,000 square miles.) She feared that Santo Domingo would forever escape from her clutches. The population of Hayti (500,000) is four-fold that of Santo Domingo, (125,000,) and is governed by a military despotism under the forms of a republic. Hayti was possessed of an armed steamer. The seaports of Santo Domingo, protected by only two small schooners, were liable to bombardment. The crisis was imminent, and the Government of Santo Domingo appealed to our Government for protection against a danger growing out of this very negotiation.

What did the Administration do? Just this: in the interest of peace and humanity it notified the Haytian authorities that a preliminary treaty of annexation had been negotiated, and that, until Congress should have expressed its decision, an invasion of the Dominican territory by any foreign Power would be regarded as an act unfriendly to the United States.

records.headline: An article from the Chicago Inter-Ocean, reprinted in the New National Era
records.summary_en: An article from the Chicago Inter-Ocean, reprinted in the New National Era, reports that Germany may seek the cession of Manzanilla Bay from Haiti following an extraction of £15,000 by a German naval squadron. The report compares Manzanilla to Samaná Bay at the opposite end of the island, which had been sought by the United States. While white colonization is reportedly abhorred by the Haitian populace, the account notes that upper classes recognize little prospect of stability unless a strong foreign power intervenes to compel Haiti and the Dominican Republic into peaceful relations. It adds, however, that many fear foreign protection would lead to complete subjugation, citing the prior experience of the Dominicans under Spanish rule.
records.summary_es: Un artículo del Chicago Inter-Ocean, reproducido en el New National Era, informa que Alemania podría procurar la cesión de la bahía de Manzanilla por parte de Haití tras la exacción de 15.000 libras por una escuadra naval alemana. El informe compara Manzanilla con la bahía de Samaná en el extremo opuesto de la isla, la cual había sido pretendida por los Estados Unidos. Aunque la colonización de personas blancas es supuestamente aborrecida por la población haitiana, el relato señala que las clases acomodadas reconocen pocas probabilidades de estabilidad a menos que una potencia extranjera fuerte intervenga para obligar a Haití y a la República Dominicana a mantener relaciones pacíficas. Añade, sin embargo, que muchos temen que la protección extranjera conduzca a una subyugación total, citando la experiencia previa de los dominicanos bajo el dominio español.

records.full_text:
1. The alleged outrage upon Hayti occurred as follows: No sooner was it known that a negotiation for annexation was pending than preparations were made by the Haytian authorities to invade their feeble neighbor, instigated to this course by the deplomatic representatives of certain European Powers, who were jealous of American suprmacy. Hayti, which comprises less than one-third of the island (10,000 square miles,) has repeatdly sought to subjugate the whole (32,000 square miles.) She feared that Santo Domingo would forever escape from her clutches. The population of Hayti (500 000) is four fold that of Santo Domingo (125,000,) and is governed by a military despotism under the forms of a republic. Hayti was possessed of an armed steamer. The seaports of Santo Domingo, protected by only two small schooners, were liable too bombardment. The crisis was iminent, and the Government of Santo Domingo appealed to our Government for protection against a danger growing out of this very negotiation. Congress was not in session at the time.

What did the Administration do? Just this: In the interest of peace and humanity it notified the Haytian authorities that a preliminary treaty of annexation had been negotiated, and that, until Congress should have expressed its decision, an invasion of the Dominican territory by any foreign Power would be regarded as an act unfriendly to the United States.

records.chapter_es: La lucha por la anexión estadounidense
records.full_text:
SAMANA OURS.

The Money Sent to Baez by New York Merchants—Trade With Santo Domingo Secured.

From the New York World, Dec. 7.
It is now three and a half years since President Grant took up the subject of the annexation of Santo Domingo. The main idea urged in favor of the plan was that it was indispensible to the prosperity of American commerce for the United States to have in their possession a substantial territory in the West Indies. In June, 1869, the President appointed an agent to obtain information about the Dominican Republic, and General Babcock was finally sent out there. In September, 1869, he negotiated a preliminary treaty, which was approved by President Grant, and in November a regular treaty with President Baez was concluded. The matter was debated in Congress, a commission was sent to the island in January, 1871, and finally in April of that year President Grant relinquished the plan.

But it has since been taken up by prominent business men of this country, who were persuaded that it would be profitable to them to secure what the Government had rejected. Some of them had visited Santo Domingo, and the result is that the steamer Tybee has just taken out, with other valuable cargo, the money required by the Baez Government for a certain specified amount of territory, including the Bay of Samana and for which Congress refused an appropriation. It is reported in business circles that one gain that will accrue to the new company will be in the shape of the port dues.

The following coloquy with Mr. C. K. Garrison gives all the particulars upon the matter that are now obtainable:

Mr. Garrison, when found at his office at the Bowling Green, was at first unwilling to communicate what he knew upon this important subject, but finding that the main facts were already known to his visitor became more communicative.

When asked, "Is it really true, that the Tybee has gone out with important lading connected with the new enterprise of the mercantile association that proposes tofollow up the Santo Domingo project?" he replied in substance, "Yes, a number of us, merchants and others, have concluded that we will accept the bargain that the government has refused. This is apart from all political considerations; is a mere matter of business."

"What shape has your action taken?"

"We have raised the money demanded and sent it out in the Tybee, and will thus gain control of the Port of Samana, the finest in the West Indies, and capable of holding the navies of the world."

"You will have special rights and privileges, I suppose—be a sort of western 'East India Company?'"

"Well, we are paying out a great deal of money, and of course we are not giving it for nothing, but expect ample returns."

"Will not this first outlay need to be followed by other large expenditures for warehouses, etc.?"

"We don't know much about what will come after. We shall move cautiously, and be governed by circumstances."

"Are only New York capitalists in the enterprise?"

"No; there are capitalists of Boston, Philadelphia and other towns in the movement."

"It appears to be a legitimate transaction. I suppose that many of you have long had mercantile dealings with those regions?"

"Yes; I, for one, have been running steamers to those islands, as far down as Brazil. I have no connection with the administration, and it is a matter of business with us all."

"This is certainly a good way to settle a vexed question, and prevent further political controversy on the subject. But what is the condition of the island? Is there much industrial activity there?"

"There is a large export trade of coffee and other tropical products; but the point of the greatest importance will be the possession by Americans of such a fine port in the West Indies?

records.chapter_es: La lucha por la anexión estadounidense
records.full_text:
The annexation of the eastern portion of Santo Domingo, known as Dominica, and formerly a colony of Spain, was very actively discussed by the public and Congress. The following are the facts of the early negotiations and treaties: Two treaties between the governments of the United States and Dominica were signed. The first was known as the Samana treaty. By this Dominica cedes the entire domain of the district described therein, which includes the Peninsula and Bay of Samana, for a term of fifty years, reserving the free navigation, for an annual rental of $15,000 gold. Four months are stipulated for ratification, during which the United States protects Dominica from foreign intervention. One year's rent was paid down, and possession duly taken.

The second, known as the annexation treaty, provides for a renunciation of sovereignty in favor of the United States, and that the Dominican Republic be incorporated on the footing of a territory, eligible to admission into the Union in the discretion of Congress. Dominica cedes her property, as specified in a schedule, but reserves all other property not scheduled; delivery not to be made nor consideration paid until Congress shall have appropriated the money. This is $1,500,000 in gold; and is in consideration of property only. Its disposition is provided for—Dominica is to apply it to her debts. But the application is to be made by a commission which the United States is to respect and protect, to be appointed by those who at the signing of the treaty constituted the present actual Dominican Government. For all debt, liquidated and unliquidated, in excess of such sum, public bonds of Dominica shall stand as security; likewise all the public lands and other property reserved from cession. After the execution of the treaty no grants or concessions of lands, or of rights in lands, were to be made, or any debt contracted. Franchises other than those are not prohibited. It is also agreed that the United States is in no event liable for Dominican debts or obligations. The cession was not to be valid unless ratified by a vote of the people.

Both treaties were signed at the city of Santo Domingo November 29, 1869, on behalf respectively of President Grant and President Baez. In execution of anticipatory instructions, an adequate naval force under the direction of a representative of the army immediately carried into effect the protection clauses. This protection has never been remitted. Hayti, either as a foreign nation or as the government de jure of the whole island, as they claim, ostensibly remonstrated.

In March, 1870, the result was received of an election held in Dominica during a fortnight, beginning under a decree of President Baez and his Senate, dated February 16, 1870. The returns indicated a general approval of the treaty. About eighty days, however, had intervened before an election was found "possible." In appropriate localities an official registry was opened, in which citizens were invited to inscribe their suffrages. On the first day of opening the polls a citizen recorded himself in the negative. He was seized on the spot and sent out of the city by the military guard, present in strong force. Several, afterwards expelled from the country by President Baez, found refuge from violence in the house of the Italian consul. President Baez, in presence of the commercial agent of the United States, threatened influential citizens with banishment if they opposed the treaty, and frequently expressed the like intolerance.

The unanimity thus obtained was so suspicious as to require negative votes by invitation. The Dominican President habitually declared the dependence of his authority upon that of the United States in force, and said that the death or expulsion of himself and his cabinet could be averted only by this annexation.

The public property of Dominica in the main was to be left to her, with the corresponding burden of her own debts and liabilities, necessarily, without prejudice to third parties. Encumbrances then became matter of essential consequence. Beyond the fact that they were large, only the most obscure and meagre data were before the United States government concerning them previous to the report of the commissioners. A person named Fabens, resident in Dominica, made, as agent of the United States, a report placing the aggregate at $600,000. With some additions since it has been reckoned at some millions. It was reported that mortgages of enormous scope, grants of public lands—of which a single one to Fabens absorbed one-fifth—perpetual navigation and commercial franchises and other monopolies, mining right, banking privileges, right to valuable woods, guano, &c., land grants and charters for railroads, for immigration societies, &c., existed; and thus there was excited the belief that by way of grant or lien all the appropriable resources of the country have fallen under private control.

Subsequent to the signing of the treaty grants and concessions of every description were solicited of the Dominican government, against zealous remonstrances of their regular United States diplomatic agent, made without encouragement from Washington. The President, on sending the report of the commissioners to Congress, accompanied it with a message, in which he took strong ground for annexation, but, as is well known, without success.

These factors have led many Dominicans to desire annexation to the United States on terms of reciprocity following its victory over slavery. SANTO DOMINGO.

ANNEXATION IN A COMMERCIAL PHASE.

VIEWS OF DR. SAMUEL G. HOWE.
What He Thinks of Santo Domingo—His Opinions Concerning the Haytians—Annexation Popular in Santo Domingo—The Great Commercial Enterprise.
To the Editor of The Tribune.
SIR: The likings and preferences of different men for different parts of the earth are sometimes accounted for, sometimes not. A mountaineer loves his home with an exceeding love, because it is finite and comprehensible to his senses; the mountain is to him a thing apart from earth; it stands out against the sky; he can compass its foot, and can take in at a glance from its green and flowery base to its cold and snowy crown. The isles of the sea, you may love them as things having definite existence and form, and space and outline; you may sail around them; you may traverse them from shore to shore, and from the high points see all their contour. Not so with a vast continent; you cannot comprehend it; cannot make it a mental unit; while thinking of one part, you lose the thought of the rest.

Most men love the islands of the West Indies for their gorgeous tropical beauty, the like of which has not been seen; his eyes have not seen the earth's glory of the Lord. I love them for their delicious climate; their soft winds coming fresh from the sea every morning, and after fanning the mountains going out again at night as cool land breezes. I love them for their clear and ever-flowing brooks; their ever flowers; their ever crystal seas. They are the Eden of the earth, which the choicest races of men in the fullness of time shall possess and regard as paradise.

Especially do I love Hayti, the mountainous, the queen of the Antilles, whose natural beauties and advantages distinguish her even among the beautiful grouped around. I take deep interest in the condition and fate of the two peoples who to-day divide her territory between them. The western end, the seat of the negro republic, is a land of rare beauty, marvelous fertility, varied production, notwithstanding the dreadful insalubrity of its seaboard; well fitted for the black man to try the experiment of self-government, and maintain the independence so gallantly won by his ancestors. It is sadly true that during the half century of that independence very little progress has been made toward civilization, even in the seaport towns, and that barbarous superstition and pagan sacrifices prevail in the interior among negroes as uncivilized as those of central Africa. Well did Frederick Douglass exclaim after a short sojourn at Port-au-Prince: "Alas! is this all that my fellow-men of color can accomplish?"

It may be, perhaps, that the black races cannot originate a new and high civilization of their own; but they can certainly imitate and carry on a civilization originated by others. But there is much in the history of Hayti to account for its present wretched condition; and there are men among Haytians who would honor any people. The French slave system was more horrid and debasing than the Spanish, which prevailed at the eastern end; and during its domination in Hayti the slaves became brutalized. Their long, bloody war for freedom was full of horrible atrocities on either side that further brutalized them. Then, after gaining their independence, they adopted the fatal policy of national isolation. They drove away most of the whites, and have continued to keep them out; they deny to them ownership of land and the right of full citizenship. Thus they have attempted to found and conduct a republic upon the narrow basis of race. Their friends abroad have sustained them in this foolish policy, and the end is the establishment of a conservative and odious aristocracy in the State, which sustains itself by a reign of terror.

But in spite of all this, we must give the black man all the aid and comfort we can, and say heartily: Vive la Republique d'Haiti, quand meme! I believe that the best way to help the Haytian is to set in his immediate neighborhood, over the mountain border, the flag of our Union, and carry thither our political and social institutions, our arts and our agriculture, that he may see them, imitate them, and profit by them. I know of no better way than to profit by the one which is now open, and obtain the right to say peace shall be kept in these regions, and they shall be opened to the peaceful spread of our commerce and our institutions.

It is for this end that I have labored, and shall labor, for the annexation of the eastern (Spanish) end of the island, now occupied by the Republic of Santo Domingo. This country is far more favored in felicitous geographical position, and salubrity of climate; is well adapted for the residence of white men, and for varied agricultural and industrial pursuits. It lies to windward, and the trade winds, drawing through the valleys between the two mountain ranges which traverse it from east to west, deposit their moisture, which is condensed on these mountains, keeping everything green to their very summits, and trickling down in constant rills and brooks. But by the time the trade winds reach the cross range which, running from north to south, separates the two republics, they have become dry and hot, and bring neither moisture nor coolness to the western end; hence proceed mainly the salubrity of the former and the insalubrity of the latter region.

Santo Domingo has been still more favored than Hayti in respect to its civil and political conditions. Its inhabitants were a mixed race of Spanish, Indian, and blacks, who live together on terms of equality; they fought side by side in the wars for driving out the Haytians and other invaders, and have a common and strong feeling of nationality. The Spaniards, during their long domination, maintained a mild form of slavery over the blacks; but with their usual liberality they accorded to the inhabitants considerable municipal rights and privileges. Hence, instead of the barbarism and the heathen practices which prevail in the interior of Hayti, we find throughout that of Santo Domingo a gentle and peaceful people, living in villages and observing the customs of civilized life. We find regular civil institutions, with civil magistrates chosen by the people; we find property pretty equally divided, and regular registries of titles, births, deaths, and the like. We find in almost every village well-bred and well-mannered men, speaking Spanish and French, and showing considerable intelligence. We find everywhere a tolerant and democratic spirit. There is not a general desire for education and improvement; but there are men who comprehend the situation of their country, and the ways and means by which to elevate it. These men give the tone to public opinion. They believe that annexation to the United States will be the greatest blessing to their country.

With the exception of here and there an enthusiast, who cries Viva la Republica, these men despair of the persistent independence of their own isle. They know that their black neighbors of Hayti never will forego the purpose, so often manifested by bloody invasions, of subjugating and dominating the whole island. This knowledge keeps them in constant dread, and paralyzes all attempts at self-improvement. To ward off these invasions the government maintains an army which keeps all the young men from work, and fits them for plunderers of the peasantry. The Government is too feeble to repel foreign invasions, and hence the apprehensions of their island being again seized upon by Spain, or some other foreign power.

These and other causes have made many Dominicans look to some foreign power which would not accord them, as Spain did, "the protection which vultures give to lambs, covering and devouring them," but aid upon equal terms of reciprocity. Since our victory over Slavery, the desire for annexation to our country has become unanimous and intense among the Dominican people. I have seen proofs enough of this fact. I saw it plainly on my official visit as Commissioner two years ago; I saw them more plainly still during a more protracted residence among the Dominicans last winter. Their best men unceasingly use their influence toward bringing about a measure to which they look as their surest guarantee of freedom, safety and prosperity.

I am more and more convinced of the truth contained in the first Presidential message upon the subject of annexation to the United States: would be a furtherance of the Monroe doctrine; that it is a national protection, asserting our just and controlling influence over the great commercial traffic soon to flow from east to west by way of the Isthmus of Darien; build up our merchant marine, furnish new markets for the products of our farms, shops and manufactories; make slavery insupportable in Cuba and Porto Rico at once, and ultimately in Brazil; and settle the unhappy condition of Cuba and its exterminating conflict; and therefore I have labored in season and out of season to bring about annexation in some shape.

It will rather thwart the one proposed by him, and therefore it is hoped that it will escape the vehement invectives and abuse heaped upon that. It is not a political measure, and cannot excite well-founded political opposition. There may be some who will oppose it in the supposed interest of the dominant party in Hayti, which continually aims at possession of the whole island, and means by force if it can.

It is a great commercial enterprise, undertaken by men of wealth and energy; and whether it yields them the rich returns they look for or not, it will open the vast resources of Santo Domingo, and establish between it and this country relations advantageous to both.
Yours, &c.,
SAMUEL G. HOWE.
Boston, Jan. 1, 1873.

records.headline: An editorial in the Tribune discusses the Samaná Bay enterprise
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Tribune discusses the Samaná Bay enterprise and disputes the assertions of Dr. Samuel G. Howe. The paper agrees that the undertaking points to the establishment of controlling American influence in the Republic of Santo Domingo and throughout the West Indies, and will be favored so far as it remains a legitimate business project. It cautions, however, that serious complications will arise, as the new owners of Samaná will demand greater protection than President Báez can supply. The editorial concludes that Washington will ultimately be required to defend American citizens, effectively placing the Samaná establishment under the United States flag.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en el Tribune analiza la empresa de la bahía de Samaná y refuta las afirmaciones del doctor Samuel G. Howe. El periódico coincide en que la iniciativa apunta al establecimiento de una influencia estadounidense preponderante en la República de Santo Domingo y en todas las Antillas, y que será vista con agrado en la medida en que siga siendo un proyecto comercial legítimo. Advierte, sin embargo, que surgirán graves complicaciones, ya que los nuevos propietarios de Samaná exigirán mayor protección de la que el presidente Báez puede brindar. El editorial concluye que el gobierno de Washington se verá finalmente obligado a defender a los ciudadanos estadounidenses, colocando prácticamente el establecimiento de Samaná bajo la bandera de los Estados Unidos.

records.headline: An article in the Dispatch quotes commentary on the Samaná concession
records.summary_en: An article in the Dispatch quotes commentary on the Samaná concession, observing that whatever productive wealth the Dominican side of the island possesses will belong to the men who obtained the grant. The quoted analysis likens the project to the historic English and Dutch East India trading companies, suggesting that the acquisition of land titles may serve as the first step toward the transfer of sovereignty and the establishment of dominant American influence in the Republic of Santo Domingo. The Dispatch remarks upon the historic irony that this commercial enterprise originates in the very region once heavily engaged in the transatlantic slave trade.
records.summary_es: Un artículo en el Dispatch reproduce un comentario sobre la concesión de Samaná, observando que cualquier riqueza productiva que posea la parte dominicana de la isla pertenecerá a los hombres que obtuvieron la concesión. El análisis citado compara el proyecto con las históricas compañías comerciales inglesa y holandesa de las Indias Orientales, sugiriendo que la adquisición de títulos de propiedad sobre la tierra puede servir como el primer paso hacia la transferencia de soberanía y el establecimiento de una influencia estadounidense dominante en la República de Santo Domingo. El Dispatch destaca la ironía histórica de que esta empresa comercial tenga su origen en la misma región que en el pasado participó activamente en la trata transatlántica de esclavos.
