records.headline: A New York Herald correspondent praises the fertility of Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: A New York Herald correspondent praises the fertility of Santo Domingo as extraordinary, remarking that the soil can cultivate anything in the botanical dictionary, though local agriculture suffers because no ploughs are used. Having secured a horse in Santiago, the writer departs for Puerto Plata after learning of local excitement caused by an alleged insult to the British flag by Dominican authorities. The correspondent describes bidding farewell to the Yaque River and traveling over the mountains past Santo Cerro, noting that companions Halsey, Oley, and Plummer proceeded toward La Vega and Cotuy en route to Santo Domingo City.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del New York Herald elogia la extraordinaria fertilidad de Santo Domingo, comentando que en su suelo puede cosecharse cuanto figura en el diccionario botánico, aunque la agricultura local carece de arados y descansa enteramente en la naturaleza. Tras conseguir un caballo en Santiago, el autor emprende viaje a Puerto Plata al enterarse de la agitación provocada por un supuesto agravio a la bandera británica por parte de las autoridades dominicanas. El corresponsal describe su despedida del río Yaque y su travesía por las montañas pasando por el Santo Cerro, señalando que sus acompañantes Halsey, Oley y Plummer continuaron hacia La Vega y Cotuy camino a la ciudad de Santo Domingo.

records.headline: The Rutland Weekly Herald comments on Samana Bay, noting its strategic
records.summary_en: The Rutland Weekly Herald comments on Samana Bay, noting its strategic location in eastern Santo Domingo near Puerto Rico and Cuba. The paper cites a New York Herald correspondent's description of the territory's rich black soil producing sugar cane, bananas, and coconuts, contrasted against an impoverished population characterized as moneyless, with worthless currency, lack of roads, and chronic dissension. The item notes that the Dominican Republic has an estimated population of 100,000 and that President Báez recently conducted a plebiscite on the Samana Bay Company contract, claiming an overwhelming affirmative vote.
records.summary_es: El Rutland Weekly Herald comenta sobre la bahía de Samaná, destacando su posición estratégica en el oriente de Santo Domingo cerca de Puerto Rico y Cuba. El periódico cita la descripción de un corresponsal del New York Herald sobre la rica tierra negra de la región, que produce caña de azúcar, plátanos y cocos, en contraste con una población desfavorecida calificada de gente sin dinero, con moneda sin valor, caminos inexistentes e interminables discordias. La nota agrega que la República Dominicana cuenta con una población estimada en 100.000 habitantes y que el presidente Báez celebró recientemente un plebiscito sobre el contrato con la Samana Bay Company, asegurando haber obtenido una votación mayoritariamente afirmativa.

records.headline: It is a pity both races cannot live on better terms
records.summary_en: According to the *New York Herald* on April 22, 1873, international animosity and border warfare between Hayti and the Dominican Republic had depopulated the border region, reducing towns like Dajabon to near-desolation. While Hayti's President Saget unsuccessfully sought a treaty of amity and commerce through the British consul general, Dominican leader Baez allegedly maintained hostilities to frighten Dominicans into supporting annexation to the United States. Additionally, the article contrasted the two nations' populations, noting that Hayti had a larger population and smaller territory with a seven-eighths black demographic, whereas the Dominican Republic was three-quarters Creole, with Creoles serving as the ruling and aristocratic element in both republics.

En tanto el presidente haitiano Saget gestionó infructuosamente un convenio de concordia y comercio con la mediación del cónsul general británico, se aseguraba que el gobernante dominicano Báez sostenía los enconos armados para intimidar a sus conciudadanos y forzarlos a cobijarse bajo la anexión a los Estados Unidos. El artículo contrastó asimismo la composición demográfica de ambos estados, refiriendo que Haití contaba con una población más densa en un territorio menor constituida en sus siete octavas partes por negros, en tanto que la República Dominicana era en sus tres cuartas partes criolla, integrando los criollos el estamento dirigente y aristocrático en ambas repúblicas.

records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* reported in April 1873 that annexing Santo Domingo would likely result in disappointment and questioned whether President Grant could guarantee the peaceable behavior of local inhabitants. The article argued that acquiring the island solely for a naval station is an extravagant burden and that annexation would only benefit New England manufactures if foreign commerce from Germany, France, and England were excluded.

La publicación arguyó que apropiarse de la isla con el único propósito de instalar una estación naval constituía un gravamen desproporcionado, y que la adhesión del territorio solo reportaría provecho a las manufacturas de Nueva Inglaterra en el caso de proscribir el comercio con Alemania, Francia e Inglaterra.

records.headline: Comparing Haiti and the Dominican Republic, a New York Herald correspondent
records.summary_en: Comparing Haiti and the Dominican Republic, a New York Herald correspondent refers to the latter as Dominica. The writer describes Santo Domingo City as cleaner and richer in historical associations than Port-au-Prince, but far behind the Haitian capital in commercial wealth. The report asserts that Haiti possesses superior harbors, scenery, and genuine coal mines, whereas Dominica relies on tobacco exports and has found only lignite. Under the subhead evaluating both nations as poor material for democracy, the correspondent argues that both are republics only nominally, stating that while Haiti's president is chosen by manipulated legislative chambers, the president of Dominica can re-elect himself at will so long as he retains control of the army.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del New York Herald compara a Haití y la República Dominicana, refiriéndose a esta última como Dominica. El autor describe a la ciudad de Santo Domingo como un lugar más limpio y rico en historia que Puerto Príncipe, pero muy a la zaga de la capital haitiana en riqueza comercial. El informe sostiene que Haití posee mejores puertos, paisajes y minas de carbón auténtico, mientras que Dominica depende de las exportaciones de tabaco y apenas cuenta con lignito. Bajo el subtítulo que evalúa a ambas naciones como mal material para la democracia, el corresponsal sostiene que las dos son repúblicas únicamente de nombre, y afirma que mientras el presidente de Haití es elegido por cámaras legislativas manipuladas, el presidente de Dominica puede reelegirse a su antojo siempre que mantenga el respaldo del ejército.

records.headline: The New York Herald's correspondent reports from La Coupe, Haiti
records.summary_en: The New York Herald's correspondent reports from La Coupe, Haiti, on an interview with General Gregorio Luperón, whom the paper also mentions in connection with an idea of uniting Haiti and Dominica. The correspondent denies reports that Luperón had already launched an invasion of Dominican territory, explaining that he had merely conducted a reconnaissance of the border with a former officer. Luperón stated that speeches by Minister Curiel promoting the Samana Bay lease as backed by United States protection had outraged local populations in Monte Cristi. Luperón displayed letters from Dominicans across the border urging him to lead a revolution against the Báez government.
records.summary_es: El corresponsal del New York Herald informa desde La Coupe, Haití, sobre una entrevista con el general Gregorio Luperón, a quien el periódico vincula asimismo con la idea de unir a Haití y Dominica. records.summary_en: An editorial notes that St. Domingo's difficulties are many and that Cabral, the revolutionary leader interviewed by a Herald correspondent, holds very decided views on them. records.headline: The New York Herald reports on heavy fighting between insurgent
records.summary_en: The New York Herald reports on heavy fighting between insurgent forces led by General Luperón and troops loyal to Dominican President Báez. Following a clash at Dajabón, Luperón retreated toward the border, where Dominican pursuit provoked an engagement with Haitian troops that left a Haitian general mortally wounded. Reinforced by General Polanco, Luperón briefly retook Dajabón with 100 men before government forces recaptured it after an eight days' siege, compelling Luperón to retreat to Altamira. The dispatch notes that Dominican government forces suffered 200 casualties, that Vice President Cáceres was captured at Altamira, halting communication between Santiago and Puerto Plata, and that Haiti dispatched a war vessel to protect its merchant shipping against Dominican seizures.
records.summary_es: El New York Herald informa sobre intensos combates entre las fuerzas insurgentes dirigidas por el general Luperón y las tropas leales al presidente dominicano Báez. Tras un enfrentamiento en Dajabón, Luperón se replegó hacia la frontera, donde la persecución dominicana provocó un choque con tropas haitianas en el que un general haitiano resultó mortalmente herido. Reforzado por el general Polanco, Luperón recuperó brevemente Dajabón con 100 hombres antes de que las fuerzas gubernamentales la reconquistaran tras un asedio de ocho días, forzándolo a retirarse a Altamira. El despacho señala que las tropas del gobierno dominicano sufrieron 200 bajas, que el vicepresidente Cáceres fue capturado en Altamira, interrumpiendo la comunicación entre Santiago y Puerto Plata, y que Haití despachó un buque de guerra para proteger a su marina mercante de incautaciones dominicanas.

records.summary_en: A telegraphic dispatch from New York in the Worcester Daily Spy reports that Dominican government forces attacked General Luperón at Dajabón, driving him toward the Haitian border. When Dominican troops pursued him across the line, Haitian forces engaged them, leaving a Haitian general mortally wounded. Aided by reinforcements sent by Polanco, Luperón temporarily reoccupied Dajabón, but government forces besieged the town for eight days and retook it, forcing Luperón to retreat to Altamira. Dominican government troops lost 100 men killed and wounded, and Vice President Cáceres was captured at Altamira, severing communication between Santiago and Puerto Plata.

Con refuerzos enviados por Polanco, Luperón retomó temporalmente Dajabón, pero las fuerzas gubernamentales sitiaron la plaza durante ocho días y la recuperaron, obligando a Luperón a retirarse a Altamira. Las fuerzas del gobierno dominicano perdieron 100 hombres entre muertos y heridos, y el vicepresidente Cáceres fue capturado en Altamira, cortando la comunicación entre Santiago y Puerto Plata.

records.headline: Quoting the Alta California, The Pacific Commercial Advertiser reports
records.summary_en: Quoting the Alta California, The Pacific Commercial Advertiser reports from New York that agents representing Dominican insurgent leaders purchased arms in the city and recently shipped one thousand stand to revolutionary territory. The report states that resistance to President Báez is intensifying because Dominicans object to the Samana Bay Company, accusing it of exploiting and exporting the country's resources without fulfilling promises to construct buildings or make material improvements. Private advices further report that Báez's army lost 100 men on the field during a June 18 battle at Caroco, leading to widespread desertions among government troops.
records.summary_es: Al citar al Alta California, The Pacific Commercial Advertiser informa desde Nueva York que agentes de los caudillos insurgentes dominicanos compraron armas en la ciudad y enviaron recientemente mil fusiles hacia territorio controlado por los revolucionarios. El reporte señala que la oposición al presidente Báez crece a diario debido al rechazo dominicano a la Samana Bay Company, a la que se acusa de extraer y exportar las riquezas del país sin cumplir sus promesas de erigir edificaciones o realizar mejoras materiales. Informes privados indican además que el ejército de Báez perdió 100 hombres en el campo de batalla el 18 de junio en Caroco, lo que desató constantes deserciones en las filas gubernamentales.

records.headline: President Báez has repelled the insurgent campaign against him
records.summary_en: President Báez has repelled the insurgent campaign against him, an editorial in the New York Herald reports, noting that General García has rejoined the government, Monte Cristi has been recaptured, a schooner carrying ammunition was seized, and General Luperón has escaped across the border into Haiti. The paper predicts that this victory offers Báez only temporary respite before Luperón returns with hundreds of men to challenge him anew. Meanwhile, the Herald observes that the Samana Bay Company appears to be doing nothing to stimulate Dominican trade, though it may have assisted Báez's recent victories to safeguard its own concessions.
records.summary_es: Un editorial del New York Herald reporta que el presidente Báez ha sofocado la campaña rebelde en su contra, destacando que el general García se ha reincorporado al gobierno, Monte Cristi fue recuperada, una goleta con municiones resultó incautada y el general Luperón huyó al otro lado de la frontera hacia Haití. El periódico prevé que esta victoria sólo brindará a Báez un respiro pasajero antes de que Luperón reaparezca con varios cientos de hombres para desafiarlo nuevamente. Entre tanto, el Herald observa que la Samana Bay Company parece no estar haciendo nada para impulsar el comercio dominicano, si bien pudo haber contribuido a los recientes triunfos de Báez con miras a proteger sus propias concesiones.

records.headline: An editorial in the Worcester Daily Spy discusses appeals for United States intervention
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Worcester Daily Spy discusses appeals for United States intervention on behalf of the Samana Bay Company against Dominican insurgents seeking to annul President Báez's territorial concessions. The paper charges that company promoters deliberately intended to embroil the United States with the Dominican Republic to force an annexation of its territory. Urging President Grant to keep clear of these complications, the editorial argues that while governments protect ordinary merchants abroad, the Samana Bay Company obtained quasi-sovereign powers—including rights to enact laws, coin money, and raise troops—and cannot claim standard diplomatic protection for its political privileges.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en el Worcester Daily Spy examina las solicitudes de intervención de los Estados Unidos a favor de la Samana Bay Company frente a los rebeldes dominicanos que buscan revocar las concesiones territoriales otorgadas por el presidente Báez. El diario acusa a los promotores de la compañía de haber buscado deliberadamente complicar a los Estados Unidos con la República Dominicana con el fin de forzar la anexión de su territorio. Al exhortar al presidente Grant a mantenerse al margen de tales enredos, el editorial razona que si bien los gobiernos protegen a comerciantes comunes en el extranjero, la Samana Bay Company adquirió facultades de cuasi-soberanía —incluido el derecho de dictar leyes, acuñar moneda y sostener milicias— y no puede reclamar protección diplomática convencional para salvaguardar sus privilegios políticos.

records.headline: In a sarcastic editorial passage, the paper mocks the provisional government Luperón set up near the Haitian frontier
records.summary_en: In a sarcastic editorial passage, the paper mocks the provisional government Luperón set up near the Haitian frontier and derides calls to send American monitors to Dominican waters. It frames the episode around men recently shot in Santo Domingo and disputes a certification published in the Nation.
records.summary_es: En un pasaje editorial sarcástico, el periódico se burla del gobierno provisional que Luperón estableció cerca de la frontera haitiana y ridiculiza los llamados a enviar monitores estadounidenses a aguas dominicanas. Enmarca el episodio en torno a hombres fusilados recientemente en Santo Domingo y disputa una certificación publicada en la Nation.

records.headline: Buenaventura Baez writes to President Grant appealing for the Dominican people, saying the agreement with the Samana Bay Company
records.summary_en: Buenaventura Baez writes to President Grant appealing for the Dominican people, saying the agreement with the Samana Bay Company has been followed by silence and indifference and that they cannot alone support the consequences of combined hatred against them. He solicits the establishment of an efficient United States protectorate to preserve them from unwarranted attacks aimed at their very existence.
records.summary_es: Buenaventura Báez escribe al presidente Grant apelando por el pueblo dominicano, diciendo que el acuerdo con la Compañía de la Bahía de Samaná ha sido seguido de silencio e indiferencia y que no pueden soportar solos las consecuencias del odio combinado contra ellos. Solicita el establecimiento de un protectorado eficaz de los Estados Unidos que los preserve de ataques injustificados dirigidos contra su propia existencia.
records.passage: the noise of its establishment has been succeeded by the most absolute silence and the most restless indifference. It not being possible for the Dominican people to continue to support alone and unaided the horrible consequence of a combined hatred, which manifests itself in disguised attacks and machinations, they appeal to the great Republic of the United States through your Excellency, soliciting the establishment of an efficient Protectorate which may preserve them from unwarranted attacks aimed at their very existence. The Dominican people believe that this will not be distasteful, even to the opponents of the plan of annexation, It would be an act of munificence and generosity whereby the Republic of the United States would risk nothing, since It would simply cover with its aegis an inoffensive and friendly people, whom Providence designed to be its natural ally, and all the sons of this people would greet with joy the day when their powerful sister should stretch out [her?] hand to save them from the dangers which encompass them, which dangers would instantly disappear in view of such a diplomatic act, If your Excellency, seeing that the fate of a people with pretensions is at stake, shall feel, as [I?] hope will be the case, a sympathetic impulse to do them justice, and shall make an effort to secure for them the protection of the Republic of the United States, you will have the immense satisfaction of having saved the future of a people of the world discovered by Columbus, without having assured any responsibility,

records.headline: The Worcester Daily Press prints an allegation in a Dominican statement
records.summary_en: The Worcester Daily Press prints an allegation in a Dominican statement that Hayti commenced a secret war using Dominican malcontents to crush the people's liberties. According to the speaker, Hayti encouraged rebellion by sheltering and arming insurgents on Haytian soil, sending them to the frontier, and assigning Haytian regular troops to aid their movements and protect their flight, thereby draining Dominican resources despite battlefield victories. To render their future more secure, the Dominican people manifested a unanimous desire for annexation to the United States, which failed and left the country amid difficulties and foreign jealousy. The statement adds that the agreement made by the Samaná Bay Company gave the finishing stroke to this situation.
records.summary_es: El Worcester Daily Press publica una declaración dominicana que alega que Haití inició una guerra secreta utilizando a descontentos dominicanos para aplastar las libertades del pueblo. Según el declarante, Haití fomentó la rebelión dando asilo y armas a los insurgentes en suelo haitiano, enviándolos a la frontera y asignando tropas regulares haitianas para apoyar sus movimientos y proteger su huida, agotando así los recursos dominicanos a pesar de las victorias en el campo de batalla. Para asegurar su futuro, el pueblo dominicano manifestó un deseo unánime de anexión a los Estados Unidos, plan que fracasó y dejó al país en medio de dificultades y recelos extranjeros. La declaración añade que el acuerdo realizado por la Samaná Bay Company dio el golpe final a esta situación.

records.headline: Baez proposes to President Grant to establish a protectorate over Santo
records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported that Mr. Báez proposed that President Grant establish a U.S. protectorate over Santo Domingo to guard against attacks and influences from Hayti, having exhausted other resources after the failure of annexation and the Samana Bay enterprise. Báez also forwarded a disavowed treaty between Hayti and Santo Domingo containing a clause against alienating territory to foreign powers, attempting to provoke national jealousy regarding European machinations. President Grant laid the communication before Congress without making any recommendations, and the scheme was deemed unlikely to receive favor from the National Legislature.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* informó que el Sr. Báez propuso al presidente Grant erigir un protectorado estadounidense sobre Santo Domingo para repeler las agresiones e influencias procedentes de Haití, habiendo agotado todos sus recursos tras frustrarse la anexión y la empresa de la Samaná Bay Company. Báez remitió asimismo un desautorizado convenio entre Haití y Santo Domingo provisto de una cláusula prohibitiva de toda cesión territorial a potencias foráneas, en una tentativa de azuzar los celos geopolíticos frente a maquinaciones europeas. El presidente Grant dio traslado de dicha comunicación al Congreso sin formular recomendación alguna, juzgándose improbable que el parlamento dispensase una acogida favorable al proyecto.

records.headline: An editorial in the New York Herald mocks Baez's appeal to General Grant
records.summary_en: An editorial in the New York Herald mocks Baez's appeal to General Grant and criticizes the President for referring to the document in his Message to Congress. The paper dismisses reports of a contemplated Haytian war against St. Domingo or a Haytian-fostered civil war by Luperon or other Dominicans as a sheer bugbear, characterizing the Dominican insurgents as a dozen breechless ragamuffins. According to the editorial, the appeal is intended to bolster the exploded Samaná Bay scheme and company, give value to its stock, and put money into Baez's pocket. The Herald concludes that the Haytian Republic is the more respectable and vigorous of the two republics and calls Baez a mere political gambler whom the United States government should avoid.
records.summary_es: Un editorial del New York Herald se burla de la apelación de Báez al general Grant y critica al presidente por hacer referencia a dicho documento en su Mensaje al Congreso. El periódico descarta los informes sobre una guerra contemplada por Haití contra Santo Domingo o una guerra civil fomentada por Haití por parte de Luperón u otros dominicanos como un mero espantajo, calificando a los insurgentes dominicanos como una docena de harapientos. Según el editorial, la súplica pretende apuntalar el fracasado plan y compañía de la Bahía de Samaná, dar valor a sus acciones y poner dinero en el bolsillo de Báez. El Herald concluye que la República Haitiana es la más respetable y vigorosa de las dos repúblicas y tilda a Báez de mero jugador político con quien el gobierno estadounidense debería tener el menor trato posible.

The rest of the island is in revolution, though business remains uninterrupted except where provisional troops move. A letter from the American consul says Puerto Plata decided against Báez and his followers became despondent, while official documents state the government wants to fulfill the Samaná Bay Company treaty and guarantee the rights granted under it.

records.headline: The Samana Bay Company
records.summary_en: An officer of the Samana Bay Company stated that a revolution in Santo Domingo would not injuriously affect the company's possessions at Samana Bay. C.S. Pussalaigue, the accredited agent of the revolutionary party, assured company officers that the revolutionaries harbor no hostility and wish to aid in the country's development. Additionally, the company owns the Samana peninsula in fee simple and seeks to acquire possession of La Vega Real.
records.summary_es: Un directivo de la Samana Bay Company declaró que una revolución en Santo Domingo no afectaría perjudicialmente las posesiones de la compañía en la bahía de Samaná. C. S. Pussalaigue, agente acreditado del partido revolucionario, aseguró a los directivos de la empresa que los revolucionarios no albergan hostilidad alguna y desean colaborar en el desarrollo del país. Además, la compañía posee la península de Samaná en dominio pleno y procura adquirir la posesión de La Vega Real.

An officer of the Samana Bay Company was questioned yesterday by a reporter of THE TRIBUNE relative to the effect the revolution in Santo Domingo would have on its possessions at Samana Bay. He stated that he did not think it would have any injurious effects. C. S. Pussalaigue, the accredited agent of the revolutionary party, who recently came to this city, has called on the officers of the Company and assured them that there is no feeling of hostility felt toward the Samana Bay Company; on the contrary, they were going to aid by all legitimate means the development of the country. The Company have been backward in promoting immigration, although thousands had applied for passage; this was because the possessions of the Company were not yet in a condition to invite immigration. The Company own the peninsula of Samana in fee simple, but they are anxious to acquire [illegible] of La Vega Real, a beautiful valley about 12 miles in width by 75 in length, extending from the head of Samana Bay to Santiago. In consequence of the delay in learning that President Baez and the Santo Domingo Legislature had agreed to the terms proposed by the Commissioners who were sent down by the Samana Bay Company, the Company were not [illegible] in taking possession of their territory before March. records.headline: A director of the Samana Bay Company denied reports that the company had failed, saying it was never in so good a condition
records.summary_en: A director of the Samana Bay Company denied reports that the company had failed, saying it was never in so good a condition and that negotiations for a considerable loan had already been concluded in London. He said the new provisional government had sent a memorial promising to respect all the company's agreements with the Baez government up to November 25, that the United States government had merely leased the Levantados islands from the company for a coaling station without yet paying anything, and that the company's engineers had been hard at work surveying its lands.
records.summary_es: Un director de la Samana Bay Company negó los informes de que la compañía había quebrado, diciendo que nunca había estado en tan buena condición y que ya se habían concluido en Londres las negociaciones para un préstamo considerable. Dijo que el nuevo gobierno provisional había enviado un memorial prometiendo respetar todos los acuerdos de la compañía con el gobierno de Báez hasta el 25 de noviembre, que el gobierno de los Estados Unidos simplemente había arrendado a la compañía las islas Levantados para una estación carbonera sin haber pagado aún nada, y que los ingenieros de la compañía habían trabajado intensamente en el levantamiento de sus tierras.

records.headline: The Tribune reports that a Havana dispatch announcing the Santo Domingo revolution closed, with General Gonzalez elected
records.summary_en: The Tribune reports that a Havana dispatch announcing the Santo Domingo revolution closed, with General Gonzalez elected President, is thought to misread earlier news, and it denies that the revolutionary government would annul the Samana Bay Company's lease. C. B. Passallaigue, agent of the Provisional Government, told a reporter that no election had been held, since the revolution's object was free elections for the whole country once order was restored, and that he had brought documents guaranteeing the company all the rights and privileges of its contract with the Baez government.
records.summary_es: The Tribune informa que un despacho de La Habana que anunciaba cerrada la revolución de Santo Domingo, con el general González electo presidente, parece ser una mala interpretación de noticias anteriores, y niega que el gobierno revolucionario fuera a anular el arrendamiento de la Samana Bay Company. C. B. Passallaigue, agente del Gobierno Provisional, dijo a un reportero que no se había celebrado ninguna elección, ya que el objeto de la revolución eran elecciones libres para todo el país una vez restaurado el orden, y que había traído documentos que garantizaban a la compañía todos los derechos y privilegios de su contrato con el gobierno de Báez.

records.headline: Under the headline "The Black and Tan Republic," an editorial
records.summary_en: Under the headline "The Black and Tan Republic," an editorial paragraph in The New York Herald remarks sarcastically that its "friend and ally, the noble Baez," who had wanted to sell out his shaky claim to the St. Domingo territory, has arrived in St. Thomas after parting from his Dominican friends. Characterizing the people of the land of Samana as mercurial and fond of change, the paper states that they shipped out Baez, who was not clever enough to sell them out even though he was rogue enough to desire to do so, and whose faux pas cost him their estimation. The editorial adds facetiously that Baez will now have to apply to President Grant for a situation, suggesting that since Cushing withdrew from the Chief Justiceship, President Grant can now offer the post to Baez.
records.summary_es: Bajo el titular «The Black and Tan Republic», una nota editorial de The New York Herald comenta sarcásticamente que su «amigo y aliado, el noble Báez», quien había querido vender sus dudosos derechos sobre el territorio de Santo Domingo, ha llegado a Saint Thomas tras haberse despedido de sus amigos dominicanos. Calificando a los habitantes de la tierra de Samaná como un pueblo voluble y afecto a los cambios, el periódico afirma que embarcaron al pobre Báez, quien no fue lo bastante astuto para venderlos aunque sí lo bastante pícaro para desear hacerlo, y cuyo traspié le hizo perder la estimación de aquellos. El editorial añade en tono burlesco que Báez tendrá ahora que solicitar un puesto al presidente Grant, sugiriendo que, dado que Cushing se retiró de la presidencia de la Corte Suprema, el presidente Grant puede ahora ofrecérsela a Báez.

records.headline: In a dispatch dated St. Thomas, January 14, 1874, under the headline
records.summary_en: In a dispatch dated St. Thomas, January 14, 1874, under the headline "Particulars of the Executive Downfall of President Baez," The New York Herald reports the latest news from St. Domingo regarding the overthrow of President Baez. According to the account, General Villanueva started from Puerto Plata with a very small force and arrived at San Pedro with only 200 men, where he was met by General Salcedo with 2,000 Dominican government troops. Villanueva asked for and was granted a four-day armistice, during which 1,300 of the government troops deserted, prompting Salcedo to retire with his few remaining men to St. Domingo city to consult the President. Villanueva followed, gaining troops along the way, and upon arriving at San Carlos demanded the surrender of the city of St. Domingo, whereupon an agreement was drawn up and President Baez retired. Quoting Baez's reply to Villanueva's first demand, the report states that Baez declared that those rising against him were of his own party, with whom he had united to prevent the sale of the Republic to Haiti, and that rather than resist and risk bringing forward the Luperon-Cabral party, he preferred to be sacrificed himself and agreed to anything.
records.summary_es: En un despacho fechado en Saint Thomas el 14 de enero de 1874, bajo el titular «Detalles de la caída ejecutiva del presidente Báez», The New York Herald informa las últimas noticias de Santo Domingo sobre el derrocamiento del presidente Báez. Según el relato, el general Villanueva partió de Puerto Plata con una fuerza muy reducida y llegó a San Pedro con solo 200 hombres, donde le salió al encuentro el general Salcedo con 2,000 soldados del gobierno dominicano. Villanueva solicitó y obtuvo un armisticio de cuatro días, durante el cual desertaron 1,300 soldados del gobierno, lo que llevó a Salcedo a retirarse con los pocos hombres restantes a la ciudad de Santo Domingo para consultar al presidente. Villanueva lo siguió, sumando tropas en el camino, y al llegar a San Carlos exigió la rendición de la ciudad de Santo Domingo, tras lo cual se redactó un acuerdo y el presidente Báez se retiró. Citando la respuesta de Báez a la primera exigencia de Villanueva, el informe señala que Báez declaró que quienes se alzaban contra él pertenecían a su propio partido, con quienes se había unido para impedir la venta de la República a Haití, y que antes que resistir y arriesgarse a propiciar el ascenso del partido de Luperón y Cabral, prefería sacrificarse él mismo y aceptaba cualquier cosa.

records.headline: The New-York Tribune reports that Buenaventura Baez, the deposed
records.summary_en: The New-York Tribune reports that Buenaventura Baez, the deposed President of the Republic of Santo Domingo, arrived in New York from St. Thomas aboard the steamer South America on Thursday. Noting that it had already published a complete history of the events that led to his downfall and the progress of the revolution, the paper states that a Tribune reporter called on the ex-President at the Brevoort House yesterday to ascertain his views regarding the revolution and the condition and prospects of the Republic of Santo Domingo. The reporter describes General Baez as a man of short stature and slight figure, with regular and comely features framed by gray whiskers and a gray mustache, an alert air, and a brisk courtesy in his manners far removed from Spanish formality. According to the Tribune, Baez is fluent and emphatic in speech and shows an eager desire to put forward his own explanation of his career and recent loss of power, though the writer remarks that his defense has much wordiness and repetition and that his positive assertions do not always meet the precise point in question.
records.summary_es: El New-York Tribune informa que Buenaventura Báez, el depuesto presidente de la República de Santo Domingo, llegó a Nueva York procedente de Saint Thomas a bordo del vapor South America el jueves. Señalando que ya había publicado una historia completa de los acontecimientos que condujeron a su caída y del desarrollo de la revolución, el periódico indica que un reportero del Tribune visitó ayer al expresidente en la Brevoort House para conocer sus opiniones respecto a la revolución y a la situación y perspectivas de la República de Santo Domingo. El reportero describe al general Báez como un hombre de baja estatura y complexión más bien delgada, de facciones regulares y agradables enmarcadas por patillas y bigote grises, porte alerta y una cortesía viva en sus modales muy distante de la solemne formalidad española. Según el Tribune, Báez es fluido y enfático al hablar y muestra un vivo deseo de exponer su propia explicación de las circunstancias de su carrera y su reciente pérdida del poder, aunque el redactor observa que en su defensa abundan la verbosidad y la repetición y que sus rotundas afirmaciones no siempre responden al punto preciso en cuestión.

records.headline: The Tribune's interview with ex-President Baez carries his account of the revolution
records.summary_en: The Tribune's interview with ex-President Baez carries his account of the revolution that overthrew him: Gen. Gonzalez, he said, still lacked two years of the thirty-eight required of a candidate for the Presidency, yet was determined to grasp the chief power by means of a revolution, though he owed his standing to Baez, who had made him Collector at Puerto Plata and afterward Governor. The pretext chosen by the agitators, Baez said, was the alleged unconstitutionality and impropriety of the alienation of Samana Bay; and the strongest proof of their bad faith was that, after the outcry against him for the sale of Samana to a foreign company, on gaining power they sent an agent to the Samana Bay Company assuring it of their good will and their desire to confirm all the arrangements previously made, and to enter into any new ones of mutual advantage. Of the Puerto Plata manifesto of November 25, with its long list of charges and its many signatures — Batista, Du Rocher, Leyba and more — Baez said the most prominent names had been used without their bearers' consent, and that several had written to the Government disavowing all connection with the agitators: the window closes as 150 men march on Santiago.
records.summary_es: La entrevista del Tribune con el expresidente Báez trae su relato de la revolución que lo derrocó: el general González, dijo, aún carecía de dos años de los treinta y ocho requeridos a un candidato a la Presidencia, y sin embargo estaba decidido a apoderarse del poder supremo por medio de una revolución, aunque debía su posición a Báez, que lo había nombrado colector en Puerto Plata y después gobernador. El pretexto escogido por los agitadores, dijo Báez, fue la supuesta inconstitucionalidad e impropiedad de la enajenación de la bahía de Samaná; y la prueba más fuerte de su mala fe fue que, tras el clamor contra él por la venta de Samaná a una compañía extranjera, al llegar al poder enviaron un agente a la Compañía de la Bahía de Samaná asegurándole su buena voluntad y su deseo de confirmar todos los arreglos hechos anteriormente y de celebrar cualesquiera nuevos de mutua ventaja. Del manifiesto de Puerto Plata del 25 de noviembre, con su larga lista de cargos y sus muchas firmas —Batista, Du Rocher, Leyba y más—, Báez dijo que los nombres más prominentes habían sido usados sin el consentimiento de sus titulares, y que varios habían escrito al Gobierno desautorizando toda conexión con los agitadores: la ventana se cierra cuando 150 hombres marchan sobre Santiago.

records.headline: After the insurgent commander obtained a four-day armistice and President Baez had made his arrangements for leaving
records.summary_en: After the insurgent commander obtained a four-day armistice and President Baez had made his arrangements for leaving the country, Baez sent the Senate a message on January 2, 1874 laying down the presidency, recalling that he had been called in 1868 when paper money had brought bankruptcy and public credit had vanished. That same afternoon Baez left Santo Domingo for St. Thomas on the French war vessel Kersaint, declaring he was in no sense an exile, having left voluntarily, and that he was tired of office and wished to rest and consult physicians about his eyes.
records.summary_es: Después de que el comandante insurgente obtuviera una tregua de cuatro días y el presidente Báez hubiera hecho sus arreglos para salir del país, Báez envió al Senado un mensaje el 2 de enero de 1874 en el que renunciaba a la presidencia, recordando que había sido llamado en 1868 cuando el papel moneda había traído la bancarrota y el crédito público había desaparecido. Esa misma tarde Báez salió de Santo Domingo hacia Saint Thomas en el buque de guerra francés Kersaint, declarando que no era en ningún sentido un exiliado, pues había salido voluntariamente, y que estaba cansado del cargo y deseaba descansar y consultar a médicos sobre sus ojos.
records.passage: [illegible] and as President Baez had made all his arrangements for leaving the country, there was no [illegible] opposition to the revolutionary march through the country. On the 2d of January, [illegible], President Baez sent the following message to the Senate: BUENAVENTURA BAEZ, General of Division, Grand Custodian and President of the Dominican Republic. HONORABLE SENATORS: When in 1868 the country was prostrated by a succession of unfortunate events, I was called to administer its general interests, My aspiration to insure its salvation did not leave me the choice of retroceding from the task of using all means to open up to it a happier destiny. records.headline: Ex-President Baez denies he is an exile in a second Tribune interview
records.summary_en: Ex-President Baez denies he is an exile in a second Tribune interview window: he left Santo Domingo voluntarily, he said, and no sentence of banishment has been pronounced against him; he had grown somewhat tired of office, of its cares and responsibilities, and desired rest and an opportunity to recruit his health and to consult the best physicians about a threatening trouble of the eyes. Of projects of regaining office he desired to say nothing, and he was chary of speech about the new Government's prospects; he still regards the men now in power as his personal friends, though they have supplanted him, and declines to say anything against them, though he hinted that stirring news about the new Government might be expected soon. For himself, he had been called four times to the Presidency, each time from a foreign country. Asked how the change of rulers might affect the interests of the Samana Bay Company, Baez replied that there is no prospect of injury to it by the revolution — the party in power will be glad enough to receive the rent from that enterprise — and that the revolutionary leaders, once in a position to declare their real views, had sent a messenger to the Company to say that the charges against him for favoring that enterprise had been only pretext: the window closes mid-sentence.

En cuanto a él, había sido llamado cuatro veces a la Presidencia, cada vez desde un país extranjero. records.headline: The Herald visited ex-President Baez at the Brevoort House
records.summary_en: The Herald visited ex-President Baez at the Brevoort House, where he had arrived late on Thursday from Santo Domingo, and prints the interview under heads promising what the recent ruler says — the causes of his fall, his betrayal by friends, the doubtful stability of the provisional Government, the Samana Bay Company, and his errand off for Washington to lobby annexation. Baez, General of Division and lately President of the republic, is described as a man of nearly sixty, short and stoutish in build, with strongly marked, war-worn features, dressed in a plain suit of black without much display of jewelry. The bloodless revolution that ousted him, the statement begins, was the result of an election agitation among the progressive party which he had represented very successfully in the Presidency for the last six years; Baez was a candidate for re-election, and Generals Villanueva, Gonzalez and others, whom he had appointed to places of trust — the window closes as their part begins.
records.summary_es: El Herald visitó al expresidente Báez en el Brevoort House, adonde había llegado tarde el jueves desde Santo Domingo, y publica la entrevista bajo encabezados que prometen lo que dice el reciente gobernante: las causas de su caída, su traición por amigos, la dudosa estabilidad del Gobierno provisional, la Compañía de la Bahía de Samaná y su viaje a Washington para gestionar la anexión. Báez, general de división y hasta hace poco presidente de la república, es descrito como un hombre de casi sesenta años, bajo y algo corpulento, de facciones fuertemente marcadas y curtidas por la guerra, vestido con un traje negro sencillo sin mucha exhibición de joyas. La revolución sin sangre que lo derrocó, comienza la declaración, fue el resultado de una agitación electoral entre el partido progresista que él había representado con mucho éxito en la Presidencia durante los últimos seis años; Báez era candidato a la reelección, y los generales Villanueva, González y otros, a quienes había nombrado para puestos de confianza —la ventana se cierra cuando comienza su parte.

According to the article, General Báez expressed sympathy for the islanders' independence and noted that while St. Domingo harbored sympathies for Spain, Cubans living in St. Domingo opposed his government because he refused to violate neutrality laws by fitting out expeditions against Spain.

are only leased, at a specified rent, for a term of years. But if the present provisional government should succeed in establishing itself it will only be glad to receive the yearly rent of $150,000 which the Samana Bay Company are paying for the rights that they have acquired.
As to the probabilities of who may be called to the Presidential chair, General Baez thinks that Caceres has at present the best chance. He says that the new men in power dare not come before the people to ask their suffrages, for then there is no doubt he would be recalled at once.
Another cause of trouble to Baez was the opposition which he suffered from the Haytiens because of his friendship for the United States. In Hayti there is a law which prohibits white men from holding or becoming possessed of real estate, and the people of that black Republic think that if Americans once got a foothold on the lovely and fertile island of St. Domingo the colored race would go to the wall. Had Baez determined upon using force to maintain himself in power (which, he asserts, might easily have been done), the worst passions of the people belonging to both Republics would have been appealed to by such freebooters and bandits as Luperon, and a sanguinary war must have ensued. The Dominicans like foreigners, especially Americans; while the Haytiens abhor all white men, particularly those of the United States.
About the ability of the Samana Bay Company to comply with the conditions of their contract there appears to be no doubt. Last year the company paid up the yearly rent of $150,000 for which the bay and its dependencies are leased. This term the rent has not been delivered over because there was no stable or legitimate government to receive it.
General Baez remembers very well the project that was set on foot some years ago with the object of establishing a new Power, to be called the Confederation of the Antilles. records.summary_en: 'An illustrious exile': a sketch of Buenaventura Báez on his arrival in New York after his fourth banishment, recapitulating his presidencies, his resistance to Santana, his expulsions by Cabral, and his negotiations to annex the island to the United States.

Baez is a remarkable man in many respects, and is deserving of more than a passing notice. He is a mulatto, about [illegible] years of age, and was born in Hayti. He gained great influence in San Domingo on account of his talents and his wealth, and after the expulsion of [Jiminez?] from the presidency was called to fill that position. At the next election, however, Santana was chosen president, but Baez refused to surrender the reins of power into his hands, and for two years successfully resisted the installation of Santana, who, up to his election to the presidency, had been Baez's warmest personal friend. Exiled on the accession of Santana, in 1858, he did not allow his restless nature to repose, but continued his intrigues for control of the island. In [illegible] he again returned to the island, was elected president a third time, but was almost immediately expelled by Cabral, his life-long enemy. Three years subsequently he again landed on his native shores, was again proclaimed president, and has retained his hold on the position till last month, when another reverse of fortune compelled his abdication. records.headline: Ex-Senator Wade, president of the late Commission of Inquiry
records.summary_en: Ex-Senator Wade, president of the late Commission of Inquiry to San Domingo, Judge Burton, its secretary and Spanish interpreter, Frederick Douglass, Senator Cameron and Representative Orth called the night before at Willard's Hotel to pay their respects to ex-President Baez, the Ledger's Washington despatch of February 27 reports. The conversation was cordial and unrestrained, the ex-President expressing deep regret over the fate of the offer of the annexation of Dominica to the United States, as the interest and destiny of the two peoples are identical, and making dark forecasts for the island: the Haytiens, he said, under the lead of renegade Dominicans, are constantly harassing the Dominicans, murdering and robbing on the borders, while the island has always been coveted by the European powers. The Chronicle, as quoted here, remarks that the arrival in Washington of so many gentlemen connected with the San Domingo commission at the same moment as Baez may be quite significant, and possibly meant business.
records.summary_es: El exsenador Wade, presidente de la difunta Comisión de Investigación a Santo Domingo, el juez Burton, su secretario e intérprete de español, Frederick Douglass, el senador Cameron y el representante Orth acudieron la noche anterior al Hotel Willard a presentar sus respetos al expresidente Báez, informa el despacho de Washington del Ledger del 27 de febrero. La conversación fue cordial y sin reservas, expresando el expresidente su profundo pesar por la suerte de la oferta de anexión de Dominica a los Estados Unidos, pues el interés y el destino de ambos pueblos son idénticos, y haciendo sombríos pronósticos para la isla: los haitianos, dijo, bajo la dirección de dominicanos renegados, hostigan constantemente a los dominicanos, asesinando y robando en las fronteras, mientras la isla siempre ha sido codiciada por las potencias europeas. El Chronicle, tal como se le cita aquí, observa que la llegada a Washington de tantos caballeros vinculados con la comisión de Santo Domingo en el mismo momento que Báez puede ser bastante significativa, y posiblemente signifique negocios.

records.headline: A sworn statement accusing ex-President Baez, by an American citizen
records.summary_en: A sworn statement accusing ex-President Baez, by an American citizen whose name this window does not reach, is printed by the Herald in its opening charges: that during 1869 and 1870, while Baez was President of the Dominican Republic, the plaintiff was arrested at his residence at Barahona, in August 1869, by an armed force under Gen. Frederico Garcia on Baez's orders, and held upwards of five months on a charge of conspiracy with armed resistance to Baez's rule; that he was then tried by a court martial of Baez's officers, upon the testimony, the filing says, of mainly convicted felons, and sentenced to be shot; that Baez pardoned him of the offence, yet required him to depart forthwith from the republic, and thereafter detained and imprisoned him for six months more: the window closes as the third charge begins.

records.headline: The case of ex-President Baez of St. Domingo
records.summary_en: The case of ex-President Baez of St. Domingo was again up in Brooklyn on a motion to vacate the order of arrest issued by Judge Pratt. An affidavit submitted by his counsel states that the complainant Hatch was an active participant in an insurrection, was captured and sentenced to death, but that the sentence was commuted to exile as a favor to the United States Government, and Baez maintains that the capture and sentence were merely the proper exercise of his powers and duties as president of the republic and denies the jurisdiction of the court.
records.summary_es: El caso del expresidente Báez de Santo Domingo volvió a verse en Brooklyn en relación con una moción para anular la orden de arresto dictada por el juez Pratt. Una declaración jurada presentada por su abogado afirma que el demandante Hatch fue participante activo en una insurrección, fue capturado y condenado a muerte, pero que la sentencia fue conmutada por el exilio como un favor al gobierno de los Estados Unidos, y Báez sostiene que la captura y la sentencia fueron simplemente el ejercicio debido de sus facultades y deberes como presidente de la república y niega la jurisdicción del tribunal.

records.headline: The Tribune's editorial on the revocation of the Samana Bay Company's lease
records.summary_en: The Tribune's editorial on the revocation of the Samana Bay Company's lease calls it another semi-tropical bubble burst: with the expiration of the troubled official life of Baez, it says, began the real difficulties of the American company; the new Government was hostile and, it is alleged, under British influence — an assertion the Tribune itself warns will probably need examination. Provisional President Gonzalez, claiming that the company is delinquent in its dues, revokes the contract and annuls the lease; and the Tribune expects next to hear of the company as a claimant for damages, with a brief in the State Department.
records.summary_es: El editorial del Tribune sobre la revocación del arrendamiento de la Compañía de la Bahía de Samaná lo llama otra burbuja semitropical reventada: con la expiración de la atribulada vida oficial de Báez, dice, comenzaron las verdaderas dificultades de la compañía estadounidense; el nuevo Gobierno era hostil y, se alega, estaba bajo influencia británica —una afirmación que el propio Tribune advierte que probablemente necesitará examen. El presidente provisional González, alegando que la compañía está en mora en sus pagos, revoca el contrato y anula el arrendamiento; y el Tribune espera oír a continuación de la compañía como reclamante de daños, con un alegato en el Departamento de Estado.

records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported on April 7, 1874, that the return of ex-President Baez to power led to the release of Carlos and Felix Baez upon the intercession of the French Consul, while business remained stagnant and government obligations were offered at an 85 percent discount. Additionally, the announcement that the treaty between the Santo Domingo Government and the Samana Bay Company had been abrogated discouraged promoters and sympathizers, prompting returning Commissioners Capt. Samuels and Gov. Fabens to hold informal consultations with company director Paul N. Spofford and other members in New York.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* informó el 7 de abril de 1874 que el regreso al poder del expresidente Báez condujo a la liberación de Carlos y Félix Báez tras la intercesión del cónsul francés, mientras que el comercio permanecía paralizado y las obligaciones gubernamentales se ofrecían con un 85 por ciento de descuento. Además, el anuncio de la abrogación del tratado entre el gobierno de Santo Domingo y la Samana Bay Company desalentó a promotores y simpatizantes, lo que motivó a los comisionados retornados, el capitán Samuels y el gobernador Fabens, a sostener consultas informales en Nueva York con el director de la compañía Paul N. Spofford y otros miembros.
records.passage: the return of ex-President Baez to power. Upon the intercession of the French Consul in their behalf, Carlos and Felix Baez were subsequently released. Business was stagnant, owing to the unsettled condition of the country and the scarcity of money. The obligations of the Government, issued at par, were offered for sale at 85 per cent discount. THE ANNOUNCEMENT IN NEW-YORK. The announcement that the treaty negotiated between the Santo Domingo Government and the Samana Bay Company had been abrogated fell with discouraging effect upon the hopes of the promoters of and sympathizers with the scheme. Capt. Samuels and Gov. Fabens, the Commissioners appointed to investigate and negotiate with the Dominican authorities, were compelled to admit that the published advices were too true, but that they hoped that the Company in a short time would be able to remedy the apparently hopeless condition of affairs. Immediately upon their landing in this city they proceeded to the office of Paul N. Spofford, a director intimately connected with the commercial interests of the island and the Company, and the consignee of the Company's steamer Tybee. Some time was spent in consultation with Mr. Spofford and other directors of the Company. As the by-laws of the Company require three days' notice before a meeting, the discussion between the members was of an informal character. Very soon the news brought by the Tybee became generally known, and many inquiries were made by persons who called for information.

The representatives of the Samana Bay Company, however, had protested against the action of the Dominican Government, and he (Gov. Fabens), with Capt. Samuels, had returned to the North in order that they might lay the matter before their directors, and subsequently before the Government. Dr. Howe, with his wife, Mrs. Julia Ward Howe, would remain at Samana, acting as Acting Governor, to protect the interests of the Company. When the Commissioners left Santo Domingo the Government had dispatched a force to take possession of the Company’s property, and as the Tybee was getting under way the Dominican steamer was also on her way to Samana. Although these events caused a great deal of discussion in Santo Domingo, he did not deem it probable that any popular tumult would occur. Gov. Fabens further said that while he could not say precisely what action the Company would take, he thought it very probable that they would call upon the United States Government for protection of its citizens, and demand that the matter be referred to arbitration. The Company had leased the Island of Levantados in Samana Bay to the United States, as a coaling station, on such terms as the United States deemed proper and equitable.
Paul N. Spofford, another of the directors, said that he did not care to connect himself with the expression of any views as yet. The Samana Bay Company would have a meeting this week and discuss the situation. He understood that the abrogation of the treaty was largely due to British influence, backed by the promised support of the British Government, the loan and full equipment of a vessel of war and the loan of an amount amounting to several millions of dollars to the Dominican Government to be repaid when convenient, without interest. He did not believe, however, that the failure of the Hartmont (English) loan, which had been the cause of some diplomatic and other correspondence between the Dominican Government, was responsible for the abrogation of the treaty.
Another director said that the Dominican Government had some time since granted concessions to the Company, and another to the Samana Surveying Company. The Samana Bay Company had not absorbed the last-mentioned Companies, and any defaults of either of the last-mentioned Company would not vitiate its grants.

The United States mail steamship Tybee, Captain Delanoy, from St. Domingo 30th ult. at this port reports the following important intelligence:—
Soon after leaving Samana Bay the Tybee fell in with the Dominican man-of-war Capotillo, bound in.

BRITISH DIPLOMACY AND TREATY MAKING.
Mr. St. John, British Consul General at Port au Prince, had been on a tour of observation to Samana Bay in Her Majesty's ship Woodlark, where he spent several days in informing himself as to the great natural advantages of the position, and had afterwards visited St. Domingo with propositions from the Haytian government for a treaty between the two republics. Among the conditions of the proposed treaty, it is said, were the cession to Hayti of the disputed territory on the frontier and the annulment of the Samana Bay Convention, made with citizens of the United States. These conditions being admitted by the Dominican government, Hayti (or England) was to loan a considerable sum to St. Domingo, payable at convenience and without interest.
The discussion of this measure was causing great excitement throughout the island.

CONSTITUTIONAL DIFFICULTIES.
The President elect, Ignacio M. Gonzalez, who styles himself "General of the National Armies and Supreme Chief of the Republic," had not yet been installed in office, as the Convention called for the purpose of framing a new constitution was still unable to agree upon the articles thereof.

THE SAMANA BAY COMPANY IN A DIFFICULTY.
The Special Commission of the Samana Bay Company, composed of Dr. Samuel G. Howe, of Boston; Captain Samuels, of Dreadnaught celebrity, and Governor Fabens, of Samana, have not succeeded in obtaining an amicable settlement of the question pending between the government and the Company, including outstanding and overdue accounts against the government, and the provisional government has declared the Samana bay Convention null and void.

AN APPEAL TO WASHINGTON.
The Commissioners have protested against this summary act as arbitrary and illegal, and, on being instigated by British-Haytian influence, demanded an arbitration upon the matters in dispute according to the terms of the Convention. The company will, in the meantime, call upon the United States government for protection against any violent proceedings on the part of the Dominican authorities.
The inhabitants of Samana, most of whom are Americans or of American descent, were at first greatly incensed against the Gonzalez government on receipt of the news of the annulment of the lease, and declared their determination to resist any attempt at enforcing it. The Commissioners explained to them that such a course would retard and perhaps defeat a just and equitable settlement of the question, and enjoined upon them to deport themselves in a peaceable manner, to pay their taxes, and, if necessary, to pay them under protest.
The paper money of the Gonzalez government was being issued in large quantities, and was already at a discount of 50 per cent. Business was entirely suspended, and the prospect for trade was very poor.

WHAT GOVERNOR FABENS SAYS.
Governor Fabens—ex-President Baez is a warm friend of the United States, and is desirous to promote the annexation of St. Domingo to this country. Baez is the representative of American ideas and Gonzales is not, the latter being strongly imbued with Haytian-English proclivities. Now, with reference to what you ask about Baez and the news from St. Domingo, I cannot tell you, for I have, as you know, just landed from my trip.
REPORTER—Governor, do you find the Americans in your troubles, seeing that there is no established government in St. Domingo?
GOVERNOR FABENS—Well (musingly) I think the United States government ought to step in and aid, in answer to our appeal, and we rely upon it to protect our interests against any over-acts of the Dominican authorities.

The Proclamation Annulling the Contract.
IGNACIO MARIA GONZALEZ, General of the National Armies, &c.:—
Whereas, in conformity with article 10 of the contract for the lease of the peninsula and bay of Samana and its islets, made in the city of St. Domingo, on the 28th of December, 1872, between the Minister of the Interior and Police and Foreign Relations, Citizens Manuel Maria Gautier and Messrs. Samuel Samuels, T. Scott Stewart and Burton S. Harrison, Commissioners of the Company styled "The Samana Bay Company," and by decree dated 19th February, 1873, of the Dominican Executive is called the "Samana Bay Company of St. Domingo," it was stipulated and decreed that the amount of rent fixed at $150,000 annually should be paid each year in advance on the 1st day of January;
Whereas, according to article 11 of the aforesaid contract, the non-payment of the annual rent at the time fixed upon, and, in case of war or other circumstance of force majeure, finally proven one month after that date at furthest, incurs the rescinding of the Convention, it being so expressly stipulated;
Whereas, when the provisional government, under date of 2d of December, 1873, ordered the withholding of the annual payment due on the 1st January of the present year, because, in virtue of the proclamation of the 25th of November previous, it had ignored the authority of General Baez, it did so solely with the object of avoiding future difficulties with the company if it should pay the late administration;
Whereas, in the official notice that it gave to the company, on the above mentioned date of 2d December, the Provisional government assured the company that it would respect the Samana Bay Company convention so far as it should be in the interest of the country and the conditions that were being fulfilled;
Whereas the company, through its Vice President, Mr. Paul Spofford, under date of 13th January of the present year, advises the Minister of Foreign Relations that the annual payment has been withheld, thus conforming to the order of the said Minister, while at the same time he states that he is awaiting official communications upon the subject;
Whereas, in virtue of the advice to which the preceding paragraph refers, the Treasury Department, by resolution of the government and by order of the Secretary of the Treasury, drew in favor of several merchants of the capital and the Minister of Foreign Affairs and Finance drafts for the sum of $147,224.14, on account of the rent due since the 1st of last January, the said drafts being presented for acceptance, and the company, in the meantime, told the government that they would not be accepted;
Whereas at the time the government drew against the company it gave it official notice of its establishment in this capital, and through the Minister of Foreign Affairs and Finance granted the company a prolongation, responding to the annual rental due, the reasons which until then it might have had for withholding the payment;
Whereas the non-payment of the amount said in advance is a sufficient cause for declaring the convention rescinded, as stipulated in the eleventh clause of the same, there being no cause on the part of the company for its inability to withhold the payment at the time mentioned;
Whereas the propositions that, verbally and in writing, have been made to the government on the 21st, 23d and 24th of the present month by the Commissioners, Samuel Samuels and Samuel G. Howe, in the name of the company, tending to modify the contract, grant extensions for the payment of the rent and to reduce the amount of said rent, are not and cannot be accepted by the government, since they would impose upon the nation a responsibility from which it could not release itself;
Whereas the Dominican government, in virtue of the communication of the 10th of January, signed by the Vice President of the company, and of the perfect right that it has as a depositor to the rent due, ought to consider said rent paid, and as such it was accepted by the government when it drew against the company, which reason it drew a portion for the amount of $147,224, and the drafts having been presented for non-acceptance, costs and damages are due, apart from the liquidation of the respective accounts of reclamation;
Whereas the company called the "Samana Bay Company of St. Domingo" has enjoyed the advantages of the lease of said bay, peninsula and keys for the time elapsed since the last payment, it is not allowed, up until the date of this decree, making use of the benefits which said lease may have produced;
Whereas, according to the terms of the mentioned eleventh clause of the convention, the right is reserved to the Dominican government of declaring null or rescinding the contract whenever the company fails to make the payment of the rent;
Whereas the government, after having taken into account the opinion of the Council of the Secretaries of State and the Council of the Government, has decreed and does hereby decree:—
ARTICLE 1.—The convention made in this city, under date of 28th of December, 1872, between the Dominican government and the company entitled the "Samana Bay Company of St. Domingo," for the lease of the peninsula and bay of Samana and of the islands and quays in those waters, is and is hereby declared from this date, in virtue of the non-fulfillment of its conditions in all its parts and null and of no value nor effect.
ART. 2. The Peninsula and Bay of Samana and the islands and keys of its waters will again from this date, as before the celebration of the Convention of the 28th of December, 1872, be ruled by the Dominican laws and authorities in the same form and manner as the provinces and districts of the Republic and islands adjacent to its territory.
ART. 3. The company will make good the amount of the account of damages incurred through the bills protested through its fault, and what concessions to the portion of the rent due since the first of January up to the date of this decree for the time that it has had the control of the said bay, peninsula and keys, until the same date.
ART. 4. The respective departments charged with the direction of the different branches of public administration will name the authorities that are to be installed in the peninsula and bay of Samana, and will take the necessary measures for the fulfillment of this decree.
Given in the National Palace of St. Domingo, the 25th of March, 1874, the 31st year of the Independence and the 11th of the Restoration.
(Signed) IGNACIO MARIA GONZALEZ.
Countersigned:—
The Minister of the Interior and Police, (Signed) P. G. ESPAILLAT.
The Minister of Foreign Relations, (Signed) J. DE LA C. ALFAU.
The Minister of Justice and Public Instruction, (Signed) T. C. DE CASTRO.
The Minister of Finance and Commerce, (Signed) J. M. COHEN.
The Minister of War and Marine, (Signed) M. M. CASTILLO.

THE DECREE AGAINST THE COMPANY.
The Samana Bay Company to all intents and purposes is dead. The investigation of the committee sent out from Washington on board the United States war vessel to report on the projected annexation of St. Domingo confirmed the idea. The people of this country may therefore congratulate themselves that the loss inflicted upon the community at large has not been larger than it is. It remains but to show below how the insolvent company has received its quietus, at the hands of the President elect of St. Domingo, Ignacio Gonzalez.
INTERVIEW WITH GOVERNOR FABENS.
Two members of the Samana Bay Commission returned to this city yesterday by the Tybee, and upon Governor Fabens, at Messrs. Spofford’s office, the following description of his visit was received.
Mr. Fabens was very courteous, but evidently very much chagrined at the unhappy fate of the enterprise. The following dialogue ensued:—
REPORTER—It is reported down town that the Samana Bay Company is dead; is that so?
GOVERNOR FABENS (hesitating)—Well, I hardly think we can say that; we have hopes of yet coming to an amicable arrangement with the Dominican government. I do not think the company can be called defunct; it is merely suffering under temporary embarrassment. When we receive proper recognition from the Dominican government we will pay over the $150,000 in gold due last 1st January. In addition to this we have claims upon that country for provisions furnished to the government, and, in addition to that, we have to receive payment for the regular performance of the mail service, &c. Our claims in the aggregate amount to about $50,000.
HIS INTERVIEW WITH THE PRESIDENT ELECT.
I had a long interview with Gonzalez, who I consider to be the head of the revolutionary party, and not the legitimate representative of the Dominican people. He has not taken the oath of office, and I therefore cannot consider him at present as the accepted Chief Magistrate. The proclamation of Gonzalez must therefore be taken for what it is worth. A new constitution, I may here remark, is being framed at St. Domingo City.
Dr. Howe has written a long letter to President Grant on the subject, while the United States Consul has also made a full report to Secretary of State Mr. Hamilton Fish, touching the occurrence.
WHERE THE SHOE PINCHES.
The publication of the decree of Gonzalez has a most prejudicial effect upon our company, for it prevents our placing on the commercial centres a loan for the company which we have had in contemplation. “Yes, sir,” said Mr. Fabens, with animation, “I think we have been very unfairly dealt with.”

records.summary_en: The steamship Tybee, from San Domingo on March 30, brings news that the British Consul-General of Port-au-Prince had toured Samana Bay and visited Santo Domingo with Haitian treaty proposals, said to include cession of the disputed frontier territory and annulment of the Samana Bay Convention in return for a large interest-free loan from Haiti or England. The same advices report that President-elect Gonzalez had not been installed because the constitutional convention could not agree, and that the Provisional Government has declared the Samana Bay Convention null and void, while the company's commissioners protested and demanded arbitration and United States protection.

records.summary_en: Based on the provided newspaper excerpt, the Provisional Government of Santo Domingo declared the Samana Bay Convention null and void after special commissioners of the Samana Bay Company failed to reach an amicable settlement. In response, the commissioners protested the act as arbitrary and illegal, demanded arbitration, and announced plans to request protection from the United States Government. Meanwhile, the island was experiencing great excitement over potential loans from Hayti or England, and the installation of President-elect González was delayed because a convention framing a new constitution had not yet agreed on all its articles.
records.summary_es: A partir del extracto periodístico facilitado, el Gobierno Provisional de Santo Domingo declaró nula y sin valor la convención de la bahía de Samaná tras el fracaso de los comisionados especiales de la Samana Bay Company en alcanzar un arreglo amistoso. En respuesta, los comisionados protestaron contra dicha medida por considerarla arbitraria e ilegal, exigieron arbitraje y anunciaron planes para solicitar la protección del Gobierno de los Estados Unidos. Entretanto, reinaba en la isla una gran agitación por posibles préstamos procedentes de Haití o Inglaterra, y la investidura del presidente electo González se hallaba demorada debido a que la convención encargada de redactar una nueva constitución aún no había acordado todos sus artículos.

records.headline: News from Santo Domingo reports the failure of the Samana Bay Company as complete, with its principal losers named
records.summary_en: News from Santo Domingo reports the failure of the Samana Bay Company as complete, with its principal losers named and the loss put at perhaps a quarter of a million dollars. The Provisional Government has declared the Samana Bay Convention null and void, after a proposed treaty with Haiti, said to include cession of disputed frontier territory and annulment of the convention, and the company's commissioners have protested and demanded arbitration.
records.summary_es: Noticias de Santo Domingo informan que el fracaso de la Compañía de la Bahía de Samaná es completo, nombran a sus principales perdedores y calculan la pérdida en quizá un cuarto de millón de dólares. El Gobierno Provisional ha declarado nula y sin efecto la Convención de la Bahía de Samaná, tras un tratado propuesto con Haití que, según se dice, incluía la cesión del territorio fronterizo en disputa y la anulación de la convención, y los comisionados de la compañía han protestado y exigido un arbitraje.
