Havana, January 26. - A rumor that Spain will sign a treaty with Santa Domingo at the end of this month assuming a protectorate over that island, causes great excitement in Santa Domingo and Hayti and serves to increase the popularity of President Baez. The rumor is somewhat strengthened by the appointment of new Spanish Consuls at several ports of the Dominican Republic. ATTEMPTED TRAIN ROBBERY. Repulsed by Plucky Express Messenger. Pueblo, (Col.,) January 28. - Last Saturday evening a west bound train on the Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railroad was boarded a few miles east of Dodge City by four men, who attempted to rob the express messenger. Two of the robbers jumped on the engine and directed the engineer and fireman to do as directed, while the other two boarded the express car. The express messenger, however, proved too plucky and repulsed them. He thinks he shot one of the robbers, as he was only three feet off and dropped when the messenger fired. The robbers escaped, but are hotly pursued by a competent party, and as the trail is plain there is little doubt of their capture. The robbers had previously bound and gagged the agent of a small station east of Dodge City and ransacked his safe. [illegible]

records.summary_en: The *Public Ledger* reported on August 3, 1878, that proponents of the annexation of St. Domingo failed to demonstrate that Dominicans were largely in favor of the project, which hindered their case in Congress and among the U.S. public. Additionally, the newspaper stated that the separate project of annexing Canada could never be accomplished without an earnest petition from Canadians and specific governmental guarantees.
records.summary_es: El *Public Ledger* consignó el 3 de agosto de 1878 que los partidarios de la anexión de Santo Domingo no consiguieron acreditar que los dominicanos respaldaran mayoritariamente la iniciativa, lo que entorpeció su acogida parlamentaria y el favor del público en los Estados Unidos. Declaró además la publicación que el proyecto independiente de incorporar el Canadá jamás fructificaría sin mediar una sincera petición del pueblo canadiense y expresas garantías constitucionales.
records.passage: matter of such minute consideration, that there is no need of trying to exhibit the moral or political principle of the transaction except under a microscope. The price we had to pay for it is big enough to see without common spectacles. If the authors of the project for annexing St. Domingo had been able to show that the Dominicans were largely in favor of it, they would have been able to make a much better show in Congress and among the people of the United States. The other project so often broached, of annexing Canada to the Union, a most undesirable thing, as we have always thought, can never be accomplished except on the earnest petition of the Canadians, and then only with guarantees that the Federal government shall not be bound by the restrictions of the old treaty between Great Britain and France, which maintains a wealthy and powerful hierarchy inside of a political authority, and leads to the chief disorders that are continually occurring in the Dominion.

records.full_text: Annexation of foreign territory to another nation ought never to take place except by a common agreement between the annexer and the annexed. The annexations to the United States have not been conducted on such principles, unfortunately for our principles. The monarchs of Spain and France sold us their possessions at the South without consulting their inhabitants, because they wanted to get rid of them, as they cost them more than they were worth. The people of Texas generally did desire annexation, but it would not have been accomplished when it was but for the determination of the Democratic party to procure more territory in which to extend slavery and create larger representation in the senate and house for the slave holding aristocracy. A bloody war had to be fought to secure this end, which might, at a later period, have been secured without war and with the deliberate and formal consent of Mexico as well as that of the people of Texas. When Alaska was annexed, there were no people to consult worth speaking of, and the advantage or disadvantage to the United States or the Alaskans is a matter of such minute consideration, that there is no need of trying to exhibit the moral or political principle of the transaction except under a microscope. The price we had to pay for it is big enough to see without common spectacles. If the authors of the project for annexing St. Domingo had been able to show that the Dominicans were largely in favor of it, they would have been able to make a much better show in congress and among the people of the United States. The other project so often broached, of annexing Canada to the Union--a most undesirable thing, as we have always thought--can never be accomplished except on the earnest petition of the Canadians, and then only with guarantees that the Federal government shall not be bound by the restrictions of the old treaty between Great Britain and France, which maintains a wealthy and powerful hierarchy inside of a political authority, and leads to the chief disorders that are continually occurring in the Dominion.

Two Dominican Conspirators Shot.

NEW YORK, Jan. 18.--A rumor prevailed throughout the city today to the effect that two well known Spanish subjects had been forcibly taken from a steamer in San Domingo, and cruelly put to death, and it created no little excitement among our Spanish and Cuban population. Senor H. Bellini, Dominican Consul in this city, when spoken to on the subject, said that General Valentine Perez and Manuel Cammino, both of whom were Dominicans and not Spanish subjects, had taken passage from Mayaguez, Porto Rico, for Porto Platte, San Domingo, on the Spanish steamer Manuel, after having combined with General Baez, ex-President of the San Domingo Republic, in a revolutionary movement for the overthrow of the existing government. Governor Lithgood, of Porto Platte, learned of the conspiracy, and when the vessel touched there demanded the men of her captain. They were delivered under protest, both claiming to be Spanish citizens, and were taken to the office of the Minister of War, when the form of trial was gone through, lasting about two hours. They were found guilty of conspiracy to overthrow the government and sentenced to be shot, and four hours after they left the vessel their bodies were riddled with bullets. They appealed for respite, but their judges were inexorable. General Perez was at one time Governor of Azua, San Domingo.

WEST INDIES.

Quiet in San Domingo--The Recent Rebellion in Hayti.
SAN DOMINGO, June 29.--Perfect tranquility prevails. The report that Congress authorized the conclusion of a treaty of commerce with the United States was inexact. Congress only directed the executive to propose to the United States free exchange of two specified products--sugar and tobacco--against any two products of the United States.
The crop of sugar in the Southern provinces this year is estimated at 10,000 hogsheads.

CAPE HAYTIEN, June 24.--It is rumored that the national assembly at Port au Prince closed owing to dissensions between Senators and Deputies. On the 20th General Teofile Parisien with his followers attacked and occupied the government house in Cape Haytien city. There was fighting all night. The government finally drove the rebels out of the city, three men being killed and wounded, and a large number of arrests made. Gen. Parisien escaped, and is said to have fled to Monte Christie on Dominican territory. General uneasiness prevails throughout the republic. Business is paralyzed and the harbor crowded with vessels waiting for cargoes, and produce comes in slowly owing to heavy rains.

ST. THOMAS, June 27.--President Guzman Blanco of Venezuela arrived at St. Nazaire on the 6th. It is rumored that he proposes to Holland the sale of the Island of Curacoa to Venezuela. Blanco before embarking at Martinique distributed 8,000 francs to the poor. The country is quiet.

THE WEST INDIES.

ST. DOMINGO PROPOSES FREE SUGAR AND TOBACCO TO THE UNITED STATES.
ST. DOMINGO CITY, June 19, Via HAVANA, July 3, 1879.
Perfect tranquillity prevails. The previous report that Congress had authorized the conclusion of a treaty of commerce with the United States was inexact. Congress has only directed the Executive to propose to the United States the free exchange of two specified products -sugar and tobacco-against any two products of the United States.
The cultivation of sugar in the southern provinces has greatly increased. The crop this year is estimated at 10,000 hogsheads, while two years ago it was scarcely as many quintals.

General Parisien escaped, and, it is said, has fled to Monte Christi, on Dominican territory.

records.summary_en: According to a dispatch from U.S. Consul Mr. Soutier at Cape Haytien, San Domingo is experiencing considerable distress because its tobacco crop cannot be sold, largely due to a new German tariff that closed that market. This loss costs Dominicans over a million dollars and the government $75,000 in duties, leading some planters to consider substituting sugar and coffee crops. Additionally, a private letter from Minister Resident and Consul General John M. Langston in Hayti reported that he has recovered from yellow fever and intends to leave for Washington soon, delayed only by an extensive revolution in the Haytien government.

La contingencia ocasiona pérdidas superiores al millón de pesos a los cosecheros y de 75.000 dólares al fisco en aduanas, incitando a varios hacendados a sustituir las vegas por cañaverales y cafetales. A Letter from the Dominican Consul.

TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN--Sir: For some time the press of this city has been giving reports respecting the trouble between Spain and San Domingo, and yesterday the Evening Telegram gave some private information received in this city, which sets forth that "should Spain bombard, as she threatens to do, the capital of San Domingo," the Dominican Government will issue letters of marque for vessels to prey on Spanish shipping.

I am not aware that Spain has made any direct threat to the Dominican Government, nor have I learned that any Spanish squadron is expected at San Domingo; but, regarding the letters of marque, the Dominican republic having no marine forces, its Constitution authorizes the Executive to issue letters of marque in case of war with any other nation.

I have not begun to buy arms and ammunition, as is reported; since the election and inauguration of Gen Cesáres Guillermo as President, his Government has been regularly buying arms and ammunition merely to equip the army.

The cause of the dispute between the two nations has been more or less misrepresented. The facts are simply these: About six months ago, on the arrival of the regular Spanish mail steamer at Porto Plata, correspondence was landed stating that there were on board two Dominican Generals, members of the Baez party, who, according to the correspondence, were going upon the Dominican frontier to start a revolution against the existing Government. The authorities of Porto Plata interviewed the Spanish Consul, asking him to give the necessary orders for the surrender of the said Generals, which the Captain did, following the instructions of his Consul, protesting at the same time against him and not against the Dominican Government. It is as well to say here that, in making his Custom House entry at Porto Plata, the Captain did not mention either in the bill of health or in the passenger list, the presence on board of the two Generals. As everybody knows, these were court martialed and shot.

My Government has done nothing against Spain, nor has it been the habit of the Dominican republic to disregard the law of nations. In all the international questions it has had, it always has behaved with moderation and dignity. In this present trouble with Spain (which my Government has in no way occasioned), President Guillermo and his Cabinet will sustain themselves at the height of their dignity.

The Dominican republic has been misrepresented, and, on account of our political commotions in this country and in Europe, it is generally believed the foreign residents there and their properties are not respected. Now, this is a great injustice; never has a foreigner suffered any inconvenience, or his property either, by any Government or revolutions; these are purely political. The country is now enjoying perfect tranquillity and foreigners are every day flowing into the republic, and with the franchises that the Government has given in favor of all agricultural establishments, large sugar, coffee and other plantations are rising up. The Government has asked of Congress authority to propose to the United States a treaty of reciprocity, and the Dominican press has been for some time, and is yet, discussing and elucidating that question. The Dominican republic has no doubt entered into an era of happiness and peace.

I hope you will have the kindness to insert this letter in your valuable paper and oblige
Your obedient servant, H. BILLINI,
Dominican Consul.
NEW YORK, Aug. 8.

records.full_text:
SPAIN AND ST. DOMINGO.

THE PRESENT TROUBLE BETWEEN THE TWO GOVERNMENTS--AN EXPLANATION BY THE DOMINICAN CONSUL GENERAL.
CONSULADO DE LA REPUBLICA DOMINICANA,
NEW YORK, August 8, 1879.
TO THE EDITOR OF THE HERALD:--
SIR--For some time the press of this city has been giving some reports respecting the trouble between Spain and St. Domingo, and yesterday some private information received in this city set forth that "should Spain bombard, as she threatens to do, the capital of St. Domingo the Dominican government will issue letters of marque for vessels to prey on Spanish shipping." I am not aware that Spain has made any direct threat to the Dominican government, nor have I learned that a Spanish squadron is expected at St. Domingo; but regarding the letters of marque, the Dominican Republic not having marine forces, its constitution authorizes the Executive to issue letters of marque in case of war with any foreign nation. I have not commenced to buy arms and ammunition, as has been reported. Since the election and inauguration of General Cesarea Guillermo as President his government has been regularly buying arms and ammunition merely to equip the army. The cause of the dispute between the two nations has been more or less misrepresented. The facts are simply these:--About six months ago, on the arrival of the regular Spanish mail steamer at Puerto Plata, information was received that there were on board two Dominican Generals members of the Baez party who were about to start a revolution on the Dominican frontier against the existing government. The authorities of Puerto Plata interviewed the Spanish Consul, asking him to give the necessary orders for the surrender of the said generals, which the captain of the steamer did, thus following the instructions of his Consul, protesting, at the same time, against the orders of the Consul, and not against the Dominican government. It is as well to state here that when making his custom house entry at Puerto Plata the captain did not mention, either in the bill of health or in the passenger list, the presence on board of the two generals. As everybody knows, they were courtmartialled and shot.

My government has done nothing against Spain, nor has it been the habit of the Dominican Republic to disregard the law of nations. In all international questions it always has behaved with moderation and dignity. In the present instance President Guillermo and his Cabinet will know how to maintain their dignity. Owing to our political commotions it is generally believed that foreign residents and their properties are not respected. This is, indeed, a great injustice. Never has a foreigner suffered any inconvenience, nor has his property been violated by any government or revolutions. The country is enjoying now perfect tranquillity, foreigners are settling down every day in the Republic, and with the franchises the government has given in favor of all agricultural establishments large sugar, coffee and other plantations are rising up. The government has asked authority of Congress to propose to the United States a treaty of reciprocity, and the Dominican press has been for some time and is yet discussing that question. The Dominican Republic has no doubt entered into an era of happiness and peace. I hope you will have the kindness to insert this letter in your valuable paper and oblige your obedient servant,
H. BILLINI, Dominican Consul.

records.full_text:
THE SCANDALS OF GRANTISM.

The San Domingo Job—Its Inception, Prosecution, and Final Failure.
I.

“If Gen. Grant, Gen. Babcock, and others high in office in Washington are so well satisfied with the real value of our prospects, and feel safe in lending their names and influence to carry them out, I cannot for the life of me see why you should hesitate. It was our intention to have sent 1,200 shares of the stock of the San Domingo Copper Company to you, as soon as Knapp shall have signed the certificates, to be distributed among officials of influence in Washington. But from the tone of your letters I suppose we shall have to do our business through some other party.”

These words, which seem like the idle boast of a confidence operator, are in reality the statement of a scandalous fact. They were written on the 21st of December, 1866, by Joseph W. Currier, then of New York, to a friend in Washington, who hesitated to embark in a scheme which looked to the raising of a million of dollars for the avowed purpose of mining copper in the island of San Domingo. Currier had been a quartermaster in the Union Army. He was speculative by nature, and circumstances made him impecunious. He was enthusiastic and credulous, but perhaps not deliberately dishonest. At this time, however, he was in the clutches of two unscrupulous knaves, who, years before, had gone from Massachusetts to the West Indies to teach the Dominicans tricks of which they never dreamt before. These were Joseph W. Fabens and William L. Cazneau. They were both natives of the Bay State. In 1863, Fabens, Cazneau, and Currier established the Great American West India Company, with an office at 5 Pine street, New York. Their rooms were fitted up in sumptuous style, and by the free use of printers’ ink they succeeded in disposing of their worthless stock to the amount of $160,000. Then they closed their doors and disappeared. But they came again in 1866, scattering far and wide their prospectus of the Great San Domingo Copper Company. They were accompanied this time by Buenaventura Baez, the deposed President of the Dominican Republic, who had been driven from the island and was ready for any sort of a job which promised him a good living without work. These conspirators explained that Cabral’s revolution had destroyed the Great American West India Company, but that the present corporation rested on a secure basis. To all doubting inquirers they whispered, “Gen. Grant is in it!” On the strength of his name they raised money from investors. Fabens took $30,000 and started for Africa to buy camels for the copper mines. He was accompanied by Baez. The 1,200 shares of stock were duly distributed among “officials of influence in Washington,” and $200,000 was raised by the sale of shares. Then the doors of the the office were closed again, and the adventurers sought safety in flight. They returned to San Domingo, where Baez reëstablished himself in the Presidency. There they remained till President Grant was inaugurated, and then they began once more their swindling operations in good earnest.

All this gratuitous service was rendered to Baez, against his enemy Cabral, that the annexation scheme might not fall through.

Babcock remained in San Domingo till August, when he returned to Washington, received further instructions from Grant, and departed almost immediately to complete his arrangements with Baez.

III.

Davis Hatch was a citizen of Connecticut who went to San Domingo in 1862 to act as agent of a New York company organized to work a salt mine in that island. The required concessions were made by the Spanish Government in 1864, but in 1865 Spain abandoned the country, and Baez, who set up as President, annulled the grants. But when Cabral overthrew and succeeded Baez, in 1866, he reconfirmed the concessions of Spain to the salt company. In 1868 Baez defeated Cabral, through an insurrection, and returned to power. In May, 1869, the city of Barahona, where Hatch resided, was deserted by Baez, and taken possession of by Cabral's forces. It was retaken in the following August by Baez, who thereupon caused the arrest of Hatch on the ground that he had sided with Cabral. He was condemned to death by a court martial, and was then pardoned by Baez on condition that he should immediately leave the island. He was quite willing to go, but was not permitted to do so. He was kept a close prisoner from the 29th of August, 1869, till the 15th of March, 1870, in flagrant violation of his rights as an American citizen. During the period of his unlawful imprisonment Babcock visited the island. J. IV.

On the fourth day of September, 1869, the bases of a treaty between the United States and the Dominican Republic were reduced to writing as agreed upon--so runs the official document--"by Gen. Orville E. Babcock, Aide-de-camp to His Excellency, Gen. Ulysses S. Grant, President of the United States of America, and his special agent to the Dominican Republic, and Mr. Manuel Maria Gautier," Secretary of State, &c., of the Dominican Republic.

The first article of this protocol will bear careful reading:

1. His Excellency, Gen. Grant, President of the United States, promises, privately, to use all his influence, in order that the idea of annexing the Dominican Republic to the United States, may acquire such a degree of popularity among members of Congress as will be necessary for its accomplishment; and he offers to make no communication to that body on the subject until he shall be certain that it will be approved by a majority. The acceptance of annexation will oblige the United States to pay the Dominican Republic the sum of $1,500,000 in coin, in order that the republic may, as a State, pay its public debt, which is estimated at the sum of $1,500,000 in coin; and the Dominican Republic, on its part, agrees to conform its Constitution to those of other States of the Union. In the event that the Dominican Republic debt should exceed $1,500,000 in coin, the excess shall be charged to the Dominican State.

In commenting on this in the Senate, Charles Sumner spoke as follows:

Here you see how this young officer, undertaking to represent the United States of America, entitles himself Aide-de-camp to His Excellency, Gen. Ulysses S. Grant, President of the United States of America, and his special agent to the Dominican Republic. Do you know any such officer in our Government as Aide-de-camp to his Excellency, the President of the United States? Does his name appear in the Constitution, in any statute, in the history of this republic anywhere? If it does, your information, sir, is much beyond mine. I have never before met any such instance. I believe this young officer stands alone in using this lofty designation. I believe still further that he stands alone in the history of free governments. I doubt whether you can find a diplomatic paper anywhere in which any person undertaking to represent his Government has entitled himself aide-de-camp to the chief of the State. The two duties are incompatible, according to all the experience of history. No aide-de-camp would be commissioned as a Commissioner, and the assumption of this exalted and exceptional character by this young officer shows at least his inexperience in diplomacy. However, he assumed it, and it doubtless produced a great effect with Baez, Cazneau, and Fabens, the three confederates.

By the other articles of this protocol (2) the price of Samana was fixed at $2,000,000. (3) Grant agreed to pay $150,000 down. (4) The United States Government agreed to protect Baez during the negotiations. (5) Absolute secrecy was enjoined. (6) Baez agreed to solicit his Senate to sell Samana.

With this basis for a treaty Babcock returned to Washington and left poor Hatch in prison.

When the success of the treaty was supposed to be assured, and not before, Davis Hatch was released. On the 13th of May, 1870, he addressed from the Island of St. Thomas a memorial to Congress claiming damages in the sum of $50,000, and asking the intervention of our Government to help him in obtaining it. A committee, consisting of James W. Nye, J. M. Howard, George H. Williams, Willard Warner, Carl Schurz, O. S. Ferry, and George Vickers, was appointed to inquire into the matter. Raymond H. Perry appeared before this committee on the 9th of June, and testified to some of the facts herein set forth. His evidence astonished the country and brought the San Domingo scheme into disrepute. Grant, Babcock, Baez, and the others found it necessary to postpone their operations.

VI.

In December, 1870, President Grant, in his annual message, asked the appointment of a commission to visit San Domingo. The Commission was accordingly appointed, and after spending nearly $100,000 of the public money, its members returned and made a glowing report to Congress, earnestly urging annexation. But in spite of the glowing picture which these enthusiasts painted, Perry's testimony was fresh in the public mind. Thereupon the conspirators resolved to destroy this objectionable witness.

So ended Grant's attempt to annex San Domingo to the United States.

A PEACEFUL ELECTION IN SAN DOMINGO.

HAVANA, July 6.--News from Puerto Plata, San Domingo, to June 22 has been received. Order prevailed during the elections for President of San Domingo. The Rev. Fernando Arturo Merino obtained a majority of the votes cast. The party of the "Blues" expected the realization of their political programme by the nomination of the Rev. Mr. Merino.

General Caman, the Haytian Commissioner, was in Puerto Plata with the object of arranging for the expulsion of Dominican political refugees from the Haytian frontiers, whence they continually infest the territory of San Domingo. The building of a railroad from Santiago to Samana was to be begun at an early day. The Republic was prospering.

THE KING IN PARIS.
LETTER FROM EUROPE--No. 60.

records.full_text:
SAN DOMINGO.

A PRONUNCIAMENTO BY GENERAL DON CESAREO GUILLERMO.
HAVANA, May 19.--The Herald's correspondent writes that the general of division in the national army and ex-president of the Dominican Republic, Don Cesareo Guillermo, has issued a revolutionary manifesto addressed to his fellow citizens. The document itself does not show where it was promulgated, and its date can only be presumed from the fact that it bears the impress of April, 1882. General Guillermo claims to have been urgently called upon by many men best known in the national political parties of the country to place himself at the head of the revolution, which he at once initiated in the Eastern province. In consequence of the evils imposed upon the nation through the dictatorship of Merino, which commenced in June, 1881, General Guillermo considers himself justified in the course he has taken, and also in deciding upon forming an expedition to open the campaign. The general refers back to the triumphs which placed the present government in power, and says that if it were possible for him to blot from the pages of history all the abominable acts which have happened since those triumphs, he would efface them at the cost of his life. The manifesto goes on in a strain of fierce denunciation against the obnoxious government which is the object of General Guillermo's wrath. He is not, however, explicit in naming the particular act of misgovernment that might justify revolution. He is no doubt a brave soldier, for his paper says for him: "All Dominicans! Here you have my sword and my life! Here I am, disposed to shed, even to the last drop, my blood, to be the first in danger and the last after victory! Therefore study my words! Long live all the parties regulated by law! Hurrah for national reconciliation!"

records.full_text:
A Suspended Law.

Since 1861 that statute of the United States known as the "Guano act" has been a dead letter, so far as the State Department is concerned. No American citizen, we believe, when he desired to avail himself of the benefit of its provisions, has ever been allowed to invoke them against unlawful interference with his business by any other power.

In order to encourage and build up an extensive and valuable domestic trade, Congress declared that whenever a citizen of the United States should discover guano on any derelict island or key, beyond the maritime jurisdiction of any other nation, he might raise the flag of the United States over it, and proceed to dig and ship the guano to this country under the laws of the coastwise trade. Such islands became by reason of such occupation appendages of the United States, subject to its jurisdiction, and entitled to its protection. They were registered in the Treasury Department, upon certain proofs of the facts, and the Treasury certificate was a conclusive and final adjudication in favor of the parties making the discovery, and adventuring their capital and labor in the business into which they were expressly invited by the public policy of the nation.

The "Guano act" was plain. Several times its provisions were submitted to the Attorney-General, and received each time the same interpretation, both as to the municipal law and the public law of the world. In a case with Venezuela it was diplomatically enforced. In a case with Hayti it was enforced by the navy, under instructions of the State Department. But Mr. SEWARD, for reasons of his own, chose to disregard it. American citizens had discovered a rich deposit of guano upon a barren and derelict islet lying in the high seas off the coast of San Domingo. They occupied it peacefully for seven months, had complied with all the conditions of the law, and established a large business. At the end of that time an armed Dominican vessel called, tore down the flag, and carried the men away prisoners. There never was a more flagrant insult to a nation, or a more indefensible outrage upon the rights of our private citizens. But Mr. SEWARD declined to seek any redress, and from that day to this there has been no instance in which the Guano act has been successfully invoked against a foreign aggressor.

Threatened Invasion of San Domingo.

ST. THOMAS, Feb. 4.—Gen. Guillermo, ex-President of San Domingo, with eleven other exiles from that republic, left here on the 29th ult. on board the British steamer Yucatan with the avowed purpose of organizing in Jamaica a formidable party to invade San Domingo and Hayti. It is reported that he has purchased the Victoria, a small steamer, which will form part of a fleet of four vessels. He is said to have in his possession letters of credit to the amount of $80,000. The Dominican Consul here has chartered the British schooner Lillie to convey to the Government of San Domingo intelligence of Gen. Guillermo’s designs.

This prelate has been for several years Nuncio in Brazil, where he went as successor of Monsignor Roncetti; the prelate who brought to Cardinal McCloskey his beretta, and who died while Nuncio at Munich.

WRITTEN FOR THE GAZETTE.
L'HISTOIRE DES HEROS D'AFRIQUE.
Dans L'Ile de Ste. Domingo.
BY PAUL GASTON.
No V.—Toussaint L'Ouverture.
Vincent Beaupre, in his celebrated "Reflections on the Tragical Drama of the Dominican Insurrection," says: "Toussaint L'Ouverture, at the head of an army, was the embodiment of the most active and the most indefatigable man that it is possible for the human mind to form a conception. His great sobriety, combined with the faculty which none but himself possessed, of never reposing, the facility with which he resumes the affairs of the cabinet after the most disastrous reverses on the field of battle, render him so eminently superior to those around him that their respect and submission were carried to the verge of fascination, and it is certain that no man of modern times ever possessed such an influence over a body of men as Toussaint exercised over his brethren of Ste. Domingo."
Such is the testimony of an enemy who had lost all his earthly possessions through the instrumentality of our hero.
Toussaint was of a prepossessing and commanding appearance, of medium stature, but of an iron frame. His dignified, calm and unaffected features, broad and well developed forhead would under any circumstances, designate him as one born to rule. Endowed by nature with lofty qualities of mind, he owed his elevation to his own energies and devotion to the welfare of his unhappy race. Like most men of energetic temperament his habits were thoughtful. In speech he arrived at his meaning by the shortest methods. So profound and original were his opinions that they have been adopted by all the chiefs who survived him. His maxims are still the guidance of the rulers of Hayti. His thoughts were vigorous as well as copious, and whatever he could not express in his native "patois" appeared tame and insipid in the polished language of France, which he was compelled to employ in official business.
While at the height of power, Toussaint himself practiced an austere sobriety bordering on abstemiousness, though his subordinate officers were reveling in luxury. Veneration for his character was not confined to Ste. Domingo, but penetrated to the heart of Europe. In generous France his name, his fame and his incomparable virtues were often pronounced in the National Councils.

YELLOW FEVER ON A FRENCH WAR VESSEL.
HAMILTON, Ont., Nov. 11.—The French war steamer Le Chasseur, Captain E. Courrequelle, arrived here on October 24 from Port au Prince, Hayti. On October 9 she received on board a distressed merchant crew of eight men in a boat from St. Marcs. One of the men was ill, and died next day of yellow fever. The remainder were put ashore at Port au Prince, and the Chasseur came north to prevent the development of yellow fever. No sickness appeared. She left Bermuda on October 27 for Guadaloupe and Martinique.

records.headline: John Mercer Langston's arrival aboard the U. S. S. Galena is announced
records.summary_en: John Mercer Langston's arrival aboard the U. S. S. Galena is announced to the Globe by a correspondent: Langston, Minister Resident and Consul General to the Republic of Hayti and Charge d'Affaires to the Dominican Republic, was given a pleasant reception by the American citizens there, of which a fuller account is promised in another communication: it was a grand sight, he writes, to see America's greatest Negro leader and San Domingo's greatest Negro President, Ulises Heureaux, clasped hand in hand, as the representatives of their common country. The letter then holds Mr. Langston up as the central figure to whom the race must turn at this eventful epoch — a crisis in the nation's history, in which, it says, the tribunal that will sit at Chicago on the third of June next will pronounce its verdict, with the Republican party and the Negro himself sitting as judges.

La carta presenta luego al Sr. Langston como la figura central a la que la raza debe volverse en esta época trascendental —una crisis en la historia de la nación, en la que, dice, el tribunal que se reunirá en Chicago el 3 de junio próximo pronunciará su veredicto, con el partido Republicano y el propio negro sentados como jueces.

SANTO DOMINGO PASSES THE FREE TRADE BILL.
HAVANA, May 13.—The British mail steamer from St. Thomas, May 5, brings Santo Domingo dispatches to May 1. According to these, the bill establishing free trade with the United States has been passed by the Dominican Congress. Senor Galvan had been appointed Commissioner, and was to proceed to Washington on the 7th inst., for the purpose of making the final arrangements. It is again ascertained that negotiations are proceeding with Washington for the lease of Samana Bay. It is reported that the government will give the bondholders of the Samana Bay Company the first claim on the money part for the lease. Advices from Cape Hayti of April 24 say that the refugees of the British Consulate there have been pardoned. A change in the entire Haytien administration is anticipated.

The Thibodaux Sentinel, SATURDAY, JULY 5 1884.
TARIFF LEGISLATION BY THE PRESIDENT.
The ease with which the Hawaiian and Mexican reciprocity treaties have been carried through the Senate has given our State Department an entirely new field of activity. By acting in conjunction with New York interests, it can contrive a new reciprocity treaty at any time providing for the free admission of certain articles agreed upon. St. Domingo, which Grant tried to annex, has been pitched upon as the proper scene of the third experiment in executive tariff legislation. It is situated with especial reference to the conveniences demanded by the exigencies requiring more free admission. Just east of it lies Spanish Port Rico. The British Bahama Islands are north-west, and Jamaica west by north. Cuba is west-north-west, and the Central and South American coasts, the Lesser Antilles, and a great number of inlets belonging to the Nether land, Denmark, France, Spain and Great Britain, etc., are accessible.
This treaty, like the Mexican, is one sided in appearance. The list of articles to be admitted free into St. Domingo is so much longer than that of articles to be admitted free into the United States, that it seems as though the United States must have got the best of the bargain, and the Dominicans must have been asleep. But since we exported to St. Domingo only $1,179,200 worth of domestic merchandise during the fiscal year ended June 30, 1883, and since we can scarcely hope to build up very much of a market among 250,000 people, it is not a matter of great consequence, except to her treasury, whether we gain free entrance for a long list of our products or not.
But short as is the list of articles which we care to admit free from San Domingo, it contains sugar and molasses. The sugar is not to be above No. 16 Dutch standard—a fact to be explained by the necessities of our refiners, who need reciprocity treaties in abundance for the procurement of raw material, and need the exclusive possession of our home market for the sugars which are fit to put on table for use. THE TREATY WITH SPAIN.
This Government has more than once been called upon of late to take action in fulfillment of international obligation with Spain. Agitation in the Island of Cuba hostile to the Spanish crown having been fomented by persons abusing the sacred rights of hospitality which our territory affords, the officers of the Government have been instructed to exercise vigilance to prevent infractions of our neutrality laws at Key West and at other points near the Cuban coast. I am happy to say that in the only instance where those precautionary measures were successfully eluded, the offenders, when found in our territory, were subsequently tried and convicted.
The growing need of close relationship of intercourse and traffic between the Spanish Antilles and their natural market in the United States led to the adoption in January last of a commercial agreement looking to that end. This agreement has since been superseded by a more carefully framed and comprehensive convention, which I shall submit to the Senate for approval. It has been the aim of this negotiation to open such a favored reciprocal exchange of productions carried under the flag of either country as to make the intercourse between Cuba and Porto Rico and ourselves scarcely less intimate than the commercial movement between our domestic ports, and to insure a removal of the burdens on shipping in the Spanish Indies, of which masters have so often had cause to complain. The negotiation of this convention has, for a time, postponed the prosecution of certain claims of our citizens, which were declared to be without the jurisdiction of the Spanish-American Claims Commission, and which we therefore remitted to diplomatic channels for adjustment. The speedy settlement of these claims will now be urged by this Government.
Negotiations for a treaty of commercial reciprocity with the Dominican Republic have been successfully concluded, and the result will shortly be laid before the Senate.

The last session of the present Congress assembled on Monday last, and will remain in session until the 4th of March next, and then adjourn and give way to the new Congress elected on the 4th of November.
The first day was occupied with the reading of President Arthur's message, which presents nothing of any great importance. It is in the usual common-place style, as the following synopsis will show:
The President says nothing could more strikingly illustrate the temper of the American citizens, his love of order and his loyalty to law, than the quiet way the election excitement passed off. Nothing could more singularly demonstrate the strength and wisdom of our political institutions.
Eight years have passed since a controversy concerning the result of a National election sharply called the attention of Congress to the necessity of providing more precise and definite regulations for counting the Electoral vote.
Our relations with all foreign powers continue to be amicable.

Whitthorne Not a Cabinet Seeker.
WASHINGTON, Dec. 6.—"They say you are to be Secretary of the Navy," said a reporter to ex-Congressman Whitthorne, of Tennessee. "They don't know what they are talking about," he replied. "I ask for nothing except that we shall have a wise, economical and progressive Democratic administration. I firmly believe that we will have such an administration under President Cleveland, but personally I expect nothing."
Signing the Treaties.
WASHINGTON, Dec. 6.—The Hawaiian treaty was signed to-day by Secretary Frelinghuysen for the United States, and Mr. Carter representing the Hawaiian Government. The San Domingoan treaty has also been signed by the Dominican Minister.

THE ST. DOMINGO TREATY.
COMMERCIAL RECIPROCITY PROPOSED.
SCHEDULES OF TARIFF CHANGES—A LONG FREE LIST OF AMERICAN PRODUCTS.
A treaty aiming at the advancement of trade between this country and St. Domingo—entitled "A convention for commercial reciprocity between the United States of America and the Dominican Republic"—is now before the United States Senate, awaiting consideration, having been negotiated and signed at Washington, December 4, 1884, by Secretary Frelinghuysen and Manuel de J. Galvan, the Dominican Minister to this country. It consists, according to the full text printed in The New-York Herald, of twenty-eight articles, of which the first provides that the following named articles of Dominican production shall be admitted into the United States free from duty:
Animals alive of all kinds for breeding purposes; asphaltum, barley, beeswax; bones, shells and other animal remains, employed as fertilizers; cocoa, crude and manufactured; coffee; cotton, hemp, sisal, henequen and other vegetable textile fibres; dyewoods and dye-stuffs of all kinds; eggs; esparto and other grasses, and pulp of, for the manufacture of paper; fish, fresh, dried, salted or smoked; fruits, vegetables and nuts, edible, of all kinds; hides and skins, undressed, whether dried, salted or pickled; hide ropes; honey, in comb or strained; India rubber and gutta percha, crude, and the milk of the same; indigo; leather, old scrap; meat, fresh, whether beef or mutton; minerals and ores; molasses and melado; palm or cocoanut oil; rock salt; sponges; Sugar, not above No. 16 Dutch standard, in color; tallow; tobacco, in leaf; wood and lumber of all kinds.

records.summary_en: Ben Perley Poore recounts how the ill feeling between President Grant and Senator Sumner grew out of a misunderstanding on the evening the San Domingo treaty was sent to the Senate: Sumner thought Grant wanted his help defending General Babcock's expenditures in Santo Domingo, while Grant meant the treaty for acquiring the Dominican Republic. When Babcock read the treaty to Sumner the next day, Sumner objected to the stipulation that Grant would use his influence to make annexation popular in Congress, and became the enemy of the whole scheme.

Cuando Babcock le leyó el tratado a Sumner al día siguiente, Sumner objetó la estipulación de que Grant usaría su influencia para hacer popular la anexión en el Congreso, y se convirtió en enemigo de todo el proyecto.

In the Senate sycophants who "carried water on both shoulders" and men who always delight in fomenting quarrels embittered Mr. Sumner against the President. One had served his country well in the camp, while the other had performed equally invaluable services in the Senate; one was a statesman, the other was a soldier. What did not appear to be wrong to the General the Senator regarded as criminal. Conscious of the value of his services in saving the Union, General Grant accepted with gratitude the voluntary offerings of grateful citizens; but Senator Sumner, who had seen too much of political life and of politicians knew too well that those who make gifts to public men expect favors in return, and that every public man should be inflexibly opposed to the reception of presents. GRANT AND SUMNER.
How the Ill-Feeling, Originating in a Misunderstanding, Was Intensified.
[Ben Perley Poore in the Boston Budget]
General Grant's difficulty with Mr. Sumner began when the President did not consult the Senator about the formation of his Cabinet. The breach was gradually widened, and in time the Senator became completely estranged from his old friend and associate in the Senate, Secretary Fish. When Mr. Motley was removed from the English mission he insisted upon regarding it as a personal insult, which he sought to repay by his opposition to the acquisition of San Domingo. General Grant endeavored to appease the offended Senator, and on the evening of the day on which the San Domingo treaty was sent to the Senate he called at Mr. Sumner's house.
General Grant found the Senator at his dinner table, with Colonel Forney and the writer, and was invited to take a seat with them. After some preliminary conversation General Grant began to talk about San Domingo, but he did not have the treaty or any memorandum of it with him. He dwelt especially upon the expenditures of General Babcock at San Domingo of a large sum taken from a secret service fund for promoting intercourse with the West India Islands, of which Mr. Seward, when Secretary of State, had prevailed on Representative Thad Stevens to have inserted in an appropriation bill during the war, and the President impressed Mr. Sumner with the idea that he feared an attack in Congress on the way much of that money had been spent.
Mr Sumner unquestionably thought that General Grant had come to enlist his services in defending the expenditure of General Babcock of $100,000 in cash and $50,000 in a light battery purchased at New York. The President meant, as Colonel Forney and the writer thought, the treaty for the acquisition of the Dominican Republic. The President and the Senator misunderstood each other. After a while General Grant promised to send General Babcock to call on the Senator the next day with copies of the papers and left. As Mr. Sumner escorted him to the door he told him that he was a Republican, and supported by a Republican administration, and that he should sustain the administration in its course if he possibly could after he had examined the papers. He meant the expenditure of Babcock, but the President meant the treaty.
The next morning General Babcock called on Senator Sumner with a copy of the treaty, which he began to read, but he had not gotten beyond the preamble, in which Babcock was styled "aid-de-camp of his Excellency, General U. S. Grant," before Mr. Sumner showed signs of disappointment. When General Babcock proceeded and read the stipulation that "His Excellency, General Grant, President of the United States, promises perfectly to use all his influence in order that the idea of annexing the Dominican Republic to the United States may acquire such a degree of popularity among the members of Congress as will be necessary for its accomplishment," Senator Sumner became the enemy of the whole scheme. He did not believe that the President of the United States should be made a lobbyist to bring about annexation by Congress.

In the senate sycophants who "carried water on both shoulders," and men who always delight in fomenting quarrels, embittered Mr. Sumner against the president. One had served his country well in the camp, while the other had performed equally invaluable services in the senate. One was a statesman, the other was a soldier. What did not appear to be wrong to the general, the senator regarded as criminal. Conscious of the value of his services in saving the union, Gen. Grant accepted with gratitude the voluntary offerings of grateful citizens, but Senator Sumner, who had seen too much of political life and of politicians, knew too well that those who make gifts to public men expect favors in return, and that every public man should be inflexibly opposed to the reception of presents. records.headline: Lucas Gibbs, Minister of Finance and Commerce of the Dominican Republic

Richard Alexander Gross serving as secretary, alongside several appointed vice-presidents and officials. Following his opening remarks, Mr. Gibbs introduced the evening's speaker, Hon. John Mercer Langston, an American citizen who expressed surprise before briefly addressing commercial relations and a reciprocal treaty.

records.headline: A speech printed by the Freeman urges the commercial treaty
records.summary_en: A speech printed by the Freeman urges the commercial treaty then pending between the Dominican Republic and the United States: San Domingo, Hayti, Venezuela and the South American republics, the speaker argues, should be made commercially great and prosperous without divesting them of their sovereignty or nationalities, so that the continent's commercial and diplomatic relations triumph as American against European competition. 'We want your products, and in exchange we want you to have ours exclusive of all others upon a reciprocal basis.' The country, he tells his hearers, is largely undeveloped and in its infancy — forests of valuable woods unexplored for want of transportation, immense virgin fields unapproachable for the same reason and for lack of capital and labor — and a new administration, just inaugurated, is about to construct its foreign policy and will be especially interested in such a measure: the window closes as the speaker recalls the steamboat's passage along the coast.

records.summary_en: According to the *St. Paul daily globe* of December 9, 1885, a commercial treaty signed with the Dominican Republic was subsequently withdrawn from the Senate for re-examination. The official concluded that entering into such engagements was inexpedient because the treaties required the United States to surrender large revenues on sugar for inadequate advantages, provided only illusory relief to consumers, risked raising embarrassing questions under favored-nation clauses, and diminished independent control over national revenues.

El mandatario concluyó que concertar tales estipulaciones resultaba improcedente, habida cuenta de que exigían a los Estados Unidos resignar cuantiosas rentas arancelarias sobre el azúcar a cambio de ventajas exiguas, brindaban un alivio ilusorio a los consumidores, arriesgaban suscitar enojosas querellas bajo las cláusulas de nación más favorecida y menoscababan el manejo soberano de los ingresos públicos.

On taking office I withdrew for re-examination the treaties signed with Spain and Santo Domingo, then pending before the senate. The result has been to satisfy me of the inexpediency of entering into engagements of this character not covering the entire tariff. These treaties contemplated the surrender, by the United States, of large revenues for inadequate considerations. Upon sugar alone duties were surrendered to an amount far exceeding all the advantages offered in exchange. Even were it intended to relieve our consumers, it was evident that, so long as the exemption but partially covered our importation, such relief would be illusory. To relinquish a revenue so essential seemed highly improvident at a time when new and large drains upon the treasury were contemplated. Moreover, embarrassing questions would have arisen under the favored nation clauses of treaties with other nations. As further objection it is evident that tariff regulation by treaty diminished that independent control over its own revenues which is essential for the safety and welfare of any government. records.headline: Recognizing the need of less obstructed traffic with Cuba and Porto
records.summary_en: The *Gloucester County Democrat* reported on December 10, 1885, that a commercial treaty had been signed by the Dominican republic following steps taken to establish less obstructed traffic with Cuba and Porto Rico. The newspaper also noted that subsequent overtures for a similar mutual extension of commercial intercourse were made by Her Britannic Majesty's government regarding British West Indian and South American dependencies, but these efforts yielded no result. Additionally, the excerpt urged Congress to recast appropriations for the diplomatic and consular service to ensure adequate salaries while returning notarial and official fees to the treasury.

Consignó asimismo la publicación que gestiones posteriores formuladas por el gobierno de Su Majestad Británica para ensanchar recíprocamente el comercio con las dependencias británicas antillanas y sudamericanas resultaron infructuosas. Por último, instó al Congreso a reformular el presupuesto del servicio diplomático y consular para dotarlo de haberes decorosos, restituyendo los derechos notariales y de cancillería al tesoro público.

THE DIPLOMATIC AND CONSULAR SERVICE. I earnestly urge that Congress recast the appropriations for the maintenance of the diplomatic and consular service on a footing commensurate with the importance of our national interests. At every post where a representative is necessary, the salary should be so graded as to permit him to live with comfort. With the assignment of ade[illegible] salaries, the so-called notarial extra-official fees, which our officers abroad are now permitted to treat as personal perquisites, should be done away with. Every act requiring the certification and seal of the officer should be taxable at schedule rates, and the fee therefore returned to the treasury. By restoring these revenues to the public use the consular service would be self-supporting, even with a liberal increase of the present low salaries. In further prevention of abuses a system of consular inspection should be instituted.

COMMERCIAL TREATIES.
The commercial relations of the United States with their immediate neighbors and with important areas of traffic near our shores suggest especially liberal intercourse between them and us. Following the treaty of 1883 with Mexico, which rested on the basis of a reciprocal exemption from customs duties, other similar treaties were initiated by my predecessor. Recognizing the need of less obstructed traffic with Cuba and Porto Rico, and met by the desire of Spain to succor languishing interest in the Antilles, steps were taken to attain these ends by a treaty of commerce. A similar treaty was afterward signed by the Dominican republic. Subsequently overtures were made by her Britannic Majesty's government for a like mutual extension of commercial intercourse with the British West Indian and South American dependencies; but without result.
On taking office, I withdrew for re-examination the treaties signed with Spain and Santo Domingo, then pending before the Senate. The result has been to satisfy me of the inexpediency of entering into engagements of this character not covering the entire traffic. These treaties contemplated the surrender by the United States of large revenues for inadequate considerations. Upon sugars alone duties were surrendered to an amount far exceeding all the advantages offered in exchange. Even had it intended to relieve our consumers, it was evident that so long as the exemption but partially covered our importation, such relief would be illusory. To relinquish a revenue so essential seemed highly objectionable at a time when new and large drains upon the treasury were contemplated. Moreover, embarrassed questions were sure to arise under the favored-nation clauses of treaties with other nations.
As a further objection, it is evident that small countries by treaty dependent lose that independent control over its own revenues which is essential for the safety and peace of any government. Emergency calling for an increase of taxation must be met as it arise, and no engagement with a foreign power should exist to hamper the action of the government.
By the fourth section of the shipping act, approved June 26, 1884, certain reductions of tonnage duties were made, and the same dues were made to apply to vessels entering the United States from any port in the West Indies, Mexico, Central America, and the isthmus as far as Aspinwall and Panama. This led to correspondence with Germany, Denmark, Portugal, and Sweden and Norway, each country claiming the favored-nation clause in their treaties with the United States, and claiming like modification in respect of vessels coming to the United States from their home ports. This government, however, holds that the privileges granted by the act are purely geographical, and apply to any vessel of any foreign power coming from any of the ports mentioned to this country and any port within the defined zone, and no warrant exists under the favored-nation clause for the extension of the same privileges in question to vessels sailing to this country from a port outside the limitation of the act.
Undoubtedly the relations of commerce with our near neighbors, whose territories form a part of the same system, should be guarded, and who find in our country a market for their products, should be given special and considerate treatment. It rests with the wisdom of Congress to say what action may increase facilities of intercourse and strengthen the bonds of a mutually profitable.

records.headline: The Sun surveys the Dominican presidential succession: the men
records.summary_en: The Sun surveys the Dominican presidential succession: the men spoken of for President include the ex-Minister of Finance, the ex-Vice-President, a general of Azua and a general of Puerto Plata, but the controlling elements are Gen. W. Heureux, commander-in-chief of the army, and Gen. Gregorio Luperon, Government delegate for the district of the Cibao, and which of the two is now more powerful is disputed. Luperon has been recognized as leader of the Blue party from the overthrow of the Baez administration and has been virtually the dictator of the republic's politics since; Heureux, his lieutenant and friend, has gradually increased in popularity and strength, and his prompt suppression of the recent Guillermo revolution, driving its leader to suicide, has helped place him where he stands. Now, for the first time, the two seem at cross purposes: Luperon is determined to dictate the nomination in the person of Gen. Pedro Bono, and if Bono declines, as at the last election, to select another; Heureux favors the ex-Minister of Finance, to whom Luperon is greatly opposed because of his affiliation with the Baez or Red party, and will oppose him even to war: the window closes as Heureux's own intentions begin.

Ahora, por primera vez, los dos parecen en desacuerdo: Luperón está decidido a dictar la nominación en la persona del general Pedro Bono, y si Bono declina, como en la última elección, a escoger a otro; Heureux favorece al exministro de Hacienda, a quien Luperón se opone fuertemente por su afiliación con el partido de Báez, o Rojo, y se le opondrá aunque sea hasta la guerra: la ventana se cierra cuando comienzan las intenciones del propio Heureux.

records.headline: The report describes the Dominican government's costly borrowing, including a recent loan of $150,000 made in Puerto Plata
records.summary_en: The report describes the Dominican government's costly borrowing, including a recent loan of $150,000 made in Puerto Plata at a stated two per cent a month, of which the government actually received far less, and the Puerto Plata syndicate's plan to issue $500,000 in paper currency. It says the country's only hopes of relief are a commercial treaty with the United States or American capital at a reasonable rate, and praises United States Consul H. C. C. Astwood for settling American claims, including a $63,000 indemnity for the widow of Piatt, an American carpenter shot by government troops.
records.summary_es: El informe describe los costosos préstamos del gobierno dominicano, incluido un préstamo reciente de $150,000 hecho en Puerto Plata a un declarado dos por ciento mensual, del que el gobierno en realidad recibió mucho menos, y el plan del sindicato de Puerto Plata de emitir $500,000 en papel moneda. Dice que las únicas esperanzas de alivio del país son un tratado comercial con los Estados Unidos o capital estadounidense a una tasa razonable, y elogia al cónsul de los Estados Unidos, H. C. C. Astwood, por resolver reclamaciones estadounidenses, incluida una indemnización de $63,000 para la viuda de Piatt, un carpintero estadounidense muerto a tiros por tropas del gobierno.

To deceive the public a recent loan was effected in Puerto Plata of $150,000 at, it was stated, two per cent. per month. The Government received from the syndicate $130,000, less seven per cent., and then agreed to pay two per cent. per month on the $150,000. so that it might appear to the public that only interest at that reduced rate was being paid. The Puerto Plata syndicate has become emboldened by its success, and is now planning to issue $500,000 in paper currency under its own guarantee, and proposes for the present making this the circulating medium of the country. This scheme has gone so far that it is understood that a well-known New York house has by this time got the order for the printing of the bills. records.headline: The Dominican Consulship.
records.summary_en: *The New York Freeman* reported on February 20, 1886, that Mr. Astwood's name was submitted for Presidential consideration for reappointment as United States Consul to San Domingo, whose affairs were described as unsettled with an anticipated upheaval due to the presidential succession. The newspaper also stated that recent reports of the assassination of President Salomon of Hayti were unfounded, praising him as a wise and discreet leader. Additionally, the excerpt criticized a note from the *Norfolk Virginian* regarding a statement made by a colored brother, Rev. Hooper Jolly, at a Methodist conference in Philadelphia.
records.summary_es: *The New York Freeman* informó el 20 de febrero de 1886 de que el pliego con la postulación del Sr. Astwood fue elevado a la consideración del presidente para su confirmación como cónsul de los Estados Unidos en Santo Domingo, demarcación cuyos asuntos se hallaban inestables y con presagios de conmociones por el relevo presidencial. Declaró asimismo el rotativo que las noticias sobre el asesinato del presidente Salomon de Haití carecían de fundamento, ponderándole como un gobernante previsor y juicioso. Fustigó asimismo una nota del *Norfolk Virginian* sobre una alocución pronunciada por un correligionario de color, el reverendo Hooper Jolly, en un congreso metodista en Filadelfia.

records.full_text:
The Hon. H. C. C. Astwood, United States Consul to San Domingo, arrived in New York last Monday, and proceeded immediately to Washington.
In the New York Sun of Tuesday, we find a communication from San Domingo City, the closing paragraph of which, bearing upon the Dominican Consulship, is here given:
H. C. C. Astwood, the United States Consul, who is an experienced consul, and the most eminent and very popular with the American residents here, has left for New York. Mr. Astwood's success in negotiating and settling American claims against the Dominican Government leads people here to hope that his efforts with his own people on behalf of his country here may prove fruitful.
Mr. Astwood succeeded in having the repudiated claims of Messrs. Remington of New York, Wanamaker & Brown of Philadelphia, and others, recognized. It was he who obtained an indemnity of $33,000 for the widow of Platt, the American carpenter, who was shot by the Government troops here in June last. The underwriters of New York, Philadelphia and Boston, in recognition of his services in breaking up and preventing numerous frauds attempted upon them, have together with Messrs. Clyde of New York and many others, petitioned the President, praying that he be continued in office. His knowledge of the language and people renders him almost indispensable to the Americans here. When the immense amount of American capital invested in sugar plantations and otherwise is considered, it is important that a suitable representative of the United States Government should be here.
It is very gratifying to note this high endorsement of Mr. Astwood's diplomatic labors. We have no doubt that President Cleveland will recognize in Mr. Astwood a capable officer of the diplomatic service, and grant the petition of those Americans who have business relations with San Domingo to reappoint Mr. Astwood.
We understand that Mr. Astwood is not anxious to retain the post, but allows his name to go before the President for consideration at the earnest solicitation of the parties above cited, who recognize in him a public servant whose place it would not be very easy to supply.
We trust the President will reappoint Mr. Astwood United States Consul to San Domingo.
The Sun's correspondent states that the affairs of San Domingo are in a very unsettled condition, and anticipates that there will be an upheavel consequent upon the Presidential succession.

records.headline: The Capital retells how Senator Sumner turned against the annexation
records.summary_en: The Capital retells how Senator Sumner turned against the annexation scheme: the stipulation was read aloud by an officer styled in the protocol 'aide-de-camp of His Excellency Gen. Ulysses S. Grant,' and when the reading reached the words by which President Grant promised 'perfectly to use all his influence in order that the idea of annexing the Dominican Republic to the United States may acquire such a degree of popularity among the members of Congress as will be necessary for its accomplishment,' Sumner showed signs of disapprobation — from that reading, the piece says, Sumner became the enemy of the whole scheme. The anecdote is printed inside a larger appeal for harmony between the President and Congress and for a united, forgiving Republican party.
records.summary_es: El Capital vuelve a contar cómo el senador Sumner se volvió contra el plan de anexión: la estipulación fue leída en voz alta por un oficial designado en el protocolo como «ayudante de campo de Su Excelencia el general Ulysses S. Grant», y cuando la lectura llegó a las palabras por las que el presidente Grant prometía «emplear perfectamente toda su influencia para que la idea de anexar la República Dominicana a los Estados Unidos adquiera el grado de popularidad entre los miembros del Congreso que será necesario para su realización», Sumner mostró señales de desaprobación; desde esa lectura, dice el artículo, Sumner se convirtió en enemigo de todo el plan. La anécdota viene impresa dentro de un llamamiento más amplio a la armonía entre el Presidente y el Congreso y a un Partido Republicano unido y dispuesto a perdonar.

Tuthill's Successor.
WASHINGTON CITY, May 22.—The president informed Congressmen Ward and Lawler, Thursday, that District Attorney Tuthill's successor would not be named for at least six weeks. He assured the two representatives that the new district attorney should be a resident of Chicago, and hoped that he might see his way clear to the appointment of their candidate, Mr. Jamieson. Mr. Ward says all the Illinois congressmen with the exception of Col. Townshend have agreed to sign a petition favoring Mr. Jamieson's appointment, and that this will be presented to the president by Col. Morrison.
Consul Recognized.
WASHINGTON CITY, May 22.—The president has recognized Carlos Lemale as consul of the Dominican republic at Chicago.

records.full_text:
SAN DOMINGO SUGAR.
Judge Coxe Decides that it Cannot be Brought In Free of Duty.
Judge Coxe of the United States Court decided yesterday in favor of the Government the suit of Joseph Netherclift & Co., one of a number of similar suits, in which San Domingo sugar importers seek to recover customs duties aggregating many hundred thousand dollars which their counsel argue was levied in violation of treaty obligations and of the tariff act of 1883. The treaty made with San Domingo in 1867 said that "no higher or other duties shall be imposed on the importations into the United States of any articles, the growth, produce, or manufacture of San Domingo, than are or shall be payable in like articles, the growth of any foreign country."
The treaty with Hawaii of 1876 made sugar free, and it was claimed that San Domingo sugar ought also to be free. Judge Wallace decided otherwise in the Bartram case, now before the Supreme Court. Congress, in 1883, declared that nothing in the Tariff act should "in any way change or impair the force or effect of any treaty between the United States and any other Government," and it was under this act that the present suits were brought.
Judge Coxe says that at the date of the act Congress found the Hawaiian treaty in full operation, a treaty which made the ports of the United States free to a group of Pacific Ocean islands, upon the express condition, however, that the island ports should be open to a much larger number of articles of United States growth and manufacture. No other similar treaty was in operation. San Domingo sugar had paid duty for sixteen years. The aim of the lawmakers was to have unchanged and unimpaired the existing state of things.
"It is hardly supposable," says the Judge, "that it was their purpose to make sweeping changes in the law, to open our ports without advantage or consideration to the industry of many countries, to destroy a vast source of revenue, and to encourage fraud by making the Dominican republic the dumping ground for the sugar and molasses of the West Indies."
District Attorney Walker and Assistant District Attorney Thomas Greenwood appeared for the Government.

AFFAIRS IN SAN DOMINGO.
The Revolution is Over and Gen. Herreux is Complete Master of the Situation.
The San Domingo revolution is over, and Gen. Herreux, for the Government, has again been victorious. The leaders of the revolution are all fugitives. Gens. Moza and Moncion, with some of the others, are in Fort aux Paix, Hayti, where they are held prisoners by the Haytian Government, and Gen. Pablo Villeneuve is in the south trying to make some conditions for surrender.
Herreux was too strong for them. Besides being better supplied with arms, money, and men, he had such a reputation as a fighter that it appears when he personally was in the field it was impossible to make the revolutionists stand their ground. In the beginning the revolutionists gained some important victories, and many thought that the issue was doubtful. With very few exceptions, the white and better class of the people were in sympathy with the Moza or revolutionary party. The latter part of last month and the beginning of this signaled a series of successes for the Government troops. While matters were at the worst for the Mozaists, a number of the young men in the city of Santo Domingo began securing arms and making arrangements for the seizing of the city. A boy, who was employed as messenger, and who was thoroughly in the confidence of the conspirators, was arrested by the authorities, who had some information or suspicion as to what was in progress. He was taken to the fort, a file of soldiers was told off, and he was informed that he had the alternative of confessing all that he knew or being shot in half an hour. He confessed, and that evening the Government authorities arrested about sixty young men who were implicated.

SAN DOMINGO'S TROUBLES OVER.
Gen. Herreux Victorious and the Leaders of the Revolution Fugitives.
NEW YORK, Oct. 26.—A Sun special from San Domingo under date of Oct. 10 says: The San Domingo revolution is over, and Gen. Herreux, for the government, has again been victorious. The leaders of the revolution are all fugitives. Gens. Moya and Moncion, with some of the others, are in Port de Paix, Hayti, where they are held prisoners by the Haytian government, and Gen. Pablo Villeneuve is in the south trying to make some conditions for surrender.
Herreux was too strong for them. Besides being better supplied with arms, money and men, he had such a reputation as a fighter that it appears that when he personally was in the field it was impossible to make the revolutionists stand their ground. In one of the former revolutions which he suppressed he marched seven of the leaders who had been taken prisoners through the streets of the capital out to the cemetery and had them shot, superintending the execution himself for fear of any mistake.

records.full_text: Gen. Herreux is a man about 40 years of age, a negro, with a slightly Jewish cast of features. It is said that he is a Haytian. His early life is clouded in obscurity, and until his bravery and intelligence were recognized by Gen. Luperon, no one had ever heard of him or his family. Since his first advancement he has gradually pushed himself on from one place to another until now he is despot or dictator, and holds absolute power over the government at Santo Domingo. Upon parade and state occasions he wears a very handsome uniform, very dazzling and grand, but when out fighting he wears the same kind of clothes as his commonest soldier, carries a rifle, and fights harder than the bravest of them.

records.headline: THE DOMINICAN REVOLUTION. CONSUL H. C. C. ASTWOOD’S ESTIMATE OF PRESIDENT CLEVELAND. He Thinks Blaine the Republican Giant—Cleveland Alone Can Stand against Him—Description of the Dominican Election and the Subsequent Revolution.
records.summary_en: Writing from Santo Domingo on December 3, 1886, United States Consul H. C. C. Astwood gives T. Thomas Fortune of The Freeman his reading of American politics—Cleveland's fairness to Black citizens, Blaine's strength for 1888—and then a full account of the Dominican election: Heureaux, the candidate of the masses, beat Casimiro N. de Moya by twenty thousand votes; Moya's party rose in arms under Benito Monción, and Heureaux's march through La Vega, Moca and Santiago ended the revolt. Astwood notes that the color line appeared in a Dominican contest for the first time.
records.summary_es: En carta desde Santo Domingo, el 3 de diciembre de 1886, el cónsul de los Estados Unidos H. C. C. Astwood ofrece a T. Thomas Fortune, de The Freeman, su lectura de la política estadounidense—la equidad de Cleveland hacia los ciudadanos negros, la fuerza de Blaine para 1888—y luego un relato completo de la elección dominicana: Heureaux, el candidato de las masas, venció a Casimiro N. de Moya por veinte mil votos; el partido de Moya se alzó en armas bajo Benito Monción, y la marcha de Heureaux por La Vega, Moca y Santiago puso fin a la revuelta. Astwood observa que la línea de color apareció por primera vez en una contienda dominicana.
