records.summary_en: According to the *Pittsburg dispatch* of January 3, 1889, French authorities in Hayti were reportedly divided between Legitime in the south and Hippolyte in the north, while a received cable stated that President Carnot gave an evasive reply to Dr. Auguste's request to recognize Hippolyte. Local merchants dismissed claims that France firmly backed Legitime, that the American squadron would have faced a French warship over the *Haytien Republic*, and that Legitime was imprisoning Americans or threatening to execute foreigners. Additionally, the Dominion Government's purchase of the British steamer *Red Rose* as a national man-of-war was widely reported as a sign of approaching war between San Domingo and Hayti due to vessel seizures, though Consul Julia of San Domingo noted that a $4,000,000 Holland loan had been made long before.
records.summary_es: A tenor del *Pittsburg dispatch* del 3 de enero de 1889, las autoridades francesas en Haití aparecían divididas entre Légitime en el sur e Hyppolite en el norte, en tanto un cable recibido daba cuenta de que el presidente Carnot dio una contestación evasiva a la petición del Dr. Auguste para que se reconociera a Hyppolite. Los hombres de negocios locales desestimaron las versiones de que Francia apoyara decididamente a Légitime, que la flotilla estadounidense se fuera a batir con un buque de guerra francés a causa del *Haytien Republic*, o que Légitime encarcelara a estadounidenses o amenazara con ajusticiar extranjeros. Asimismo, la compra por el gobierno dominicano del vapor británico *Red Rose* para transformarlo en buque de guerra fue juzgada señal de inminente guerra entre Santo Domingo y Haití por incidentes navales, si bien el cónsul de Santo Domingo Julia aclaró que un empréstito holandés de 4.000.000 de pesos se concertó mucho antes.

[SPECIAL TELEGRAM TO THE DISPATCH.]
NEW YORK, January 2.—A week ago last Saturday, Dr. Auguste sailed from this port for Paris. It was common report at the time, credited generally by merchants having business with Hayti, that he had gone there on a mission from Hippolyte, the leader of the revolutionary forces of the North of Hayti. The belief was strengthened by the knowledge that the French authorities in Hayti were astride the fence. In the South they were openly for Legitime. In the North they sided with Hippolyte.
It was reported yesterday that a cable had been received from Paris by a merchant of this city stating that Dr. Auguste had had an interview with President Carnot, of the French republic. Dr. Auguste asked that Hippolyte be recognized. President Carnot replied evasively. The cabled statements that France stands with Legitime through thick and thin, and that the American squadron would not have taken the Haytien Republic away without a fight had a French man-of-war been on the spot, are scouted by Haytian merchants in this city. France stands, they say, exactly as the United States stands.
The statements in an afternoon paper that Legitime was imprisoning Americans and had declared that he would shoot every foreigner who interfered with Haytian politics if he had to shoot 500, is not believed genuine by merchants in this city having relations with Hayti.
The purchase of the British tramp steamer Red Rose by the Dominion Government as a national man-of-war has been widely heralded as an indication of approaching war between San Domingo and Hayti, the result, it has been stated, of Haytian seizures of Dominican vessels in Dominican waters. Consul Julia, of San Domingo, talked last night, for the first time of the new Dominican navy. The Holland loan of $4,000,000, he said, was made long before any difficulty arose between North and South Hayti, and was made solely for the purpose of reorganizing the army and procuring a navy for ordinary purposes of national self-defense. The Dominican navy was to consist of four vessels, and an agent is now in Europe negotiating for their purchase. The first of them, and the only one so far purchased, was the Red Rose. She is now due in San Domingo. She will be called El Presidente.

SUICIDE OF THE PRESIDENT OF AN IRON FOUNDRY COMPANY IN ARLINGTON, N. J. Samuel Beckett, of the firm of Beckett McDowell, manufacturing machinists, No. 120 Liberty-st., and president of an iron foundry and machine company at Arlington, N. J., was found dead in his bed yesterday morning, at his house in Grand-st., in Arlington. Death had been caused by suffocation from gas. Mr. Beckett retired on Thursday night, and slept alone in a room adjoining one occupied by his wife and children. Nothing was heard of him during the night, At 7 a m. his wife went to the room and found it filled with gas. A rubber tube was found connected with the gas jet near the bed, and the jet was turned on full head. It was apparent that he had inhaled the gas by inserting the tube in his mouth. Dr. Exton, a local physician, was called in, and pronounced the man dead. He granted a certificate of burial. Mr. Beckett had been depressed in mind by business reverses. About eighteen months ago cellonite factory in Arlington blew up, and badly damaged surrounding property, including the works of the iron company. The cost of repairs drained the company's resources. The specialty of the company is mining

records.full_text:
MYSTERY ON THE MERCEDES.
CONSUL JULIEN SAYS SHE IS HIS.
MINISTER PRESTON CONTRADICTS HIM—IS SHE INTENDED FOR HYPPOLITE?
From information obtained yesterday from Minister Preston and the detectives employed by him it is fairly certain that the Mercedes is intended for the Hyppolite Navy. The money for her purchase was furnished by Jimines, Haustedt & Co., No. 5 South William-st.; she was purchased in the name of Carlos Julien, the Dominican Consul, and sailed from here under the Dominican flag. Mr. Jimines ran for Vice-President on the ticket with General Hyppolite recently; Oscar Hurtlinger, a member of the firm of Jimines, Haustedt & Co., is a nephew of Consul Julien, and another of the firm is his brother-in-law.
The first act of the firm of Jimines, Haustedt & Co. was to send a large consignment of arms and ammunition to Hyppolite; they also sent a large consignment on the steamer Saginaw through the favor of Consul Julien. President Herraux, of Santo Domingo, had got President Legitime's consent to land some arms and ammunition at Monte Christi, upon the representation that they were for Santo Domingo, and he so informed Consul Julien, and they were to be sent on the steamer Saginaw. Instead of the Santo Domingo consignment going, it is alleged that Jimines, Haustedt & Co. sent down a similar quantity for Hyppolite and Herraux's purchase did not go.
Minister Preston's detectives and General Contreras were in Boston when the Mercedes (then the Novelty) sailed from there on Thursday for New-York, and they had considerable information about her. When they traced her to this port on Friday it was too late to take any action to prevent her sailing, and they deferred appealing to Collector Magone until yesterday morning. But the boat sailed long before daylight, passing outside of Sandy Hook at 3:40. Her manifest at the Custom House shows that she had no freight, and carried 200 tons of coal and "no passengers." However, Mr. Hurtlinger sailed upon her, and under ordinary circumstances would have been a passenger. It was the impression that as soon as she got outside she would pull down the Dominican flag and hoist the Haytian colors, and would be intercepted by some vessel which would transfer guns to her. It is believed by Mr. Preston's detectives that she had some guns in her coal bunkers intended for the Madrid, which vessel is now being transformed into an armor-belted cruiser in the Erie Basin.
Carlos Julien, the Dominican consul, met a Tribune reporter with a happy smile yesterday, and was perfectly willing to unbosom himself regarding his part in the story of the mysterious Mercedes, otherwise known as the Novelty, now that she was under way for Samana. In fact, he seemed proud of it. He said that he was the owner of the Mercedes, and that he had bought her from a Boston firm about two weeks ago, but merely for a private speculation. He paid, he declared, $60,000 for her, and expects to make money by selling her. "You see," continued the consul, "they need vessels in the South, and they are willing to pay for them. I know that the Haytian Government is in great need of proper boats. I know that General Hyppolite needs them, and I know that General Legitime needs them, and whoever is the highest bidder shall have the Mercedes. That may be, for all I know, my own government. I sailed her under the Dominican flag in order to make the sale easier. I know nothing about the make-up of the crew. Should the speculation be profitable, however, I may repeat the operation, and send other vessels South. The Mercedes carried no arms of any kind, her cargo consisting of two hundred tons of coal."
Minister Preston contradicted Mr. Julien's statements. "That vessel," said he, "was bought with Haytian money. We have known this for two weeks. She will be used as a pirate and privateer in the Northern navy. Mr. Julien has no money to buy her with."
The superintendent of the Merritt Wrecking Company was indignant over the report that the Mercedes had taken guns on board while lying at Stapleton. He denounced it as utterly untrue, saying that she had taken no cargo on board, and that no lighter had been alongside of her when she was lying at the Merritt dock.

HIPPOLYTE'S VICTORY.
The News Confirmed by the Captain of a Blockade Runner.
LEGITIME THREE TIMES BEATEN.
Sixteen Prisoners Captured in the Engagement at Montrouis.
GEN. PIQUANT'S INGLORIOUS ESCAPE.
A Navy for Hippolyte Almost at His Hand, About as Good as New.
[SPECIAL TELEGRAM TO THE DISPATCH.]
NEW YORK, January 26.—The steamer Wensleydale, Captain Coull, arrived here from Port-de-Paix this evening. She took provisions shipped by Hugo Kainor & Co. to that "blockaded" Hatian port and sold out at a big profit. She brought logwood back for the Green Point Dye Works.
Captain Coull says he entered Port-de-Paix on the evening of the 8th, with all the lights burning and the Legitimist gunboat Belize in sight. When she whistled the Belize made off and disappeared. The town was hungry. The garrison was small and half clothed. The soldiers were armed chiefly with old-fashioned horse-pistols, and the artillery consisted of old cannon four or five feet long.
There were two passengers on the Wensleydale—B. DePendry, a French-Canadian schoolmaster, who is on his way home after teaching two years in Port-de-Paix, and Frederick Elie, who described himself as a merchant on business, but is believed to have come straight from Hippolyte, at Cape Haytien.
LATE NEWS CONFIRMED.
Mr. DePendry confirmed the late news that Hippolyte had beaten Legitime's forces in three successive engagements. They were at Las Cahobas, Mirobalais, and Achaies. In the Montrouis engagement, which was reported here from Port-au-Prince as a victory for the Legitimists, he says the Northern forces badly whipped General Piquant, and took as many as 16 prisoners. General Piquant fled, closely pursued, and made for the coast, where the Toussant l'Ouverture was lying. In such close quarters did he find himself that he didn't dare to wait for the Toussant's boat to get to him, but jumped into the ocean and swam to meet the boat, while his pursuers popped their pistols at him from the shore.
Two weeks ago the Toussant L'Ouverture attacked Cape Haytien again, and fired shells for a whole day. Fort Piccolet replied. Only one shell reached the town. Mr. DePendry said that Hippolyte was putting off an aggressive campaign until his new navy was ready for action. The plan then was to march the entire Northern army straight for Port-au-Prince, while the gunboats worked around to the harbor.
A NAVY ON THE SPOT.
Hippolyte will not have to wait for the arrival of the Madrid. He has a navy on the spot. Mr. DePendry says that a courier arrived at Cape Haytien recently, overland from Hippolyte's agent in San Domingo, with the news that President Hereaux has sold his new gunboat, El Presidente, to Hippolyte. The gunboat was the Red Rose, and was purchased recently in France by Hereaux. The news also came that the Mercedes had reached Samana and had been promptly sold to Hippolyte. This is the boat recently purchased on speculation by the Dominican Consul in this city.
Mr. DePendry said that the armament had been brought by the Ozama from New York, and was being put aboard the boats in Dominican waters. One of them was fitting up in Monte Cristi. The guns will be handled by American gunners. Ten of them, he said, arrived by the Ozama, with the guns. It will be remembered that the Ozama took nine Gatling guns and a long heavy box that was supposed to be a piece of heavier ordnance.
Minister Preston said a cable message had informed him that there had been a fire in Port-au-Prince. Two or three private houses were burned, the result of an oil explosion. If the fire was so small, it seems rather peculiar that Legitime should cable the news at $1 35 a word.

SHE WASN'T SUNK.
A Clyde Steamer Returns from a Haytien Cruise.
NEW YORK, Feb. 9.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—There is considerable stir among the merchants of the Haytien trade over the arrival of the Clyde steamship Ozama, which a Haytien gun boat was expected to send to the bottom, if found in Haytien waters. But the Ozama had not only been in Haytien waters, but she remained two days at Cape Haytien and took a full cargo of coffee. She had on board General Segundo Imbert, vice president of the republic of San Domingo. General Imbert did not leave San Domingo of his own accord. General Henriux, president of the republic, mildly suggested that his presence was not desired and placed $2,000 at his disposal, requesting him to make immediate arrangements for his departure. The vice president, so the story goes, took the hint and secured passage on the Ozama when she touched at Monte Cristo. When the steamer left General Henriux went on board a Dominican gunboat lying in the harbor and accompanied the Ozama some distance out to sea. The Haytien gunboat is said to have been watching the Ozama, but she made no hostile movement. The Ozama continued her way to Cape Haytien, where she arrived January 30. The American steel cruiser Atlanta, which had arrived that morning, was lying off Port Picolet and the Clyde steamer entered the port with colors flying.
Major Colwel, commander of the Ozama, said: "There was not the slightest pretense of a blockade and no Haytien gunboats were in sight. The Atlanta, on rounding to off the port, fired a salute of twenty-one guns and the fort responded with her thirty-two pounder. General Hippolyte, I was told, went on board the Atlanta and was received with the same honors tendered Legitime on his visit to Rear Admiral Luce on board the Galena at Port-au-Prince."
A dispatch was received at Cape Haytien from St. Marc January 31 which announced that a body of Legitime's troops, under General Belize, attempted to land from three gunboats at that place. The invaders were repulsed by the soldiers under General Montploint. Later reports, still unconfirmed at the time of the Ozama sailing, were that 700 of Legitime's troops landing at Saline had been captured by Montploint's men. This probably relates to the battle reported on Wednesday last. One of the Ozama's passengers from Turk's Island said General Alexis Nord has succeeded in reaching Cape Haytien and had assumed command of Hippolyte's forces. General Nord went from Fortune Island in a schooner which touched at Turk's Island and then proceeded to Monte Cristo, where Nord landed and found his way to the Cape.

Who Owns the Madrid?
NEW YORK, Feb. 16.—Consul Julia, of San Domingo, applied to the deputy collector of port for clearance papers for the steamer Madrid, which is supposed to have been purchased for Hippolyte. He presented two certificates, one showing that he represented the owner of the vessel and the other certifying that she was owned by the Dominican government. Minister Preston, of Hayti, appeared in the collector's office at this time and begged the deputy collector not to clear the vessel. He said the vessel was intended for Hippolyte, and it would be a violation of law to allow her to clear. The deputy collector declined to clear the Madrid until he had looked into the matter, and asked both gentlemen to call again. Collector Magone will probably give his decision at that time.

records.summary_en: The *New-York tribune* reported that authorities investigated a vessel, formerly named the *Madrid* and renamed the *Conserva*, suspected of being fitted for war against a government at peace with the United States by Haitian rebels and Dominican officials. Mr. de Chambrun argued that an alliance existed between Santo Domingo and the Haitian insurgents, while Acting Collector McClelland postponed the case due to defective certificates despite appeals from Consul Julia and others.
records.summary_es: El *New-York tribune* dio cuenta de las averiguaciones practicadas por las autoridades sobre un buque, denominado primitivamente *Madrid* y rebautizado *Conserva*, sospechoso de ser artillado para hacer la guerra contra un gobierno amigo de los Estados Unidos por cuenta de rebeldes haitianos y funcionarios dominicanos. El Sr. de Chambrun alegó la connivencia entre el gobierno de Santo Domingo y los sediciosos haitianos, en tanto el administrador interino de aduana McClelland dilató la resolución a causa de certificaciones anómalas, pese a las instancias del cónsul Julia y otros personeros.
records.passage: They maintained that it was evident that the vessel was intended for war purposes against a Government with which the United States is at peace; that the evidence in the Carondelet case proved that the vessel was bought with the money furnished by General Hyppolite, the leader of the Haytian rebels, and that the Dominican officials were aiding and abetting them, as proven by the transfer of the Madrid to Mr. Julia, the changing of her name to the Conserva, and the application to clear her from this port under the Dominican flag for Samana, where Consul Julia's brother is the Haytian Consul. The new point made by Mr. de Chambrun was that an alliance had been made between Santo Domingo and the Haytian insurgents. While the matter was being discussed before Acting Collector McClelland, the crowd of Haytians and Dominicans indulged in some loud and acrimonious talk, but the Acting Collector quieted this and then decided to postpone further consideration of the case until the defective certificates could be corrected. DETAINING THE MADRID.
A CRAFTY RUSE TO SLIP OUT TO SEA.
DOES SHE WANT TO OVERTAKE THE CARONDELET?
Santo Domingo and Hayti, or that portion of the island represented by the Legitime party, were on the verge of war in the Custom House yesterday, and not only did Deputy Collector Charles P. McClelland, who is acting Collector in the absence of Mr. Magone at Washington, act as peacemaker, but it required the full command of his keen observation and his legal ability to avoid making a mistake upon nice technicalities. His suspicions were awakened upon the presentation of a certificate, carefully and shrewdly written, to the effect that "Citizen Leoncio Julia, Dominican Consul at this port, representing his Government," had purchased the steamship Madrid. At the same time an application was made for a clearance of the vessel under her new name, the Conserva, "in command of Captain J. Henry Aukers and twenty-three of a crew, with 400 tons of coal for the use of the ship, and ballast and stores, for Samana, Santo Domingo.
The certificate was signed by Manuel de Jesus Galvan, jr., as "acting secretary" for the Dominican Consul, who also engaged Campbell & Gardiner as the brokers. To the brokers Senor Galvan gave another certificate of sale which was to the effect that the Madrid had been "transferred and sold to Citizen Leoncio Julia, Dominican Consul at this port, as the representative of his Government." Soon after the application for a clearance, Minister Preston with Charles A. de Chambrun, the counsel for the Haytian Legation at Washington for the last fifteen years, appeared to protest against giving the Madrid a clearance. This protest was supported by an affidavit of Counsel de Chambrun.
They maintained that it was evident that the vessel was intended for war purposes against a Government with which the United States is at peace; that the evidence in the Carondelet case proved that the vessel was bought with the money furnished by General Hyppolite, the leader of the Haytian rebels; and that the Dominican officials were aiding and abetting them as proven by the transfer of the Madrid to Mr. Julia, the changing of her name to the Conserva, and the application to clear her from this port under the Dominican flag for Samana, where Consul Julia's brother is the Haytian Consul. The new point made by Mr. de Chambrun was that an alliance had been made between Santo Domingo and the Haytian insurgents.
While the matter was being discussed before Acting Collector McClelland, the crowd of Haytians and Dominicans indulged in some loud and acrimonious talk, but the Acting Collector quieted this and then decided to postpone further consideration of the case until the defective certificates could be corrected. Then Consul Julia was sent for, but even his urgent appeal and flood of apologies, combined with those of his secretary, Captain Aukers and others could not induce Mr. McClelland to construe his interpretation of the language of the two certificates in the interest of the professed new owners of the vessel. The Madrid lay at Pier A, Erie Basin, last night, and was ready to sail at any moment. It was stated that there was a desire to get her away at once to go down the coast and meet the Carondelet in one of the inlets on the New-Jersey shore, and after receiving the guns and ammunition on board the latter to proceed to Samana and there be turned over to the Haytians. The Carondelet is then to put into Newport News, go to Samana and get a cargo of logwood and coffee and return to this port.

records.headline: The Tribune reports the clearance of the American steamer Madrid
records.summary_en: The Tribune reports the clearance of the American steamer Madrid, now the Dominican gunboat Conserva: Minister Preston received word from Acting Collector McClelland that the question of giving the vessel clearance had been referred to President Cleveland, and Consul L. Julia then appeared with his certificate, dated New York, February 15, 1889, that he had bought the American steamer Madrid, of New Orleans, of the burden of 560 58-100 tons, for account and on behalf of the Dominican Republic, that she had been legally transferred to him as his Government's representative, and that her name was changed to Conserva, sailing now under the Dominican flag. The United States Attorney advised that clearance could not be legally withheld, and it was granted at once; her cargo is 400 tons of coal, ballast and stores for ship's use, under Captain Ankers with a crew of twenty-three. The report adds that the steamer Carondelet, loaded with arms and ammunition from keelson to main deck, waits in an inlet along the coast to transfer her cargo to the Conserva, while word has been sent to Legitime's navy to watch for her coming to Samana.

Shipping circles downtown are interested about the sudden disappearance of General Contreras, the "military attache" of Legitime's Haytian Consulate in this city. He had heard, but could not say how true it was, that the General had shipped on the Madrid in the guise of a sailor; he had heard, also, that the doughty General had intentions of blowing up that vessel as soon as she was out to sea, and for that purpose had provided himself with a package of dynamite, intending to sink Hyppolite's warship if he had to sacrifice himself in the attempt.

Of this vessel, or of the rebellion at Santo Domingo City, they heard nothing said, the better class hesitating to speak their minds even to foreigners; the opinion in shipping circles is that the vessel was El Presidente, one of the vessels purchased by the Dominican officials ostensibly for the Dominican Government — but a report a few days old, that this vessel and others purchased here were recently driven out of Samana Bay because the Dominican Government would no longer continue its alliance with General Hyppolite, the leader of the Haytian insurrection, leads to the belief that the vessel which fired on the schooner was part of Hyppolite's navy.

records.full_text:
HAYTI AND DOMINGO.
Two Republics in Which the People Are Vastly Different.
FALSE IMPRESSIONS CORRECTED
About the Latter, Which Is an Inviting Field for Americans.
NO WARS FOR THE PAST TEN YEARS
BOSTON, July 26.—It is a singular fact, but it is nevertheless true, that the majority of Americans regard San Domingo and the Republic of Hayti as one and the same country. Hon. H. C. C. Astwood, United States Consul at San Domingo for the past eight years, was in town a day or two ago, and in response to a question put to him, said:
"Yes, I find that the major portion of the people of our country have a very erroneous impression of San Domingo. San Domingo, as you well know, was discovered by Columbus. Its original name was Hispaniola, or Little Spain. The island was afterward divided between the French and Spaniards. The easterly or Spanish portion was two-thirds of the island and was called Quigualla. It was discovered on a Sunday, and so Columbus christened it San Domingo, after the great saint. In the western or French section slavery was introduced, and hence the population was largely made up of Africans or blacks. Strange to say, slavery was not introduced to any great extent in the eastern end of the island. The native Caribs, or Indians, numbering several millions, were utilized by the Spaniards in working the gold mines, building a walled city and constructing immense fortifications, now to be seen in a perfect state of preservation at San Domingo City and many other portions of the republic. American tourists, including several from Boston, have said to me recently that it is exceedingly strange that San Domingo has remained in obscurity, with its splendid relics of antiquity, which, if generally known, would bring thousands of Americans who visit the West Indies. The population of the eastern portion, known as
THE DOMINICAN REPUBLIC,
are chiefly descendants of the Caribs and the Spaniards, making a race in appearance not unlike the Spaniards themselves. San Domingo is often taken for Hayti in speaking of the revolutionary tendencies of the latter country. This is a great mistake. The two peoples are distinct in every particular—in language, customs and their general deportment. The Dominican is kind, hospitable and very attentive to strangers. You may travel through the republic, unarmed or without protection, and the humblest and poorest man or woman will greet you kindly in his home and have you partake of whatever accommodation it affords, and will absolutely refuse any compensation that you may offer. This is the character of the whole people.
"In their revolutionary upheavals, which are fast disappearing, life and property are respected, and especially those of strangers. The cases are isolated where this has been otherwise, except by naturalized Cubans, Porto Ricans or persons of Spanish extraction, who interfere with the politics of the country and are maltreated, and then appeal to their Governments as having been outraged. These instances are often published without any explanation, to the great detriment of the country. The Spanish portion of the Dominican Republic is just as beautiful as nature could have made it. There is an immense area in almost virgin state, capable of supporting in luxury and ease quite 10,000,000 of people. The population is a sparse one, numbering not more than 400,000. It abounds in beautiful woods, such as mahogany, satin wood, fustic, etc. There are scarcely any roads or means of conveyance to have these valuable woods shipped to foreign countries."
Referring to the Government, Consul Astwood said it was a very liberal one. It is composed of a President, Vice President, Supreme Court and a National Congress made up of 12 districts. The President is invested with the power to appoint the following Cabinet officers: The Secretary of State and Interior Police, the Secretary of State of Foreign Relations, the Secretary of State of Finance and Commerce, the Secretary of State of Improvement and Public Work, the Secretary of State of Justice and Public Instruction and the Secretary of State of War and Marine. This Cabinet must be confirmed by the Congress. All
ACTS OF THE GOVERNMENT,
other than laws, are transacted by the Executive power, and each Minister gives a detailed account of the officers of his department through the President to Congress, which meets on the 27th of February of each year and continues in session 90 days. All contracts and concessions granted by the Executive power must be submitted to Congress for its approval and published in the official paper, after having received the signature of the Corresponding Secretary of State before it can become a law. All laws emanating from Congress, after a third reading at three distinct meetings, are forwarded to the President for execution. If not returned within eight days they become laws. A two-thirds vote of Congress will set aside the Executive veto. The Congress is made up of two Representatives from each province and from each district. There are six provinces and six districts, or 22 members, who form the National Congress.
The President, Vice President, members of the Congress and Judges of the Supreme Court are chosen by an electoral college by primaries in each district. The vote of each college district is forwarded to the National Congress, the members of which count the vote and declare the election.
Every foreigner has, under the Constitution, the same right to acquire property and engage in business, without let or hindrance as a Dominican. His property is subject to the protection of the Government just so long as he does not surrender his nationality. Aliens may become naturalized after a residence of one year, by making declaration of intention to the competent authorities. The country has developed rapidly in recent years, owing to the large amount of foreign capital which is being invested principally by Americans.
There is a great tendency to Americanize the country. The President is a very liberal man, and admires the progressive spirit of the Yankees. He is very solicitous to have them come to San Domingo, and offers every inducement and facility in the way of
GRANTING VALUABLE FRANCHISES.
He has given the Bay State Fruit Company, of Boston, of which Mr. William M. Snow is the President, a very profitable concession to develop the fruit trade. This company has already established a large plantation, and I am told that the bananas are now being brought here on steamships. If this company would increase its capital San Domingo would become one of the most important fruit producing islands in the West Indies, on account of proximity to the United States. Its most distant points would be about 1,600 miles, so you see an ordinary 12-knot steamer could make the trip in six days. The republic is rapidly being spanned by railroads constructed by Americans. Mr. Nathaniel McKay, a New Yorker, is building an iron bridge across the Ozama river, connecting San Domingo City with the historical town of Pagarito. records.full_text:
Consul Astwood Tells of the Inhabitants and Government of San Domingo.
From the Boston Herald.
It is a singular fact, but it is nevertheless true, that the majority of Americans regard San Domingo and the Republic of Hayti as one and the same country. Hon. H. C. C. Astwood, United States Consul to San Domingo for the past eight years, was in town a day or two ago, and in response to a question put to him by a Herald representative, said:
"Yes, I find that the major portion of the people of our country have a very erroneous impression of San Domingo. San Domingo, as you well know, was discovered by Columbus. Its original name was Hispaniola, or Little Spain. The island was afterwards divided between the French and Spaniards. The eastern, or Spanish portion, was two-thirds of the island, and was called Quigualla. It was discovered on a Sunday, and so Columbus christened it San Domingo, after the great saint. In the western, or French section, slavery was introduced, and hence the population was largely made up of Africans or blacks. Strange to say, slavery was not introduced to any great extent in the eastern end of the island. The native Caribs or Indians, numbering several millions, were utilized by the Spaniards in working the gold mines, building a walled city and constructing immense fortifications, now to be seen in a perfect state of preservation at San Domingo city and many other portions of the Republic. American tourists, including several from Boston, have said to me recently that it is exceedingly strange that San Domingo has remained in obscurity, with its splendid relics of antiquity, which, if generally known, would bring thousands of Americans who visit the West Indies. The population of the eastern portion, known as the Dominican Republic, are chiefly descendants of the Caribs and the Spaniards, making a race in appearance not unlike the Spaniards themselves. San Domingo is often taken for Hayti in speaking of the revolutionary tendencies of the latter country. This is a great mistake. The two peoples are distinct in every particular—in language, custom and their general deportment. The Dominican is kind, hospitable and very attentive to strangers. You may travel through the Republic, armed or without protection, and the humblest and poorest man or woman will greet you kindly in his home and have you partake of whatever accommodations it affords, and will absolutely refuse any compensation that you may offer. This is the character of the whole people.
"In their revolutionary upheavals, which are fast disappearing, life and property are respected, and especially those of strangers. The cases are isolated where this has been otherwise, except by naturalized Cubans, Porto Ricans or persons of Spanish extraction, who interfere with the politics of the country and are maltreated, and then appeal to their government as having been outraged. These instances are often published without any explanation, to the great detriment of the country. The Spanish portion of the Dominican Republic is just as beautiful as nature could have made it. There is an immense area in almost virgin state, capable of supporting in luxury and ease quite 10,000,000 of people. The population is a sparse one, numbering not more than 400,000. It abounds in beautiful woods, such as mahogany, satin wood, fustic, etc. There are scarcely any roads or means of conveyance to have these valuable woods shipped to foreign countries."
Referring to the government, Consul Astwood said it was a very liberal one. It is composed of a president, vice-president, supreme court and a national congress made up of twelve districts. The President is invested with the power to appoint the following cabinet officers: The secretary of state and interior police, the secretary of state of foreign relations, the secretary of state of finance and commerce, the secretary of state of improvement and public works, the secretary of state of justice and public instruction and the secretary of state of war and marine. The cabinet must be confirmed by the congress. All acts of the government, other than laws, are transacted by the executive power, and each minister gives a detailed account of the officers of his department through the President to Congress, which meets on the 27th of February of each year and continues in session ninety days. All contracts and concessions granted by the executive power must be submitted to Congress for its approval and published in the official paper, after having received the signature of the corresponding secretary of state before it can become a law. All laws emanating from Congress, after a third reading of the district meetings, are forwarded to the President for execution. If not returned within eight days, they become laws. A two-thirds vote of Congress will set aside the executive veto. The congress is made up of two representatives from each province and from each district. There are six provinces and six districts, or twenty-two members, who form the national congress.
The President, vice-President, members of Congress and judges of the supreme court are chosen by an electoral college by primaries in each district. The vote of each college district is forwarded to the national congress, the members of which count the vote and declare the election.
Every foreigner has, under the constitution, the same right to acquire property and engage in business, without let or hindrance as a Dominican.

records.full_text:
In his official report to Jefferson Davis, Secretary of War, relative to his reconnoissance and survey of the bay of Samana, "for the purpose of obtaining a Naval station in that first of bays in the Antilles," Captain McClellan made the important statement that "it is to be observed that the Haytian portion of the island possesses more good harbors than Dominica. That of the Mole of St. Nicolas is from its position the most interesting to us, commanding the Windward Passage even more completely than that of Samana does the Mona Passage. It is so well-known that I will merely mention that it is a good harbor for large vessels, and was under the French strongly fortified."
Commander Selfridge sixteen years later was sent in the United States steamer Nipsic (the predecessor of the Nipsic which was injured in the hurricane at Apia, Samoa,) to the bay of Samana with instructions "to examine whether there is at that place a good position for a coal depot, and whether the United States Government can obtain such a spot without any expense." In his report Commander Selfridge stated: "If it is the desire of the Government to possess a port in the Island of Hayti, either by purchase or lease, I know of no port in the West Indies in convenience of approach, facility of defence, salubrity of position, or of the strategic situation, that the port of St. Nicolas Mole, at the north-western extremity of Hayti possesses."

JANUARY.

records.headline: The Advertiser prints a general description of Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The Advertiser prints a general description of Santo Domingo and its government: its president is elected to serve four years, but the frequency of insurrections renders the term of office uncertain; the republic keeps but a small army of infantry, cavalry and artillery, a regiment being stationed in the capital of each province, and it is a good deal in debt after many financial ups and downs. The area of Santo Domingo, embracing the eastern portion of the island, is estimated at over 18,000 square miles, with a population estimated at 616,000; Puerto Plata, the chief port, has 18,000 inhabitants. The principal exports are lignum vitae, logwood, mahogany, fustic, tobacco and cocoa; the exports of sugar are on the increase, those of mahogany declining. A railroad at Samana has been finished and is being extended, large sugar plantations and factories are at work in the south and west, the telegraph lines are being extended, and primary instruction is free and compulsory, with over 300 schools at last reports.
records.summary_es: El Advertiser publica una descripción general de Santo Domingo y su gobierno: su presidente es elegido para servir cuatro años, pero la frecuencia de las insurrecciones hace incierta la duración del cargo; la república mantiene solo un pequeño ejército de infantería, caballería y artillería, con un regimiento estacionado en la capital de cada provincia, y está bastante endeudada después de muchos altibajos financieros. La superficie de Santo Domingo, que comprende la parte oriental de la isla, se estima en más de 18,000 millas cuadradas, con una población estimada de 616,000 habitantes; Puerto Plata, el puerto principal, tiene 18,000 habitantes. Las principales exportaciones son palo de tinte (lignum vitae), campeche, caoba, fustete, tabaco y cacao; las exportaciones de azúcar van en aumento y las de caoba en declive. Un ferrocarril en Samaná ha sido terminado y se está extendiendo, grandes plantaciones e ingenios azucareros trabajan en el sur y el oeste, las líneas telegráficas se están extendiendo, y la instrucción primaria es gratuita y obligatoria, con más de 300 escuelas según los últimos informes.

records.headline: The Freeman discourses on the island's two republics in an essay
records.summary_en: The Freeman discourses on the island's two republics in an essay: the Dominican Republic, originally settled by the Spanish, occupies the eastern two-thirds of the island, while the Haytian Republic occupies the western third, and the Dominican Republic is seldom mentioned, the writer believes, on account of the really good government found there — an actual proof, he says, that the Negro is capable of self-government in its highest form. If the World's Fair is held, the Dominican Republic will have an exhibit, and President Heureaux will visit the Fair and tour the United States. Ulises Heureaux is a remarkable man, the paper continues: born at Puerto Plata in 1846, he has risen by his own efforts step by step from the ranks of the army until he became general, the idol of his people, and finally President: the window closes inside the Freeman's admiring description of him.

Si se celebra la Feria Mundial, la República Dominicana tendrá una exhibición, y el presidente Heureaux visitará la Feria y recorrerá los Estados Unidos. Ulises Heureaux es un hombre notable, continúa el periódico: nacido en Puerto Plata en 1846, ha ascendido por su propio esfuerzo, paso a paso, desde las filas del ejército hasta llegar a general, ídolo de su pueblo, y finalmente Presidente: la ventana se cierra dentro de la elogiosa descripción que el Freeman hace de él.

records.headline: An American company is now constructing a railroad in San Domingo

Pell of New York; the engineer of the road is a Frenchman who has resided seven years in the Dominican republic.

HAYTI OR SAN DOMINGO.
The United States, It Is Said, Is Looking Toward Annexation.
NEW YORK, July 29.—The Times' Portland, Me., special says that a gentleman formerly prominent in two Republican administrations, and who is now at Bar Harbor, intimates that the United States is likely to annex Hayti or San Domingo, and that Mr. Blaine's views on sugar duties have a bearing on this point. A Dominican statesman recently paid a hurried visit to Mr. Blaine. Minister Douglass' return from Hayti may have some connection with this matter.

INVADED BY HAYTI.
THE TROOPS OF THE BLACK REPUBLIC ON DOMINICAN SOIL.
A Battle in Which Many Were Killed and Wounded—Great Indignation—The Cause of the Trouble.
NEW YORK, Aug. 23.—A special cable to the Herald from the city of Santo Domingo, via Havana, says:
Information has reached this capital that on the night of August 20 about 800 Haytian troops stationed near the frontier of the Dominican republic invaded the territory of this country.
The Dominican Government at once dispatched an armed force to drive out the intruders. The Dominican troops were successful and repulsed the enemy, killing twenty-three men and wounding a number of others. The Dominicans had but four soldiers injured.
Great indignation is felt here at Hayti's action in this invasion of Dominican soil, and the Dominican Cabinet has been called together by President Ulise Huerreaux to consider the advisability of declaring war against Hayti.
President Huerreaux said to-day that the real cause of the trouble was that in 1875 and 1876 a treaty for commercial purposes was entered into between the Haytian and Dominican governments which at the same time defined the boundaries of the two countries. A special stipulation of this treaty was that Hayti was to make use of a portion of Dominican territory which she needed, and which Santo Domingo was to allow to be so used on condition that Hayti should pay annually to the Dominican Government $150,000 as long as she retained possession of the loaned territory. Hayti was, moreover, to permit all imports from Santo Domingo to enter into Hayti free of duty. Hayti has not paid the $150,000 for a number of years, and now owes something over $2,000,000.
Hayti, however, alleges that there is so much rum imported from Santo Domingo that the Haytian revenues are greatly suffering. Hayti wishes to make an end to her bargain and at the same time retain possession of the loaned land.
Senors Francisco Leonte Vasquez and Manuel De J. Galvan, the consul general and consul, respectively, of the Dominican Government in this city, state that they have received no official intimation from their government that any outbreak or invasion had occurred on the island.
They knew that there was some sort of trouble brewing between Hayti and Santo Domingo, but they could not say to what extent it had developed. They had also heard it said that private advices had been received by persons here that there had been a distubance between the two countries, but they had learned none of the particulars.

records.summary_en: *The National Tribune* reviewed the 19th-century history of Hispaniola, quoting writer Samuel Hazard from the 1871 American commission on Santo Domingo. The article recounted the reigns of early Haitian leaders, Spain's temporary reoccupation of Santo Domingo, the transfer of Columbus's supposed remains to Havana, and Santo Domingo's 1821 independence followed by Boyer's annexation.

El artículo relató los mandatos de los primeros gobernantes haitianos, la reocupación temporal de Santo Domingo por parte de España, el traslado de los supuestos restos de Colón a La Habana y la independencia de Santo Domingo en 1821 seguida de la anexión por parte de Boyer.

records.chapter_es: Azúcar, deuda y caudillos
records.full_text:
IMPRESSING STEVEDORES.
Domingo upon the approach of the insurgents under the leadership of Toussaint l'Ouverture, who was the first revolutionary chief. L'Ouverture committed many atrocious acts. On Jan. 3, 1801, he had all the white women, children and old men of San Domingo City gathered in groups in the market place, with squads of black soldiers over each party, and had given orders to massacre them all. But a terrific storm coming on, with terrible thunder and sharp lightning, just as he was about to have his orders put in execution, his superstitious fears were aroused and he let them all go free.
It was a fearful retribution which fell on Hayti. Under the Spanish yoke the original Indian inhabitants of the island were worked to death in the mines, while under the French dominion captured Indians from other French possessions were sent there to be killed with toil. Under the joint ownership the coasts of Africa were scoured for negroes, who were brought in chains, and under the lash had to wear their lives away for their cruel taskmasters, to spend the product of their blood in luxury and idleness.
In 1804, from which year Haytien independence is dated, Dessalines was selected as Governor-General for life. He covered his name with infamy by ordering the slaughter of all the whites on the island, after he had promised them protection, because, as he said, France would not acknowledge their independence. Oct. 8, 1804, having downed all opposition, he assumed the title of Jacques I, Emperor of Hayti, and established a royal court of blacks, a travesty on the monarchies of Europe. Many of the white people had been secreted during his massacres by faithful slaves, and finding this out at Cape St. Francois, he issued a proclamation that justice (?) was satisfied, and directing all whites who escaped the massacre to appear on the public plaza to be sent away. When they did so they were taken and shot, and
HIS BRUTAL ACTS
so incensed many of his followers that his soldiers rose against him. The career of Emperor Jacques I was finished in 1806 at Point Rouge, a short distance from Port au Prince, and his mantle fell on Christophe, whose career was horrible and tyrannical, and who assumed the title of Emperor Henry I. Mr. Hazard, who accompanied the San Domingo Commissioners to Hayti when the United States were trying to acquire Samana Bay, in giving his views of Haytien history, says:
"It seems a peculiarity of these negroes when in power in this island, that no sooner do they begin to feel a little assured in their position than the negro's instinct of display, love of power, or some inherent element of cruelty induces them to commit acts that bring on their own ruin, while horrifying the world with deeds of bloodshed."
So Christophe ruled with rod of iron until 1820, when the people rose against him, and, attacked on all sides, he killed himself. Petion, who had been opposing him for years and had successfully maintained himself in the south-west part of the island, now acted as President for a while, until Boyer was chosen. He is looked upon as the best ruler the island ever had.
The Spaniards soon reoccupied San Domingo after the great outburst of 1803, but seeing the disorganized condition of affairs, removed the remains of Christopher Columbus from the Cathedral in the city of St. Domingo, which he had founded, to the Cathedral in Havana, where they now are. In 1821 the Dominicans gained their independence from Spain, and then Boyer marched over from Hayti and attacked them while they were weak, and he united the whole island under one Government, ruling until 1842, when a revolution shook him up and he had to flee, and Gen. Herard, or Riviere, succeeded him, and the Dominicans, in 1844, shook off the yoke of Hayti.
Herard raised an army and marched against them, but he got decently trounced and run out, and when he reached home they banished him and put Guerrier in his place. This colored gentleman died very suddenly next year, and Pierrot was selected to succeed him, but party oppositions were so bitter that he got scared and resigned,—
THREW UP THE SPONGE.
His successor, Gen. Riche, had scarcely got the chair warm before he died, and in 1847 the gay duck Faustin Soulouque was inducted into power. To 'make himself solid' he marched against Domingo with 5,000 men in 1849, but he was attacked at Las Carreras by Santana with 400 men and driven back. He returned home, and to stop talk hung all those who found fault with his campaign. He then formed a strong party and proclaimed himself Emperor under the title of Faustine I, and was crowned with great pomp. He had Princes and noblemen of all grades, and was surrounded by black guards. He erected a huge frame building near Port au Prince, elegantly fitted it up, and called it the Tuilleries, which name it yet retains.
The ebony Earls, Marquises and Counts put on so many airs that the unfortunate darkies who were not so rank became jealous and formed a revolution under Gen. Geffrard in 1859; so Faustine I folded his imperial purple about him, and seizing on all the valuables and loose change around the Tuilleries, skipped for Kingston, Jamaica, where he had been laying up savings for 10 years.
Geffrard then became President of Hayti, and some of the opposition party tried to assassinate him. They fired into his sitting-room, missing him but killing his daughter.
The opposition party was headed by Salnave, and called themselves the 'Lizards,' while Geffrard's party called themselves 'Cacos,' after a black parrot that feeds on lizards. These two parties represented the factions which have been fighting each other since the Haytiens gained their independence; but the balance of power is held by the 'Piquints,' or backwoodsmen, who always go with the party that pays the best. The Salnave party got the best of Geffrard, however, and he had to leave after Soulouque to Jamaica, well loaded, like his imperial predecessor, with public treasure. Salnave was then elected President in 1867, but soon proclaimed himself Emperor and doled out titles to his followers, one of them being
"DUKE OF MARMALADE,"

records.full_text:
An Important San Domingo Colony from the United States.
The New York World of Sunday contains a splendid article by Lieut. C. H. ROCKWELL of the American Navy, in which he describes with much eloquence and sympathy a visit he made to the colony of Afro-Americans who settled on the Bay of Samana in 1824 and 1825. About 2,000 of these people settled there upon the invitation of President BOYER.
Lieut. ROCKWELL found that the colonists had greatly increased in numbers, that they were prosperous, highly intelligent and hospitable, and that they had clung to the English language, while having acquired the Spanish language, which is generally spoken in Santo Domingo. Lieut. ROCKWELL draws the following picture of the condition of the people:
These sturdy elements of character have not failed to receive recognition even there. The present government estimates the whole colony very highly, and all the offices, from the governor down, are held by the descendants of the American emigrants. There is absolute peace and quietness in the district. The country is vigilantly patrolled, the people seem innocently happy and their hospitality is boundless. There is ample room for many thousands. The people are anxious to receive and welcome and help all who will come. The country is healthy, and its natural resources are boundless.
In conclusion he says:
Here is one emigration and colonization of colored people which has been a success. There is ample room for more; kind, willing hands and hearts to receive them, and a smiling paradise ready for occupancy. The political and social regeneration of the island of Santo Domingo is a possibility for the colored race of the United States.
If the Dominican Republic would offer such inducements to actual settlers as the United States offer to foreigners, we dare say that a very large number of Afro-Americans would take advantage of them, to their own and the betterment of the Dominican government. A hundred thousand could go of the most desirable of the people, and would go if offered fair inducements. We trust the matter will be looked into. What has the Afro-American press to say about the matter? Now is a good time to discuss it.

records.headline: A traveling Odd Fellow's letter in the Age describes the Odd Fellow lodges
records.summary_en: A traveling Odd Fellow's letter in the Age describes the Odd Fellow lodges in Puerto Plata and Santo Domingo: at Puerto Plata he stopped two days, was received by the local lodge, and a large committee waited on him to express their welcome and offer the lodge's hospitality whenever he might visit; at San Domingo he officiated under the vouching of the Honorable H. C. C. Astwood, who established the San Domingo Lodge and under whose direction the work was translated into the Spanish language. The lodge room there, he writes, puts their own old lodge room at home to shame — longer and wider by about ten feet in each dimension, its floor of tiles, its walls kalsomined sky blue, and its borders and ceiling decorated with the emblems of Odd Fellowship, the regalia, altars and insignia all imported from the United States.
records.summary_es: La carta de un viajero de la Orden de los Odd Fellows en el Age describe las logias de la orden en Puerto Plata y Santo Domingo: en Puerto Plata se detuvo dos días, fue recibido por la logia local, y una numerosa comisión lo visitó para expresarle su bienvenida y ofrecerle la hospitalidad de la logia siempre que la visitara; en Santo Domingo ofició bajo el aval del Honorable H. C. C. Astwood, quien estableció la Logia de Santo Domingo y bajo cuya dirección el ritual fue traducido al español. El salón de la logia allí, escribe, avergüenza a su antiguo salón en casa: más largo y más ancho por unos diez pies en cada dimensión, con piso de losetas, paredes encaladas de azul celeste, y bordes y techo decorados con los emblemas de la Odd Fellowship, con las insignias, altares y emblemas importados todos de los Estados Unidos.

records.headline: The Tribune prints the Dominican special envoy's presentation of his credentials
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints the Dominican special envoy's presentation of his credentials at Washington: the envoy, accredited by an official letter from the President of the Dominican Republic as Minister Plenipotentiary on special mission, tells President Harrison he is charged to propose a commercial arrangement between the two countries in conformity with the recent tariff legislation of the United States, and expresses the sentiments and good disposition with which the Dominican Government and people are animated toward the United States. President Harrison replies that he does not doubt a friendly exchange of views will promptly lead to a conclusion of mutual advantage, and that it will give him great pleasure to promote not only this special work but everything tending to promote peace and good will, welcoming the minister cordially to the capital; a short but cordial exchange of views followed before the envoy took leave.
records.summary_es: El Tribune publica la presentación de credenciales del enviado especial dominicano en Washington: el enviado, acreditado por una carta oficial del Presidente de la República Dominicana como ministro plenipotenciario en misión especial, dice al presidente Harrison que está encargado de proponer un arreglo comercial entre los dos países conforme a la reciente legislación arancelaria de los Estados Unidos, y expresa los sentimientos y la buena disposición con que el Gobierno y el pueblo dominicanos están animados hacia los Estados Unidos. El presidente Harrison responde que no duda de que un intercambio amistoso de pareceres conducirá prontamente a una conclusión de ventaja mutua, y que le dará gran placer promover no solo esta labor especial sino todo lo que tienda a promover la paz y la buena voluntad, dando al ministro una cordial bienvenida a la capital; siguió un breve pero cordial intercambio de pareceres antes de que el enviado se retirara.

records.headline: The Pawtucket Tribune relays Washington talk of a coaling station
records.summary_en: The Pawtucket Tribune relays Washington talk of a coaling station at Samaná Bay: it is perhaps not generally known, the paper says, that Admiral Gherardi left Port au Prince four weeks ago under cable orders to go direct to Samana Bay and examine into its fitness for a coaling station, and that while he was there Gen. Heureaux, the president of San Domingo, came from San Domingo City in his yacht and was closeted with the admiral for several hours, only his secretary of war and a lieutenant of the admiral's staff present. There is no doubt, the paper continues, that the subject of the conversation was the establishment of a naval station on Samana Bay, and that the price is the friendship and moral support of the United States in the present difficulty between San Domingo and Hayti; Secretary Tracy is very much in earnest, feeling in Washington runs far from friendly to Hayti after its government's late action, and as between the two republics the preference will probably now be given to San Domingo.

records.headline: The Sun notes talk among the colored people of the invitation
records.summary_en: The Sun notes talk among the colored people of the invitation to settle in San Domingo extended to all American Negroes by Gen. Heureux, president of the Dominican republic: there is room for a million of them in San Domingo, which has a rich soil, a tropical climate and marvelous resources, and a population of only 350,000. The colored people here, however, are not inclined to accept President Heureux's invitation, as there is no security for peace in San Domingo and the Government is in constant danger from the Haytians; moreover, they prefer the United States, of which they are natives, to any other country in the world — yet they appreciate the hospitable intent of the Dominican President and the kindly welcome he offers them.

SAMANA AS A NAVAL STATION.
Santa Barbara Harbor May Possibly be a Substitute for Mole St. Nicolas.
WASHINGTON, May 27.—It would be strange if after twenty years of neglect the project for the acquisition of a foothold in Samana Bay should now be revived. President Baez, on receiving the news of the rejection by the United States Senate of the famous San Domingo treaty of 1869, put on record the prediction that it would some day be renewed. In the broad form of annexation the scheme is no nearer fruition now than then; but in the very limited particular of securing a repair and coaling station for our war vessels within the Dominican republic there is a prospect of its again coming to the front.
There is little doubt that the State and Navy departments were somewhat chagrined at Hayti's refusal to cede the use of Mole St. Nicolas as a naval station. The indirect but powerful aid which the affair of the steamship Haytian Republic gave to the cause of Hippolyte, when the latter was in arms against Légitime, had hardly been expected to lead up to the futile negotiations lately carried on by Admiral Gherardi and Minister Douglass. It is true that the action of our Government in that affair was directed to the interests of its own citizens and the maritime rights of neutrals in general rather than to interfering for one party in the civil war on the island. It is also probable that the promises of French help with which M. de Sesmaisons buoyed up the hopes of Légitime's followers were not grounded on any assurances from his Government, so that the counter-interference of our own country to prevent European control of Hayti would not have been called for. Still, Hippolyte's cause did undoubtedly receive much moral and some material strength from the United States. But the real ground of the disgust of the Washington authorities is doubtless rather the folly of Hayti in failing to see its own advantage in ceding the use of Mole St. Nicolas, with its resulting local and general benefits to her. Of course the ability of a great power like the United States to conquer and annex Hayti, if that were its object, is too obvious for dispute; while its willingness to take merely a lease of the desired lands and water privileges, and even to receive them through the medium of a private corporation, was a further guarantee of its moderate aims.
But the revival of the Samana project, which is believed to have begun when Admiral Gherardi was ordered a few weeks ago to visit that bay, where Gen. Ulises Heureaux, the President of San Domingo, held a long private interview with him on the flagship, is not to be ascribed to mere official pique. It is true that, should this substitute scheme be carried out, Hayti would probably soon recognize that she had thrown away an opportunity. But the Samana Bay project rests on its intrinsic merits. Situated at the northeastern end of the island, on the south side of Samana peninsula, the bay could hold the war fleets of the whole world. At the western end it receives the Yuma, the chief river of San Domingo. As a strategic position it is of great value, since it opens into the Mona Passage, the principal entrance to the Caribbean Sea for vessels from Europe, and is hardly a day's steaming from the Windward Passage at the other end of the island. As a sheltered place for repairs and coaling, no better need be asked in the West Indies, while it is sufficiently near the Nicaragua Canal to serve in keeping a watch upon that future highway of commerce.
The port of Santa Barbara, which would be the particular region leased, is on the north shore of Samana Bay. The entrance is narrow, from a line of reefs and islets parallel with the shore, but the harbor within is deep enough for large vessels. It could be perfectly covered by batteries, but the true defence would be at the entrance of Samana Bay, where the channel is less than a mile wide in consequence of a cluster of reefs and small islands. Batteries there placed would easily shut out any hostile ships from the entire bay. At the head of Santa Barbara harbor is a village from which a railroad runs westward, and there it is proposed to build a dry dock for repairs.
One thing tolerably clear is that if a reasonable proposal to lease the port of Santa Barbara is made to the Dominican republic it will be accepted. As is well known, this republic occupies the larger part of the island, having an area of about 18,000 square miles, of which only an insignificant part would be taken. Even as early as 1850, only half a dozen years after its independence of Hayti had been declared, San Domingo talked of annexation to the United States, and shortly after the close of our civil war its Government expressed willingness to lease Samana Bay, this being a rival proposition to the St. Thomas annexation project at that time mooted. In 1869 President Grant intrusted Gen. Babcock and Mr. R. H. Perry with negotiations, the result of which was a treaty signed on the 29th of November for the annexation of the whole republic. The money consideration named was $1,500,000, and Gen. Grant, in transmitting the treaty to the Senate, said that he had reason to believe that a European power stood ready to offer $2,000,000 for Samana Bay alone. He argued that the annexation would be in the line of the Monroe doctrine, especially in its aiding the United States to command the Isthmus of Darien. The treaty called for a popular vote in San Domingo, which proved to be almost unanimous for annexation; but it failed to secure the approval of our Senate. In 1873 the bay privileges and peninsula of Samana were ceded to a company formed in the United States, but the following year its rights were declared to be annulled for the non-payment of the stipulated rent. What seems clear is that if even the annexation project was so favored in the island, the present less objectionable form of a concession such as we already hold at Pago Pago from Samoa and at Pearl Island from Hawaii, could be easily procured.

records.summary_en: The Gazette reprints, in its briefs, the New York Sun's item on President Heureux's invitation: the colored people are talking about the invitation to settle in San Domingo extended to all American Negroes by General Heureux, the president of the Dominican republic, there being room for a million of them in San Domingo, with its rich soil, tropical climate, marvelous resources and a population of only 350,000. They are not inclined to accept the invitation, as there is no security for peace in San Domingo and the government is in constant danger from the Haitians; moreover they prefer the United States, of which they are natives, to any other country in the world — yet they appreciate the hospitable intent of the Dominican president and the kindly welcome he offers them.

records.full_text:
VIEWS UPON THE LITTLE REPUBLIC.
ADVANTAGES TO BE DERIVED FROM RECIPROCITY—FEATURES OF INTEREST.
Minister Galvan, who represents the Government of San Domingo in this country, and who is at work on a reciprocity treaty between the United States and his Government, is now in New-York, where he expects to remain until the treaty has been signed and the official announcement of it has been made.
A Tribune reporter found him yesterday at his hotel in Union Square. He speaks fairly good English, but his oldest son, who acts as his secretary, also fills the place of interpreter at times. The Minister received the reporter pleasantly, and signified his willingness to discuss San Domingo affairs as freely as the circumstances of his official place would permit.
"In what condition are the negotiations for reciprocity treaty between San Domingo and this country?" he was asked.
"I cannot say anything about that just at present," he replied. "The conditions are such now that I cannot discuss the matter. I will say, however, that the treaty as proposed will be a benefit to both countries. It will aid San Domingo, because if our sugar is let in here free of duty it will stimulate and extend the sugar-growing business of my country. Planters then will have the knowledge that in the United States they can find a steady market. The benefits to your country will come in the admission of American manufactures at such reduced rates of duty that your manufacturers can compete with the other foreign countries in the contest for trade."
"Is there any prospect of your Government ceding the United States a coaling station on Samana Bay?" he was asked.
"Of that I am unable to speak. Nothing has been said to me by my Government about it, and the subject has not been broached in any way by any of the representatives of your country. The bay is probably one of the finest on the globe. It has plenty of water for the largest ships.
"No, I do not think that there will be trouble between the Governments of Hayti and San Domingo. The two countries are not on good terms, owing to Hayti's breach of the treaty of 1874. The Haytians do not want to attack the Dominicans."
GENERAL U. HEUREAUX, President of Santo Domingo.
Everybody knows what a keen observer Nathaniel McKay is, and that he is well up in men, manners and customs as well as in figures. He recently made a voyage to San Domingo, and during his trip he collected many interesting facts and statistics. Mr. McKay had the other day a talk with a Tribune reporter about his journey and the information he had picked up by the way.
"The climate of San Domingo is pleasant, and a voyage to this ancient city in the winter would be one of the most enjoyable that a man could take for his health. The greatest distance out of sight of land is between New-York and Turks Islands; the rest of the time you sail among the islands, day and night. The sea voyage would be much preferable to a trip to Florida. The steamers of the Clyde line are fitted and furnished in the best manner; the food is in abundance and of the best kind; the beds on the ships are excellent."

records.headline: The Record prints a geographical description of Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The Record prints a geographical description of Santo Domingo and its great bay: the cape and town of Isabella, where Columbus first established himself, are on the northern coast of the territory the description calls Dominica, and the city of San Domingo, where he finally planted his colony and where his body was deposited when returned from Spain — remaining 240 years until finally taken to Havana — is on the southern coast. The Bay of Samana is beyond doubt the grandest harbor of the Antilles, extending some thirty miles from east to west by nine or twelve from north to south; the peninsula that forms it is a grand promontory of steep, irregular hills ranging from a few hundred to 2,000 feet, covered with dense underbrush, vines and timber and watered by mountain streams that sometimes fall in beautiful cascades. The predominant rock is limestone, with schist, quartz and mica slate also occurring, and bituminous coal is found of exceeding richness; the harbor's entrance, for vessels drawing more than eight feet, is contracted to about 2,000 yards by a broad coral reef, north of which lie five small islands, the largest of about 100 acres.
records.summary_es: El Record publica una descripción geográfica de Santo Domingo y su gran bahía: el cabo y el pueblo de Isabela, donde Colón se estableció primero, están en la costa norte del territorio que la descripción llama Dominica, y la ciudad de Santo Domingo, donde finalmente plantó su colonia y donde su cuerpo fue depositado al ser devuelto de España —permaneciendo 240 años hasta ser finalmente llevado a La Habana— está en la costa sur. La bahía de Samaná es sin duda el puerto más grandioso de las Antillas, con unas treinta millas de este a oeste por nueve o doce de norte a sur; la península que la forma es un gran promontorio de colinas escarpadas e irregulares que van de unos pocos cientos a 2,000 pies, cubiertas de densa maleza, enredaderas y bosques y regadas por arroyos de montaña que a veces caen en hermosas cascadas. La roca predominante es la caliza, con esquistos, cuarzo y mica también presentes, y se encuentra carbón bituminoso de extraordinaria riqueza; la entrada del puerto, para buques de más de ocho pies de calado, se estrecha a unas 2,000 yardas por un amplio arrecife de coral, al norte del cual hay cinco islotes, el mayor de unas 100 acres.

The then recent experiences of the people, however, under foreign domination rendered the proposition inopportune. Although, as the Assistant Secretary reported, the measure commended itself to the better judgment of the leading minds of the Dominion republic, it would require time to satisfy the minds of the people that the occupation of Samana by the United States would be a far different matter from its recent temporary control by Spain, and that our presence and friendship would save them from the very evils which they dreaded, and bring peace and prosperity to take the place of their unhappy discords. The negotiations were, however, broken off; but on the 24th of November in the same year our commercial agent again wrote that an informal proposal had been made to him for a lease of Samana and the following month President Baez, after consulting the magnates of the republic, made arrangements for submitting a proposition for the protection of the United States to a popular vote.
Such was the condition of these negotiations when the administrtion of Mr. Johnson ceased and General Grant was elected President. General Babcock was now sent as a commissioner to act in conjunction with Mr. Perry, the commercial agent of the United States, to negotiate a treaty for the annexation of the whole territory of the republic to the United States, or for a lease of the peninsula and bay of Samana.
In February, 1870, the proposition for annexation was submitted to the people and was approved by an almost unanimous vote. Mr. Perry in his dispatches said: "The whole people desire annexation to the United States."
The treaty, however, failed to receive the requisite two-thirds of the United States Senate, and General Grant again called attention to it in his annual message at the next session of Congress. He said: "I now firmly believe that the moment it is known that the United States have entirely abandoned the project of accepting as a part of its territory the island of Santo Domingo a free port will be negotiated for by European nations. In the bay of Samana a large commercial city will spring up to which we will be tributary without receiving corresponding benefits, and then will be seen the folly of our rejecting so great a prize."
After referring to the fact that the Government and people of St. Domingo had voluntarily sought this annexation—that they were a weak power, yet possessing one of the richest territories under the sun, capable of suporting in luxury 10,000,000 of people—he presented at great length the commercial advantages to be secured, and finally argued that "the acquisition of St. Domingo is an adherence to the Monroe doctrine; that it is a measure of national protection; that it is asserting our just claim to a controlling influence over the great commercial traffic soon to flow from east and west by way of the isthmus—that it is to build up our merchant marine; that it is to furnish new markets for the products of our farms, shops, and manufactories; that it is to extend the area of freedom and to furnish our citizens with the necessaries of life at a cheaper rate than ever before." In fine, he concluded: "So convinced am I of the advantages to flow from the acquisition of St. Domingo and of the great disadvantage—I might say calamities—to flow from non-acquisition that I believe the subject has only to be investigated to be approved."
But this eloquent and patriotic appeal fell unheeded upon the dull ears of an unappreciative Senate, and the matter has strangely remained in abeyance through successive administrations from that day to this, until so disheartened had the authorities and the people of the little republic finally become that they plaintively referred to it in recently declining to be represented at the World's Fair in 1893.
It is true that President Baez and others prophesied that it would some day be renewed. And this has now come to pass. But the renewal now proceeds from the side of the United States, and not until our humble supplications at the other end of the island have been peremptorily rejected. The vigorous increase of our navy, our rapidly augmenting commerce with the southern republics, and the new impetus to be given to isthmian transit by the Nicaragua Canal, and soon, perhaps, by a ship railway at Tehuantepec, all so forcibly urged by General Grant in his repeated appeals to Congress, contribute to impress upon the mind as a matter of imminent importance.—Chicago Times.

records.headline: The Press and Banner prints the geographical description of the bay
records.summary_en: The Press and Banner prints the geographical description of the bay to which the United States has been invited: the Bay of Samana is on the other extreme of the island, in the territory the description calls Dominica, commanding the Mona Passage, the principal channel to the Caribbean Sea and the Spanish Main; Isabella, where Columbus first established himself, is on its northern coast, and the city of Santo Domingo, where his body lay 240 years before being taken to Havana, on the southern. The bay is beyond doubt the grandest harbor of the Antilles, extending some thirty miles from east to west by nine or twelve from north to south, its peninsula a grand promontory of steep hills up to 2,000 feet, covered with dense growth and watered by mountain streams; limestone predominates, quartz and mica slate occur, and bituminous coal is found of exceeding richness, while the entrance is contracted to about 2,000 yards by a coral reef for vessels drawing more than eight feet.

records.full_text:
AFFAIRS IN SAN DOMINGO.
That Republic Has Not Been Affected by the Troubles in Haiti.
[SPECIAL TELEGRAM TO THE DISPATCH.]
NEW YORK, July 24.—Thomas Simpson, United States Consul at Puerto Plata, San Domingo, is at the Astor Hotel. He expects to return to San Domingo to-morrow afternoon. In an interview this morning he said: "The revolutionary disturbances in Haiti have had no apparent effect on San Domingo. Formerly there was a reciprocity treaty between the two republics, but this is in force no longer. Some months ago representatives of the two powers met at San Domingo and tried to frame a new treaty, but were not successful."
"The President of San Domingo is a native of the United States, and his son is my Vice Consul. However, they are not in favor of annexation with the United States. As far as reciprocity is concerned, I believe there is no particular interest, though the Dominicans are not opposed to it." Mr. Simpson said he believed that with the friendly relations existing between this country and San Domingo a sentiment could easily be created in the latter country in favor of leasing Samana to the United States.
