records.headline: The Record-Visitor tells how Columbus's remains came to rest
records.summary_en: The Record-Visitor tells how Columbus's remains came to rest at Santo Domingo: in 1795, when the eastern part of the island came under French dominion, the Spaniards exhumed from the vaults of the cathedral a coffin they judged to contain the body of Columbus and transferred it to Havana. But in 1877 a new vault was discovered in San Domingo, near that opened in 1795, and the coffin found in it bore inscriptions showing that the mortal remains of Christopher Columbus were certainly contained in it; the body previously exhumed was that of his son Diego. At present the remains of the illustrious navigator still repose in the cathedral of San Domingo, capital of the Dominican Republic and one of the most ancient cities founded in America by Europeans; his principal descendant today, the Duke of Veragua, a grandee of Spain, has confided to the Academy of Madrid the task of awarding in 1892 a prize of $6,000 to the author of the best history of his immortal ancestor.
records.summary_es: El Record-Visitor cuenta cómo los restos de Colón llegaron a reposar en Santo Domingo: en 1795, cuando la parte oriental de la isla pasó a dominación francesa, los españoles exhumaron de las bóvedas de la catedral un ataúd que juzgaron contenía el cuerpo de Colón y lo trasladaron a La Habana. Pero en 1877 se descubrió en Santo Domingo una nueva bóveda, cerca de la abierta en 1795, y el ataúd hallado en ella llevaba inscripciones que demostraban que ciertamente contenía los restos mortales de Cristóbal Colón; el cuerpo exhumado anteriormente era el de su hijo Diego. En la actualidad, los restos del ilustre navegante reposan aún en la catedral de Santo Domingo, capital de la República Dominicana y una de las ciudades más antiguas fundadas en América por europeos; su principal descendiente hoy, el duque de Veragua, grande de España, ha confiado a la Academia de Madrid la tarea de premiar en 1892 con $6,000 al autor de la mejor historia de su inmortal antepasado.

records.headline: The Sun argues the strategic case for Samana Bay on expert testimony
records.summary_en: The Sun argues the strategic case for Samana Bay on expert testimony: according to the best testimony obtainable, the harbor might be fortified by a system of defenses not very costly to build, and it would have over St. Thomas the marked advantage of commanding the Mona Pass, one of the two chief strategic points in the Antilles. The two great nautical routes between Europe and the Gulf of Mexico and Central America, the Sun continues, are the Mona Pass, on the south side of the island of San Domingo, and the Mole St. Nicolas route, or Windward Passage, on the northern or Haytian side of the island; the power that occupies these two points and fortifies them will control the principal waterways between Europe and the Gulf of Mexico. Were an interoceanic canal built across Central America, the occupation of both the Mole St. Nicolas and Samana Bay would prove of invaluable importance to the United States, and the Mole lies barely thirty miles from the Cuban coast.

Las dos grandes rutas náuticas entre Europa y el golfo de México y la América Central, continúa el Sun, son el paso de la Mona, en el lado sur de la isla de Santo Domingo, y la ruta del Môle St. Nicolas, o paso de los Vientos, en el lado norte o haitiano de la isla; la potencia que ocupe esos dos puntos y los fortifique controlará las principales vías acuáticas entre Europa y el golfo de México. Si se construyera un canal interoceánico a través de la América Central, la ocupación tanto del Môle St. Nicolas como de la bahía de Samaná resultaría de inestimable importancia para los Estados Unidos, y el Môle dista apenas treinta millas de la costa cubana.

Bismarck received him kindly but finally dismissed him with the remark that the United States would not tolerate German interference in those quarters.

According to Gen. Taylor's statement to a trusted friend, he was most kindly received, and listened to with the utmost interest. But finally the Prince dismissed him with the remark that the United States would not tolerate German interference in those quarters. About the same time, when Ferdinand de [Lesseps?], then on his way back from Panama to France, stopped at Washington, Mr. [Evarts?], then Secretary of State, exacted from the French Government a declaration to the effect that France would never have anything to do with the enterprise of the Panama Canal; and the French Minister at Washington, having been authorized to execute such a declaration, signed it and placed it in the hands of the Secretary of State. These various illustrations disclose a noteworthy situation which has not yet been fully apprehended by the general public. records.full_text:
RECIPROCITY WITH SAN DOMINGO.
President Harrison's Proclamation Giving the List of Duty-Free Articles.
WASHINGTON, Aug. 1.—The President to-day issued a proclamation announcing reciprocity with San Domingo, under the tariff act of last October, which, with a view to securing reciprocal trade, exempted from duty sugars, molasses, coffee and hides imported into the United States. By this treaty the following articles manufactured in the United States will be admitted free of duty into the Dominican republic from and after Sept. 1, 1891:
Live animals; meats of all kinds, excepting smoked corn; corn-meal and starch; oats, barley, rye and buckwheat, and flour of these grains; hay; bran and straw; trees; plants, vines and seeds; cotton-seed oil and meal-cake; pitch tar, turpentine and rosin; coal; mineral waters; ice machines; mining machinery; agricultural implements; railway material; wrought and cast-iron and steel, in pigs, bars, rods, beams, etc., and wire nails, screws and pipes; zinc, tin and lead, and roofing material; copper in bars, plates, nails, etc., and copper and lead pipe; bricks, cement, lime, stone, marble and paving tiles; fence wire, telegraph wire and apparatus; wood and lumber of all kinds; material for ship-building; school furniture; books, pamphlets, printed matter and paper for newspapers; inks, gold and silver coin and bullion.
The following articles are to be admitted into the Dominican republic at a reduction of duty of 25 per centum:
Butter, cheese and condensed milk; fish of all kinds; fruits and vegetables of all kinds; cotton, manufactured, spun or twisted, and in fabrics of all kinds, woven or knit, and the same fabrics mixed with other vegetable or animal fibres in which cotton is the equal or greater component part; boots and shoes; writing paper, blank books, wall paper, paper for wrapping and packing, for cigarettes in cardboard boxes and bags, sandpaper and pasteboard; tin-plate and tinware for arts, industries and domestic uses; cordage, rope and twine of all kinds; woodenware implements for household use
The proclamation closes with the following language: "And whereas, the special plenipotentiary of the United States has by my direction given assurance to the envoy extraordinary and minister plenipotentiary of the Dominican republic at Washington that this action of the government of the Dominican republic in granting exemption of duties to the products and manufactures of the United States of America on their importation into the Dominican republic is accepted as a due reciprocity for the action of Congress as set forth in Section 3 of said act;
"Now, therefore, be it known that I, Benjamin Harrison, President of the United States of America, have caused the above-stated modifications of the tariff laws of the Dominican republic to be made public for the information of the citizens of the United States of America. In testimony whereof I have hereunto set my hand and caused the seal of the United States to be affixed. Done at the city of Washington, the first day of August, one thousand, eight hundred and ninety-one, and of the independence of the United States of America the one hundred and sixteenth.
"BENJAMIN HARRISON.
"William A. Wharton, Acting Secretary of State."
The correspondence preceding the proclamation of the treaty was brief, consisting of but two letters exchanged between Senor Galvan, Minister of the Dominican Republic, and Hon. John W. Foster, special plenipotentiary of the United States, both bearing date June 4, 1891. The schedules submitted by Senor Galvan were accepted with the exception of the following sentence, which is omitted from the treaty:
"It is understood that the packages or coverings in which the articles named in the foregoing schedules are imported shall be free of duty if they are usual and proper for the purpose."

records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported on specific assurances given by the Dominican government under the new reciprocity arrangement with the United States. Santo Domingo pledged not to raise export duties on free-list goods, to extend any future export duty reductions to American shipments, and to prevent discriminatory municipal taxes on United States products. The treaty permitted reasonable customs regulations to verify the origin of goods while protecting Dominican revenue without imposing undue restrictions on importers.

El tratado permitía reglamentaciones aduaneras razonables para verificar el origen de las mercancías protegiendo los ingresos fiscales dominicanos, sin imponer restricciones indebidas a los importadores.

RECIPROCITY.
Provisions of the New Trading Arrangement with San Domingo to go into Effect Sept. 1.
NEW YORK, July 30.—A Washington dispatch announces the conclusion of an important treaty of reciprocity between the United States and the republic of San Domingo. The treaty was negotiated by Maquel De J. Galvin, minister plenipotentiary and envoy extraordinary, on the part of San Domingo and John W. Foster, special commissioner, on the part of the United States, and was signed in Washington June 4. Under the terms of the McKinley bill the treaty does not require ratification by the senate. As Senor Galvin was specially authorized by his government to carry on the negotiations and was granted full power to sign the convention the treaty will go into force without delay. September 1 is the day fixed upon. The full text will be officially published within a few days. Both Secretary Blaine and the president have approved the treaty.
Secretary Suarez, of the Dominican legation, has just returned to this city from a flying trip to San Domingo, where he laid the text of the convention before President Heureaux and received his indorsement on July 4. The treaty follows closely the lines laid down in the convention with Brazil. In the opening sections the authority of the McKinley act for the free entry of sugar, molasses, coffee, cocoa and hides is referred to and in reciprocity for these concessions the admission into Dominican ports is authorized of goods enumerated in two schedules which are appended, the one schedule without any duty and the other with a reduction of 25 per cent. upon the duty now levied. In the free schedule are enumerated various breadstuffs, potatoes, hay and oats, pork and fish, cotton-seed oil, agricultural implements, mining and mechanical tools and material for the construction and equipment of railways.
The admission into Dominican ports of a large number of articles with a reduction of 25 per cent. on the present duty is authorized by a clause in the treaty and a schedule appended including cured and canned meats and vegetables, manufactures of cotton, iron and steel not included in the free schedule, unmanufactured leather, lumber, and manufactures of wood, etc.
In exchange for $1,715,000 worth of sugar the United States last year sent to San Domingo a trifle over $925,000 worth of goods which included wheat, flour, lard, cottons, iron and steel manufacture and wood manufactures. A good deal of New England capital is invested in the island.

records.headline: The Democrat prints a geographical description of Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The Democrat prints a geographical description of Santo Domingo and its great bay: the Bay of Samaná, to which the United States has been invited, is at one extreme of the island, in the territory the description calls Dominica, commanding the Mona passage, the principal channel to the Caribbean Sea and the Spanish Main, while the island's northwesternmost point is in Haytian territory. The cape and town of Isabela, where Columbus first established himself, are on the northern coast of Dominica, and the city of Santo Domingo, where he finally planted his colony and where his body rested 240 years after its return from Spain before being taken to Havana, is on the southern coast. The bay is beyond doubt the grandest harbor of the Antilles, extending some thirty miles from east to west by nine or twelve from north to south; the peninsula that forms it is a grand promontory broken into exceedingly steep, irregular hills ranging from a few hundred to 2,000 feet, covered with a dense growth of underbrush, vines, and timber and watered by numerous mountain streams that sometimes fall in beautiful cascades. The predominant rock is limestone, with schistose rocks, quartz, and an abundance of mica slate also occurring, and bituminous coal is found of exceeding richness.

El cabo y el pueblo de Isabela, donde Colón se estableció primero, están en la costa norte de Dominica, y la ciudad de Santo Domingo, donde finalmente plantó su colonia y donde su cuerpo descansó 240 años tras su devolución desde España antes de ser llevado a La Habana, está en la costa sur. La bahía es sin duda el puerto más grandioso de las Antillas, con unas treinta millas de este a oeste por nueve o doce de norte a sur; la península que la forma es un gran promontorio quebrado en colinas sumamente escarpadas e irregulares que van de unos pocos cientos a 2,000 pies, cubiertas de densa maleza, enredaderas y bosques y regadas por numerosos arroyos de montaña que a veces caen en hermosas cascadas. La roca predominante es la caliza, con rocas esquistosas, cuarzo y una abundancia de esquisto micáceo también presentes, y se encuentra carbón bituminoso de extraordinaria riqueza.

records.headline: The Times tells how the remains of Columbus came to rest in the cathedral of San Domingo
records.summary_en: The Times tells how the remains of Columbus came to rest in the cathedral of San Domingo in the Dominican Republic: in 1795, when the eastern part of the island came under French dominion, the Spaniards exhumed from the vaults of the cathedral a coffin they judged contained the body of Columbus and transferred it to Havana. But in 1877 a new vault was discovered in San Domingo, near that opened in 1795, and the coffin found in it bore inscriptions which showed that the mortal remains of Christopher Columbus were certainly contained in it; the body previously exhumed was that of his son Diego. At present the mortal part of the illustrious navigator still reposes in the cathedral of San Domingo, capital of the Dominican Republic and one of the most ancient cities founded in America by Europeans; his principal descendant today is the Duke of Veragua, a grandee of Spain, who has confided to the Academy of Madrid the task of awarding in 1892 a prize of $6,000 to the author of the best history of his immortal ancestor.

Pero en 1877 se descubrió en San Domingo una nueva bóveda, cerca de la abierta en 1795, y el ataúd hallado en ella llevaba inscripciones que demostraban que los restos mortales de Cristóbal Colón estaban ciertamente contenidos en él; el cuerpo exhumado anteriormente era el de su hijo Diego. En la actualidad, la parte mortal del ilustre navegante reposa aún en la catedral de San Domingo, capital de la República Dominicana y una de las ciudades más antiguas fundadas en América por europeos; su principal descendiente hoy es el duque de Veragua, grande de España, que ha confiado a la Academia de Madrid la tarea de premiar en 1892 con $6,000 al autor de la mejor historia de su inmortal antepasado.

RESOLUTIONS OF INQUIRY—PROVISION FOR COMMITTEE CLERKS.
Washington, Jan. 13.—In the House to-day Mr. Wise, of Virginia, offered a resolution authorizing the Committee on Interstate and Foreign Commerce to sit during the sessions of the House, to send for persons and papers, and to administer oaths in pursuing inquiry touching any matter of proposed legislation referred to it. Mr. Bynum, of Indiana, said that no such power had ever before been conferred upon a committee. He suggested that the latter part of the resolution be eliminated; and this was acceded to by Mr. Wise. The resolution as amended was adopted.
Mr. Stone, of Kentucky, offered a resolution (which was agreed to) calling on the Secretary of the Treasury for a tabular statement of all goods imported into Porto Rico and the Dominican Republic since the reciprocity treaty went into effect. Also a resolution (which was agreed to) calling on the Secretary of State for copies of all communications between the United States and those countries, Cuba, Salvador and Brazil on the subject of reciprocity.

THE TRADE TREATIES.
Representative STONE, of Kentucky, has introduced in Congress a resolution, which was adopted, calling upon the secretary of the treasury for a tabular statement of all goods imported into Porto Rico and the Dominican republic under the operation of the reciprocity treaty, and upon the secretary of state for copies of all communications between the United States and Spain, San Salvador and Brazil on the subject of reciprocal trade relations with the United States. The aim of this is to ascertain whether there has been any practical benefit to our people from reciprocity as applied to these nations.
The scope of the proposed inquiry is a limited one. It might very well be applied to all the Central and South American countries, and no doubt will eventually be extended to embrace the whole of them. There is little doubt that this country is paying, or is proposing to pay, dear for the much-vaunted reciprocity whistle, and that the reciprocal trade relations mean a market for manufactures and products of our coast states, without material benefits to western agriculturists, merchants and people generally.
The latest treaty is with San Salvador and gives it, free of duty, all kinds of machinery, agricultural implements, lumber, wagons, iron and steel products, furnaces, building material, coal, fruits, cereals, and preparations of flour, all of which when imported into the United States are taxed from 35 to 100 per cent. In none of the reciprocity treaties is taxation reduced upon articles brought to the United States.
It is to be hoped that a complete overhauling will be given by Congress to the whole business of negotiating these treaties and the effect they have had and are likely to have upon our commerce.

EFFECTS WITH VARIOUS COUNTRIES.
Mr. Hale went on to state the effects of the reciprocity arrangements made with Brazil, Cuba and Porto Rico, the Dominican Republic, Germany, the Hawaiian Islands and the British West Indian colonies. As to Brazil, he said that the increased trade with that country of nearly $2,000,000 in the last seven or eight months indicated unerringly that the United States would under that arrangement maintain a trade with Brazil that would bring American exportations to that country nearly or quite up to the importations from it. As to Cuba, he said that the passage of the reciprocity provision in the tariff bill brought the Cuban sugar planter face to face with the question whether new advantages should be given to the trade of the United States by him or he should see his own industry ruined and his plantation abandoned. When that negotiation was opened the representatives of the State Department found the Spanish government fully impressed with the belief that the power given to the President by section 2 of the tariff act would never be enforced.
THE TREATY WITH SPAIN.
All of the arguments originally advanced against the amendment and the articles in democratic newspapers predicting that nothing would come of it had been carefully gathered by the Spanish authorities, and the United States negotiators were told that Spain and Cuba had expected the benefit of free sugar without being obliged to give anything in return; but when they were assured that the President would carry the law into execution in good faith, the Spanish government at once entered upon the negotiation of an arrangement which culminated in a treaty having two sets of provisions. Large favors had been obtained, especially for American agricultural products. All kinds of meats, heretofore paying heavy duties, were now admitted to Cuba entirely free. Lard, which had been sent to Cuba to the extent of nearly $2,500,000 a year under a duty of 4 1/2 cents a pound, was now admitted free. The exportation of lard would now be increased enormously. So also with fish (fresh and salt), oats, barley, rye, cotton-seed oil, hay, fruits (fresh and preserved), vegetables, all kinds of wood and lumber, wagons, sewing machines, raw petroleum and coal. Then, as to flour, the duty, providing which had been $5.61 per barrel, (equivalent to prohibition) had been reduced to about ninety cents a barrel. With this small duty, the cheapness of American flour and the advantage in freights by nearness of the market this country was given a complete monopoly of the Cuban flour market and the industry of the Spanish wheat grower and miller had been in effect destroyed. The added trade gained with Cuba alone on this would prove the wisdom of the reciprocity feature of the tariff act of 1890. The same results applied to corn and cornmeal, the duties of which had been reduced from 66 cents per 100 kilograms to 11 cents, making it a mere nominal tax and giving to the United States complete control of the market in these articles.
THE POLITICAL FUTURES OF SPANISH ISLANDS.
The good effects of this treaty touched the political futures of these islands of the Spanish main as well as the commercial future. The control which under this treaty the United States would have of the commerce of Cuba would lead more largely to the investment of American capital in that island. It would attach Cuba more and more to the United States. It would make it less dependent upon Spain and less valuable to her as a colony, because heretofore it had been kept largely as a market for Spanish goods. When Cuba ceased to have commercial or financial value for Spain the interests of that country in its possession would diminish and Cuba would naturally attain independence or become a part of the great United States system. Reciprocity with American republics and American colonies brought them all nearer to the United States in every way.
In reply to questions from Mr. Vest Mr. Hale explained that the new treaty with Spain would not take full effect until July, 1892, but that in the meantime there was a transitory arrangement in force.
THE DOMINICAN REPUBLIC.
As to the Dominican Republic, Mr. Hale said that although its trade was small it was important that that republic should be included in the scope of the new treaties. The fourth reciprocity arrangement, he said, had been concluded with Germany and was important both in a commercial and a political and a commercial view. A reduction of duty on a very important list of American agricultural products had been obtained. One immediate effect of the reciprocity provision of the tariff act, so far as Germany was concerned, in the power given to the President to levy duty on German sugar was to bring about an agreement removing the prohibition on American pork into German ports in September last, and this had been followed by Sweden and Norway, Denmark, France, Italy and Austria. It was here as in Cuba and in Brazil that the tremendous leverage of the power of the President to reimpose the duty on sugar had worked and brought about these concessions to American trade.

records.summary_en: *The Morning Call* reported on the United States Navy's strategic interest in acquiring a coaling station at Samaná Bay, highlighting its superior harbor and its commanding position along shipping routes to a future Nicaragua canal. However, the correspondent noted that complications existed because the Samaná Bay Company held prior treaty claims, necessitating that the State Department resolve the company's damage claims against the Dominican government before securing a title.
records.summary_es: *The Morning Call* informó sobre el interés estratégico de la Armada de los Estados Unidos en adquirir una estación carbonera en la bahía de Samaná, destacando su magnífico puerto y su posición dominante a lo largo de las rutas de navegación hacia un futuro canal de Nicaragua. Sin embargo, el corresponsal señaló que existían complicaciones debido a que la Samaná Bay Company poseía reclamos derivados de tratados previos, lo que exigía que el Departamento de Estado resolviera los reclamos por daños y perjuicios de la compañía contra el gobierno dominicano antes de asegurar un título de propiedad.
records.passage: our Government has kept aloof. "Now, however, the United States has a navy and it is necessary to provide coaling stations for it. It finds that the bay of Samana is the most available point at which to coal its vessels, because of its excellent advantages from a marine point of view. Engineers have declared it to be the best place for a coaling station in the whole West Indies, as it is easily approached without danger from reefs or shoals, while it is a matter of peril to undertake to reach many of the other islands, so hemmed in are they by dangers to the navigator. "Another thing, the station is in the direct line to the Nicaragua canal and, when that shall have been opened to navigation, there will be no better point from which it can be readily reached from the East. It is a good place for a war-vessel to lie while awaiting orders or for any other purpose, as it is the healthiest of all the islands of the West Indian group. While the rumors prompted alarm in Haiti and diplomatic inquiries from Germany, France, and Britain, the United States State Department issued a formal denial, clarifying that no cession had occurred or was being sought.

Washington, June 8. — The report from Paris that Samana Bay, Santo Domingo, has been ceded to the United States is officially denied at the State Department. An officer of that Department said this afternoon that no such cession has been made to or is sought by this Government, and that Minister Durham has not taken up a permanent residence in Santo Domingo and is probably on his way to Hayti, being accredited to both countries. The official added that whatever excitement or uneasiness prevails in San Domingo is in no wise due to any action on the part of the United States. THE CAUSE OF THE AUSTRIAN MINE DISASTER. Vienna, June 8. — The Austrian Social Democratic Congress has made a report on the Birkenberg mine disaster, in which it is alleged that the immense loss of life in the mine was due to the officials driving the miners back from the shaft when they were trying to escape just after the fire broke out. These officials, the report declares, told the men there was no danger.

records.full_text: PARIS, June 8.—A dispatch received in this city from Kingston, Jamaica, states that great excitement has been caused in San Domingo by the announcement that the report that Samana Bay, in the eastern part of the terminus of the Sanchez Lavega Railway, Dominican Republic, had been ceded to the United States had been confirmed. The Haitian Minister, the dispatch adds, has become alarmed, owing to the fact that Mr. John S. Durham, the American Minister to Haiti and Charge d'Affaires to San Domingo, has taken a residence at the city of San Domingo. The Haitian Consul at Port au Prince, the dispatch further says, has received instructions from his Government to state to the representatives of France and England regarding the state of affairs in the Dominican Republic, and it is added that the report has caused great uneasiness in Haiti.

records.full_text:
The United States Buys Samana Bay.

PARIS, June 8.—A dispatch from Kingston, Jamaica, says great excitement was caused in San Domingo by the announcement that the port of Samana bay, in the western part of the island, had been ceded to the United States and the cession confirmed. The Haitian minister is alarmed, owing to the fact that American Minister Durham, of Haiti, who is in charge of affairs at San Domingo, has taken residence in the city of San Domingo. The German consul at Port-au-Prince has received instructions to come to an understanding with the representatives of France and England with regard to taking steps to safeguard the autonomy of San Domingo.

[Samana bay is on the south side of the peninsula of Samana. It is about forty-three miles in length from east to west, by about eight miles broad, and at its west end receives the Yuma, the largest river in the Dominican republic. It forms one of the finest harbors in the world, and may be regarded as a most important maritime position, in reference to the trade of the Gulf of Mexico and the interoceanic routes across Central America, both in a commercial and military point of view.]

records.summary_en: *The National Tribune* reported that European nations lodged diplomatic protests against the United States-Dominican reciprocity treaty, demanding identical trade privileges under existing most-favored-nation pacts. The Dominican government defended the treaty, explaining that special concessions were necessary because the United States accounted for the majority of Dominican trade and provided essential markets for its sugar, coffee, and hides. Facing persistent European pressure, President Heureaux appealed to Washington for diplomatic backing.

El gobierno dominicano defendió el tratado explicando que las concesiones especiales eran necesarias debido a que Estados Unidos representaba la mayor parte del comercio dominicano y ofrecía mercados fundamentales para su azúcar, café y cueros. Ante la persistente presión europea, el presidente Heureaux apeló a Washington en busca de respaldo diplomático.

The story of the persecution of the "Black Republic" by the European powers mentioned — for "persecution" the State Department officials call it — is an interesting one, and dates back one year, when negotiations looking to the ratification of the reciprocity treaty between that country and the United States were concluded. The European powers mentioned above followed these negotiations with a jealous eye, as they were the only countries outside of the United States which had any considerable commerce with the island, and it was very manifest that the adoption of such a favorable treaty would give our country a practical monopoly of San Domingo's import trade. These Nations at first protested individually, and subsequently united in a joint protest, and argued that under their respective treaties with San Domingo each was to be placed on a similar footing to that enjoyed by any other Nation with whom the Republic might form a treaty. Harrison reported that successful reciprocal trade agreements under Section 3 of the tariff act had been concluded with numerous countries, including the Dominican Republic, Brazil, Spain for its Caribbean colonies, and the German Empire.

Harrison informó que se habían concertado acuerdos comerciales recíprocos exitosos, en virtud de la Sección 3 de la ley arancelaria, con numerosos países, entre ellos la República Dominicana, Brasil, España para sus colonias caribeñas y el Imperio alemán.
records.passage: lished and maintained for their protection and comfort. Our relations with other nations are now undisturbed by any serious controversy. Commercial Agreements. A treaty providing for the arbitration of the dispute between Great Britain and the United States as to the killing of seals in the Bering sea was concluded on the 29th of February last. records.summary_en: The *St. Paul Daily Globe* detailed the collapse of the Dutch Westendorp concession, which had issued millions in bonds to finance a railway between Puerto Plata and Santiago that remained largely unbuilt. Facing default and exhausted credit, the Dutch financiers negotiated a transfer of their Dominican debt claims and customs-collection rights to an American syndicate organized by New York financiers.
records.summary_es: El *St. Paul Daily Globe* detalló el colapso de la concesión holandesa Westendorp, que había emitido millones en bonos para financiar un ferrocarril entre Puerto Plata y Santiago que permanecía en su mayor parte sin construir. Ante la suspensión de pagos y el agotamiento del crédito, los financieros holandeses negociaron la transferencia de sus reclamaciones sobre la deuda dominicana y de sus derechos de recaudación aduanera a un consorcio estadounidense organizado por financistas neoyorquinos.
records.passage: be emitted by the Amsterdam financiers. They floated the bonds at [illegible] per cent of the face value with interest at [illegible] per cent. The purpose of the bonds was internal improvements. San Domingo languishes because she has not modern methods of transportation from the interior to the seaboard. A railway between Puerto Plata and Santiago de Los Caballeros, an inland city, has long been the subject of discussion. The bonds were issued to complete and equip the railway. Only about eleven miles of road are finished, and in addition to the first $6,000,000 of bonds the country has become responsible for about $1,800,000 additional. The export and import duties amount to about $1,200,000 per annum. Of course work on the railway ceased and, as there was no credit to be obtained, San Domingo was left in the condition of a man who wishes to borrow without available collateral. "The Dutchmen became weary of waiting, and last winter a representative of the Westerndorps crossed to New York to ascertain if the San Domingo claims could not be transferred to citizens of the great republic. records.headline: Madrid, Feb., 20.—The Minister of the Colonies has received a dispatch
records.summary_en: A Madrid dispatch says the Captain-General of Cuba reported great popular excitement in Santo Domingo over the concession of the customs, with an accompanying grant of land, to an American syndicate, with President Heureaux fiercely denounced and every sign of an imminent revolution. A Spanish vessel had left Cuba for Santo Domingo to protect Spanish interests, amid fears the concession was only a prelude to a United States attempt on Dominican independence, and Madrid had asked for specific information before deciding whether to send a protest to Washington.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de Madrid dice que el capitán general de Cuba informó de una gran agitación popular en Santo Domingo por la concesión de las aduanas, con una cesión de tierras que la acompañaba, a un consorcio estadounidense, con el presidente Heureaux fieramente denunciado y todos los indicios de una revolución inminente. Un buque español había salido de Cuba rumbo a Santo Domingo para proteger los intereses españoles, ante el temor de que la concesión fuera solo el preludio de un intento de los Estados Unidos contra la independencia dominicana, y Madrid había pedido información específica antes de decidir si enviaría una protesta a Washington.
records.passage: Madrid, Feb. 20. — The Minister of the Colonies has received a dispatch from Rodriguez Arias, Captain-General of Cuba, stating that great popular excitement prevails in Santo Domingo, in consequence of the concession of the customs, with an accompanying grant of land, to an American syndicate. General Heureaux, the President of Santo Domingo, is fiercely denounced by the people, and there is every sign of a revolution being imminent. A Spanish vessel has left Cuba for Santo Domingo to protect Spanish interests in the Republic. The excitement among the people of Santo Domingo is based on a fear that the concession to the syndicate is only a prelude to an attempt by the United States upon Dominican independence. The telegram from Captain-General Arias hints at interference by the United States in Dominican affairs. The Minister of the Colonies has sent a cable dispatch to the Captain-General asking for specific information as to any action [illegible] the United States [illegible] and the decision whether or not the Spanish Government will send a protest to Washington against any course on the part of the United States that intrenches upon or menaces the independence of Santo Domingo. records.summary_en: *The Indianapolis Journal* reported that Dominican President Ulises Heureaux moved ruthlessly to crush a suspected conspiracy by ordering the summary arrest and execution of prominent political opponents in the capital. In one raid, government troops surrounded the residence of Dr. Theick, fatally shooting his wife and servants, while Theick narrowly escaped through a window and fled abroad to Jamaica.
records.summary_es: *The Indianapolis Journal* informó que el presidente dominicano Ulises Heureaux actuó de manera despiadada para aplastar una supuesta conspiración al ordenar el arresto sumario y la ejecución de prominentes opositores políticos en la capital. En una redada, tropas gubernamentales rodearon la residencia del Dr. Theick, matando a tiros a su esposa y a sus sirvientes, mientras que Theick escapó milagrosamente por una ventana y huyó al extranjero rumbo a Jamaica.
records.passage: for some time that he would strike a blow which he hoped would crush the opposition and put an end to the plot against him. A few days ago President Heureaux discovered what he announced was a conspiracy against him, with which many leading men of the Dominican capital were alleged to be connected. President Heureaux ordered that all the leaders of the conspiracy be arrested and shot. Soldiers were sent to surround the residences of all the suspected persons. Dr. Theick's house was one of the first visited. When the soldiers appeared he knew their visit meant death to himself, and he hastened preparations to escape. The soldiers opened fire and riddled Mrs. Theick and the servants with bullets. The Doctor leaped from a window, mounted a horse and fled. He made his way to Cape Hayti, and from there sailed to Kingston, reaching here in safety. His own departure was so hurried that he did not learn the fate of the other men whom Heureaux had sentenced to death. Generals Arnaux and Momplasier, exiles from Hayti, have been arrested here by order of the government of Jamaica. They are accused of violating international law by fitting out and arming a vessel in August, 1893, to be employed in ousting Hippolyte from the presidency of the black republic. General Momplasier was formerly Minister of the Interior of Hayti. Senator Morgan Recovering. Southampton, March 7. The condition of Senator John T. records.headline: A Paris dispatch of March 20 in the Tribune reports the rumor of French troops
records.summary_en: A Paris dispatch of March 20 in the Tribune reports the rumor of French troops and its denial: nothing is known in Paris to confirm the advices said to have been received in Madrid to the effect that French troops had landed in San Domingo. The concern felt in government circles at Madrid in regard to a French or American intervention in the Dominican Republic has been caused probably, the dispatch says, by the reading of dispatches published in a New-York paper on March 7, according to which a man whose nationality the dispatch does not indicate had arrived at Kingston, Jamaica, and related there that soldiers had been sent by President Heureaux to capture him, as he was accused of conspiring against the Dominican Government, and that he had succeeded in escaping by a back door while his wife and children were riddled by the bullets of the troops. This story has not yet been denied or confirmed; at any rate, the dispatch says, it is certain that no American intervention or 'aggression,' as the Madrid cable dispatch puts it, has occurred in Santo Domingo. As to the report that French troops had been landed there, it is denied from Paris; the only foundation for such a report may be found in a rumor recently circulated in the naval circles of the French: the window closes within the sentence.

records.summary_en: *The Sun* commented on Spanish apprehensions regarding the Dominican Republic, asserting that Spain could neither re-establish colonial control nor prevent voluntary annexation by the United States. The editorial noted that under the Monroe Doctrine, European powers—including Spain and France—were strictly barred from acquiring territory or interfering in the political destinies of New World republics.
records.summary_es: *The Sun* comentó sobre los temores españoles respecto a la República Dominicana, aseverando que España no podía restablecer el control colonial ni impedir una anexión voluntaria por parte de los Estados Unidos. El editorial señalaba que, en virtud de la Doctrina Monroe, a las potencias europeas —incluidas España y Francia— se les prohibía terminantemente adquirir territorios o intervenir en los destinos políticos de las repúblicas del Nuevo Mundo.

The annexation of San Domingo is nowhere talked of or dreamed of here at the present time, but does Spain imagine that if the people of the United States and the people of San Domingo wished to join fortunes she would have the right or power to prevent it? On the other hand, if the secret of this otherwise inexplicable [illegible] in Madrid is the [illegible] on the part of Spain to regain her old control in San Domingo, she may as well abandon it. She could not be suffered to acquire as her own either the eastern or the western part of the Island. That would conflict with American policy as embodied in the Monroe doctrine. This policy and doctrine, however, may relieve Spain from her latest source of anxiety — the supposed designs of France upon San Domingo. For it does not even accord to France the right to transfer to herself Cuba, which is now not free but under European domination. records.headline: Sage to Congress after the rejection of the An nexation treaty
records.summary_en: The *St. Croix Avis* revisited President Grant's arguments for annexing the Dominican Republic, emphasizing its heightened relevance with the planned construction of the Nicaragua Canal. The article argued that acquiring Santo Domingo and its strategic harbor at Samaná Bay would enable the United States to safeguard the Mona Passage and counterbalance British naval influence in the Caribbean.
records.summary_es: El *St. Croix Avis* retomó los argumentos del presidente Grant a favor de la anexión de la República Dominicana, destacando su creciente relevancia ante la proyectada construcción del canal de Nicaragua. El artículo sostenía que la adquisición de Santo Domingo y de su puerto estratégico en la bahía de Samaná permitiría a los Estados Unidos proteger el paso de la Mona y contrarrestar la influencia naval británica en el Caribe.
records.passage: sage to Congress after the rejection of the Annexation treaty, President Grant said: The acquisition of San Domingo is an adherence to the Monroe Doctrine; it is a measure of national protection; it is asserting our just claim to a controlling influence over the great commercial traffic soon to flow from west to east by way of the Isthmus of Darien. So convinced am I of the advantage to flow from the acquisition of San Domingo, and of the great disadvantages — I might almost say calamities — to flow from non-acquisition, that I believe the subject has only to be investigated to be approved. The building and control of the Nicaragua Canal by this government immensely increases the importance of the consideration urged by the patriotic President in favour of bringing the Dominican republic under the Stars and Stripes. Great Britain has Jamaica to command that waterway. With San Domingo in our possession we could promptly checkmate any hostile designs against the canal in case of war. It commands Mona Passage, through which lies the direct route of European commerce from the Atlantic to the Caribbean Sea and the coasts of South and Central America. Samana Bay offers a safe and commodious harbour, one of the finest in the world, whose entrance is guarded by cliffs and coral reefs on all sides. To obtain San Domingo would be to cut in two the cordon of fortified stations drawn by England from Halifax via the Bermudas and the Bahamas, around our Eastern and Southern coasts. records.summary_en: *The Morning Call* reviewed early United States diplomatic and naval missions to the Dominican Republic, including Lieutenant David D. Porter's 1846 survey of Dominican finances and Samaná Bay's strategic harbors. The paper also recalled the 1851 joint mission of Robert M. Walsh alongside British and French commissioners to negotiate an end to Haitian military incursions against the Dominican Republic.
records.summary_es: *The Morning Call* examinó las primeras misiones diplomáticas y navales de los Estados Unidos en la República Dominicana, incluida la inspección efectuada en 1846 por el teniente David D. Porter sobre las finanzas dominicanas y los puertos estratégicos de la bahía de Samaná. El diario también recordó la misión conjunta de 1851 de Robert M. Walsh junto con comisionados británicos y franceses para negociar el cese de las incursiones militares haitianas contra la República Dominicana.
records.passage: [illegible] dropped anchor off the ancient city of San Domingo, May 6, [illegible]. Lieutenant Porter found the Dominican finances in a deplorable condition. The small amount of specie in the country was in the hands of usurers. The currency consisted of paper and copper tokens, and twenty paper dollars were equivalent to one [illegible] silver. On his return to Washington, Porter made a full report in duplicate, one for the State and the other for the Navy Department, but both of these papers disappeared from the departments prior to the breaking out of the Civil War in 1861. The report was highly favorable in tone, commending the excellent harbor at Samana Bay, and pointing to its strategical advantages as a naval station. In 1851 President Fillmore and Secretary of State Webster commissioned Robert M. Walsh as special agent of the Government to Hayti and San Domingo to co-operate with the British and French commissioners in bringing about a cessation of the warfare that the Haytians had been waging on the peacefully inclined and numerically inferior San Dominicans. The United States steamer Saranac conveyed Commissioner Walsh to Port-au-Prince, where he met the French and English commissioners, and during a stay of some weeks had two interviews with Emperor Faustin I. With the French and English commissioners he then went to San Domingo and reported the results of their negotiations at Hayti to President Baez of the Dominican republic. Perry in negotiating an annexation treaty and a lease for Samaná Bay. The results of General Babcock's examination were deemed favorable to the maintenance of the American policy, and he was instructed to return to San Domingo to aid Raymond H. records.summary_en: *The Seattle Post-Intelligencer* reported that an armed insurgent force led by General Pablo Reyes and Horacio Vásquez crossed from Haiti into Dajabón on March 10 to invade the Dominican Republic. Dominican government forces commanded by Governor Anderson repulsed the invasion, resulting in twelve deaths during the combat. Haitian President Florvil Hyppolite cooperated by disarming the retreating insurgents and deporting their leaders aboard the steamer *Ozama* to Turks Island.
records.summary_es: *The Seattle Post-Intelligencer* informó que una fuerza insurgente armada encabezada por el general Pablo Reyes y Horacio Vásquez cruzó desde Haití hacia Dajabón el 10 de marzo para invadir la República Dominicana. Las fuerzas gubernamentales dominicanas, comandadas por el gobernador Anderson, repelieron la invasión, con un saldo de doce muertos durante el combate. El presidente haitiano Florvil Hyppolite cooperó desarmando a los insurgentes en retirada y deportando a sus líderes a bordo del vapor *Ozama* hacia las islas Turcas.
records.passage: AN EPHEMERAL REVOLUTION. How the Late Invasion of San Domingo Was Squelched. NEW YORK, April 2. — Advices from Cape Haytien, under the date of March 26, say: An invasion of Santo Domingo occurred at Dajabon, on the borders between Santo Domingo and Haiti, on March 10. The attacking force consisted of [illegible] men, under the insurgent leaders, Gen. Pablo Reyes, R. Vasquez and others. Two men were killed. The insurgents were repulsed by a force of 200 Dominican soldiers, led by Gov. Anderson, of Samana, and aides, and ten of the Dominicans lost their lives. By order of President Hyppolite, of Haiti, the insurgents were disarmed and brought here. The rebels, including Gens. Pablo Reyes and H. records.headline: The Bee prints news from Santo Domingo of an insurrection against President Heureaux
records.summary_en: The Bee prints news from Santo Domingo of an insurrection against President Heureaux and of the issue the insurrectionists raise: a statement quoted in the report says that troops are massed on the border of Santo Domingo, but that the writer is also officially informed this is only a measure of caution and there is no danger of a battle. News of a more serious nature has been received, however, from Santo Domingo: it is said that under the leadership of General Ygnacio Ma. Gonzales, the discontented citizens of that republic have started an insurrection against President Heureaux. Gonzales was secretary of foreign affairs under the previous administration, which retired February 27. The issue raised by the insurrectionists is opposition to the supposed policy of annexation to the United States: Gonzales had circulated reports that President Heureaux is scheming for the annexation of the republic. The majority of the citizens of Santo Domingo, the report adds, oppose any change of government.
records.summary_es: El Bee publica noticias de Santo Domingo sobre una insurrección contra el presidente Heureaux y sobre la cuestión que los insurrectos plantean: una declaración citada en el informe dice que hay tropas apostadas en la frontera de Santo Domingo, pero que el autor está también informado oficialmente de que esto es solo una medida de precaución y que no hay peligro de batalla. Sin embargo, se han recibido noticias de naturaleza más grave de Santo Domingo: se dice que, bajo la dirección del general Ygnacio Ma. Gonzales, los ciudadanos descontentos de esa república han iniciado una insurrección contra el presidente Heureaux. Gonzales fue secretario de Relaciones Exteriores bajo la administración anterior, que se retiró el 27 de febrero. La cuestión planteada por los insurrectos es la oposición a la supuesta política de anexión a los Estados Unidos: Gonzales había hecho circular noticias de que el presidente Heureaux trama la anexión de la república. La mayoría de los ciudadanos de Santo Domingo, añade el informe, se opone a cualquier cambio de gobierno.

records.summary_en: *The Morning Call* reported that President Ulises Heureaux toured Dominican border outposts while Haitian President Hyppolite cracked down on Dominican dissidents. Hyppolite arrested and expelled General Gregorio Luperón and other insurgent leaders from Haitian soil, calling upon Heureaux to reciprocate by apprehending and deporting Haitian dissidents seeking refuge in the Dominican Republic.
records.summary_es: *The Morning Call* informó que el presidente Ulises Heureaux recorrió los puestos fronterizos dominicanos mientras el presidente haitiano Hyppolite reprimía a los disidentes dominicanos. Hyppolite arrestó y expulsó del territorio haitiano al general Gregorio Luperón y a otros cabecillas insurgentes, instando a Heureaux a corresponder deteniendo y deportando a los disidentes haitianos que buscaran refugio en la República Dominicana.
records.passage: to Preserve the Peace. Puerto Plata, San Domingo, April 10. — President Heureaux is on a tour of inspection of the Dominican outposts on the frontier of Hayti. News has been received here that President Hyppolite, after his arrival at Cape Haytien, arrested Luperon and other Dominican rebel leaders. He made them leave the republic, their forces were disarmed and the leaders escorted under a strong guard to the frontier. Hippolyte then sent a message to President Heureaux requesting him to reciprocate in maintaining the peace of both republics. Kingston, Jamaica, April 10. — The Commandant at Aux Cayes has been arrested here on a charge of conspiring with Manigate and others to start a revolution in Hayti. He has been imprisoned. LANTRY'S LUCK. Baird Made a Will on Board of the Majestic. London, April 10. — The Exchange Telegraph Company says that the property of George Abingdon Baird, or "Squire" Abingdon, will not go intact to his family as has been stated. A will made by Baird aboard the steamer Majestic during his voyage to the United States has been found among his effects, it is said, and under its provisions Mrs. Langtry will receive a large property.

records.summary_en: The *Omaha Daily Bee* reported that Haiti and the Dominican Republic settled their diplomatic disputes after Haitian President Hyppolite apologized and offered indemnity for border raids linked to General Luperón. Presidents Heureaux and Hyppolite formed an alliance barring political exiles from organizing in either nation and pledged to coordinate against foreign aggression. The agreement also stipulated that neither republic would cede naval bases like Samaná Bay or Môle Saint-Nicolas to foreign powers without mutual consent.
records.summary_es: El *Omaha Daily Bee* informó que Haití y la República Dominicana resolvieron sus disputas diplomáticas luego de que el presidente haitiano Hyppolite se disculpara y ofreciera una indemnización por las incursiones fronterizas vinculadas al general Luperón. Los presidentes Heureaux y Hyppolite conformaron una alianza que prohibía a los exiliados políticos organizarse en cualquiera de las dos naciones y se comprometieron a coordinar acciones contra agresiones extranjeras. El acuerdo estipulaba además que ninguna de las dos repúblicas cedería bases navales como la bahía de Samaná o Môle Saint-Nicolas a potencias extranjeras sin consentimiento mutuo.
records.passage: between the two republics were settled. On behalf of Hayti President Hippolyto formally apologized for the encouragement Hayti had given General Luperon in his raid over the Santo Domingo border. He promised to pay indemnity. President Heureaux was satisfied with this apology and promise of indemnity. He has issued orders for the withdrawal of his troops from the border line. Traffic is thus reopened. An alliance was entered into between the two republics by which they agree to deny the right of refuge in either republic to political exiles from the other. Heureaux also enters into alliance to operate with Hayti on all questions of foreign interferences. President Heureaux and the war ship El Presidente have gone to the city of Santo Domingo. Hippolyto's forces that were massed about Cape Haytien have started on their return to Port-au-Prince. Hippolyte, his cabinet and his family will remain at Cape Haytien and return the visit of Heureaux in August. The German man-of-war [Gneisenau?] has sailed for Cuba. The United States ship Kearsarge is the only foreign war vessel now in these waters. Under the agreement between Presidents Hippolyto and Heureaux all hope of Europe securing either Samana Bay or the Mole St. Nicholas as a coaling station is lost. The treaty has been revised, and under the terms the presidents of the republics are bound not to cede either port without the consent of the other. records.headline: The Sun argues in an editorial against Spain attacking Dominica
records.summary_en: The Sun argues in an editorial against Spain attacking Dominica over the Cuban recruits: we would not like to see Spain attack Dominica because recruits for the Cuban revolutionary force have been raised there. Spain has the right to drive away, capture, or destroy any hostile vessel that may approach Cuban shores from any quarter, but she had better not attack Dominica for failing to prevent the departure from Samaná of an unfriendly transport, any more than she would attack Jamaica for a like failure, or Mexico, or the United States. The Dominican Republic is a very feeble institution, but if it were attacked by any foreign government, that government might find itself involved in serious complications; Spain can work her will in Cuba and Porto Rico, but nowhere else on this side of the sea.

records.headline: Under the head 'Columbus' Remains,' the Courier prints the letter of F. L. Vasquez of the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: Under the head 'Columbus' Remains,' the Courier prints the letter of F. L. Vasquez of the Dominican Republic to the American press, dated at New York, May 2: in reference to the story from Chicago that an attempt had been made to steal the ashes of Columbus, said to be deposited in the convent of La Rabida, Vasquez declares it officially that the precious remains of Columbus are now in the city of San Domingo, honored and guarded with jealous reverence and care as a sacred obligation by the government he has the honor to represent. His government, he writes, has rejected with indignation several propositions to remove the remains, and will always look upon any suggestion of that kind as unworthy of serious consideration; a magnificent monument in the principal plaza of San Domingo, in front of the cathedral, is to be erected, where it is hoped the sacred relic will rest undisturbed for many centuries to come. That the remains of Columbus are in San Domingo, he concludes, is indisputable, the evidence therefor being so ample and conclusive that no intelligent person who examines it can thereafter entertain the slightest doubt.
records.summary_es: Bajo el título «Columbus' Remains», el Courier publica la carta de F. L. Su gobierno, escribe, ha rechazado con indignación varias proposiciones de trasladar los restos, y siempre considerará cualquier sugerencia de esa clase como indigna de seria consideración; un magnífico monumento en la plaza principal de San Domingo, frente a la catedral, habrá de erigirse, donde se espera que la sagrada reliquia descanse sin perturbación por muchos siglos venideros. Que los restos de Colón están en San Domingo, concluye, es indiscutible, siendo la evidencia al respecto tan amplia y concluyente que ninguna persona inteligente que la examine podrá abrigar después ni la menor duda.

records.headline: The Eagle reprints an extract by Carl Schurz from Harper's Magazine
records.summary_en: The Eagle reprints an extract by Carl Schurz from Harper's Magazine, carrying the expansionist argument in its own terms: if we do not take Cuba, some other power will take it, and that power may be hostile; let us take it ourselves. Santo Domingo is only a few miles distant from Cuba, also a country of rich resources; other powers several times tried to get it; if in the hands of a hostile power it would 'threaten' Cuba; it also 'commands' the Caribbean Sea; the Dominican Republic, occupying the larger part of the island, offered to join us once, and will wish to do so again; to acquire the Haitian Republic we shall have to fight; it will cost men and money, but we can easily beat the negroes. We must have Santo Domingo; Puerto Rico will come as a matter of course with Cuba. All the more necessary will it be to have possession of the mainland bordering and 'commanding' the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea on the western side: we must have all the 'keys' to the seas and to the land, or at least as many as we can possibly get, one to protect another, and once well launched on this course we shall hardly find a stopping-place north of the Gulf of Darien, and we shall have an abundance of reasons, one as good as another, for not stopping even there.

Debemos tener Santo Domingo; Puerto Rico vendrá como cosa natural con Cuba. records.headline: The Tribune notes new financial arrangements in Europe for the Dominican debt
records.summary_en: The Tribune notes new financial arrangements in Europe for the Dominican debt and the conversion of its railroad bonds: the financial agent of the San Domingo Government at Brussels, Belgium, has issued a circular inviting the holders of the Dominican Railroad 6 per cents of 1888 to present their titles for conversion into bonds of the Dominican 4 per cent loan. The old coupons, which have not been paid, will be converted into scrip of the same loan. The note comes at a time when cable dispatches announce the approaching triumphal visit of President Heureaux of the Dominican Republic to his former enemy and now great friend, General Hyppolite, President of Hayti.

records.headline: The Press prints the latest advices on the reported uprising
records.summary_en: The Press prints the latest advices on the reported uprising in Santo Domingo and Consul Vasquez's account of it: the latest advices received are to the effect that the movement is well under way and the government has not as yet succeeded in suppressing it, and a general exiled by President Heureux has gone back to San Domingo for the purpose of aiding the insurgents. At New York, December 22, F. L. Vasquez, consul from the Dominican Republic, was asked about the reported uprising against President Ulysse Heureux at San Domingo: he admitted that there was some trouble there, thought it was caused principally by a number of American exiles who are continually plotting against the government, and said he received a cable yesterday afternoon stating that the revolt had taken place but that it has been quickly suppressed and the government is stronger than ever before; the cable, he said, gave no further details, and from an authoritative source he was sure the trouble was at an end.

records.summary_en: *The Jersey City News* reported that Dominican soldiers fired upon a landing boat from the American schooner *Henry Crosby* near Azua, critically wounding a sailor and injuring the first officer. The schooner's captain sailed to Azua and filed a formal report with the United States Consul General in Santo Domingo, who forwarded the complaint to Washington. The unprovoked attack was believed to have resulted from soldiers mistaking the crew for insurgents attempting to land and overthrow President Heureaux.
records.summary_es: *The Jersey City News* informó que soldados dominicanos abrieron fuego cerca de Azua contra un bote de desembarco de la goleta estadounidense *Henry Crosby*, hiriendo de gravedad a un marinero y lesionando al primer oficial. El capitán de la goleta navegó hacia Azua y presentó un informe formal ante el cónsul general de los Estados Unidos en Santo Domingo, quien remitió la queja a Washington. Se creía que el ataque no provocado se debió a que los soldados confundieron a la tripulación con insurgentes que intentaban desembarcar para derrocar al presidente Heureaux.

records.headline: The Star reviews the quarrel between President Heureaux and France
records.summary_en: The Star reviews the quarrel between President Heureaux and France over the Banco Nacional: it had been declared that the president had broken open the bank and abstracted the cash therein, about 200,000 francs, but the Santo Domingo authorities assert that no money was touched and that the documents abstracted consisted merely of securities deposited against a contract never executed; the president said that he had demanded the return of these documents from the French authorities of the bank and that his application had been refused, and later he himself refused the proposition of the French admiral, De Libran, to deposit the money or the securities in the hands of a responsible third party until arbitration should have decided upon the merits of the case. France, the Star says, was satisfied with sending occasionally one or two men-of-war to maneuver off the Dominican coast and with suspending diplomatic relations; meanwhile Heureaux keeps in prison a French merchant named Bolmare, whose only crime, it is said, is that he started a soap factory in competition with one in which the president had an interest. Heureaux is the more interested in picking no quarrel with the United States on account of the decrease in his financial resources: in 1888 the customs revenues were given in guarantee at Amsterdam to Dutch bankers, who took up a loan whose amount the window does not print legibly; the revenues were stated then as amounting to $1,500,000, they fell to $1,305,101 in 1892, and they are collected by an American syndicate, which has acquired the rights and the concession granted in 1888 to the Amsterdam bankers.

Francia, dice el Star, se contentó con enviar de vez en cuando uno o dos buques de guerra a maniobrar frente a la costa dominicana y con suspender las relaciones diplomáticas; mientras tanto, Heureaux mantiene en prisión a un comerciante francés llamado Bolmare, cuyo único crimen, se dice, es haber establecido una fábrica de jabón en competencia con una en la que el presidente tenía interés. records.summary_en: *The Abbeville Press and Banner* reported that Captain Stubbs of the American schooner *Henry Crosby* anchored near Old Azua after losing his bearings and dispatched a longboat to determine their location. Dominican soldiers on the beach opened fire without warning, striking a sailor in the back of the head and wounding the chief officer. Captain Stubbs proceeded to Azua and lodged a formal complaint with the American consul for transmission to Washington.
records.summary_es: *The Abbeville Press and Banner* informó que el capitán Stubbs, de la goleta estadounidense *Henry Crosby*, fondeó cerca de Azua Vieja tras perder el rumbo y envió un bote para determinar su ubicación. Soldados dominicanos apostados en la playa abrieron fuego sin previo aviso, alcanzando a un marinero en la parte posterior de la cabeza e hiriendo al primer oficial. El capitán Stubbs se dirigió a Azua y presentó una queja formal ante el cónsul estadounidense para su transmisión a Washington.
records.passage: December 11, but the populace of San Domingo City, which is eighty-four miles from Azua, were still talking of the affair when the Clyde came away, two days later. Old Azua harbor is ten miles away from Azua, and in approaching the first named Captain Stubbs, of the Crosby, lost his bearings. His schooner dropped anchor and the captain ordered four of his sailors in the long boat in charge of the chief mate to ascertain the exact position of the craft. As the boat drew near the beach a dozen soldiers in Dominican uniform were seen running toward the surf. Without warning of any kind the men leveled their carbines at the occupants of the long boat and fired. A bullet from the first volley hit one of the rowers in the back of the head, and a second shot from another round laid low the chief officer. The uninjured men then hurried back to the Crosby with their mates. All were thoroughly frightened, but Captain Stubbs was beside himself in anger. He was for going ashore and dealing vengeance then and there. But he weighed anchor instead and went to Azua, where he sent a complaint to the American Consul at St. Domingo City. records.headline: General Heureaux's letter is dated from Azua, where the political outrages
records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported on an official communication from Dominican President Ulises Heureaux to Vice President Figuereo announcing the summary execution of several political opponents. Heureaux stated that General Eugenio Generoso Marchena and five associates were executed at La Clavellina for the murder of a government delegate, while three others were shot at Los Jovillos for attempting to assassinate Heureaux. Seven other accused conspirators were spared execution and transferred to prison in the capital.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* informó sobre una comunicación oficial del presidente dominicano Ulises Heureaux al vicepresidente Figuereo en la que anunciaba la ejecución sumaria de varios opositores políticos. Heureaux declaró que el general Eugenio Generoso Marchena y cinco colaboradores fueron fusilados en La Clavellina por el asesinato de un delegado gubernamental, mientras que otros tres fueron pasados por las armas en Los Jovillos por intentar atentar contra la vida de Heureaux. Otros siete acusados de conspiración se salvaron de la ejecución y fueron trasladados a prisión en la capital.
records.passage: citizens. General Heureaux's letter is dated from Azua, where the political outrages for complicity in which those men met their death occurred, as well as the firing upon the American schooner Henry Crosby, and it is addressed to General Figuereo, Vice-President of the Republic, then acting as Executive at the capital. The document says, among other things: "Having carefully sifted the facts and reached the full conviction of the guilt of the accused of the said ambushes and assassinations, acting with justice and with the consciousness of duty, which impose now hard and painful measures, I gave the order to shoot, in the place called 'La Clavellina,' where General Joaquin Campos, Delegate of the General Government, had been assassinated, General Eugenio Generoso Marchena, José Concha, Oliverio Reyes, José Maria Guzman, José Reyes and Carlos Baez Figueroa. And in the place called 'Los Jovillos,' where was the ambush of those who sought to assassinate me on my journey from Neiba to this city (Azua), I have given orders that José Pérez, Pablo Baez and Lorenzo Brito shall be executed. "Although important documents referring to those occurrences incriminate Senors Alfredo Blandino, Abraham Ortiz, Antonio Romano, Manuel [illegible], Prospero [Freites?], Agapito [Felix?] and José Polin [Reyes?], yet, believing that a sufficient example has been made, I have felt bound not to have them executed, and I have put them in the jail of the capital, where they shall remain until otherwise disposed of." records.passage: The two men, however, decamped at Port de Paix. At this port another Dominican, also a refugee from his own land, was put on the El Callao to be taken to Anagua, but he also left the vessel when she touched at Cape Haytien. A WAR SHIP ON THE WATCH. While the vessel lay off the harbor of Cape Haytien, the officers noticed out toward the island of Tortugas a warlike little steamer of about 800 tons. She was brigantine rigged and was painted black. She was cruising about and seemed to be keeping a sharp lookout on all the shipping. The description is said to answer to that of one of the Haytien gunboats, and it is thought that she may be on the lookout for the two vessels said to have been purchased by the friends of Gen. Manigat to take part in his proposed revolt against the government of Hippolyte. NOTHING HEARD FROM SMYTHE. records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported on escalating authoritarian measures by President Heureaux, who restricted foreign travel and arrested suspected political opponents across the country. Following Heureaux's armed seizure of $60,000 from a French bank, the bank’s Dominican attorney, Jacinto de Castro Peynado, was imprisoned for his arguments during legal proceedings against the government. Additionally, Dominican troops blocked the son of a former Spanish consul from landing in Santo Domingo, threatening him with rifles until he departed on the steamer.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* informó sobre la escalada de medidas autoritarias adoptadas por el presidente Heureaux, quien restringió los viajes al extranjero y arrestó a presuntos opositores políticos en todo el país. Tras la incautación armada por parte de Heureaux de 60.000 dólares de un banco francés, el abogado dominicano de la entidad bancaria, Jacinto de Castro Peynado, fue encarcelado a causa de sus alegatos en los procedimientos judiciales contra el gobierno. Además, tropas dominicanas impidieron el desembarco en Santo Domingo del hijo de un excónsul español, amenazándolo con fusiles hasta que abandonó el lugar a bordo del vapor.

records.headline: The Tribune reports the release of the French soap manufacturer
records.summary_en: The Tribune reports the release of the French soap manufacturer held in San Domingo: the Paris papers say that the French citizen whose case was mentioned in the Tribune of February has been set at liberty after more than one year of imprisonment. He was a soap manufacturer, and consequently a competitor of President Heureaux, who is interested in a soap factory, and he had not done any act justifying his arrest. He was released through the efforts of the Spanish Consul, who has had charge of French affairs in San Domingo since the suspension of diplomatic relations between that Republic and France. President Heureaux, meanwhile, is desirous of avoiding the conflict which threatened to cause a war between his Government and France, while the latest telegraphic dispatches from the Republic of San Domingo report the possibility of a conflict with Spain; he has not yet surrendered the 950,000 francs which he took arbitrarily from the safe of the Banco Nacional, a Franco-Dominican establishment.
records.summary_es: El Tribune informa de la liberación del fabricante de jabón francés detenido en San Domingo: los periódicos de París dicen que el ciudadano francés cuyo caso fue mencionado en el Tribune de febrero ha sido puesto en libertad después de más de un año de prisión. Era un fabricante de jabón, y por consiguiente un competidor del presidente Heureaux, que tiene interés en una fábrica de jabón, y no había hecho ningún acto que justificara su arresto. Fue liberado gracias a las gestiones del cónsul español, que se ha hecho cargo de los asuntos franceses en San Domingo desde la suspensión de las relaciones diplomáticas entre esa República y Francia. El presidente Heureaux, mientras tanto, desea evitar el conflicto que amenazaba con causar una guerra entre su Gobierno y Francia, mientras los últimos despachos telegráficos de la República de San Domingo informan de la posibilidad de un conflicto con España; aún no ha entregado los 950,000 francos que tomó arbitrariamente de la caja fuerte del Banco Nacional, un establecimiento franco-dominicano.

records.headline: The Tribune prints a story from San Domingo, received by way of Panama
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints a story from San Domingo, received by way of Panama and dated March 2, reporting that the two sons of ex-President Baez had been shot by order of President Heureaux: the elder son had previously been sentenced to imprisonment for life for plotting to overthrow the existing government, and when the younger was also discovered to be implicated, Heureaux determined that both should die; soon after the younger Baez's arrest, the President sent word to the Baez family that the two had need of two broadcloth suits. Among the victims, the story adds, was Francis Pintado, an alleged dynamiter, brother of the Spanish consul to San Domingo, who was himself ejected from the island without recourse to diplomatic formalities.
records.summary_es: El Tribune publica un relato de San Domingo, recibido por vía de Panamá y fechado el 2 de marzo, según el cual los dos hijos del expresidente Báez habían sido fusilados por orden del presidente Heureaux: el hijo mayor había sido condenado antes a prisión perpetua por conspirar para derrocar al gobierno existente, y cuando se descubrió que el menor también estaba implicado, Heureaux determinó que ambos debían morir; poco después del arresto del menor de los Báez, el presidente hizo saber a la familia Báez que los dos necesitaban dos trajes de paño fino. Entre las víctimas, añade el relato, estaba Francis Pintado, presunto dinamitero, hermano del cónsul español en San Domingo, quien fue expulsado de la isla sin recurso a formalidad diplomática alguna.

records.headline: The Times prints a story of the execution of the two Baez brothers
records.summary_en: The Times prints a story of the execution of the two Baez brothers in the Dominican Republic: when the younger was also discovered to be implicated in the plot to overthrow the existing government, President Heureaux determined that both should die; soon after the younger's arrest, the President sent word to the Baez family that the two brothers had need of two broadcloth suits — this was on February 2 — and the clothes were sent, and the next morning the youths were told to put the black suits on, and when they had complied they were told that the freedom of the jail yard was given them, and in the yard a squad of soldiers' bullets speedily put an end to their lives. This, it is said, makes twelve martial executions in the Dominican Republic in sixty days; among the twelve was that of Francis Pintado, an alleged dynamiter, brother of the Spanish consul to San Domingo, the consul himself having been ejected from the island without recourse to any of the diplomatic formalities.
records.summary_es: El Times publica un relato de la ejecución de los dos hermanos Báez en la República Dominicana: cuando se descubrió que el menor también estaba implicado en el complot para derrocar al gobierno existente, el presidente Heureaux determinó que ambos debían morir; poco después del arresto del menor, el presidente hizo saber a la familia Báez que los dos hermanos necesitaban dos trajes de paño fino —esto fue el 2 de febrero— y los trajes fueron enviados, y a la mañana siguiente se dijo a los jóvenes que se pusieran los trajes negros, y cuando hubieron obedecido se les dijo que se les concedía la libertad del patio de la cárcel, y en el patio las balas de un pelotón de soldados pusieron fin rápidamente a sus vidas. Esto, se dice, eleva a doce las ejecuciones militares en la República Dominicana en sesenta días; entre los doce estaba la de Francis Pintado, presunto dinamitero, hermano del cónsul español en San Domingo, habiendo sido el propio cónsul expulsado de la isla sin recurso a formalidad diplomática alguna.

records.headline: The Tribune quotes a just-returned traveler's high praise of President Heureaux.
records.summary_en: The Tribune quotes a just-returned traveler's high praise of President Heureaux. 'He is a fine man. He is a born leader and is just the man to lift his country to prosperity. He has a keen sense of moral responsibility. His word is as good as his bond in all contracts, public or private.' The party which has just returned from San Domingo, the item adds, consisted of Smith M. Weed, his son and daughter, W. Brown, Dr. Boyer, Professor J. Lawrence Laughlin, and Charles W. Wells.
records.summary_es: El Tribune cita los grandes elogios de un viajero recién regresado al presidente Heureaux: «Es un hombre excelente. records.summary_en: *The Lusk Herald* reported imminent conflict between France and the Dominican Republic after French warships appeared off Santo Domingo City to take soundings. Heureaux reportedly responded that the Dominican treasury lacked the money to meet the demand.
