records.full_text:
MAY BOMBARD SAN DOMINGO.

France Demands Indemnity for Confiscation of a French Bank.
New York special: A dispatch to the World, dated Puerto Plat, San Domingo, January 18, says:
“Trouble seems imminent between France and the Dominican Republic. A French man of war appeared off San Domingo City a few days ago and began to take soundings. Soon after she departed another appeared. The latter was boarded by a pilot, who was informed that his services were not needed, and when he asked the commander his intention, he was told it was none of his business.”

The San Domingo authorities had a dispute with a bank a few years ago, and eventually took $60,000 from it. The bank was backed by French capitalists, and the bankers laid the case before the French Government. France demanded that the money be returned to the bank, but diplomatic negotiations seem to have resulted in nothing. The World correspondent learns upon trustworthy authority that the French ultimatum has already been sent in and demands the restoration of the $60,000 and $20,000 as indemnity. President Heuraux, it is said, has declared that he has no money to pay it with.

Dispatches for the Britsh Admiral at Jamaica passed this port probably asking him to look after British interests in case of bombardment.

records.headline: The Republican takes the Dominican affair of twenty-five years
records.summary_en: The Republican takes the Dominican affair of twenty-five years ago as its text in an editorial against annexation and the pending Hawaii proposition: the doctrine of the true grandeur of nations, it says, was preached where that other crime against San Domingo and against the principles of republican government was defeated, the hot and inconsiderate defense of the doctrine of national greed and conquest which the junior senator from Massachusetts has given to the country in the parallel case of Hawaii. We predict for these imperialists, the editorial says, the same fate which overtook the jingoists in the Dominican affair 25 years ago: if the proposition to annex an island adjacent to the American coast was then regarded as hostile to republican principles and ruled out of order, what must be said of this pending proposition to reach out 2,000 miles into the Pacific for more territory? It is something not to be listened to by any person who has regard for the safety of republican institutions, and the editorial quotes Washington's Farewell Address against quitting our own ground to stand upon foreign ground.

Es algo que no debe escuchar ninguna persona que se preocupe por la seguridad de las instituciones republicanas, y el editorial cita el discurso de despedida de Washington contra abandonar nuestro propio suelo para pisar suelo extranjero.

records.summary_en: The *Evening Star* reported that the San Domingo Improvement Company appealed to the United States State Department for protection against French naval threats to seize Dominican customs revenues, which were pledged to secure company bonds. Dominican chargé d'affaires Alejandro Wos y Gil and company representative Smith Weed conferred with Secretary of State Walter Q. Gresham, quien posteriormente instruyó al embajador estadounidense en París para que advirtiera a Francia que los Estados Unidos se opondrían a cualquier acción que comprometiera los derechos financieros estadounidenses en Santo Domingo.

The Dominican government has taken no direct action in the matter, and has left it to the company to appeal to the State Department for protection, although the Dominican chargé, Mr. Gil, has accompanied Mr. Smith Weed, the company's representative, to Washington from New York, and has heard the statements he has made to Secretary Gresham. The Secretary has been impressed with the justice of Mr. Weed's claims, and about two weeks ago he cabled to Mr. Eustis, our ambassador to France, and instructed him to inform the French government that the United States could not look with indifference upon its proposed action. He was to represent that an American company had large interests in Santo Domingo, and to express the hope of the United States government that the French government would not be unmindful of the interests of that company in whatever course it pursued. records.headline: The Courier prints a travel sketch of San Domingo, opening with the approach
records.summary_en: The Courier prints a travel sketch of San Domingo, opening with the approach to the city from the sea: as the city of San Domingo, the capital of the Dominican Republic, is approached from the sea, one is struck by the quaintness of an old, dilapidated tower which rises up from a formidable-looking stone wall along the beach, and on coming nearer the wall and tower become plainly noticeable as only a harmless mass of ruins. In order to become thoroughly interested in the place and its ruins, the sketch — printed under the head 'Where Columbus Is Buried' — says, one must go ashore and meet one of the old inhabitants and hear some of his blood-curdling yarns dating back to the times when pirates were bold; and after he has told all the stirring stories he has ever heard, and the relative merits of cock-fighting and bull-fighting have been discussed, and a hope has been expressed that there would soon be another revolution, it becomes comparatively easy to draw the conversation toward Columbus. The window closes in the sketch's opening movement, with the old inhabitant beginning to point out and explain.

records.summary_en: *The Anaconda Standard* recounted the political fallout from President Grant’s attempt to annex Santo Domingo, highlighting the favorable report by commissioners Benjamin Wade, Samuel Gridley Howe, and Andrew D. White. The proposal provoked a fierce Senate battle led by Charles Sumner, causing the treaty’s defeat, a lasting personal breach between Grant and Sumner, and Sumner's removal as chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

La propuesta provocó una encarnizada batalla en el Senado liderada por Charles Sumner, lo que ocasionó el fracaso del tratado, un distanciamiento personal duradero entre Grant y Sumner y la destitución de este último como presidente del Comité de Relaciones Exteriores del Senado.

These gentlemen visited San Domingo. They studied the situation thoroughly, became convinced that President Grant was right and so reported. Then the trouble began. There followed in the senate one of the most ill-tempered debates ever heard in congress. Charles Sumner led in the opposition — he made a terrific attack on the president's conduct; he went farther than most of the senators felt was right. The annexation scheme failed, and the smoke of the battle hung heavily and long. Thereafter General Grant and Senator Sumner had no personal intercourse. A few months afterward, by action of the senate, Sumner lost the chairmanship of the committee on foreign relations, and he refused committee appointments to which he was assigned. From that time until the close of his life Senator Sumner, brilliant as had been his career and splendid his ability, was in an uncomfortable place, although, just as the end was approaching, he appeared to be treated by the republican senators with renewed friendliness. records.headline: The Tribune prints the first part of a published statement by a Dominican exile:
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints the first part of a published statement by a Dominican exile: the barbarous executions ordered by 'the little tyrant Heureaux' in the department of Cibao and the district of Monte Cristi, where universal discontent is openly manifested against the President of the Dominican Republic, who is prolonging unconstitutionally the presidential period from four to eight years with the criminal object of obtaining re-election and continuing in power against the wish of the majority of the nation, resolved the writer at once to go to Hayti, with the idea of crossing over the frontier and uniting himself with the many friends of recognized political importance who have taken refuge in those places, to decide what would be best to do under the circumstances. He therefore embarked, incognito, at Ponce in the steamer Manuela on November 25 last, reaching Puerto Plata on the 26th at 3 p.m., on the same day that the man-of-war Independencia was expected with General Heureaux on board from Sanchez and Samana; continuing his voyage that same afternoon to Cape Haytien, he reached that port on the morning of the 27th and disembarked without inconvenience, and though he had to present himself at the office of the commandant of the port, a strong partisan of Heureaux on account of relationship, he managed to pass through undiscovered, but unfortunately in crossing over from the office to the hotel he was seen and recognized by one of the numerous spies of the Dominican Government who infest that port. The window closes there.

Se embarcó, pues, de incógnito, en Ponce, en el vapor Manuela, el 25 de noviembre pasado, llegando a Puerto Plata el 26 a las 3 p.m., el mismo día en que se esperaba el buque de guerra Independencia con el general Heureaux a bordo, procedente de Sánchez y Samaná; continuando su viaje esa misma tarde hacia Cabo Haitiano, llegó a ese puerto en la mañana del 27 y desembarcó sin inconveniente, y aunque tuvo que presentarse en la oficina del comandante del puerto, un fuerte partidario de Heureaux por razón de parentesco, logró pasar inadvertido, pero desafortunadamente, al cruzar de la oficina al hotel, fue visto y reconocido por uno de los numerosos espías del Gobierno dominicano que infestan ese puerto. La ventana se cierra ahí.

records.headline: The Tribune prints the conclusion of the statement of A. F. Morales
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints the conclusion of the statement of A. F. Morales, dated at St. Thomas in December 1895: it was stated that it was not desirable that the writer should be allowed to go to 'the little English island so near to San Domingo,' and he was therefore kept in prison at the Cape until the next morning, when the German steamer arrived in which they decided to embark him for St. Thomas; but as that steamer had to remain in port several days receiving cargo, the commandant of the port took him on board in the custody of two officers, who conducted him from the prison to the Suevia under a numerous escort. It remains now, he writes, publicly to thank the many Dominicans who came to see him in prison, placing themselves entirely at his service, and also the inhabitants of the Cape for their cordial manifestation of sympathy, accompanying him in great number from the port office to the door of the prison and back again, with many marks of respect and significant murmurs of disapprobation for the servile attitude assumed by the government of Hyppolite in favor of his worthy colleague Heureaux.

records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported that the Spanish government awarded the Grand Cross of Isabel the Catholic to Dominican President Ulises Heureaux in recognition of his friendly neutrality during the Cuban insurrection. Spanish officials valued Heureaux's cooperation in preventing Dominican ports from being used as staging grounds for insurgent filibustering expeditions to Cuba.

Las autoridades españolas valoraron la cooperación de Heureaux para evitar que los puertos dominicanos fueran utilizados como puntos de partida de expediciones filibusteras insurgentes hacia Cuba.

Heureaux. Private letters received since explain the affair in the following manner: Gen. Ramon Castillo, Minister of War, asked President Heureaux some months ago for 1,000 rifles and the necessary ammunition to suppress, as he said, an outbreak against the president, which was going to occur in the province of San Pedro Macori. He described so vividly the importance of the conspiracy, and the urgency of suppressing it with a strong hand, that the 1,000 rifles were given to him, and, besides, he was ordered to go directly to San Pedro Macori and take command of the government forces. He did so, but time passed, and President Heureaux heard no more of the rebel movement. Instead of that, what he heard was that Gen. 'How can I be sentenced to death without a trial? How can I be sentenced without my judge first hearing my defense?' All his pleading was of no avail; the soldiers of El Pacificador fired on him and he fell dead, pierced by several bullets. 'At last justice is done,' exclaimed Jose Estay, when a doctor certified the death of Castillo. 'Not yet, sir,' answered President Heureaux, approaching him. 'Another sentence has to be executed before we can say that justice is satisfied. That sentence is yours, Gen. Jose Estay.' After these words the unfortunate Estay was carried to the place where Castillo was shot and the soldiers of El Pacificador again did their duty. records.summary_en: The Tribune prints an account of the arrangement by which Spanish consuls in the Bahamas act for the government of Santo Domingo: if Spanish consuls in the Bahamas were authorized to act in the name of the Santo Domingo government, they would be able to detect and stop more easily any filibustering expedition organized under Dominican colors, given the known pro-Cuban sympathies of all Dominicans. General Heureaux was much praised by the Havana papers for his devotion to Spanish interests, but the fact is that he was merely using Spanish consuls as his own spies; the Dominican dictator is aware that the people of the island are thoroughly tired of his rule, and that revolutionary attempts will not be delayed much longer, being about to sally forth from some of the Bahama islands, and Heureaux has made the Spanish consuls his own agents and informers, since they act as Dominican consuls and are bound to report to Santo Domingo any information of interest to his government; while the Spaniards proclaim that they have secured an effective ally in the person of General Heureaux, who transfers to them his consular service, the Spanish consular service in the Bahamas will act henceforth for the Dominican dictator, who will be the only one benefited by the arrangement.

records.summary_en: The *Richmond Dispatch* published an account from a former American diplomat concerning an unfinished protocol submitted by Dominican President Ulises Heureaux as the basis for a new treaty. After verbally briefing Secretary Sherman in Washington, the diplomat decided to disclose the details following the acceptance of his resignation. He explained that Heureaux had requested his visit to Santo Domingo in March to receive the proposed terms and related memoranda.
records.summary_es: El *Richmond Dispatch* publicó el relato de un exdiplomático estadounidense acerca de un protocolo inconcluso presentado por el presidente dominicano Ulises Heureaux como base para un nuevo tratado. Tras informar verbalmente al secretario Sherman en Washington, el diplomático decidió revelar los detalles luego de que se aceptara su renuncia. Explicó que Heureaux había solicitado su visita a Santo Domingo en marzo para recibir los términos propuestos y los memorandos pertinentes.
records.passage: THE PROTOCOL. "In answer to your direct question, and with a knowledge of the deep interest you manifest in everything affecting the foreign relations of the United States, I will give you an outline of the unfinished protocol submitted to me by General Heureaux, President of the Dominican republic, for presentation to my government as the basis of a new treaty between the two countries. On my arrival in Washington I made a verbal report to Secretary Sherman, because I had not arranged the memoranda submitted by President Heureaux, and hastily taken in a note-book on the eve of my departure, and the Secretary, who appeared interested in the matter, suggested that I go home, and after I had recruited my strength, make him a formal report as to the proposed convention and the general conditions in Haiti and San Domingo. Now, inasmuch as the acceptance of my resignation, tendered the [illegible] of March, has released me from the obligations of my position, I deem it at least permissible to give you for the press the information you desire, although I can only surmise the source from which you acquired a knowledge of the matter in question. "While at Port-au-Prince in February, I received an official letter from General Heureaux, asking me to visit his capital before returning to this country, to receive an important communication. records.summary_en: The *San Francisco Call* reported that former minister Smythe negotiated the outline of a treaty with President Heureaux granting the United States a coaling station in Santo Domingo free of charge. In return, the Dominican government requested reciprocal coaling privileges in American ports and the removal of U.S. import duties on Dominican sugar. The report highlighted naval experts' views on the strategic necessity of acquiring West Indian coaling stations.
records.summary_es: El *San Francisco Call* informó que el exministro Smythe negoció las bases de un tratado con el presidente Heureaux que concedía a los Estados Unidos una estación carbonera en Santo Domingo de forma gratuita. A cambio, el gobierno dominicano solicitaba privilegios recíprocos de aprovisionamiento de carbón en puertos estadounidenses y la eliminación de los derechos de importación de Estados Unidos sobre el azúcar dominicano. El informe destacó la opinión de expertos navales sobre la imperiosa necesidad estratégica de adquirir estaciones carboneras en las Antillas.

records.summary_en: The *Watertown Republican* reported that the Dominican government offered to grant the United States a naval coaling station without financial cost. According to former diplomat Mr. Smythe, the proposed treaty covered commerce, navigation, extradition, and reciprocity, offering a site at Samana Bay or east of Santo Domingo. The sole condition attached to the concession was that Dominican naval vessels be granted coaling facilities in American ports.
records.summary_es: El *Watertown Republican* informó que el gobierno dominicano ofreció conceder a los Estados Unidos una estación naval carbonera sin costo financiero alguno. Según el exdiplomático Sr. Smythe, el tratado propuesto abarcaba comercio, navegación, extradición y reciprocidad, y ofrecía un emplazamiento en la bahía de Samaná o al este de Santo Domingo. La única condición vinculada a la concesión era que a los buques navales dominicanos se les otorgaran facilidades para aprovisionarse de carbón en puertos estadounidenses.

records.headline: In order that this independence of tho Congress shall bo complete
records.summary_en: The *Evening Bulletin* analyzed legal questions regarding the proposed annexation of Hawaii, citing the Dominican precedent for provisionally maintaining local governance machinery until Congress legislates for a newly incorporated territory. The report outlined how treaties, local statutes, and labor systems would be adapted under American authority. It specifically noted provisions safeguarding congressional authority and prohibiting the entry of Chinese laborers.
records.summary_es: El *Evening Bulletin* analizó cuestiones jurídicas relativas a la proyectada anexión de Hawái, citando el precedente dominicano para mantener de manera provisional la estructura del gobierno local hasta que el Congreso legisle sobre un territorio recién incorporado. El informe describió cómo se adaptarían los tratados, estatutos locales y regímenes laborales bajo la autoridad estadounidense. Señaló específicamente disposiciones que salvaguardaban la autoridad del Congreso y prohibían la entrada de trabajadores chinos.
records.passage: of the annexed territory, the citizenship and elective franchise of its inhabitants and the manner in which laws of the United States are to be extended to the islands. In order that this independence of the Congress shall be complete and unquestionable, and pursuant to the recognized doctrine of public law that treaties expire with the independent life of the contracting state, there has been introduced out of abundant caution an express proviso for the determination of all treaties heretofore concluded by Hawaii with foreign nations and the extension to the islands of the treaties of the United States. This leaves Congress free to deal with such especial regulation of the contract labor system of the islands as circumstances may require. There being no general provision of existing statutes to prescribe the form of Government for newly incorporated territory, it was necessary to stipulate, as in the Dominican precedent, for continuing the existing machinery until provision shall be made by law for the Government, as territory of the United States, of the dominion thus incorporated into the union, but having in view the peculiar status created in Hawaii by laws enacted in execution of the treaties heretofore concluded between Hawaii and other countries, only such Hawaiian laws are thus provisionally continued as shall not be incompatible with the Constitution or the laws of the United States or with the provisions of this treaty. records.headline: The Tribune reprints a Chicago Times-Herald item on the coinage
records.summary_en: The Tribune reprints a Chicago Times-Herald item on the coinage the United States mint makes for foreign governments: the work is being done for the Dominican Republic, and the dollars will be sent to Santo Domingo; the design for the coins was furnished by the Dominican treasury department and in no respect, excepting shape, resembles the dollar of the United States. It has long been the custom of the United States to make the money of several South American countries, the item says, and as an act of comity and good will the work is done at the actual cost of labor and material; the present order from Santo Domingo also includes 800,000 half dollars, 875,000 quarter dollars, and 750,000 dimes; the mint bureau has just filled an order from Costa Rica for a large quantity of gold coins, and so pleased is Costa Rica that it has ordered through its minister at Washington 40,000 more coins of gold; and the first work of this kind done by the United States was in 1876, when $100,000 worth of minor coins were turned out for the government of Venezuela.

Hace mucho que es costumbre de los Estados Unidos hacer el dinero de varios países sudamericanos, dice la nota, y como un acto de cortesía y buena voluntad el trabajo se hace al costo real de la mano de obra y el material; el pedido actual de Santo Domingo incluye también 800,000 medios dólares, 875,000 cuartos de dólar y 750,000 monedas de diez centavos; la oficina de la moneda acaba de cumplir un pedido de Costa Rica de una gran cantidad de monedas de oro, y tan complacida está Costa Rica que ha ordenado, por medio de su ministro en Washington, 40,000 monedas de oro más; y el primer trabajo de esta clase hecho por los Estados Unidos fue en 1876, cuando se produjeron $100,000 en monedas menores para el gobierno de Venezuela.

records.headline: The Union prints an item on the foreign coinage of the United States
records.summary_en: The Union prints an item on the foreign coinage of the United States mint, the work for the Dominican Republic being already begun at Philadelphia: already the work has been started at the mint in Philadelphia, and within a few days 300,000 of them will be turned out; they will be only 35 per cent silver, the balance being copper and nickel, but they will circulate at full value. records.full_text:
REVOLUTION FOR SAN DOMINGO.

It Is Being Brewed in New York by Enemies of President Hereaux.

New York, Oct. 21.—The Journal and Advertiser says: Efforts to crystalize the opposition to President Hereaux of San Domingo, the Spanish speaking republican that shares with the French speaking republic of Hayti the West Indian island of Hayti, into a revolution, are said to be nearing completion in this city.

The leader of the movement in New York is given Moscoso, who arrived here last July and is said to have been constantly busy ever since with secret meetings with the purpose in view. He is one of Hereaux's implacable foes and his friends here declare that he is the most available man to lead a revolt against the Dominican ruler. Moscoso was long ago recognized by Hereaux as a dangerous man and Hereaux was scheming to put him in prison and thus get him where he could not endanger the administration, when Moscoso got wind of his intention and promptly skipped out of the country. He went to the neighboring island of Porto Rica, the usual refuge of Dominican exiles, and was nearly assassinated there shortly after. Moscoso's friends openly declare their belief that the would-be assassins were in the pay of President Hereaux, the desperate method having been resorted to, they claim, because Moscoso was rapidly effecting his plans to return secretly to San Domingo and start an uprising, which Hereaux wanted to prevent by any means. Moscoso's assailants in Pence, Porto Rica, came very near killing him. He was taken unawares and stabbed once before he realized his danger, and then managed to escape only because one of the men thinking a fatal blow had been struck ran away, and the other was too scared and bewildered at the flight of his companion to follow up his attack. Moscoso is barely 35 years of age. He was educated in this country and speaks languages with fluency. His personal bravery is extolled as highly as his mental accomplishments, and his following at home is declared to be large and enthusiastic. He refuses to discuss his plans, but talks readily when President Hereaux's administration is mentioned. He makes no secret of his opposition to the president, whom he freely denounces.

Dominican exiles are not numerous in New York but they make up in determination what they lack in numbers. They declare they mean to stake their all in Mocoso's movement and basing their hopes on recent advices chief seaport, are confident that it will be successful.

Hereaux has been president of Santo Domingo three terms, a much longer period than any of his predecessors. His enemies declare that he has been able to retain the reins of president so long because he has been unscrupulous in carrying out his secret intention of making himself dictator for life by stifling opposition by means of bribery and intimidation. In consequence the best and most influential of the country have either been stultified or banished. It is even charged that a number have been unlawfully put to death at the president's instigation.

records.summary_en: *The Sun* reported that an English company was replacing an American syndicate in managing Dominican customs duties and railroad concessions to secure foreign loan payments. The article traced the concession back to an earlier multimillion-dollar loan by the Amsterdam firm Westendorp & Co., which had financed a railroad from Puerto Plata to the interior. It noted that customs revenues subsequently declined due to poor crops, administrative mismanagement, and widespread smuggling.
records.summary_es: *The Sun* informó que una compañía inglesa estaba sustituyendo a un consorcio estadounidense en la administración de las aduanas y concesiones ferroviarias dominicanas para asegurar el pago de empréstitos extranjeros. El artículo remontó el origen de la concesión a un préstamo multimillonario previo de la firma de Ámsterdam Westendorp & Co., la cual había financiado un ferrocarril desde Puerto Plata hacia el interior. Señaló además que las rentas aduaneras disminuyeron con posterioridad debido a malas cosechas, mala gestión administrativa y un contrabando generalizado.
records.passage: character not unusual; and, in fact, the English company is practically taking the place of an American syndicate that received, several years ago, a like control of the import and export duties, to cover a loan. The railroad concessions and control which the American syndicate has hitherto enjoyed also pass to its British successor, the latter paying to the former whatever the Dominican Government still owes it on account of its loan. We may further point out that the original holder of these customs privileges was the Amsterdam banking firm of Westendorp Co., which made a loan of several million dollars to San Domingo eight or nine years ago. It was stipulated that "Westendorp Co. should appoint their own agents in collecting the duties, that these duties were not to be altered without their consent, and that Holland should be the arbiter in disputes between them and San Domingo." The Amsterdam firm thereupon floated its bonds, and of a total amount of $6,600,000, American capitalists, we think, took about $2,800,000. San Domingo, with the proceeds, cancelled some old debts and began work on the railroad running from Puerto Plata to the interior. records.headline: The Sun doubts that San Domingo has made any stipulation whatever
records.summary_en: The Sun doubts that San Domingo has made any stipulation whatever in regard to the possession of Samana Bay: it recalls a time when the customs duties of San Domingo, then pledged to the American syndicate, were seized in the prosecution of some claims of a foreign power's citizens — the United States Government itself having claims of long standing against San Domingo which it had not sought to settle by force — and says the difficulty, it believes, was amicably smoothed over, though for a time it caused uneasiness. Yet the strategic importance of the bay, from its opening upon the Mona Passage, makes its future an object of watchfulness for the United States Government, and since the collection of the export and import duties of San Domingo is to pass from an American to an English syndicate, American authorities, after Mr. Powell's letter, will naturally await assurances that no political or territorial control can thereby pass to the British Government.

Sin embargo, la importancia estratégica de la bahía, por su apertura sobre el paso de la Mona, hace de su futuro un objeto de vigilancia para el gobierno de los Estados Unidos, y como el cobro de los derechos de exportación e importación de San Domingo va a pasar de un sindicato americano a un sindicato inglés, las autoridades americanas, tras la carta del Sr. Powell, esperarán naturalmente seguridades de que ningún control político o territorial pueda pasar con ello al gobierno británico.

records.headline: About thirty years ago an attempt was made by the Grant
records.summary_en: *The Saint Paul Globe* published a letter comparing the proposed annexation of Hawaii to President Grant's unsuccessful effort to annex Santo Domingo in 1869 and 1870. The writer recalled that despite strategic arguments, joint resolution efforts, and a favorable commission report, the annexation treaty failed in the Senate. The author argued that past fears of foreign powers absorbing Santo Domingo proved unfounded and hoped Hawaii would avoid annexation.
records.summary_es: *The Saint Paul Globe* publicó una carta en la que comparaba la proyectada anexión de Hawái con la infructuosa tentativa del presidente Grant de anexionar Santo Domingo en 1869 y 1870. El autor recordaba que, a pesar de los argumentos estratégicos, de los esfuerzos por lograr una resolución conjunta y de un informe favorable de la comisión, el tratado de anexión fracasó en el Senado. El autor sostuvo que los temores pasados de que potencias extranjeras absorbieran a Santo Domingo resultaron infundados y expresó su deseo de que Hawái evitara la anexión.
records.passage: HISTORY REPEATS. Similarity in Hawaiian and Santo Dominican Cases. To the Editor of the Globe. About thirty years ago an attempt was made by the Grant administration to annex Santo Domingo, the second largest island in the West Indies, which ingloriously failed, as I hope the present administration will fail in its attempt to annex the Hawaiian islands. Then, as now, a treaty had been signed for annexation between President Grant and the president of the Santo Domingo republic on Sept. 9, 1869, which treaty was rejected by the senate. In December, 1870, inspired by the president's annual message, another attempt was made to annex said island by passing a joint resolution, which then, as it is now claimed, could be accomplished by a majority vote. This was met and it was held that no territory could be annexed without a treaty which must be ratified by a two-thirds vote of the senate. Finally, a commission of visiting statesmen was appointed, who, in due time, reported favorably, but the whole thing was abandoned in the long run, and no "foreign power" has thus far expressed any desire to absorb that republic. Then, as now, it was strongly urged how indispensable that island was to us for military and naval reasons. Then, as now, certain great patriots were much distressed lest some foreign power would absorb that island and its dusky inhabitants. records.summary_en: *The Sun* highlighted the strategic value of Samana Bay as a coaling station along the Mona Passage between Santo Domingo and Puerto Rico, citing its sheltered anchorage and defensible geography. The article reviewed the rejection of President Grant's annexation project 28 years prior, which led the Dominican Republic to refuse any sale, cession, or lease of its territory. It emphasized that current American interest did not contemplate territorial annexation or permanent fortifications.
records.summary_es: *The Sun* destacó el valor estratégico de la bahía de Samaná como estación carbonera en el paso de la Mona, entre Santo Domingo y Puerto Rico, señalando su fondeadero protegido y su ventajosa geografía defensiva. El artículo repasó el rechazo al proyecto de anexión del presidente Grant ocurrido 28 años atrás, lo que llevó a la República Dominicana a negarse a cualquier venta, cesión o arrendamiento de su territorio. Subrayó que el interés estadounidense en ese momento no contemplaba anexiones territoriales ni fortificaciones permanentes.
records.passage: desired coaling station during the various negotiations for acquiring a foothold there. An American company held land in the neighborhood many years ago, and a coal pile was established on Carenero Island. Samana Bay not only gives anchorage enough for the fleets of the world, but it is exceedingly well situated for our purpose. It is true that Mole St. Nicolas, on the Windward Passage, between Hayti and Cuba, has strategic advantages, that route being shorter from our ports to the Isthmus, but Samana Bay lies on the Mona Passage, a route which is taken by the merchant vessels that go to South America between San Domingo and Porto Rico. It is healthful, under the trade winds which blow into it, and it is capable of defence, its narrow entrance being commanded by Levantada Island, while the bold headlands on the north shore give a plunging fire. But we are to assume that there is no question whatever of fortifications now, since no annexation of territory is undertaken, nor even any lease from the Dominican Government. It will be remembered that the old project of acquiring Samana Bay as a coaling station, under President Grant's Administration, about twenty-eight years ago, developed into the form of annexing all San Domingo, and this the Senate did not approve. But afterward the little republic took the ground not only that she would not be annexed, but that she would not sell, cede, or even lease us any territory at all. records.headline: The Graphic prints part of a survey of the West Indies in wartime
records.summary_en: The Graphic prints part of a survey of the West Indies in wartime: the passage opens with the closing words of the story of Christophe's citadel — that the secrets of the citadel they had just completed should never be divulged. There are quite a million people on the island, the survey says, but they dally on the way to civilization; there is no army, and Hayti's only use to the United States would be in lending it a harbor: there are no harbors on the north coast, but Port au Prince, in the republic of Hayti, is a well-protected port lying behind the island of Gonave; in the Dominican Republic there are the harbors of Santo Domingo and Puerto Plata, which would make convenient bases for operations in the Caribbean. The Mona Passage, only 60 miles wide, separates Hayti from the beautiful island of Porto Rico, which the survey calls a valuable possession and, taken altogether, the most important of all the West Indies after Cuba, its exports estimated at more than a quarter of a million dollars a few years ago and its staples sugar and coffee.

Hay en la isla cerca de un millón de personas, dice el estudio, pero se demoran en el camino de la civilización; no hay ejército, y el único uso de Haití para los Estados Unidos sería prestarles un puerto: no hay puertos en la costa norte, pero Puerto Príncipe, en la república de Haití, es un puerto bien protegido situado detrás de la isla de Gonave; en la República Dominicana están los puertos de Santo Domingo y Puerto Plata, que harían bases convenientes para las operaciones en el Caribe. El paso de la Mona, de solo 60 millas de ancho, separa a Haití de la hermosa isla de Puerto Rico, que el estudio llama una posesión valiosa y, en conjunto, la más importante de todas las Indias Occidentales después de Cuba, con exportaciones estimadas en más de un cuarto de millón de dólares hace algunos años y con azúcar y café como productos principales.

records.headline: The Gazette prints a quoted argument for American coaling harbors
records.summary_en: The Gazette prints a quoted argument for American coaling harbors: of harbors in the Atlantic, the best the United States could probably secure is St. Thomas, or, if not this, then Samana Bay, in the Dominican Republic; in the great Pacific, north of the equator, there is only one, Pearl Harbor, near Honolulu. The writer of this has been in all these three places, the argument continues, and knows of what he is speaking; certainly, no time should be lost in securing one harbor in the Atlantic and one in the Pacific as stepping stones on the line of the American coast, of immense value in connection with the isthmian canal; then comes the canal itself, and the question of dry docks large enough for the greatest vessels of today.
records.summary_es: El Gazette publica un argumento citado en favor de puertos americanos de carboneo: de los puertos del Atlántico, el mejor que los Estados Unidos probablemente podrían asegurarse es Santo Tomás, o, si no este, la bahía de Samaná, en la República Dominicana; en el gran Pacífico, al norte del ecuador, solo hay uno, Pearl Harbor, cerca de Honolulu. El autor de esto ha estado en estos tres lugares, continúa el argumento, y sabe de lo que habla; ciertamente, no debe perderse tiempo en asegurarse un puerto en el Atlántico y uno en el Pacífico como escalones en la línea de la costa americana, de inmenso valor en conexión con el canal ístmico; luego viene el propio canal, y la cuestión de los diques secos, lo bastante grandes para los mayores buques de hoy.

will not only be safe, out have facilities
for coaling and repairing, without
asking the consent or permission of
any one.
"Of these in the Atlantic ocean, the
best one we could probably secure is
St. Thomas, or, if not this, then
Samana Bay, in the Dominican Republic.
In the great Pacific ocean, north
of the equator, there is only one, Pearl
Harbor, -near Honolulu. The writer of
this has been in all these three places,
and knows of what he is speaking.
Certainly, no time should be lost in securing
one harbor in the Atlantic and
one in the Pacific as stepping stones on
tho line of our coast, and as places
which will be of immense value to us
in connecion with the isthmian canal.
"Then next comes the canal itself,
and we can take no wiser step and
make no greater move than in forming
some company which will put itself in
touch with the present Panama Canal
Company, and arrange to have the
work completed and the canal open for
commerce in a few years.
"Then there is the question of dry
docks, large enough for the greatest
vessels of today. We need several of
them on our Atlantic, Pacific and Gulf
coast, and also at Pearl Harbor, and
whichever other one -we may own near
the Atlantic end of the canal.

records.headline: Under the head 'Coining for South America,' the Alert reports
records.summary_en: Under the head 'Coining for South America,' the Alert reports that the United States government is minting silver dollars for the Dominican Republic: the design was furnished by the San Domingo treasury department and differs very little from the American dollar; it has been the custom of the United States government, as an act of comity and good will, to make the money of several South American countries, and the work is done at the actual cost of labor and material; the dollars being minted for San Domingo only contain 35 percent silver, yet answer admirably for the purposes of effecting exchanges there as elsewhere, and Costa Rica is also having coins minted by this government. The editorial protests that for the increasing needs of the United States the government is minting no additional silver dollars: the people of South American states get the benefit, and the trade of those distant republics, not America's own, is stimulated thereby.
records.summary_es: Bajo el título «Coining for South America», el Alert informa que el gobierno de los Estados Unidos está acuñando dólares de plata para la República Dominicana: el diseño fue suministrado por el departamento del tesoro de San Domingo y difiere muy poco del dólar americano; ha sido costumbre del gobierno de los Estados Unidos, como acto de cortesía y buena voluntad, hacer el dinero de varios países sudamericanos, y el trabajo se hace al costo real de la mano de obra y el material; los dólares que se acuñan para San Domingo solo contienen un 35 por ciento de plata, pero responden admirablemente a los fines del cambio allí como en cualquier parte, y Costa Rica también está haciendo acuñar monedas por este gobierno. El editorial protesta porque para las crecientes necesidades de los Estados Unidos el gobierno no está acuñando dólares de plata adicionales: el pueblo de los estados sudamericanos recibe el beneficio, y el comercio de esas repúblicas distantes, no el de la propia América, es el estimulado con ello.

records.headline: The Graphic reprints the closing passage of a Chicago Times-Herald item
records.summary_en: The Graphic reprints the closing passage of a Chicago Times-Herald item on the coinage the United States mint makes for foreign governments: happily, the coins are not intended for circulation in this country; the work is being done for the Dominican Republic, and the dollars will be sent to Santo Domingo; the design for the coins was furnished by the Dominican treasury department and in no respect, excepting shape, resembles the dollar of the United States. It has long been the custom of the United States to make the money of several South American countries, and as an act of comity and good will the work is done at the actual cost of labor and material; the present order from Santo Domingo also includes 800,000 half dollars, 375,000 quarter dollars and 750,000 dimes. The mint bureau has just filled an order from Costa Rica for a large quantity of gold coins, and Costa Rica, so pleased with the coinage, has ordered through its minister at Washington 40,000 more coins of gold; and the first work of this kind done by the United States was in 1876, when $100,000 worth of minor coins were turned out for the government of Venezuela.

Hace mucho que es costumbre de los Estados Unidos hacer el dinero de varios países sudamericanos, y como un acto de cortesía y buena voluntad el trabajo se hace al costo real de la mano de obra y el material; el pedido actual de Santo Domingo incluye también 800,000 medios dólares, 375,000 cuartos de dólar y 750,000 monedas de diez centavos. La oficina de la moneda acaba de cumplir un pedido de Costa Rica de una gran cantidad de monedas de oro, y Costa Rica, tan complacida con la acuñación, ha ordenado, por medio de su ministro en Washington, 40,000 monedas de oro más; y el primer trabajo de esta clase hecho por los Estados Unidos fue en 1876, cuando se produjeron $100,000 en monedas menores para el gobierno de Venezuela.

records.headline: Among the Herald's war dispatches: a copyrighted cablegram of the World
records.summary_en: Among the Herald's war dispatches: a copyrighted cablegram of the World from its correspondent George Bronson Rea, dated Puerto Plata, San Domingo, May 8: Dominican officials report heavy cannonading off the north of Monte Cristi, about 50 miles from here, and it is believed there that Rear Admiral Sampson's squadron is engaging the Spanish Cape Verde fleet; the firing began about 9 o'clock this morning and was terrific. Sampson came here, the cablegram continues, with orders to find the fleet and reduce it, and after destroying the Spanish ships will begin a strict blockade and, if necessary, will bombard and capture Porto Rico; and a St. Thomas dispatch of May 8, printed in the same columns, reports that the American fleet under Rear Admiral Sampson has not yet arrived off Porto Rico and no fighting has yet occurred in that quarter.
records.summary_es: Entre los despachos de guerra del Herald: un cablegrama del World con derechos reservados, de su corresponsal George Bronson Rea, fechado en Puerto Plata, San Domingo, el 8 de mayo: funcionarios dominicanos informan de un intenso cañoneo frente al norte de Monte Cristi, a unas 50 millas de aquí, y se cree allí que la escuadra del contralmirante Sampson está combatiendo con la flota española de Cabo Verde; el fuego comenzó hacia las 9 de esa mañana y fue terrible. Sampson vino aquí, continúa el cablegrama, con órdenes de encontrar la flota y destruirla, y tras destruir los buques españoles comenzará un bloqueo estricto y, si es necesario, bombardeará y capturará Puerto Rico; y un despacho de Santo Tomás del 8 de mayo, publicado en las mismas columnas, informa que la flota americana al mando del contralmirante Sampson aún no ha llegado frente a Puerto Rico y que no ha ocurrido combate alguno en ese frente.

records.headline: Under the head 'Pretty Naval Problem,' the Globe sets out the positions of the fleets:
records.summary_en: Under the head 'Pretty Naval Problem,' the Globe sets out the positions of the fleets: Admiral Sampson, with that portion of his fleet which took part in the bombardment of San Juan, is at Puerto Plata, the principal seaport of the Dominican Republic, situated on the north coast of the island; the auxiliary cruiser Yale sailed this morning from St. Thomas, going in a westerly direction, and the Montgomery, according to the report, is still at that place; the Harvard is at St. Pierre for repairs and will not be available for some days; the flying squadron under Schley, and the Oregon, with the Marietta and the Nictheroy as consorts, do not at present seem to be active factors in the problem. That the object of the Spanish commander is to reach the coast of Cuba, and perhaps Cienfuegos, is indicated by the latest reports of his movements, the Globe judges; if the Spanish fleet can be bottled up in a Cuban port, Sampson will be capable of taking care of it without other aid.
records.summary_es: Bajo el título «Pretty Naval Problem», el Globe expone las posiciones de las flotas: el almirante Sampson, con la parte de su flota que tomó parte en el bombardeo de San Juan, está en Puerto Plata, el principal puerto marítimo de la República Dominicana, situado en la costa norte de la isla; el crucero auxiliar Yale zarpó esta mañana de Santo Tomás, en dirección oeste, y el Montgomery, según el informe, permanece aún en ese lugar; el Harvard está en St. Pierre en reparaciones y no estará disponible por algunos días; la escuadra volante al mando de Schley, y el Oregon, con el Marietta y el Nictheroy como consortes, no parecen por el momento factores activos en el problema. Que el objeto del comandante español es llegar a la costa de Cuba, y quizá a Cienfuegos, lo indican los últimos informes de sus movimientos, juzga el Globe; si la flota española puede ser embotellada en un puerto cubano, Sampson será capaz de encargarse de ella sin otra ayuda.

records.summary_en: *The Indianapolis Journal* reported from Haiti regarding proposed constitutional changes concerning foreign property rights. Haitian Foreign Minister Brutus St. Victor denied claims that the government intended to repeal Article 6 of the constitution, which prohibited alien ownership of real estate, stating the public was not prepared for such reform. St. Victor also declined to disclose specific government plans to address the rising premium on paper currency.
records.summary_es: *The Indianapolis Journal* informó desde Haití sobre las propuestas de reforma constitucional relativas a los derechos de propiedad de los extranjeros. El ministro de Asuntos Exteriores haitiano, Brutus St. Victor, desmintió las versiones de que el gobierno pretendiera derogar el artículo 6 de la constitución, que prohibía a los extranjeros la propiedad de bienes inmuebles, afirmando que la opinión pública no estaba preparada para tal cambio. St. Victor declinó asimismo revelar planes gubernamentales específicos para hacer frente al creciente sobreprecio del papel moneda.

records.headline: The Plain Dealer prints part of a West Indies survey in wartime
records.summary_en: The Plain Dealer prints part of a West Indies survey in wartime: a moment's consideration of the history of the two republics, Hayti in the west and San Domingo in the east, the only countries in the West Indies whose form of government is like our own, except, of course, the republic of Cuba. Toussaint L'Ouverture's successful struggle against France and his capture by treachery, followed by the complete expulsion of the French, is one of liberty's favorite tales; the Spanish invaded San Domingo in 1861, and their defeat left the islanders free; the Haytians have experimented with kings and discarded them, and the treasure of one of these despots, Christophe, remains buried under the rank vegetation among the ruins of a stronghold he built, whose architect and all the workmen were thrown from the parapets so that the secrets of the citadel they had just completed should never be divulged. There are quite a million people on the island; there is no army, or Hayti's only use to us would be in lending us a harbor: there are no harbors on the north coast, but Port au Prince, in the republic of Hayti, is a well-protected port lying behind the island of Gonaive, while in the Dominican republic there are the harbors of Santo Domingo and Porto Plata, which would make convenient bases for operations in the Caribbean; and the Mona passage, only 60 miles wide, separates Hayti from Porto Rico.
records.summary_es: El Plain Dealer publica parte de un estudio de las Indias Occidentales en tiempo de guerra: una breve consideración de la historia de las dos repúblicas, Haití en el oeste y Santo Domingo en el este, los únicos países de las Indias Occidentales cuya forma de gobierno es como la nuestra, excepto, por supuesto, la república de Cuba. La exitosa lucha de Toussaint L'Ouverture contra Francia y su captura por traición, seguida de la completa expulsión de los franceses, es uno de los relatos favoritos de la libertad; los españoles invadieron Santo Domingo en 1861, y su derrota dejó libres a los isleños; los haitianos han experimentado con reyes y los han descartado, y el tesoro de uno de esos déspotas, Christophe, permanece enterrado bajo la exuberante vegetación entre las ruinas de una fortaleza que construyó, cuyo arquitecto y todos los obreros fueron arrojados desde las almenas para que los secretos de la ciudadela que acababan de completar nunca fueran revelados. Hay cerca de un millón de personas en la isla; no hay ejército, o el único uso de Haití para nosotros sería prestarnos un puerto: no hay puertos en la costa norte, pero Puerto Príncipe, en la república de Haití, es un puerto bien protegido situado detrás de la isla de Gonaive, mientras que en la república dominicana están los puertos de Santo Domingo y Puerto Plata, que serían bases convenientes para las operaciones en el Caribe; y el paso de la Mona, de solo 60 millas de ancho, separa a Haití de Puerto Rico.

records.headline: The Jersey City News prints the closing passage of the Associated Press dispatch
records.summary_en: The Jersey City News prints the closing passage of the Associated Press dispatch on the steamer Fanita: she was to touch at Monte Cristi, Dominican Republic, or at the keys just outside, to fill up the empty portion of her hold, and she has on board Chris Roberts, of Great Inagua, the most famous pilot of the West Indies. The captain of the Fanita, when that vessel was here, said the portion of her cargo which was not landed consisted of coal, but there is good reason to suppose that it is something very different from coal; and proof that the Fanita is under serious suspicion was afforded this morning by the excited conduct of the Spanish consul here, who denounces the taking on board the steamer of Spanish-speaking roustabouts and the sudden sailing of the vessel without the permission of the Dominican consul, classes this as a great outrage and an act of piracy, and has entered a formal protest with the Haytien authorities and telegraphed to his diplomatic chief at Santo Domingo this morning about the Fanita. There are large numbers of Cubans in Santo Domingo who eagerly desire to return to Cuba and take part in the war, and the correspondent here of the Associated Press is informed that the Spaniards of this place believe that it may be part of the mission of the Fanita to afford these Cubans transportation, at the same time furnishing them with arms and ammunition.

records.headline: Among the El Paso Herald's dispatches is a report on the Jiminez expedition:
records.summary_en: Among the El Paso Herald's dispatches is a report on the Jiminez expedition: a revolutionary expedition from Hayti landed at Monte Cristi, San Domingo, on Thursday under the leadership of Senor Jiminez, formerly a New York merchant; the Dominican government had been advised of the movement of the troops and was waiting to capture the party; General Augustin Morales, a leader of the expedition, was shot without ceremony; and the whole party will probably be executed.
records.summary_es: Entre los despachos del El Paso Herald hay un informe sobre la expedición de Jiminez: una expedición revolucionaria procedente de Haití desembarcó en Monte Cristi, Santo Domingo, el jueves bajo el liderazgo del señor Jiminez, antes comerciante en Nueva York; el gobierno dominicano había sido avisado del movimiento de las tropas y estaba esperando para capturar al grupo; el general Augustin Morales, uno de los líderes de la expedición, fue fusilado sin ceremonia; y es probable que todo el grupo sea ejecutado.

records.summary_en: The Standard prints the Associated Press Fanita dispatch of June 2: the Clyde line steamer, which arrived there yesterday half empty, bringing from New York some provisions for the navy, which she landed at Matthewstown, Great Inagua, in the Bahamas, slipped out last night with between 50 and 75 Dominicans added to the crew; she was to touch at Monte Cristi, Dominican Republic, or at the keys just outside, to fill up the empty portion of her hold, and she has on board Chris Roberts, the most famous pilot of the West Indies. The captain of the Fanita, when there, said a portion of her cargo which was not landed consisted of coal, but there is good reason to suppose it is something very far from coal; and there are large numbers of Cubans in Santo Domingo who eagerly desire to return to Cuba to take part in the war, and the Spaniards of Cape Haytien believe it may be part of the mission of the Fanita to afford these Cubans transportation, at the same time furnishing them with arms and ammunition.

records.headline: Under the head 'Expedition Captured,' the New Mexican prints
records.summary_en: Under the head 'Expedition Captured,' the New Mexican prints a dispatch to the Herald from Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic: a revolutionary expedition was landed at Monte Cristi from Hayti under the leadership of Senor Jimenez, formerly a merchant in New York; the government had been advised of the movement, troops were waiting for the party, and all were captured; the leader, Jimenez, was reserved for examination, but General Augustin was shot without delay; President Heureaux will arrive at Monte Cristi tomorrow, and it is almost certain that the whole party will be executed.

records.headline: The Intelligencer prints part of the Associated Press feature
records.summary_en: The Intelligencer prints part of the Associated Press feature on the revolution the steamer Fanita carried to Monte Cristi: General Villanueva, who fought bravely against President Heureaux's alleged usurpation and was exiled, has been living at Great Inagua for some time past, and the Fanita is said to have stopped there in order to take him on board. The preparations for the revolution are said to have been very elaborate, and there is a strong belief there that the revolutionists are sure of success; but, on the other hand, the Dominican consul there says he has a report that the revolutionists have been defeated at Monte Cristi, a report not generally believed. The advices received there on the subject say that the Fanita arrived at Monte Cristi at 3 o'clock yesterday afternoon, and that the revolutionists had no difficulty in taking the town; the most circumstantial reports have it that the revolutionists are now in considerable force, and that under Generals Morales and Villanueva they are marching on Puerto Plata, while another detachment is moving against Santiago de los Caballeros, on the Yaque river, one hundred miles east of there; General Garcia, another important Dominican leader, is said to be taking part in the revolution, and it is expected there will be a rising at Santo Domingo, the capital of the republic; and General Jimenez is a merchant who has business houses there, at Monte Cristi, at Puerto Plata and at Hamburg, in his youth he served in the army, and for many years he has been very popular in the Dominican Republic.
records.summary_es: El Intelligencer publica parte del reportaje de la Associated Press sobre la revolución que el vapor Fanita llevó a Monte Cristi: el general Villanueva, que peleó valientemente contra la alegada usurpación del presidente Heureaux y fue exiliado, ha estado viviendo en Gran Inagua desde hace algún tiempo, y se dice que la Fanita se detuvo allí para recogerlo a bordo. Se dice que los preparativos de la revolución fueron muy elaborados, y hay una fuerte creencia allí de que los revolucionarios están seguros del éxito; pero el cónsul dominicano allí dice que tiene un reporte de que los revolucionarios han sido derrotados en Monte Cristi, reporte que no es creído en general. Los avisos recibidos allí sobre el asunto dicen que la Fanita llegó a Monte Cristi a las 3 de la tarde de ayer, y que los revolucionarios no tuvieron dificultad en tomar la ciudad; los reportes más circunstanciados sostienen que los revolucionarios están ahora en fuerza considerable, y que bajo los generales Morales y Villanueva marchan sobre Puerto Plata, mientras otro destacamento se mueve contra Santiago de los Caballeros, sobre el río Yaque, cien millas al este de allí; el general García, otro importante líder dominicano, se dice que toma parte en la revolución, y se espera que haya un levantamiento en Santo Domingo, la capital de la república; y el general Jimenez es un comerciante que tiene casas de negocio allí, en Monte Cristi, en Puerto Plata y en Hamburgo, en su juventud sirvió en el ejército, y por muchos años ha sido muy popular en la República Dominicana.

records.summary_en: *The News & Observer* reported that an armed uprising against Dominican President Heureaux had begun at Monte Cristi, near the Haitian border. The Clyde Line steamer *Fanita* reportedly departed Cape Haitien carrying 150 Dominican insurgents concealed in its hold, alongside rebel leaders General Juan Isidro Jimenes and General Villanueva. Observers in Haiti described the revolutionary expedition as well prepared and expressed strong confidence in its potential success.
records.summary_es: *The News & Observer* informó que se había iniciado un levantamiento armado contra el presidente dominicano Heureaux en Monte Cristi, cerca de la frontera con Haití. Se informó que el vapor *Fanita*, de la Clyde Line, zarpó de Cabo Haitiano transportando a 150 insurgentes dominicanos ocultos en sus bodegas, junto a los cabecillas rebeldes, los generales Juan Isidro Jimenes y Villanueva. Observadores en Haití describieron la expedición revolucionaria como bien preparada y manifestaron gran confianza en su posible éxito.

The Santiago advices to Cape Haytien, in referring to the sunken vessel as auxiliary cruiser, probably mistake her character. The Merrimac is a collier, and always has been a collier. Cape Haytien, Hayti, June 3. — 11:40 a. m. — The mystery surrounding the movements of the Clyde Line steamer Fanita is now said to be fully explained. It appears established beyond a doubt that the reports of an uprising in the republic of Santo Domingo against the power of President Heureaux are correct. The initial blow was struck at Monte Cristo, on the borders of Hayti, the nearest Dominican port to Cape Haytien. It would appear as though the Fanita had 150 Dominicans on hand while here, who remained in the hold of the ship so as to escape attention. General Juan Ysidro Jimenes and General Villanueva are believed to have been on board. It is also noted that the former has long been in the public eye in Santo Domingo as a desirable man for the presidency. records.headline: The Salt Lake Herald prints part of the Associated Press feature
records.summary_en: The Salt Lake Herald prints part of the Associated Press feature on the Fanita revolution: the reports of an uprising in the republic of Santo Domingo against the power of President Heureaux are correct; the initial blow was struck at Monte Cristi, on the borders of Hayti, the nearest Dominican port to Cape Haytien. It would appear that the Fanita, instead of having on board only 17 Dominicans, probably had 330 on board; she arrived at Cape Haytien on June 1 half empty, bringing from New York provisions for the navy, which she landed at Matthewtown, in the Bahama Islands, and slipped away about 10 o'clock the same night, to fill up the empty portion of her hold; she had on board Chris Roberts, the most famous pilot of the West Indies. General Ysidro Jimenez and General Pablo Villanueva are believed to have been on board; Jimenez has long been in the public eye in Santo Domingo as a desirable man for the presidency, and Villanueva fought bravely against President Heureaux's alleged usurpation and was exiled. The preparations for the revolution are said to have been very elaborate, and there is a strong belief there that the revolutionists are sure of success.
records.summary_es: El Salt Lake Herald publica parte del reportaje de la Associated Press sobre la revolución de la Fanita: son correctos los reportes de un levantamiento en la república de Santo Domingo contra el poder del presidente Heureaux; el golpe inicial fue dado en Monte Cristi, en los límites de Haití, el puerto dominicano más cercano a Cabo Haitiano. Parecería que la Fanita, en lugar de tener a bordo solo 17 dominicanos, probablemente tenía 330 a bordo; llegó a Cabo Haitiano el 1 de junio medio vacía, trayendo de Nueva York provisiones para la marina, que desembarcó en Matthewtown, en las islas Bahamas, y escapó cerca de las 10 de esa misma noche, para llenar la parte vacía de su bodega; llevaba a bordo a Chris Roberts, el piloto más famoso de las Indias Occidentales. Se cree que el general Ysidro Jimenez y el general Pablo Villanueva iban a bordo; Jimenez ha estado por largo tiempo ante la vista pública en Santo Domingo como un hombre deseable para la presidencia, y Villanueva peleó valientemente contra la alegada usurpación del presidente Heureaux y fue exiliado. Se dice que los preparativos de la revolución fueron muy elaborados, y hay una fuerte creencia allí de que los revolucionarios están seguros del éxito.

records.summary_en: The Times prints the closing passage of the Associated Press feature on the Fanita revolution, with the consul's report of its defeat: the revolutionists are now in considerable force, and under Generals Morales and Villanueva they are marching on Puerto Plata, while another detachment is moving against Santiago de los Caballeros, on the Yaque river, 103 miles east of there; and General Garcia, another important Dominican leader, is said to be taking part in the revolution, and there is said to be a rising at Santo Domingo, the capital of the Dominican republic. President Heureaux, according to a common saying among the Dominicans, has killed off all the prominent men on whom he could lay hands and who might be rivals, and is said to have recently resumed the arbitrary execution of his opponents, sometimes openly, sometimes stealthily, the tragic disappearances of men of political note having been frequent of late in the republic. This afternoon the Dominican consul there received a dispatch from President Heureaux saying that an attempted revolution at Monte Cristi had been defeated, that General Jiminez fled at the first fire of the government troops, taking refuge on board the Fanita, and that all the others who landed, with the exception of three, had been killed; two of the prisoners are Pablo Villanueva, son of General Villanueva, and a laborer, and they will be executed today with other prisoners; General Morales, the Haytian general, and several Dominicans who shipped there are among the killed, and another person was killed on board the steamer Fanita.

El presidente Heureaux, según un dicho común entre los dominicanos, ha eliminado a todos los hombres prominentes a los que pudo echar mano y que pudieran ser rivales, y se dice que recientemente ha reanudado la ejecución arbitraria de sus oponentes, a veces abiertamente, a veces a escondidas, habiendo sido frecuentes en los últimos tiempos en la república las trágicas desapariciones de hombres de nota política. Esta tarde el cónsul dominicano allí recibió un despacho del presidente Heureaux diciendo que un intento de revolución en Monte Cristi había sido derrotado, que el general Jiminez huyó al primer fuego de las tropas del gobierno, refugiándose a bordo de la Fanita, y que todos los demás que desembarcaron, con la excepción de tres, habían sido muertos; dos de los prisioneros son Pablo Villanueva, hijo del general Villanueva, y un jornalero, y serán ejecutados hoy con otros prisioneros; el general Morales, el general haitiano, y varios dominicanos que se embarcaron allí están entre los muertos, y otra persona fue muerta a bordo del vapor Fanita.

records.summary_en: The *Indianapolis Journal* reported that insurgent forces led by Generals Morales and Villanueva were advancing on Puerto Plata and Santiago de los Caballeros against Dominican President Heureaux. The report profiled revolutionary leader General Juan Isidro Jimenes, an established merchant with business houses in Europe and the Caribbean who had organized the movement from New York. It noted that Jimenes enjoyed wide popularity and had previously resided in Paris to escape Heureaux's hostility toward political rivals.
records.summary_es: El *Indianapolis Journal* informó que fuerzas insurgentes encabezadas por los generales Morales y Villanueva avanzaban sobre Puerto Plata y Santiago de los Caballeros contra el presidente dominicano Heureaux. El informe trazó un perfil del líder revolucionario general Juan Isidro Jimenes, un consolidado comerciante con casas comerciales en Europa y el Caribe que había organizado el movimiento desde Nueva York. Señalaba que Jimenes gozaba de amplia popularidad y que previamente había residido en París para escapar de la hostilidad de Heureaux hacia sus rivales políticos.

General Jiminez is a merchant who has business houses here at Monte Cristo, at Puerto Plata and at Hamburg. In his youth he served in the army and for many years he has been very popular in Santo Domingo. President Heurreaux, according to a common saying among the Dominicans, has killed off all the prominent men on whom he could lay hands and who might be rivals. The President's hatred for General Jiminez is especially marked, but the latter has kept out of his reach, residing chiefly in Paris. records.summary_en: The *Richmond Dispatch* reported that an attempted revolution against Dominican President Heureaux met swift defeat at Monte Cristi. According to an official dispatch from Heureaux, insurgent leader General Jimenes fled aboard the steamer *Fanita* under fire, while Haitian General Morales and several others were killed. Dominican authorities captured several prisoners, including General Villanueva's son, who were slated for execution.
records.summary_es: El *Richmond Dispatch* informó que un intento de revolución contra el presidente dominicano Heureaux fue rápidamente derrotado en Monte Cristi. Según un parte oficial de Heureaux, el líder insurgente general Jimenes huyó bajo fuego a bordo del vapor *Fanita*, mientras que el general haitiano Morales y varios otros perecieron. Las autoridades dominicanas capturaron a varios prisioneros, entre ellos el hijo del general Villanueva, quienes estaban destinados a ser ejecutados.

HEUREUX'S BLOODTHIRSTNESS. President Heureux, according to a common saying among the Dominicans, has killed off all the prominent men on whom he could lay hands, and who might be rivals. President Heureux is said to have recently resumed the arbitrary execution of his opponents, sometimes openly, sometimes stealthily. The tragic disappearances of men of political note have been frequent of late in Dominica. General Pablo Reyes is said to be among the officers who have risen. THE REVOLT PUT DOWN. LATER. — This afternoon the Dominican Consul here received a dispatch from President Heureux, saying that an attempted revolution at Monte Cristo had been defeated; that General Jiminez fled at the first fire of the government troops, taking refuge on board the Fanita, and that all others who landed, with the exception of three, had been killed. Two of the prisoners are Pablo Villanueva, son of General Villanueva, and a laborer. They will be executed to-day, with other prisoners. According to the impression which prevails at Cape Haytien, the Fanita, when she left there, had a tried and resolute body of men on board, and also carried a heavy supply of arms and ammunition; it is charged that she skilfully worked up the impression that she was engaged in an expedition to Cuba, and was going to Monte Cristi to take on more men. The advices received there on the subject say that the Fanita arrived at Monte Cristi at 3 o'clock yesterday afternoon, and that the revolutionists had no difficulty in taking the town; the most circumstantial reports have it that the revolutionists are now in considerable force, and that under Generals Morales and Villanueva they are marching on Puerto Plata, while another detachment is moving against Santiago de los Caballeros, on the Yaque river, 100 miles east of Cape Haytien; General Garcia, another important Dominican leader, is said to be taking part in the revolution, and it is expected there will be a rising at Santo Domingo, the capital of the Dominican republic; and General Jiminez is a merchant who has business houses at Cape Haytien, at Monte Cristi, at Puerto Plata and at Hamburg, in his youth he served in the army, and for many years he has been very popular in the Dominican Republic.

records.headline: The Post-Intelligencer prints the closing passage of the Associated Press feature
records.summary_en: The Post-Intelligencer prints the closing passage of the Associated Press feature on the Fanita revolution: General Jiminez, a man of mild temperament, has several times been a candidate for the presidency, and his father was formerly president of the republic. A correspondent of Puerto Plata cables the confirmation of the accounts of the repulse of the revolutionary party at Monte Cristi: General Augustin Morales and another officer were killed, five of the insurgents were taken prisoners and shot this morning, and the others escaped in the steamer Fanita; President Heureaux left the capital this morning with three men-of-war, and the correspondent, in concluding his dispatch, says the revolutionary movement is regarded in Puerto Plata as of no consequence. The Dominican consul at Cape Haytien reasserts that Jiminez escaped on the Fanita, saying that had Jiminez been killed President Heureaux would have informed him of the fact; and this afternoon the consul received a dispatch from President Heureaux saying that the attempted revolution at Monte Cristi had been defeated, that Jiminez fled at the first fire of the government troops, taking refuge on board of the Fanita, and that all the others who landed, with the exception of three, had been killed, two of the prisoners being Pablo Villanueva, son of General Villanueva, and a laborer, who will be executed with the other prisoners.

Un corresponsal de Puerto Plata cablegrafía la confirmación de los relatos de la repulsa del partido revolucionario en Monte Cristi: el general Augustin Morales y otro oficial fueron muertos, cinco de los insurgentes fueron tomados prisioneros y fusilados esta mañana, y los demás escaparon en el vapor Fanita; el presidente Heureaux salió de la capital esta mañana con tres buques de guerra, y el corresponsal, al concluir su despacho, dice que el movimiento revolucionario es considerado en Puerto Plata como de ninguna consecuencia. El cónsul dominicano en Cabo Haitiano reafirma que Jiminez escapó en la Fanita, diciendo que si Jiminez hubiera sido muerto el presidente Heureaux se lo habría informado; y esta tarde el cónsul recibió un despacho del presidente Heureaux diciendo que el intento de revolución en Monte Cristi había sido derrotado, que Jiminez huyó al primer fuego de las tropas del gobierno, refugiándose a bordo de la Fanita, y que todos los demás que desembarcaron, con la excepción de tres, habían sido muertos, siendo dos de los prisioneros Pablo Villanueva, hijo del general Villanueva, y un jornalero, que serán ejecutados con los demás prisioneros.

records.headline: The Leader prints part of the Associated Press feature on the Fanita revolution:
records.summary_en: The Leader prints part of the Associated Press feature on the Fanita revolution: Jimenez has long been in the public eye in Santo Domingo as a desirable man for the presidency, and General Villanueva, who fought bravely against President Heureaux's alleged usurpation and was exiled, has been living at Great Inagua for some time past, and the Fanita is said to have stopped there in order to take him on board. The preparations for the revolution are said to have been very elaborate, and there is a strong belief at Cape Haytien that the revolutionists are sure of success, but, on the other hand, the Dominican consul there says he has a report that the revolutionists have been defeated at Monte Cristi, a report not generally believed. According to the impression which prevails at Cape Haytien, the Fanita, when she left there, had a tried and resolute body of men on board and also carried a heavy supply of arms and ammunition, and it is charged that she skilfully worked up the impression that she was engaged in an expedition to Cuba and was going to Monte Cristi to take on more men. The advices received there on the subject say that the Fanita arrived at Monte Cristi at 3 o'clock Thursday afternoon, and that the revolutionists had no difficulty in taking the town; the most circumstantial reports have it that the revolutionists are now in considerable force, and that under Generals Morales and Villanueva they are marching on Puerto Plata, while another detachment is moving against Santiago de los Caballeros, on the Yaque river, 100 miles east of Cape Haytien; and General Garcia, another important Dominican leader, is said to be taking part in the revolution.

Se dice que los preparativos de la revolución fueron muy elaborados, y hay una fuerte creencia en Cabo Haitiano de que los revolucionarios están seguros del éxito, pero, por otro lado, el cónsul dominicano allí dice que tiene un reporte de que los revolucionarios han sido derrotados en Monte Cristi, reporte que no es creído en general. Según la impresión que prevalece en Cabo Haitiano, la Fanita, cuando salió de allí, tenía a bordo un cuerpo de hombres probados y decididos y también llevaba un pesado suministro de armas y municiones, y se le imputa haber trabajado hábilmente la impresión de que estaba ocupada en una expedición a Cuba y que iba a Monte Cristi a recoger más hombres. records.summary_en: The *Daily Morning Journal and Courier* reported that Dominican President Heureaux mobilized three warships after insurgent leader General Jimenes escaped aboard the steamer *Fanita* following the defeat at Monte Cristi. The report highlighted Jimenes's past role in financing President Hyppolite in Haiti and noted the significant use of a Clyde Line steamer in the conspiracy. It also reported that Heureaux had resumed arbitrary executions and forced disappearances of prominent political opponents.
records.summary_es: El *Daily Morning Journal and Courier* informó que el presidente dominicano Heureaux movilizó tres buques de guerra luego de que el líder insurgente general Jimenes escapara a bordo del vapor *Fanita* tras la derrota en Monte Cristi. El informe resaltó el papel pasado de Jimenes en la financiación del presidente Hyppolite en Haití y señaló el uso significativo de un vapor de la Clyde Line en la conspiración. Asimismo, informó que Heureaux había reanudado las ejecuciones arbitrarias y las desapariciones forzadas de destacados opositores políticos.
records.passage: ers escaped in the steamer Fanita. President Heureaux left the capital this morning with three men-of-war. The correspondent, in concluding his dispatch, says the revolutionary movement is regarded at Puerto Plata as of no consequence. The Dominican consul here at Cape Haytien reasserts positively that General Jimenes escaped on the Fanita. He says that had Jimenes been killed President Heureaux would have informed him of the fact. General Jimenes was regarded as the wheelhorse of the revolution which put Hippolyte in power in Hayti, managing the financial end of the movement. When he was here the last time it was understood that President Heureaux warned him to leave Dominica for his own safety. Last April his principal partner came here from Hamburg to replace him in the direction of the business. The fact that the Clyde company furnished the conspirators with a steamer is regarded as very significant of the completeness of the preparations and the prospect of their success, since the Clyde steamship concession is the most valuable held under the Dominican government. President Heureaux is said to have recently resumed the arbitrary execution of his opponents, sometimes openly, sometimes stealthily. The tragic disappearances of men of political note have been frequent of late in Dominica. HAWAIIAN ANNEXATION. President McKinley Discusses Question With Several Representatives.
