records.headline: The Courier completes its assassination dispatch: the remains of President Heureaux
records.summary_en: The Courier completes its assassination dispatch: the remains of President Heureaux will probably be taken to San Domingo for the funeral services; upon the announcement of the president's death, the direction of affairs was assumed, and at present calmness prevails everywhere in the republic. Under the head 'Assassination Confirmed,' a Washington item of July 27 says the State Department today received a dispatch from the United States consul at Puerto Plata — 'President Heureaux was assassinated' — and Consul Read at San Domingo also confirms the report, but neither gives any details; and a Port au Prince, Hayti, item says nothing is known at the Dominican legation there or at other quarters regarding the assassination of Ulysses Heureaux, president of the republic of San Domingo. Under the head 'President Sympathizes,' a Washington item of July 27 says the official confirmation of Heureaux's death was forwarded to the president at Lake Champlain today, and he directed the following to be forwarded in his name to President Figuereo, Heureaux's successor: 'In the name of the American people and my own, I offer your excellency and the Dominican nation the most sincere condolences by reason of the death of President Heureaux.' Under the head 'Details of the Assassination,' a Cape Haytien item of July 27 says the details of the murder of President Heureaux, of Santo Domingo, received there are to the effect that he was assassinated as he was about to leave on horseback for Santiago de las Caballeros; the assassin was Ramon Caceros.
records.summary_es: El Courier completa su despacho del asesinato: los restos del presidente Heureaux serán probablemente llevados a Santo Domingo para los servicios fúnebres; tras el anuncio de la muerte del presidente, la dirección de los asuntos fue asumida, y al presente prevalece la calma en todas partes en la república. Bajo el título «Assassination Confirmed», una nota de Washington del 27 de julio dice que el Departamento de Estado recibió hoy un despacho del cónsul de los Estados Unidos en Puerto Plata — «El presidente Heureaux fue asesinado» — y el cónsul Read en Santo Domingo también confirma el reporte, pero ninguno da detalles; y una nota de Puerto Príncipe, Haití, dice que nada se sabe en la legación dominicana allí ni en otros lugares respecto al asesinato de Ulysses Heureaux, presidente de la república de Santo Domingo. Bajo el título «President Sympathizes», una nota de Washington del 27 de julio dice que la confirmación oficial de la muerte de Heureaux fue enviada al presidente en Lake Champlain hoy, y él dirigió que lo siguiente se enviara en su nombre al presidente Figuereo, el sucesor de Heureaux: «En nombre del pueblo americano y en el mío propio, ofrezco a su excelencia y a la nación dominicana las más sinceras condolencias por motivo de la muerte del presidente Heureaux». Bajo el título «Details of the Assassination», una nota de Cabo Haitiano del 27 de julio dice que los detalles del asesinato del presidente Heureaux, de Santo Domingo, recibidos allí son al efecto de que fue asesinado cuando estaba a punto de partir a caballo para Santiago de los Caballeros; el asesino fue Ramon Caceros.

records.headline: The Courier completes its details of the assassination: the body of the president
records.summary_en: The Courier completes its details of the assassination: the body of the president was taken to the palace of the governor of Moca; Heureaux's death has caused a panic; Juan Isidoro Jimines, who took part in the attempted insurrection in June, 1898, is a candidate for the presidency; it is reported that General Maximo Gomez, who is a native of Santo Domingo, also aspires to the presidency; the father of Caceros, the assassin, was put to death by order of Heureaux in 1884; and Vice President Figuereo has taken precautions to prevent disorder and has taken command of the troops, and so far all is quiet.

records.headline: The Democrat prints a dispatch from Hayti of July 27 on the assassination of President Heureaux:
records.summary_en: The Democrat prints a dispatch from Hayti of July 27 on the assassination of President Heureaux: the authorities have sent troops in pursuit of the assassin, and the news of the president's death spread rapidly and has caused much commotion among the inhabitants of the country; it is believed by many that the murder was the result of a political conspiracy; the vice president has taken precautions to prevent disorder and has taken command of the troops to that end, but up to the present time all is quiet. Details of the murder of President Heureaux are to the effect that he was assassinated while about to leave on horseback for Santiago de las Caballeros: the assassin, Raymond Caceres, surrounded by several accomplices, as he was talking with several friends, fired upon him twice with a revolver — the first bullet struck the left side and penetrated his heart, and the second bullet killed an old man who was standing near the president; the assassin and his friends then fled to escape the shots fired after them by the friends of the president; and the body of the president was taken to the palace of the governor of Moca, and the president's death has caused a panic.
records.summary_es: El Democrat publica un despacho de Haití del 27 de julio sobre el asesinato del presidente Heureaux: las autoridades han enviado tropas en persecución del asesino, y la noticia de la muerte del presidente se extendió rápidamente y ha causado mucha conmoción entre los habitantes del país; se cree por muchos que el asesinato fue el resultado de una conspiración política; el vicepresidente ha tomado precauciones para prevenir el desorden y ha tomado el mando de las tropas con ese fin, pero hasta el presente todo está tranquilo. Los detalles del asesinato del presidente Heureaux son al efecto de que fue asesinado mientras estaba a punto de partir a caballo para Santiago de los Caballeros: el asesino, Raymond Caceres, rodeado por varios cómplices, mientras él hablaba con varios amigos, disparó sobre él dos veces con un revólver — la primera bala alcanzó el costado izquierdo y le penetró el corazón, y la segunda bala mató a un anciano que estaba parado cerca del presidente; el asesino y sus amigos huyeron entonces para escapar de los disparos que les hicieron tras ellos los amigos del presidente; y el cuerpo del presidente fue llevado al palacio del gobernador de Moca, y la muerte del presidente ha causado un pánico.

records.headline: The Democrat completes its assassination dispatch: the remains of President Heureaux
records.summary_en: The Democrat completes its assassination dispatch: the remains of President Heureaux will probably be taken to Santo Domingo for the funeral services; upon the announcement of the president's death, the direction of affairs was assumed, and at present calmness prevails everywhere in the republic; and it prints a sketch of the dead president: Ulysses Heureaux, who for 17 years had been president of the republic of Santo Domingo, was a sort of Napoleon in this negro republic of the West Indies: it was a queer sight for visitors to this bankrupt little republic on the eastern end of the island of Haiti to see a ruler with the airs of a czar, the politeness of a Parisian, at times the morals of a sultan, and a defiant bravado that made him a dictator, and all this under the thin guise of a republican form of government. Heureaux was 53 years old; he was born in Puerto Plata, the nearest city to the little town of Moca, where he was assassinated Tuesday; he became a common soldier, and by bravery, brains and dash soon won high command; all the West Indies at one time or another have fought Spain — Santo Domingo did, and Heureaux became a general in that war; he was a fighter, a fearless, reckless one, whom bullets could not stop, and he received several of them in his body, but did not mind them; finally, when warfare palled, he became a politician, and his success in that exciting game was so great that his military record was overshadowed; and in 1882 Heureaux was elected president of the republic.
records.summary_es: El Democrat completa su despacho del asesinato: los restos del presidente Heureaux serán probablemente llevados a Santo Domingo para los servicios fúnebres; tras el anuncio de la muerte del presidente, la dirección de los asuntos fue asumida, y al presente prevalece la calma en todas partes en la república; y publica un esbozo del presidente muerto: Ulysses Heureaux, que por 17 años había sido presidente de la república de Santo Domingo, era una especie de Napoleón en esta república negra de las Indias Occidentales: era un espectáculo extraño para los visitantes de esta pequeña república en bancarrota en el extremo oriental de la isla de Haití ver a un gobernante con los aires de un zar, la cortesía de un parisino, a veces la moral de un sultán, y una bravata desafiante que lo hacía un dictador, y todo esto bajo la fina apariencia de una forma republicana de gobierno. Heureaux tenía 53 años; nació en Puerto Plata, la ciudad más cercana al pequeño pueblo de Moca, donde fue asesinado el martes; se hizo soldado raso, y por bravura, inteligencia y arrojo pronto ganó alto mando; todas las Indias Occidentales en un momento u otro han luchado contra España — Santo Domingo lo hizo, y Heureaux se hizo general en esa guerra; era un luchador, uno temerario y sin miedo, a quien las balas no podían detener, y recibió varias de ellas en su cuerpo, pero no les hacía caso; finalmente, cuando la guerra cansó, se hizo político, y su éxito en ese juego emocionante fue tan grande que su historial militar fue eclipsado; y en 1882 Heureaux fue elegido presidente de la república.

records.summary_en: The Journal completes its assassination dispatch: the remains of President Heureaux will probably be taken to Santo Domingo for the funeral services; and it prints a sketch of the dead president: Ulysses Heureaux, who for seventeen years had been president of the Republic of Santo Domingo, was a sort of Napoleon in this negro republic of the West Indies, but a Napoleon who, after years of autocratic power, had assumed the manners of an Oriental despot: it was a queer sight for visitors to this bankrupt little republic on the eastern end of the island of Hayti to see a ruler with the airs of a czar, the politeness of a Parisian at times, the morals of a sultan and a defiant bravado that made him a dictator, and all this under the thin guise of a republican form of government. Heureaux was fifty-three years old; he was born in Puerto Plata, the nearest city to the little town of Moca, where he was assassinated yesterday; his parents were poor; he became a common soldier and by bravery, brains and dash soon won high command; all the West Indies at one time or another have fought Spain — Santo Domingo did, and Heureaux became a general in that war; he was a fighter, a fearless, reckless one, whom bullets could not stop, and he received several of them in his body, but did not mind them; finally, when warfare palled, he became a politician, and his success in that exciting game was so great that his military record was overshadowed; and in 1882 Heureaux was elected President of the Republic, and with four re-elections continued in power.

records.headline: The Journal's sketch of Heureaux continues with anecdotes of his rule:
records.summary_en: The Journal's sketch of Heureaux continues with anecdotes of his rule: stumbling upon a group of suspects, he learned their whole plans, and the next day he sent for the men, and there was a seance of terror in the palace. Another time Heureaux went alone to a place where he knew conspirators were meeting; bursting into the room he confronted them, slowly looked around the group, and then dramatically pointed his finger at each, exclaiming, 'You here?'; he was one man in the power of fifty — they were plotting his death, and had him now in their hands, but not one dared move against him; the next day the conspirators were summoned to the palace and lined up before the President, and no ancient despot ever gloated more over victims than Heureaux did over these conspirators, whom he had defied with his bravado, and before sundown they were shot. Enemies accused President Heureaux of the crimes of Oriental monarchs: he rid himself of troublesome opponents, they declared, by poison; secret assassination was another of his favorite methods of heading off plots, and insurrections were nipped in the bud by almost indiscriminate executions; and men were sent on journeys of state and never reached their destinations.
records.summary_es: El esbozo del Journal sobre Heureaux continúa con anécdotas de su gobierno: tropezando con un grupo de sospechosos, aprendió todos sus planes, y al día siguiente hizo venir a los hombres, y hubo una sesión de terror en el palacio. En otra ocasión Heureaux fue solo a un lugar donde sabía que los conspiradores se estaban reuniendo; irrumpiendo en el cuarto los confrontó, miró lentamente alrededor del grupo, y luego apuntó dramáticamente con su dedo a cada uno, exclamando: «¿Usted aquí?»; era un hombre solo en poder de cincuenta — estaban tramando su muerte, y lo tenían ahora en sus manos, pero ni uno se atrevió a moverse contra él; al día siguiente los conspiradores fueron citados al palacio y alineados ante el Presidente, y ningún déspota antiguo se regocijó más sobre sus víctimas que Heureaux sobre estos conspiradores, a quienes había desafiado con su bravata, y antes de la puesta del sol fueron fusilados. Los enemigos acusaron al presidente Heureaux de los crímenes de los monarcas orientales: se deshizo de oponentes molestos, declararon, por veneno; el asesinato secreto era otro de sus métodos favoritos de cortar las conspiraciones, y las insurrecciones eran cortadas de raíz por ejecuciones casi indiscriminadas; y los hombres eran enviados a viajes de estado y nunca llegaban a sus destinos.

records.headline: The Journal's sketch of Heureaux, continuing, gives the Liberals' verdict
records.summary_en: The Journal's sketch of Heureaux, continuing, gives the Liberals' verdict on his rule: that was the way Heureaux maintained his power. Secret assassination was another of his favorite methods of heading off plots, and insurrections were nipped in the bud by almost indiscriminate executions; men were sent on journeys of state and never reached their destinations, and others were arrested and nothing more heard of their fate. Three years ago General Castillo, Minister of War, thought the opportunity favorable for starting a revolution for his own benefit: there was some trouble in the province, and Castillo got 1,000 rifles from the President on the plea of sending them to the province to put down the rebellion — of course, Castillo saw that they fell into the hands of his friends. Heureaux was for a time fooled, but discovered what was going on; he ordered General Estay, governor of the province, to execute Castillo, but the order was not carried out; by a neat stratagem the President enticed Castillo to the capital and arrested him, and the Minister was put aboard a war ship and taken to the province, where he was shot, and General Estay, surprised and protesting, was executed also because he had not obeyed orders. During the past two years Heureaux had lively times with the Jimenes insurrection that would not completely down, although he succeeded in driving Jimenes and General Morales out of the country; despotism was wearing on the people, and Heureaux was waning a bit in popular favor, and besides, Heureaux was piling up the national debt of the country.
records.summary_es: El esbozo del Journal sobre Heureaux, continuando, ofrece el veredicto de los Liberales sobre su gobierno: esa era la manera en que Heureaux mantenía su poder. El asesinato secreto era otro de sus métodos favoritos de cortar las conspiraciones, y las insurrecciones eran cortadas de raíz por ejecuciones casi indiscriminadas; los hombres eran enviados a viajes de estado y nunca llegaban a sus destinos, y otros eran arrestados y nada más se supo de su suerte. Hace tres años el general Castillo, ministro de Guerra, creyó favorable la oportunidad para comenzar una revolución para su propio beneficio: había algún disturbio en la provincia, y Castillo consiguió 1,000 rifles del Presidente con el pretexto de enviarlos a la provincia para sofocar la rebelión — por supuesto, Castillo se aseguró de que cayeran en manos de sus amigos. Heureaux estuvo por un tiempo engañado, pero descubrió lo que estaba pasando; ordenó al general Estay, gobernador de la provincia, ejecutar a Castillo, pero la orden no se llevó a cabo; por una estratagema ingeniosa el Presidente atrajo a Castillo a la capital y lo arrestó, y el Ministro fue puesto a bordo de un buque de guerra y llevado a la provincia, donde fue fusilado, y el general Estay, sorprendido y protestando, fue ejecutado también porque no había obedecido las órdenes. Durante los últimos dos años Heureaux tuvo tiempos animados con la insurrección de Jimenes que no se dejaba sofocar por completo, aunque logró expulsar a Jimenes y al general Morales del país; el despotismo estaba cansando al pueblo, y Heureaux estaba perdiendo un poco de favor popular, y además, Heureaux estaba acumulando la deuda nacional del país.

records.headline: The Times prints a dispatch on the assassination and the State Department's confirmation of it:
records.summary_en: The Times prints a dispatch on the assassination and the State Department's confirmation of it: three men at once opened fire upon the president with revolvers, mortally wounding him; the names of the assassins are Juan Pichardo, Horacio Vasquez, and Ramon Caceres, all prominent residents of Moca; the murderers of the president made their escape, and it is not probable that they will be captured; and business is paralyzed, but at present the country is quiet. The State Department received this morning from Campbell L. Maxwell, American consul general at Santo Domingo, an official confirmation of the assassination of President Heureaux; and through the State Department, President McKinley sent a cablegram of condolence to President Figuereo: 'Lake Champlain, via Washington, July 27, 1899. His Excellency Wenceslao Figuereo, President of the Dominican Republic, Santo Domingo: In the name of the American people, and in my own, I offer to your Excellency and the Dominican Nation most sincere condolences, by reason of the death of President Heureaux. William McKinley.' It was said at the State Department this afternoon that the assassination of President Heureaux will probably not disturb the diplomatic relations between that country and the United States, and that, unless it shall appear that American business interests on the island are in danger by a possible revolution or political agitation growing out of the tragedy, no action will be taken by this Government beyond the official expression of sympathy with the inhabitants of the Republic.

records.headline: The Gazette completes its assassination dispatch: the remains of President Heureaux
records.summary_en: The Gazette completes its assassination dispatch: the remains of President Heureaux will probably be taken to Santo Domingo for the funeral services; General Wenceslao Figuereo, immediately upon the announcement of the President's death, assumed the direction of affairs, and at present calmness prevails everywhere in the republic. President Heureaux was a soldier during his entire lifetime: one of his arms was paralyzed from a wound he received by a rifle ball in battle; he is described by Americans familiar with his career as a man without fear, and when there was any disturbance or revolution in any part of the republic, he mounted his horse and went pellmell himself to the front as leader, and learned all the details of the revolution as well as the causes leading to it; President Heureaux was about fifty-four years of age, he spoke English fluently, and treated everybody who approached him with courtesy. The Gazette also prints a Puerto Plata item of July 27: it is learned that President Heureaux met his death at the hands of three men as he was entering a friend's house: the three fired at Heureaux with revolvers, and one shot entered the heart, causing instant death; friends of the President returned the fire, but the assassins fled and their whereabouts are not known; Heureaux was at Moca on one of his periodical trips to investigate affairs on the island; and the assassination is believed to be due to the personal animosity of Caceres, the chief assassin, whose father was executed by orders of Heureaux in 1884.

records.headline: The Intelligencer prints the close of its assassination dispatch
records.summary_en: The Intelligencer prints the close of its assassination dispatch and the Washington and New York items: upon the announcement of the president's death the direction of affairs was assumed; at present calmness prevails everywhere in the republic; and the remains of President Heureaux will probably be taken to Santo Domingo for the funeral services. The Washington item, of July 26, says that no information was received up to half past 9 o'clock tonight from the consular representatives of the United States in Santo Domingo regarding the assassination there today of President Heureaux, and that, pending official advices of the assassination, no formal action will be taken by this government; Secretary Long said he could not recall that there were any ships of the United States navy now in Santo Domingo waters, and that, should the developments of the next few days show a feeling of unrest and uncertainty regarding the future affairs of the island, a United States man-of-war will be dispatched to that vicinity to look out for the protection of American interests. Under the head 'Was a Model Executive,' the New York item says that Senor Don Alejandro Woss y Gil, consul general of the Dominican republic, when seen at his home here tonight, could scarcely credit the news of the assassination of his president, Senor Ulysses Heureaux: "President Heureaux did wonders to make our people happy and give us prosperity. He was serving his second term, and in a year would have finished his labors as president. He was formerly minister of the interior and also served as secretary of war. Moca is a town three days' ride by horse from Santo Domingo."

records.headline: The Standard prints part of an article on the annexation attempt
records.summary_en: The Standard prints part of an article on the annexation attempt under Grant: a speech quoted in the article declares that "the idea of annexing the Dominican republic to the United States may acquire such a degree of popularity among members of congress as will be necessary for its accomplishment," and asks, "Shall I read the rest of the document? It is in the same tenor. There are questions of money in it, cash down, all of which must have been particularly agreeable to the three confederates." After the delivery of this speech Grant and Sumner had no personal intercourse; public opinion did not justify the course of Senator Sumner; no further attempt was made by the president to urge the acquisition of San Domingo upon congress, it being evident that neither the Senate nor the House could be induced to approve the scheme, and the administration was necessarily compelled to abandon it; but defeat did not change General Grant's view of the question, and in his last annual message to congress, in December, 1876, nearly six years after the controversy closed, he recurred to the subject to record once more his approval of it.
records.summary_es: El Standard publica parte de un artículo sobre el intento de anexión bajo Grant: un discurso citado en el artículo declara que «la idea de anexar la República Dominicana a los Estados Unidos puede adquirir tal grado de popularidad entre los miembros del congreso como será necesario para su realización», y pregunta: «¿Leo el resto del documento? Es del mismo tenor. Hay en él cuestiones de dinero, en efectivo, todo lo cual debe haber sido particularmente agradable a los tres confederados». Después de la pronunciación de este discurso, Grant y Sumner no tuvieron más trato personal; la opinión pública no justificó el curso del senador Sumner; no se hizo ningún intento más por el presidente de instar la adquisición de Santo Domingo ante el congreso, siendo evidente que ni el Senado ni la Cámara podrían ser inducidos a aprobar el plan, y la administración se vio necesariamente obligada a abandonarlo; pero la derrota no cambió la opinión del general Grant sobre la cuestión, y en su último mensaje anual al congreso, en diciembre de 1876, casi seis años después de cerrada la controversia, volvió sobre el tema para registrar una vez más su aprobación.

records.headline: The Times prints a New York item of July 26 on the assassination
records.summary_en: The Times prints a New York item of July 26 on the assassination: private despatches received late this afternoon in this city from Santo Domingo reported that Gen. Ulysses Heureaux, president of the Dominican Republic, had been assassinated at Moca at 4:30 o'clock in the afternoon; the despatches were without details, but the crime was undoubtedly inspired by political motives. Alejandro Wos y Gil, who preceded Heureaux as president of the republic, is its consul general at New York and charge d'affaires; he heard the news this afternoon, but had no particulars, and said tonight that he did not believe the report of the assassination: "In fact," he said, "I feel sure that it is false. There have been a number of similar rumors within the past two years, but they have always been contradicted next day. The meagre details of the alleged murder also argue to me that the report is unfounded. I am positive that I would have been notified either by the officials of my own country or by the United States government at Washington if the president had been killed. I received a cipher cable despatch from him on Monday. Now, the village of Moca is three days' journey by horse from the place from which the cable was sent. There are no railroads between the two places, and I am positive that it would have been impossible for the president to have gone to Moca and for the news of his murder there to have reached a place from which the news could be cabled here in so short a time."
records.summary_es: El Times publica una nota de Nueva York del 26 de julio sobre el asesinato: despachos privados recibidos tarde esta tarde en esta ciudad desde Santo Domingo reportaron que el general Ulysses Heureaux, presidente de la República Dominicana, había sido asesinado en Moca a las 4:30 de la tarde; los despachos no traían detalles, pero el crimen fue indudablemente inspirado por motivos políticos. Alejandro Wos y Gil, que precedió a Heureaux como presidente de la república, es su cónsul general en Nueva York y encargado de negocios; oyó la noticia esta tarde, pero no tenía particulares, y dijo esta noche que no creía el reporte del asesinato: «De hecho», dijo, «estoy seguro de que es falso. Ha habido un número de rumores similares dentro de los pasados dos años, pero siempre han sido contradichos al día siguiente. Los escasos detalles del alegado asesinato también me arguyen que el reporte es infundado. Estoy positivo de que habría sido notificado, ya por los funcionarios de mi propio país o por el gobierno de los Estados Unidos en Washington, si el presidente hubiera sido muerto. Recibí de él un despacho cifrado por cable el lunes. Ahora bien, el pueblo de Moca está a tres días de camino a caballo desde el lugar desde el cual se envió el cable. No hay ferrocarriles entre los dos lugares, y estoy positivo de que habría sido imposible que el presidente hubiera ido a Moca y que la noticia de su asesinato allí hubiera alcanzado un lugar desde el cual la noticia pudiera ser cablegrafiada aquí en tan corto tiempo».

records.headline: The Times' sketch of Heureaux's career continues with the executions
records.summary_en: The Times' sketch of Heureaux's career continues with the executions: men who had conspired against Heureaux were executed; in June, 1895, it was reported that his enemies had succeeded in killing him, but he had escaped, and it was thought he had succeeded in downing all the opposition to him; he was elected to the presidency in 1887, and the constitution of the republic was changed so as to permit him to succeed himself; he was already in his second term in 1893, and the attempts upon his life have all been made since then; in spite of the conspiracies that had begun in his second term he was twice again re-elected and was in his fourth term; while the prosperity under his administration has been unusual for Santo Domingo, it has not been such as to mark a material advance in the republic's general condition; the president's policy has been a progressive one, but the nation has not gone forward with any degree of rapidity in the way of civilization; under Heureaux American and English capital has been welcomed and railroads have been begun and have been extended, and the telegraphic facilities of the country, by which most of the chief towns are now connected, were furthered at his instance. Under the head 'The Castillo Rebellion,' the sketch continues: in the spring of 1896 the president found himself called upon to deal with a conspiracy against his power in the province of San Pedro de Macoris; General Ramon Castillo, his minister of war, had shortly before asked for 1,000 rifles to put down an incipient rebellion in that province, and had gone there in command to restore order, as he said.
records.summary_es: El esbozo del Times sobre la carrera de Heureaux continúa con las ejecuciones: los hombres que habían conspirado contra Heureaux fueron ejecutados; en junio de 1895 se reportó que sus enemigos habían logrado matarlo, pero él había escapado, y se pensaba que había logrado acabar con toda la oposición contra él; fue elegido a la presidencia en 1887, y la constitución de la república fue cambiada de modo que se le permitiera sucederse a sí mismo; ya estaba en su segundo período en 1893, y los intentos contra su vida han sido todos hechos desde entonces; a pesar de las conspiraciones que habían comenzado en su segundo período, fue dos veces más reelegido y estaba en su cuarto período; aunque la prosperidad bajo su administración ha sido inusual para Santo Domingo, no ha sido tal que marque un avance material en la condición general de la república; la política del presidente ha sido progresista, pero la nación no ha avanzado con ningún grado de rapidez en el camino de la civilización; bajo Heureaux, el capital americano e inglés ha sido bienvenido y los ferrocarriles han sido comenzados y extendidos, y las facilidades telegráficas del país, por las cuales la mayoría de los pueblos principales están ahora conectados, fueron impulsadas a su instancia. Bajo el título «The Castillo Rebellion», el esbozo continúa: en la primavera de 1896 el presidente se vio llamado a lidiar con una conspiración contra su poder en la provincia de San Pedro de Macorís; el general Ramon Castillo, su ministro de guerra, había pedido poco antes 1,000 rifles para sofocar una rebelión incipiente en esa provincia, y había ido allí al mando para restaurar el orden, según dijo.

records.headline: The Times' sketch continues with the order to kill Castillo
records.summary_en: The Times' sketch continues with the order to kill Castillo in San Pedro de Macoris, and, under the head 'Other Plots,' with the later conspiracies: in June, 1898, there was a good deal of discontent in Santo Domingo, owing partly to commercial and industrial depressions, and, when the operations of the Spanish-American war caused more or less excitement in the West Indies, Juan Jiminez, a former New York merchant who before had had political aspirations in Santo Domingo, led an attack upon Heureaux's power; he sailed with an expedition from the Bahamas for Cape Haitien and went thence to Monte Cristo, a town of Santo Domingo which he had founded; Jiminez landed in an American ship, the Fanita; General Garcia, who was in charge of affairs for him at Monte Cristo, was unprepared for action, but the two conspirators, together with Gen. Augustin Morales and eleven men, essayed to carry out their purpose and called upon the governor to surrender; the governor had twenty soldiers, who opened fire on the insurrectionists, killing five of them; Jiminez escaped to his ship; all the others except Garcia were captured, and Jiminez's secretary had turned informer; Jiminez went to Great Inagua, where he was arrested; he was tried at Nassau and acquitted, and since then he has carried on a propaganda against the administration of President Heureaux. In 1891 there was a carefully laid dynamite plot to blow up Heureaux; Heureaux has been described as humane when not thwarted, but ferocious when provoked by attempts on his authority; he was diplomatic and could speak four languages.

records.headline: The Spy prints the close of the assassination dispatch and the Washington item of July 26:
records.summary_en: The Spy prints the close of the assassination dispatch and the Washington item of July 26: the remains of President Heureaux will probably be taken to San Domingo for the funeral services. The Washington item, under the head 'No Official News,' says that no information was received up to half past 9 o'clock tonight from the consular representatives of the United States in San Domingo regarding the assassination there today of President Heureaux, and that, pending official advices of the assassination, no formal action will be taken by this government: Hon. William F. Powell, the minister to Hayti, is also charge d'affaires to San Domingo, while this government is directly represented in the republic in the person of Campbell L. Maxwell, who is consul general, and John A. Read, who is vice consul; officials here recall that attempts have been made heretofore on the life of Mr. Heureaux; Secretary Hay paid a brief tribute to the work of the deceased president, saying he understood that he had given the country a good administration; and Secretary Long said he could not recall that there were any ships of the United States navy in San Domingo waters, and that, should the developments of the next few days show a feeling of uncertainty regarding the future affairs of the island, a United States man-of-war will be dispatched to that vicinity to look out for the protection of American interests.
records.summary_es: El Spy publica el cierre del despacho del asesinato y la nota de Washington del 26 de julio: los restos del presidente Heureaux serán probablemente llevados a Santo Domingo para los servicios fúnebres. La nota de Washington, bajo el título «No Official News», dice que no se recibió hasta las nueve y media de esta noche ninguna información de los representantes consulares de los Estados Unidos en Santo Domingo respecto al asesinato allí hoy del presidente Heureaux, y que, pendientes los avisos oficiales del asesinato, no se tomará ninguna acción formal por este gobierno: el honorable William F. Powell, el ministro en Haití, es también encargado de negocios en Santo Domingo, mientras este gobierno está directamente representado en la república en la persona de Campbell L. Read, que es vicecónsul; los funcionarios aquí recuerdan que se han hecho antes intentos contra la vida del señor Heureaux; el secretario Hay rindió un breve tributo a la obra del presidente fallecido, diciendo que entendía que él había dado al país una buena administración; y el secretario Long dijo que no podía recordar que hubiera ninguno de los buques de la marina de los Estados Unidos en aguas de Santo Domingo, y que, si los acontecimientos de los próximos días muestran un sentimiento de incertidumbre respecto a los asuntos futuros de la isla, un buque de guerra de los Estados Unidos será despachado a esa vecindad para velar por la protección de los intereses americanos.

records.headline: The Age-Herald prints details of the murder of President Heureaux
records.summary_en: The Age-Herald prints details of the murder of President Heureaux, received at Cape Haytien in a dispatch of July 27: he was assassinated as he was about to leave on horseback for Santiago de los Caballeros; the assassin, Ramon Caceros, surrounded by several accomplices, approached the president as he was talking with some friends and fired twice with a revolver; the first bullet struck the president in the left side and penetrated the heart, causing instant death; the second bullet killed an old man who was standing near the president; the assassin and his accomplices then fled to avoid the shots fired at them by the president's friends, and it is not known whether any of them were wounded; the body of the president was taken to the palace of the governor of Moca; President Heureaux's death has caused a panic; it is said that one Juan Isidoro Jiminez, who took part in the attempted insurrection of June, 1898, is a candidate for the presidency; and it is reported that General Maximo Gomez, formerly president of the Cuban insurrectionists, who is a native of San Domingo, also aspires to the presidency.

records.headline: The Age-Herald completes its account of the assassination aftermath
records.summary_en: The Age-Herald completes its account of the assassination aftermath: the successor assumes the presidential functions, acting with the ministers, and has informed the widow of President Heureaux that the body of her husband will be interred at Santiago de los Caballeros, orders for carrying out the plan having been given to the governors of Santiago; it is concurrently reported that this course was decided on in order to avoid the excitement and manifestations which would be the result of the removal of the remains to the city of Santo Domingo; foreseeing the possibility of disturbances, and in order to prepare for any emergency, General Pepin, governor of Santiago, has taken important precautionary measures and has decided to demand that arms and ammunition be forwarded to him from Santo Domingo; and advices from Santiago received here at a late hour report that the situation there is becoming more serious. Under the head 'A Political Crime,' a Fort de France dispatch of July 27 says that the body of President Heureaux has been taken to Santiago de los Caballeros; the president's widow has requested that the remains be transported by railway to Puerto Plata and from there to Santo Domingo by sea, but the government of Santiago fears disorder if the body should be removed from there by train; the government of Santiago confirms the general opinion that the assassination of the president was a political crime; and it is reported that the assassin's party is gathering forces preparatory to an attack on the government troops.
records.summary_es: El Age-Herald completa su relato de las secuelas del asesinato: el sucesor asume las funciones presidenciales, actuando con los ministros, y ha informado a la viuda del presidente Heureaux que el cuerpo de su esposo será enterrado en Santiago de los Caballeros, habiéndose dado a los gobernadores de Santiago las órdenes para llevar a cabo el plan; se reporta concurrentemente que este curso se decidió para evitar la excitación y las manifestaciones que serían el resultado del traslado de los restos a la ciudad de Santo Domingo; previendo la posibilidad de disturbios, y para prepararse para cualquier emergencia, el general Pepin, gobernador de Santiago, ha tomado importantes medidas precautorias y ha decidido demandar que se le envíen armas y municiones desde Santo Domingo; y avisos de Santiago recibidos aquí a hora avanzada reportan que la situación allí se está volviendo más seria. Bajo el título «A Political Crime», un despacho de Fort de France del 27 de julio dice que el cuerpo del presidente Heureaux ha sido llevado a Santiago de los Caballeros; la viuda del presidente ha pedido que los restos sean transportados por ferrocarril a Puerto Plata y de allí a Santo Domingo por mar, pero el gobierno de Santiago teme desorden si el cuerpo fuera removido de allí por tren; el gobierno de Santiago confirma la opinión general de que el asesinato del presidente fue un crimen político; y se reporta que el partido del asesino está reuniendo fuerzas en preparación para un ataque contra las tropas del gobierno.

records.headline: The Argus prints the Santiago dispatch on the assassination
records.summary_en: The Argus prints the Santiago dispatch on the assassination aftermath: the remains will be interred at Santiago de los Caballeros, and orders for the carrying out of this plan have been given to the governor of Santiago; it is currently reported that this course was decided upon in order to avoid the excitement and manifestations which would be the result of the removal of the remains to the City of Santo Domingo; foreseeing the possibility of disturbances, and in order to be prepared for any emergency, General Pepin, governor of Santiago, has taken important precautionary measures and has decided to demand that arms and ammunition be forwarded to him from Santo Domingo; and advices from Santiago report that the situation there is becoming more serious. Under the head 'It Was a Political Assassination,' the paper continues: the governor of Santiago confirms the general opinion that the assassination of President Heureaux was a political crime; it is reported that the assassin's party is gathering forces preparatory to an attack on the government troops; it has been learned that Caceros' companions when President Heureaux was killed were Juan Pichardo and Horacio Vasquez, the latter the brother of a deputy in parliament; a financial crisis having arisen in Santo Domingo, and an insurrection being feared owing to the number of malcontents, President Heureaux went to the north and west of the island to prepare for what might happen, and he was about to leave Moca for Santiago de los Caballeros when he was killed.
records.summary_es: El Argus publica el despacho de Santiago sobre las secuelas del asesinato: los restos serán enterrados en Santiago de los Caballeros, y las órdenes para llevar a cabo este plan han sido dadas al gobernador de Santiago; se reporta corrientemente que este curso se decidió para evitar la excitación y las manifestaciones que serían el resultado del traslado de los restos a la ciudad de Santo Domingo; previendo la posibilidad de disturbios, y para estar preparado para cualquier emergencia, el general Pepin, gobernador de Santiago, ha tomado importantes medidas precautorias y ha decidido demandar que se le envíen armas y municiones desde Santo Domingo; y avisos de Santiago reportan que la situación allí se está volviendo más seria. Bajo el título «It Was a Political Assassination», el periódico continúa: el gobernador de Santiago confirma la opinión general de que el asesinato del presidente Heureaux fue un crimen político; se reporta que el partido del asesino está reuniendo fuerzas en preparación para un ataque contra las tropas del gobierno; se ha sabido que los compañeros de Caceros cuando el presidente Heureaux fue muerto eran Juan Pichardo y Horacio Vasquez, este último hermano de un diputado en el parlamento; habiendo surgido una crisis financiera en Santo Domingo, y temiéndose una insurrección debido al número de descontentos, el presidente Heureaux fue al norte y al oeste de la isla para prepararse para lo que pudiera suceder, y estaba a punto de partir de Moca para Santiago de los Caballeros cuando fue muerto.

records.summary_en: The Leader completes the details dispatch and prints a Washington item of July 28: he was about to leave on horseback for Santiago de los Caballeros; the assassin, Ramon Caceros, surrounded by several accomplices, approached the president as he was talking with some friends and fired twice with a revolver; the first ball struck the president in the left side and penetrated the heart, causing instant death; the second bullet killed an old man who was standing near the president; the assassin and his accomplices then fled to avoid the shots fired at them by the president's friends, and it is not known whether any of them were wounded; the body of the president was taken to the palace of the governor of Moca; President Heureaux's death has caused a panic; it is said that one Juan Isidoro Jiminez, who took part in the attempted insurrection of June, 1898, is a candidate for the presidency; it is reported that Gen. Maximo Gomez, formerly president of the Cuban insurrectionists, who is a native of Santo Domingo, also aspires to the presidency; and the father of Caceros, the assassin, was put to death by order of President Heureaux in 1881. records.headline: The Fisherman and Farmer prints the Fort de France dispatch
records.summary_en: The Fisherman and Farmer prints the Fort de France dispatch and the Washington item of July 26: Ulises Heureaux, president of the Dominican Republic, was assassinated at Moca, Santo Domingo, at half past four o'clock this afternoon; the name of the murderer is Ramon Caceros; he succeeded in making his escape, but an energetic pursuit was at once begun and it is probable he will soon be captured; and at present calmness prevails everywhere in the republic. The Washington item says that no information was received up to 9:30 o'clock tonight from the consular representatives of the United States in Santo Domingo regarding the assassination there today of President Heureaux, and that, pending official advices of the assassination, no formal action will be taken by this government: Hon. W. F. Powell, the minister to Hayti, is also charge d'affaires to Santo Domingo, while this government is directly represented in the republic in the person of Campbell L. Maxwell, who is consul-general, and John A. Read, who is vice consul; officials here recall that attempts have been made heretofore on the life of Mr. Heureaux; Secretary Hay paid a brief tribute to the work of the deceased president, saying he understood that he had given the country a good administration; and, should the developments of the next few days show a feeling of unrest and uncertainty regarding the future affairs of the island, a United States man-of-war will be dispatched to that vicinity to look out for the protection of American interests.
records.summary_es: El Fisherman and Farmer publica el despacho de Fort de France y la nota de Washington del 26 de julio: Ulises Heureaux, presidente de la República Dominicana, fue asesinado en Moca, Santo Domingo, a las cuatro y media de esta tarde; el nombre del asesino es Ramon Caceros; logró hacer su escape, pero una persecución enérgica se comenzó de inmediato y es probable que pronto sea capturado; y al presente prevalece la calma en todas partes en la república. La nota de Washington dice que no se recibió hasta las 9:30 de esta noche ninguna información de los representantes consulares de los Estados Unidos en Santo Domingo respecto al asesinato allí hoy del presidente Heureaux, y que, pendientes los avisos oficiales del asesinato, no se tomará ninguna acción formal por este gobierno: el honorable W. records.headline: The News prints a Kingston dispatch of July 28 on the Jimenez plot:
records.summary_en: The News prints a Kingston dispatch of July 28 on the Jimenez plot: advices from Santo Domingo to a Dominican at Kingston, Jamaica, describe the existence of a well-planned and widespread plot by adherents of Jimenez to depose President Heureaux, which it was thought was sure to succeed, and the assassination of President Heureaux is regarded there as an indication of the success of the plot. The Washington item, under the head 'The Entering Wedge,' reports that a naval vessel is to be sent immediately to Santo Domingo; this is a measure of precaution rather than one of necessity at the present time, for Minister Powell has not suggested any such action to the government, but it is deemed well, in view of the press reports indicating the disturbed condition of affairs, to have a representative of the United States authority within reach of the minister to protect American interests should the need arise.

records.headline: The Register prints a sketch of Heureaux's career: he was born
records.summary_en: The Register prints a sketch of Heureaux's career: he was born in Puerto Plata, San Domingo, in 1846; he became a private soldier in 1862 and was soon after appointed commandant in the district of Puerto Plata; he served continuously in the war against Spain from 1868 to 1874; twice he was exiled for political reasons; for two years he retired to private life, and again in 1878 assumed command to put down a Spanish uprising; he had been wounded many times and narrowly escaped several plots to kill him; during the recent Spanish-American war a filibustering expedition, alleged to have been fitted out in a port in the southern part of the United States, made an attempt to land in San Domingo, but was met and checked by Heureaux's prompt action, and at that time his assassination was rumored and had undoubtedly been planned; Gen. Heureaux was re-elected president of San Domingo at a general election, November 1, 1898, and was serving his fourth term; Gen. Heureaux was first elected president, September 1, 1882, to succeed Fernando A. Merino, when the national party, of which he was an active representative, was powerful; General Maximo Gomez, former president of the Cuban insurrectionists, who is a native of San Domingo, also aspires to the presidency; the father of Caceros, the assassin, was put to death by order of President Heureaux in 1884; and a financial crisis having arisen in Santo Domingo, and an insurrection being feared owing to the number of malcontents, President Heureaux went to the north and west of the island to prepare for all eventualities.

records.headline: The Times continues its New York item with Consul General Gil's reaction:
records.summary_en: The Times continues its New York item with Consul General Gil's reaction: Alejandro Wos y Gil, consul general and charge d'affaires of the Dominican Republic in this city, who had received no answer to his message of inquiry, was much shocked when he read the despatches verifying the reports received last night: "It is very sad news," he said. "I had hoped that this rumor, like many others I have heard in the course of the past year, would prove false." Consul General Gil then expressed the opinion that the president's death would not have a serious effect upon the republic. Mr. York, of the Santo Domingo Improvement Company, was very positive that no serious results would follow the president's death: "The affairs of the country are in a sound, healthy condition and things will go on as usual. The fact that the President was assassinated does not mean that there is any general discontent among the citizens of the country. That would be a false assumption. Discontented persons with murderous instincts are to be found in every country, but as a rule they do not represent the great body of the people. You will appreciate the extent of my confidence in the strength of the Government when I tell you my wife and children sail for Santo Domingo today on the Clyde line steamship Carib. I am sorry to hear of General Heureaux's death, very sorry, but it will surely not affect the country seriously." Moca is the principal town of the Espaillat province; it is situated in the mountains on the north coast of the island, and has no railroad communication.
records.summary_es: El Times continúa su nota de Nueva York con la reacción del cónsul general Gil: Alejandro Wos y Gil, cónsul general y encargado de negocios de la República Dominicana en esta ciudad, que no había recibido respuesta a su mensaje de indagación, quedó muy impresionado cuando leyó los despachos que verificaban los reportes recibidos anoche: «Es una noticia muy triste», dijo. «Había esperado que este rumor, como muchos otros que he oído en el curso del año pasado, resultara falso». El cónsul general Gil expresó entonces la opinión de que la muerte del presidente no tendría un efecto serio sobre la república. El señor York, de la Santo Domingo Improvement Company, estuvo muy positivo de que no seguirían resultados serios a la muerte del presidente: «Los asuntos del país están en una condición sana y saludable y las cosas seguirán como de costumbre. El hecho de que el presidente fue asesinado no significa que haya ningún descontento general entre los ciudadanos del país. Esa sería una suposición falsa. Personas descontentas con instintos asesinos se encuentran en todo país, pero por regla general no representan al gran cuerpo del pueblo. Usted apreciará la extensión de mi confianza en la fuerza del gobierno cuando le diga que mi esposa e hijos zarpan hoy para Santo Domingo en el vapor Carib de la línea Clyde. Siento oír de la muerte del general Heureaux, lo siento mucho, pero seguramente no afectará seriamente al país». Moca es el pueblo principal de la provincia Espaillat; está situado en las montañas en la costa norte de la isla, y no tiene comunicación por ferrocarril.

records.headline: The Republican prints the Fort de France dispatch on the assassination
records.summary_en: The Republican prints the Fort de France dispatch on the assassination: Gen. Ulises Heureaux, president of the Dominican republic, was assassinated at Moca at 4:30 o'clock Wednesday afternoon; the name of the murderer is Ramon Caceros; he succeeded in making his escape, but an energetic pursuit was at once begun and it is probable that he will soon be captured; the vice-president, Gen. Wenceslao Figuereo, immediately upon the announcement of the president's death assumed the direction of affairs; at present calmness prevails everywhere in the republic; and the body of President Heureaux will probably be taken to San Domingo for the funeral services.

records.headline: The Telegram prints the details of the assassination at Moca
records.summary_en: The Telegram prints the details of the assassination at Moca: the assassin, surrounded by several accomplices, approached the president as he was talking with some friends and fired twice with a revolver; the first bullet struck the president in the left side and penetrated to the heart, causing instant death; the second bullet killed an old man who was standing near the president; the assassin and his accomplices then fled to avoid the shots fired at them by the president's friends, and it is not known if any of them was wounded; the body of the president was taken to the palace of the governor of Moca; President Heureaux's death has caused a panic; it is said that one Juan Isidoro Jiminez, who took part in the attempted insurrection of June, 1898, is a candidate for the presidency; it is reported that General Maximo Gomez, former president of the Cuban insurrectionists, who is a native of Santo Domingo, also aspires to the presidency; and the father of Caceres, the assassin, was put to death by order of President Heureaux in 1881. The other account, under the head 'Another Version of the Affair,' says that a financial crisis having arisen in Santo Domingo, and an insurrection being feared owing to the number of the malcontents, President Heureaux went to the north and west of the island to prepare for all eventualities; he was about to leave Moca for Santiago de los Caballeros when he was killed; booted and spurred, ready to mount his horse, he sat under the gallery of a house in the Rue Colon talking with two friends at 4:30 in the afternoon, when an old man approached to ask for alms.
records.summary_es: El Telegram publica los detalles del asesinato en Moca: el asesino, rodeado por varios cómplices, se acercó al presidente mientras él hablaba con algunos amigos y disparó dos veces con un revólver; la primera bala alcanzó al presidente en el costado izquierdo y le penetró hasta el corazón, causando la muerte instantánea; la segunda bala mató a un anciano que estaba parado cerca del presidente; el asesino y sus cómplices huyeron entonces para evitar los disparos que les hicieron los amigos del presidente, y no se sabe si alguno de ellos fue herido; el cuerpo del presidente fue llevado al palacio del gobernador de Moca; la muerte del presidente Heureaux ha causado un pánico; se dice que un tal Juan Isidoro Jiminez, que tomó parte en la insurrección intentada de junio de 1898, es candidato para la presidencia; se reporta que el general Maximo Gomez, antiguo presidente de los insurrectos cubanos, que es nativo de Santo Domingo, también aspira a la presidencia; y el padre de Caceres, el asesino, fue condenado a muerte por orden del presidente Heureaux en 1881. La otra versión, bajo el título «Another Version of the Affair», dice que habiendo surgido una crisis financiera en Santo Domingo, y temiéndose una insurrección debido al número de descontentos, el presidente Heureaux fue al norte y al oeste de la isla para prepararse para todas las eventualidades; estaba a punto de partir de Moca para Santiago de los Caballeros cuando fue muerto; con botas y espuelas, listo para montar su caballo, estaba sentado bajo la galería de una casa en la Rue Colon hablando con dos amigos a las 4:30 de la tarde, cuando un anciano se acercó a pedir limosna.

records.headline: The Bee completes its assassination items with a report on the political crime
records.summary_en: The Bee completes its assassination items with a report on the political crime and a Puerto Plata item of July 27: the body of President Heureaux has been taken to Santiago de las Caballeros; the president's widow has requested that the body be transported by railway to Puerto Plata and from there to Santo Domingo by sea, but the governor of Santiago fears disorder if the body should be removed from there by train; the governor of Santiago confirms the general opinion that the assassination of President Heureaux was a political crime; it is reported that the assassin's party is gathering forces preparatory to an attack on the government troops; and it has been learned that Cacero's companions when President Heureaux was killed were Juan Pichardo and Horacio Vasquez, the latter a brother of a deputy in Parliament. The Puerto Plata item says President Heureaux, who was assassinated in Moca yesterday afternoon, had gone there to see Jacobo Lara; the president, at the entrance to the city, was fired at by four individuals; enemies of the government are trying to disturb the peace; General Wenceslao Figuereo, who succeeds to the presidency, will continue the plan of retiring paper money; and President Heureaux went to Moca attended by only six persons.

records.headline: The Journal prints the close of an interview, Erwin York's statement
records.summary_en: The Journal prints the close of an interview, Erwin York's statement, and a Fort de France item of July 28: the speaker prophesies that the United States will eventually be compelled to interfere to establish peace in the island, just as this country did in Cuba, declares that he favors the policy of peace and will be glad to return to his country and support such a policy if it is inaugurated by Gen. Figuereo, the vice president, who succeeds to the head of the government, and warns that if something is not quickly done to establish order and peace more revolutionary expeditions will follow, like that of Gen. Jimines and Gen. Morales, who led a band from Cuba against Heureaux. Erwin York, secretary of the Santo Domingo improvement company which controls the country's finances, said: 'Should the new administration attempt to repudiate our contracts we shall certainly, as American citizens, call upon the Washington administration for protection. I do not believe there will be any revolution.' The contract with the improvement company was signed by President Heureaux in 1883; it gives to the company the railroads and the right to collect the customs, and in return for those concessions the company has assumed the national debt of the country, which is principally held by the United States. Under the head 'Murder Was Political,' the Fort de France dispatch says Vice President Figuereo, who assumes the presidential functions acting with the ministers, has informed the widow of President Heureaux that the body of her husband will be interred at Santiago de las Caballeros.

records.headline: The Bulletin prints the panic item, completes its dispatch
records.summary_en: The Bulletin prints the panic item, completes its dispatch, and gives another account from Fort de France: the second bullet killed an old man who was standing near the president; the assassin and his accomplices then fled to avoid the shots fired at them by the president's friends; it is not known whether any of the men were wounded; and the body of the president was taken to the palace of the governor of Moca. President Heureaux's death has caused a panic: one Juan Isidoro Jimines, who took part in the attempted insurrection of June, 1898, is said to be a candidate for the presidency; General Maximo Gomez, formerly president of the Cuban insurrectionists, who is a native of Santo Domingo, also aspired to the presidency; and the father of Caceros, the assassin, was put to death by order of President Heureaux in 1884. Under the head 'Another Account,' a financial crisis having arisen in Santo Domingo and an insurrection being feared, owing to the number of malcontents, President Heureaux went to the northwest of the island to prepare for all eventualities, and was to leave Moca for Santiago de las Caballeros when he was killed: booted and spurred, ready to mount his horse, he sat under the gallery of a house in the Rue Colon, talking with two friends at 4:30 p. m., when an old man approached to ask for alms, and just as the president gave the old man some money, Caceros, the assassin, rushed forward quickly and fired twice from his revolver, one bullet striking the heart of the president, killing him instantly, and the other killing the old man by his side.

records.headline: The Sun prints the consul general's account of the assassination
records.summary_en: The Sun prints the consul general's account of the assassination news in a New York item: Alejandro Woss y Gil, the consul general of the Dominican Republic in this city, had received no word from his home government directly yesterday confirming the assassination of President Heureaux, but two cablegrams were taken to him by Secretary Erwin D. York of the Santo Domingo Improvement Company; one came from the manager of the Santo Domingo Railroad, dated at Puerto Plata, and read: 'Gen. Heureaux assassinated at Moca Wednesday afternoon. Country quiet'; the other came from the city of Santo Domingo and contained a similar announcement. The consul general said the country was prosperous, with no serious question for the government to settle except the paper issue of the currency, and this he thought would be taken up and disposed of in a satisfactory manner by Vice-President Figuereo, whom he declared to be a very able man. Mr. York, whose company has charge of the collection of the revenue of the Dominican Republic as the representative of foreign bondholders, also expressed confidence in the vice president, who will now become the executive, and thought the death of President Heureaux was not the precursor of revolution: 'The government in Santo Domingo,' he said, 'has been stable for many years now, and I know of no party or faction that has been threatening it.'
records.summary_es: El Sun publica el relato del cónsul general sobre el asesinato en una nota de Nueva York: Alejandro Woss y Gil, el cónsul general de la República Dominicana en esta ciudad, no había recibido palabra de su gobierno directamente ayer confirmando el asesinato del presidente Heureaux, pero dos cablegramas le fueron llevados por el secretario Erwin D. York de la Santo Domingo Improvement Company; uno venía del gerente del Ferrocarril de Santo Domingo, fechado en Puerto Plata, y decía: «Gen. Heureaux asesinado en Moca el miércoles por la tarde. País tranquilo»; el otro venía de la ciudad de Santo Domingo y contenía un anuncio similar. El cónsul general dijo que el país estaba próspero, sin ninguna cuestión seria que el gobierno tuviera que resolver excepto la emisión en papel de la moneda, y esto él pensaba sería tomado y dispuesto de una manera satisfactoria por el vicepresidente Figuereo, a quien declaró ser un hombre muy capaz. El señor York, cuya compañía tiene a su cargo la cobranza de la renta de la República Dominicana como representante de los tenedores de bonos extranjeros, también expresó confianza en el vicepresidente, que ahora se convertirá en el ejecutivo, y pensó que la muerte del presidente Heureaux no era el precursor de una revolución: «El gobierno en Santo Domingo», dijo, «ha sido estable por muchos años ahora, y no conozco ningún partido o facción que lo haya estado amenazando».

records.summary_en: The Gazette prints a Puerto Plata dispatch of July 28 on the burial and the grave condition of the island: the body of President Heureaux was interred in the cathedral at Santiago de los Caballeros last evening, after impressive services; affairs in the island are in a grave condition and the government is taking active measures to prevent an insurrection; a small armed force last night made a demonstration about Moca and fired several shots; it is reported that a number of exiles from Santo Domingo, driven into Hayti by Heureaux, are arming and preparing to cross the frontier and join an insurrection under Caceres, the chief assassin of Heureaux; and business in the town of Santo Domingo is paralyzed and disorder is feared.

records.headline: The Democrat prints a Puerto Plata dispatch of July 28 and the opening of a sketch of Heureaux's career:
records.summary_en: The Democrat prints a Puerto Plata dispatch of July 28 and the opening of a sketch of Heureaux's career: President Heureaux, who was assassinated in Moca Wednesday, had gone there to see Jacobo Lara; he was attended by only six persons; the president, at the entrance to the city, was fired at by four individuals; the situation is critical, and enemies of the government are trying to disturb the peace; General Wenceslao Figuereo, the vice president, succeeds to the presidency, and will continue the plan of retiring paper money. Ulises Heureaux was born in 1846 and became president of the Dominican republic in 1886; he ruled with a firm hand, putting down insurrection after insurrection, and shooting the leaders very often without trial; he was immensely wealthy, and his term of office would have expired in October, 1901; he himself had caused reports to be circulated that he had been seized by revolutionists, imprisoned, and subsequently shot, to throw his enemies off their guard, so that they would betray themselves; he was twice exiled for political reasons; and his military career dated from 1862, when he enlisted as a private soldier to assist in driving the Spaniards from his native land, in a war that lasted three years and was followed by the Baez revolution, in which Colonel Heureaux also took a prominent part, conspicuous for his dash and bravery.
records.summary_es: El Democrat publica un despacho de Puerto Plata del 28 de julio y el comienzo de una semblanza de la carrera de Heureaux: el presidente Heureaux, que fue asesinado en Moca el miércoles, había ido ahí a ver a Jacobo Lara; fue atendido por solo seis personas; el presidente, a la entrada de la ciudad, fue atacado a tiros por cuatro individuos; la situación es crítica, y enemigos del gobierno están tratando de perturbar la paz; el general Wenceslao Figuereo, el vicepresidente, sucede a la presidencia, y continuará el plan de retirar el papel moneda. records.headline: This article describes Santo Domingo as long disturbed by dissensions and revolutionary movements, naming Juan
records.summary_en: This article describes Santo Domingo as long disturbed by dissensions and revolutionary movements, naming Juan Jiminez, a former merchant of Monte Christi and permanent candidate for the presidency, as one of the chief troublemakers. It recounts how Jiminez in June 1898 organised a filibustering expedition against the Heureaux government and landed at Monte Christi, but failed, his men being killed or captured while he escaped, and how another invasion was hourly expected there in July; it also describes the country's recent acute financial crisis, when the rate of exchange on New York rose more than 100 per cent and a commercial panic followed.
records.summary_es: Este artículo describe a Santo Domingo como perturbado durante mucho tiempo por disensiones y movimientos revolucionarios, y señala a Juan Jiménez, antiguo comerciante de Monte Cristi y candidato permanente a la presidencia, como uno de los principales agitadores. Cuenta cómo Jiménez organizó en junio de 1898 una expedición filibustera contra el gobierno de Heureaux y desembarcó en Monte Cristi, pero fracasó, pues sus hombres fueron muertos o capturados mientras él escapaba, y cómo en julio se esperaba allí otra invasión de un momento a otro; también describe la reciente crisis financiera aguda del país, cuando el tipo de cambio sobre Nueva York subió más del 100 por ciento y siguió un pánico comercial.
records.passage: iron rule was such bitter hatred on the part of his enemies that they tried to assassinate him in both June and December of 1898. But he escaped, and his opponents feared more than ever his smile which he graciously accorded to each one doomed by him to be shot against the "long, brick wall." Santo Domingo has been disturbed by internal dissensions and revolutionary movements for a long period, one of the chief trouble-makers being Juan Jiminez, formerly a prosperous merchant of Monti Christi, and who considers himself a permanent candidate for the presidency, his father having at one time been president of the republic. Jiminez, in June, 1898, organized a filibustering expedition against the Heureaux government, making a successful landing at Monti Christi. The attempt, however, failed, all Jiminez's men being killed or captured. Jiminez himself escaped, and, on July [illegible] last, it was reported that panic reigned at Monti Christi, where another invasion by Jiminez's followers was hourly expected. The country has also recently passed through an acute financial crisis, owing to the peculiar financial system of the country. Last September the increase in the rate of exchange on New York was more than 100 percent, and a commercial panic ensued, and public discontent attained such force that the situation of the Heureaux government was considered most critical,

records.headline: The Globe prints the burial decision for Santiago de los Caballeros
records.summary_en: The Globe prints the burial decision for Santiago de los Caballeros and the governor's precautions: Vice President Figuereo, who assumes the presidential functions acting with the ministers, has informed the widow of President Heureaux that the body of her husband will be interred at Santiago de los Caballeros, and orders for the carrying out of this plan have been given to the governor of Santiago; this course was decided on in order to avoid the excitement and manifestations which would result from the removal of the remains to the city of Santo Domingo. Foreseeing the possibility of disturbances, Gen. Peppin, governor of Santiago, has taken important precautionary measures, and has ordered that arms and ammunition be forwarded to him from Santo Domingo; advices from Santiago received at a late hour say the situation is becoming more serious. The governor of Santiago confirms the general opinion that the assassination of President Heureaux was a political crime; it was reported that the assassin's party are gathering preparatory to an attack upon the government troops; and it has been learned that Cacero's companions when President Heureaux was killed were Juan Picharde and Horacio Vasquez, the latter a brother of a deputy in parliament. President Heureaux's death has caused a panic: one Juan Isidore Jiminez, who took part in the attempted insurrection of June, 1898, is said to be a candidate for the presidency; and Gen. Maximo Gomez, formerly president of the Cuban insurrectionists, who is a native of Santo Domingo, also aspires to the presidency.
records.summary_es: El Globe publica la decisión del entierro para Santiago de los Caballeros y las precauciones del gobernador: el vicepresidente Figuereo, que asume las funciones presidenciales actuando con los ministros, ha informado a la viuda del presidente Heureaux que el cuerpo de su esposo será enterrado en Santiago de los Caballeros, y órdenes para la ejecución de este plan han sido dadas al gobernador de Santiago; este curso fue decidido para evitar la excitación y las manifestaciones que resultarían del traslado de los restos a la ciudad de Santo Domingo. Previendo la posibilidad de disturbios, el gen. Peppin, gobernador de Santiago, ha tomado importantes medidas precautorias, y ha ordenado que armas y municiones le sean enviadas desde Santo Domingo; avisos de Santiago recibidos a última hora dicen que la situación se está volviendo más seria. El gobernador de Santiago confirma la opinión general de que el asesinato del presidente Heureaux fue un crimen político; se reportó que el partido del asesino se está reuniendo en preparación de un ataque a las tropas del gobierno; y se ha sabido que los compañeros de Cacero cuando el presidente Heureaux fue muerto fueron Juan Picharde y Horacio Vasquez, el último hermano de un diputado en el Parlamento. La muerte del presidente Heureaux ha causado un pánico: se dice que un tal Juan Isidore Jiminez, que tomó parte en el intento de insurrección de junio de 1898, es candidato a la presidencia; y el gen. Máximo Gómez, ex presidente de los insurrectos cubanos, que es nativo de Santo Domingo, aspira también a la presidencia.

records.headline: After the assassination of President Heureaux, Vice President Figueroa, who assumes the presidential functions
records.summary_en: After the assassination of President Heureaux, Vice President Figueroa, who assumes the presidential functions, informed the president's widow that the body would be buried at Santiago de los Caballeros rather than taken to Santo Domingo, for fear of hostile manifestations there. Government officials expect an uprising: arms and ammunition have been ordered sent to Santiago, the assassin's party is reported to be gathering to attack the government troops, and the president was shot down at Moca by Ramon Caceres just as he gave alms to an old man who had asked for help.

Las autoridades del gobierno esperan un levantamiento: se ha ordenado enviar armas y municiones a Santiago, se informa que el partido del asesino se está reuniendo para atacar a las tropas del gobierno, y el presidente fue derribado a tiros en Moca por Ramón Cáceres justo cuando daba limosna a un anciano que le había pedido ayuda.

FORT DE FRANCE, July 27.—[illegible] financial crisis having arrived in Santo Domingo and an insurrection being feared owing to the number of malcontents, President Heureaux went to the north and west of the island to prepare for all eventualities. He was about to leave Moca for Santiago de los Caballeros when he was killed. Booted and spurred, ready to mount his horse, he sat under the gallery of a house in the Rue Colon, talking to two friends, at 4:30 in the afternoon, when an old man approached to ask for alms. Just as the president gave the old man some money, Caceros, the assassin, rushed forward quickly and fired twice from his revolver. One bullet struck the heart of the president, killing him instantly, and the other killed the old man by his side. The crime was committed so rapidly that the friends of the president were not able to interfere in time to prevent it, but they fired a number of shots at Caceros, who ran away, accompanied by several persons. The assassin's party returned the fire of the president's friends and Caceros escaped. It is not known whether he was wounded or not. The authorities immediately sent troops to pursue him. The body of President Heureaux was taken to the house of the governor of Moca. The news of the president's death spread rapidly and caused much emotion among the inhabitants of the island. York's opinion of the murder under the head 'Deed of a Fanatic': Vice President Figuero has taken precautions to prevent disorder, and has taken command of the troops to that end, but up to the present all is quiet. E. D. York, secretary of the Santo Domingo Improvement company, who has large interests in Santo Domingo and supported President Heureaux, said in New York on July 27 that the assassination was the act, no doubt, of some fanatical native, who thought he was making a martyr of himself, and that it only illustrates the temper of the race; that Gen. Heureaux, in his opinion, was in every way what President Diaz is to Mexico, and with a firm hand had put the country in a substantial and prosperous condition; that two months ago he was in the interior of the island, and from personal observation never had it experienced such a period of prosperity, with over 100 miles of road in the interior, the sugar and coffee crops the largest known in years, and, while prices are not as high, the exports the highest known; and that the currency question was causing the administration no little uneasiness, the government trying to move from an old silver basis to the modern gold standard, the transition having occasioned no little bitterness and discontent.

records.headline: The Herald prints an editorial paragraph on the death of President Heureaux
records.summary_en: The Herald prints an editorial paragraph on the death of President Heureaux and the danger of disorder in the West Indies: the death of President Heureaux of the Dominican republic emphasizes, it says, the danger of preserving order among the hotblooded races of the West Indies; assassination in the Spanish-American republics is no uncommon occurrence, preceding and almost invariably following every political revolution, and almost every campaign assumes the seriousness of civil war before an election is reached; but in this particular republic President Heureaux was especially popular and pleasing in his administration of public affairs, and no reason for the murder can be divined except that such acts are an expression of a race characteristic.
