records.headline: The Intelligencer prints an editorial on the three serious possibilities
records.summary_en: The Intelligencer prints an editorial on the three serious possibilities which directly concern Americans in San Domingo: the first is the extent of American investments on the island; the second reason is the approximation of the interests of the people of the Dominican republic to our own, both in a material and sentimental way, it being regarded that in no other of the islands of the West Indies, with the exception of Cuba and Porto Rico, is the confidence so strong in the United States, and this country has been looked to rather than any other country for good favor when needed; and the Sun and other papers commenting on the situation, as well as naval and military officers, point out the new political and strategic relations proceeding from our possession of Porto Rico on one side and our occupation of Cuba on the other. These are logical arguments for the exercise of watchfulness on the part of our government; and in view of the fact that the death of Heureaux is followed by disorder and insurrection, naval vessels to protect our interests will be necessary for the waters of San Domingo — in all probability this course will be taken, for the matter is too serious to be ignored.
records.summary_es: El Intelligencer publica un editorial sobre las tres serias posibilidades que conciernen directamente a los americanos en San Domingo: la primera es la extensión de las inversiones americanas en la isla; la segunda razón es la aproximación de los intereses del pueblo de la República Dominicana a los nuestros, tanto en el sentido material como en el sentimental, considerándose que en ninguna otra de las islas de las Indias Occidentales, con la excepción de Cuba y Puerto Rico, es tan fuerte la confianza en los Estados Unidos, y se ha mirado a este país más que a ningún otro en busca de buen favor cuando se ha necesitado; y el Sun y otros periódicos que comentan la situación, así como oficiales navales y militares, señalan las nuevas relaciones políticas y estratégicas que proceden de nuestra posesión de Puerto Rico por un lado y nuestra ocupación de Cuba por el otro. Estos son argumentos lógicos para el ejercicio de la vigilancia por parte de nuestro gobierno; y en vista del hecho de que la muerte de Heureaux es seguida de desorden e insurrección, buques navales para proteger nuestros intereses serán necesarios para las aguas de San Domingo — en toda probabilidad este curso será tomado, pues el asunto es demasiado serio para ser ignorado.

records.headline: The Intelligencer prints an editorial on the killing of Heureaux
records.summary_en: The Intelligencer prints an editorial on the killing of Heureaux, whom the paper calls despotic, and on the succession that follows: the leaders of the uprising will offer the presidency to General Gomez, the hero of the Cuban insurrection; Gomez has been identified with San Domingo, and it is practically his home; coupled with the statement is the assertion that his choice for President would likely prove acceptable to all parties. If this is true, and the United States is not compelled to take possession, Gomez, who is so brave a champion of human liberty, would be a decided improvement over the late ruler; and even should the United States assume simply a protectorate, it could not do better than place the matter in his hands, if his popularity among the Dominicans is so great as reported.
records.summary_es: El Intelligencer publica un editorial sobre la muerte de Heureaux, a quien el periódico llama despótico, y sobre la sucesión que sigue: los líderes del levantamiento ofrecerán la presidencia al general Gómez, el héroe de la insurrección cubana; Gómez ha estado identificado con San Domingo, y es prácticamente su hogar; unida a la afirmación está la aseveración de que su elección como Presidente probablemente resultaría aceptable a todos los partidos. Si esto es cierto, y los Estados Unidos no se ven obligados a tomar posesión, Gómez, que es un campeón tan valiente de la libertad humana, sería una mejora decidida sobre el difunto gobernante; e incluso si los Estados Unidos asumieran simplemente un protectorado, no podrían hacer mejor que poner el asunto en sus manos, si su popularidad entre los dominicanos es tan grande como se reporta.

records.headline: The Monitor prints a dispatch announcing the assassination of President Heureaux
records.summary_en: The Monitor prints a dispatch announcing the assassination of President Heureaux at Moca: Gen. Ulysses Heureaux, president of the Dominican republic, was assassinated last Wednesday at Moca; the name of the murderer is Ramon Caceres; he succeeded in making his escape, but an energetic pursuit was at once begun and it is probable that he will soon be captured; calmness prevails everywhere in the republic; and the remains of President Heureaux were taken to San Domingo for the funeral and burial.
records.summary_es: El Monitor publica un despacho que anuncia el asesinato del presidente Heureaux en Moca: el gen. records.headline: The Sun prints a Washington item of July 31 on the movements of the warships
records.summary_en: The Sun prints a Washington item of July 31 on the movements of the warships for San Domingo: the Navy Department received a telegram to-day reporting the departure of the gunboat Machias from San Juan, Porto Rico, for San Domingo City yesterday; the Machias left St. Thomas, Danish West Indies, yesterday morning for San Juan, and after landing Capt. Snow, commandant of the Porto Rico naval station, proceeded without delay to San Domingo waters, and probably got to the Dominican capital to-day; the cruiser New Orleans, which left Newport, R. I., for San Domingo City early yesterday morning, is expected to join the Machias there on Friday or Saturday; and no official news of the situation in the Dominican republic has been received here.

records.headline: The Washington officials are not crossing any bridges until they come
records.summary_en: The *Evening Times-Republican* reported that Washington officials were prepared to intervene and establish a protectorate over the Dominican Republic if violent conflict erupted over the succession to the assassinated President Heureaux. Cuban newspapers debated remarks by General Maximo Gomez's secretary suggesting foreign intervention would be required to maintain order on the island. Meanwhile, Dominican Vice President Wenceslao Figuereo reportedly accepted the presidency to maintain constitutional continuity.
records.summary_es: El *Evening Times-Republican* informó que las autoridades en Washington estaban preparadas para intervenir y establecer un protectorado sobre la República Dominicana si estallaba un conflicto violento por la sucesión del asesinado presidente Heureaux. Periódicos cubanos debatieron declaraciones del secretario del general Máximo Gómez en las que sugería que se requeriría una intervención extranjera para preservar el orden en la isla. Entretanto, según se informó, el vicepresidente dominicano Wenceslao Figuereo asumió la presidencia para asegurar la continuidad constitucional.

records.headline: The Republican prints an item of July 28 headed 'Look to Uncle Sam':
records.summary_en: The Republican prints an item of July 28 headed 'Look to Uncle Sam': an exiled leader of the Liberal party of Santo Domingo, Gen. Abelardo A. Moscoso, now living in New York, said last night: 'The death of President Heureaux will, I think, surely be followed by long state of disorder and revolution. I want to emphasize this prophecy — that the United States will eventually be compelled to interfere to establish peace in the island, just as this country did in Cuba. I favor the policy of peace. I shall be glad to return to my country and support such a policy if it is inaugurated by Gen. Figuereo, the vice-president, who succeeds to the head of the government. But if something is not quickly done to establish order and peace, more revolutionary expeditions will follow, like that of Gen. Jiminez and Gen. Morales, who led a band from Cuba against Heureaux.' The secretary of the Santo Domingo Improvement Company, which controls the country's finances, said yesterday: 'Should the new administration attempt to repudiate our contracts we shall certainly, as American citizens, call upon the Washington administration for protection' — the contract with the Improvement Company being the railroads and the right to collect the customs, and in return for these concessions the company has assumed the national debt.

records.headline: The Journal prints an interview with Señor Lluberes, who had arrived
records.summary_en: The Journal prints an interview with Señor Lluberes, who had arrived from St. John, Porto Rico, to rest here several days before leaving for Europe, and who left Santo Domingo before the assassination of President Heureaux and was shocked on learning the news: the report of a revolution in his country, which the Journal's representative brought him, was news to him; he was in a position to say, however, that nothing serious would result from it, and that General Wenceslao Figuereo, who succeeds General Heureaux as President, is strong enough to protect American interests; the dispatching of war ships by the United States to the scene of disturbance is a natural movement of a country in a case of this kind — there are many Americans in Santo Domingo who have large interests there, and the action of this country in sending war ships will be regarded by his countrymen as a precautionary measure. Señor Lluberes was very evasive when asked his opinion of a possibility of annexation of the Dominican Republic by the United States, and how his people would receive such a proposition; he would only say that he had never heard the subject discussed in his country, and that it would be a question to be settled only by the people. 'I do not believe the report that the real mission of the New Orleans and Machias is to force the annexation of Santo Domingo,' he said.
records.summary_es: El Journal publica una entrevista con el señor Lluberes, que había llegado de San Juan, Puerto Rico, para descansar aquí varios días antes de partir para Europa, y que salió de Santo Domingo antes del asesinato del presidente Heureaux y quedó impactado al conocer la noticia: el reporte de una revolución en su país, que el representante del Journal le trajo, era noticia para él; estaba en posición de decir, sin embargo, que nada serio resultaría de ello, y que el general Wenceslao Figuereo, que sucede al general Heureaux como Presidente, es suficientemente fuerte para proteger los intereses americanos; el despacho de buques de guerra por los Estados Unidos a la escena de disturbio es un movimiento natural de un país en un caso de esta clase — hay muchos americanos en Santo Domingo que tienen grandes intereses allí, y la acción de este país al enviar buques de guerra será considerada por sus compatriotas como una medida precautoria. El señor Lluberes fue muy evasivo cuando se le preguntó su opinión sobre una posibilidad de anexión de la República Dominicana por los Estados Unidos, y cómo su pueblo recibiría tal proposición; solo diría que nunca había oído el tema discutido en su país, y que sería una cuestión a ser resuelta solo por el pueblo. «No creo el reporte de que la verdadera misión del New Orleans y el Machias es forzar la anexión de Santo Domingo», dijo.

records.headline: The Times prints part of an editorial on Santo Domingo and annexation
records.summary_en: The Times prints part of an editorial on Santo Domingo and annexation: the country might have been had without bloodshed and heavy expenditure through the forces of 'benevolent assimilation,' which would have been set in motion; what we foolishly refused to accept then as a free offering we may have to fight for in the not distant future; nothing has occurred since 1871 to kill the spirit of genuine Americanism which animated the request of the Dominicans for annexation to this country — it represents one of those impulses of a people which can be chilled but not slain by indifference; but the natural enemies of the project have grown stronger through organization than they were twenty-eight years ago, and it will now require an effort on our part, either through the slow processes of diplomacy or the undue aggressions of war, to compose the differences in the little Republic before we can set up our authority there; our solemn obligation to Porto Rico and Cuba admonishes us of our duty in Santo Domingo; if we permit disorder to reign there we may expect to see the infectious spirit of anarchy communicated to the nearby islands, and if we allow old Maximo Gomez and the other leaders driven from the island by the despotic Heureaux to return and ply their trade, we may expect to see rebellion break out in our own new possessions; and this can be prevented in only one way, and that is a very simple way — run up the Stars and Stripes at San Domingo City and take possession of the country.
records.summary_es: El Times publica parte de un editorial sobre Santo Domingo y la anexión: el país podría haberse obtenido sin derramamiento de sangre y sin gran gasto a través de las fuerzas de la «asimilación benévola», que se habrían puesto en movimiento; lo que tontamente rehusamos aceptar entonces como una oferta gratuita puede que tengamos que pelear por ello en un futuro no distante; nada ha ocurrido desde 1871 que mate el espíritu de genuino americanismo que animó la solicitud de los dominicanos de anexión a este país — representa uno de esos impulsos de un pueblo que pueden ser enfriados pero no muertos por la indiferencia; pero los enemigos naturales del proyecto se han hecho más fuertes a través de la organización que lo que eran hace veintiocho años, y ahora requerirá un esfuerzo de nuestra parte, ya a través de los lentos procesos de la diplomacia o de las indebidas agresiones de la guerra, para componer las diferencias en la pequeña República antes de que podamos establecer nuestra autoridad allí; nuestra solemne obligación hacia Puerto Rico y Cuba nos amonesta de nuestro deber en Santo Domingo; si permitimos que el desorden reine allí podemos esperar ver el espíritu infeccioso de la anarquía comunicado a las islas cercanas, y si permitimos que el viejo Máximo Gómez y los otros líderes expulsados de la isla por el despótico Heureaux regresen y ejerzan su oficio, podemos esperar ver estallar la rebelión en nuestras propias nuevas posesiones; y esto puede prevenirse de una sola manera, y es una manera muy simple — izar las Barras y Estrellas en la ciudad de Santo Domingo y tomar posesión del país.

records.headline: The Journal prints part of an editorial urging the acquisition of Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The Journal prints part of an editorial urging the acquisition of Santo Domingo as a more desirable acquisition than Porto Rico, for, with over five times the area, it has only two-thirds the population, so that the opportunities remaining open for development are much greater; it has 18,045 square miles, almost exactly the area of New Hampshire and Vermont combined, with something over 600,000 inhabitants; unlike Haiti, the black republic on the same island, it does not have a majority of negroes; the bulk of its land is available for cultivation; it is rich in all varieties of tropical woods and plants; it is solvent, and its standard of value is the United States gold dollar; with the acquisition of Santo Domingo we should almost complete our cordon of defence of the Nicaragua Canal; of course nobody would urge the forcible annexation of an unwilling people, but if the former sentiments of the Dominicans toward the United States still exist, or are likely to revive, we should be ready to take advantage of them; and we ought to have a couple of war ships always at hand, with instructions to meet any friendly overtures in the proper spirit before the opportunity goes by.

records.headline: The Transcript completes a cable item on the revolution in Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The Transcript completes a cable item on the revolution in Santo Domingo and prints two dispatches: according to a private cablegram, demoralization is growing through the death of the president, and in the event of the revolution succeeding it is probable that Jiminez and the other reputed leaders will agree to retire, offering the presidency to General Maximo Gomez, who would prove acceptable to all parties, and a deputation is reported to be going to Cuba to confer with General Gomez. Under the head 'The Situation Critical,' a Puerto Plata dispatch of July 31 says the situation is critical and an outbreak momentarily expected; the friends of the government are under arms and ready for action to protect property and preserve the peace; the burial of President Heureaux was conducted with fitting honors; Governor Pepin had assembled troops in Moca, and the governor of La Vega Real has 1,000 men; the minister of the treasury has arrived at Moca in hot haste; the government is taking steps for the protection of business and the finance of the country, and expects to carry out the cancellation of the state bank notes; and in Puerto Plata there is an urgent demand that the government send a sufficient force to Moca to hunt down the assassins of the president. Under the head 'Telegraph Wires Cut,' a Cape Haytien dispatch of July 31 says advices just received from the Dominican frontier say the insurgents have cut the telegraph wires in the neighborhood of Santiago de los Caballeros and also near Moca.

records.headline: The Eagle prints part of a sketch of the late President Heureaux
records.summary_en: The Eagle prints part of a sketch of the late President Heureaux, a man of unbending will, endowed with much intellectual force, and possessed of great courage, he strove honestly for the people of his fatherland, but with methods which found their only counterpart in the middle ages; in the less than fifty years of his life, he rose from a peasant to the dictatorship of San Domingo, and in the thirteen years of his administration he materially advanced the country in civilization, welding out of a mass of brigands an army of considerable strength, and building up a financial system which brought prosperity to his people; his people looked upon him either with a devotion akin to idolatry, or with horror and fear, for his vigorous personality admitted of no lukewarm sentiment — whether they loved or hated him, they obeyed him without question; thirty years ago, an ill-clad, half-starved boy from the hills of the interior, he joined as a private the so-called army, a lawless, impotent mob controlled by corrupt politicians and incompetent generals; despite a withered arm, which was almost useless, Heureaux developed into a good soldier, and soon rose from the ranks to an under officership; his genius for organization developed, and by rapid promotions the young officer advanced until he became commander in chief; then came the turbulent days of 1885-'86, and in the disorder of the time Heureaux found his opportunity — with his power as head of the army, he forced his election as president.
records.summary_es: El Eagle publica parte de un bosquejo del difunto presidente Heureaux, un hombre de voluntad inflexible, dotado de mucha fuerza intelectual y poseedor de gran valor, que se esforzó honestamente por el pueblo de su patria, pero con métodos que encontraron su único contrapeso en la edad media; en los menos de cincuenta años de su vida, se elevó de campesino a la dictadura de San Domingo, y en los trece años de su administración avanzó materialmente el país en civilización, soldando de una masa de bandidos un ejército de fuerza considerable, y construyendo un sistema financiero que trajo prosperidad a su pueblo; su pueblo lo miraba ya con una devoción parecida a la idolatría, o con horror y miedo, pues su vigorosa personalidad no admitía ningún sentimiento tibio — lo amaran o lo odiaran, le obedecían sin cuestión; hace treinta años, un muchacho mal vestido y medio hambriento de las lomas del interior, se unió como soldado raso al llamado ejército, una muchedumbre sin ley e impotente controlada por políticos corruptos y generales incompetentes; a pesar de un brazo marchito, que era casi inútil, Heureaux se desarrolló en un buen soldado y pronto se elevó de las filas a una suboficialidad; su genio para la organización se desarrolló, y por rápidas promociones el joven oficial avanzó hasta llegar a ser comandante en jefe; entonces vinieron los días turbulentos de 1885-86, y en el desorden de la época Heureaux encontró su oportunidad — con su poder como jefe del ejército, forzó su elección como presidente.

records.headline: The Eagle prints part of a sketch of President Heureaux and his courage:
records.summary_en: The Eagle prints part of a sketch of President Heureaux and his courage: it was difficult to secure from Dominicans expressions of opinion on any subject touching the president or his policy, but when it was possible to find a Dominican who was willing to talk of the life of Heureaux, the stories told had the flavor of old-time romance; one of the striking instances of the president's personal courage is to be found in the story of his suppression of the 'Santiago' rebellion a few years ago — Santiago is inland from the famous Samana Bay, and at a distance from the capital which made it possible for the residents to foment trouble with the possibility of escaping immediate punishment; here a band of malcontents from all parts of the island gathered and soon succeeded in enlisting the sympathies of almost the entire population of the town, and, encouraged by the fact that the terrible president was several days' journey distant, the ringleaders finally became bold enough to issue a manifesto declaring Heureaux a monstrous tyrant, and urging an uprising, and great posters were printed bearing the picture of a coffin and calling on all patriots to aid in ridding the fatherland of its oppressor; the government secret service soon apprised the president of the affair, and in his usual picturesque manner he proceeded with preparations for revenge: he ordered made a tough black coffin, and, putting it aboard his little armoured yacht, he took a detail of soldiers and sailed around the coast for Santiago, and, landing with thirty soldiers, he started on the twenty-five-mile horseback journey.

records.headline: A profile of President Heureaux tells how his brother-in-law, the husband of the half sister for whom he had a real
records.summary_en: A profile of President Heureaux tells how his brother-in-law, the husband of the half sister for whom he had a real affection, was advanced rapidly in the government service, warned once after joining a plot to assassinate the president, and found within six months plotting again. Heureaux gave a state breakfast in the young man's honor, seated him at his side, and as the meal ended told him he was going to be shot in five minutes; the official was then shot in the courtyard while the president's sister screamed from the windows above, and the uncoffined body was quickly buried in a flower garden.
records.summary_es: Un perfil del presidente Heureaux cuenta cómo su cuñado, el esposo de la media hermana por quien sentía un verdadero afecto, fue ascendido rápidamente en el servicio del gobierno, advertido una vez tras unirse a un complot para asesinar al presidente, y descubierto en menos de seis meses conspirando de nuevo. Heureaux ofreció un desayuno de Estado en honor del joven, lo sentó a su lado y, al terminar la comida, le dijo que iba a ser fusilado en cinco minutos; el funcionario fue fusilado entonces en el patio mientras la hermana del presidente gritaba desde las ventanas de arriba, y el cuerpo sin ataúd fue enterrado rápidamente en un jardín de flores.

records.summary_en: This profile of Heureaux recounts how he walked among men who had been swearing to take his life, told them they were not nearly so anxious for his life as they believed, and let them go free without taking any action. It describes his polished manner and entertaining conversation, his three-story palace in Santo Domingo covering a block, and the keen slight he felt because the aristocratic Dominicans refused to admit him to their social circles on account of his blood.
records.summary_es: Este perfil de Heureaux relata cómo caminó entre hombres que habían estado jurando quitarle la vida, les dijo que no estaban ni de lejos tan ansiosos por su vida como ellos creían, y los dejó ir libres sin tomar ninguna medida. Describe su trato cortés y su conversación entretenida, su palacio de tres pisos en Santo Domingo que ocupa una manzana, y el desaire que sentía agudamente porque los dominicanos aristocráticos se negaban a admitirlo en sus círculos sociales a causa de su sangre.
records.passage: "I wished to show you," Heureaux said, "that you are not nearly so anxious for my life as you believed. I know you all, but I shall take no action. You are free." And he turned and went away. He kept [illegible] left the country. Heureaux had the features of a full-blooded negro. His manner was polished and his conversation entertaining. The aristocratic Dominicans, who are of pure Spanish blood, refused to admit him to their social circles because of his negro blood, and he felt their slight keenly. Little was known of his family history or his parentage, and he was always reticent about the incidents of his life before he became famous. His palace in Santo Domingo is a three-story building covering a block, and built in the typical style of the tropics. records.summary_en: The Transcript prints the Moscoso interview, the warships item, and the opening of a Havana item: General Abelardo A. Moscoso, an exiled leader of the Liberal party of Santo Domingo, now living in New York, said: 'The death of President Heureaux will, I think, surely be followed by a long state of disorder and revolution. I want to emphasize this prophecy — that the United States will eventually be compelled to interfere to establish peace in the island, just as this country did in Cuba. I favor the policy of peace. I shall be glad to return to my country and support such a policy if it is inaugurated by General Figuereo, the vice president, who succeeds to the head of the government. But if something is not quickly done to establish order and peace, more revolutionary expeditions will follow that of General Jiminez and General Morales, who led a band from Cuba against Heureaux.' Under the head 'Precautionary Measure,' a Washington item of July 29 says Secretary Long has sent telegraphic orders to the cruiser New Orleans, at Newport, directing that she proceed at once to San Domingo, and at the same time an order was sent to the gunboat Machias, at St. Thomas, to leave for San Domingo; it is expected that the New Orleans will be able to leave during the day, and the Machias will be in San Domingo waters within a day or two; and this action was not due to the receipt of any official advices indicating possible trouble, but entirely to the desire to be forehanded in dealing with any possible disturbance. A Havana item of July 29 opens under the head 'Gomez Says All Papers Lie.'

Bido; and Minister of Posts and Telegraphs, J. R. Vidal. The country is quiet and no fears of disturbances are entertained, and the United States gunboat Machias arrived here from Porto Rico yesterday. Under the head 'Our Recognition to Be Prompt,' the Washington item of August 1 says the State Department will not delay in recognizing the new government set up by Figuereo, but as soon as United States Minister Powell notifies the department that the Vice-President has assumed the presidential office and is at the head of a de facto government, the Minister will be instructed to extend the formal recognition of the United States Government.

records.headline: The Spy prints a Santo Domingo dispatch headed 'How It Happened'
records.summary_en: The Spy prints a Santo Domingo dispatch headed 'How It Happened', in which the latest story of the assassination of President Heureaux received here agrees with previously published accounts in nearly all particulars; according to advices just at hand, President Heureaux was with the administrator of finances in Moca, when a beggar came to the house and requested a gratuity; the president went to the door of the house in answer to the appeal of the mendicant, but he had no sooner made his appearance than a shot was fired, wounding him; despite his wounds, Gen. Heureaux started toward the street, firing his revolver as he advanced; and six more shots were fired, all taking effect in the president's body. The United States gunboat Machias arrived here from Porto Rico today, August 1. The assassins of President Heureaux and their seconds are in a mountainous district about 25 miles northward of Moca, and Señor Don Cordero, the late minister of the interior, has taken the field against them with 400 men.
records.summary_es: El Spy publica un despacho de Santo Domingo titulado «How It Happened», en el cual la última historia del asesinato del presidente Heureaux recibida aquí concuerda con las versiones previamente publicadas en casi todos los particulares; según avisos recién a mano, el presidente Heureaux estaba con el administrador de finanzas en Moca, cuando un mendigo vino a la casa y pidió una gratificación; el presidente fue a la puerta de la casa en respuesta al llamamiento del mendigo, pero apenas había hecho su aparición cuando se disparó un tiro, hiriéndolo; a pesar de sus heridas, el gen. Heureaux avanzó hacia la calle, disparando su revólver al avanzar; y se dispararon seis tiros más, todos haciendo efecto en el cuerpo del presidente. La cañonera Machias de los Estados Unidos llegó aquí hoy, 1 de agosto, desde Puerto Rico. Los asesinos del presidente Heureaux y sus segundos están en un distrito montañoso a unas 25 millas al norte de Moca, y el señor don Cordero, el antiguo ministro del interior, ha tomado el campo contra ellos con 400 hombres.

records.headline: The Spy prints an editorial on the island and the Dominican Republic:
records.summary_en: The Spy prints an editorial on the island and the Dominican Republic: the conflict between Hippolyte and Legitime furnished the most constant and exciting items of news from the West Indies, and all the force and ability of the extraordinary Heureaux were required to restore order in the republic; the condition of the island is of vastly more importance to the United States now than it was a dozen years ago, and the affairs of the islands therefore deserve the more consideration; the island of Hispaniola, Hayti or Santo Domingo, as it has been at various times called, is divided into two republics — the western third of the territory is occupied by the republic of Hayti, which dates back to 1800, and is of French character, even the language being a French patois; the remaining two-thirds, representing an area of some 19,000 square miles, or somewhat more than the combined areas of New Hampshire and Vermont, constitute the Dominican republic; the language is Spanish, and the people are of mixed French, Spanish, English and African blood; the soil is wonderfully fertile, bearing tobacco, cotton, sugar cane, cocoa, coffee, fruits and valuable woods; the scenery is mountainous and picturesque, and under proper government the country would be a pleasant place of residence; and while the island has not been remarkable for prosperity, there is a certain rich class which indulges in educational aspirations, and not a few of its sons have been sent to this country or to Europe to study, and two sons of the late President Heureaux are said to be studying law and medicine in Paris.

records.headline: The Enterprise prints the Fort de France assassination dispatch
records.summary_en: The Enterprise prints the Fort de France assassination dispatch and a sketch of President Heureaux: Gen. Ulises Heureaux, president of the Dominican Republic, was assassinated at Moca, Santo Domingo; the name of the murderer is Ramon Caceros; he succeeded in making his escape, but an energetic pursuit was at once begun, and it is probable that he will soon be captured; Vice President General Wenceslao Figuereo, immediately upon the announcement of the president's death, assumed the direction of affairs; at present calmness prevails everywhere in the republic; and the remains of President Heureaux will probably be taken to Santo Domingo for the funeral services. President Heureaux was a soldier during his entire lifetime: one of his arms was paralyzed from a wound he received by a rifle ball in battle; he is described by Americans familiar with his career as a man without fear, and when there was any disturbance or revolution in any part of the republic, he mounted his horse and went pell-mell himself to the front as leader, and learned all the details of the revolution as well as the causes leading to it; he went as a soldier, not as President or General, and thus was unknown by his people; he generally traveled on horseback and made frequent excursions through the country, and when on such trips he avoided hotels and private houses and slept along the roadside; he had a wonderful career, and was held in high regard by the majority of his people; and he participated in many battles, and always with success.
records.summary_es: El Enterprise publica el despacho del asesinato de Fort de France y un bosquejo del presidente Heureaux: el gen. Ulises Heureaux, presidente de la República Dominicana, fue asesinado en Moca, Santo Domingo; el nombre del asesino es Ramón Caceros; logró escapar, pero se inició de inmediato una persecución enérgica, y es probable que pronto sea capturado; el vicepresidente general Wenceslao Figuereo, inmediatamente después del anuncio de la muerte del presidente, asumió la dirección de los asuntos; en el presente prevalece la calma en todas partes de la república; y los restos del presidente Heureaux probablemente serán llevados a Santo Domingo para los servicios fúnebres. El presidente Heureaux fue un soldado durante toda su vida: uno de sus brazos estaba paralizado por una herida que recibió de una bala de rifle en batalla; es descrito por americanos familiarizados con su carrera como un hombre sin miedo, y cuando había cualquier disturbio o revolución en cualquier parte de la república, montaba su caballo e iba precipitadamente él mismo al frente como líder, y aprendía todos los detalles de la revolución así como las causas que la motivaron; iba como soldado, no como Presidente o General, y así era desconocido por su pueblo; generalmente viajaba a caballo e hacía frecuentes excursiones a través del país, y cuando en tales viajes evitaba hoteles y casas privadas y dormía a la orilla del camino; tuvo una carrera maravillosa y era tenido en alta estima por la mayoría de su pueblo; y participó en muchas batallas, y siempre con éxito.

records.headline: The Review completes a cable item on the revolution in Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The Review completes a cable item on the revolution in Santo Domingo and prints two dispatches: according to a private cablegram, demoralization is growing through the death of the president, and in the event of the revolution succeeding it is probable that Jiminez and the other reputed leaders will agree to retire, offering the presidency to General Maximo Gomez, who would prove acceptable to all parties, and a deputation is reported to be going to Cuba to confer with General Gomez. Under the head 'The Situation Critical,' a Puerto Plata dispatch of August 1 says the situation is critical and an outbreak momentarily expected; the friends of the government are under arms and ready for action to protect property and preserve the peace; the burial of President Heureaux was conducted with fitting honors; Governor Pepin had assembled troops in Moca, and the governor of La Vega Real has 1,000 men; the minister of the treasury has arrived at Moca in hot haste; the government is taking steps for the protection of business and the finance of the country, and expects to carry out the cancellation of the state bank notes; and in Puerto Plata there is an urgent demand that the government send a sufficient force to Moca to hunt down the assassins of the president. Under the head 'Telegraph Wires Cut,' a Cape Haytien dispatch of August 1 says advices just received from the Dominican frontier say the insurgents have cut the telegraph wires in the neighborhood of Santiago de los Caballeros and also near Moca.
records.summary_es: El Review completa una nota cablegráfica sobre la revolución en Santo Domingo y publica dos despachos: según un cablegrama privado, la desmoralización está creciendo a través de la muerte del presidente, y en el evento de que la revolución triunfe es probable que Jiminez y los otros líderes reputados acuerden retirarse, ofreciendo la presidencia al general Máximo Gómez, que probaría ser aceptable a todos los partidos, y se reporta que una diputación va a Cuba a conferenciar con el general Gómez. Bajo el título «The Situation Critical», un despacho de Puerto Plata del 1 de agosto dice que la situación es crítica y que un estallido es esperado momentáneamente; los amigos del gobierno están bajo las armas y listos para la acción para proteger la propiedad y preservar la paz; el entierro del presidente Heureaux fue conducido con honores apropiados; el gobernador Pepín había reunido tropas en Moca, y el gobernador de La Vega Real tiene 1,000 hombres; el ministro de la tesorería ha llegado a Moca en gran prisa; el gobierno está tomando pasos para la protección de los negocios y las finanzas del país, y espera llevar a cabo la cancelación de los billetes del banco del estado; y en Puerto Plata hay una demanda urgente de que el gobierno envíe una fuerza suficiente a Moca para cazar a los asesinos del presidente. Bajo el título «Telegraph Wires Cut», un despacho de Cabo Haitiano del 1 de agosto dice que avisos recién recibidos de la frontera dominicana dicen que los insurgentes han cortado los cables telegráficos en el vecindario de Santiago de los Caballeros y también cerca de Moca.

records.headline: The News prints part of a statement in defense of General Gomez
records.summary_en: The News prints part of a statement in defense of General Gomez, and an interview with the ex-President of Venezuela: the statement says that Gomez strove to obtain independence for the island for thirty years, and his efforts have been little recognized; those make a mistake who think he aspires to anything in Santo Domingo or Cuba — God forbid that he should even be an employe of high rank; he thinks it a veritable misfortune to be president, as on the field of battle a brave man exposes his life, while in the presidential chair he exposes his honor, even if he has no valor; Jiminez is the man he hopes will be president of the Dominican Republic; those in Cuba to whom he is a cause of worry need not be disturbed at seeing his family, which only came here from a pious motive, which being fulfilled, he and his family will abandon the land which has repaid his many efforts with rancor; and those who want posts need not fear that he wants the dictatorship — he goes home leaving the field free. A New York item of August 1 prints Dr. Laurens Villanova, ex-President of Venezuela, who is at present in New York: asked this morning through his interpreter whether it was true that the South American countries were about to form an offensive and defensive alliance against the United States on account of its 'Imperialism policy,' he replied that he had not heard of it, but thought that such an alliance ought to be made; and asked, 'Do the South American nations fear the United States?' the ex-President shrugged his shoulders and said something in Spanish.
records.summary_es: El News publica parte de una declaración en defensa del general Gómez, y una entrevista con el expresidente de Venezuela: la declaración dice que Gómez se esforzó por obtener la independencia de la isla por treinta años, y que sus esfuerzos han sido poco reconocidos; aquellos se equivocan que piensan que él aspira a algo en Santo Domingo o Cuba — Dios prohíba que él sea siquiera un empleado de alto rango; piensa que es una verdadera desventura ser presidente, pues en el campo de batalla un hombre valiente expone su vida, mientras en la silla presidencial expone su honor, aun si no tiene valor; Jiminez es el hombre que él espera será presidente de la República Dominicana; aquellos en Cuba a quienes él es causa de preocupación no necesitan ser disturbados al ver a su familia, que solo vino aquí por un motivo piadoso, el cual siendo cumplido, él y su familia abandonarán la tierra que ha repagado sus muchos esfuerzos con rencor; y aquellos que quieren puestos no necesitan temer que él quiera la dictadura — se va a casa dejando el campo libre. Una nota de Nueva York del 1 de agosto publica al Dr. Laurens Villanova, expresidente de Venezuela, que está al presente en Nueva York: preguntado esta mañana a través de su intérprete si era cierto que los países sudamericanos estaban a punto de formar una alianza ofensiva y defensiva contra los Estados Unidos por razón de su «política de Imperialismo», replicó que no había oído de ello, pero pensaba que tal alianza debía hacerse; y preguntado, «¿Temen las naciones sudamericanas a los Estados Unidos?» el expresidente se encogió de hombros y dijo algo en español.

INSTANTLY KILLED.
Joseph H. Thyng Crushed by a Falling
Pulley in Suncook.
SUNCOOK, July 27.—Joseph H. Thyng,
a machinist, while at work last night in
the China mill removing shafting and pul
leys, was instantly Kkilled, about midnight,
by being crushed under a falling pulley.
He was 24 years of age and belongs in
Lakeport and has worked here but a few
months. A wife survives. Mr. Thyng
was a corporal in Company K, First New
Hampshire, in the Spanish-American war.
The remains were taken to Lakeport to
day on the afternoon train.

records.headline: The Censor prints a dispatch from Santo Domingo and a sketch of President Heureaux:
records.summary_en: The Censor prints a dispatch from Santo Domingo and a sketch of President Heureaux: the former reports that immediately upon the announcement of the president's death, Vice President Gen. Wenceslao Figuereo assumed control of the government; several attempts have been made before to take the life of President Heureaux, but they were frustrated — on one occasion, while passing through the arched entrance to the palace between lines of guards, his quick eye caught one of the soldiers, who appeared to lower his rifle in his direction, and, quickly pulling a revolver, he shot the man in his tracks, passed on to his private office, and gave orders to remove a dead man lying at the main entrance; Gen. Heureaux was born in Porto Plata in 1846, and served in the war against Spain from 1868 to 1874; later he was put at the head of the advanced Dominicans, who sought to improve their country by inducing foreign capital to locate on the island; as he advanced, the wealthy inhabitants joined his forces, and when he arrived at the gates of the historic city of Santo Domingo he was chosen president of the republic, and served his term of four years; at the expiration of every four years an electoral college assembles in the city to vote for a president for the following term, but owing to Gen. Heureaux's popularity and ability he has always been unanimously re-elected, and was serving his fifth term.

records.headline: The Tribune prints the closing part of a statement on the situation
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints the closing part of a statement on the situation in Santo Domingo: there is no fear that the insurrectionists will interfere in any way with the property of foreigners on the island; notwithstanding the many revolutions which have taken place in Santo Domingo since it attained its independence, in no instance has either life been taken or property molested of any foreigner, with the single exception of the action of Heureaux, who opened the vaults of the French bank because of a personal quarrel with one of its directors; women and children are safe at all times, as the Dominicans never stoop to war with the helpless, nor do they ever sack or pillage, but fight for what they believe to be right in the open, as men and soldiers should do; Mr. Jiminez and General Gomez are warm personal friends — in fact, both reside in the same house in Havana; as Heureaux was a usurper, the Vice-President is equally so, but bloodshed and insurrection would cease at once if the latter would announce that a legal, public election would take place on August 16, which is the Independence day of the country; the entire country is aroused to the necessity of a change to a government where life is secure, and it recognizes that the former Vice-President and the present pretending President is but one of the accomplices of Heureaux, and as such has no confidence in him; and there is but one man who at this time represents the people and their best interests, and that is Jiminez, and if an opportunity is given to the people they will prove it by their ballots — but if none is afforded in that way, then force will be used.
records.summary_es: El Tribune publica la parte final de una declaración sobre la situación en Santo Domingo: no hay temor de que los insurreccionistas interfieran en ninguna manera con la propiedad de los extranjeros en la isla; a pesar de las muchas revoluciones que han tenido lugar en Santo Domingo desde que alcanzó su independencia, en ningún caso ha sido tomada vida ni molestada propiedad de ningún extranjero, con la sola excepción de la acción de Heureaux, que abrió las bóvedas del banco francés por una querella personal con uno de sus directores; las mujeres y los niños están seguros en todo tiempo, pues los dominicanos nunca se rebajan a guerrear con los indefensos, ni saquean ni pillan jamás, sino que pelean por lo que creen correcto a campo abierto, como hombres y soldados deben hacer; el señor Jiminez y el general Gómez son amigos personales cálidos — de hecho, ambos residen en la misma casa en La Habana; como Heureaux fue un usurpador, el vicepresidente es igualmente eso, pero el derramamiento de sangre y la insurrección cesarían de inmediato si este último anunciara que una elección legal y pública tendría lugar el 16 de agosto, que es el día de la Independencia del país; el país entero está despertado a la necesidad de un cambio a un gobierno donde la vida sea segura, y reconoce que el anterior vicepresidente y el presente presidente pretendiente es solo uno de los cómplices de Heureaux, y como tal no tiene confianza en él; y hay un solo hombre que en este tiempo representa al pueblo y sus mejores intereses, y ese es Jiminez, y si una oportunidad es dada al pueblo ellos lo probarán por sus votos — pero si ninguna es ofrecida de esa manera, entonces se usará la fuerza.

records.headline: The Tribune prints a dispatch headed 'Figuero Takes the Reins'
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints a dispatch headed 'Figuero Takes the Reins', the Santo Domingo dispatch of August 1, in which the Vice-President, Wenceslao Figuereo, as a result of the assassination of President Heureaux on July 28, has taken charge of the Government of Santo Domingo as President, and has formed a cabinet as follows: Minister of the Interior, F. D. Morales; Minister of War and Marine, Tilo Palino; Minister of Foreign Affairs, E. Henriquez; Minister of Finance, J. de J. Alvarez; Minister of Justice, Sebastian Valverde; Minister of Agriculture, T. Cordero Bido; Minister of Posts and Telegraphs, Jaime R. Vidal; Sub-Secretary of the Interior, Braulio Alvarez; and Sub-Secretary of Justice, Pedro T. Perez. The country is quiet, and no fears of disturbances are entertained. This place was visited during the afternoon of July 27 by a severe tornado, which blew at the rate of forty miles an hour; three coasting vessels loaded with produce and anchored in the outer harbor were wrecked, and about fifteen men perished; and the damage done ashore was not of much importance. The dispatch also opens the latest story of the assassination of President Heureaux received here, which agrees with previously published accounts in nearly all particulars: according to advices just at hand, President Heureaux was with the Administrator of Finances in Moca, when a beggar presented himself and requested a gratuity, and the President went to the door of the house in answer to the appeal.

records.headline: The Tribune prints part of a letter written in defense of General Gomez:
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints part of a letter written in defense of General Gomez: in it, he strove to obtain independence for the island for thirty years, and his efforts have been little recognized; the sweat on the horse is hardly dry when the rage of those who did not dare to take the field by his side falls upon him; insults will not affect him more than if they were directed against the Czar of Russia by a person with whom he had no connecting links; what, however, is irritating and painful, and has no logical explanation, is the desire to injure him, to despise the Dominican, to insult the stranger who believes he has done much for Cuba — they would insult the old Dominican Republic, which has brilliantly served the Cuban cause more than any Latin people, with money, love and blood; the Dominicans are called savages because their President was killed by the angered hands of vengeance — why then not call other nations savages on account of assassinations committed in them? In this connection the writer cites the instances of the killing of President Garfield of the United States, Señor Canovas del Castillo, the Spanish Premier, and President Carnot, of the French Republic; and, continuing, the writer says that some Cubans think they can get at him by means of this unfortunate occurrence, accusing him of aspiring to fill the place made vacant by the act of the assassin, forgetting that he aspires still higher; and the history of his life proves that he prefers liberating those writing things against him — if Cuba cannot see a position to offer him after all his efforts, how could he see one in Santo Domingo?

records.headline: The Tribune completes the assassination dispatch with a sketch of President Heureaux:
records.summary_en: The Tribune completes the assassination dispatch with a sketch of President Heureaux: the assassination was at half past four o'clock Wednesday afternoon; the name of the murderer is Ramon Caceros; he succeeded in making his escape, but an energetic pursuit was at once begun; Vice President Gen. Wenceslao Figuereo, immediately upon the announcement of the president's death, assumed the direction of affairs; at present calmness prevails everywhere in the republic; and the remains of President Heureaux will probably be taken to Santo Domingo for the funeral services. Ulysses Heureaux, the late president of Santo Domingo, was born about 1838; little is known of his early life except that he was a power in the politics of the little West Indian republic when he was a young man; his first real prominence was attained during the war with the Spaniards in 1866, when he commanded the Santo Domingo army; after the cessation of hostilities he became very prominent in politics; he held several positions of trust and honor, and finally, in 1882, he was elected president; he served one term; in 1887 he again was placed in the presidential chair, and has been elected continuously ever since; and Heureaux faced dozens of revolutions during his long period of office holding, but he always came out victorious.
records.summary_es: El Tribune completa el despacho del asesinato con un bosquejo del presidente Heureaux: el asesinato fue a las cuatro y media de la tarde del miércoles; el nombre del asesino es Ramón Caceros; logró escapar, pero se inició de inmediato una persecución enérgica; el vicepresidente gen. Wenceslao Figuereo, inmediatamente después del anuncio de la muerte del presidente, asumió la dirección de los asuntos; en el presente prevalece la calma en todas partes de la república; y los restos del presidente Heureaux probablemente serán llevados a Santo Domingo para los servicios fúnebres. Ulysses Heureaux, el difunto presidente de Santo Domingo, nació cerca de 1838; poco se sabe de su vida temprana excepto que era un poder en la política de la pequeña república de las Indias Occidentales cuando era un hombre joven; su primera prominencia real fue alcanzada durante la guerra con los españoles en 1866, cuando comandó el ejército de Santo Domingo; después de la cesación de hostilidades llegó a ser muy prominente en la política; ocupó varias posiciones de confianza y honor, y finalmente, en 1882, fue elegido presidente; sirvió un término; en 1887 fue de nuevo puesto en la silla presidencial, y ha sido elegido continuamente desde entonces; y Heureaux enfrentó docenas de revoluciones durante su largo período de tenencia del cargo, pero siempre salió victorioso.

records.headline: The Post prints fragments of a Santo Domingo dispatch of August 1:
records.summary_en: The Post prints fragments of a Santo Domingo dispatch of August 1: business men are urged to be patient; Jiminez is suspected to be in the neighborhood; news from Moca and Santiago indicate a calmer feeling today; President Figuereo has issued a manifesto outlining his programme, and it is expected that a general amnesty will be proclaimed; and the United States gunboat Machias arrived.

records.headline: The Journal completes the Fort de France assassination dispatch
records.summary_en: The Journal completes the Fort de France assassination dispatch, prints President McKinley's message of condolence, and opens the July 28 details dispatch: the president's friends fired at the assassins, but it is not known whether any of them were wounded; the body of the president was taken to the palace of the governor of Moca; President Heureaux's death has caused a panic; it is said that Juan Isidoro Jimines, who took part in the attempted insurrection of June, 1898, is a candidate for the presidency, and that General Maximo Gomez, formerly president of the Cuban insurrectionists, a native of San Domingo, also aspires to the presidency; and the father of Caceres, the assassin, was put to death by order of President Heureaux in 1884. President McKinley's message, sent by direction through the State Department, offers to President Figuereo and the Dominican nation the most sincere condolences of the American people and his own. Wenceslao Figuereo is the officer next in line to President Heureaux and succeeds to the office of president. The July 28 dispatch says a financial crisis having arisen in San Domingo, and an insurrection being feared owing to the number of malcontents, President Heureaux went to the north and west of the island to prepare for all eventualities; he was about to leave Moca for Santiago de las Caballeros when he was killed.
records.summary_es: El Journal completa el despacho del asesinato de Fort de France, publica el mensaje de condolencia del presidente McKinley y abre el despacho de detalles del 28 de julio: los amigos del presidente dispararon contra los asesinos, pero no se sabe si alguno de ellos fue herido; el cuerpo del presidente fue llevado al palacio del gobernador de Moca; la muerte del presidente Heureaux ha causado pánico; se dice que Juan Isidoro Jimenes, quien tomó parte en la intentona insurreccional de junio de 1898, es candidato a la presidencia, y que el general Máximo Gómez, anteriormente presidente de los insurrectos cubanos, nativo de Santo Domingo, también aspira a la presidencia; y el padre de Cáceres, el asesino, fue ejecutado por orden del presidente Heureaux en 1884. El mensaje del presidente McKinley, enviado por su dirección a través del Departamento de Estado, ofrece al presidente Figuereo y a la nación dominicana las más sinceras condolencias del pueblo estadounidense y las suyas propias. Wenceslao Figuereo es el oficial que sigue en línea al presidente Heureaux y le sucede en el cargo de presidente. El despacho del 28 de julio dice que, habiendo surgido una crisis financiera en Santo Domingo, y temiéndose una insurrección por el número de descontentos, el presidente Heureaux fue al norte y al oeste de la isla para prepararse ante cualquier eventualidad; estaba a punto de salir de Moca hacia Santiago de los Caballeros cuando fue asesinado.

records.headline: The Tribune prints an editorial on Santo Domingo: the national debt of the Dominican republic
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints an editorial on Santo Domingo: the national debt of the Dominican republic has for some time been under the financial control of a company dominated by New York financiers, who bought it in cheaply from a syndicate in Holland, which had been unable to collect the interest; this American company took prompt possession of the Dominican custom houses and is now virtually the controlling power in the island; in addition to that, the leading steamship line is an American one, so that no matter what form of government exists down there, there is always a strong reason for American watchfulness. Under the Monroe doctrine, not likely since the Spanish war to be challenged by any European power, the only government which could intervene for purposes of pacification is that of the United States; the sending of warships and marines to the vicinity of Puerto Plata means that if a responsibility of this kind shall come through native chaos it will not be shirked; the United States is not aching for any more tropical wards, but if a further paternal oversight shall fall to it in the line of unsought duty the job will be accepted and completed with, let us hope, neatness and dispatch.
records.summary_es: El Tribune publica un editorial sobre Santo Domingo: la deuda nacional de la República Dominicana ha estado durante algún tiempo bajo el control financiero de una compañía dominada por financieros de Nueva York, quienes la compraron barata a un sindicato en Holanda, el cual no había podido cobrar los intereses; esta compañía estadounidense tomó pronta posesión de las aduanas dominicanas y es ahora virtualmente el poder controlador en la isla; además de eso, la línea de vapores principal es estadounidense, de modo que no importa qué forma de gobierno exista allí, siempre hay una fuerte razón para la vigilancia estadounidense. Bajo la doctrina Monroe, no siendo probable que desde la guerra española la desafíe ninguna potencia europea, el único gobierno que podría intervenir con fines de pacificación es el de los Estados Unidos; el envío de buques de guerra e infantes de marina a las cercanías de Puerto Plata significa que si una responsabilidad de este tipo llega a través del caos nativo no será eludida; los Estados Unidos no ansían más pupilos tropicales, pero si una adicional tutela paternal le corresponde en la línea del deber no buscado, el trabajo será aceptado y completado con, esperemos, pulcritud y rapidez.

records.headline: The Avalanche completes the assassination dispatch with a sketch of the late President Heureaux:
records.summary_en: The Avalanche completes the assassination dispatch with a sketch of the late President Heureaux: the announcement of the president's death brought Vice-President Gen. Wenceslao Figuereo to the control of the government. Several attempts have been made before to take the life of President Heureaux, but they were frustrated: on one occasion, while passing through the arched entrance to the palace between lines of guards, his quick eye caught one of the soldiers, who appeared to lower his rifle in his direction; quickly pulling a revolver he shot the man dead in his tracks, passed on to his private office, where he gave orders to remove a dead man lying at the main entrance. Gen. Heureaux was born in Puerto Plata in 1840 and served in the war against Spain from 1868 to 1874; later he was put at the head of the advanced Dominicans, who sought to improve their country by inducing foreign capital to locate on the island; as he advanced all the wealthy inhabitants joined his forces, and when he arrived at the gates of the historic city of Santo Domingo he was chosen president of the republic and served his term of four years; at the expiration of every four years an electoral college assembles in the city to vote for a president for the following term, but owing to Gen. Heureaux's popularity and ability he has always been unanimously re-elected, and was serving his fifth term.

records.headline: The Democrat prints a Cape Haitien dispatch of July 30 and the Moscoso statement
records.summary_en: The Democrat prints a Cape Haitien dispatch of July 30 and the Moscoso statement from New York: the funeral of President Heureaux of San Domingo took place at 5 o'clock last evening in Santiago de las Caballeros; the population was panic stricken, but there was no disorder; a report has been received here to the effect that the adversaries of the government attacked Moca last night; the news of the death of the president was hardly credited here by the people generally until last evening, when undoubted confirmation was received, and then there was great rejoicing among the Dominican exiles, many of whom live in and around Cape Haitien; these exiles, who were driven out of their country by Heureaux, are now preparing to arm themselves and enter San Domingo, where they expect their chief, Don Juan Isidor Jiminez, to join them; and the Dominican government is making preparations on a large scale to maintain itself. Gen. Abelardo A. Moscoso, an exiled leader of the Liberal party of San Domingo, now living in New York, said last night: 'The death of President Heureaux will, I think, surely be followed by a long state of disorder and revolution. I want to emphasize this prophecy — that the United States will eventually be compelled to interfere to establish peace in the island, just as she did in Cuba. I favor the policy of peace. I shall be glad to return to my country and support such a policy if it is inaugurated by Gen. Figuera, the vice-president, who succeeds to the head of the government.'

records.headline: The Journal prints part of an editorial on Santo Domingo and annexation:
records.summary_en: The Journal prints part of an editorial on Santo Domingo and annexation: Congress authorized the president to appoint a commission to investigate conditions and inclinations in the Dominican republic; this commission reported in 1871 that the people preferred independence, but believed that permanent independence was impossible, and therefore favored annexation; owing to radical differences of opinion, however, the subject was dropped with the printing of the report. There is probably no political significance in the sending of the cruisers New Orleans and Machias to Santo Domingo, as such action is entirely in accordance with precedent and is a prudential measure whenever American interests are threatened by such local disturbances; at the same time, in view of possible events, it may prove advantageous in more ways than one to have naval representation at hand in case of revolution. To say the least, the people of Santo Domingo would not ask in vain at this time for annexation to the United States; at the same time there is not the slightest possibility that they shall ever be annexed against their will.

records.headline: The Press-Journal prints part of an item on the crisis in Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The Press-Journal prints part of an item on the crisis in Santo Domingo and a Havana item headed 'Gomez on His Dignity': of the conspiracy which resulted in the assassination of President Heureaux, it is believed to be probable that it was planned and executed by partisans of Jiminez, the revolutionary leader; it is known that Heureaux had lived in fear of assassination for many months, and had frankly announced that he proposed to continue in the presidency as long as he lived; German interests in the republic are considerable, and President Heureaux was strongly backed by them; the future of the republic may depend largely upon the course taken by the foreign element in this crisis, and the course of the German government in the present crisis will be watched with considerable interest by the American government; the finances of San Domingo are in a bad way, and merchants doing business there have little hope of any material improvement, unless this government in some way takes control of matters. In the Havana item, General Gomez declared that a majority of the alleged interviews with him, published in the local papers, were entirely without foundation, and that he has decided to write himself anything he may hereafter have to say to the press: 'I believe all papers lie,' said Gomez, 'and that those of one country are in this respect no better than those of another. In future I will give over my own signature, or through the Associated Press alone, anything intended for publication.' General Gomez refused to discuss the presidency of the Dominican republic.

records.headline: The Courier completes a sketch of President Heureaux, with an account of the Dominican Republic:
records.summary_en: The Courier completes a sketch of President Heureaux, with an account of the Dominican Republic: Heureaux, after the cessation of hostilities, became very prominent in politics; he held several positions of trust and honor, and finally, in 1882, he was elected president; he served one term; in 1887 he again was placed in the presidential chair, and has been elected continuously ever since; Heureaux faced dozens of revolutions during his long period of office holding, but he always came out victorious. Last year, when the war between Spain and the United States was at its height, an expedition of filibusters was fitted out in the United States against Heureaux's government; it was given out that the expedition was intended for Cuba, but after the Americans had ceased to watch it a straight course was laid for the Dominican republic; Heureaux, however, had been apprised of the expedition, and when it reached Santo Domingo he was prepared to give it a warm reception; the filibusters were defeated. Under the head 'The Dominican Republic,' the paper says the republic occupies the eastern portion of the island of Hayti, which next to Cuba is the largest of the West Indian islands; its inhabitants are of Spanish, African and Indian descent and use the Spanish language; the president is assisted by a cabinet, and the legislative body is composed of 22 deputies elected by indirect popular vote; the population is estimated at between 416,000 and 610,000; the capital, Santo Domingo, has a population of 25,000; there are about 3,000 schools in the republic, and 40 newspapers are published.

Bajo el título «The Dominican Republic», el periódico dice que la república ocupa la porción oriental de la isla de Haití, que junto a Cuba es la mayor de las islas de las Indias Occidentales; sus habitantes son de ascendencia española, africana e india y usan el idioma español; el presidente es asistido por un gabinete, y el cuerpo legislativo se compone de 22 diputados elegidos por voto popular indirecto; la población se estima entre 416,000 y 610,000; la capital, Santo Domingo, tiene una población de 25,000; hay unas 3,000 escuelas en la república, y se publican 40 periódicos.

records.headline: The Avalanche prints a Washington item on the warship orders
records.summary_en: The Avalanche prints a Washington item on the warship orders and the situation in Santo Domingo: Secretary Long Friday issued orders detaching the cruiser New Orleans from the North Atlantic squadron at Newport and directing her to proceed at once to Santo Domingo city; orders were issued also to the Machias at St. Thomas, to proceed to the same point via San Juan; these orders were made at the instance of the State Department and as a precautionary measure owing to the disturbed conditions following the assassination of President Heureaux of San Domingo. The trouble between the Government of San Domingo and its creditors has reached an acute stage; the creditors, who are almost entirely Americans, have begun to clamor for an American protectorate, which would necessarily be the first step in the direction of annexation. Political plots are already shaping themselves: the adherents of Gen. Jiminez seek to put him at the head of affairs, while the friends of Gen. Maximo Gomez are talking of making him the ruler of the republic; it is said by officers who have recently been in San Domingo that interference by this Government would be welcomed by a large proportion of the inhabitants of the island.
records.summary_es: El Avalanche publica una nota de Washington sobre las órdenes de los buques de guerra y la situación en Santo Domingo: el secretario Long emitió el viernes órdenes separando al crucero New Orleans de la escuadra del Atlántico Norte en Newport y dirigiéndolo a proceder de inmediato a la ciudad de Santo Domingo; también se emitieron órdenes al Machias, en Santo Tomás, de proceder al mismo punto vía San Juan; estas órdenes fueron dadas a instancia del Departamento de Estado y como medida precautoria debido a las condiciones perturbadas que siguieron al asesinato del presidente Heureaux de Santo Domingo. El problema entre el gobierno de Santo Domingo y sus acreedores ha llegado a una etapa aguda; los acreedores, que son casi enteramente estadounidenses, han comenzado a clamar por un protectorado estadounidense, que sería necesariamente el primer paso en dirección de la anexión. Las conspiraciones políticas ya toman forma: los partidarios del gen. Jimenes buscan ponerlo a la cabeza de los asuntos, mientras los amigos del gen. Máximo Gómez hablan de hacerlo gobernante de la república; dicen oficiales que han estado recientemente en Santo Domingo que la interferencia de este gobierno sería bienvenida por una gran proporción de los habitantes de la isla.

records.headline: The Observer prints part of an editorial on the San Domingo Improvement Company:
records.summary_en: The Observer prints part of an editorial on the San Domingo Improvement Company: a company incorporated in New Jersey, known as the 'San Domingo Improvement Company of New York,' has acquired a concession in the republic; in 1888 the fiscal agents of the Dominican republic entered into convention with an Amsterdam firm for a loan of about $3,760,000, and to meet the payments on the loan the Holland company was given the right to collect directly the receipts from all custom houses in the republic, and the indebtedness was made a mortgage upon all the revenues of the country; in 1893 the rights of the Amsterdam bankers were transferred to the New York company, and by act of the Santo Domingo Congress the right of the Americans to collect the customs and port dues was reaffirmed. In the event of a revolution it will require the presence of several American warships to preserve the interest of the American company, and as a civil war would seriously reduce the revenues the administration may feel warranted to extend its protection to the extent of exerting force to maintain peace.

records.headline: The Gazette prints a Puerto Plata assassination dispatch of July 28
records.summary_en: The Gazette prints a Puerto Plata assassination dispatch of July 28 and part of a sketch of President Heureaux: President Ulysses Heureux of the republic was assassinated at Moca, a town in the interior, at 4:30 o'clock this afternoon; the murderer, whose name is Roman Caceros, succeeded in escaping, but an energetic pursuit has begun by the authorities, and it is possible that he will be captured; Vice-President Wenceslao Figuereo, immediately upon the announcement of the President's death, assumed the direction of affairs; at present calmness prevails everywhere in the republic; the body of President Heureux will probably be taken to San Domingo for the funeral services. The sketch says Gen. Ulysses Heureaux had numerous enemies, but seemed to possess a charm against death; as a politician he had great talent and boldness; he himself caused reports to be circulated that he had been seized by revolutionists, imprisoned and subsequently shot, done to throw his enemies off their guard so that they would betray themselves; he was born at Porto Plata in 1846; becoming a private soldier in 1862, he volunteered in the native uprising against the Spaniards, which lasted about three years, and when the Spaniards left the island Heureaux had risen to the rank of colonel; he was a leader in the attempts to drive from power Bonaventura Baez, who, in 1867, usurped absolute power in the island.

records.headline: The Gazette prints an account of the republic it calls Dominica
records.summary_en: The Gazette prints an account of the republic it calls Dominica and the details of the murder received at Cape Haytien: Dominica is the eastern part of the island, the western part being Haiti; it has been under French, Spanish and English domination at times, but has been a republic since 1841; the population is of mixed white, Indian and African descent, with few pure blacks; in November 1868, Bonaventura Baez, then president of Dominica, signed with President Grant a treaty for the annexation of the country to the United States, but the Senate at Washington refused to ratify it, though a commission which visited the island reported favorably. The details of the murder, received at Cape Haytien July 27, are to the effect that President Heureaux of Santo Domingo was assassinated as he was about to leave on horseback for Santiago de las Caballeros; the assassin, Ramon Caceros, surrounded by several accomplices, approached the President as he was talking with some friends and fired twice with a revolver; the first bullet struck the President in the left side and penetrated the heart, causing instant death; the second bullet killed an old man who was standing near the President; the assassin and his accomplices then fled to avoid the shots fired at them by the President's friends, and it is not known whether any of them was wounded; the body of the President was taken to the palace of the governor of Moca; President Heureaux's death has caused a panic.
records.summary_es: El Gazette publica una relación de la república que llama Dominica y los detalles del asesinato recibidos en Cabo Haitiano: Dominica es la parte oriental de la isla, siendo Haití la parte occidental; ha estado bajo dominación francesa, española e inglesa en ocasiones, pero ha sido una república desde 1841; la población es de ascendencia mezclada blanca, india y africana, con pocos negros puros; en noviembre de 1868, Buenaventura Báez, entonces presidente de Dominica, firmó con el presidente Grant un tratado para la anexión del país a los Estados Unidos, pero el Senado en Washington se negó a ratificarlo, aunque una comisión que visitó la isla informó favorablemente. Los detalles del asesinato, recibidos en Cabo Haitiano el 27 de julio, son en el sentido de que el presidente Heureaux de Santo Domingo fue asesinado cuando estaba a punto de salir a caballo hacia Santiago de los Caballeros; el asesino, Ramón Caceros, rodeado por varios cómplices, se acercó al presidente mientras este hablaba con algunos amigos y disparó dos veces con un revólver; la primera bala alcanzó al presidente en el lado izquierdo y le penetró el corazón, causándole la muerte instantánea; la segunda bala mató a un anciano que estaba de pie cerca del presidente; el asesino y sus cómplices huyeron entonces para evitar los disparos que les hicieron los amigos del presidente, y no se sabe si alguno de ellos fue herido; el cuerpo del presidente fue llevado al palacio del gobernador de Moca; la muerte del presidente Heureaux ha causado pánico.

Ulysses Heureaux, who for 17 years had been president of the republic of Santo Domingo, was a sort of Napoleon, who, after years of autocratic power, had assumed the manners of an oriental despot; Heureaux was 53 years old; he was born in Puerto Plata, the nearest city to the little town of Moca, where he was assassinated Tuesday; his parents were poor; he became a common soldier and by bravery, brains and dash soon won high command; all the West Indies at one time or another have fought Spain — Santo Domingo did, and Heureaux became a general in that war; he was a fighter, a fearless, reckless one, whom bullets could not stop; in 1882 Heureaux was elected president of the republic and with four re-elections continued in power to the day of his death.

records.summary_en: The Herald prints a Cape Haytien dispatch of July 28 on the murder headed 'Heureaux's Assassination': details of the murder of President Heureaux, of Santo Domingo, received here are to the effect that he was assassinated as he was about to leave on horseback for Santiago de las Caballeros; the assassin, Ramon Caceros, surrounded by several accomplices, approached the president as he was talking with some friends and fired twice with a revolver; the first bullet struck the president in the left side and penetrated the heart, causing instant death; the second bullet killed an old man who was standing near the president; the assassin and his accomplices then fled to avoid the shots fired at them by the president's friends; the president's death has caused a panic.
records.summary_es: El Herald publica un despacho de Cabo Haitiano del 28 de julio titulado «Heureaux's Assassination»: los detalles del asesinato del presidente Heureaux, de Santo Domingo, recibidos aquí son en el sentido de que fue asesinado cuando estaba a punto de salir a caballo hacia Santiago de los Caballeros; el asesino, Ramón Caceros, rodeado por varios cómplices, se acercó al presidente mientras este hablaba con algunos amigos y disparó dos veces con un revólver; la primera bala alcanzó al presidente en el lado izquierdo y le penetró el corazón, causándole la muerte instantánea; la segunda bala mató a un anciano que estaba de pie cerca del presidente; el asesino y sus cómplices huyeron entonces para evitar los disparos que les hicieron los amigos del presidente; la muerte del presidente ha causado pánico.

records.headline: The Herald prints a Fort de France dispatch of July 29 on the unrest
records.summary_en: The Herald prints a Fort de France dispatch of July 29 on the unrest headed 'Santo Domingo in a State of Unrest': the funeral services over the remains of President Heureaux, which took place at Santiago de las Caballeros last evening, were attended by a large number of people; the city of Santo Domingo is in a state of great unrest and business is entirely suspended; the people fear an outbreak; last night a band of armed men attacked Moca; the government has taken measures to put down the threatened insurrection.

Fort de France, July 29. The funeral
services over the remains of President
Heureaux, which took place at Santi

The city of Santo Domingo is in a state

break. Last night a band of armed
