records.headline: The Tribune continues its description of the republic's products
records.summary_en: The Tribune continues its description of the republic's products and climate: honey, molasses, cocoanuts, dyewoods and many other articles are exported, the records showing that about £5,000,000 worth of various products leave the republic every year. As to the climate, a writer says: 'It must be healthful when one may see by the records that the death rate is only eight to the thousand inhabitants. There are no densely populated places, yellow fever is unknown, and intermittent fevers may be avoided, as in Europe, with the smallest precautions. There is scarcely a section of the republic where the trade winds do not blow all day long; the mountain ranges run east and west, and the valleys between them, as well as the mountain sides, receive the trade winds, which blow continually from the east in that latitude. The city of Puerto Plata, on the north coast, and the interior cities of La Vega, Moca and Santiago, in the Royal Plain (Vega Real) of Columbus, are kept healthful and comfortable all the year by this wind, which removes miasmatic emanations. On the south the great sugar-raising plains are between the mountains and the Caribbean Sea. Although Santo Domingo city, the capital, is situated only 18½ degrees from the equator, and Puerto Plata, the northern port, 20 degrees, and the temperature in winter is quite mild, the thermometer does not rise high in midsummer.'
records.summary_es: El Tribune continúa su descripción de los productos de la república y el clima: se exportan miel, melaza, cocos, maderas tintóreas y muchos otros artículos, y los registros muestran que cada año salen de la república productos por valor de unas 5.000.000 de libras. En cuanto al clima, un escritor dice: 'Debe de ser saludable cuando se puede ver en los registros que la tasa de mortalidad es de solo ocho por cada mil habitantes. No hay lugares densamente poblados, la fiebre amarilla es desconocida, y las fiebres intermitentes pueden evitarse, como en Europa, con las más pequeñas precauciones. Apenas hay una sección de la república donde los vientos alisios no soplen durante todo el día; las cordilleras corren de este a oeste, y los valles entre ellas, así como las laderas de las montañas, reciben los vientos alisios, que soplan continuamente desde el este en esa latitud. La ciudad de Puerto Plata, en la costa norte, y las ciudades del interior de La Vega, Moca y Santiago, en la Vega Real de Colón, se mantienen saludables y confortables todo el año gracias a este viento, que elimina las emanaciones miasmáticas. En el sur, las grandes llanuras azucareras están entre las montañas y el mar Caribe. Aunque la ciudad de Santo Domingo, la capital, está situada a solo 18½ grados del ecuador, y Puerto Plata, el puerto del norte, a 20 grados, y la temperatura en invierno es bastante suave, el termómetro no sube mucho en pleno verano'.

records.headline: The Register prints the Havana dispatch on the departure of Gen. Juan Isidro Jiminez:
records.summary_en: The Register prints the Havana dispatch on the departure of Gen. Juan Isidro Jiminez: the general, accompanied by six Cubans and four natives of Santo Domingo, is believed to have left here this afternoon for the Dominican republic; it has not yet been ascertained how the party left, but if, as it is thought, they went on one of the Herrera line steamers for the north coast, expecting to obtain a schooner at Nuevitas, they will probably be arrested or prevented from continuing their journey; Gen. Jiminez claimed to be ill yesterday, but the many visitors whom he received this morning led to the belief that the movement was on foot; one thing only is certain, and that is that he has gone, taking his baggage with him, as did also his companions; and the authorities are making a close investigation in order to discover in which direction the party went. The dispatch is headed 'General Jiminez.'

records.summary_en: The Post-Intelligencer prints the close of a Washington item and a New York special to the Herald from Havana of August 5: Minister Powell has cabled the State Department that the presence of a United States warship may be required, if the present threatening condition continues, to insure the safety of the United States legation and consulates. General Jiminez to-day displayed a cipher cablegram which he received from an agent in Santo Domingo, reading: 'Revolution commences to-day in Dajabon and La Vega. Send definite answer when you arrive. Must be as early as possible. — Franco.' Jiminez has replied: 'Be there by last of month with party. Delay so as to avoid bloodshed. Think present government will retire before then.' Jiminez declared that he had stands of arms in Cuba ready to be used, and that a party of Americans in the United States is preparing to sail at once; when asked if he did not think the United States would stop his expedition, he smiled and said: 'Has the United States enough vessels to guard the entire coast of Cuba and the Isle of Pines that can be spared? Never fear, we will have no trouble in sailing, and we will sail soon.' Jiminez is said to be backed by Gomez and other prominent Cuban army officers. The special closes with the report that General Jiminez, accompanied by six Cubans and four natives of Santo Domingo, is believed to have left Havana this afternoon for the Dominican republic.

records.headline: The State Journal prints the closing part of a dispatch on the revolution
records.summary_en: The State Journal prints the closing part of a dispatch on the revolution in Santo Domingo: men have taken up arms in Santo Domingo in favor of Don Juan Isidro Jiminez and occupy the provinces of Chagui and Curabo, as far as Jose de las Matas, as well as the towns of Guayabin, Sabineta, Manzanillo and Dajabon, abandoned by the troops of the government of Santo Domingo; more than half these troops are said to have gone over to the camp of General Pacheco, who is reported to have more than 800 well armed men under his command; General Guellito, governor of Monte Cristi, who it is claimed has already lost half his troops, who have gone over to the enemy, is in a desperate position and unable to attack the revolutionary troops, and it is added that he will be obliged to capitulate; and numbers of Dominicans are arriving in Hayti by sea in order to join, by crossing the frontier, the camp of General Pacheco.

records.headline: A profile of Heureaux recounts how he showed a group of conspirators, told them they were not nearly so anxious for his life
records.summary_en: A profile of Heureaux recounts how he showed a group of conspirators, told them they were not nearly so anxious for his life as they believed, said he would take no action, and let them go free, keeping his word that none would be punished, though the majority left the country. It also describes his polished manner and entertaining conversation, and his palace in Santo Domingo, a three-story building covering a block.
records.summary_es: Un perfil de Heureaux relata cómo mostró a un grupo de conspiradores, les dijo que no estaban ni de lejos tan ansiosos por su vida como creían, dijo que no tomaría ninguna medida, y los dejó libres, cumpliendo su palabra de que ninguno sería castigado, aunque la mayoría abandonó el país. También describe sus modales refinados y su conversación amena, y su palacio en Santo Domingo, un edificio de tres pisos que ocupa una manzana.
records.passage: but I shall take no action. "You are free." And he turned and went away. He kept his word and none of the conspirators was punished, but the majority of them left the country. Heureaux had the features of a full-blooded negro. His manner was polished and his conversation entertaining. The aristocratic Dominicans, who are of pure Spanish blood, refused to admit him to their social circles because of his negro blood, and he felt their slight keenly. Little was known of his family history or his parentage, and he was always reticent about the incidents of his life before he became famous. His palace in Santo Domingo is a three-story building covering a block, and built in the typical style of the tropics. Its plaster walls and green window slats are all that can be seen by the tourist.—Chicago Tribune. [illegible] BY A TOOTHPICK. [illegible] Illustrating Means Used in Identification of Criminals. records.headline: Advices from Santo Domingo on August 7 report that word of an approaching hurricane has been received from various parts of the country
records.summary_en: Advices from Santo Domingo on August 7 report that word of an approaching hurricane has been received from various parts of the country and that the barometer there is falling rapidly. The Dominican warships have sailed for a port of refuge on the south coast, and the United States cruiser New Orleans is still there, with steam up and ready to leave at any moment.

records.headline: The Journal prints the close of a Cape Haytien dispatch and a Puerto Plata dispatch of August 7
records.summary_en: The Journal prints the close of a Cape Haytien dispatch and a Puerto Plata dispatch of August 7 headed 'Trying to Keep Order': General Guellito, governor of Monte Cristi, is thus placed in a dangerous position and is unable to attack the revolutionists, and it is added that he will be obliged to capitulate; numbers of Dominicans are arriving in Hayti by sea in order to reach the revolutionary army by crossing the frontier, thus augmenting the force of General Pacheco. The Puerto Plata dispatch says Minister of Finance Señor Alvarez and Senator Cordero, with 100 men, went to Monte Cristi yesterday, where they united with 700 men who had been assembled in behalf of the government for the restoration of order; American steamships are also watching the coast to prevent the landing of an insurrectionary expedition, should any such attempt be made; it is claimed the governor of Monte Cristi has 3,000 men under arms for the preservation of the peace, but the situation is considered very grave; and the United States gunboat Machias has left the port of Santo Domingo for Punta Macoris, but the cruiser New Orleans still remains here.
records.summary_es: The Journal publica el cierre de un despacho de Cabo Haitiano y un despacho de Puerto Plata del 7 de agosto, titulado 'Trying to Keep Order': el general Guellito, gobernador de Monte Cristi, queda así en una posición peligrosa e incapaz de atacar a los revolucionarios, y se añade que se verá obligado a capitular; numerosos dominicanos están llegando a Haití por mar para alcanzar el ejército revolucionario cruzando la frontera, aumentando así la fuerza del general Pacheco. El despacho de Puerto Plata dice que el ministro de Hacienda, señor Alvarez, y el senador Cordero, con 100 hombres, fueron ayer a Monte Cristi, donde se unieron a 700 hombres que habían sido reunidos a favor del gobierno para el restablecimiento del orden; vapores americanos también vigilan la costa para impedir el desembarco de una expedición insurreccional, si se intentara alguna; se afirma que el gobernador de Monte Cristi tiene 3,000 hombres en armas para la preservación de la paz, pero la situación se considera muy grave; y el cañonero estadounidense Machias ha salido del puerto de Santo Domingo hacia Punta Macoris, pero el crucero New Orleans aún permanece aquí.

AS WASHINGTON VIEWS IT. WASHINGTON, [illegible] — Notwithstanding the growing turbulence in San Domingo, as disclosed in Press dispatches, neither the State nor Navy Departments had received anything up to the close of office hours today to show that our officials there were apprehensive over the developments. The authorities here are proceeding on the theory that the existing order of affairs is regular, and this will continue to be the course observed. Only in the event that the insurrection becomes strong enough to establish a de facto form of government is there any likelihood that its claim could be taken into consideration as against the de jure government.

records.headline: The Messenger prints a Cape Haytien dispatch of August 3 on the Dominican revolt:
records.summary_en: The Messenger prints a Cape Haytien dispatch of August 3 on the Dominican revolt: it has just become known that an armed insurrection has broken out at La Vega, a town seventy-eight miles northwest of Santo Domingo, in favor of Jiminez, who aspires to the presidency in succession to the late President Heureaux; later advices from the Dominican republic indicate that the revolution is growing in strength; and at Santiago de la Cruz 500 well armed men have risen under the command of General Ramon Pacheco, and General Reyes, who is very influential in those districts, has joined the insurgents with several other generals, each commanding fairly important forces. The dispatch is headed 'Unrest in West India Republics.'
records.summary_es: The Messenger publica un despacho de Cabo Haitiano del 3 de agosto sobre la revuelta dominicana: se acaba de saber que ha estallado una insurrección armada en La Vega, pueblo situado a setenta y ocho millas al noroeste de Santo Domingo, a favor de Jiminez, quien aspira a la presidencia en sucesión del fallecido presidente Heureaux; informaciones posteriores de la República Dominicana indican que la revolución gana fuerza; y en Santiago de la Cruz se han levantado 500 hombres bien armados bajo el mando del general Ramón Pacheco, y el general Reyes, muy influyente en esos distritos, se ha unido a los insurgentes con varios otros generales, cada uno al mando de fuerzas bastante importantes. El despacho lleva por título 'Unrest in West India Republics'.

records.headline: The Weekly Post prints a Puerto Plata dispatch of August 7:
records.summary_en: The Weekly Post prints a Puerto Plata dispatch of August 7: Señor Alvarez, the minister of finance, and Señor Cordero, with 100 men, went to Monte Cristi yesterday and united there with 700 men who had been assembled in behalf of the government for the restoration of order; armed steamers are watching the coast to prevent the landing of an insurrectionary expedition, should such a thing be attempted; the governor of Monte Cristi has 3,500 men under arms for the preservation of the peace, and the situation is considered grave. The capital dispatch, headed 'Situation at the Capital', says the United States gunboat Machias has left here for Punta Macoris; news from the interior indicates that tranquillity prevails, but business continues depressed and the want of drafts is greatly felt; the government is endeavoring to ameliorate the financial condition; advices that a hurricane is approaching have been received from various parts of the republic of Dominica, and the barometer here is falling rapidly; the Dominican warships have sailed for Caldera, a port of refuge on the south coast; the United States cruiser New Orleans is still here, with steam up and ready to leave at any moment; the American steamer Carib, from New York July 28 for Turks Island, which is now at Samana, is anxiously expected; and as provisions are very scarce and prices high, the poor people are suffering severely, their earnings not being in proportion to the prices now asked for the necessaries of life.

records.headline: The Post prints the Cape Haytien, Puerto Plata, and Santo Domingo dispatches of August 7
records.summary_en: The Post prints the Cape Haytien, Puerto Plata, and Santo Domingo dispatches of August 7 in heavily degraded type: partisans of Don Juan Jiminez have taken up arms in Santo Domingo on the plains of Chaguel and San Jose de las Matas and in the towns of Guayabin, Sabaneta, Manzanillo and Dajabon, abandoned by the troops of the government of Santo Domingo; more than half of these troops are said to have gone over to the camp of General Pacheco; General Guellito, governor of Monte Christo, who it is claimed has lost half his troops, who have gone over to the enemy, it is believed will capitulate; and numbers of Dominicans are arriving in Hayti by sea, crossing the frontier to join the force of General Pacheco. The Puerto Plata dispatch says Señor Alvarez, the minister of finance, and Señor Cordero, with a hundred men, went to Monte Christo yesterday and united there with 700 men assembled in behalf of the government for the restoration of order; steamers are watching the coast to prevent the landing of an insurgent expedition, should such a thing be attempted; and the governor of Monte Christo has 3,000 men under arms for the preservation of the peace, the situation being considered grave. The Santo Domingo dispatch says the United States gunboat Machias has left here for Punta Manacoris; the United States cruiser New Orleans remains here; advices from the interior indicate that tranquillity prevails, but business continues depressed and the want of drafts is generally felt, and the government is endeavoring to ameliorate the prevailing condition. A Washington item of August 7 adds that, notwithstanding the growing turbulence in Santo Domingo as disclosed in press dispatches, neither the State nor the Navy Department had received anything up to the close of office hours to-day.
records.summary_es: The Post publica los despachos de Cabo Haitiano, Puerto Plata y Santo Domingo del 7 de agosto, en tipos muy degradados: partidarios de don Juan Jiminez han tomado las armas en Santo Domingo en las llanuras de Chaguel y San José de las Matas y en los pueblos de Guayabín, Sabaneta, Manzanillo y Dajabón, abandonados por las tropas del gobierno de Santo Domingo; se dice que más de la mitad de esas tropas se han pasado al campamento del general Pacheco; el general Guellito, gobernador de Monte Christo, de quien se afirma que ha perdido la mitad de sus tropas, pasadas al enemigo, se cree que capitulará; y numerosos dominicanos están llegando a Haití por mar, cruzando la frontera para unirse a la fuerza del general Pacheco. El despacho de Puerto Plata dice que el señor Alvarez, ministro de Hacienda, y el señor Cordero, con cien hombres, fueron ayer a Monte Christo y se unieron allí a 700 hombres reunidos a favor del gobierno para el restablecimiento del orden; vapores vigilan la costa para impedir el desembarco de una expedición insurgente, si tal cosa se intentara; y el gobernador de Monte Christo tiene 3,000 hombres en armas para la preservación de la paz, considerándose grave la situación. El despacho de Santo Domingo dice que el cañonero estadounidense Machias ha salido de aquí hacia Punta Manacoris; el crucero estadounidense New Orleans permanece aquí; avisos del interior indican que prevalece la tranquilidad, pero el comercio continúa deprimido y la falta de letras de cambio se siente en general, y el gobierno se esfuerza por mejorar la situación prevaleciente. Una nota de Washington del 7 de agosto añade que, a pesar de la creciente turbulencia en Santo Domingo revelada en los despachos de prensa, ni el Departamento de Estado ni el de Marina habían recibido nada hasta el cierre de las oficinas hoy.

records.headline: First move of the revolution: the Dominican revolutionary troops assembled at Ouanaminthe have crossed the frontier
records.summary_en: First move of the revolution: the Dominican revolutionary troops assembled at Ouanaminthe have crossed the frontier and taken Dajabón, the garrison retiring to Fort Blair; Jiménez is expected to land and take command, and the Haitian government moves to keep him out of its territory.
records.summary_es: Primer movimiento de la revolución: las tropas revolucionarias dominicanas reunidas en Juana Méndez han cruzado la frontera y tomado Dajabón, retirándose la guarnición al Fuerte Blair; se espera que Jiménez desembarque y tome el mando, y el gobierno haitiano actúa para mantenerlo fuera de su territorio.
records.passage: FIRST MOVE in the New Haytian Revolution — Jiminez Shows His Hand. Port-au-Prince, Hayti, Aug. [illegible] — The revolutionary Dominican troops, which assembled at [Ouanaminthe?], have crossed the frontier and taken possession of Dajabon. The garrison at that place retired to Fort Blair, a strategic position commanding the town. The foreign population and Haytian consul have left the place. It is considered probable that Jiminez, the leader of the revolution, will attempt to make a landing on the island shortly in order to join the revolutionary troops at Dajabon and take direct command of the movement. The Haytian government is taking measures to prevent Jiminez from landing in its territory

records.headline: The Globe prints the closing part of the Santo Domingo dispatch of August 7:
records.summary_en: The Globe prints the closing part of the Santo Domingo dispatch of August 7: advices that a hurricane is approaching have been received from various parts of the republic of Dominica, and the barometer here is falling rapidly; the Dominican warships have sailed for Caldera, a port of refuge on the south coast; the United States cruiser New Orleans is still here, with steam up and ready to leave at any moment; the American steamer Carib, from New York July 28 for Turk's Island, which is now at Samana, is anxiously expected; and, as provisions are very scarce and prices high, the poor people are suffering, their earnings not being in proportion to the price now asked for the necessities of life.
records.summary_es: The Globe publica la parte final del despacho de Santo Domingo del 7 de agosto: se han recibido avisos de que se acerca un huracán desde varias partes de la república de Dominica, y el barómetro aquí baja rápidamente; los buques de guerra dominicanos han zarpado hacia Caldera, un puerto de refugio en la costa sur; el crucero estadounidense New Orleans sigue aquí, con vapor levantado y listo para partir en cualquier momento; el vapor americano Carib, que salió de Nueva York el 28 de julio hacia la Isla Turca y que ahora está en Samaná, es esperado con ansiedad; y, como las provisiones son muy escasas y los precios altos, la gente pobre sufre, pues sus ganancias no están en proporción con el precio que ahora se pide por los artículos de primera necesidad.

records.headline: The Messenger prints the closing part of the Havana interview
records.summary_en: The Messenger prints the closing part of the Havana interview with General Jiminez: the present government, he had said, could not possibly last beyond the 15th of this month. 'I did hear,' he continued, 'that Heureaux was sending men to Cuba to kill me, but I knew nothing whatever regarding the plot to kill him. I had no connection and have no connection with Ramon Caceres, who did the shooting. I do not believe that the United States will interfere with my government in San Domingo, which will be a government peaceful and helpful to all, for the United States did not interfere with the government of Heureaux, who robbed and murdered for fourteen years.' General Jiminez admits that he has often been to the United States incognito, but says he has not had interviews with official persons; he considers that there is no need of promoting expeditions to land in San Domingo, as there already are a thousand men waiting for him, a force which he deems quite sufficient for his purposes; referring to the future relations of San Domingo with the United States, he expressed a desire to be on friendly terms with Washington, and said he believed he could count upon American sympathy; Gomez he referred to as esteemed by Dominicans, but not sought for as president; and the people of San Domingo, he declares, are impetuous, and are urging him to come to them at once, but for a time he prefers delay, as 'each day is worth a battle won.'

records.headline: The News prints a dispatch from Santo Domingo on the revolution
records.summary_en: The News prints a dispatch from Santo Domingo on the revolution: the revolutionary Dominicans have crossed the frontier and have taken possession of Dajabon; the garrison at that place retired to Fort Belair, a strategic position commanding the town; the foreign population and the Haytian consul left the place; it is considered that Jiminez, the leader of the revolution, will attempt to make a landing on the island shortly in order to join the revolutionary troops at Dajabon and take direction of the movement; the Haytian government is taking measures to prevent Jiminez from landing in its territory; it is very difficult at present to obtain information regarding the events transpiring in the Dominican Republic; and it is reported that the exiled Dominicans assembled at Ouanaminthe, Hayti, crossed the frontier of Santo Domingo and captured the town of Dajabon.
records.summary_es: The News publica un despacho desde Santo Domingo sobre la revolución: los dominicanos revolucionarios han cruzado la frontera y han tomado posesión de Dajabón; la guarnición de ese lugar se retiró a Fuerte Belair, una posición estratégica que domina el pueblo; la población extranjera y el cónsul haitiano abandonaron el lugar; se considera que Jiminez, el líder de la revolución, intentará desembarcar en la isla en breve para unirse a las tropas revolucionarias en Dajabón y tomar la dirección del movimiento; el gobierno haitiano está tomando medidas para impedir que Jiminez desembarque en su territorio; en la actualidad es muy difícil obtener información sobre los acontecimientos que ocurren en la República Dominicana; y se reporta que los dominicanos exiliados reunidos en Ouanaminthe, Haití, cruzaron la frontera de Santo Domingo y capturaron el pueblo de Dajabón.

records.headline: The Eagle opens a narrative feature on Don Juan Isidro Jiminez
records.summary_en: The Eagle opens a narrative feature on Don Juan Isidro Jiminez, the present aspirant to the presidential chair, who was the leading opponent of the late President Heureaux: it accounts for some hitherto mysterious movements of the steamship Fanita, which was libeled in Mobile, liberated and sailed, ostensibly for Cuba with arms for the insurgents, but in reality made a daring dash for San Domingo to take the island by storm, only to meet with defeat and flight; it explains the interest the War Department took in the trial of Jiminez on British soil, in the Bahamas, and how the United States settled with the little island republic; and, on the whole, considering the present unsettled condition of San Domingo, and the possibility of Jiminez gaining the ascendency, the recital will be of interest. San Domingo, the feature says, is a very beautiful, fruitful, but not a very big island; in fact, there is room for but one big man there at a time — this was the conviction of the late President Heureaux, who was the one big man; there was another, however, Don Juan Isidro Jiminez, a rich merchant with immense plantations on the island, great warehouses and commercial branches in New York, Hamburg and other cities of the world, and a great traveler, which contributed to his longevity; but every time he landed the island sagged considerably in that direction, and this displeased President Heureaux, whose palace was in the interior, and who rarely went to the shore for fear that the island would capsize with his weight.
records.summary_es: The Eagle abre un reportaje narrativo sobre don Juan Isidro Jiminez, el actual aspirante a la silla presidencial, quien fue el principal opositor del fallecido presidente Heureaux: da cuenta de algunos movimientos hasta ahora misteriosos del vapor Fanita, que fue embargado en Mobile, liberado y zarpó, ostensiblemente hacia Cuba con armas para los insurgentes, pero en realidad hizo una audaz carrera hacia San Domingo para tomar la isla por asalto, solo para encontrarse con la derrota y la huida; explica el interés que el Departamento de Guerra tomó en el juicio de Jiminez en suelo británico, en las Bahamas, y cómo los Estados Unidos se arreglaron con la pequeña república isleña; y, en conjunto, considerando la actual situación inestable de San Domingo y la posibilidad de que Jiminez alcance el ascendiente, el relato será de interés. San Domingo, dice el reportaje, es una isla muy hermosa y fértil, pero no muy grande; de hecho, allí solo hay espacio para un gran hombre a la vez: esa era la convicción del fallecido presidente Heureaux, quien era el gran hombre; había otro, sin embargo, don Juan Isidro Jiminez, un rico comerciante con inmensas plantaciones en la isla, grandes almacenes y sucursales comerciales en Nueva York, Hamburgo y otras ciudades del mundo, y un gran viajero, lo que contribuyó a su longevidad; pero cada vez que desembarcaba, la isla se hundía considerablemente en esa dirección, y eso disgustaba al presidente Heureaux, cuyo palacio estaba en el interior y que rara vez iba a la costa por temor a que la isla volcara con su peso.

records.headline: The Eagle continues its narrative feature with the island trade
records.summary_en: The Eagle continues its narrative feature with the island trade and the dinner at which President Heureaux warns General Jiminez against his growing popularity: the trade runs from the exportation of logwood to the French wine growers to the importation of Ansonia clocks, which were quite recherché among the Dominican elite as neck ornaments. 'General Jiminez,' the president said gravely, 'it is with interesting apprehension that the presidential prerogative views your growing popularity. You are a rich man, a benevolent man, and a just man, so far as you can judge by foreign standards. You are well liked at the custom house, so I understand, and it seems to be mutual.' General Don Juan smiled proudly. 'Now General, while you are growing richer, the presidential prerogative regrets to say the island is growing poorer. I am going to perform a grand coup. I am going to float a many million dollar loan with the Americans, and I am going to rebond the customs of San Domingo as security. I am going to allow the foreigner to sit in the seat of customs, and you know, General Jiminez, these people have riches back of their heads. Take heed, then. Make yourself less popular. Popularity is a growing disease on the island. Check yours in the incipient stage or it will be fatal. Remember, during my sixteen years of divine prerogative gentlemen of the island have been picked off because of these growing pains of popularity.'
records.summary_es: The Eagle continúa su reportaje narrativo con el comercio de la isla y la cena en la que el presidente Heureaux advierte al general Jiminez sobre su creciente popularidad: el comercio va desde la exportación de palo de tinte a los viticultores franceses hasta la importación de relojes Ansonia, que eran muy recherché entre la élite dominicana como adornos para el cuello. 'General Jiminez', dijo el presidente gravemente, 'es con interesante aprensión que la prerrogativa presidencial ve su creciente popularidad. Usted es un hombre rico, un hombre benévolo y un hombre justo, hasta donde se puede juzgar por patrones extranjeros. Usted es bien apreciado en la aduana, según entiendo, y parece que es mutuo'. El general don Juan sonrió con orgullo. 'Ahora, General, mientras usted se hace más rico, la prerrogativa presidencial lamenta decir que la isla se hace más pobre. Voy a realizar un gran golpe. Voy a negociar un préstamo de muchos millones de dólares con los americanos, y voy a volver a afianzar las aduanas de San Domingo como garantía. Voy a permitir que el extranjero se siente en el puesto de aduanas, y usted sabe, general Jiminez, que esa gente tiene riquezas tras la cabeza. Tenga cuidado, entonces. Hágase menos popular. La popularidad es una enfermedad creciente en la isla. Controle la suya en su etapa inicial o será fatal. Recuerde, durante mis dieciséis años de prerrogativa divina, caballeros de la isla han sido eliminados por esos dolores crecientes de la popularidad'.

records.headline: The Eagle prints, in a later part of its narrative feature
records.summary_en: The Eagle prints, in a later part of its narrative feature, a statement in behalf of Jiminez: the revolutionists will not interfere in any way with the property of foreigners on the island; notwithstanding the many revolutions which have taken place in San Domingo since it attained its independence, in no instance has either life been taken or property molested of any foreigner, with the single exception of the action of Heureaux, who opened the vaults of the French bank because of a personal quarrel with one of its directors; women and children are safe at all times, as the Dominicans never stoop to war with the helpless, nor do they ever sack or pillage, but fight for what they believe to be right in the open, as men and soldiers should do. 'The entire country is aroused to the necessity of a change to a government where life is secure, and it recognizes that the former vice president and the present pretending president is but one of the accomplices of Heureaux, and as such has no confidence in him. There is but one man who at this time represents the people and their best interests, and that is Jiminez, and if an opportunity is given to the people they will prove it by their ballots. But if none is accorded in that way, then force will be used.'
records.summary_es: The Eagle publica, en una parte posterior de su reportaje narrativo, una declaración a favor de Jiminez: los revolucionarios no interferirán en modo alguno con la propiedad de los extranjeros en la isla; a pesar de las muchas revoluciones que han tenido lugar en San Domingo desde que alcanzó su independencia, en ningún caso se ha quitado la vida ni se ha molestado la propiedad de ningún extranjero, con la única excepción de la acción de Heureaux, quien abrió las bóvedas del banco francés por una disputa personal con uno de sus directores; las mujeres y los niños están seguros en todo momento, pues los dominicanos nunca se rebajan a hacer la guerra a los indefensos, ni saquean ni pillan, sino que luchan por lo que creen justo a campo abierto, como deben hacerlo los hombres y los soldados. 'Todo el país está despertado ante la necesidad de un cambio hacia un gobierno donde la vida esté segura, y reconoce que el exvicepresidente y el actual presidente pretendiente no es más que uno de los cómplices de Heureaux, y como tal no tiene confianza en él. Solo hay un hombre que en este momento representa al pueblo y sus mejores intereses, y ese es Jiminez, y si se le da una oportunidad al pueblo, lo probará con sus votos. Pero si no se le concede de esa manera, entonces se usará la fuerza'.

records.headline: The Silver State prints the close of a dispatch on the revolution
records.summary_en: The Silver State prints the close of a dispatch on the revolution, a Puerto Plata dispatch of August 9 headed 'Arms Seized', and a Philadelphia item of August 9 headed 'Don't Like Sam': the forces of Don Juan Isidro Jiminez, the leader of the revolution, are being augmented every day, and news from every part of the Dominican Republic is favorable to him. The Puerto Plata dispatch says the Haytien government has seized at Fort Liberte arms and ammunition destined for Dominican insurgents; several Dominicans in Hayti have been arrested for violating the neutrality laws, among them Francisco Deetjen, in whose keeping arms were found; President Sam of Hayti has wired the Dominican government that insurgents will not be permitted to use Haytien territory as a base of operations; and the force for the government under the command of Minister Cordero has encountered insurgents led by General Pablo Reyes. The Philadelphia item says three officers representing the insurgents of San Domingo and two civilians, representing those who do not like the manner in which President Sam manages affairs in Hayti, have been here three days endeavoring to find vessels to carry munitions of war recently purchased in New Haven; to avoid suspicion, all the members of the party crossed the Windward passage in small boats and embarked on a steamship at Guantanamo, landing last week in New York; those from San Domingo were delayed by the capsizing of a boat; and they claim that there is little danger in landing contraband war material anywhere on the coast of either country, except near the principal ports, as the coasts are not patrolled.
records.summary_es: The Silver State publica el cierre de un despacho sobre la revolución, un despacho de Puerto Plata del 9 de agosto titulado 'Arms Seized', y una nota de Filadelfia del 9 de agosto titulada 'Don't Like Sam': las fuerzas de don Juan Isidro Jiminez, el líder de la revolución, aumentan cada día, y las noticias de todas partes de la República Dominicana le son favorables. El despacho de Puerto Plata dice que el gobierno haitiano ha incautado en Fuerte Libertad armas y municiones destinadas a los insurgentes dominicanos; varios dominicanos en Haití han sido arrestados por violar las leyes de neutralidad, entre ellos Francisco Deetjen, en cuyo poder se encontraron armas; el presidente Sam, de Haití, ha cablegrafiado al gobierno dominicano que no se permitirá a los insurgentes usar el territorio haitiano como base de operaciones; y la fuerza del gobierno bajo el mando del ministro Cordero se ha encontrado con insurgentes dirigidos por el general Pablo Reyes. La nota de Filadelfia dice que tres oficiales que representan a los insurgentes de San Domingo y dos civiles, que representan a quienes no les gusta la manera en que el presidente Sam maneja los asuntos en Haití, llevan tres días aquí tratando de encontrar buques para transportar municiones de guerra compradas recientemente en New Haven; para evitar sospechas, todos los miembros del grupo cruzaron el Paso de los Vientos en pequeños botes y se embarcaron en un vapor en Guantánamo, desembarcando la semana pasada en Nueva York; los de San Domingo se retrasaron por el vuelco de un bote; y afirman que hay poco peligro en desembarcar material de guerra de contrabando en cualquier punto de la costa de cualquiera de los dos países, excepto cerca de los puertos principales, pues las costas no son patrulladas.

records.headline: The Post-Intelligencer prints the Dajabon dispatch: the revolutionary Dominicans
records.summary_en: The Post-Intelligencer prints the Dajabon dispatch: the revolutionary Dominicans have crossed the frontier and have taken possession of Dajabon; the garrison at that place retired to Fort Belair, a strategic position; the foreign population and the Haytien consul left the place; and the Haytien government is taking measures to prevent Jiminez from landing in its territory. A Fort de France item of August 8 adds that it is very difficult at present to obtain information regarding the events transpiring in the Dominican republic, but that it is reported the exiled Dominicans assembled at Ouanaminthe, Hayti, crossed the frontier of Santo Domingo and captured the town of Dajabon. A Havana item of the same date says General Juan Isidro Jiminez, the aspirant to the presidency of the republic, says that several Dominican generals have already declared in his favor, in spite of his advice to them to delay definite action; he denies that the Dominican government has the force under arms attributed to it, and asserts that the present executive will not be able to make an effective resistance, owing to the scarcity of resources and sympathizers. The dispatch is printed in heavily degraded type.

Una nota de Fort de France del 8 de agosto añade que en la actualidad es muy difícil obtener información sobre los acontecimientos que ocurren en la República Dominicana, pero que se reporta que los dominicanos exiliados reunidos en Ouanaminthe, Haití, cruzaron la frontera de Santo Domingo y capturaron el pueblo de Dajabón. Una nota de La Habana de la misma fecha dice que el general Juan Isidro Jiminez, aspirante a la presidencia de la república, dice que varios generales dominicanos ya se han declarado a su favor, a pesar de su consejo de retrasar la acción definitiva; niega que el gobierno dominicano tenga la fuerza en armas que se le atribuye, y afirma que el actual ejecutivo no podrá oponer una resistencia efectiva, debido a la escasez de recursos y simpatizantes. records.headline: The State Journal prints the close of a dispatch on the revolution
records.summary_en: The State Journal prints the close of a dispatch on the revolution, a New York item of August 9 headed 'Can't Land in Hayti', and a Philadelphia item of August 9 headed 'Filibusters Active': the forces of Don Juan Isidro Jiminez, leader of the revolution, are being augmented every day and the news from all parts of the Dominican republic is favorable to him. The New York item, a Herald dispatch from Port Au Prince, Hayti, says word comes from Monte Christi that Dominican troops have been hurried there; the Haytien government is prepared to prevent Jiminez from landing on Haytien territory; all is quiet in Port Au Prince; and suspects are being interrogated by the authorities. The Philadelphia item, from a morning paper, says three officers representing the insurgents of San Domingo and two civilians, representing those who do not like the manner in which President Sam manages affairs in Hayti, have been here three days endeavoring to find vessels to carry munitions of war recently purchased in New Haven; to avoid suspicion, all the members of the party crossed the Windward passage in small boats and embarked on a steamship at Guantanamo, landing last week in New York; those from San Domingo were delayed by the capsizing of a boat; and they claim that there is little danger in landing contraband war material anywhere on the coast of either country, except near the principal ports, as the coasts are not patrolled, because neither of the governments has war vessels to do the work.

La nota de Nueva York, un despacho del Herald desde Puerto Príncipe, Haití, dice que llegan noticias de Monte Christi de que tropas dominicanas han sido enviadas allí con urgencia; el gobierno haitiano está preparado para impedir que Jiminez desembarque en territorio haitiano; todo está tranquilo en Puerto Príncipe; y los sospechosos están siendo interrogados por las autoridades. La nota de Filadelfia, de un periódico matutino, dice que tres oficiales que representan a los insurgentes de San Domingo y dos civiles, que representan a quienes no les gusta la manera en que el presidente Sam maneja los asuntos en Haití, llevan tres días aquí tratando de encontrar buques para transportar municiones de guerra compradas recientemente en New Haven; para evitar sospechas, todos los miembros del grupo cruzaron el Paso de los Vientos en pequeños botes y se embarcaron en un vapor en Guantánamo, desembarcando la semana pasada en Nueva York; los de San Domingo se retrasaron por el vuelco de un bote; y afirman que hay poco peligro en desembarcar material de guerra de contrabando en cualquier punto de la costa de cualquiera de los dos países, excepto cerca de los puertos principales, pues las costas no son patrulladas, porque ninguno de los dos gobiernos tiene buques de guerra para hacer ese trabajo.

records.headline: Ties can be paid In American sold or na tional silver
records.summary_en: The *Indianapolis Journal* reported on Dominican fiscal measures requiring a portion of customs duties to be paid in paper currency, which would be publicly burned each month to retire the circulating paper notes. Concurrently, Dominican revolutionary forces crossed from Ouanaminthe, Haiti, and captured the border town of Dajabon, forcing the local garrison to retreat to Fort Belair. The report noted expectations that rebel leader General Jimenes would soon land to take direct command, despite Haitian efforts to prevent his transit.
records.summary_es: El *Indianapolis Journal* informó sobre las medidas fiscales dominicanas que exigían el pago de una porción de los aranceles aduaneros en papel moneda, el cual se quemaría públicamente cada mes para retirar los billetes en circulación. Al mismo tiempo, fuerzas revolucionarias dominicanas cruzaron desde Ouanaminthe, Haití, y tomaron la localidad fronteriza de Dajabón, obligando a la guarnición local a replegarse hacia Fort Belair. El informe señalaba la expectativa de que el líder rebelde general Jimenes desembarcara en breve para asumir el mando directo, pese a los esfuerzos haitianos por impedir su paso.
records.passage: ties can be paid in American gold or national silver or paper money, but [illegible] per cent. of the same must be paid in paper money to a special commission named by the government in the different ports. This commission will be instructed to burn publicly the amount received during each month. The law is to remain in force until all paper money in circulation shall have been taken up. According to a former law now in force a certain part of the export dues is applied for the same purpose. A favorable change in the financial situation is expected if the government bill is approved by Congress. Judging by the latest news received from the interior of the republic the country is quiet. PORT-AU-PRINCE, Haiti, Aug. 8. — The revolutionary Dominican troops which assembled at Ouanaminthe have crossed the frontier and have taken possession of Dajabon. The garrison at that place retired to Fort Belair, a strategic position commanding the town. The foreign population and the Haitian consul left the place. It is considered probable that Jimenez, the leader of the revolution, will attempt to make a landing on the island shortly to join the revolutionary troops at Dajabon and take direct command of the movement. The Haitian government is taking measures to prevent Jimenez from landing in its territory. Cable Notes. Mr. Choate will leave London to-day for a three weeks tour in Scotland. M'KINLEY'S VISITORS Canadian Officers Pay Respects Will Visit the Catholic Summer School. Hotel Champlain, N. Y., Aug. 9. President McKinley today promised Father Lavella, the president of the Catholic summer school of America, that he would visit the summer school grounds, which are near the hotel, next Tuesday forenoon. Major General Hutton, aide to the queen, and commander of her majesty's troops in Canada, and Major Laurence G. records.headline: The Eagle prints the closing words of a dispatch on the revolution
records.summary_en: The Eagle prints the closing words of a dispatch on the revolution, a Puerto Plata dispatch of August 9, and two New York items of August 9: the news from all parts of the Dominican republic is favorable to Jiminez. The Puerto Plata dispatch says the Haytien government has seized at Fort Liberte arms and ammunition destined for Dominican insurgents; several Dominicans in Hayti have been arrested for violating the neutrality laws, among them Francisco Deetjen, in whose keeping arms were found; President Sam, of Hayti, has wired the Dominican government that insurgents will not be permitted to use Haytien territory as a base of operations; and the force for the government under the command of Minister Cordero has encountered insurgents led by General Pablo Reyes. A special to the Herald from Washington says General Brooke was given instructions today to prevent at all hazards any filibustering expedition in Jiminez's interests leaving Cuba; the charge d'affaires of the Dominican republic in this country has called the attention of the authorities to the contemplated expedition and he was assured that everything possible would be done to prevent any such proceedings. A dispatch to the Herald from Port Au Prince, Hayti, says word comes from Monte Christi that Dominican troops have been hurried there; the Haytien government is prepared to prevent Jiminez from landing on Haytien territory; all is quiet in Port Au Prince; and suspects are being interrogated by the authorities.

El despacho de Puerto Plata dice que el gobierno haitiano ha incautado en Fuerte Libertad armas y municiones destinadas a los insurgentes dominicanos; varios dominicanos en Haití han sido arrestados por violar las leyes de neutralidad, entre ellos Francisco Deetjen, en cuyo poder se encontraron armas; el presidente Sam, de Haití, ha telegrafiado al gobierno dominicano que no se permitirá a los insurgentes usar el territorio haitiano como base de operaciones; y la fuerza del gobierno bajo el mando del ministro Cordero se ha encontrado con insurgentes dirigidos por el general Pablo Reyes. Una nota especial al Herald desde Washington dice que el general Brooke recibió hoy instrucciones de impedir a toda costa que cualquier expedición filibustera en interés de Jiménez salga de Cuba; el encargado de negocios de la república dominicana en este país ha llamado la atención de las autoridades sobre la expedición proyectada y se le aseguró que se haría todo lo posible para impedir tales procedimientos. records.headline: The Democrat prints the closing part of the interview with General Jiminez
records.summary_en: The Democrat prints the closing part of the interview with General Jiminez, opening with followings of 800 men: Dominican government paper, General Jiminez says, is unsalable; men of all colors in Santo Domingo are joining his cause, but most of his generals are colored; when questioned regarding a dispatch from Cape Haitien published by the Discusion, representing that the Haitian government is unfavorable to his pretensions and is prepared to prevent him from landing on Haitian territory, General Jiminez replied that the Haitian government was in a 'very rotten condition'; he estimates the revenue of the Dominican republic under a good government at not less than 2,500,000, an amount more than enough to meet governmental expenses and the interest on the public debt; when he attains to the presidency, he hopes to go ahead promptly with public works and to carry on other necessary improvements, but he insists that 'the first necessity of Santo Domingo is honest men in her administration'; and as to the possibility that the existing government may prevent his entering the country, he ridicules it, as, to quote his words, 'Santo Domingo is practically mine.'
records.summary_es: El Democrat publica la parte final de la entrevista con el general Jiménez, que se abre con partidarios de 800 hombres: el papel del gobierno dominicano, dice el general Jiménez, no tiene venta; hombres de todos los colores en Santo Domingo se están uniendo a su causa, pero la mayoría de sus generales son de color; al ser interrogado sobre un despacho de Cabo Haitiano publicado por la Discusión, que representa que el gobierno haitiano es desfavorable a sus pretensiones y está preparado para impedirle desembarcar en territorio haitiano, el general Jiménez respondió que el gobierno haitiano estaba en una «condición muy podrida»; estima los ingresos de la república dominicana bajo un buen gobierno en no menos de 2,500,000, una cantidad más que suficiente para cubrir los gastos del gobierno y los intereses de la deuda pública; cuando alcance la presidencia, espera avanzar prontamente con las obras públicas y llevar a cabo otras mejoras necesarias, pero insiste en que «la primera necesidad de Santo Domingo son hombres honestos en su administración»; y en cuanto a la posibilidad de que el gobierno existente le impida entrar al país, se burla de ella, pues, para citar sus palabras, «Santo Domingo es prácticamente mío».

records.headline: The Tribune prints part of an editorial item on the San Domingo Improvement Company:
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints part of an editorial item on the San Domingo Improvement Company: the American interest at stake in the republic, the item says, is due to a concession which a company incorporated in New Jersey and known as the 'San Domingo Improvement Company of New York' has acquired in the republic; in 1888 the fiscal agents of the Dominican republic entered into convention with an Amsterdam firm for a loan, and to meet the payments on the loan the Holland company was given the right to collect directly the receipts from all custom houses in the republic, and the indebtedness was made a mortgage upon all the revenues of the country; in 1893 the rights of the Amsterdam bankers were transferred to the New York company, and by act of the Santo Domingo Congress the right of the Americans to collect the customs and port dues was reaffirmed; and in the event of a revolution it will require the presence of several American warships to preserve the interest of the American company, and as a civil war would seriously reduce the revenues the administration may feel warranted to extend its protection to the extent of exerting force to maintain peace.

records.summary_en: The *Age-Herald* reported that the Dominican revolutionary movement in favor of Juan Isidro Jimenes was expanding rapidly, with the province of La Vega in revolt. Government troops commanded by General Francisco Tiriano deserted en masse upon confronting rebel General Ramon Pacheco at Dajabon, giving the insurgents control of the Yaque River crossings and isolating Monte Cristi. The paper also noted cordial relations between Haiti and the United States, marked by approval for an American meteorological station at Cape Haitien.

records.headline: The Journal and Courier prints the close of General Jiminez's interview:
records.summary_en: The Journal and Courier prints the close of General Jiminez's interview: he said to-day that funds are being daily placed to his credit in Paris and that he had refused over 800 tenders of service on the part of the Cubans and Americans who were ready to pay their expenses; in reply to these offers he had asserted that he had neither need nor desire to organize expeditions; to-day, he continued, he had received advices that two more Dominican generals had declared themselves in his favor, with followings of 800 men; and as to the possibility that the existing government may prevent his entering the country, he ridicules it, as, to quote his words, 'Santo Domingo is practically mine.'
records.summary_es: El Journal and Courier publica el cierre de la entrevista del general Jiménez: dijo hoy que diariamente se están colocando fondos a su crédito en París y que ha rechazado más de 800 ofertas de servicio de parte de cubanos y estadounidenses que estaban listos para pagar sus gastos; en respuesta a esas ofertas había asegurado que no tenía necesidad ni deseo de organizar expediciones; hoy, continuó, había recibido noticias de que dos generales dominicanos más se habían declarado a su favor, con partidarios de 800 hombres; y en cuanto a la posibilidad de que el gobierno existente le impida entrar al país, se burla de ella, pues, para citar sus palabras, «Santo Domingo es prácticamente mío».

Deputation Examining Island.
St. Johns, N. F., Aug. 9. A deputa
tion of Finlanders is here inspecting the
country with a view to arranging for
the immigration of thousands of Fin-
landers who are emigrating because of
the tyranny of the Russian government.
Joseph Chamberlain, British secretary
of state for the colonies, sent with them
a Hpeeial re.mest to the governor of

records.summary_en: The *Houston Daily Post* reported that the Dominican rebellion against the government was expanding, with the province of La Vega in open revolt. Haitian authorities arrested several Dominicans and seized weapons destined for the insurgents, with President Sam declaring Haiti would not allow its territory to serve as an insurgent base. Meanwhile, Dominican government troops sent to confront rebel leader General Ramon Pacheco at Dajabon deserted to the insurgent side, cutting communications with Monte Cristi.
records.summary_es: El *Houston Daily Post* informó que la rebelión dominicana contra el gobierno continuaba expandiéndose, hallándose la provincia de La Vega en abierta insurrección. Autoridades haitianas arrestaron a varios dominicanos e incautaron armas destinadas a los insurgentes, declarando el presidente Sam que Haití no permitiría que su territorio sirviera de base para los sublevados. Mientras tanto, las tropas del gobierno dominicano enviadas para enfrentar al líder rebelde general Ramón Pacheco en Dajabón desertaron al bando insurgente, cortando las comunicaciones con Monte Cristi.

The Philadelphia item says a morning paper reports that three officers representing the insurgents of San Domingo and two civilians representing those who do not like the manner in which President Sam manages affairs in Hayti have been here three days endeavoring to find vessels to carry munitions of war recently purchased in New Haven; to avoid suspicion, all the members of the party crossed the Windward passage in small boats and embarked on a steamship at Guantanamo, landing last week in New York; those from San Domingo were delayed by the capsizing of a boat; they claim that there is little danger in landing contraband war material anywhere on the coast of either country except near the principal ports, as the coasts are not patrolled, because neither of the governments has war vessels to do the work; and what they claim are needed are small steam tugs to take out their purchases and remove cargoes landed on the eastern shores of Cuba some months ago.

records.headline: The Bee prints the closing part of the Puerto Plata dispatch
records.summary_en: The Bee prints the closing part of the Puerto Plata dispatch: the Haytien government has seized at Fort Liberte arms and ammunition destined for Dominican insurgents; several Dominicans in Hayti have been arrested for violating the neutrality laws, among them Francisco Deetjen, in whose keeping arms were found; President Sam of Hayti has wired the Dominican government that insurgents will not be permitted to use Haytien territory as a base for operations; and the force for the government under the command of Minister Cordero has encountered insurgents led by General Pablo Reyes. A dispatch to the Herald from Port au Prince, Hayti, says word was received from Monte Christo that Dominican troops had been hurried there, that the Haytien government is prepared to prevent Jiminez from landing on Haytien territory, that all is quiet in Port au Prince, and that suspects are being interrogated by the authorities. A special to the Herald from Washington says General Brooke was given instructions today to prevent at all hazards any filibustering expedition in Jiminez's interests leaving Cuba, and that the charge d'affaires of the Dominican republic in this country has called the attention of the authorities to the contemplated expedition and was assured that everything possible would be done to prevent any such proceedings. The Port au Prince dispatch begins a report that the latest news from Santo Domingo says the revolutionary movement is extending and that the province of Vega is in arms, and that it is impossible to obtain any details here; the city is calm.
records.summary_es: El Bee publica la parte final del despacho de Puerto Plata: el gobierno haitiano ha incautado en Fuerte Libertad armas y municiones destinadas a los insurgentes dominicanos; varios dominicanos en Haití han sido arrestados por violar las leyes de neutralidad, entre ellos Francisco Deetjen, en cuyo poder se encontraron armas; el presidente Sam de Haití ha telegrafiado al gobierno dominicano que no se permitirá a los insurgentes usar el territorio haitiano como base de operaciones; y la fuerza del gobierno bajo el mando del ministro Cordero se ha encontrado con insurgentes dirigidos por el general Pablo Reyes. Un despacho al Herald desde Puerto Príncipe, Haití, dice que se recibió noticia de Monte Cristi de que tropas dominicanas habían sido enviadas allí con urgencia, que el gobierno haitiano está preparado para impedir que Jiménez desembarque en territorio haitiano, que todo está tranquilo en Puerto Príncipe, y que los sospechosos están siendo interrogados por las autoridades. Una nota especial al Herald desde Washington dice que el general Brooke recibió hoy instrucciones de impedir a toda costa que cualquier expedición filibustera en interés de Jiménez salga de Cuba, y que el encargado de negocios de la república dominicana en este país ha llamado la atención de las autoridades sobre la expedición proyectada y se le aseguró que se haría todo lo posible para impedir tales procedimientos. El despacho de Puerto Príncipe comienza un informe de que las últimas noticias de Santo Domingo dicen que el movimiento revolucionario se extiende y que la provincia de La Vega está en armas, y que es imposible obtener detalles aquí; la ciudad está tranquila.

records.headline: The Sun prints part of an item on the San Domingo Improvement Company:
records.summary_en: The Sun prints part of an item on the San Domingo Improvement Company: the American interest at stake in the republic, the item says, is due to a concession which a company incorporated in New Jersey and known as the 'San Domingo Improvement Company of New York' has acquired in the republic; in 1888 the fiscal agents of the Dominican republic entered into convention with an Amsterdam firm for a loan of about $3,750,000, and to meet the payments on the loan the Holland company was given the right to collect directly the receipts from all custom houses in the republic, and the indebtedness was made a mortgage upon all the revenues of the country; in 1893 the rights of the Amsterdam bankers were transferred to the New York company, and by act of the Santo Domingo Congress the right of the Americans to collect the customs and port dues was reaffirmed; and in the event of a revolution it will require the presence of several American warships to preserve the interest of the American company, and as a civil war would seriously reduce the revenues the administration may feel warranted to extend its protection to the extent of exerting force to maintain peace.

records.headline: The Times prints the Dajabon dispatch and a Havana dispatch of August 9:
records.summary_en: The Times prints the Dajabon dispatch and a Havana dispatch of August 9: the Dominican revolutionary troops which assembled at Ouanaminthe have crossed the frontier and taken possession of Dajabon; the garrison retired to Fort Belair, a strategic position commanding the town; the foreign population has left the place; it is considered probable that Jiminez, who leads the revolution, will attempt landing on the island shortly, join the revolutionary troops at Dajabon and take the direction of their movements; and the Haytien government is taking measures to prevent Jiminez from landing in its territory. The Havana dispatch says General Juan Isidro Jiminez, who was interviewed yesterday, said he was in daily receipt of about twenty-five cablegrams from Santo Domingo, where all was going well; to the interviewer he exhibited a letter, which he said was from a person of influence, advising him not to risk participancy in an expedition, as the result was assured and was only a matter of time; according to the writer, if anything happened to Jiminez the people of Santo Domingo would regard it as a great loss, inasmuch as their ideals and hopes regarding good government were bound up in him; and moreover, the writer holds, the system needed a man in some respects like Heureaux, whereas the present executive, Figuereo, though trying to work on the lines followed by Heureaux, was mean, unpopular and incapable of carrying on the administration with the necessary vigor.

records.headline: The Age-Herald's reprinted editorial from the Chicago Times-Herald continues:
records.summary_en: The Age-Herald's reprinted editorial from the Chicago Times-Herald continues: San Domingo's political history has been varied almost beyond parallel; an uninhabited, wild region separates it from Hayti, and the political hostility between the two governments is a fixed and ineradicable fact; Hayti has been growing and ascending, while San Domingo has been declining and lapsing into poverty; within less than a century San Domingo has been successively under Spanish, French, Haytian, independent, Spanish and again independent flags; in 1865 Spain withdrew its authority for the last time, and San Domingo has been independent ever since; the present republic was founded earlier, however, in 1844, and its constitution is modeled to a considerable extent upon that of the United States; there is a congress of twenty-two deputies, chosen under a restricted suffrage, while the executive is chosen by an electoral college for a term of four years; the country is divided into ten districts, each administered by a governor appointed by the president, and the governors in turn appoint prefects over the communes and cities; and under President Heureaux there has been comparative quiet and a revival of prosperity, the insurrection in Cuba leading to emigration which San Domingo was glad to welcome.

records.headline: The Transcript prints the close of the Cape Haytien dispatch
records.summary_en: The Transcript prints the close of the Cape Haytien dispatch and two New York items of August 10: the government commander sent from Monte Cristo to attack General Ramon Pacheco at Dajabon, the headquarters of the revolutionists, was abandoned when he arrived in front of the enemy by his troops, who, without firing a shot, deserted and entered the camp of General Pacheco; the advanced posts of the latter are at Las Aguas, and the revolutionists are masters of the fords across the river Yaque, thus cutting off communication between Monte Cristo and the interior; and the forces of Don Juan Isidro Jiminez, leader of the revolution, are being augmented every day and the news from all parts of the Dominican republic are favorable to him. The first New York item says the Haytien government has seized at Fort Liberte arms and ammunition destined for Dominican insurgents, and that several Dominicans in Hayti have been arrested for violating the neutrality laws, among them Francisco Deetjen, in whose keeping arms were found. records.headline: The Post prints a report of the Porto Plata hurricane damage
records.summary_en: The Post prints a report of the Porto Plata hurricane damage: the hurricane passed over Porto Plata and appears to have ravaged the north of the Dominican republic; all communication between Porto Plata and the interior, not including Santo Domingo, is interrupted, and it is impossible to obtain a correct account of the damage done, although it is thought to be important; the railway from Porto Plata to Santo Domingo is no longer working; and evidently the hurricane swept over Cape Haytien with less violence, and therefore with correspondingly less damage. records.headline: The Silver Star prints part of an item on the San Domingo Improvement Company:
records.summary_en: The Silver Star prints part of an item on the San Domingo Improvement Company: the American interest at stake in the republic, the item says, is due to a concession which a company incorporated in New Jersey and known as the 'San Domingo Improvement Company of New York' has acquired in the republic; in 1888 the fiscal agents of the Dominican republic entered into convention with an Amsterdam firm for a loan of about $3,750,000, and to meet the payments on the loan the Holland company was given the right to collect directly the receipts from all custom houses in the republic, and the indebtedness was made a mortgage upon all the revenues of the country; in 1893 the rights of the Amsterdam bankers were transferred to the New York company, and by act of the Santo Domingo Congress the right of the Americans to collect the customs and port dues was reaffirmed; and in the event of a revolution it will require the presence of several American warships to preserve the interest of the American company, and as a civil war would seriously reduce the revenues the administration may feel warranted to extend its protection to the extent of exerting force to maintain peace.

records.summary_en: Dispatches on the hurricane in The Indianapolis Journal state that the storm passed over Porto Plata and appears to have ravaged the northern Dominican Republic. Because all communication between Porto Plata and the interior, not including San Domingo, is interrupted, no accurate account of the damage can yet be obtained, though losses are believed to be heavy. The railroad from Porto Plata to San Domingo is out of service, and the hurricane later passed over Cape Haitien with reduced violence.

El ferrocarril de Porto Plata a San Domingo dejó de funcionar y el huracán pasó finalmente sobre Cape Haitien con menor violencia.

records.headline: A Washington dispatch of August 10 in the Omaha Daily Bee reports
records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch of August 10 in the Omaha Daily Bee reports that the Navy Department has received no further news of the West Indian hurricane and considers all American naval vessels in those waters safe, with the New Orleans the only vessel still out. Regarding ships in Dominican ports, the dispatch notes that the vessel printed as "Machlas" is at San Pedro de Macoris, San Domingo, while the New Orleans steamed out of Santo Domingo harbor the previous Tuesday in anticipation of the storm. A brief fragment at the top of the column also notes a disrupted link to Santo Domingo and adds that the hurricane eventually swept over Cape Haytien with less violence and correspondingly reduced damage.
records.summary_es: Un despacho desde Washington fechado el 10 de agosto en el Omaha Daily Bee informa que el Departamento de Marina no ha recibido nuevas noticias sobre el huracán de las Antillas y considera a salvo a todos los buques navales estadounidenses en esas aguas, siendo el New Orleans el único que permanece fuera de puerto. En cuanto a las naves en puertos dominicanos, el parte señala que el buque impreso como "Machlas" se encuentra en San Pedro de Macoris, San Domingo, mientras que el New Orleans zarpó del puerto de Santo Domingo el martes anterior en previsión de la tormenta. Un breve fragmento al inicio de la columna menciona además una conexión interrumpida hacia Santo Domingo y añade que el huracán pasó finalmente sobre Cape Haytien con menor violencia y daños proporcionalmente menores.

records.headline: A dispatch from Puerto Plata, Santo Domingo, dated August 10
records.summary_en: A dispatch from Puerto Plata, Santo Domingo, dated August 10, in The New York Journal and Advertiser states that the full severity of the cyclone on the island cannot yet be determined because communication with the interior is cut off and even the railway from Puerto Plata to San Domingo City has been disabled. The report asserts that the northern part of the Dominican Republic was largely laid waste and predicts that accurate accounts, once received, will likely show heavy loss of life, ruined growing crops, and families left homeless and starving. With apparently diminishing violence, the storm passed from Cape Haytien toward eastern Cuba on a track pointing toward the southern coast of the United States.

El informe sostiene que la parte norte de la República Dominicana quedó en gran medida arrasada y prevé que, cuando lleguen reportes precisos, probablemente se comprobará la pérdida de muchas vidas, la destrucción de cultivos en pie y familias sin hogar y hambrientas. Con violencia aparentemente decreciente, la tormenta pasó desde Cape Haytien hacia el extremo oriental de Cuba en dirección a la costa sur de los Estados Unidos.

records.headline: Commenting editorially on Dominican affairs, The Age-Herald describes
records.summary_en: Commenting editorially on Dominican affairs, The Age-Herald describes the island between Cuba and Porto Rico as fertile, well watered, and suited to tropical crops, while characterizing its population in racial terms as divided between the Black inhabitants of Hayti and the mulatto population of San Domingo, claiming it would become one of the richest countries in the world if occupied exclusively by white people. Turning to the rebellion, the paper states that General Jiminez is organizing expeditions abroad while Generals Pocheco and Reyes and a dozen other home generals lead the internal movement, adding that Figuero will be fortunate to withstand the Jiminez faction's attacks. The editorial concludes that the United States does not want the island no matter how strongly Dominicans again seek annexation, unless as an agricultural destination for a million Black emigrants from the American South alongside Liberia, Hayti, and San Domingo.
records.summary_es: En un comentario editorial sobre los asuntos dominicanos, The Age-Herald describe la isla situada entre Cuba y Porto Rico como fértil, húmeda y apta para cultivos tropicales, al tiempo que caracteriza racialmente a su población como dividida entre los habitantes negros de Hayti y los mulatos de San Domingo, afirmando que sería uno de los países más ricos del mundo si estuviera ocupada exclusivamente por personas blancas. Respecto a la rebelión, el periódico señala que el general Jiminez organiza expediciones en el exterior mientras los generales Pocheco y Reyes y una docena más de generales locales encabezan el movimiento interno, y añade que Figuero tendrá suerte si logra resistir los ataques de la facción de Jiminez. El editorial concluye que los Estados Unidos no desean la isla por más que los dominicanos soliciten nuevamente la anexión, salvo que se busque un destino agrícola para un millón de emigrantes negros del sur estadounidense junto con Liberia, Hayti y San Domingo.

records.headline: A Havana special dispatch in The Savannah Tribune reports a Wednesday interview
records.summary_en: A Havana special dispatch in The Savannah Tribune reports a Wednesday interview with General Juan Isidro Jiminez, whom the paper describes as the aspirant to the presidency of the "Republic of Dominica" (the Dominican Republic). Jiminez stated that funds were being placed daily to his credit in Paris and that he had declined more than 800 offers of service from Cubans and Americans ready to pay their own expenses. Ridiculing the possibility that the incumbent government of the Dominican Republic could prevent him from entering the country, he declared, "Santo Domingo is practically mine."
records.summary_es: Un despacho especial desde La Habana en The Savannah Tribune recoge una entrevista del miércoles con el general Juan Isidro Jiminez, a quien el periódico describe como aspirante a la presidencia de la "Republic of Dominica" (la República Dominicana). Jiminez afirmó que diariamente se depositaban fondos a su favor en París y que había rechazado más de 800 ofrecimientos de servicio por parte de cubanos y estadounidenses dispuestos a pagar sus propios gastos. Al ridiculizar la posibilidad de que el gobierno vigente de la República Dominicana impida su entrada al país, declaró: "Santo Domingo es prácticamente mío".

records.headline: Advices from Kingston, Jamaica, dated August 11 in The Scranton Tribune cite
records.summary_en: Advices from Kingston, Jamaica, dated August 11 in The Scranton Tribune cite an August 3 mail dispatch from Santo Domingo via Hayti confirming cable reports on the spread and significance of the revolution across the Dominican Republic. Prominent civil and military figures are taking the field on the understanding that Jiminez is the prime mover and will soon arrive with munitions of war, while Generals Ramon Pacheco and Pablo Reyes, leading armed followers that include regular soldiers, are marching rapidly westward to cut off Monte Christi from reinforcements and link up with insurgents from Hayti ahead of Jiminez's expedition. The dispatch attributes the uprising's popularity to the name of Gomez and notes that if he declines the presidency or Jiminez ultimately opposes his election, prominent leaders are already considering a plebiscite on renewing an earlier vote for American annexation or an American protectorate.

According to the report, prominent men in civil and military circles are taking the field in the belief that Jiminez is the prime mover and will arrive shortly. Attributing the revolution's popularity to the use of Gomez's name, the dispatch adds that if Gomez declines to accept Jiminez's presidency or finally opposes his election, prominent leaders are already weighing a plebiscite on whether the country would prefer to renew the 1871 vote for American annexation or an American protectorate rather than elect another dictator.

records.headline: Two Dominican items appear in this column of the New-York Tribune
records.summary_en: Two Dominican items appear in this column of the New-York Tribune, opening with the close of a dispatch stating that arrivals from an armed steamer departed immediately with their staffs for Santiago de los Caballeros, and that the government will permit foreign money to enter and circulate freely without restriction while beginning the retirement of banknotes on August 17. Under the heading "Plans of the Revolutionists," an August 11 Kingston, Jamaica, dispatch relays an August 3 mail report from San Domingo via Hayti describing prominent civil and military men taking the field behind Jiminez, who is expected shortly from Cuba with munitions of war, while Generals Ramon Pacheco and Pablo Reyes march westward with armed followers including regular soldiers to cut off Monte Christi from reinforcements and join insurgents from Hayti. The dispatch adds that the revolution owes its popularity to Gomez's name and that if he declines the presidency or Jiminez finally opposes his election, leaders are considering a plebiscite to renew the 1871 vote for American annexation or an American protectorate rather than elect another dictator.
records.summary_es: Dos notas dominicanas aparecen en esta columna del New-York Tribune, comenzando con el cierre de un despacho según el cual recién llegados de un vapor armado partieron de inmediato con sus estados mayores hacia Santiago de los Caballeros, y el gobierno permitirá la libre entrada y circulación de moneda extranjera sin restricciones e iniciará el retiro de billetes bancarios el 17 de agosto. Bajo el título "Plans of the Revolutionists", un parte desde Kingston, Jamaica, del 11 de agosto transmite un informe por correo desde San Domingo del 3 de agosto vía Hayti que describe a hombres prominentes civiles y militares saliendo a campaña tras Jiminez, a quien se espera pronto desde Cuba con pertrechos de guerra, mientras los generales Ramon Pacheco y Pablo Reyes marchan hacia el oeste con seguidores armados que incluyen soldados regulares para aislar a Monte Christi de refuerzos y unirse a los insurgentes de Hayti. El despacho añade que la revolución debe su popularidad al nombre de Gomez y que, si este declina la presidencia o Jiminez se opone finalmente a su elección, los líderes contemplan un plebiscito para renovar el voto de 1871 por la anexión estadounidense o un protectorado estadounidense antes que elegir a otro dictador.
