records.summary_en: The *San Francisco Call* reported that pressure was mounting in Washington for President Roosevelt to establish an American protectorate over the Dominican Republic to end persistent revolutionary instability. While Secretary of State Hay opposed such an intervention, President Roosevelt was considering steps to protect American commercial investments, though final decisions awaited ratification of the Panama Canal treaty. The report highlighted that six American, German, and French warships were guarding foreign interests, with European governments receptive to American measures restoring order.
records.summary_es: El *San Francisco Call* informó que crecía la presión en Washington para que el presidente Roosevelt estableciera un protectorado estadounidense sobre la República Dominicana a fin de terminar con la constante inestabilidad revolucionaria. Aunque el secretario de Estado Hay se oponía a dicha intervención, el presidente Roosevelt consideraba medidas para proteger las inversiones comerciales estadounidenses, si bien las decisiones definitivas aguardaban la ratificación del tratado del Canal de Panamá. El informe subrayó que seis buques de guerra estadounidenses, alemanes y franceses custodiaban los intereses extranjeros, mostrándose los gobiernos europeos receptivos ante medidas estadounidenses que restablecieran el orden.

records.summary_en: A dispatch from Monte Cristi dated February 6 reports that the Clyde Line steamship New-York arrived that morning followed by the Dominican gunboat Presidente, and that when lighters went out to bring ashore ammunition forming part of her cargo, the gunboat fired on them and the revolutionists on shore replied with cannon and Mausers. The New-York left for Puerto Plata, the gunboat was hit twice by round shot and by many bullets during half an hour of firing, and the failure to land the ammunition is called a serious blow to General Jiminez, whose attack on Santiago de los Caballeros had been fixed for Sunday.
records.summary_es: Un despacho desde Monte Cristi fechado el 6 de febrero informa que el vapor New-York de la línea Clyde llegó esa mañana seguido por el cañonero dominicano Presidente, y que cuando las lanchas salieron a traer a tierra municiones que formaban parte de su carga, el cañonero disparó contra ellas y los revolucionarios en la costa respondieron con cañones y fusiles Mauser. El New-York partió hacia Puerto Plata, el cañonero fue alcanzado dos veces por balas de cañón y por muchas balas de fusil durante media hora de tiroteo, y el fracaso en desembarcar las municiones se califica como un golpe serio para el general Jiminez, cuyo ataque a Santiago de los Caballeros estaba fijado para el domingo.
records.passage: the cruisers Montgomery and Detroit, now at Culebra, have been ordered from there to Porto Plata. The Clyde Liner New-York Fails to Land Cargo at Monte Christi. Monte Christi, Santo Domingo, Feb. 6. — The Clyde Line steamship New-York, which sailed from New-York on January 30, arrived here this morning. It was followed by the Dominican gunboat Presidente. Lighters were sent alongside the New-York, to bring ashore some ammunition, which formed part of her cargo. When the lighters had nearly reached the steamship the gunboat fired on them, and the revolutionists on shore replied with cannon and Mausers. Being in danger, the New-York thereupon left Monte Christi for Porto Plata. The firing continued for half an hour, after which the gunboat sailed for Porto Plata. She was hit twice by round shot, and apparently by many bullets, for she stopped and lowered boats, evidently to plug the holes made in her hull. The failure to land the ammunition is a serious blow to General Jiménez, for whom it was intended, and may cause him to lose the ground he had already gained. An attack on Santiago de los Caballeros had been fixed for Sunday.

records.headline: A United States naval report tells of the commander going aboard the Newark to interview General Morales after a charge
records.summary_en: A United States naval report tells of the commander going aboard the Newark to interview General Morales after a charge that Morales had violated asylum granted by the American consular agent at Samana to two men; Morales replied the men were taken not from the consulate but from a farm outside the town belonging to the agent, and the commander warned him to respect the American flag and consulate. The report also covers Morales's decree closing Monte Cristi and Macoris, the firing on the Clyde liner New-York's lighters at Monte Cristi and the agreement to deposit her cargo at Puerto Plata, and the insurgents holding La Vega and the southeastern peninsula while Santo Domingo City is closely invested by about 1,200 men.
records.summary_es: Un informe naval de los Estados Unidos relata que el comandante subió a bordo del Newark para entrevistar al general Morales tras la acusación de que Morales había violado el asilo concedido por el agente consular americano en Samana a dos hombres; Morales respondió que los hombres no fueron tomados del consulado sino de una finca fuera de la ciudad perteneciente al agente, y el comandante le advirtió que respetara la bandera y el consulado americanos. El informe también cubre el decreto de Morales que cerró Monte Cristi y Macoris, los disparos contra las lanchas del vapor New-York de la línea Clyde en Monte Cristi y el acuerdo de depositar su carga en Puerto Plata, y que los insurgentes ocupan La Vega y la península del sureste mientras la ciudad de Santo Domingo está estrechamente sitiada por unos 1,200 hombres.

records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported allegations by General Francisco Leonte Vásquez that Dominican insurgents deliberately targeted Americans to provoke armed United States intervention. Vásquez claimed government troops discovered incriminating letters at Santiago de los Caballeros written by revolutionary Governor Desiderio Arias to rebel leader Juan Isidro Jimenes. According to Vásquez, these documents explained the deadly attack on machinist Johnson of the USS *Yankee* and the gunfire directed against the American steamer *New York*.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* informó sobre las denuncias formuladas por el general Francisco Leonte Vásquez en el sentido de que los insurgentes dominicanos atacaban deliberadamente a estadounidenses para provocar una intervención armada de los Estados Unidos. Vásquez afirmó que las tropas del gobierno hallaron cartas incriminatorias en Santiago de los Caballeros escritas por el gobernador revolucionario Desiderio Arias al líder rebelde Juan Isidro Jimenes. Según Vásquez, estos documentos explicaban el ataque mortal contra el maquinista Johnson del USS *Yankee* y los disparos dirigidos contra el vapor estadounidense *New York*.

WANT U. S. TO INTERVENE. Statement of General Vasquez as to San Domingo Insurrectionists.

That the Dominican insurrectionists are waging a war against Americans and American Interests for the express purpose of causing the intervention of the United States In the affairs of San Domingo was the direct accusation made yesterday by General Francisco Leonte Vasquez, who has just returned to this city from the scene of conflict. He brings with him, he says, documentary proof in substantiation of his assertions, and [in?] these might be found the explanation for the killing of the machinist, Johnson, of the United States gunboat Yankee, and the firing on the Clyde Line steamer New-York by the revolutionists. The documents on which General Vasquez bases his charges are two letters addressed to General Juan Isidro Jiménez, chief of the rebellion, by General Desiderio Arias, one of his subordinates, which were intercepted at Santiago de los Caballeros by the government army, of which General Vasquez was in command until a few weeks ago.

records.summary_en: The *Wahpeton Times* reported that Captain Miller of the USS *Columbia* refused to permit Dominican President Morales to blockade domestic ports against American shipping after the gunboat *Presidente* turned away the American schooner *W. R. Perkins*. In San Pedro de Macorís, insurgents seized and armed the Clyde Line tugboat *Burro*, while the steamer *Cherokee* received a naval convoy from the USS *Hartford*. The report also noted domestic arrests and the deportation of several Dominican political figures to Cuba.
records.summary_es: El *Wahpeton Times* informó que el capitán Miller, del USS *Columbia*, se negó a permitir que el presidente dominicano Morales bloqueara los puertos nacionales al comercio marítimo estadounidense, luego de que el cañonero *Presidente* rechazara a la goleta estadounidense *W. R. Perkins*. En San Pedro de Macorís, los insurgentes incautaron y artillaron el remolcador *Burro* de la Clyde Line, mientras que el vapor *Cherokee* recibió escolta naval del USS *Hartford*. El informe dio cuenta asimismo de detenciones internas y de la deportación de varias figuras políticas dominicanas hacia Cuba.

President Morales, of the Dominican republic, has been refused permission to blockade his own ports to keep out the revolutionists, as shown by the following report, to the navy department by Capt. James E. Miller, commanding the cruiser Columbia: "This morning (Feb. 18) the American three-masted schooner W. R. Perkins came in from the eastward and our boarding boat went alongside. The captain informed me that he had been warned off Macoris and not allowed to enter by the gunboat Presidente, and was told that he must proceed to this port. "Immediately upon receipt of this information I communicated with the minister, requesting him to communicate with President Morales and inform him that I would not recognize his right to blockade Macoris and refuse entrance to vessels flying the American flag. The minister informs me that the president demurred at first, but finally agreed to the fact." Rebels Seize American Tug. San Domingo. March 3. United States Minister Powell has been informed that the insurgents at San Pedro de Macoris have seized the tug boat Burro, belonging to the Clyde line of New York, and armed her. The Clyde line steamer Cherokee has gone to Azua de Compostela, convoyed by the United States training ship Hartford. Many arrests have been made here and several politicians were sent out of the country yesterday on board the steamer Julia of the Cuba line. Edward C. records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* recounted political maneuvers during President Buenaventura Báez's historical efforts to annex the Dominican Republic to the United States. The account recalled how Báez jailed political opponents to guarantee passage of the treaty until an American politician persuaded him that a small dissenting vote would look less suspicious. It also detailed an earlier attempt to lease Samana Bay surveyed by Captain George B. McClellan, which collapsed when British and French warships arrived to oppose American acquisition.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* relató las maniobras políticas durante las gestiones históricas del presidente Buenaventura Báez para anexionar la República Dominicana a los Estados Unidos. La crónica recordó cómo Báez encarceló a opositores políticos para asegurar la aprobación del tratado hasta que un político estadounidense lo convenció de que una pequeña votación disidente resultaría menos sospechosa. Detalló asimismo una tentativa anterior para arrendar la bahía de Samaná, inspeccionada por el capitán George B. McClellan, la cual fracasó al llegar buques de guerra británicos y franceses para oponerse a la adquisición estadounidense.

When the report reached the ears of a prominent New-York politician who was at the Dominican Capitol, and who was greatly interested in the treaty, he went at once to Baez and remonstrated:

“Jail methods will ruin the whole business,” he said. “This thing must be done on the square, or it will fall through.” Baez at first shrugged his shoulders, and when he did speak he only said: “But you want it unanimous, don't you? “Not at all. A unanimous vote always creates suspicion. A small minority vote gives a far better impression.” “All right.” said Baez. “You can have that. Anything you want you can have in San Domingo.” Baez summoned several representatives, and there was a hurried conference. The treaty was passed with a “small minority.” Twenty years before the failure of this annexation scheme this government made a treaty with San Domingo to rent in perpetuity the great sheltered Bay of Samana. The father of the present Mayor of New-York accompanied the commission sent to negotiate for the territory, and Captain McClellan, as he was known then, made a survey of that part of the Dominican coast. Just before the treaty could be ratified, however, news of its purpose leaked out. England and France both took alarm, and dispatched warships to Samana Bay. At the sight of European cannon the San Domingo statesmen forgot all about the treaty.

records.full_text:
U. S. RECEIVERSHIP FOR SANTO DOMINGO

The Novel Scheme Which Roosevelt Will Probably Put Into Effect—Island Would Have Been Annexed to This Country in 1869 But for the Opposition of Chas. Sumner.

By Jacob Waldeck.
WASHINGTON, Jan. 10.—Santo Domingo, torn by revolution, misgoverned and despoiled, is soon to feel the chastening influence of "the big stick." A century of turmoil, bloodshed, robbery and disorder is to be terminated by the intervention of the United States.

Officials of the highest rank in the administration say that such action is inevitable. President Roosevelt is said, on the best authority, to hold that view of the case. It is a question of time, but of months, rather than years. American officials and American marines will inaugurate a reign of good order and a season of debt-paying in the country.

They don't call it that in diplomatic language, but the proposed order of things in Santo Domingo seems to be nothing more or less than a receivership. It will be

Something Brand New
in American history. The republic will bear a relation to this country unlike Porto Rico, which was annexed; unlike the Philippines, which were hitched on behind, and unlike Cuba, which is the object of a benevolent guardianship. Santo Domingo is to be regulated. It is to be told to pay its debts and be good.

The plan is to place men in the custom houses to collect the revenue of the country. They are to see that a fair share of this money goes to the creditors, and that public officials, instead of looting the public treasury, conduct the government on an economical basis. One custom house, that of Puerto Plata, is now in the hands of an American as a result of arbitration, last summer, over a claim of $5,000,000 owned by New Yorkers. They advanced a lot of money about 10 years ago and took a blanket mortgage on the government. The proceeds at Puerto Plata are being devoted to their claim.

Opinion as to the new deal is divided among the people. Creditors, business men and most of the people of the cities favor it. Those living in the interior are, as a rule, opposed to foreign interference. So are the insurgent chiefs, who fear that a settled order of things may interfere with the revolution industry and keep them from digging their hands into the treasury.

A Land of Chaos.
In the past the order of things has been very much unsettled. The country has been in a chronic state of revolution. There have been nearly a dozen presidents in five years.

From the standpoint of novelty it would seem that the people ought to welcome a receivership. The country has had autocratic, monarchial and republican forms of government. It has also had no government; there having been prolonged seasons of anarchy. Te people have been ruled by despots, emperors and presidents. Mostly despots, though, for whatever the title of the man who happened to be ruling for a short period, he has usually paid no attention to law. Men whom he hasn't liked he has caused to be shot. Any money lying around that he fancied he has appropriated. If money was scarce he negotiated loans at extravagant rates from foreigners. The lenders got Chadwick rates in the way of interest and bonuses, and could rest serene in the fact that when the day for settlement came their governments would force San Domingo to pay.

Another class of men who may embarrass the administration, when intervention takes place, are now flocking to Santo Domingo. They are "investors." A lot of them, Americans, are going over to the republic from Porto Rico. They

Scent Rich Profits
and are eager to be early on the ground. Tehir option is to pick up property at anarchy rates and sell at prices incident to American rule. Santo Domingo, in its climate and resources, has been described by all travelers who have visited the country as one of the most attractive and richest spots in the world. It has not been developed because for 100 years there has been little or no respect for personal or property rights. As a result of this condition it has been possible for years to buy the best of sugar land and land covered with magnificent forests at a nominal price. A good many Americans have taken advantage of the opportunity. They have made no attempt to develop their holdings, but have patiently awaited the day when order should be restored in the country. Others are now crowding in to get the benefit of the bargains offered. They are confident that this country will, in some form, soon enforce order, and they are equally confident that when the United States finally withdraws it will exact guarantees for the protection of their interests.

Came Close to Annexation.
The question of adding the territory of the republic to the United States has been raised at intervals for half a century. It confronted Lincoln in the closing days of the civil war, but he was busy with bigger problems, and consigned it to a pigeonhole. Grant took it up in 1869. Men contended in those days that Santo Domingo would be a more valuable acquisition than Cuba, Haiti or Porto Rico. The fine climate, valuable forests, rich soil, sparse population and small public debt were all said to be in its favor. At that time the debt to be assumed by this country would have been only $1,500,000. Now it would be $32,000,000, secured by Dominican bonds, while Spain would put in a claim for other millions that, the dons say, they were to receive if the republic should ever, by consent of its people, become annexed to another country.

De B. Randolph Keim, a Pennsylvania editor who is also an official of the bureau of insular affairs, brought the first proposition of annexation to this country. He went to the island in 1869 as the correspondent of a New York newspaper.

records.summary_en: The *Springfield Weekly Republican* argued that foreign capitalists and commercial planters in the Dominican Republic actively encouraged political unrest to terminate indigenous rule. It cited State Department admissions that American firms had supplied money and weapons to opposing Dominican factions while simultaneously petitioning Washington for naval protection. The editorial noted that President Morales, having secured power through United States naval support, signed the customs receivership agreement to align with foreign property interests.
records.summary_es: El *Springfield Weekly Republican* sostuvo que los capitalistas y hacendados comerciales extranjeros en la República Dominicana fomentaban activamente la inestabilidad política para poner fin al gobierno autóctono. Citó admisiones del Departamento de Estado respecto a que firmas estadounidenses habían suministrado dinero y armas a facciones dominicanas rivales mientras pedían simultáneamente protección naval a Washington. El editorial señaló que el presidente Morales, habiendo asegurado el poder mediante el apoyo naval estadounidense, firmó el acuerdo de administración aduanera para alinearse con los intereses de los propietarios extranjeros.

The Dominican planters and all the foreign capitalists concerned in the republic have had a strong economic object in bringing the native rule to a close. There is, indeed, reason for thinking that the frequent revolutions of late years have been secretly encouraged, and even fomented in part, by the foreign interests.. For proof of this, we may quote what appeared on March 16 last in the Washington Star, the paragraph having all the appearance of being inspired by the state department. “It is admitted at the ‘state department," said the Star, “that ‘some representations have been made in a ‘forcible way to American firms and indi ‘viduals having an interest in San Domingo ‘that they have small ground for complaint ‘of revolutionary disturbances affecting •their interests unfavorably so long as they themselves are in the. habit of furnishing •arms, ammunition and money to both sides •engaged in this fratricidal strife.” It is necessary to point out, also, that President Morales, now the head of the Dominican government, who has voluntarily, it appears, signed the agreement for the American receivership, represents the property interests of the republic more than his late opponents did. records.summary_en: The *Springfield Weekly Republican* detailed the finalized protocol providing for American administration of Dominican customs until foreign creditor claims were settled. The modified convention affirmed the Monroe Doctrine, guaranteed Dominican territorial integrity, and allotted 45 percent of gross customs revenues directly to the Dominican government for its operating budget. The agreement stipulated that future tariff modifications required approval from the President of the United States and prohibited increases in the national public debt.

La convención modificada reafirmaba la Doctrina Monroe, garantizaba la integridad territorial dominicana y asignaba el 45 por ciento de los ingresos aduaneros brutos directamente al gobierno dominicano para su presupuesto operativo. El acuerdo estipulaba que las futuras modificaciones arancelarias requerían la aprobación del presidente de los Estados Unidos y prohibía cualquier incremento de la deuda pública nacional.

records.headline: This editorial examines the legal basis claimed for American customs operations in Santo Domingo, centered on the arbitration
records.summary_en: This editorial examines the legal basis claimed for American customs operations in Santo Domingo, centered on the arbitration award of July 14, 1904, which authorized the United States Financial Agent to extend his control to Monte Cristi, Sanchez and Samana if the collections at Puerto Plata proved insufficient to meet the monthly installment of $37,500 payable under the award. Morgan said Cromwell acted to frustrate the Reader syndicate's plan for Dominican concessions and to promote a syndicate holding a mass of claims against Latin-American republics, including a large part of the Dominican debt; the Senate was divided over whether he made his case, and the treaty was expected to be recommitted without a vote.

records.summary_en: The *Washington Times* reported on the private negotiations conducted by Mr. Reader, whose wife had sought to act as Dominican fiscal agent to negotiate the sale of Samana Bay and settle foreign debts. Although President Morales initially favored the private proposals, United States Minister Dawson instructed Dominican authorities on January 9 to terminate talks with Reader and deal exclusively with Washington. Following the arrival of Commander Dillingham on an American gunboat, official state negotiations commenced, prompting Reader to abandon his mission and return to New York.

Aunque el presidente Morales favoreció en un principio las propuestas privadas, el ministro estadounidense Dawson instruyó a las autoridades dominicanas el 9 de enero para que cesaran las conversaciones con Reader y trataran exclusivamente con Washington. records.headline: A travel narrative follows the old Camino Real, the royal road running 150 miles north from Santo Domingo City to Cotui
records.summary_en: A travel narrative follows the old Camino Real, the royal road running 150 miles north from Santo Domingo City to Cotui, La Vega and Moca, describing the ancient Spanish roads as broad paths cut a hundred feet wide through the forest, with no ditching, drainage, macadam or bridges, and the Isabella River crossed in native dugout canoes while the horses swim. It describes the savanna country of red clay loam and an inland town, Savanna Grande, as a row of one-story palm-wood huts thatched with palm leaves around a green central square, and the travelers' night stop at the home of Don Emiliano Tejera, a wealthy power in Dominican politics housed in thatched native houses with dirt floors.
records.summary_es: Una crónica de viaje sigue el viejo Camino Real, la vía real que corre 150 millas al norte desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo hasta Cotuí, La Vega y Moca, describiendo los antiguos caminos españoles como senderos anchos abiertos de cien pies a través del bosque, sin zanjas, drenaje, macadán ni puentes, y el río Isabela cruzado en canoas nativas de un solo tronco mientras los caballos nadan. Describe la región de sabana de arcilla roja y un pueblo del interior, Sabana Grande, como una fila de chozas de un piso de madera de palma techadas con hojas de palma alrededor de una plaza central verde, y la parada nocturna de los viajeros en la casa de don Emiliano Tejera, un hombre rico y poderoso en la política dominicana alojado en casas nativas de techo de palma y piso de tierra.

records.headline: A feature calls Santo Domingo the garden of the western tropics, with soil for cocoa, tobacco, tropical fruits
records.summary_en: A feature calls Santo Domingo the garden of the western tropics, with soil for cocoa, tobacco, tropical fruits, sugar cane, coffee, vanilla and rubber, mahogany forests in its mountainous interior, and constant verdure, and says that freed from its financial incubus it need not lag behind its sister republics. It then traces the career of President Carlos F. Morales, born at Puerto Plata to a prosperous merchant's family, ordained a priest after seminary study, who renounced the priesthood after eight years, edited an opposition newspaper, was arrested and narrowly escaped being shot, lived through revolt and exile, served in Congress and as governor of Puerto Plata, and last year headed the movement that drove out Jiminez and Wos y Gil and assumed control, proclaiming an election for next June.
records.summary_es: Un reportaje llama a Santo Domingo el jardín de los trópicos occidentales, con suelo para cacao, tabaco, frutas tropicales, caña de azúcar, café, vainilla y caucho, bosques de caoba en su interior montañoso y verdor constante, y dice que libre de su peso financiero no tiene por qué quedarse atrás de sus repúblicas hermanas. Después recorre la carrera del presidente Carlos F. Morales, nacido en Puerto Plata en la familia de un comerciante próspero, ordenado sacerdote tras estudiar en un seminario, quien renunció al sacerdocio después de ocho años, editó un periódico de oposición, fue arrestado y escapó por poco de ser fusilado, vivió entre revueltas y exilios, sirvió en el Congreso y como gobernador de Puerto Plata, y el año pasado encabezó el movimiento que expulsó a Jiminez y a Wos y Gil y asumió el control, proclamando una elección para el próximo junio.

records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch reports that, to thwart a revolutionary movement at Macoris against President Morales of Santo Domingo, the State Department has asked the Navy Department to send a warship to that port, and instructions were telegraphed to Rear Admiral Bradford at Guantanamo. records.summary_en: The *Birmingham Age-Herald* criticized President Roosevelt for enforcing the unratified Dominican customs treaty through executive action, using warships to protect Customs Receiver George R. Colton. The editorial argued that neither Roosevelt nor President Morales held constitutional authority to bind their nations without legislative approval, and warned the policy risked committing the United States to guaranteeing debts throughout Spanish America. The article predicted that Senate Democrats would firmly oppose ratification, noting rumors that the administration might seek a congressional joint resolution to validate the receivership.
records.summary_es: El *Birmingham Age-Herald* criticó al presidente Roosevelt por aplicar el tratado aduanero dominicano no ratificado mediante una acción ejecutiva, empleando buques de guerra para proteger al receptor de aduanas George R. Colton. El editorial sostenía que ni Roosevelt ni el presidente Morales tenían autoridad constitucional para comprometer a sus naciones sin aprobación legislativa, y advertía del riesgo de que esta política comprometiera a los Estados Unidos a garantizar deudas en toda Hispanoamérica. El artículo vaticinaba que los demócratas en el Senado se opondrían con firmeza a la ratificación, señalando rumores de que el gobierno intentaría obtener una resolución conjunta del Congreso para validar la administración aduanera.

records.summary_en: The *Free Lance* reported on the repressive governance of Dominican President Morales, stating he had executed approximately 200 political opponents and maintained a coded blacklist of prominent citizens. Meanwhile, the State Department in Washington announced a policy of non-intervention in internal Dominican strife, regarding the conflict as domestic as long as foreign interests remained safe. Officials cautioned, however, that the United States would intervene militarily if violence threatened American lives or interfered with customs collections.

Entretanto, el Departamento de Estado en Washington anunció una política de no intervención en las disputas internas dominicanas, considerando el conflicto como doméstico mientras los intereses extranjeros estuvieran a salvo. No obstante, los funcionarios advirtieron que los Estados Unidos intervendrían militarmente si la violencia amenazaba vidas estadounidenses o interfería con la recaudación de aduanas.

records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported on impending military clashes at Santiago between forces loyal to provisional President Ramón Cáceres and rebel units allied with former President Jimenes and fugitive President Morales. An American observer arriving from Monte Cristi, Hugh M. Creighton, asserted that the United States should sustain Morales, arguing the conflict erupted because Morales refused financial demands from Cáceres's political faction. Creighton noted that the 45 percent customs revenue allocated by the American receivership adequately met lawful state expenses but left no funds for political patronage.

Creighton, afirmó que los Estados Unidos debían respaldar a Morales, argumentando que el conflicto estalló porque este rechazó las demandas financieras de la facción política de Cáceres. Creighton señaló que el 45 por ciento de los ingresos de aduanas asignado por la administración estadounidense cubría adecuadamente los gastos legítimos del Estado, pero no dejaba fondos para el clientelismo político.

TALE ON SANTO DOMINGO. “Morales Represents Best Element on Island,” Says Observer. Hugh M. Creighton arrived on the steamer [Seminole?], from Monte Cristi, Santo Domingo. Mr. Creighton said:

I was in Santo Domingo three weeks, and was in constant contact with all classes of Dominicans. I became convinced that, unless the government at Washington asserts itself promptly, and with a firm hand sustains President Morales, who is still the constitutional head of the government, the prestige of the United States, with the best element on the island, which is being dissipated by delay, will entirely disappear. The present trouble, as I learned from business men, grows out of the inability of President Morales to respond to the demands made on him by the faction headed by Vice-President Caceres for money. The 4 per cent that is derived from the customs collections, under the supervision of the United States agent, is sufficient for all the legitimate needs of the government, but it affords no margin out of which to pay levies that may be made by political ‘‘grafters.”

records.summary_en: The *Springfield Weekly Republican* reported that former President Juan Isidro Jimenes traveled to Monte Cristi to seek the presidency with the backing of fugitive President Morales and broad northern support. The paper profiled insurgent leader General Demetrio Rodríguez, an American-educated commander who had previously controlled customs revenues in Monte Cristi before being defeated by General Céspedes. It noted that Céspedes, originally a key supporter of Morales, had turned against the president in fierce opposition to the fiscal convention with the United States.

El periódico reseñó al líder insurgente, general Demetrio Rodríguez, un militar educado en los Estados Unidos que anteriormente había controlado los ingresos de aduanas en Monte Cristi antes de ser derrotado por el general Céspedes. Señaló además que Céspedes, quien en un principio fue un firme partidario de Morales, se volvió contra el mandatario en feroz oposición a la convención fiscal con los Estados Unidos.

According to the reports brought to Cape Haytien by messengers, a large part of the population of northern San Domingo is in Favor of Gen Jiminez. Gen Demetrio Rodriguez had long been a prominent factor in the affairs of San Domingo. He was a graduate of Fordham college. New York, spoke English fluently, and was described as an affable and scholarly man and a born leader of men. He resided about 25 miles from Monte Christi; and was considered to be one of the most formidable of Morales's opponents. At the close of the last revolution Rodriguez only consented to lay down his arms under the promise of being allowed to collect the customs and other revenues in the province of Monte Christi. Gen Cespedes, who defeated Gen Rodriguez, was one of the leading men in the movement which placed Morales in the presidential chair of San Domingo, but Cespedes quarreled with Morales on account of the latter's transactions with the American government, and when the enemies of Morales became active Cespedes hastened to join issue with them in their opposition to the Morales government and the fiscal agreement between the United States and San Domingo.

records.summary_en: The *Springfield Weekly Republican* published an interview from San Juan with ousted Dominican President Carlos F. Morales, who affirmed that national salvation depended on the ratification of the pending customs convention by both nations. Morales noted that while provisional President Cáceres and various rebel factions had come to endorse the convention, political stability remained precarious under Cáceres's minority government. Morales recounted suffering a fractured ankle when a vine rope broke while scaling a cliff during his escape from the Dominican capital.

Morales, quien afirmó que la salvación nacional dependía de la ratificación de la convención aduanera pendiente por ambas naciones. Morales señaló que, si bien el presidente provisional Cáceres y varias facciones rebeldes habían llegado a respaldar la convención, la estabilidad política continuaba siendo precaria bajo el gobierno minoritario de Cáceres. Morales relató que sufrió una fractura de tobillo al romperse una cuerda vegetal mientras escalaba un risco durante su huida de la capital dominicana.

records.summary_en: A dispatch from Cape Haitien on January 16 reports a bloody and probably final battle near Guayubin, where the troops of General Caceres, temporary president of San Domingo, defeated the insurgents, with several generals on both sides killed or wounded. Former president Morales, interviewed at San Juan, said the future salvation of Santo Domingo depends entirely on ratification of the pending convention by the United States Senate and the Dominican congress.

records.summary_en: The *Stark County Democrat* reported on a Senate speech by Senator Benjamin Tillman condemning President Roosevelt's Dominican policy and the enforcement of the unratified customs treaty. Tillman criticized the administration for prioritizing European bondholders and ridiculed the executive *modus vivendi* as an unconstitutional usurpation of Senate authority. Warning against imperial expansion, Tillman asserted that unless the Senate firmly rejected the administration's actions, the United States would permanently dominate and occupy Santo Domingo.

records.summary_en: The *Springfield Weekly Republican* reported that a peace treaty ending the Dominican insurrection was signed aboard the United States cruiser *Yankee* at Monte Cristi. Foreign Minister Emiliano Tejera stated that the rapid restoration of peace was made possible by decisive military action and the American financial *modus vivendi*, which deprived the insurgents of customs revenues. Under the capitulation terms, Monte Cristi returned to government control, rebel General Desiderio Arias was permitted to go into exile in Puerto Rico, and remaining insurgents were granted amnesty.
records.summary_es: El *Springfield Weekly Republican* informó que se firmó a bordo del crucero estadounidense *Yankee*, en Monte Cristi, un tratado de paz que puso fin a la insurrección dominicana. El ministro de Relaciones Exteriores Emiliano Tejera declaró que el rápido restablecimiento de la paz fue posible gracias a la enérgica acción militar y al *modus vivendi* financiero estadounidense, que privó a los insurgentes de las rentas aduaneras. Bajo los términos de la capitulación, Monte Cristi volvió al control del gobierno, se le permitió al general rebelde Desiderio Arias exiliarse en Puerto Rico y se concedió amnistía a los insurgentes restantes.
records.passage: TREATY OF PEACE SIGNED. [illegible] of the Failure of the San Domingo Revolution. A treaty of peace between the insurgent generals at Monte Cristi and the government was signed Wednesday last week on board the American cruiser Yankee, says a dispatch from San Domingo. Monte Cristi is now in the hands of the constitutional government forces. Emiliano [Tejera?], minister of foreign affairs, said to the Associated Press Wednesday: “I attribute the prompt collapse of the insurrection to the vigor of the government's military operations, to the financial modus vivendi which restrained the revolutionists from seizing the custom-houses, and to the fact that the government is a constitutional one.” The Dominican government in receiving the surrender of Monte Cristi permitted the revolutionary governor, Gen Arias, to depart for Porto Rico, and granted general amnesty to the other revolutionists. records.headline: Herald correspondence from Santo Domingo, dated March 3, reports that General Ramon Caceres will not resign the presidency
records.summary_en: Herald correspondence from Santo Domingo, dated March 3, reports that General Ramon Caceres will not resign the presidency, because a change of administration would involve internal disturbances, and that the demand for him to remain was almost universal. His cousin Horacio Valdez, head of the Horacist party and the man in whose favor Caceres wished to withdraw, was the first to urge him to reconsider, and after petitions and a mass meeting in Columbus plaza a crowd marched to Caceres's house, where he told them he would postpone his resignation until the danger to the republic ceased, later issuing a public address accepting what he called the new sacrifice.
records.summary_es: Una correspondencia del Herald desde Santo Domingo, fechada el 3 de marzo, informa que el general Ramón Cáceres no renunciará a la presidencia, porque un cambio de administración implicaría disturbios internos, y que la demanda de que permaneciera fue casi universal. Su primo Horacio Valdez, jefe del partido horacista y la persona en cuyo favor Cáceres deseaba retirarse, fue el primero en instarlo a reconsiderarlo, y tras las peticiones y una reunión masiva en la plaza Colón una multitud marchó a la casa de Cáceres, donde les dijo que pospondría su renuncia hasta que cesara el peligro para la república, y después emitió un mensaje público aceptando lo que llamó el nuevo sacrificio.

records.summary_en: The Evening Times published a statement from Dominican revolutionists detailing their aims to reform land taxes, modify tariffs, eliminate export duties, and establish habeas corpus protections. The statement asserted that Generals Morales and Jimenez had reached an understanding, while former President Horacio Vasquez had deserted President Caceres. It also alleged that Dominican Minister of Finance Federico Velasquez was seeking to secure half of the $1,300,000 deposited for foreign creditors to fund government war expenses.

El manifiesto aseguraba que los generales Morales y Jimenes habían alcanzado un entendimiento, mientras que el expresidente Horacio Vásquez había abandonado al presidente Cáceres. Alegaba además que el ministro de Hacienda dominicano Federico Velásquez procuraba asegurarse la mitad de los 1.300.000 dólares depositados para los acreedores extranjeros con el propósito de costear los gastos bélicos del gobierno.

It is our purpose, if we are victorious, as I am certain we shall be, to establish land taxes, modify the tariff and remove the pernicious export duties, which retard the progress of our industries. We also want the right of habeas corpus, which is unknown in our country. As matters are, the government puts in Jail and exiles citizens without any process of law. records.summary_en: The Evening Star reported that Dominican representative Mr. Joubert conferred in Washington with Dr. Hollander and other U.S. officials regarding the situation in Santo Domingo. Joubert dismissed reports of a major revolutionary uprising at Monte Cristi as rumors from enemies of President Caceres and denied claims that customs funds held by the United States would be divided before treaty ratification. Joubert and Dominican Finance Minister Velasquez planned to travel to New York, where Velasquez would study American institutions.

Joubert desestimó los informes sobre un gran levantamiento revolucionario en Monte Cristi calificándolos de rumores de los enemigos del presidente Cáceres, y negó que los fondos de aduanas custodiados por los Estados Unidos fueran a dividirse antes de la ratificación del tratado. Joubert y el ministro de Hacienda dominicano Velásquez planeaban viajar a Nueva York, donde Velásquez estudiaría las instituciones estadounidenses.

records.summary_en: The article reports a Dominican government proclamation for Monte Cristi province, countersigned by President Caceres, declaring that peace negotiations having failed, the government will end the war however violent and severe the means, placing the district under siege and threatening summary shooting even for women found carrying cartridges. Exiled revolutionist General Berroa, speaking in New York alongside ex-President Jiminez, called the decree simply despotic, said 700 to 1,000 well-armed revolutionists were in the field, and said the revolution would stop only when constitutional rights, political prisoners and the exiles were dealt with justly.
records.summary_es: El artículo informa de una proclama del gobierno dominicano para la provincia de Monte Cristi, refrendada por el presidente Cáceres, que declara que, habiendo fracasado las negociaciones de paz, el gobierno terminará la guerra por violentos y severos que sean los medios, pone el distrito en estado de sitio y amenaza con fusilamiento sumario incluso para las mujeres a las que se encuentren cartuchos. El general revolucionario exiliado Berroa, hablando en Nueva York junto al expresidente Jiménez, calificó el decreto de simplemente despótico, dijo que había entre 700 y 1,000 revolucionarios bien armados en campaña, y afirmó que la revolución solo cesaría cuando los derechos constitucionales, los presos políticos y los exiliados fueran tratados con justicia.

records.summary_en: The Evening Star detailed the financial provisions of the proposed Dominican treaty, outlining how customs revenues would cover receivership expenses, interest, bond amortization, and payments to the Dominican government. Collection costs were capped at five percent, with $100,000 monthly allocated to the loan's fiscal agent and annual collections over $3,000,000 applied to the sinking fund. The terms also prohibited the Dominican Republic from increasing its public debt or modifying import duties without the consent of the U.S. President.

records.summary_en: The New-York Tribune reported that the Dominican modus vivendi proved financially beneficial, resulting in $3,000,000 deposited in New York, increased revenues, four U.S.-built coastguard cutters, and reduced smuggling. records.full_text:
TREATY RATIFIED BY SAN DOMINGO

Departure in United States' Relations to Small Republics

CONTROLS CUSTOM HOUSE

United States Now Becomes Legally a Trustee In a Financial Sense.

Will Discourage Revolutions.

Santo Domingo, May 3.—The new treaty between the United States and Santo Domingo intended to replace the treaty which has been pending before the United States Senate for the last two years was ratified by the Dominican congress today.

The Dominican treaty marks a new departure from the relations of the United States to the smaller republics of the western hemisphere, for in the case of Santo Domingo the United States now becomes legally a trustee in a financial sense, and must go so far in the preservation of order and the accompanying discouragement of revolutions as is incident to the control of the custom house.

The treaty really had its birth in a revolution. While the American government was pressing for a settlement of the claims of its citizens against Santo Domingo in December, 1904, President Morales being beset by revolutionists in the hope of securing the moral support of the United States, entered into an agreement with Captain Dillingham of the American navy by which the Dominican custom houses were to be occupied by the Americans and the foreign indebtedness of the country discharged from the receipts. Rejected at Washington, this agreement gave place March 31, 1905, to a modus vivendi which has operated up to this time. This placed an American collector in charge and provided for the deposit in New York of 55 per cent of the customs receipts for the benefit of the Dominican creditors. The modus vivendi did not save Morales from political destruction, as he was deported by the revolutionists and his vice president, General Caceres, installed as president. But the modus vivendi did lead to the deposit in New York of $3,000,000 which will now be placed to the credit of the Dominican government. That government has had more available money since the modus vivendi was established than any other time in its history. The Dominican government also finds itself in possession of four coast guard cutters built in the United States.

The modus vivendi was formed after a treaty pending before the United States Senate when Secretary Root assumed office. He recast the document, and February 19, last, the treaty which has just been ratified was submitted to the Senate. The way had been paved by an agreement between Federico Velasquez, the Dominican minister of finance, and the creditors of the republic whereby the latter agreed to a 50 per cent reduction in their claims if these were settled in cash.

A New York banking house undertook to advance the money for this purpose, accepting $20,000,000 5 per cent fifty-year bonds, which will now be promptly issued. Thus all of the creditors of Santo Domingo will be embodied in this New York firm.

The new treaty provides in its first article for the appointment by the President of a receiver of customs to collect the Dominican revenues as long as the bonds are outstanding, a period estimated at twenty to forty years. This collector is to pay the expenses of receivership, the interest on the bonds and the annual sums required for a mortization of the bonds, and then turn the balance over to the Dominican government. On the first day of each month he is to pay $100,000 to the fixed agent of the loan. When the customs receipts exceed $3,000,000 annually, then one-half of the surplus shall be applied to the sinking fund.

records.summary_en: The New-York Tribune reported on an interview with the former Dominican president, who described being detained in a palace during a visit to Port-au-Prince. He asserted that the era of Dominican revolutions had ended, praised President Caceres and the American customs receivership, but expressed firm opposition to annexation by the United States. He also stated his desire to return to Santo Domingo once a general amnesty was granted and recounted how political betrayal had forced his past flight.

Afirmó que la era de las revoluciones dominicanas había concluido, elogió al presidente Cáceres y a la receptoría de aduanas estadounidense, pero manifestó su firme oposición a una anexión por parte de los Estados Unidos. Declaró además su deseo de regresar a Santo Domingo tan pronto se concediera una amnistía general y relató cómo la traición política había forzado su huida en el pasado.

in any capacity. records.summary_en: The New-York Tribune reported Consul General Medina's statement announcing the surrender of Dominican insurgent General Candelario de la Rosa and the pacification of refractory districts. Medina asserted that American revenue administration had restored national credit, enabling debt payments and attracting American capital into central pine forestry and railroad construction. He maintained that the government was fully prepared to counter any revolutionary efforts from Dominican exiles in Puerto Rico.

The consul general says that he has just received dispatches from Santo Domingo informing him of the surrender of General Candelario de la Rosa, who had for some time been giving the government trouble. He says that the hopes of the revolutionists are vain: that the government is prepared to meet every contingency, and that he is keeping a sharp watch on the Dominican exiles residing in Porto Rico. In referring to the actual condition in Santo Domingo, Consul General Medina makes the following statement:

At no time has the Dominican Republic been in such a favorable condition as at present. The fact that honest, strong and intelligent men are at the head of public affairs has raised the credit of the country. American control of the revenues has been the means of insuring a steady income, thus enabling the government not only to attend to its own needs but also to pay off the heavy debt that weighed down the country. With the assurance of lasting peace, capital is flowing into the republic. Within the last five or six months American companies have undertaken the tapping of the vast pine forests which cover the centre of the island, and the turpentine and lumber obtained will be a source of increased revenue. records.headline: A Washington report describes a new plan to settle the Dominican Republic's debt after the original bond sale to a New York firm
records.summary_en: A Washington report describes a new plan to settle the Dominican Republic's debt after the original bond sale to a New York firm fell through because of the money market. Foreign creditors recognized in the original project would receive an immediate pro rata cash payment from the $3,500,000 accumulated in the National City Bank from 55 per cent of the republic's customs revenues over two years, with the bond sale postponed or bonds issued directly by the Dominican government for the remainder, in a settlement to be discussed with Senor Velasquez at the State Department.
records.summary_es: Un informe de Washington describe un nuevo plan para saldar la deuda de la República Dominicana después de que la venta original de bonos a una firma de Nueva York fracasara por la situación del mercado monetario. Los acreedores extranjeros reconocidos en el proyecto original recibirían un pago inmediato en efectivo, a prorrata, del fondo de $3,500,000 acumulado en el National City Bank procedente del 55 por ciento de las rentas aduaneras de la república durante dos años, y la venta de bonos se pospondría o los bonos serían emitidos directamente por el gobierno dominicano por el resto, en un acuerdo que se discutiría con el señor Velásquez en el Departamento de Estado.

In consideration of this payment the sale of the bonds of the republic to some syndicate which will advance the cash to settle the remainder of the debt will be postponed until a more opportune time. A variation of this plan, which also will be considered by a conference to-morrow at the State Department between the officials and Senor Velasquez, the Dominican Secretary of Commerce and Finance, looks to the distribution of the accumulated cash as in the first case, but provides for the immediate issue to the creditors of bonds for the remainder of the obligation, which will be issued directly by the Dominican government. In either case it is contemplated that the Morton Trust Company and Speyer Co., who have acted as the fiscal agents for the Dominican government, will continue in that capacity and aid in carrying out the terms of the new agreement. records.summary_en: The New-York Tribune reported on a debt settlement plan proposed by Dominican Finance Minister Velasquez to distribute cash deposited in the National City Bank pro rata and issue $16,000,000 in forty-year 5 percent bonds to foreign creditors. With no New York banking syndicate willing to underwrite the liquidation directly, Velasquez hoped European and American claimants—including the Santo Domingo Improvement Company—would accept the arrangement. The report noted that the United States would continue collecting Dominican customs duties to service the bonds and maintain a sinking fund.

Al no hallarse ningún sindicato bancario neoyorquino dispuesto a suscribir la liquidación directamente, Velásquez esperaba que los acreedores europeos y estadounidenses —incluida la Santo Domingo Improvement Company— aceptaran el arreglo. No syndicate has been found in New York which cared to undertake the liquidating of the debt, but Señor Velasquez hopes that the creditors, in view of the cash payment he is prepared to offer and the gilt edge character of the securities, will accept his new proposition. The creditors include citizens of Belgium, France, Italy and the United States. The largest known American creditor is the Santo Domingo Improvement Company, with an adjudicated claim of $4,000,006. It is understood that a number of the foreign claims have been purchased by American bankers, and there is some suspicion that American interests have been at work to prevent the liquidation of this debt as originally planned, but it is hoped by the Dominican and American authorities that the new plan will be accepted by the creditors and that the entire liquidation may thus be accomplished. The United States, to all intents and purposes, will continue to collect the Dominican customs and supervise the payment of interest and the accumulation of a sinking fund to meet the maturity of the securities. records.summary_en: The New-York Tribune reported that the U.S. Secret Service arrested Giordani in New York, uncovering his role as the financial agent of a Haitian revolutionary movement under General Fermin. Giordani had previously contracted the printing of 1,500,000 "Deux Gourdes" banknotes, half of which had been stored in a New York warehouse after an earlier failed uprising. Federal authorities intervened to prevent the remaining currency from being shipped to finance active insurgent forces in Haiti.

UU. arrestó a Giordani en Nueva York, descubriendo su papel como agente financiero de un movimiento revolucionario haitiano encabezado por el general Fermin. Giordani había contratado previamente la impresión de 1.500.000 billetes de «Deux Gourdes», la mitad de los cuales se hallaban almacenados en un depósito neoyorquino tras un fracasado levantamiento anterior. Las autoridades federales intervinieron para impedir que el resto del papel moneda fuera despachado para financiar a fuerzas insurgentes activas en Haití.

According to such facts as can be learned apart from the formal wording of the complaint, Giordani has for five years resided for the greater portion of the time in New York as the financial representative of the Haytian revolutionary movement, and several years ago, after presenting proper authorization, had printed by the Hamilton Bank Note Company £1,500,000 of beautifully engraved and “yellow backed” “Doux Gourdes” bills of the proposed new Haytian government.

At the time one-half of this currency was sent to Hayti to pay off the insurgent troops then in the field, serving under General Fermin. But before the golden bills arrived in the southern republic the revolutionary movement had met with failure, and. according to information in the possession of the federal authorities, the consignment of revolutionary currency was burned upon its arrival. Since that time the other half of the money has reposed quietly in a New York warehouse. records.summary_en: The Semi-Weekly Herald reviewed the outcome of the 1905 Dominican customs arrangement instituted by President Roosevelt to avert foreign military intervention over unpaid debts. Despite initial domestic controversy and Senate delays over Roosevelt's executive authority, the system transferred 45 percent of collections to the Dominican government and 55 percent to debt liquidation. The paper noted that the policy achieved a total transformation in the country, stabilizing public finances and virtually eliminating civil insurrections.
records.summary_es: The Semi-Weekly Herald analizó los resultados del arreglo aduanero dominicano de 1905 instituido por el presidente Roosevelt para eludir una intervención militar extranjera por deudas impagas. Pese a la controversia nacional inicial y las demoras en el Senado en torno a las atribuciones ejecutivas de Roosevelt, el sistema transfirió el 45 por ciento de la recaudación al gobierno dominicano y el 55 por ciento a la liquidación de la deuda. El periódico destacó que esta política logró una transformación total en el país, estabilizando las finanzas públicas y eliminando prácticamente las insurrecciones civiles.
records.passage: outlook was apparently hopeless. San Domingo was deeply in debt, and as it had for some time previous ceased to meet obligations, its foreign creditors were clamoring for a settlement and were threatening to collect their claims by force. Realizing that something would have to be done to avert the dangerous complications which were manifestly impending, Mr. Roosevelt instituted negotiations which resulted in the execution in February, 1905, of an agreement whereby officials appointed by the United States government were to collect the customs' receipts and after paying 45 per cent of the same to the Dominican authorities were to apply the remaining [illegible] per cent to the liquidation of the outstanding indebtedness. It will not have been forgotten how bitterly the president was criticised for his action in the premises. He was charged with having exceeded the bounds of his constitutional powers and for months the ratification of the Dominican treaty was delayed by the obstructive tactics of the hostile minority in the senate. Kingston, Jamaica, Nov. 5.—A revolutionary Santo Domingo junta has established headquarters here, and this morning a sloop belonging to it took out clearance papers for Hayti. Her destination, however, is believed to be some point on the Dominican coast. On board the sloop are some of the principal revolutionary leaders. Attempts are being made here to charter a steamer in order to make a descent on Santo Domingo with a President Designate and his staff. ESTRADA DEFEATED. Zelaya's Forces Reported Moving on Rama.

Managua, Nicaragua, Nov. 4 (Delayed in transmission).—Government troops defeated the revolutionists in a sharp engagement to-day, many of General Estrada's followers being killed, wounded or captured. The government lost fifteen men, including General Castillo [Chamorro?]. President Zelaya's forces attacked the rebel general, Fornos Diaz, at Paso las Lajas, capturing that point, which had been defended by four hundred men. The rebels fled in the direction of Rama and were pursued. The above dispatch, which the correspondent was unable to get through yesterday, refers doubtless to the battle of Thursday, concerning which conflicting reports reached New Orleans and Washington. Sympathizers at New Orleans with the Nicaraguan rebels received advices saying that General Estrada was gaining ground and had taken Paso las Lajas. records.summary_en: The Evening Star detailed extensive public works and infrastructure projects advancing in the Dominican Republic, including the purchase and expansion of the Puerto Plata-Santiago railroad and new branch lines. The Dominican government reduced port fees, dredged the Ozama River, surveyed irrigation systems in Monte Cristi and Azua, and initiated macadamized highway construction between the capital and San Cristobal. The report lauded the country's economic potential, civic improvements, and the hospitality of its citizens.

El gobierno dominicano redujo las tasas portuarias, dragó el río Ozama, realizó estudios para sistemas de irrigación en Monte Cristi y Azua, e inició la construcción de una carretera macadamizada entre la capital y San Cristóbal. El informe alabó el potencial económico del país, sus mejoras urbanas y la hospitalidad de sus habitantes.

Taft noted that despite lower customs revenues caused by economic conditions and anticipated tariff revisions, debt service payments were maintained and burdensome private concessions were retired. The message also reviewed U.S. diplomatic interventions regarding corporate claims in Nicaragua and Chile.

El mensaje examinó además las intervenciones diplomáticas estadounidenses relativas a reclamaciones corporativas en Nicaragua y Chile.

records.headline: Wiping Out a Republic's Debt
records.summary_en: The Evening Journal reported on the fiscal success of American Customs Receiver W. E. Pulliam in the Dominican Republic, noting that his administration reduced tariffs by 15 percent by shifting tax burdens from necessities to luxuries. Customs receipts exceeded expectations and were projected to reach at least $3,000,000 for the year, far surpassing the required $2,000,000 benchmark. The report asserted that backing from the U.S. Navy had suppressed revolutionary attempts and held up the Dominican financial system as a model for Honduras.
records.summary_es: The Evening Journal informó sobre el éxito financiero del receptor de aduanas estadounidense W. E. Pulliam en la República Dominicana, destacando que su administración redujo los aranceles en un 15 por ciento trasladando la carga tributaria de los artículos de primera necesidad a los de lujo. La recaudación aduanera superó las expectativas y se proyectaba alcanzar al menos 3.000.000 de dólares en el año, sobrepasando con creces la meta requerida de 2.000.000 de dólares. WIPING OUT A REPUBLIC'S DEBT

Honest Administration is Saving Santo Domingo. Honduras Asks for Help

NEW TARIFF LAWS HAVE HELPED COUNTRY

WASHINGTON, Aug. 11—The recent suggestion that this government assume a protectorate over Honduras and enter into a joint protectorate with Great Britian, France and Germany over Liberia, makes a review of this country's protectorate of Santo Domingo of timely interest. It will be recalled that the United States in March, 1905, entered into a treaty with the Dominican Republic to arrange its financial difficulties. The republic owed about $20,000,000, and its foreign creditors were pressing hard. Under a treaty, which the Senate reluctantly ratified, an American collector of customs was appointed for the republic, who received all customs receipts and divided them in the proportion of 45 per cent. for the republic and 55 per cent. for the creditors. Under the old Spanish law, which the Dominican republic never repealed, all expenses of the government are paid them for revenues derived from, imports and exports, property paying no taxes whatever.

In the five years that this government has assumed control of the Dominican custom-houses, the republic's debt has been reduced by $7,000,000 and the government, although receiving only 45 per cent. of the revenues has had more money to expend on administration and on public improvements than ever before when all the receipts went into the national treasury. The reason is not far to seek, for the American administration of the customs is honest. There have been naturally several abortive attempts at revolutions from hungry patriots whose souls shudder at the thought that the country's revenues are going into the country's treasury, but behind the American collector of customs, Mr. W. E. Pulliam, stands the American navy, and the net result of these revolutons has been only a decrease in the population of Santo Domingo, for those revolutionists who are not buried where they fall are safely tucked away in Dominican dungeons.

Result of New Tariff.
So well has Mr. Pulliam administered the revenues of the republic that a year ago last month he submitted a new tariff downward by about 15 per cent. Up to that time the Spanish principal of revenue taxation prevailed—namely, placing the heaviest possible duties on the necessities of life and permitting the luxuries to come in with the lightest possible duty. Mr. Pulliam introduced the American idea of letting the necessities of life come in free of duty, or nearly free, while the burden of taxation rested upon the luxuries. It was stipulated that an annual collection of $2,000,000 must be shown if the new tariff should remain in effect for more than a year. The tariff has now been adopted, and after a few months of a transition period, during which the business men of Santo Domingo adgusted themselves to new conditions, the receipts more than surpassed Mr. Pulliam's expectations. For the past three months the custom receipts have passed each month the quarter-million mark. At this rate the revenues for the current year will be at least $3,000,000, or one million more than the stipulated amount.

With this splended display of what American tariff and honesty will accomplish, it is small wonder that Honduras,, whose foreign creditors are pressing her hard for their money, and that Liberia, which faces dissolution as a republic, have appealed to this country for a similar protectorate. Although the State Department is strongly inclined to accede to both requests, it would be premature to say that the request will be granted. The Senate is bitterly opposed to any more such arrangements, although the example of Santo Domingo is encouraging. In the case of Liberia this country has only a sentimental interest, for Liberia owes its inception to American philanthropists.. It was the legislature of Maryland, whose generous appropriations nearly a century ago founded the Province of Maryland and peopled it with freed men from Maryland. The present republic if Liberia is a development of that settlement, but it is acknowledged on every hand that the republic is a failure. If this country enters into a joint protectorate with Great Britain, France and Germany, it will only mean a postponement of the fatal day.

No more Protectorates.
As for Honduras, a protectorate over that little republic would seem to be a logical corollary of the Monroe Doctrine, but the Senate, as already stated, is so bitterly opposed to any more of these treaties that Secretary Knox is at this moment unable to see his way clear to establishing a protectorate there. The Senate holds that if, following the example in Santo Domingo, this country takes up Honduras, it is only a question of time when an American receiver will be in charge of the customs of every petty republic in Central and South America, a condition not to be regarded with toleration.

records.summary_en: The Yorkville Enquirer reported that Dominican authorities arrested former Admiral Catrain as he attempted to sneak aboard a German steamer in Santo Domingo to join an insurrection led by deposed President Morales. Catrain, who had previously commandeered the gunboat *Independencia* during Morales's 1906 ouster before receiving amnesty, was suspected of returning to command a revolutionary vessel. Dominican officials discounted Morales's assertions to his followers that the United States supported his return to power.

records.summary_en: The Yorkville Enquirer commented on Dominican political instability and former President Morales's campaign to regain the presidency by force, arguing that the country needed a strong leader comparable to Mexico's Porfirio Diaz. The article questioned whether Morales could improve upon the incumbent administration or justify plunging the nation into civil war. It noted that if threatened, the Dominican government could invoke a treaty clause originally drafted by Morales himself to request American intervention to protect debt obligations.
records.summary_es: The Yorkville Enquirer comentó sobre la inestabilidad política dominicana y la campaña del expresidente Morales para reconquistar la presidencia por la fuerza, argumentando que el país precisaba de un líder fuerte semejante al mexicano Porfirio Díaz. El artículo cuestionaba si Morales podría mejorar la gestión del gobierno en funciones o justificar que se sumiera a la nación en una guerra civil. Señalaba que, de verse amenazado, el gobierno dominicano podría recurrir a una cláusula del tratado redactada en su momento por el propio Morales para solicitar la intervención estadounidense en salvaguarda de los compromisos de la deuda.
records.passage: beloved by Columbus and the cradle of American civilization, for the first university in the New World was established in Santo Domingo, is at present living in the sixteenth century. Is it to be wondered at under the circumstances that the little republic is a prey to the worst evils that battened upon Europe during that era? Santo Domingo undoubtedly needs a despotic ruler with a determination to make it progress, a man of the Porfirio Diaz type, who will do for it what Diaz has done for Mexico. Whether Morales is capable of doing this or not can not be surmised. His term of office was too short to permit an influence either in pro or in contra, but his passage was marked by undeniable progress. Morales's plans of government, whatever they may be, should he succeed in reaching the presidency, are unknown, but unless he can materially better the present administration he would not be justified in carrying civil war into his country. records.summary_en: The Topeka State Journal reported on President Taft's speech defending his foreign policy against critics of "Dollar Diplomacy," advocating pending treaties with Nicaragua and Honduras modeled on the Dominican arrangement. Taft emphasized that American customs collection in Santo Domingo had ensured debt repayments and fostered national reconstruction. He countered Senate objections that such treaties created entangling alliances for American banking interests rather than promoting regional stability.

Broadly speaking President Taft said the proposed treaties with these countries before the senate would secure for them a financial agent in the United States who would settle their existing debts on a just basis and who would point the road to peace and prosperity to two republics, rich in natural resources but torn by strife and revolution. The president pointed out the efficacy of a similar arrangement with Santo Do mingo where this government collects the customs and sees that foreign debts are paid, exercises a benefit supervision that Mr. Taft said has accrued to the upbuilding of Santo Domingo. Taft highlighted that 55 percent of customs collections provided unprecedented domestic revenues while 45 percent went toward debt extinction, reducing costly American naval patrols to a minimum. He urged applying the Dominican model to resolve chronic revolutions and financial distress in Honduras and Nicaragua.

records.summary_en: The Salt Lake Tribune discussed political reactions following the assassination of Dominican President Ramon Caceres, noting his past role in killing dictator Ulises Heureaux in 1899. Officials recalled Caceres's rise through cabinet and vice-presidential posts to the presidency in 1905, expressing concern that rival politicians might seize on his death to provoke unrest. The War Department noted that the assassination disrupted an exceptional four-year period of peace in a nation previously plagued by annual revolutions.
records.summary_es: The Salt Lake Tribune analizó las reacciones políticas tras el magnicidio del presidente dominicano Ramón Cáceres, recordando su participación en la muerte del dictador Ulises Heureaux en 1899. Los funcionarios rememoraron el ascenso de Cáceres a través de carteras ministeriales y la vicepresidencia hasta alcanzar la presidencia en 1905, expresando inquietud de que políticos rivales aprovecharan su deceso para provocar alteraciones. El Departamento de Guerra advirtió que el magnicidio truncó un excepcional período de cuatro años de paz en una nación anteriormente asolada por revoluciones anuales.

records.summary_en: The Richmond Virginian reported that war appeared imminent between Haiti and the Dominican Republic amid revolutions in both countries, following the assassination of Haiti's President Leconte and rebel capture of the border town Dajabon. Santo Domingo prepared to declare war after hundreds of Haitians allegedly assisted Dominican insurgents, massing 4,000 troops along the border. The region also faced severe agricultural drought and famine, while civil strife escalated concurrently in Nicaragua.

Santo Domingo se preparaba para declarar la guerra luego de que cientos de haitianos presuntamente auxiliaran a los insurgentes dominicanos, concentrando 4.000 soldados a lo largo de la frontera. La región padecía además una severa sequía agrícola y hambruna, mientras la guerra civil se intensificaba a la par en Nicaragua.

Mexico, Santo Domingo, Nicaragua.

It appears that the criticism of Senor Didapp, the representative of the Mexican revolutionists in Washington, and former Mexican Consul General to Spain, Turkey, and later at Norfolk, Va., is pretty well founded when, in his public utterances, he criticises Secretary Knox’s “dollar diplomacy,” which he maintains is making a mess of it in all Pan-American affairs, especially so in Mexico and Nicaragua.

As regards the former, Senor Didapp says that, unable to protect American lives and property by showing a firm attitude toward Madero, the department has been forced to the expedient of assisting the Mexican government by allowing Mexican troops to cross American territory in their attempt to get closer to the revolutionists. This, adds the senor, under the rules of international law, is equivalent to a declaration of war against the revolutionists on the part of the United States.

While The Herald believes that he is wrong in this contention, because the Mexican revolutionists are not yet recognized as belligerents by the Powers, yet it is a queer way of upholding the laws of neutrality. If this is considered fair on the part of the United States, then it would hardly be a greater violation of neutrality to throw a few brigades of United States regulars across the Rio Grande for the purpose of re-enforcing the Madero armies.

It would seem, therefore, that there is some ground for the contention of Senor Didapp that our government already has “intervened” when it allowed Mexican troops to cross American soil on their way to attack the revolutionists.

Secretary Knox, while away on a mission which an Assistant Secretary could well have fulfilled, leaves Pan-American affairs in a badly muddled condition, and the question may be permitted what good his recent trip to Central America has accomplished. His peace efforts have made a dismal failure of preserving the peace in Nicaragua.

The object of our proposed treaty with that country has been to authorize the executive branch of the United States government, with the consent of Congress, to intervene in Nicaragua, as it did in Santo Domingo in the alleged interest of the protection of American lives and property and the maintenance of public order. We know what that has meant to the Dominicans. Neither was property protected nor order maintained. The natives were overawed by the aid of the American forces. All debts of that republic, since the year one of its existence, were combined into bonds, and these exchanged for pieces of paper called Dominican-American “guaranteed national bonds.” These bonds have the interest guaranteed by the United States, but not the principal, by the collection of customs moneys.

If seriously looked into it will be found that Americans hold large blocks of the old debts of Nicaragua. The State Department had such an easy time in the Senate in the Dominican intervention deal that it also may have given assurances to Nicaraguan professional patriots with bundles of old scrip. But the Senate balked, because, were the United States to side with one faction against another, it would make it quite uncomfortable for American industrial expansionists.

It looks to The Herald that, when the smoke has cleared away, the United States will be found collecting Nicaraguan customs duties in the interest of American pioneers. This is known as “Dawsonizing the Monroe Doctrine,” for it avoids annexing the republics, while it obliterates them from the map as international factors of discord. Despite the fact that the Senate has refused to sanction the grabbing of a neighboring republic's custom-house, it would seem that those interested in the possibilities of spoil possess sufficient power to have the State Department spread United States marines over Nicaragua interior towns. This is apparently evidenced by the fact, quite palpable, that a battalion of American marines had been dispatched to Granada, which is not on the line of communication between Washington and Minister Weitzel, in order to rescue some girls alleged to be held in a French college.

What we should like to know is what these girls, this purely domestic affair, have to do with the Nicaraguan question?
