records.headline: In December he was designated as secretary of the Inaugu ration
records.summary_en: The Sun reported on the appointment of Walter W. Vick as general receiver of Dominican customs, emphasizing the requirement that he maintain strict political neutrality. The article credited the American receivership with securing revenues from aspiring revolutionists and providing seven years of uninterrupted domestic peace until disturbances resumed in 1912. Vick's mandate was to preserve the integrity and security of customs collections across all contending political factions.
records.summary_es: The Sun informó sobre la designación de Walter W. Vick como receptor general de las aduanas dominicanas, enfatizando la exigencia de que mantuviera una estricta neutralidad política. El artículo atribuía a la receptoría estadounidense el mérito de haber puesto los caudales a salvo de las ambiciones revolucionarias y de brindar siete años de ininterrumpida paz interna hasta el resurgimiento de los disturbios en 1912. La misión de Vick consistía en preservar la integridad y seguridad de la recaudación de aduanas frente a todas las facciones políticas en pugna.

In December he was designated as secretary of the Inauguration committee and opened headquarters in Washington, from which he directed the arrangements as the personal representative of the President elect. His new appointment involves a radical change. Instead of being in politics he must maintain absolute neutrality In such matters in the Dominican republic. One of the advantages supposed to lie in the American receivership is that the customs revenues are by it removed to neutral hands and are no longer to be preyed upon by aspiring revolutionists or grafting officials. From [illegible], when the first temporary arrangement went into effect, until [illegible], Santo Domingo had its first long period of freedom from revolution and internal strife. The neutralization of the customs receipts has been regarded as the cause of this peace in the turbulent republic. In 1912 there was continued political disturbance, but even during the revolution the custom houses remained unmolested by either faction In the struggle. It will be Mr. Vick's task to continue this absolute security of the customs receipts and maintain perfect neutrality toward all the contending political factions in the Island.

records.headline: Colonel Harry Betancourt, who served under the anti-government banner, recounts the machete cavalry charge at the battle of La
records.summary_en: Colonel Harry Betancourt, who served under the anti-government banner, recounts the machete cavalry charge at the battle of La Vega, where about a hundred men on each side, half-clad rebels with spurs strapped to naked ankles, fought hand to hand with cane knives in place of sabres. He says seventy-five per cent of the combatants on either side were killed or disabled, that he was the only United States citizen holding a command, and that three battles were fought that day around La Vega, with an interval of two hours between each.
records.summary_es: El coronel Harry Betancourt, que sirvió bajo la bandera antigubernamental, relata la carga de caballería con machetes en la batalla de La Vega, donde unos cien hombres de cada bando, rebeldes semidesnudos con espuelas atadas a los tobillos descalzos, lucharon cuerpo a cuerpo con cuchillos de caña en lugar de sables. Dice que el setenta y cinco por ciento de los combatientes de cada bando resultaron muertos o incapacitados, que él fue el único ciudadano de los Estados Unidos con un mando, y que ese día se libraron tres batallas alrededor de La Vega, con un intervalo de dos horas entre cada una.

We fought three battles that day about La Vega, actually three battles, with an interval of two hours between each. In each of these encounters Gen. Pichardo received a wound. He fought in the most dangerous spots. He died of his injuries a few days later. "Some of our troopers were boys only 15 years old. Yet they felt the battle power and tingle of the militant demigod. They held themselves stiffly erect, although scores of them had only their horse's backbone for a saddle. Heads high, and with the lofty, confident air of a field marshal, they eagerly and anxiously listened for the command to charge. "Every machete held in the black or brown hand had been sharpened to a razor edge. For two days the sharpening had gone on in our bivouac outside La Vega. In some cases there was a scabbard, but in most cases there wasn't. The sharp edges of the great knives caused many injuries to the men themselves. After the last battle on October 2, when government forces near Puerto Plata attacked the rebels, Commander Louis M. Nulton of the Nashville and customs receiver Walter W. Vick helped bring the deadlocked peace commissions to Santo Domingo City, where a final agreement was reached on Tuesday evening at a conference Sullivan attended.

records.summary_en: The Raymer Enterprise reviewed the history of the Dominican customs receivership, noting that removing customs revenues from political grasp had ended chronic revolutions and established domestic peace between 1905 and 1912. The article recalled that President Roosevelt intervened in 1905 to prevent European creditor nations from seizing Dominican customs to collect $20,000,000 in defaulted debts. Newly appointed Receiver Walter W. Vick was charged with maintaining strict administrative neutrality and safeguarding revenue security.

El artículo recordó que el presidente Roosevelt intervino en 1905 para evitar que las potencias acreedoras europeas se apoderaran de las aduanas dominicanas para cobrar 20.000.000 de dólares en deudas morosas. El recién designado receptor Walter W. Vick tenía por misión preservar una rigurosa neutralidad administrativa y resguardar los fondos fiscales.

The neutralization of the customs receipts has been regarded as the cause of this peace in the turbulent republic. It says the removal of the customs revenues to neutral hands gave Santo Domingo its first long period of freedom from revolution, from 1905 to 1912, and recounts how European creditors in 1904 demanded settlement of a debt of about $30,000,000, leading to the modus vivendi, the treaty that took effect on July 8, 1907, and a $20,000,000 bond issue.

Dice que el traslado de los ingresos aduaneros a manos neutrales dio a Santo Domingo su primer largo período sin revoluciones, de 1905 a 1912, y cuenta cómo los acreedores europeos exigieron en 1904 el arreglo de una deuda de unos 30.000.000 de dólares, lo que llevó al modus vivendi, al tratado que entró en vigor el 8 de julio de 1907 y a una emisión de bonos de 20.000.000 de dólares.

records.headline: France and Germany Warn Government to Meet Financial Obligations
records.summary_en: France and Germany have warned Haiti that its customhouses will be seized unless arrangements are made to meet its outstanding financial obligations, according to reports reaching Washington. Secretary of State Bryan said no notice of such a step had reached the United States, but the cabinet discussed the situation at length. Officials noted that no treaty or arrangement would allow the United States to take charge of Haitian customs as it did in Santo Domingo, and pointed out that four American warships were already in Haitian waters while the German cruiser Strassburg lay in Dominican waters, within a few hours' sail of Port-au-Prince. Haiti's minister in Washington, Ulrich Duvivier, protested that his country was not a defaulting debtor and that the debts claimed were indemnities demanded by irresponsible foreigners.
records.summary_es: Francia y Alemania han advertido a Haití que sus aduanas serán embargadas si no se toman medidas para cumplir con sus obligaciones financieras pendientes, según informes llegados a Washington. El secretario de Estado Bryan declaró que no había llegado a los Estados Unidos ninguna notificación de tal medida, pero el gabinete discutió la situación extensamente. Las autoridades señalaron que ningún tratado ni acuerdo permitiría a los Estados Unidos hacerse cargo de las aduanas haitianas como lo hizo en Santo Domingo, e indicaron que cuatro buques de guerra estadounidenses ya se encontraban en aguas haitianas, mientras el crucero alemán Strassburg estaba en aguas dominicanas, a pocas horas de navegación de Puerto Príncipe. El ministro de Haití en Washington, Ulrich Duvivier, protestó que su país no era un deudor moroso y que las deudas reclamadas eran indemnizaciones exigidas por extranjeros irresponsables.

records.summary_en: The Montgomery Advertiser reported widespread insurrections across the Dominican Republic, including uprisings at Azua, Monte Cristi, and La Romana, where American plantation owners requested State Department protection. President Bordas remained gridlocked against insurgent forces despite ruling through decree and receiving customs funding. With Minister Sullivan and Collector Vick stepping down, the U.S. government remained hesitant to deploy force, considering instead sending a prominent mediator to reconcile the factions.
records.summary_es: The Montgomery Advertiser informó sobre levantamientos generalizados en toda la República Dominicana, incluyendo revueltas en Azua, Monte Cristi y La Romana, donde hacendados azucareros estadounidenses solicitaron amparo al Departamento de Estado. El presidente Bordas se mantenía empantanado contra las fuerzas insurgentes no obstante gobernar por decreto y recibir caudales de aduana. Con la renuncia del ministro Sullivan y del recaudador Vick, el gobierno de los EE. UU. vacilaba en recurrir a las armas, evaluando en su lugar el envío de un destacado mediador para aproximar a las facciones.
records.passage: Today's reports showed no Improvement. Meanwhile revolutions have broken out in other sections—at Azua, where the government navy found it necessary to destroy the custom house: along the line of railway, between Sanchez and Samana Bay, at Monte Cristi and at La Romana in the southeast. records.summary_en: The Freeman reported that Dominican insurgents fired upon the gunboat *Machias* before rebel leaders boarded the vessel to assure American non-combatant safety. The paper noted that four simultaneous insurrections were underway while Minister Sullivan returned to Washington, prompting anxiety over the United States' obligations under its treaty semi-protectorate. With Collector Vick resigned, the State Department considered dispatching an impartial emissary to avert full military intervention while maintaining naval vessels in Dominican waters.

El periódico señaló que estallaban cuatro insurrecciones paralelas mientras el ministro Sullivan volvía a Washington, lo que despertaba alarma acerca de las obligaciones de los Estados Unidos bajo su semiprotectorado emanado de los tratados. Con la dimisión del recaudador Vick, el Departamento de Estado contemplaba el despacho de un emisario neutral para conjurar una intervención militar plena, conservando buques de guerra en aguas dominicanas.

With four separate revolutions raging simultaneously and the American minister to the country returning home after several months of fruitless efforts to restore peace, the little republic of San Domingo is causing grave anxiety on the part of the Washington government which is morally bound to maintain order there under the semi-protectorate created by treaty. Official opinion here is slowly crystallizing into a conviction that only through powerful outside influence and probably that of the United States can these chaotic conditions be terminated and a stable government set up. Mr. Vick, the American collector of customs, has resigned, and now Minister Sullivan is returning to the United States, leaving Secretary White in charge of the American Legation, and without any definite assurance that he will ever resume his official duties. The State Department is reluctant to intervene forcibly in San Domingo, and it is expected that an effort will be made to send some strong man to the republic who may secure the confidence of all elements and bring them together. records.summary_en: The Manning Times reported escalating conflict at Puerto Plata, where the gunboat *Machias* exchanged fire with shore combatants and used its main guns to silence President Bordas's artillery after non-combatant safety was violated. The revenue cutter *Algonquin* evacuated 42 American and Puerto Rican refugees from the besieged city amid heavy crossfire between federal forces and Legalista rebels. Meanwhile, a U.S. naval squadron patrolled Dominican coastal ports while Washington sought a mediator to restore peace.

El guardacostas *Algonquin* evacuó a 42 refugiados estadounidenses y puertorriqueños de la ciudad sitiada en medio del recio fuego cruzado entre tropas gubernamentales y rebeldes legalistas. Mientras tanto, una escuadra naval de los EE. UU. patrullaba los puertos de la costa dominicana mientras Washington procuraba un mediador para restablecer la paz.

Other vessels are on the Haitien end of the island. Reckless firing. Dominican rebels sent several shots against the hull of the American gunboat Machias in Puerto Plata harbor late Tuesday night and drew upon themselves a warning volley from the Machias' three-pounders and automatic rifles. The shooting from shore stopped immediately. A few days ago the gunboat used her main battery of four-inch guns to silence President Bordas' batteries, which were bombarding the rebel garrison holding the city, in violation of the agreement that the lives of foreigners and other non-combatants would not be endangered by artillery fire. One woman died during the voyage from the effects of starvation. The condition of those remaining in Santo Domingo was reported to be pitiable, as it was almost impossible to obtain foodstuffs, the prices of which were prohibitive. A report was brought here by the Algonquin that an American bluejacket on board the gunboat Machias had been shot in the leg by a bullet from the shore. Solon Menos, the Haitien minister, conferred today with Secretary Bryan and urged that intervention would result in a number of counter revolutions, necessitate the dissolution of the present government, and even the abdication of the president. "I count on the spirit of justice of the American people," said Minister Menos, referring to intervention, "to restrain them from taking the step which would be so harmful to Haiti." Present mobilization of marines in the vicinity of the islands, the minister explained, had been officially explained by the state department as a precautionary step taken to avert possible trouble, and was not, he felt sure, an indication that plans actually existed for the landing of United States troops at Haiti. records.headline: Doubtless take steps to protect their interests is they deem it
records.summary_en: The New Hampshire Farmer and Weekly Union contrasted unrest in the Caribbean, noting that while Dominican disturbances were likely to prompt U.S. armed intervention, the country presented fewer military and diplomatic difficulties than neighboring Haiti. European nations maintained smaller financial interests in Santo Domingo, whereas Haitian instability threatened foreign defaults. The Wilson administration sought guarantees that Haitian customs revenues would be managed to satisfy foreign debts in a manner analogous to the Dominican receivership.
records.summary_es: The New Hampshire Farmer and Weekly Union contrastó las revueltas en el Caribe, observando que, si bien era probable que las perturbaciones dominicanas provocaran una intervención militar estadounidense, dicho país planteaba menores dificultades bélicas y diplomáticas que el vecino Haití. Las naciones europeas conservaban intereses financieros más reducidos en Santo Domingo, al tiempo que la inestabilidad haitiana ponía en riesgo moratorias con el exterior. La administración Wilson demandaba garantías de que los ingresos de las aduanas de Haití fueran administrados para cancelar deudas foráneas de modo análogo a la receptoría dominicana.
records.passage: doubtless take steps to protect their interests if they deem it necessary, but none of those countries is going to risk an affront to the United States so long as there is a possibility that this government will take steps to protect their interests for them. Although there are disturbances in the Dominican republic that will probably lead to armed intervention by the United States, it does not present as difficult a military problem as Haiti, and the political importance is not so great. records.summary_en: The Washington Times reported on congressional and departmental hearings investigating Minister James M. Sullivan's conduct and appointment under Dominican treaty relations. Witnesses detailed political influence and lobbying efforts involving customs appointments, while Assistant Secretary of State John B. Osborne testified that he had previously warned Santo Domingo against accumulating unauthorized debt. Osborne also noted receiving communications from former Customs Receiver Walter W. Vick that severely criticized Sullivan's actions.

Osborne testificó haber alertado previamente a Santo Domingo sobre la acumulación de deudas no autorizadas. Osborne mencionó además haber recibido comunicaciones del exreceptor de aduanas Walter W. Vick en las que se reprobaban con dureza los actos de Sullivan.

'INSIDE INFORMATION' AT SULLIVAN PROBE

Revelations Made by Harry J. Overman, Brother of Senator From South Carolina.

Inside information as to the influences at work on the appointment of American representatives in the Dominican government was brought out yesterday at the first session of the Sullivan hearing here.

Harry J. Overman, file clerk in the office of the Secretary of the Senate and a brother of Senator Lea S. Overman of North Carolina, testified concerning his efforts to obtain appointment as deputy receiver of customs at Santo Domingo under the treaty relations between the Dominican republic and the United States. He declared that he had been urged to apply for the place by a man named Gold, who, he said, suggested that William C. Beer would be a good person to support him for the place. Beer, he said he was told by Gold, could influence Secretary of State Bryan through John H. Grey, of Wilmington, Del.

Md. Overman testified that inasmuch as his own brother was unwilling to use his position to further his candidacy he was compelled to do much of the work himself. He said that he had met Mr. Beer at a hotel in Washington in company with Minister Sullivan.

John E. Osborne, First Assistant Secretary of State, stated that prior to the appointment of Mr. Sullivan, he had gone to Haiti and Santo Domingo on a secret mission for the Government. While there, he stated, he had warned the Dominican government against increasing its indebtedness.

Regarding the Sullivan case, Secretary Osborne said that he knew practically nothing except that he had received personal letters from Mr. Vick, criticising the conduct of the minister.

Others who were present were Joseph P. Tumulty, Secretary to the President; Assistant Secretary of State, Philips; Assistant Secretary of War Breckenridge, and Brigadier General McIntyre, chief of the Bureau of Insular Affairs, War Department.

At the outset of today's session Charles H. Strong, attorney, conducting the examination for Comimssioner Phelan, announced that the entire scope of the investigation was to inquire into the fitness, competence, and conduct of Minister Sullivan.

“The Commissioner intends,” he said, “to run down any legitimate clue bearing on this case without fear or favor for anybody in or out of public office. He means to sift the case to the bottom. Necessarily, inasmuch as the lines upon which this investigation is being conducted are wholly different from court procedure, much hearsay testimony, or even gossip, must creep into the evidence. But as a result of this hearsay evidence we have already been able to unearth things of the utmost importance.”

records.summary_en: The Springfield Weekly Republican reported on ongoing proceedings in the Phelan investigation into Minister James M. Sullivan, reviewing personal debts and legal judgments submitted into the record alongside testimonials on his behalf. State Department investigator Harry S. Dickey and former Vice Consul Charles H. Albrecht praised Sullivan's diplomatic rapport, attributing the controversy to personal hostility from former Receiver Walter W. Vick. Representative Hamill also testified, denying any connection to commercial interests in advocating for Sullivan's appointment.

records.summary_en: The Evening Public Ledger criticized systemic customs fraud and graft in Haiti, contrasting the island's fertile resources with the economic harm caused by official corruption. The article detailed how the wife of former President Nord Alexis evaded customs duties by smuggling goods and disguising valuable coffee shipments as untaxed cottonseed. It concluded that establishing an honest, stable administration would allow Haiti to realize its natural agricultural potential.

records.summary_en: The Washington Herald reported that a Haitian rebel commander fled toward Monte Cristi in the Dominican Republic to recruit men and procure arms, raising concerns of renewed destabilization along the border. Officials noted rising unrest and riots within Santo Domingo, where a compromise coalition government instituted under U.S. auspices was widely regarded as failing. American naval forces faced strain, having withdrawn the cruiser *Nashville* from Dominican waters to handle military operations and disarmament efforts in Haiti.
records.summary_es: The Washington Herald informó que un jefe insurgente haitiano huyó en dirección a Monte Cristi, en la República Dominicana, para reclutar partidarios y obtener armamento, desatando la alarma ante una nueva alteración en la línea fronteriza. Los funcionarios observaron una creciente conmoción y disturbios en Santo Domingo, donde se consideraba un fracaso el gobierno de concertación auspiciado por los Estados Unidos. La fuerza naval estadounidense se veía exigida tras haber retirado el crucero *Nashville* de aguas dominicanas para atender las operaciones castrenses y de desarme en Haití.

records.summary_en: A feature describes the Dominican Republic as naturally one of the richest spots in the world, with Puerto Plata, a town of some 10,000 or 12,000 inhabitants, linked by railway to Santiago de los Caballeros, La Vega and Moca in the Cibao, and San Pedro de Macoris as the sugar port, with thousands of acres in sugar cane and millions of dollars of American capital invested. In the capital it points out relics of Columbus, including the ruins of the house of Diego Colon and the cathedral crypt from which, the Dominicans claim, the Spaniards mistakenly removed the remains of a brother of Columbus instead of the discoverer's.

En la capital señala reliquias de Colón, incluidas las ruinas de la casa de Diego Colón y la cripta de la catedral de la que, según afirman los dominicanos, los españoles retiraron por error los restos de un hermano de Colón en lugar de los del descubridor.

records.summary_en: This feature describes Macoris, where thousands of acres are devoted to sugar cane, millions of dollars of American capital are invested, and the plantations, equipped with the most modern machinery, are worked by coloured labourers from the English and Danish West Indies. It then tours the capital, Santo Domingo City, with the ruins of the first church, San Nicolas, the house of Diego Colon, the ceiba tree to which Columbus's caravels were tied, and a macadam boulevard running twenty miles toward Bani, and insists the climate is healthy, with no serious epidemic since the cholera outbreak of the early sixties.

records.headline: This descriptive feature presents Santo Domingo City, the capital, seventy miles from La Romana and forty from Macoris
records.summary_en: This descriptive feature presents Santo Domingo City, the capital, seventy miles from La Romana and forty from Macoris, as a place of modern life amid relics of the fifteenth century, including the ruins of the first church, San Nicolas, the bones Dominicans claim are those of Christopher Columbus in the cathedral, and the ruins of the house of Diego Colon, his son. Washington warned Dominican officials that it viewed congressional impeachment proceedings against Jimenes as a veiled revolutionary plot, granting him an eight-day respite to reply. The excerpt also detailed a concurrent constitutional clash in Haiti, where Caperton backed President Dartiguenave against a rebellious parliament.

WASHINGTON, May 5.—Rear Admiral Caperton, commanding the American naval forces in Dominican waters, is under broad instructions to use whatever force is necessary to maintain the constitutional government in the Dominican Republic. The Admiral recently went to the capital with instructions from Washington which declared the United States considered the impeachment of President Jiminez a thinly veiled revolutionary plot. If necessary Admiral Caperton may land bluejackets and marines. PORT AU PRINCE, Haiti, May 5. The Haitian Cabinet has resigned. Parliament has entered a protest with the American Government and Congress against what it declares to be a violation of the rights of the legislative branch of the Government. President Dartiguenave, of Haiti, and his Cabinet have been in controversy with Parliament over the framing of a new constitution to conform with the treaty with the United States. records.summary_en: American marines, fully equipped, were landed on the outskirts of Santo Domingo City, first from the cruiser Prairie to protect the American legation after disorders in which several persons were killed or wounded. Advices said the serious situation caused by hostilities between the factions of President Jimenes and General Arias had become quiet after Jimenes resigned, a step he took to prevent threatened armed intervention by the United States. Five additional destroyers and the supply ship Panther were to sail for the Dominican Republic, and the French armored cruiser Marseillaise had arrived in port.

Los informes decían que la grave situación causada por las hostilidades entre las facciones del presidente Jimenes y el general Arias se había calmado después de que Jimenes dimitiera, paso que dio para evitar la amenazada intervención armada de Estados Unidos. records.headline: This feature calls the Dominican Republic, and indeed the whole island, naturally one of the richest spots in the world
records.summary_en: This feature calls the Dominican Republic, and indeed the whole island, naturally one of the richest spots in the world, with remarkably fertile soil: cotton near Monte Cristi backed by American and English capital, Puerto Plata linked by railway to the cacao and tobacco towns of the Cibao, Samana Bay with the town of Samana and the port of Sanchez, and San Pedro de Macoris as the sugar port, where thousands of acres of cane and millions of dollars of American capital are worked with modern machinery. It also tours the capital's relics, including the ruins of the first church of San Nicolas, the bones Dominicans claim are those of Christopher Columbus, and the ruins of the house of Diego Colon.
records.summary_es: Esta crónica califica a la República Dominicana, y en verdad a toda la isla, como naturalmente uno de los lugares más ricos del mundo, con un suelo notablemente fértil: algodón cerca de Monte Cristi respaldado por capital estadounidense e inglés, Puerto Plata unida por ferrocarril a las ciudades del Cibao productoras de cacao y tabaco, la bahía de Samaná con la ciudad de Samaná y el puerto de Sánchez, y San Pedro de Macorís como puerto azucarero, donde se trabajan miles de acres de caña y millones de dólares de capital estadounidense con maquinaria moderna. Recorre también las reliquias de la capital, incluidas las ruinas de la primera iglesia de San Nicolás, los huesos que los dominicanos afirman que son los de Cristóbal Colón y las ruinas de la casa de Diego Colón.
records.passage: ducted clubs. Club Union and Casino de la Juventud, where there are frequent social entertainments. Automobiles are plentiful and the ride from the capital to San Cristobal along the new macadam boulevard is most attractive. Automobiles can be procured for $1 an hour. There are several hotels in the city, of which the Hotel Francis is the best known. There is quite a large foreign colony at the capital and in Macoris and Puerto Plata. The whole trip from New York, including a stop at all ports, is about eight or nine days. A very erroneous impression prevails that the climate of Santo Domingo is unhealthy. From its geographical position it cannot be unhealthy. The winds have a clean sweep across the island, and there has been no serious epidemic there since the cholera outbreak some time in the early sixties.

records.headline: But after six or seven years of peace trouble broke out
records.summary_en: The *Perth Amboy evening news* reported on U.S. intervention in Santo Domingo, stating that severe unrest in 1914 and 1915 forced the United States to deploy marines and warships to restore quiet. The article asserted that Dominicans reluctantly accepted external peace enforced under the Monroe Doctrine after customs administration alone failed to prevent renewed revolutions. It characterized the military interventions in Santo Domingo, Haiti, and Nicaragua as costly, altruistic sacrifices made for regional security rather than territorial gain.
records.summary_es: El *Perth Amboy evening news* informó sobre la intervención de los Estados Unidos en Santo Domingo, indicando que los graves disturbios acaecidos en 1914 y 1915 obligaron a Washington a movilizar infantes de marina y escuadras navales para restaurar la calma. El artículo aseveraba que la población dominicana aceptaba a regañadientes una paz exterior impuesta al amparo de la Doctrina Monroe, luego de que la sola administración aduanera resultara ineficaz para evitar la reaparición de revueltas. Calificaba los desembarcos militares en Santo Domingo, Haití y Nicaragua como sacrificios onerosos y altruistas en favor de la seguridad continental antes que en búsqueda de engrandecimiento territorial.
records.passage: still left a greater net Income for the use of the government than It had ever had before. "For a long time it was thought that, deprived of the opportunity of securing customs house revenues through the seizure of ports, revolution could not support themselves. But after six or seven years of peace trouble broke out again, and during 1914 and 1915 it became so serious that the United States was forced to Intervene in behalf of peace and to demand, with marines on shore and naval guns trained and pointed on the ports, that the country return to a state of quiet. And so today the Dominicans, realizing that the Monroe doctrine is determined to afford them protection, from their own excesses, their own bitter passions and blind purposes, have accepted the inevitable and have secured the blessings of peace from without when they could not attain that end themselves. It is a reluctant acquiescence they yield, but a wholesome one, none the less. 'It has not been without effort or without expense, nor yet without the actual sacrifice of blood and life that our country has stepped in to play the role of Good Samaritan to the people of Santo Domingo, Haiti and Nicaragua, who had lost the blessings of peace and were unable to regain them. In Haiti alone we lost one officer and six marines and had a number wounded. But out of this altruistic effort are growing results of which a nation that covets no territory, that seeks only its own security and the welfare of its unfortunate neighbors may well be proud.

records.summary_en: The *Pinedale roundup* reported that the U.S. Navy proclaimed military rule in Santo Domingo to quell political chaos and establish a financial and police protectorate similar to that in Haiti. Approximately 1,800 American marines were tasked with maintaining order and supervising native government operations until January elections, including the disbursement of $600,000 in accumulated export duties. The intervention followed the overthrow of President Jiminez by General Arias and Washington's refusal to recognize the newly chosen government of Frederico Enriquez.

Cerca de 1.800 infantes de marina estadounidenses fueron comisionados para preservar el orden y supervisar las funciones administrativas del país hasta los comicios de enero, incluyendo la entrega de 600.000 dólares en derechos de exportación retenidos. La intervención se produjo tras el derrocamiento del presidente Jimenes por el general Arias y la negativa de Washington a reconocer al electo gobernante Francisco Henríquez y Carvajal (mencionado como Frederico Enriquez).
records.passage: been proclaimed in Santo Domingo by the United States navy to suppress existing political chaos in the little republic and pave the way for guaranteeing future quiet by establishing there such a financial and police protectorate as the American government now exercises over Haiti. Eighteen hundred American marines will maintain order for the present, and at least until elections are held in January their officers will supervise the conduct of government by native officials and disburse the customs revenues which American receivers have been collecting by treaty arrangement for nine years. The navy proclamation, issued Thursday, apparently has been put into effect without bloodshed. records.summary_en: The *Evening journal* recounted the service of Private Hogan of the Fourth Regiment of Marines, who deployed to Santo Domingo aboard the *Tennessee* to quell civil rebellion. Hogan took part in a June 8 skirmish in which one marine was wounded and an estimated sixty insurgents were killed or wounded, and he later observed the wreck of the *Memphis*. He described Dominican rebels as poorly organized, barefoot forces who frequently removed front rifle sights and relied on sniping tactics against American troops.

Hogan intervino en un combate el 8 de junio en el que un infante de marina fue herido y se calculó en sesenta los insurgentes muertos o heridos, presenciando tiempo después el naufragio del crucero *Memphis*. Describió a los alzados dominicanos como combatientes descalzos y de escasa disciplina militar, que solían retirar el punto de mira de sus fusiles y hostigar con francotiradores a las tropas estadounidenses.

records.headline: There were assassinations, there were betrayals, there were con spiracies, there
records.summary_en: The *Norwich bulletin* recounted the chronic political instability and recurring civil wars in Santo Domingo that left the republic heavily indebted to foreign creditors. When foreign warships threatened bombardment to enforce debt claims, Dominican authorities entered into an agreement with the United States in 1905 to take over the collection of customs. Under this treaty, American authorities restructured the nation's tariffs to tax luxuries and guaranteed payments to satisfy European claims.
records.summary_es: El *Norwich bulletin* rememoró la crónica inestabilidad política y las constantes guerras civiles en Santo Domingo que abocaron a la república a un pesado endeudamiento con acreedores extranjeros. Al amenazar cañoneros extranjeros con bombardear los puertos para hacer efectivas sus reclamaciones, las autoridades dominicanas celebraron un acuerdo con los Estados Unidos en 1905 para confiarles la recaudación aduanera. Bajo este convenio, los funcionarios estadounidenses modificaron los aranceles nacionales gravando los artículos de lujo y aseguraron pagos para saldar los reclamos europeos.
records.passage: bulletin. "Revolution had followed revolution almost with clocklike regularity. There were assassinations, there were betrayals, there were conspiracies, there were wars within and wars without — war with Haiti over boundary questions and civil war over the control of the government. Debts were piled up without thought of the day of payment or even provisions for meeting the interest charges. "So long and so steady was the orgy of revolution, speculation, debt making and interest-dodging that the nation's credit grew worse than that of its individual citizens. Finally, the day of reckoning came. Foreign warships approached the ports whose harbors had given refuge to the great discoverer Columbus and whose capital city contains what undoubtedly are his ashes, and demanded that the claims of their subjects be satisfied — claims for money advanced, claims for property wantonly destroyed — and they demanded it at the point of big naval guns. "In a predicament from which they were powerless to extricate themselves, the Dominicans were ready enough to negotiate a treaty turning over the control of the country's customs to the United States, if, in return therefor, the United States would protect them from angry European creditors and rejuvenate their treasury. "And so it was that in [illegible] the United States undertook to serve as treasurer of Santo Domingo and to vouch for her debts. The tariff was quickly revised, the American authorities urging that duties be laid on luxuries rather than upon necessities.

records.full_text:
U. S. MARINE DIES IN FIGHT

One American Is Killed and One Severely Wounded by Santo Domingo Bandits.

Washington, Jan. 24.—A night fight between native bandits and American marines in the Dominican republic, resulting in the death of one marine and the severe injury of another, was reported to the navy department.

Captain Knapp, commanding the American cruiser forces, reported the fight occurred Saturday night in the vicinity of the Porvenir sugar plantation, near Macoris, the scene of two similar encounters recently. Private J. R. Olson of the Fiftieth company was killed and Corporal George Wilson of the Fifty-second company was shot in the neck.

records.headline: An Associated Press correspondent writing from Santo Domingo on February 13 reports that peace, expected by everyone
records.summary_en: An Associated Press correspondent writing from Santo Domingo on February 13 reports that peace, expected by everyone to be permanent, has at last been established through the intervention of the United States in a country that has had approximately fifty presidents in seventy years, not one chosen without revolution. Captain Knapp, head of the temporary military government, faces the work of establishing good government, a sound educational system, agriculture and transportation, with an education commission headed by Archbishop Adolfo Nouel already appointed and a great highway of more than 200 miles planned across the Cibao to Monte Cristi.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal de la Associated Press que escribe desde Santo Domingo el 13 de febrero informa que la paz, que todos esperan permanente, se ha establecido por fin mediante la intervención de los Estados Unidos en un país que ha tenido aproximadamente cincuenta presidentes en setenta años, ninguno elegido sin revolución. El capitán Knapp, jefe del gobierno militar temporal, enfrenta la tarea de establecer un buen gobierno, un sistema educativo sólido, la agricultura y el transporte, con una comisión de educación encabezada por el arzobispo Adolfo Nouel ya nombrada y una gran carretera de más de 200 millas proyectada a través del Cibao hasta Monte Cristi.

There is a so-called school system in existence, but those in a position to know say there is not a public school building in the republic and estimates of illiteracy run as high as 90 per cent. Teachers have drawn salaries from the government when they had no pupils to teach and subventions are said to have been granted to private schools which existed only in name. Great Highway Planned. The report concluded that the country's lack of coal and poor overland transit routes posed the greatest obstacles to its industrial development.

The most famous of Dominican resources, and the one about which the American consul receives the most inquiries, is its gold. In the Cibao range and in the San Cristobal region there are placers which have been known and worked for centuries. In the days of the Spanish occupation it is said that the invaders gathered great stores of this treasure by trading with the Indians little silver hawkbells for their fill of gold. Nowadays the peon women wash gold out of these same streams with wooden bowls, making a few dollars a week, and by a law of the land the common people are protected in their right to work these placers. The forest resources are another example of unused wealth. One of the largest Dominican imports is lumber, and yet there are extensive forests of pine, oak and chestnut, as well as mahogany, satinwood, lignum vitae and rosewood. The most serious lack in Santo Domingo is coal, which will probably limit the future industrial development of the island more than anything else. There is an abundance of iron ore and also lead and copper, but no mineral fuel has so far been discovered except lignite. Another striking and so far undeveloped resource is two mountains of rock salt, said to be remarkably pure. They are in Barahona province. The article analyzed the country's social structure, explaining that approximately twenty elite families controlled virtually all political offices and land while avoiding property taxes. It observed that pervasive political corruption and sinecures had long characterized native governance prior to the American occupation.

They recognize that some stronger power must restore confidence in law and government and initiate the reconstruction of the country. They are not, however, looking toward annexation. It is easy to prove that the Dominicans are a lazy, disorderly people, and also hard to see how they could be anything else under present conditions. As in most small Latin-American countries, there are just two native classes — the very rich and the very poor. The upper class here is said to consist of not more than twenty large families. These hold all the political offices and own nearly all the land. They are wealthy, intelligent and well educated. Every law is designed to benefit them. records.summary_en: The *Omaha daily bee* reported that the government of President Jimenez collapsed after its revenues were withheld by American authorities, and Admiral Knapp refused Jimenez's request for a month's salary. Jimenez subsequently departed the country to lecture in Latin America against American despotism in Santo Domingo. The article noted that Knapp's proclamation established a military government intended as a temporary measure, keeping native courts and municipal administrations intact while imposing press censorship.
records.summary_es: El *Omaha daily bee* informó que la administración del presidente Jimenes se desmoronó luego de que las autoridades estadounidenses retuvieran sus fondos fiscales, habiéndose negado el almirante Knapp a pagar a Jimenes un mes de sueldo solicitado. Acto seguido, Jimenes abandonó la nación para dictar conferencias por Hispanoamérica denunciando la opresión estadounidense en Santo Domingo. El artículo apuntaba que la proclama de Knapp fundaba un gobierno militar con carácter provisional, manteniendo operando a los tribunales del país y los cabildos locales pero implantando la censura de prensa.
records.passage: Just exactly what happened to the Jimenez government after this is hard to state in official language, but is sufficiently clear; its political jugular vein has been severed, its golden life blood drained. It did not resign, it did not revolt; simply faded and died. To the cabinet officers was tendered the high and chaste honor of serving on without pay, but they unaccountably failed to respond. President Jimenez sent a messenger to Admiral Knapp to explain that his excellency was in a state of financial need and to request that his salary for one month be paid. This was refused. President Jimenez then sailed away and is said to have taken the lecture platform in other Latin American countries and devoted his abilities to an exposition of the greedy and underhand methods by which the eagle of the north is sinking the talons of despotism into the vitals of free and democratic government in Santo Domingo. Schoenrich concluded from 1877 cathedral excavations that Spain had mistakenly removed the remains of Diego Columbus, leaving Christopher Columbus's body in Santo Domingo.

records.summary_en: The *New-York tribune* published the proclamation of the U.S. military occupation in Santo Domingo, which stated that the intervention aimed to restore internal order and treaty compliance rather than end Dominican sovereignty. Dominican statutes and civil courts remained operational for regular matters, while military tribunals were established to try offenses against the occupation or its personnel. As his forces prepared to shell Puerto Plata unless the city surrendered by two o'clock, and Washington had sent two contingents of Marines to Puerto Plata and Monte Cristi to stand by, the American commander warned him that the first gun fired would result in the landing of Marines and a general cleaning out of the belligerents.

records.headline: One year was the limit if he failed to "make good
records.summary_en: The *Richmond planet* recounted the outbreak of civil war in Santo Domingo after a provisional president, appointed for a one-year trial term, issued a manifesto ten months later refusing to relinquish office. The declaration provoked widespread public outrage, prompting citizens to take up arms under the banner of liberty to remove the administration. While the president armed supporters with government artillery, fighters in Puerto Plata organized resistance, plunging the country into open conflict.
records.summary_es: El *Richmond planet* relató el estallido de la guerra civil en Santo Domingo después de que un presidente provisional, designado para un período de prueba de un año, emitiera un manifiesto diez meses después negándose a dejar el cargo. La declaración provocó una indignación pública generalizada, lo que llevó a los ciudadanos a alzarse en armas bajo el estandarte de la libertad para deponer a la administración. Mientras el presidente armaba a sus partidarios con artillería gubernamental, combatientes en Puerto Plata organizaron la resistencia, sumiendo al país en un conflicto abierto.

records.full_text:
OUR CARIBBEAN EMPIRE

The average citizen of the United States is blissfully ignorant of the extent to which this government has established a colonial empire in the Caribbean regions. In Nicaragua the government is practically in the hands of the United States marines. The natives complain not merely that they are ruled without their consent but that they are subject to the whims of our navy department which in this matter is responsible neither to congress nor the people. The American government is also charged with unwarranted interference in Guatemala, Costa Rica and Honduras. At a recent conference at Clark university, Judge Otto Schoenrich, a conservative citizen, born in America, who has held high judicial posts in Porto Rico and is familiar with all the Caribbean countries, read a paper reviewing the record of the American administration of the two island republics, Santo Domingo and Haiti. The first, it will be recalled, is Spanish-speaking and predominantly white; the second French-speaking and Negro. In 1916 our navy took over the government of Santo Domingo, and administers it through the marines against the wishes of the people. “Law and order” have been established. Roads have been built and a beginning has been made at popular education. The reason for our intervention was the failure of the Dominican government to live up to its agreement in the matter of its foreign debt. Foreign bondholders now get their interest regularly! Judge Schoenrich, however, charges that in accomplishing these things the United States government has maintained a censorship so rigid as to apply to every public statement “from the utterances of the chief justice to an advertisement for a servant girl.” Until recently the words, national, revolution, freedom of thought and speech could not appear in a Dominican publication. One unfortunate bookseller was originally sentenced to five years in prison for circulating a speech by the speaker of the Porto Rican house of representatives. Later his sentence was graciously commuted to banishment. Judge Schoenrich also reports serious charges of torture in connection with the administration of the provost courts.

In the neighboring republic of Haiti conditions are even more unsatisfactory. There we intervened on the nominal authority of a treaty, but the Haitian congress only ratified that treaty with 23 reservations which we ignored. In 1916 marines dispersed the congress and in 1917 dispersed a constituent assembly. Tell it not to Trotzky! Judge Schoenrich says there are three governments: the Haitian, the government of the American treaty officials, and the government of the American military. The first is impotent, the second inefficient, and the third indifferent. In the interior districts of the island the officers of the marines exercise despotic powers and the natives charge that a marine can do no wrong to a Haitian. From Haiti also come ugly stories of torture, autocratic and unjust trials of civilians by provost court, and denials of civil liberty. A few months ago armed Haitians, either bandits or revolutionists according to the point of view, actually marched on the capital city where there was vigorous fighting before they were dispersed. The Haitian debt was largely held by the people, who, lacking proper banking facilities, put their savings into national bonds. Under American occupation payment on these was suspended although it was guaranteed in the treaty. The people sold their holdings at low prices. The bonds, it is believed, are now held by New York bankers, and negotiations are under way looking to their payment at par.

It is only fair to say that such criticisms as these were vigorously attacked at the Clark university conference by defenders of the American regime. They are, however, supported by other testimony. Archbishop Nouel of Santo Domingo in a letter to the American minister (we go through the farce of maintaining a minister plenipotentiary in a country ruled by an American rear admiral) complains not only of torture, of the denial of liberty, but of a faulty system of taxation and waste in its expenditure. Emphatically the situation requires investigation. The navy department is ruling three republics without their consent primarily in the interests of their American creditors, with a blissful irresponsibility even as regards congress or the American public. Supposing that conditions in Nicaragua, Santo Domingo, and Haiti prior to our intervention were as bad as their critics assert—it is a sorry world if we can discover no way of helping to educate “backward” people without subjecting them to flagrant economic and political imperialism.

Porto Rico welcomed American annexation and her case is not on all fours with her neighbor’s. Nevertheless, our territorial rule leaves something to be desired. During the year 1917-’18 only 142,846 children out of 427,668 of school age were actually enrolled in the public schools. The total wealth of the island is in the hands of 15 per cent of the population; 14 per cent is in the hands of native Porto Ricans; 67 per cent in the hands of Americans. Wages, housing, and health conditions are wretched. The extension of this sort of thing in Mexico and the Caribbean countries is not our idea of civilizing people.—The World Tomorrow.

records.summary_en: The *Richmond times-dispatch* published a report by Military Governor Rear Admiral Thomas Snowden detailing administrative progress in Santo Domingo. Snowden reported that internal revenue collections had increased from $700,000 to approximately $3,500,000 annually and that regressive taxes were replaced with direct property taxes. He stated that the republic's floating debt was cleared, the 1908 loan was on course to be retired thirty years early by 1926, and administrative savings were funding new schools, highways, and sanitation projects.

records.summary_en: The *Pine Bluff daily graphic* reported that Julio M. Cestero of the Dominican junta issued a statement asserting that Dominican citizens never sought U.S. intervention and continually demanded the return of their national sovereignty. In a concurrent release, Secretary of State Colby defended American policy, stating that military intervention in Haiti was prompted by chronic bloodshed and the 1915 lynching of President Guillaume Sam in the French legation. Colby maintained that the United States acted under the Monroe Doctrine to restore order and preempt European military intervention.
records.summary_es: El *Pine Bluff daily graphic* informó que Julio M. Cestero, de la junta dominicana, emitió una declaración afirmando que los ciudadanos dominicanos nunca solicitaron la intervención de Estados Unidos y que exigían continuamente la restitución de su soberanía nacional. En un comunicado simultáneo, el secretario de Estado Colby defendió la política estadounidense, señalando que la intervención militar en Haití fue provocada por el derramamiento de sangre crónico y el linchamiento en 1915 del presidente Guillaume Sam en la legación francesa. Colby sostuvo que Estados Unidos actuó en virtud de la Doctrina Monroe para restablecer el orden y prevenir una intervención militar europea.

Referring to the recent declarations by Senator Harding and Secretary of the Navy Daniels, Cestero declared the citizens of the Dominican republic "have never sought the present American intervention" and have never ceased to ask for "restoration of their freedom and sovereignty." "As is well known, for many years, prior to 1915, the island of Haiti was the scene of chronic disorders. records.summary_en: The *Ogden standard-examiner* reported Secretary of State Colby's statement that the United States hoped to withdraw from Haiti as its mission to stabilize the republic neared completion. records.summary_en: The *Evening star* published a historical overview of the Dominican Republic, detailing its initial settlement by Spain, the eradication of indigenous inhabitants, and the importation of enslaved Africans. The article described how an eighteenth-century uprising abolished slavery and expelled colonizers, followed by shifts between Spanish and Haitian rule until the Dominican Republic secured independence in 1844. It observed that despite preserving Spanish language and institutions, the nation experienced frequent political coups and revolutions throughout its history.
records.summary_es: El *Evening star* publicó una reseña histórica de la República Dominicana, detallando su colonización inicial por parte de España, la desaparición de los pobladores indígenas y la importación de africanos esclavizados. El artículo describió cómo un levantamiento en el siglo XVIII abolió la esclavitud y expulsó a los colonizadores, seguido de sucesivas alternancias entre el dominio español y el haitiano hasta que la República Dominicana consolidó su independencia en 1844. Observó que, a pesar de conservar la lengua y las instituciones españolas, la nación experimentó frecuentes golpes políticos y revoluciones a lo largo de su historia.

After a turbulent history, during which the native Indians were exterminated and thousands of African slaves were imported, the latter, assisted by mulatto freemen, rose, in the last years of the eighteenth century, abolished slavery, and drove their oppressors from the island. Though the land of the Dominican Republic reverted for a while to Spanish control, and later was conquered by the Republic of Haiti, with which it shares the island, it established its independence in 1844 and has retained its individuality since. Johnson characterized the occupation of Haiti as pure economic exploitation, describing native resistance fighters as patriots rather than outlaws. records.headline: The possibility that the island of Haiti might become a pawn
records.summary_en: The *Springfield weekly Republican* discussed prospective U.S. withdrawal from Santo Domingo, observing that wartime strategic concerns and foreign debt disputes had prompted military guardianship over the island of Hispaniola. Acting Secretary of State Davis noted that the occupation grew out of the 1907 convention establishing an American customs receivership and barring unauthorized debt expansion. The article observed that Dominican authorities later violated the convention by increasing public debt to finance the suppression of domestic rebellions.
records.summary_es: El *Springfield weekly Republican* analizó la proyectada retirada de Estados Unidos de Santo Domingo, observando que las preocupaciones estratégicas en tiempos de guerra y las disputas por la deuda externa habían motivado la tutela militar sobre la isla de La Española. El secretario de Estado interino Davis señaló que la ocupación derivó de la convención de 1907, la cual estableció la receptoría general de aduanas estadounidense y prohibió el aumento no autorizado de la deuda. El artículo indicó que las autoridades dominicanas violaron posteriormente dicha convención al incrementar la deuda pública para financiar la represión de rebeliones internas.
records.passage: steps looking to its withdrawal suggests an experience in guardianship of an interesting sort. The public would like to hear more about it. It is more than a coincidence, of course, that the period of military occupation has been commensurate with the latter half of the war and the early stage of international adjustment. The possibility that the island of Haiti might become a pawn in the great game explains in part, no doubt, the relation of the United States toward the island's two little republics during the past few years. It was important that they should be assured stable and responsible government of some sort in view of foreign claims upon their resources and foreign appreciation of their strategic location. The present status of Santo Domingo, or the Dominican Republic, is a direct outgrowth, however, of conditions existing long before the war. It was in 1907, in the administration of President Roosevelt, that a treaty was concluded, as Acting Secretary of State Davis explains, by which Santo Domingo agreed to the appointment of an American receiver-general of customs for the purpose of meeting the obligations of the national debt and also agreed that the debt should not be increased without the approval of the United States. This course was held to be desirable because of the danger of European intervention prompted by the Dominicans' failure to pay the interest on their foreign loans. records.summary_en: The *Evening star* reported that the United States initiated steps toward withdrawing forces from Santo Domingo and establishing a native governing commission to restore self-government. The report recounted that naval officers instituted military rule in 1916 after provisional president Francisco Henriquez y Carvajal refused terms of a proposed treaty. Under the occupation, Dominican school enrollment grew from 18,000 to 100,000 pupils, and gross annual revenues expanded from $4,600,000 to over $7,000,000.

Durante la ocupación, la matrícula escolar dominicana aumentó de 18 000 a 100 000 alumnos, y los ingresos fiscales brutos anuales se incrementaron de 4 600 000 dólares a más de 7 000 000 de dólares.

records.headline: It is frequently said that a revolution would follow the departure
records.summary_en: The *Dearborn independent* argued that an immediate withdrawal of American marines from Haiti would quickly lead to revolution and governmental collapse. The article contrasted the French colonial period's agricultural prosperity with the nation's condition following Toussaint L'Ouverture's uprising and Jean-Jacques Dessalines's 1804 declaration of independence. It asserted that more than a century of post-independence conflict and despotic leadership had ruined the country's plantations and civil institutions.

records.summary_en: The *Evening star* reported that President Harding, Secretary Hughes, and Secretary Denby approved a proclamation establishing procedures for withdrawing the military government from the Dominican Republic. The plan directed primary assemblies to convene within a month to choose electors, who would elect senators and deputies and nominate judges under the Dominican constitution. Delegates appointed by the military governor would then negotiate an evacuation convention to ratify military government acts, validate a $2,500,000 public works loan, and extend customs receivership duties.
records.summary_es: El *Evening star* informó que el presidente Harding, el secretario Hughes y el secretario Denby aprobaron una proclama que establecía el procedimiento para retirar el gobierno militar de la República Dominicana. Delegados designados por el gobernador militar negociarían luego una convención de evacuación para ratificar las disposiciones del gobierno militar, convalidar un préstamo de 2 500 000 dólares para obras públicas y prorrogar las funciones de la receptoría de aduanas.

During the occupation, the United States oversaw the construction of schools and highways funded through a $2,500,000 loan. Officials warned that American marines would remain and military rule would continue unless the Dominican government provided binding assurances that these financial commitments would be fulfilled.

Las autoridades advirtieron que los infantes de marina estadounidenses permanecerían y el régimen militar continuaría a menos que el gobierno dominicano brindara seguridades vinculantes de que se cumplirían dichos compromisos financieros.

The Government finds itself in the position of the person who has adopted a ward, has given to it a rudimentary education and has incurred obligations for its further improvement, and desires to assure itself that these obligations will be observed. It might happen that the ward would prove unwilling to carry out the terms of these obligations. That is the situation in which the Government of the United States finds itself. During its occupation the United States started the construction of schools, roads and other improvements, and negotiated a minimum loan of $2,500,000 to insure the completion of those improvements for the advantage of the Dominican people. Before evacuating the republic the Government of the United States wants assurance doubly sure that those obligations will be taken care of. Without such assurances the American marines will remain in the island and the present military Government will continue. records.summary_en: The *Chicago whip* reported on continued resistance to the U.S. occupation of Haiti, mocking claims of mutual devotion between Haitians and military authorities while officials acknowledged that ending martial law would spark immediate revolt. The paper published a statement by Haitian Hague delegate Pierre Hudicourt, who traveled to Washington to formally protest the occupation before the Senate. Hudicourt condemned the invasion as an assault on national sovereignty driven by foreign commercial interests and urged the American public to demand military withdrawal.

records.full_text:
THE AMERICAN EMPIRE

[Selected]

In none of the lands that America has guided and protected during the last generation is more interesting than the great island often called Haiti, but more correctly known as Santo Domingo—the island which lies between Cuba and Porto Rico. It is unquestionably the finest of the West Indies—a land of lofty mountains clothed with splendid forests and a rich variety of minerals; a land of spacious plateaus and fertile plains that are capable of producing the finest of sugar, tobacco and other tropical products. Santo Domingo would appear predestined by nature to be the richest and most prosperous of the West Indies. As a matter of fact it lost its early prosperity long ago, and for more than a century has been sunk in a backwardness and misery from which, under recent American guidance, it is only now beginning to emerge. The story of the turbulent past of Santo Domingo and of its new start is a story well worth telling.

As its double name suggests, the island of Santo Domingo, which has an area of some thirty thousand square miles (about half the area of New England), is divided politically into two distinct nations. The western third forms the republic of Haiti; the eastern two-thirds constitutes the Dominican Republic. Haiti is a nation of Negroes; it has only a few mulattoes and no native whites. The people speak a corrupt French and look to France for their culture. The Dominican Republic, on the other hand, is a Spanish-speaking land, much like Cuba and Porto Rico. It has a considerable white or near-white upper class, a peasantry of mixed blood (Indian, white and African) and relatively few full-blooded Negroes.

Christopher Columbus discovered Santo Domingo, and the island was the first Spanish colony in the New World. It had a fine start, for at first the whole colonizing energy of Spain flowed into that relatively small insular area. Within thirty years multitudes of colonists had covered the land with towns of stone. Even now, after four centuries of decay, Santo Domingo, the capital city, still shows those stately mansions proudly described by an early Spanish historian as “so fair and large that they may well receive any lord or noble of Spain.”

During those thirty years the blood of a million Indians paid for the ingots of gold and silver that amazed the Spanish court. But at the end of that exciting period the bloodshed ceased. Mexico and Peru were conquered, the mines of Santo Domingo became insignificant beside the mines of the mainland, and the Indian workers were dead. The restless, fortune-hunting conquistadores who had made up the bulk of the population of Santo Domingo flocked away to the more tempting Spanish Main; and depopulated Spanish Santo Domingo almost sank into oblivion.

So matters stood for perhaps a hundred years. Then, just about the time when our ancestors were settling the Atlantic seaboard of North America, the coming of the French revived the prosperity of Santo Domingo. The Spaniards had colonized only the eastern part of the island—the part now known as the Dominican Republic; they had left the western part, which is today known as Haiti, virtually uninhabited, and the deserted coasts became the haunt of the famous buccaneers. The buccaneers were mainly French, and in time France claimed the region they had occupied, introduced respectable immigrants and made it a colony known as the French part of Santo Domingo. Like the Spaniards, the French devoted themselves to agriculture, and soon showed what marvelous productiveness the island had. During the eighteenth century French Santo Domingo was by far the most flourishing colony in the West Indies. Covered with fine plantations and cultivated to the very mountain crests, the French part of Santo Domingo, though only a trifle larger than the state of Massachusetts, furnished not only France but half Europe with sugar, coffee and other tropical products.

In order to obtain the labor necessary for so many plantations the French brought in multitudes of Negro slaves, who soon vastly outnumbered the white population. When the French Revolution convulsed France and its colonies, the Negroes of French Santo Domingo took advantage of the situation, revolted and after a long struggle succeeded in expelling the whites. Then they declared their independence, and in the year 1804 set up the republic of Haiti, the old Indian name for the land. About twenty years later the eastern part of the island threw off Spanish rule and became the Dominican Republic.

But independence meant neither peace nor prosperity. Having gained their freedom, the Haitians and the Dominicans began to misuse it. Both peoples showed from the first an utter lack of capacity for orderly self-government. The “Black Republic” of Haiti quickly degenerated into an absurd burlesque of France. The government sedulously copied French political forms; and the republic was sometimes styled a kingdom, sometimes an empire. One of the rulers of Haiti especially distinguished himself by creating a whole nobility headed by four princes and fifty-nine dukes; innumerable marquises, counts and barons completed the pompous galaxy that surrounded the “imperial” throne. Meanwhile Haiti itself went to rack and ruin. An endless succession of black and mulatto “generals” at the head of tatterdemalion “armies” fought ferociously for the spoils of office and kept the land plunged in a horrid and interminable anarchy. Revolution succeeded revolution and in those senseless civil wars the fine, well-constructed towns that the French had left were destroyed and replaced by squalid shacks, and the broad plantations and shaded highroads of the countryside again became bush and forest.

In the Spanish (Dominican) Republic colonial prosperity was destroyed because the Haitians repeatedly invaded and conquered it. How the Haitians ruled their own country suggests how they ruled the Dominicans; and finally, when the Dominicans at last succeeded in expelling them, the Dominican Republic continued to flounder in the bog of misgovernment and revolution.

By the beginning of the present century things had become so bad that European intervention seemed certain. Both republics had piled up huge foreign debts that they could not pay. Some of the creditors were Americans, but most of them were Europeans, particularly Englishmen, Frenchmen and Germans.

Now, it soon became clear that whatever the United States might think about its duty in the matter, the European nations would not put up with conditions much longer. In fact, European warships were already appearing off the coast and threatening to bombard the ports unless the money that was due was paid. But if European powers seized the ports of Santo Domingo, what would become of the Monroe Doctrine, one of the corner stones of our foreign policy?

Faced with that critical situation, President Roosevelt succeeded in 1905 in getting the Dominican government to sign an agreement that permitted the United States to adjust the Dominican debt and to administer the customs for the benefit of creditors. The effects of American intervention were instantly felt.

Hitherto the goal of every revolutionist had been the nearest customhouse, because the customs were almost the only source of revenue. If a revolutionist could seize a customhouse, he could maintain an army. But when the United States took charge of the customhouses, the customs officials turned over 45 per cent of the revenue to the Dominican government for its current expenses and applied the remaining 55 per cent to paying the foreign debt. At once the customhouses ceased to be prizes for revolutionists, because an American collector with American naval forces behind him was in charge. Revolutions promptly stopped, and for nearly ten years the Dominican Republic enjoyed unprecedented peace and prosperity. The country developed rapidly; roads, harbors, schools and public buildings were constructed, and the public debt was steadily reduced.

Then came the World War. The withdrawal of American naval vessels to European waters was the signal for fresh revolutions. A series of uprisings threatened to undo all that had been accomplished. In 1916 the United States intervened with armed force. American marines landed, deposed the revolutionary government and set up a military administration headed by an American naval officer. Under American military rule the republic was completely disarmed, banditry was suppressed, and order was firmly established.

Meanwhile, across the border in Haiti, conditions had gone from bad to worse. Between 1908 and 1915 seven presidents were successively overthrown, assassinated or driven into exile. When the World War broke out, German influence in Haiti was strong, and there was danger that Germany might seize a naval base on the island. In July, 1915, after a particularly shocking massacre of political prisoners, American marines landed at Port-au-Prince. A treaty was negotiated between the United States and Haiti under which the United States assumed control of the finances and police of the republic.

Under American supervision the gendarmery was organized, public works were pushed forward, and the country was cleared of the cacos, or mountain bandits, who had terrorized the population for generations. Today both republics on the island of Santo Domingo are peacefully developing their immense natural resources under American guidance and protection.

Regarding Haiti, the committee concluded that reducing marine forces would inevitably lead to renewed brigandage and revolution. While acknowledging administrative blunders and instances of cruelty toward natives, the report maintained that the occupation had established peace, solvency, and security.

En cuanto a Haití, la comisión concluyó que reducir los efectivos de infantería de marina conduciría inevitablemente a un rebrote del bandolerismo y la revolución. Pese a reconocer desatinos administrativos y casos de crueldad hacia la población nativa, el informe sostuvo que la ocupación había establecido paz, solvencia financiera y seguridad.

The report justified the intervention as necessary to protect the Monroe Doctrine against German influence and French troop landings following the collapse of Haitian credit. However, the committee admitted that U.S. authorities had made mistakes in selecting personnel and defining administrative responsibilities.

No obstante, la comisión admitió que las autoridades estadounidenses habían cometido errores en la selección de personal y en la definición de las responsabilidades administrativas.

records.summary_en: The *Evening star* detailed an agreement between Dominican leaders and American authorities to establish a provisional government preparatory to ending the military occupation. Under the arrangement, executive departments would be transferred to Dominican ministers, expenditures would follow established budgets, and American troops would concentrate into select centers while the national police preserved order. Full American evacuation was conditioned on a newly elected constitutional government ratifying executive orders and the 1918 and 1922 bond issues.
records.summary_es: El *Evening star* detalló un acuerdo entre dirigentes dominicanos y autoridades estadounidenses para establecer un gobierno provisional preparatorio para poner fin a la ocupación militar. En virtud del pacto, los departamentos ejecutivos se transferirían a ministros dominicanos, los gastos se ajustarían a los presupuestos establecidos y las tropas estadounidenses se concentrarían en determinados centros mientras la policía nacional preservaba el orden. La evacuación estadounidense definitiva quedaba condicionada a que un nuevo gobierno constitucional electo ratificara las órdenes ejecutivas y las emisiones de bonos de 1918 y 1922.

records.summary_en: The *Pleasantville press* reported that a Senate committee led by Senator Medill McCormick described the American record in Haiti as one of both achievement and failure, admitting instances of military cruelty and administrative mistakes. The committee maintained that intervention was necessary to defend the Monroe Doctrine against European threats following the collapse of Haitian credit and public order. It concluded that under the bilateral treaty, the occupation had successfully established national peace, financial solvency, and security.

La comisión sostuvo que la intervención fue indispensable para defender la Doctrina Monroe de amenazas europeas tras el descalabro del crédito y del orden público en Haití. Concluyó que, en el marco del tratado bilateral, la ocupación había logrado instaurar la paz nacional, la solvencia económica y la seguridad.

records.summary_en: Following the State Department's agreement to withdraw American military forces from San Domingo, the provisional government of the Dominican Republic will assume administrative powers from the date of its installation. It will legislate to regulate the holding of elections, reorganize provincial and municipal government and enable the Dominican people to amend the constitution as they deem appropriate, and from that date it will be alone responsible for its acts, ending seven years of American military government.

Legislará para regular la celebración de elecciones, reorganizará los gobiernos provinciales y municipales y permitirá al pueblo dominicano enmendar la constitución como lo considere apropiado, y desde esa fecha será el único responsable de sus actos, poniendo fin a siete años de gobierno militar estadounidense.

records.summary_en: The *Birmingham age-herald* commented that the planned withdrawal of American troops after seven years proved the success of the U.S. mission to stabilize the Dominican Republic and prepare it for self-government. The editorial cited extensive road construction, suppression of banditry, sanitary improvements, and fiscal reforms as permanent benefits of the occupation. It argued that the impending military evacuation refuted accusations that the United States harbored imperialistic designs in Santo Domingo.
records.summary_es: El *Birmingham age-herald* comentó que la planeada retirada de las tropas estadounidenses tras siete años demostraba el éxito de la misión de Estados Unidos para estabilizar la República Dominicana y prepararla para el autogobierno. El editorial citó la extensa construcción de caminos, la supresión del bandolerismo, las mejoras sanitarias y las reformas fiscales como beneficios permanentes de la ocupación. Sostuvo que la inminente evacuación militar refutaba las acusaciones de que Estados Unidos albergaba designios imperialistas en Santo Domingo.
records.passage: result of the state department's decision to withdraw American troops from the Dominican republic. The American occupation of Santo Domingo lasted for seven years, and while there has been much criticism of the government for its Dominican policy, the task of restoring order and placing the Dominican people in a position to govern themselves has apparently been accomplished. Furthermore, by the building of roads, the protection of private property, the breaking up of banditry, sanitation and government economies, the republic and its people are in far better case than they otherwise would have been. The withdrawal of American troops should put an end to the accusations that the United States was pursuing a high-handed and imperialistic policy in its treatment of Santo Domingo.
