Today, a woman in her 30’s she is credited with being the first person to grow human cancer in animals. The result of her work may speed up science's efforts to find a cure for the dread malady. Dr. Helene Wallace Toolan, a small, pretty woman with curly brown hair and grey eyes, is an associate at the Sloan-Kettering Institute research unit of the Memorial Center for Cancer and Allied Diseases. Dr. Toolan, an example of the women of our time who have become VIP’s in fields once considered for men only, works with her six assistants in one of the liveliest laboratories in the Institute. records.summary_en: The Evening Star reviewed the history of Caribbean political conflicts, tracing how Venezuelan exiles and Romulo Betancourt helped form the Caribbean Legion to invade Rafael Trujillo's Dominican Republic. Following the collapse of those invasion attempts, legion remnants aided Jose Figueres in establishing power in Costa Rica during the 1948 revolution. Dictators Trujillo and Anastasio Somoza accused Figueres of harboring communist conspirators and reforming the legion to attack their regimes, charges Figueres dismissed as dictatorial paranoia.
records.summary_es: El *Evening Star* repasó la historia de los conflictos políticos del Caribe, reseñando cómo los exiliados venezolanos y Rómulo Betancourt colaboraron en la formación de la Legión del Caribe para invadir la República Dominicana de Rafael Trujillo. Tras el fracaso de aquellas intentonas de invasión, los remanentes de la legión ayudaron a José Figueres a afianzarse en el poder en Costa Rica durante la revolución de 1948. Los dictadores Trujillo y Anastasio Somoza acusaron a Figueres de cobijar a conspiradores comunistas y reorganizar la legión para atacar a sus regímenes, señalamientos que Figueres desestimó considerándolos paranoia dictatorial.

When the old military regime was overthrown, its leaders obtained territorial asylum in the Dominican Republic. There, under the tutelage of President Rafael Trujillo Molina, they plotted a counter-revolution. Learning about this, Betancourt and party helped organize an expedi tionary force of asylees from Carib bean totalitarian regimes to invade the Dominican Republic. This force, named the Caribbean Legion, trained in Cuba and failed at two attempts to invade Trujillo's land. It then disintegrated. Costa Rican Adventure Remnants of the legion figured in a revolution that broke out in Costa Rica late in 1948. A conserva tive invalidated the free election of a liberal president. Jose Figueres mobilized a group of young liberals and forced the Conservative-Com munist coalition out, set himself up as provisional president, and even tually turned the government over to the constitutionally elected presi dent. Betancourt is in Costa Rica, with his friend, Figueres. Dr. Joaquin Balaguer, minister of education, has said that in two more years “we will have no more illiteracy in the Dominican Republic.”’ A government census in 1950 disclosed that there were 830,537 illiterates. records.summary_en: Hurricane Katie beat a path across the Dominican Republic, slamming into the south shore with 115-mile winds the night before, but the mountains of Hispaniola distorted the storm and weakened her winds to about 40 or 50 miles an hour. At noon her center was near Puerto Plata, moving northeast at about 14 miles an hour, and she was expected to regain hurricane force over the open Atlantic without threatening the United States mainland.

records.summary_en: New York detectives searched the Dominican freighter Fundación in Brooklyn for four hours after the Dominican revolutionary leader Nicolás Silfa charged that Jesús de Galíndez, a foe of Generalissimo Rafael Trujillo, had been thrown alive into a steaming boiler aboard the ship. The detectives questioned the 36 crew members and found not a single solid clue to Galíndez's fate, though the boilers' openings were large enough to squeeze a man through. A representative of the Ward Lines, which controls the Dominican Steamship Line, said opening a boiler door while it was fired would burn a man to a crisp, and Silfa, in a statement afterwards, repeated his charge that Galíndez's body was thrown into the firebox on Trujillo's orders.

It also says that “1957 will bring the culmination of important jointly achievements between the two sister nations and a direct inter KNOW THY NEIGHBOR By ANTONIO RUIZ HAITI In all the seaports, the chief cities of the Republic of Haiti, beautiful green mountains form the background of the charming landscape. Of the total area of the country of 10,700 square miles, 8,000 square miles are mountains. There are three principal ranges with several large plains lying be tween them and along their out er fringes. One range, including large groups known as La Horte and La Selle, extends from east to west along the lower peninsula, while the other two stretch from the southeast to the northeast across the mainland an northern peninsula. The highest mountain in Haiti is Morne La Selle in the southeast, which reaches an altitude of 8,700 feet above sea level. There are four plains of major importance in the country: the North Plain, lying along the northern east coast be tween the mountains and the sea; the Central Plain, a large interior flatland, bordering the Dominican Republic, and the Artibonite and Cul-de-Sac Plains, which spread eastward from the Gulf of Gonave. Haiti has numerous rivers, most of them short, rapid streams coursing down the mountain slopes into the sea. The Artibonite River, however, which drains the Arti bonite Plain on its way to the Gulf of Gonave, has a length of 200 miles from its headwaters in the Dominican Republic to its mouth.

U. S. Government Rejects
Dominican Statements on
Murphy’s Disappearance

WASHINGTON, March 16 (UP) The United States rejected today the Dominican government explanation about the mysterious disappearance of the North American aviator Gerald L. Murphy, in the Dominican Republic.

23 years old Murphy disappeared in the Dominican Republic on December 3rd. last.

In official note, delivered by the United States Embassy in Ciudad Trujillo, the U. S. government rejected the explanation offered by the Dominican government that Murphy was assassinated by the Dominican pilot Octavio de la Maza, who later committed suicide at Ciudad Trujillo, leaving a letter in which he confessed his crime.

A copy of the note delivered in Ciudad Trujillo was handed today to the Dominican Ambassador in Washington, Dr. Joaquín Salazar.

The note urges the Dominican Government to continue “vigorously” the investigation on the disappearance of Murphy, who was said to have been the pilot who took to the Dominican Republic professor Jesús de Galíndez, who disappeared in New York on March 12, 1956. It has also been said Murphy was murdered because he talked too much.

Last January, the Dominican Government delivered to the State Department an alleged letter-confession of pilot de la Maza and other documents, all of which have been carefully examined by the FBI.

The note delivered today by the U. S. Government says:

“Upon examination of these documents and evidence, this Government has reached the conclusion that, if the handwriting samples submitted by Dominican authorities as belonging to Maza are really his, that means the suicide note was not written by de la Maza.”

Other points rejected by the State Department over the explanation are:

1. That Murphy did not know any person with political influence in the Dominican Republic. The U. S. investigation, says the Department of State, shows that Murphy had “good relations” with high Dominican officials, including the then Undersecretary of the Army, now Consul General in New York, Arturo Espaillat.

2. That Murphy’s income while in the Dominican Republic was $350 per month. The investigation shows, the note says, that the missing pilot had a capital substantially bigger than what Dominican authorities say.

“The Government of the United States is gravely concerned by the disappearance of one of its citizens in the Dominican Republic — the note says — and assumes this concern is shared by the Dominican Government.”

Murphy, as de la Maza, worked for the Dominican Air Line, and disappeared when he had announced his intention to return to the United States for good.

As soon as the contents of the note were revealed, Rep. Charles O. Porter, who has realized a personal investigation on Murphy’s disappearance, said the note shows the need of a Congress investigation of the relations of the United States with the Dominican Republic.

records.full_text:
Rebels Seize
Army Station
In Venezuela

By ARISTEDES MOLEON

CARACAS, Venezuela (AP) — Rebels seized control of an army regiment’s headquarters at San Cristobal near the Colombian border today in an attempt to set off nationwide revolt against President Romulo Betancourt’s government.

Betancourt ordered soldiers to San Cristobal to quell the uprising, and pledges of support came to him at once from military, political and civilian sources.

The moderate Venezuelan President announced he would use all constitutional powers to crush the rebellion, but would not suspend constitutional guarantees in this oil-rich nation.

The strong military garrison at Caracas announced its support at once for Betancourt’s government.

Leaders of the nation’s three major political parties spoke over a national radio network, appealing to their followers in San Cristobal to vigorously oppose the insurrection.

The rebels seized control of the Simon Bolivar army regiment’s headquarters at San Cristobal.

Gen. Pedro Jose Quevado, commander of the Venezuelan armed forces, urged “my companions in arms to set an example of common sense and maturity” and support the constitutional government.

The head of the Central Workers Organization, Jose Gonzalez Navarro, called for its 1,200,000 members to go on strike. He said this would be a demonstration of opposition to the “criminal” insurrection which, he declared, was counting on the support of the Dominican Republic.

The government had announced last Saturday that it had smashed a plot for an armed invasion of Venezuela from Colombia by officers who were dismissed from the army for their support of former dictator Gen. Marcos Perez Jimenez.

Venezuelan naval craft and air force planes were patrolling the coast today on the lookout for two fishing boats which the minister of defense, General Jose Lopez Henrique, said had sailed from Spain with arms for the plotters.

Betancourt, a moderate with a reputation as a social reformer, has faced a series of minor uprisings, threats and harassments since he took office early in 1959. He was elected a year after the overthrow of Perez Jimenez, now in exile in Florida.

Venezuela, a tropical country, lies on the northern hump of South America facing the Caribbean. It has about six million people, and because of the nation’s rich resources, has the highest per capita income in South America.

records.full_text:
Change For Better Hoped
U.S. Watches Trend In D.R.

WASHINGTON (AP)—Secretary of State Dean Rusk set out today on his delayed trip to join President Kennedy in Europe, signalling a belief that the assassination of Dominican dictator Rafael L. Trujillo will not result in the immediate turmoil officials had feared.

Rusk had been scheduled to leave Wednesday to back up Kennedy in his talks in Paris with French President Charles de Gaulle and later in Vienna with Soviet Premier Khrushchev. Instead he was held here to take personal charge of dealing with the Dominican situation.

That decision underscored the anxiety with which American officials were watching for clues as to which way the Caribbean country will shift.

Rusk’s plane was due in Paris at 9 a.m. Paris time Friday.

Just before takeoff, Rusk told newsmen at National Airport that there is no way of knowing at this time what kind of government will finally take over in the Dominican Republic.

U.S. authorities said information seeping out from tightly censored Ciudad Trujillo indicated the Trujillo group, under figurehead President Jouquin Balaguer, still was in control.

President Kennedy and Rusk, in telephone contact between Paris and Washington, were said to be agreed that the Dominican situation was of such top priority that Rusk could do more by setting the U.S. course as the situation clears than by speeding off to the summit talks.

Informed sources said both the President and the secretary of state had the recent Cuban invasion fiasco very much in mind and were determined to avoid any mistake on the neighboring Caribbean island. They feel the outcome will affect the whole of U.S.-Latin American affairs.

Balking Washington strategists was a scarcity of solid information. Officials said they did not yet know who engineered the assassination or who might be behind the figurehead president who continued in office, Joaquin Balaguer. They said their evidence did not point to pro-Communist Cuba or other foreign manipulators.

The only post-assassination communication from the U.S. Consulate in Ciudad Trujillo reported by late Wednesday was a brief message from Consul General Henry Dearborn saying the capital was calm and he knew of no injury to the 5,200 citizens in the country.

Some U.S. authorities foresaw a struggle for power, both within the Trujillo group and between it and the large elements of Dominican society persecuted during the dictator’s 31-year rule. A continued harsh rightwing regime without Trujillo’s personal leadership, they reasoned, would set off revolt—perhaps pro-Castro the next time.

The United States had several lures to attract Trujillo’s successors down the democratic path, a main aim of Kennedy’s “alliance for progress” Latin American program.

One is resumption of U.S. aid, cut off when Washington joined the other American Republics last year in breaking diplomatic relations and normal commercial ties with Trujillo. Another is a boost in U.S. sugar purchases. The Dominican economy has been sagging.

The United States could also take a leading role in a move by the hemisphere organization, the Organization of American States, in readmitting a progressive Dominican regime to the American family.

Washington congressional reaction was mixed.

Sen. George Smathers, D-Fla., recommended that U.S. Marines be landed in the Dominican Republic to prevent a Communist takeover.

Sens. Homer E. Capehart, R-Ind., Olin D. Johnston, D-S.C., and Allen J. Ellender, D-La., saw a Red Castroite takeover in prospect as a result of Trujillo’s death.

The sole holdover was newly appointed Defense Minister Santos Mélido Marte, who succeeded Major General José René Román following the latter's arrest for complicity in Rafael Trujillo's assassination.

records.summary_en: The *Evening Star* reported that President Joaquín Balaguer declared his government in full control following the expulsion of returning members of the Trujillo family. Speaking as U.S. warships patrolled offshore, Balaguer announced the armed forces solidly backed his administration and pledged to unveil new measures to establish democratic institutions.
records.summary_es: El *Evening Star* informó que el presidente Joaquín Balaguer declaró a su gobierno en pleno control tras la expulsión de los miembros de la familia Trujillo que pretendían retornar. Hablando mientras buques de guerra estadounidenses patrullaban frente a las costas, Balaguer anunció que las fuerzas armadas respaldaban slidamente a su administración y prometió revelar nuevas medidas para instaurar instituciones democráticas.
records.passage: CIUDAD TRUJILLO, Dominican Republic, Nov. 22 (AP).—President Joaquin Balaguer says the Dominican armed forces have lined up solidly behind him and that threats by antidemocratic diehards to topple his government have been eliminated. Mr. Balaguer, in a radio address last night, claimed the government had emerged in full control from the crisis prompted by the return of two Trujillo family leaders last week. Their return raised speculation of a resurgence of Trujillo rule and brought a covey of United States warships hovering offshore. Mr. Balaguer declared that the crisis was created by the "ambitious and senselessness of some men of rural mentality.” He said they included two cabinet members but offered no further identification. Mr. Balaguer’s address on the state of the nation obviously was intended in part to squelch reports of rumblings in military ranks over some of his military appointees named to succeed exiled Trujillos. He said there was “propaganda tending to create a false impression” that threats of a coup d’etat remained but warned Dominicans not to take stock in such reports. Opposition Leaders Welcomed As lights from United States warships still twinkled off shore, Mr. Balaguer said he would announce new plans tomorrow to hasten the installation of democratic processes in the land after three decades of the late Generalissimo Rafael Trujillo’s feudal dictatorship. records.headline: This Spanish-language essay argues that the immense majority of the Dominican people accept Trujillo's tyrannical regime
records.summary_en: This Spanish-language essay argues that the immense majority of the Dominican people accept Trujillo's tyrannical regime only out of an imperative need for collective survival, hate and fear it, and should be regarded as the despot's passive victims rather than held responsible for it. It says three things should not be counted against that majority: having enrolled in Trujillo's political parties, whose membership the regime tied to civil rights, having held public employment, which is service to the state and not to the regime, and having worked in a business of Trujillo or his followers, given the persecution system known as the 'lepra'.
records.summary_es: Este ensayo en español argumenta que la inmensa mayoría del pueblo dominicano acepta el régimen tiránico de Trujillo solo por una imperiosa necesidad de supervivencia colectiva, lo odia y le teme, y debe ser considerada víctima pasiva del déspota en lugar de hacérsele responsable de él. Dice que tres cosas no deben contarse en contra de esa mayoría: haberse inscrito en los partidos políticos de Trujillo, cuya militancia el régimen vinculó a los derechos civiles, haber servido un empleo público, que es servir al estado y no al régimen, y haber trabajado en una empresa de Trujillo o de sus secuaces, dado el sistema de persecución conocido como la «lepra».

records.summary_en: The *Evening Star* reported the inauguration of a transitional Council of State in Santo Domingo, with opposition leader Rafael Bonnelly sworn in as vice president to eventually succeed President Joaquín Balaguer. The seven-member council included Antonio Imbert and Luis Amiama Tió, the sole surviving conspirators of the plot that assassinated Rafael Trujillo.

El consejo de siete miembros incluía a Antonio Imbert y a Luis Amiama Tió, los únicos conspiradores sobrevivientes de la trama que dio muerte a Rafael Trujillo.

Mr. Balaguer drew up the plan for an interim government and promised to quit when the Organization of American States lifts its economic and diplomatic sanctions against the Dominican Republic. Following lukewarm approval of the council plan by opposition factions, President Kennedy announced that the United States favored lifting the sanctions imposed against the old Trujillo regime for plotting to assassinate President Romulo Betancourt of Venezuela. Mr. Bonnelly represents the National Civic Union, major opposition faction which agreed to give the Balaguer plan a chance after weeks of off-and-on negotiations. records.summary_en: The *Evening Star* reported that OAS Secretary General José A. Mora and Inter-American Development Bank President Felipe Herrera scheduled missions to Santo Domingo to assess reconstruction aid under the Alliance for Progress. Mora planned discussions with President Joaquín Balaguer and incoming interim leader Rafael Bonnelly to prepare substantial technical and financial assistance programs.
records.summary_es: El *Evening Star* informó que el secretario general de la OEA, José A. Mora, y el presidente del Banco Interamericano de Desarrollo, Felipe Herrera, programaron misiones a Santo Domingo para evaluar la ayuda a la reconstrucción en el marco de la Alianza para el Progreso. Mora tenía previsto mantener conversaciones con el presidente Joaquín Balaguer y con el mandatario interino entrante Rafael Bonnelly a fin de estructurar cuantiosos programas de asistencia técnica y financiera.
records.passage: This group has been described as a “pre-planning” mission to investigate what aid the Dominican Republic needs under the inter-American Alliance for Progress sponsored by the Kennedy administration. Bank Chief to Visit Felipe Herrera, president of the Inter-American Development Bank, also is scheduled to make a personal visit to investigate the possibility of low cost loans for Dominican reconstruction. The Inter-American Development Bank, with assets of over $1 billion, is the hemispheric institution which also administers a $394 million Social Progress Trust fund voted by Congress for the Alliance for Progress. Secretary General Mora’s visit is to last four days. Sources close to him say he will meet with Dominican President Joaquin Balaguer and Rafael Bonnelly, the chief representative of the democratic opposition on the new Council of State. President Balaguer, who is a holdover from the Trujillo regime, has said he will resign once the OAS sanctions are lifted. OAS sources expected, therefore, that most of Secretary General Mora’s dealings would be with Mr. Bonnelly. who will become interim President, and members of his group, the National Civic Union. Experts Gather Data In his statement here, Mr. Mora noted that experts of the OAS are busy collecting data which will be used in planning a technical co-operation program in both economic and social fields. A source close to Mr. Mora said a major aim of his visit is to lend more prestige to these efforts of the experts.

For the first 10 years of the Trujillo regime, Dr. Bonnelly stayed clear of any association with the govern ment, but in the 1940s he joined the official family. He was also rector of Santo Domingo University, a job in which he still takes pride since it gave him a chance to teach and direct what Dominicans consider the hemisphere’s oldest institution of learning. records.summary_en: The *Evening Star* reported that the Dominican Council of State headed by Rafael Bonnelly implemented significant economic reforms, including doubling sugar workers' minimum wages and launching public works. The transitional government confiscated the extensive holdings of the Trujillo family—redistributing an estimated 40 percent of the nation's wealth—while counting on pledged United States assistance for economic recovery.

El gobierno de transición confiscó los cuantiosos bienes de la familia Trujillo —redistribuyendo cerca del 40 por ciento de la riqueza nacional— mientras confiaba en la asistencia prometida por Estados Unidos para la recuperación económica.

It is the creed of basically conservative men with social consciences, men who believe in evolution, not revolution. Rather than drama, they want stability. They have already raised the basic wage of sugar workers 100 per cent—to a minimum of $3.25 per day. These and other lesser wage increases—plus confiscation of the huge Trujillo holdings—are estimated to have redistributed 40 per cent of the wealth of the country already. An emergency public works program emphasizing manpower more than scarce materials is also making the first minor dent in widescale unemployment. “We are open for foreign investment,” affirmed Mr. Bonnelly, “and we want it. But that investment must benefit both the Dominican people and the investors. It will be channeled through our new planning commission.” U. S. Aid Important It was a gentle—but clear—slap at the small trickle of North American “businessmen” who have arrived to speculate on the Dominican future. They check in at the best hotel in town and then pursue new officials with a high-pressure sales pitch. But the new leaders are far more intent on how the United States Government lives up to its commitments of all-out aid. This potential aid is the third and by far the strongest trump in government hands. By general consensus the aid is essential to swift economic recovery.

Obviously we take the position nowadays that armed intervention cannot be undertaken in this hemisphere, barring a spectacular threat to our security like the presence somewhere of Soviet rockets. There are ways, however, of accomplishing these things. For one thing, as we pointed out the other day, there is economic pressure. Our purchases from Haiti are not extensive. But, for instance, could we not get along without Haitian coffee while Duvalier remains in power? Duvalier could be toppled, as he should be, by the Haitians themselves— relatively few of them. The men to topple him are there and, sooner or later, one of them will organize the job. They need guns, grenades and explosives. records.summary_en: The *Evening Star* reported that the Organization of American States unanimously referred the latest border dispute between Haiti and the Dominican Republic to an investigatory fact-finding commission. U.S. officials acknowledged having little independent information regarding the rebel invasion in northern Haiti, while a representative for insurgent leader General Léon Cantave reported only minor skirmishes.

Funcionarios estadounidenses reconocieron disponer de escasa información independiente sobre la invasión rebelde en el norte de Haití, mientras un representante del líder insurgente, general Léon Cantave, reportó únicamente escaramuzas menores.
records.passage: strictly by the hemispheric principle of non-intervention, and that the invasion had been consequence of the dictatorial nature of the Duvalier regime. Like A Charade The performance on all sides had the earmarks of an oft repeated charade. It took the council exactly, four minutes of open debate—after an hour of private talk in an upstairs conference room—to approve unanimously the resolution turning the dispute over to the fact-finding commission. To a great extent, the attitude in the OAS reflects a similar outlook in the United States State Department. Officials admit that they have almost no first-hand information about how the northern invasion is proceeding—if it is proceeding. The United States Embassy in Haiti, which has been whittled down to a skeleton staff to show displeasure with the Duvalier regime, has no on-the-spot representatives in the Cap Haitian area. Since telephone communications in Haiti broke down years ago, contact is reduced to radio talks with the estimated 125 American residents of the area. But no one in Washington seems to be able to discover whether any fighting actually has taken place and whether government or rebel forces have suffered any casualties. Private sources in Port au Prince claimed Cantave was still on Haitian soil pressing his drive to topple Duvalier. A rebel spokesman in the Dominican Republic accused Duvalier’s regime of issuing false victory claims to try and discourage Haitians from joining the invaders. Exile sources in the Dominican Capital of Santo Domingo insisted two rebel columns had thrust down past Cap Haitien, Haiti’s second city, and a third was moving across the northwest peninsula in an apparent squeeze on Gonaives, the country’s third largest city. Rebel informants claimed the invasion force started at 500 strong but was swelled as it advanced by defections from Duvalier’s forces. Haitian Ambassador Fern D. Baguidy told a special committee of the Organization of American States in Washington Wednesday that "danger still exists because of the enmity of Dominican President Juan Bosch" toward Duvalier. Baguidy reiterated charges that the Dominican Republic collaborated with the invading force. The Dominican government and invasion leaders have denied the invasion was launched from Dominican soil. records.summary_en: The paper reports Haiti's government marshaled its regular army and civilian armed forces to combat rebel bands entrenched in mountains near the Dominican border, after Haitian exile invaders crossed from the Dominican border at Capotille into the Mont Organisé area. Reports also spoke of rumors of reprisals against disloyal civilians by the Tonton Macoutes, President Duvalier's security force, with official sources tight-lipped.

Los informes también hablaban de rumores de represalias contra civiles desleales por los Tonton Macoutes, la fuerza de seguridad del presidente Duvalier, con fuentes oficiales reservadas.

records.headline: Virginia Prewett reports that ex-President Juan Bosch's forces in the Dominican Republic are for the first time
records.summary_en: Virginia Prewett reports that ex-President Juan Bosch's forces in the Dominican Republic are for the first time acquiring partial army support through a quiet agreement with former president Joaquin Balaguer, who has a respectable army following and now swings his influence to the Bosch cause. Balaguer sent his reform party's secretary general, Nicolas Silfa, to Santo Domingo by air on October 17 to advise on supporting the constitutional cause, but Silfa was turned back from the airport because his name is blacklisted by the junta, and the new alignment comes as Brigadier General Elias Wessin y Wessin challenges a combination headed by General Antonio Imbert for control of the power apparatus in Santo Domingo.
records.summary_es: Virginia Prewett informa que las fuerzas del expresidente Juan Bosch en la República Dominicana están adquiriendo por primera vez un apoyo parcial del ejército mediante un acuerdo discreto con el expresidente Joaquín Balaguer, que tiene un respetable seguimiento en el ejército y ahora inclina su influencia hacia la causa de Bosch. Balaguer envió a Santo Domingo por avión el 17 de octubre al secretario general de su partido reformista, Nicolás Silfa, para asesorar sobre el apoyo a la causa constitucional, pero Silfa fue devuelto desde el aeropuerto porque su nombre está en la lista negra de la junta, y la nueva alineación llega cuando el general de brigada Elías Wessin y Wessin desafía a una combinación encabezada por el general Antonio Imbert por el control del aparato de poder en Santo Domingo.

records.summary_en: At its mid-year meeting in Santo Domingo, the Inter American Press Association resolved again to protest Brazilian government discrimination against Copley News Service correspondent Louis Stein, whose foreign office accreditation Brazil has refused to restore for a year. The board wound up its meeting in a flurry of activity, passing hard-hitting resolutions that included a fresh denunciation of Fidel Castro's dictatorship in Cuba. The association directed its president, John R. Reitemeyer, to communicate the protest to the government of Brazil once again and to request that Stein's credentials be restored without further delay.

La junta concluyó su reunión en un torbellino de actividad, aprobando resoluciones enérgicas que incluyeron una nueva denuncia de la dictadura de Fidel Castro en Cuba. records.headline: Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: George L. Rosenblatt's travel feature opens on Santo Domingo, the oldest city in the New World, founded by Christopher Columbus's brother Bartholomew, with the celebrated founding date set at August 4, 1496. A few hours' stroll through the Colonial Zone shows the firsts of the hemisphere: the first cathedral, the first hospital, the first university and the first commercial street. Foremost among the sights is the Cathedral of Santa María la Menor, the first cathedral established in the New World, which the article presents as the last resting place of Christopher Columbus, whose ornate tomb stands inside the cathedral and whose coffin is traditionally opened to view on Columbus Day.
records.summary_es: El reportaje de viajes de George L. Rosenblatt se abre con Santo Domingo, la ciudad más antigua del Nuevo Mundo, fundada por Bartolomé, hermano de Cristóbal Colón, con la fecha de fundación celebrada fijada el 4 de agosto de 1496. Unas pocas horas de paseo por la Zona Colonial muestran las primicias del hemisferio: la primera catedral, el primer hospital, la primera universidad y la primera calle comercial. Entre los lugares se destaca la Catedral de Santa María la Menor, la primera catedral establecida en el Nuevo Mundo, que el artículo presenta como el último descanso de Cristóbal Colón, cuya tumba adornada se encuentra dentro de la catedral y cuyo ataúd se abre tradicionalmente a la vista el Día de Colón.

records.headline: Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: In the next stretch of George L. Rosenblatt's Santo Domingo feature, the walk continues to the Ozama Fort and its Tower of Homage, both built in the first decade of the 1500s, a short block from the cathedral. From the top of the tower visitors can scan a panorama of the old city: the Ozama River and the port to the east, the bridges to the north, the harbor mouth where the Ozama empties into the Caribbean Sea to the south, and the rooftops of the old city to the west. The feature then passes the Casa de Bastidas, a sprawling sixteenth-century home now a museum and crafts outlet, and notes the sun clock on Calle Las Damas, an eighteenth-century device that still keeps fairly good time.
records.summary_es: En el siguiente tramo del reportaje de George L. Rosenblatt sobre Santo Domingo, el paseo continúa hacia la Fortaleza Ozama y su Torre del Homenaje, ambas construidas en la primera década del siglo XVI, a una manzana de la catedral. Desde lo alto de la torre los visitantes pueden contemplar un panorama de la ciudad vieja: el río Ozama y el puerto al este, los puentes al norte, la desembocadura del puerto donde el Ozama desemboca en el mar Caribe al sur, y los tejados de la ciudad vieja al oeste. El reportaje pasa luego por la Casa de Bastidas, una amplia casa del siglo XVI hoy convertida en museo y tienda de artesanías, y menciona el reloj de sol de la calle Las Damas, un artefacto del siglo XVIII que todavía da la hora con bastante exactitud.

records.headline: Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The final stretch of George L. Rosenblatt's page-one feature carries the walk north along Calle Las Damas to the Columbus Castle, built by Christopher Columbus's son Diego and now a museum of sixteenth-century court life. Descending the stairs at the northern edge of the castle, the reader reaches La Atarazana, the oldest shopping street in the New World, which dates from the 1500s. The feature pauses at the Casa de Bastidas, with its shaded garden courtyard, and at the eighteenth-century sun clock on Las Damas, described as simple and more remarkable for having survived intact than for any intrinsic quality.
records.summary_es: El tramo final del reportaje de primera página de George L. Rosenblatt lleva el paseo hacia el norte por la calle Las Damas hasta el Castillo de Colón, construido por Diego, hijo de Cristóbal Colón, y hoy museo de la vida cortesana del siglo XVI. Al bajar las escaleras del extremo norte del castillo, el lector llega a La Atarazana, la calle comercial más antigua del Nuevo Mundo, que data del siglo XVI. El reportaje se detiene en la Casa de Bastidas, con su patio ajardinado sombreado, y en el reloj de sol del siglo XVIII de Las Damas, descrito como sencillo y más notable por haber sobrevivido intacto que por cualquier cualidad intrínseca.

records.summary_en: In this continuation of George L. Rosenblatt's Santo Domingo feature, the walk resumes on La Atarazana, where a lunch at the Fonda de la Atarazana ends in a tropical downpour that traps the writer in the restaurant, watching the rain on the brick tiles of the patio. The feature continues to the Casa del Cordón, built in 1503 and believed to be the first stone house in the Americas, and to Puerta del Conde, where the flag of the Dominican Republic first flew in 1844. Through the gate stands the shrine of La Trinitaria, where the three Founding Fathers — Juan Pablo Duarte, Francisco del Rosario Sánchez and Ramón Mella — are entombed. The writer closes with his impressions of the Dominican people, whom he finds gentle and unobtrusive, and with a long taxi ride driven by Victor, a man who spoke no English but with whom he talked baseball, and who charged about eleven dollars for a two-hour excursion.
records.summary_es: En esta continuación del reportaje de George L. Rosenblatt sobre Santo Domingo, el paseo se reanuda en La Atarazana, donde un almuerzo en la Fonda de la Atarazana termina en un aguacero tropical que retiene al escritor en el restaurante, observando la lluvia sobre los ladrillos del patio. El reportaje continúa hasta la Casa del Cordón, construida en 1503 y considerada la primera casa de piedra de las Américas, y hasta la Puerta del Conde, donde ondeó por primera vez la bandera de la República Dominicana en 1844. Tras la puerta se encuentra el santuario de La Trinitaria, donde están sepultados los tres Padres de la Patria —Juan Pablo Duarte, Francisco del Rosario Sánchez y Ramón Mella—. El escritor cierra con sus impresiones del pueblo dominicano, al que encuentra amable y discreto, y con un largo viaje en taxi conducido por Víctor, un hombre que no hablaba inglés pero con quien conversó de béisbol, y que cobró unos once dólares por una excursión de dos horas.
